heading: O1 - Multi-agent architecture, orchestration, uncertainty hand-off and audit trail

papers.title: MDAgents: An Adaptive Collaboration of LLMs for Medical Decision-Making
papers.authors: Kim Y, Park C, Jeong H, Chan YS, Xu X, McDuff D, Lee H, Ghassemi M, Breazeal C, Park HW
papers.aim: To let LLM agents decide how much teamwork a medical question really needs, instead of fixing one setup for every case.
papers.method: A moderator agent first rates the case complexity. Easy cases go to one doctor agent, medium cases go to a multi-disciplinary team that discusses, and hard cases go to an integrated care team that writes a final report.
papers.result: Best accuracy on 7 of 10 medical benchmarks (MedQA, PMC-VQA, Path-VQA etc). Adding moderator review and external medical knowledge gave a further clear gain.
papers.tools: GPT-4 / GPT-4V, Gemini-Pro, prompt engineering, role-play agents, majority voting
papers.gap: Only question-answer benchmarks. No real patient pathway, no calibrated confidence, and the human doctor is not part of the loop.
papers.relation: Same idea as our orchestrator that routes tasks. But they route by question difficulty, we want to route by measured uncertainty and send hard cases to a real clinician.
papers.limitations: High API cost, LLM hallucination, and results come from public QA sets, not hospital data. Future: real clinical data and human review.
papers.methodologyDetail: MDAgents is a training-free, prompt-based pipeline run on commercial LLM APIs. The authors took ten public medical benchmarks covering text (MedQA, PubMedQA, DDXPlus, SymCat, JAMA, MedBullets), image+text (Path-VQA yes/no subset, PMC-VQA, MIMIC-CXR-VQA) and video+text (MedVidQA with GPT-4-made options). From each they randomly sampled 50 questions and ran every method with 3 random seeds, reporting mean accuracy and SD. Step 1: a moderator agent, prompted as a general practitioner, reads the query and labels it low (a GP can answer alone), moderate (GP plus specialist team) or high (multi-department team). Step 2: a recruiter agent names up to N specialist roles and a communication hierarchy. Step 3: low cases go to one primary-care agent with 3-shot prompting. Moderate cases go to a multi-disciplinary team: each expert gives an initial answer, then they talk in rounds and turns, each choosing whom to address; if answers disagree, the moderator reviews the log and gives feedback, and a new round starts. High cases go to an integrated care team where an initial assessment team, diagnostic teams and a final review team each write a report through a lead clinician. Step 4: a decision agent reads the single answer, the discussion log, or the reports and gives the final answer, using ensembles such as temperature ensembles or voting. Consensus was tracked with Shannon entropy of agent answers. They compared against 6 single-agent prompting methods and 8 multi-agent methods, all on GPT-4(V) (Gemini-Pro(Vision) for video). Ablations fixed the complexity level, varied agent number (best N=3, 9.3 API calls), temperature (0.3 vs 1.2), added MedRAG and moderator review (71.8% to 80.3%), and changed collaboration style. Finally, 3 physicians rated complexity of 50 MedQA questions; ICC was about 0.27 and LLM-physician correlation was near zero. To adapt this, one would replace the LLM complexity label with a calibrated uncertainty score and add a clinician-deferral branch.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark (in-silico) evaluation of a training-free LLM multi-agent framework on public medical QA datasets. Institutions: MIT, Google Research, Seoul National University Hospital (USA/South Korea). Plus a small annotation study with 3 physicians rating question complexity.
papers.datasets: Ten public benchmarks (50 random test samples each in main runs; 100 in Table 12 runs). Text: MedQA (USMLE, English test set 1,273 questions, 5 options); PubMedQA (yes/no/maybe, test size 500); DDXPlus (synthetic patients, 134K, differential diagnosis); SymCat (synthetic, 369K records; 801 conditions, 376 symptoms); JAMA Clinical Challenge (1,524 cases, 4 options); MedBullets (308 USMLE Step 2/3 questions). Image+text: Path-VQA (3,391 pathology QA; only yes/no questions used); PMC-VQA (227K VQA pairs on 149K images; test 50K); MIMIC-CXR-VQA (377,110 chest radiographs from 227,827 studies; test 1,531). Video+text: MedVidQA (3,010 questions; test 155; multiple-choice options generated by GPT-4). Physician study: 50 MedQA questions balanced over USMLE steps 1-3. No patient-level inclusion/exclusion criteria (benchmark data).
papers.preprocessing: No training, so no train/validation split. 50 randomly sampled test questions per dataset, run with 3 random seeds. Path-VQA restricted to yes/no questions for standard accuracy. MedVidQA extended with GPT-4-generated distractor options. 3-shot prompting for low-complexity cases; zero-shot for moderate and high. No image preprocessing reported.
papers.modelDetails: Four stages (Algorithm 1). (1) Complexity check: moderator LLM (acting as GP) labels query low / moderate / high using a fixed prompt with definitions. (2) Recruitment: recruiter LLM recruits up to N experts and states a communication hierarchy (e.g. Pulmonologist == Neonatologist > Cardiologist). (3a) Low: one primary care agent answers with few-shot prompting, ans = Agent(Q). (3b) Moderate: MDT agents give initial answers, then discuss for up to R rounds with T turns each; each agent chooses whom to talk to; consensus is checked by parsing opinions; if no consensus, moderator reviews the log and gives feedback to each agent. (3c) High: Integrated Care Team: Initial Assessment Team, diagnostic teams, then Final Review and Decision Team; each team led by a lead clinician writes a report. (4) Decision agent combines answer / interaction log / reports, using ensemble methods such as temperature ensembles or majority voting. Consensus measured with Shannon entropy H = -sum p(x) log2 p(x) over agent answers. Optional extras: MedRAG retrieval and moderator review. Exact R and T values: Not reported in main text.
papers.training: Training-free (inference only via API). Temperatures tested: low T = 0.3 and high T = 1.2. Best agent number N = 3 (peak 83.5%). API calls per question: Solo 5-shot CoT-SC 6.0; Group MedAgents (N=5) 20.3; MDAgents (N=3) 9.3. Mean inference time: low 14.7 s, moderate 95.5 s, high 226 s. Hardware managed by API providers. Optimizer, epochs, batch size: not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on multiple-choice / yes-no answers, mean +/- SD over 3 seeds, 50 samples per dataset. Compared Solo, Group and Adaptive settings. Ablations: fixed complexity (low/moderate/high) vs adaptive; moderator review and MedRAG; number of agents; temperature; collaboration style (sequential/parallel, with/without discussion). Complexity analysis on 25 MedQA questions each solved 10 times at each level. Physician study: 3 physicians (2 PGY-2 internal medicine, 1 GP) rated 50 MedQA questions as -1/0/1; agreement by ICC; LLM ratings compared to physician majority by Pearson correlation.
papers.baselines: Solo: zero-shot, few-shot, few-shot CoT, CoT-SC, Ensemble Refinement, Medprompt. Group single-model: majority voting, weighted voting, Borda count, MedAgents, Meta-Prompting. Group multi-model: ReConcile, AutoGen (4 agents), DyLAN (4 agents, 4 rounds).
papers.results: GPT-4(V), 50 samples: MDAgents MedQA 88.7 +/- 4.0 vs best solo CoT-SC 83.9 +/- 2.7 and ReConcile 81.3 +/- 3.0; PubMedQA 75.0 +/- 1.0 vs ReConcile 79.7 +/- 3.2 (not best); Path-VQA 65.3 vs 62.1 (weighted voting); PMC-VQA 56.4 vs 53.4 (Medprompt); MedVidQA (Gemini) 56.2 vs 57.8 (weighted voting); DDXPlus 77.9 vs 72.7 (CoT); SymCat 93.1 vs 91.9 (majority voting); JAMA 70.9 vs 71.0 (ER); MedBullets 80.8 vs 77.0 (MedAgents); MIMIC-CXR 55.9 vs 53.5. Adaptive vs fixed complexity on text: 81.2% vs low 64.2%, moderate 71.6%, high 65.8%. 64% of text queries were labelled high; 55% of image+text and 87% of video+text labelled low. Knowledge ablation: base 71.8%, +MedRAG 75.2%, +medical knowledge initialisation 76.0%, +moderator review 77.6%, +both 80.3%. Collaboration on high-complexity image+text: sequential no discussion 39.0%, sequential + discussion 45.0%, parallel no discussion 56.0%, parallel + discussion 59.0%. Full MedQA (GPT-4o mini): MDAgents 83.6% vs ReConcile 80.2%, CoT-SC 77.2%. LLM picks the best complexity level with probability a = 0.81 +/- 0.29 (b = 0.11, c = 0.08).
papers.statistics: Mean +/- SD over 3 seeds. Significance p < 0.05 claimed vs Solo and Group (test type not named). Physician inter-rater reliability: ICC2k = 0.269 [-0.14, 0.55], ICC3k = 0.280 [-0.15, 0.57]. Pearson correlation of LLM complexity vs physician majority: gpt-4o-mini -0.090, gpt-4o 0.022, gpt-4 0.070, gemini-1.5-flash 0.110.
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/mitmedialab/MDAgents. Data: public benchmarks. Annotation interface: https://dxagents.github.io/2024/05/01/medqa.html.

papers.title: MedAgents: Large Language Models as Collaborators for Zero-shot Medical Reasoning
papers.authors: Tang X, Zou A, Zhang Z, Li Z, Zhao Y, Zhang X, Cohan A, Gerstein M
papers.aim: To improve medical reasoning of LLMs without any training, by making several LLM 'experts' discuss a case.
papers.method: Five steps: gather domain experts, each expert writes analysis, summarise into a report, experts discuss and vote until agreement, then final decision.
papers.result: Beat zero-shot chain-of-thought and self-consistency on MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA and medical parts of MMLU.
papers.tools: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, role-playing prompts, consensus voting
papers.gap: Errors still come from missing domain knowledge and wrong retrieval. Text only, multiple-choice questions only.
papers.relation: Supports our design of specialised agents (MRI, pathology, diagnosis). Gives a simple way to resolve disagreement between agents before escalation.
papers.limitations: No uncertainty value, no audit log, no image input. Future work they mention: better knowledge grounding.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedAgents is a prompt-only, zero-shot pipeline. The authors used nine public exam-style datasets: MedQA (USMLE), MedMCQA (Indian entrance exams), PubMedQA (abstract-based yes/no/maybe) and six MMLU medical subtasks. They randomly sampled 300 questions per dataset and ran GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 through Azure OpenAI, with temperature 1.0 and top_p 1.0. For each question with k options (4, or 3 for PubMedQA), Step 1 asks the LLM to name m = 5 question-domain experts and n = 2 option-domain experts (m = 4 for PubMedQA). Step 2 prompts the LLM to act as each question expert and write an analysis, then as each option expert to analyse the options given the question analyses. Step 3 has a report-assistant role merge all analyses into a report with 'key knowledge' and 'total analysis'. Step 4 is the consultation loop: every expert votes yes or no on the report; experts who vote no write modification requests; the LLM revises the report; this repeats until all vote yes or 5 attempts are used. Step 5 has a decision-maker role read the final report and choose the answer. Accuracy was compared with zero-shot, few-shot, CoT and self-consistency (5 samples, temperature 0.7) prompting, and with Flan-PaLM results. Ablations removed stages on MedQA (CoT 55.0% to 67.0% with all stages), varied the number of question agents (1-8) and option agents (1-5), removed relevant or irrelevant experts (20 samples), and used identical-domain agents (300 samples). Finally, two authors grouped 40 error cases into lack of knowledge, mis-retrieval, consistency and CoT errors. Cost was about 1.4 US cents and 40 s per question. To reproduce, one needs only the prompts from the paper appendix and an LLM API; to adapt for imaging, the expert analyses would need image-reading tools and a calibrated vote-confidence threshold for deferral.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark (in-silico) evaluation of a training-free LLM framework. Institutions: Yale University (USA) and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (China). Human error analysis of sampled failure cases.
papers.datasets: MedQA (USMLE, 4 options, test size 1,273); MedMCQA (AIIMS and NEET PG exams, 4 options, test size 6.1K); PubMedQA (question + abstract context, yes/no/maybe, 500); MMLU medical subtasks (anatomy, clinical knowledge, college medicine, medical genetics, professional medicine, college biology; total 1,089). 300 examples randomly sampled from each dataset for experiments. Error analysis: 40 random error cases from MedQA and MedMCQA. Domain-variation study: 20 samples. No patient-level inclusion/exclusion (exam questions).
papers.preprocessing: No training data split (zero-shot). Random sample of 300 questions per dataset. Number of options k = 4, except PubMedQA k = 3. No other preprocessing reported.
papers.modelDetails: Five stages. (1) Expert gathering: LLM, given a system role and prompt, proposes m question-domain experts and n option-domain experts (m = 5, n = 2; PubMedQA m = 4, n = 2). (2) Analysis proposition: each question expert writes an analysis of the question; each option expert analyses the options using the question analyses. (3) Report summarisation: a 'medical report assistant' LLM extracts key knowledge and a total analysis into one report. (4) Collaborative consultation (Algorithm 1): each expert votes yes/no on the report; 'no' voters propose modifications; the report is revised; repeat until all vote yes or maximum attempts t = 5. (5) Decision making: a decision-maker LLM answers using the unanimous report. Temperature 1.0 and top_p 1.0 for all generations. No uncertainty or deferral rule.
papers.training: No training. Inference via Azure OpenAI GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4. Temperature 1.0, top_p 1.0; self-consistency baseline uses 5 samples at temperature 0.7. Cost about USD 1.41 per 100 questions; about 40 s per question. Hardware: not reported (API).
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on 300 random samples per dataset, zero-shot. Compared with zero-shot and few-shot settings with and without CoT and SC. Ablation of stages on MedQA. Number-of-agents study (1 to 8 question agents; 1 to 5 option agents). Domain-variation study (remove most/least relevant or random experts, 20 samples). Agent-quantity study with 6, 5, 4 same-domain agents (300 samples). Human error analysis of 40 error cases in four categories.
papers.baselines: Flan-PaLM few-shot CoT and CoT+SC (reported numbers); GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 zero-shot, few-shot, zero-shot CoT, few-shot CoT, zero-shot CoT+SC, few-shot CoT+SC; open-source models MedAlpaca-7B, BioMedGPT-10B, BioMedLM-2.7B, BioBERT-large, SciBERT-large, BERT-large.
papers.results: GPT-4 MedAgents: MedQA 83.7, MedMCQA 74.8, PubMedQA 76.8, Anatomy 83.5, Clinical knowledge 91.0, College medicine 87.6, Medical genetics 93.0, Professional medicine 96.0, College biology 94.3, average 86.7 (vs zero-shot 80.6, zero-shot CoT 80.8, zero-shot CoT+SC 83.0, few-shot CoT+SC 85.4). GPT-3.5 MedAgents: MedQA 64.1, MedMCQA 59.3, PubMedQA 72.9, Anatomy 65.2, Clinical knowledge 77.7, College medicine 69.8, Medical genetics 79.0, Professional medicine 82.1, College biology 78.5, average 72.1 (vs zero-shot 67.8, zero-shot CoT+SC 70.9, few-shot CoT+SC 71.6). Ablation (MedQA, GPT-3.5): direct 49.0, CoT 55.0, +analysis 62.0, +summary 65.0, +consultation 67.0. Open-source: MedAlpaca-7B MedQA 55.2 / MedMCQA 45.8; BioMedGPT-10B 50.4 / 42.2. Domain variation (GPT-3.5, 20 samples): full 63.8/58.9; remove most relevant 60.5/55.4; remove least relevant 66.2/61.5; random 62.2/56.3. Agent quantity (GPT-3.5): 6 different domains 64.1/59.3; 6 same 59.2/58.1; 5 same 57.5/57.3; 4 same 55.9/57.0. Errors: 77% from lack or mis-retrieval of domain knowledge.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no significance tests or confidence intervals).

papers.title: Agent Hospital: A Simulacrum of Hospital with Evolvable Medical Agents
papers.authors: Li J, Wang S, Zhang M, Li W, Lai Y, Kang X, Ma W, Liu Y
papers.aim: To build a simulated hospital where patient, nurse and doctor agents interact, so doctor agents can improve from cases without labelled data.
papers.method: Whole hospital flow is simulated (triage, registration, consultation, exam, diagnosis, treatment, follow-up). Doctor agents use MedAgent-Zero, storing successful cases and lessons from failures.
papers.result: After treating a very large number of simulated patients, doctor agents reported about 93% accuracy on a respiratory subset of MedQA.
papers.tools: LLM agents (GPT-3.5/GPT-4), memory / experience base, simulated environment
papers.gap: All simulated. Not tested with real clinicians or real patients. Simulated patients may be too simple.
papers.relation: Their hospital flow is close to our pathway (intake, MRI, pathology, diagnosis, surgery planning, follow-up). Idea: we can test our orchestrator in a simulated pathway before using registry data.
papers.limitations: Simulation bias, no safety check, no human validation step. Future: link with real hospital systems.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first built a 2D hospital simulation (Tiled and Phaser) with 16 areas, 42 doctor agents and 4 nurse agents. To decide departments, GPT-4 classified MedQA test questions into 32 departments: 21 clinical and 11 non-clinical. For the 21 clinical departments they listed 339 common diseases (DXY list plus GPT-4 additions) and took symptoms, examination findings and treatment plans from Baidu Health Encyclopedia. Synthetic patients were then generated step by step: pick a disease, generate demographics, medical history, symptoms and examination reports (with severity mild, moderate or severe), and a quality-control agent checks the record against the knowledge base. For each department and task they made 20,000 training and 200 separate test patients. A doctor agent built on a frozen GPT model receives a structured prompt (role, patient information, candidate list of tests or diseases, and retrieved memories). It must choose examinations, give a diagnosis and suggest treatment. If correct, the question-answer pair is saved in a task-specific medical case base. If wrong, the agent compares with ground truth and writes a short rule; the rule is tested on new Q&A pairs and saved in the experience base only if it gives the right answer. Doctors also 'read books': textbook content is converted into multiple-choice items and added to the case base. At inference, the question is embedded with text-embedding-ada-002 and the top-3 similar cases and top-4 rules (cosine similarity) are inserted into the prompt; an extra step judges whether retrieved rules help. Performance was measured before and after evolution on the 200 test patients per department (exam 66.14% to 98.76%, diagnosis 76.98% to 95.31%) and on the full MedQA test set, where it reached 92.22% with GPT-4o. Ablations removed each memory and varied top-k. To adapt it, one could store clinician-confirmed brain-tumour cases and validated correction rules as memory for the agents.
papers.studyDesign: Simulation study with synthetic (LLM-generated) patients plus retrospective benchmark evaluation on MedQA. Institution: Institute for AI Industry Research (AIR) and Department of Computer Science, Tsinghua University, China.
papers.datasets: Synthetic patient agents: 32 departments (21 clinical, 11 non-clinical) derived by GPT-4 classifying MedQA test questions; 339 diseases across 21 clinical departments (common diseases from DXY list, supplemented by GPT-4). Disease knowledge (symptoms, examination findings, treatment plans) from Baidu Health Encyclopedia. Per clinical department and task: training set 20,000 and test set 200 synthetic patients (respiratory department also run to 50,000). Real-world test: MedQA (USMLE) full test set; MedQA training data added to case base only in the 'Hybrid' variant. Medical textbooks/documents converted to multiple-choice questions for the 'reading books' step. No real patients.
papers.preprocessing: Patient generation in 5 steps: choose disease; generate basic information (name, gender, age); generate medical history; generate symptoms; generate examination reports (severity mild/moderate/severe) guided by the knowledge base; a quality-control agent checks consistency with the knowledge base. Only basic information, history and symptoms are shown to the doctor agent (examination results added for the diagnosis task). Medical documents reformatted into multiple-choice Q&A. Split: 20,000 training / 200 test patients per department with no overlap.
papers.modelDetails: Simulacrum: 16 functional areas, 42 doctor agents, 4 nurse agents, 8 event types (disease onset, triage, registration, consultation, examination, diagnosis, medicine dispensary, convalescence) plus 'reading books'. MedAgent-Zero doctor evolution: structured prompt with (1) role instruction, (2) patient information, (3) candidate choice list (doctor may propose new options), (4) retrieved personal experience. Medical case base: question-answer pairs stored when the answer is correct, one base per task. Experience base: on a wrong answer, the agent compares with ground truth and writes a natural-language principle; the principle is validated on Q&A pairs and kept only if it leads to a correct answer, otherwise discarded; principles are reformatted with manually selected examples; an extra judgement step checks if retrieved top-K experiences are helpful. Retrieval: text-embedding-ada-002 vectors, cosine similarity; best setting top-3 medical cases and top-4 experiences. No uncertainty threshold or deferral rule.
papers.training: No gradient training; base LLM frozen. Evolution by treating up to 20,000 synthetic patients per department (50,000 in respiratory analysis). Base models GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o, o1-preview. Hyperparameters: top-k cases 3, top-k experiences 4 (tested 2-8 experiences and 2-5 cases). Hardware, time and cost: not reported.
papers.evaluation: Virtual world: accuracy on examination selection, diagnosis and treatment-plan tasks on 200 held-out synthetic patients per department, before vs after evolution; cumulative and segment accuracy per 1,000 patients. Real world: accuracy on the full MedQA test set; department-level comparison on 8 departments; ablation without case base or without experience base; Hybrid variant with MedQA training data; hyperparameter sweep of top-k; two qualitative case studies (MedQA IDs 73 and 340).
papers.baselines: Direct prompting, Chain-of-Thought, MedAgents, Medprompt (and Medprompt*) on GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o, o1-preview.
papers.results: Department diagnosis (21 departments, 200 test patients each): overall examination 66.14% to 98.76% (+32.62), diagnosis 76.98% to 95.31% (+18.33); e.g. Cardiology exam 52.5% to 96.0%, diagnosis 68.0% to 93.5%; Psychiatry exam 23.5% to 99.5%; Immunology diagnosis 67.5% to 87.5%. Rheumatic heart disease diagnosis rose from 9% (GPT-3.5 base) to 82%. Respiratory diagnosis started near 66% and rose sharply over first 10,000 patients. MedQA accuracy (GPT-3.5 / GPT-4 / GPT-4o / o1-preview): Direct 58.29 / 78.16 / 88.22 / 95.05; CoT 64.02 / 83.11 / 90.42 / -; MedAgents 66.30 / 84.45 / 89.24 / -; Medprompt 73.76 / 89.47 / 91.52 / 95.36; MedAgent-Zero 74.31 / 89.71 / 92.22 / 96.15; Hybrid 76.83 / 91.20 / 92.77 / 96.15. Ablation (GPT-4 / GPT-4o): without experience base 87.75 / 90.65; without case base 87.75 / 91.36; full 89.71 / 92.22; Hybrid 90.50 / 92.77. Top-k: best 92.22 at 3 cases and 4 experiences.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no significance tests; confidence band shown only for fitted segment-accuracy curves).
papers.availability: Not available (no code or data link given in the paper).

papers.title: AgentClinic: a multimodal agent benchmark to evaluate AI in simulated clinical environments
papers.authors: Schmidgall S, Ziaei R, Harris C, Reis E, Jopling J, Moor M
papers.aim: To test LLM doctors in an interactive, step-by-step clinical setting instead of static exam questions.
papers.method: Doctor agent must take history, order tests from a measurement agent and give diagnosis. Patient agents can carry cognitive and demographic biases. Includes image cases from NEJM.
papers.result: Models that score high on MedQA lose a lot of accuracy in the sequential setting. Bias and tool use change results noticeably.
papers.tools: Multiple LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, Llama etc), multimodal LLMs, simulated patients
papers.gap: Still simulated dialogue. Diagnosis only, no treatment or surgical step.
papers.relation: Good evidence that static accuracy is misleading, which supports our O4 argument. Their sequential test setup can be used to stress-test our agent chain.
papers.limitations: Synthetic cases, limited images. Future: more specialties and real clinical evaluation.
papers.notes: Preprint of O4-P21 (AgentClinic, npj Digital Medicine)
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors turned existing diagnostic cases into interactive role-play scenarios. They sampled 215 USMLE cases from MedQA, 200 single-diagnosis patients from MIMIC-IV (the first 200 out of about 6,000 with one diagnosis, with their lab and microbiology events), 120 of 932 NEJM image challenges, 260 MedMCQA specialty case reports from 9 specialties, and 749 MedQA cases translated into six other languages by GPT-4 and corrected by native speakers. GPT-4 filled a JSON OSCE template for each case (doctor objective; patient demographics, history and symptoms; exam findings and test results; correct diagnosis), and the authors checked each case by hand. Each part of the template goes to a different agent. The patient agent knows only symptoms and history and answers in 1-3 sentences. The measurement agent holds the test results and replies when the doctor writes 'Request Test: X'. The doctor agent, the model under test, starts with a short objective and may use N = 20 turns in total for questions and tests, then must write 'Diagnosis Ready: ...'. A GPT-4 moderator compares this free text with the true diagnosis. Patient, measurement and moderator roles use GPT-4. They tested more than 11 doctor LLMs and three physicians under the same rules, and varied N (10 to 30) and the patient LLM. They injected cognitive and implicit bias text into doctor or patient prompts and asked biased patients to rate confidence, compliance and consultation from 1 to 10. They added tools: zero-shot, one-shot and reflection CoT, adaptive RAG over the web or 18 textbooks, and a notebook kept across patients. For NEJM, images were given at the start or only on request. Results are mean accuracy with 95% CIs from the standard error over runs. Three clinicians rated 20 dialogues for realism and empathy. For our work, the same template could encode brain-tumour cases with MRI and pathology on request, and a 'defer' action could be scored.
papers.studyDesign: Simulation benchmark study using retrospective case data (exam questions, de-identified EHR, published case challenges) with LLM agents; small clinician reader study and human physician comparison. Institutions: Stanford University, Johns Hopkins University (USA), Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein (Brazil), ETH Zurich (Switzerland).
papers.datasets: AgentClinic-MedQA: 215 cases from USMLE (MedQA) questions, text. AgentClinic-MIMIC-IV: 200 cases; from about 40,000 MIMIC-IV patients (about 34,000 with multiple diagnoses) the first 200 of about 6,000 single-diagnosis patients were taken, with lab, microbiology and record data; race: White 66.0%, Black 11.0%, Asian 8.5%, Multiple 6.0%, Hispanic 5.5%, Unknown 2.5%, Native American 0.5%. AgentClinic-NEJM: 120 cases randomly sampled from 932 NEJM image challenges, text + images (open-ended; image types e.g. physical 56 (42%), CT 19 (16%), dermatology 16 (13%), histopathology 13 (11%), radiography 12 (10%), ophthalmology 11 (9%), MRI 6 (5%), biopsy 6 (5%)). AgentClinic-Spec: 260 case reports from MedMCQA across 9 specialties. AgentClinic-Lang: 749 cases from AgentClinic-MedQA translated into Chinese, Hindi, Korean, Spanish, French, Persian (plus English). 23-24 bias types (cognitive and implicit).
papers.preprocessing: Each case converted into a structured JSON OSCE template (objective for doctor; patient demographics, history, symptoms, past medical and social history, review of systems; physical exam findings and vital signs; test results; correct diagnosis) using GPT-4, then manually validated. Information split by agent: objective to doctor, history and symptoms to patient, exam/test results to measurement agent, diagnosis to moderator. Multilingual cases translated by GPT-4 and corrected by native speakers. NEJM multiple-choice options removed (open-ended). No train/test split (evaluation only).
papers.modelDetails: Doctor agent prompt: limited to MAX_INFS questions (default N = 20 patient + measurement interactions); can write 'Request Test: [test]' and finally 'Diagnosis Ready: [diagnosis]'. Patient agent answers in 1-3 sentences and must not reveal the diagnosis. Measurement agent returns results in 'Results: ...' format from the case file. Moderator agent compares the free-text diagnosis to ground truth. Bias: text added to system prompt of patient or doctor (e.g. self-diagnosis, recency bias, race, gender, education, religion, socioeconomic, sexual orientation, cultural). Tools: zero-shot CoT, one-shot CoT, reflection CoT, adaptive RAG (command 'Research [database] [query]' over web or 18 textbooks), notebook memory persisting across patients. Patient-centric follow-up: patient agent rates confidence, compliance and consultation 1-10. Multi-agent variants: Multi-Agent Debate and MedAgents as doctor. Images given at start or on request from the measurement/instrument agent. No uncertainty or deferral rule.
papers.training: No training (inference only). Interaction budget N = 20 (also tested 10, 15, 25, 30). GPT-4 used for patient, measurement and moderator agents. Sampling temperature, hardware and cost: Not reported (o1-preview noted as about 20x more costly than GPT-4o).
papers.evaluation: Primary metric: diagnostic accuracy judged by the moderator agent against the ground-truth diagnosis. 95% confidence intervals from standard error of the mean over multiple runs. Comparisons: 11+ doctor LLMs; human physicians (3) on AgentClinic-MedQA with the same constraints; effect of interaction budget; effect of patient LLM; bias effects as normalised accuracy (Accuracy_bias / Accuracy_no-bias); patient-perception ratings; specialty and language breakdowns; tool use; multimodal NEJM with image-at-start vs image-on-request; information coverage analysis (manual review); clinician reader study: 3 clinicians (MDs) rated 20 dialogues on doctor realism, patient realism, measurement realism and empathy (1-10).
papers.baselines: Static MedQA accuracy of the same models; human physicians (n = 3); different doctor LLMs compared with each other; unbiased vs biased agents; no-tool vs tool settings; multi-agent frameworks (Multi-Agent Debate, MedAgents).
papers.results: AgentClinic-MedQA: Claude-3.5 62.1% (95% CI 55-68), OpenBioLLM-70B 58.3 +/- 4.2, humans 54 +/- 28.5, GPT-4 51.6% (44-58), Mixtral-8x7B 37.1%, GPT-3.5 36.6% (30-42), GPT-4o 34.2% (27-40), MedLlama3-8B 31.4, Meditron-70B 29.1, PMC-Llama-7B 23.6, Llama 3 70B 19.0% (13-24), Llama 2 70B 4.5% (2-7); o1-preview 80.6 +/- 5.6. MIMIC-IV: Claude-3.5 42.9% (37-50), OpenBioLLM 38.1, PMC-Llama 34.3, GPT-4 34.0% (28-40), Mixtral 29.5%, GPT-3.5 27.5%, Meditron 25.5, GPT-4o 24.0%, Llama 2 13.5%, Llama 3 8.5%. Interaction budget (GPT-4): N=10 25%, N=15 38%, N=20 52%, N=25 48%, N=30 43%. Patient LLM: GPT-4 52%, GPT-3.5 48%, Mixtral 46%. Bias (GPT-4, base 52%): patient cognitive 48%, doctor cognitive 50.3%, patient implicit 51.3%, doctor implicit 50.5%; Mixtral (base 37%): doctor cognitive 29%, patient cognitive 35%, implicit avg 32.7%. GPT-4 refused bias instructions 25 of 215 times (gender bias). Specialty average: Claude-3.5 66.7%, GPT-4 55.7%, GPT-3.5 51.8%, GPT-4o 37.7%, Llama3-70b 27.5%, GPT-4o-mini 5.2%. Language average: Claude-3.5 48.4%, GPT-4 20.9%, GPT-4o 20.5%, GPT-3.5 19.5%, Llama3-70b 6.2%, GPT-4o-mini 4.1%. Tools: Claude-3.5 best 56.1% with notebook; GPT-4 best 43.9% with web RAG; Llama3-70b +19.7 with notebook and +18.7 with reflection; GPT-3.5 fell with all tools (e.g. -9.2 with book RAG). NEJM: image at start Claude 37.2, GPT-4 27.7, GPT-4o 21.4, GPT-4o-mini 8.0; on request 35.4, 25.4, 19.1, 6.1. Multi-agent: MedAgents Claude 65.2 +/- 3.6, GPT-4 53.1, GPT-4o 40.1; Debate Claude 64.1, GPT-4 51.7, GPT-4o 37.9. Information coverage 67% (72% when correct, 63% when wrong). Clinician ratings: doctor 6.2, patient 6.7, measurement 6.3, empathy 5.8.
papers.statistics: 95% confidence intervals from standard error of the mean across runs (e.g. Claude-3.5 MedQA 62.1% [55%, 68%]); SD reported for many results. No hypothesis tests or inter-rater agreement statistics reported for the clinician reader study.
papers.availability: Project and code: https://agentclinic.github.io/ (open-source benchmark). MIMIC-IV requires PhysioNet credentialed access.

papers.title: Development and validation of an autonomous artificial intelligence agent for clinical decision-making in oncology
papers.authors: Ferber D, El Nahhas OSM, Wolflein G, Wiest IC, Clusmann J, et al., Kather JN
papers.aim: To check if an LLM that can call specialised oncology tools can make better clinical decisions than the LLM alone.
papers.method: GPT-4 acts as the central agent and calls tools: vision transformers for mutation prediction from histology, MedSAM for radiology segmentation, OncoKB, PubMed search, and retrieval from oncology guidelines. Tested on 20 realistic multimodal patient cases.
papers.result: Decision accuracy went from about 30% (GPT-4 alone) to about 87% with tools. Most tool calls were correct and most answers cited guidelines.
papers.tools: GPT-4, RAG over guidelines, vision transformers, MedSAM, OncoKB API, PubMed
papers.gap: Only 20 cases, not prospective, no deferral rule. Errors in one tool can flow silently to the final answer.
papers.relation: Closest design to ours: an orchestrator + imaging tool + pathology tool. Our extra contribution is passing uncertainty between tools and forcing clinician check when confidence is low.
papers.limitations: Small evaluation set, GPT-4 dependency, privacy issue with cloud LLM. Future: larger validation, local models.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first built a knowledge base. They collected guideline documents from six sources (MDCalc, UpToDate, MEDITRON, ASCO, ESMO, Onkopedia), filtered them by keywords, and converted PDFs with GROBID into structured text. They cleaned the text, marked headers and saved it as jsonlines. They split text into chunks of 512, 256 and 128 tokens with 50-token overlap, embedded them with OpenAI text-embedding-3-large (3,072 dimensions) and stored them in a Chroma vector database, about 6,800 documents in total. Next they defined tools in JSON: GPT-4V for CT/MRI reports, MedSAM for segmentation, pre-trained vision transformers for MSI, KRAS and BRAF on TCGA histology (features pre-extracted with STAMP), OncoKB, Google search, PubMed search and a calculator. GPT-4 (gpt-4-0125-preview, temperature 0.1) received a free-text patient case and a multi-part question, made a plan and called tools, in parallel or in chains (for example, segment two scans, then compute the area ratio to judge progression). In the second stage, built in DSPy, GPT-4 wrote 10-14 sub-queries with Chain-of-Thought. For each sub-query it retrieved 40 passages, reranked them, kept the top 10, then merged and deduplicated them. It wrote an answer strategy, a response with a citation for every one or two sentences, a self-check against sources, and suggestions for missing information. To test the system they wrote 11 fictional gastrointestinal cancer cases with 1-2 CT/MRI slices each, histology in 7 cases and genomic data in 4 cases, with 3-4 subtasks per question. Four oncologists blindly rated outputs, using majority vote and the more adverse rating on ties. They measured tool use (32/33), correctness (131/140), harm (3/140), completeness (63/67), helpfulness (33/37) and citation accuracy (141/171). To adapt this, replace the tools with brain MRI segmentation and grading models, use local LLMs, and add a deferral step to clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Proof-of-concept development and evaluation study using fictional (simulated) patient cases built from public and in-house images; retrospective use of public images (TCGA, TCIA) and images from University Hospital Aachen, Germany. Institutions: NCT Heidelberg, EKFZ TU Dresden, University of St Andrews, MSKCC, Google Cloud and others (Germany, UK, USA). Blinded manual evaluation by 4 certified oncology clinicians. Ethics approval TU Dresden (BO-EK-444102022). Experiments run on 4 and 13 March 2024.
papers.datasets: (1) Knowledge base: about 6,800 medical documents and clinical scores from six sources: MDCalc (clinical scores), UpToDate and MEDITRON guidelines (general recommendations), ASCO, ESMO and German/English Onkopedia (DGHO) oncology guidelines; keyword-filtered for the use case. (2) Evaluation set: 11 fictional multimodal patient cases in gastrointestinal oncology (colorectal, pancreatic, cholangiocellular, hepatocellular cancer). Each has a short history; 3/11 cases have one CT/MRI slice and the others two slices (6/11 sequential liver follow-up, 1 lung follow-up, 1 simultaneous liver and lung staging). Images from the web, The Cancer Imaging Archive (Colorectal-Liver-Metastases collection) and University Hospital Aachen. Histology (TCGA) in 7/11 cases; genomic variants (mutations, gene fusions) in 4 cases. Each query has multiple subtasks (average 3-4). Reference standard: 33 expected tool calls, 67 expected completeness items (5-10 keywords per case), 37 sub-questions. Inclusion/exclusion criteria: Not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Guideline PDFs converted with GROBID to TEI XML; text pulled from XML; removal of hyperlinks, graphics, corrupted tables, malformed characters and IP addresses; headers marked with '#', blank lines between paragraphs; saved as jsonlines with metadata. MEDITRON guidelines used as provided jsonlines. Text chunked into 512, 256 and 128-token segments with 50-token overlap, embedded with text-embedding-3-large (3,072 dimensions) and stored with metadata in one Chroma collection. Histology feature vectors (STAMP step 1) pre-computed before agent runs. Cases framed as hypothetical scenarios for GPT-4V. No train/validation/test split (no model training).
papers.modelDetails: Two-stage pipeline. Stage 1 (tools): given patient context and question, GPT-4 makes a plan and iteratively calls tools defined in JSON (short description and input parameters); calls can run in parallel or in chains (e.g. MedSAM areas of two scans passed to the calculator to compute a ratio; example progression factor 3.89). GPT-4V reports each image separately, then compares them. Pathology ViTs predict MSI/MSS, KRAS and BRAF status. OncoKB gives evidence for mutations, copy number changes and fusions. Tool choice is left to the agent (manual prompting possible, used in cases D and X). Stage 2 (RAG in DSPy, Algorithm 1): Chain-of-Thought generates 10-14 sub-queries (main text says up to 12); for each, retrieve n=40 passages by cosine similarity, rerank, keep top k=10; merge, deduplicate and number sources; generate an answer strategy (CoT), then a cited response, then suggestions for missing information. Each statement (max two sentences) must carry a citation, enforced with DSPy suggestions and one self-check iteration against the source text. No uncertainty or deferral rule is defined.
papers.training: No model training or fine-tuning. Off-the-shelf models via the OpenAI API: gpt-4-0125-preview and gpt-4-vision-preview, temperature 0.1 (set empirically), no other hyperparameters changed. Pathology ViTs and MedSAM are previously trained models. Hardware and run time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Blinded manual evaluation by 4 certified oncology clinicians; final label by majority vote, ties resolved toward the more adverse rating (correct, irrelevant, wrong). Metrics: tool use = actual/expected tool calls; helpfulness = sub-questions answered / all sub-questions; correctness, incorrectness and harmfulness = proportion of statements (answers split at citations or topic change; 140 statements); completeness = proportion of predefined expected keywords/interventions covered (67); citation accuracy = correct/irrelevant/wrong for 171 citations, checked against the source chunk by ID. No external validation and no comparison arm.
papers.baselines: None in arXiv v1 (no comparison with GPT-4 alone or other agents).
papers.results: Tool use 97% (32/33; one failed call for patient Z, one omitted call for patient Le); about 3 tool calls per case on average (1 for cases T and Z, 8 for case X). Correctness 93.6% (131/140), incorrect 4.3% (6/140), harmful 2.1% (3/140). Completeness 94% (63/67; 4 missed). Helpfulness 89.2% (33/37). Citations: correct 82.5% (141/171), irrelevant 11/171, wrong 3/171. Pathology tools correct in 7/7 cases; GPT-4V led to correct disease-trajectory assessment in all radiology cases despite some errors.
papers.statistics: Descriptive proportions only; majority vote of 4 raters. No confidence intervals, statistical tests or inter-rater agreement coefficients reported.
papers.availability: Code: authors planned release upon journal publication (not available in arXiv v1). Full model outputs and tool results in Supplementary Tables 3-7. Public data: TCGA, TCIA.

papers.title: MMedAgent: Learning to Use Medical Tools with Multi-modal Agent
papers.authors: Li B, Yan T, Pan Y, Luo J, Ji R, Ding J, Xu Z, Liu S, Dong H, Lin Z, Wang Y
papers.aim: To build one multimodal medical agent that learns which tool to call for a given image task.
papers.method: Instruction-tuned LLaVA-Med on a tool-use dataset. Tools cover grounding, segmentation, classification, report generation and retrieval across several imaging modalities.
papers.result: Did better than open-source medical models and GPT-4o on most tested tasks, and new tools can be added easily.
papers.tools: LLaVA-Med, MedSAM, Grounding DINO, BiomedCLIP, instruction tuning
papers.gap: Tool choice is learned but there is no confidence check on tool outputs.
papers.relation: Shows a trained router is possible. Our MRI agent and pathology agent could be called the same way, but we add uncertainty to each call.
papers.limitations: Fixed tool list, mostly 2D images, not brain MRI volumes. Future: more tools and modalities.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors chose LLaVA-Med (60K-IM, 7B) as the core of the agent and gave it six tools for seven tasks. Because no medical grounding model handled many modalities, they fine-tuned Grounding DINO on six segmentation datasets (WORD 9,309 CT images, FLARE 4,797 CT, VinDr-CXR 4,394 X-rays, Montgomery 566 X-rays, BraTS 14,720 brain MRI images, Cellseg 229 histology images) after turning each mask into a tight bounding box, and also kept COCO and Flickr30k. MedSAM does box-prompted segmentation; Grounding DINO plus MedSAM does text-prompted segmentation; BiomedCLIP classifies against 11 text labels; ChatCAD writes chest X-ray reports; ChatCAD+ retrieves from the Merck Manual (1,972 entries). They then used GPT-4o with one-shot prompts to create 48K instruction dialogues in a fixed format: Thoughts (which tool), Actions (API name and parameters), Value (answer). The mix was 15K VQA, 10K detection, 3K RAG and 5K each for segmentation, classification, report generation and grounded segmentation. They trained with LoRA (rank 128), AdamW, a cosine schedule peaking at 2e-4, batch size 48 and 15 epochs, about 72 hours on two A100 80GB GPUs, with an auto-regressive loss on tool calls and final answers. At run time the model reads the image and question, emits a tool call, receives the tool result and writes the answer. For testing they built 70 unseen questions (30 grounding, 20 report generation, 10 classification, 10 RAG). GPT-4 scored each answer 1-10, and scores were divided by GPT-4o's score. They also tested 193 open-ended questions and four VQA benchmarks (4K training and 300 test pairs each). To add a new tool they generated 5K samples and fine-tuned with learning rate 1e-6 and batch size 10, reaching 100% selection in 2K steps. For our project, the same recipe could train a local orchestrator for brain MRI tools, with a deferral output added.
papers.studyDesign: Methods development and benchmark evaluation (retrospective, public datasets only). Institutions: Stanford University, Harvard Medical School, Virginia Tech, MSU, CUHK, Tsinghua University, Duke University (USA/China). No patients recruited.
papers.datasets: Grounding DINO fine-tuning (Appendix Table 5): WORD (CT abdomen, 9,309 images, 14 organ labels), FLARE2021 (CT abdomen, 4,797 images, 11 organs), VinDr-CXR (chest X-ray, 4,394 images, 14 findings), Montgomery County X-ray (566 images, lung), BraTS (brain MRI, 14,720 images, tumour), Cellseg (histology, 229 images, cell); plus COCO and Flickr30k to keep natural-image ability. Instruction tuning: 48K samples = 15K augmented VQA (from LLaVA-Med 60K inline mentions, PMC articles), 10K detection, 3K RAG, 5K each for segmentation, classification, MRG and G-Seg. RAG source: Merck Manual (1,972 diseases/procedures); RAG instruction data from 1,000 generated chest X-ray reports, 1,000 GPT-4o medical reports and 1,000 GPT-4o patient questions. MRG tool trained on MIMIC-CXR. Evaluation set: 70 questions = 10 Merck Manual RAG concepts + 60 unseen images (10 organ grounding, 10 disease grounding, 10 cell grounding, 20 X-ray MRG, 10 classification). Open-ended dialogue: 193 questions on 50 images from PMC-15M (143 conversation, 50 description; X-ray 37, MRI 38, histology 44, gross 34, CT 40). VQA benchmarks: VQA-RAD, SLAKE, PATH-VQA (each 150 open + 150 closed test), PMC-VQA (300 closed); 4K training pairs each. Inclusion/exclusion criteria: Not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Segmentation masks converted to bounding boxes using the minimal outer rectangle of each object; box coordinates and labels used as grounding labels. Instruction data generated by GPT-4o with one-shot prompting, a fixed system prompt per tool and example conversations; dialogue format with Thoughts, Actions (API name and params) and Value. Captions for evaluation images built from labels when missing (e.g. 'A CT scan showing the kidney organ'). VQA: 4K random image-text pairs for training and 300 for test per benchmark. Image resolution and normalisation: Not reported. Augmentation: VQA instructions augmented following LLaVA-Plus.
papers.modelDetails: Four-step workflow: (1) user gives instruction Xq and image Iq; (2) the MLLM (action planner) produces a formatted tool call Xtool; (3) the tool runs on Iq and returns Xresult; (4) the MLLM aggregates Xq, Iq and Xresult into the final answer Xanswer. Output has three fields: Thoughts (can it answer alone, or which tool is needed), Actions (list of API name + params; empty list means no call), Value (round 1: chosen tool; round 2: final answer). Tools: VQA by backbone LLaVA-Med; classification by BiomedCLIP using cosine similarity between image and text embeddings over a closed set of 11 labels (e.g. 'brain MRI', 'chest X-ray', 'hematoxylin and eosin histopathology'); grounding by fine-tuned Grounding DINO; B-Seg by MedSAM with a box prompt; G-Seg chains Grounding DINO then MedSAM; MRG by ChatCAD; RAG by ChatCAD+ cosine-similarity retrieval from the Merck Manual. Loss: auto-regressive loss on Xtool and Xanswer tokens. No uncertainty or deferral rule; a tool can be swapped by changing its API name.
papers.training: Initialised from LLaVA-Med 60K-IM; LoRA rank 128; 15 epochs; batch size 48; AdamW; cosine learning-rate schedule peaking at 2e-4; about 72 hours on two NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. New-tool experiment: 5K extra instruction samples, learning rate 1e-6, batch size 10, one A100 80GB, 100% selection within 2K steps. Grounding DINO fine-tuning hyperparameters: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: GPT-4 rates each answer from 1 to 10 for helpfulness, relevance, accuracy and level of detail, given image captions (or reports for MRG). Absolute score = GPT-4 score; relative score = S_model / S_GPT-4o (%). For open-ended dialogue the reference is GPT-4 instead of GPT-4o. VQA benchmarks scored on open and closed questions (metric not defined in detail). Tool selection accuracy measured. Segmentation evaluated qualitatively only. No cross-validation and no clinician evaluation.
papers.baselines: GPT-4o (reference), Med-Flamingo, RadFM, LLaVA-Med, LLaVA-Med (Tool in Test, given tool outputs), Yi-VL-34B, Qwen-VL-Chat, LLaVA-34B.
papers.results: Relative scores (% of GPT-4o) for grounding cell/organ/disease, classification, MRG, RAG, overall, and absolute overall: MMedAgent 97.50/102.29/125.89, 81.11, 121.49, 85.55, overall 109.48, abs 8.66. LLaVA-34B 76.75/84.85/80.75, 96.04, 80.27, 91.64, overall 86.52, abs 6.84. Qwen-VL-Chat overall 76.21 (abs 6.03). LLaVA-Med (Tool in Test) 65.31 (5.17). Yi-VL-34B 64.08 (5.07). LLaVA-Med 60.68 (4.80). RadFM 45.38 (3.59). Flamingo-Med 14.68 (1.16). Open-ended dialogue overall: MMedAgent 51.42 vs LLaVA-Med 50.94 (conversation 54.49 vs 53.30; description 39.75 vs 38.90; X-ray 58.37 vs 56.58; MRI 35.09 vs 40.84; histology 56.88 vs 54.71; gross 51.88 vs 48.47; CT 52.79 vs 50.68). VQA (MMedAgent vs LLaVA-Med): VQA-RAD open 58.31 vs 28.23, closed 86.72 vs 61.40; SLAKE open 79.39 vs 39.17, closed 86.34 vs 52.16; PATH-VQA open 39.16 vs 12.30, closed 90.38 vs 54.05; PMC-VQA 39.50 vs 27.48. Tool selection accuracy 100%.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no confidence intervals, statistical tests or rater agreement).
papers.availability: Code and web UI: https://github.com/Wangyixinxin/MMedAgent. Datasets used are public.

papers.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
papers.authors: Wu Q, Bansal G, Zhang J, Wu Y, Li B, Zhu E, Jiang L, Zhang X, Zhang S, Liu J, Awadallah AH, White RW, Burger D, Wang C
papers.aim: To give a general open-source framework for building applications from several agents that talk to each other.
papers.method: 'Conversable' agents that can be LLMs, tools or humans. Developer defines the conversation pattern. A human proxy agent can ask a person for input at set points.
papers.result: Worked on maths, retrieval QA, coding, decision making tasks and reduced the coding effort to build multi-agent systems.
papers.tools: Python, OpenAI LLMs, tool execution, human-input modes
papers.gap: Not designed for safety-critical use. No standard way of logging decisions for audit.
papers.relation: Possible implementation framework for our prototype. The human proxy agent maps nicely to our clinician validation point.
papers.limitations: Chat-based state is hard to verify. Future: better control flow and evaluation tools.
papers.methodologyDetail: AutoGen is a Python library, so the 'method' is a design pattern rather than a trained model. A developer first defines agents. Each agent is a ConversableAgent with send, receive and generate_reply functions. An AssistantAgent is backed by an LLM (GPT-4 or GPT-3.5-turbo) with a default system prompt that tells it to write code, fix errors and reply 'TERMINATE' when finished. A UserProxyAgent stands in for the human: it can ask a person for input (human_input_mode 'ALWAYS', 'NEVER' or conditional) and it executes code or function calls suggested by the assistant. Second, the developer programs the conversation: once a chat starts, each agent replies automatically to the message it receives until a termination condition, a maximum number of auto replies, or a 'TERMINATE' message. Custom reply functions, function calls and a GroupChatManager (select speaker with a role-play prompt, get its reply, broadcast) allow dynamic multi-agent flows. The authors then built six applications and tested them. For math they ran an assistant plus user proxy on 120 level-5 MATH problems and the full 5,000-problem test set (69.48% vs 55.18% for GPT-4). For retrieval-augmented QA they chunked 5,332 Natural Questions documents, embedded them with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 in Chroma, answered 6,775 queries, and let the assistant say 'UPDATE CONTEXT' to fetch more chunks (F1 25.88%, recall 66.65%). For ALFWorld (134 unseen tasks, 3 attempts) they added a grounding agent that gives commonsense rules when errors repeat (69% vs 54%). For OptiGuide they split work among Commander, Writer and Safeguard agents and tested 100 safe/unsafe coding tasks (F1 96% vs 88%). A 4-agent group chat solved 11 of 12 tasks with GPT-4. For our project, the same pattern can host imaging, pathology, guideline and planning agents with a clinician proxy agent that is called when the system is uncertain.
papers.studyDesign: Framework (software) paper with benchmark experiments and small pilot/user studies. Microsoft Research, Pennsylvania State University, University of Washington, Xidian University (USA/China). No patients or clinical data.
papers.datasets: A1 MATH: 120 randomly selected level-5 problems (20 from each of six categories, geometry excluded) and the whole test set (5,000 problems); 2 level-5 problems x 3 trials for qualitative study. A2 Natural Questions: 5,332 non-redundant context documents and 6,775 queries from HuggingFace (W/O-interactive check on first 500 questions); code-generation case with FLAML. A3 ALFWorld: 134 unseen tasks, 6 task types. A4 OptiGuide: 100 coding tasks (half safe, half unsafe) for safeguard test; 10 random questions for user study; 2,000 questions across five OptiGuide applications (netflow, facility, tsp, coffee, diet) for interaction count. A5: 12 manually crafted complex tasks. A6: chess games (qualitative). Extra: MiniWoB++ 49 tasks.
papers.preprocessing: Retrieval-augmented chat: documents split into chunks of a set size (size not reported), embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and stored in Chroma. No training data splits (no model training). Other preprocessing: Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: ConversableAgent is the base class; AssistantAgent (LLM-backed, human_input_mode='NEVER', default system message telling it to write Python code, fix errors and reply 'TERMINATE' when done) and UserProxyAgent (human_input_mode='ALWAYS' by default, executes code or function calls) are subclasses. Auto-reply: when an agent receives a message it calls generate_reply and answers unless a termination condition holds; custom reply functions can be registered. Control can be by natural language (prompts), by code (termination condition, max auto replies, human input mode) or by switching between them (function calls). GroupChatManager repeats: select next speaker (role-play prompt), ask it to respond, broadcast the message. Applications: A1 assistant + user proxy (human_input_mode='ALWAYS' for human-in-the-loop); A2 retrieval user proxy + retrieval assistant with interactive retrieval (assistant replies 'UPDATE CONTEXT' to fetch the next most similar chunks; stops when no documents remain); A3 assistant + executor + grounding agent that injects commonsense rules when repeated errors appear; A4 Commander, Writer and Safeguard agents (Safeguard checks code safety before execution); A5 four-agent group chat (user proxy, engineer, critic, executor); A6 two player agents + board agent that checks move legality. No uncertainty or confidence thresholds.
papers.training: No model training. Uses GPT-4 and GPT-3.5-turbo through the API; ReAct baseline run with text-davinci-003 via its official code. Temperature, hardware and run time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Benchmarks: MATH success ratio (accuracy); NQ F1 and recall following Adlakha et al. (2023); ALFWorld success rate over 3 attempts (average and best of 3); OptiGuide safeguard F1 and recall on unsafe-code detection; user time and number of user prompts; group chat number of successes, average LLM calls, termination failures on 12 tasks; MiniWoB++ success rate. Ablations: no interactive retrieval ('I don't know' instead of 'UPDATE CONTEXT'), 2 vs 3 agents, single vs multi-agent safeguard, task-based vs role-play speaker selection, no board agent.
papers.baselines: Vanilla GPT-4, ChatGPT + Code Interpreter, ChatGPT + Plugin (Wolfram Alpha), Multi-Agent Debate, LangChain ReAct, AutoGPT, BabyAGI, CAMEL, MetaGPT (preliminary), DPR (dense passage retrieval), ReAct (text-davinci-003), RCI (MiniWoB++), single-agent OptiGuide.
papers.results: MATH 120 level-5 (GPT-4): AutoGen 52.5%, ChatGPT+Code 48.33%, ChatGPT+Plugin 45.0%, GPT-4 30.0%, Multi-Agent Debate 26.67%, LangChain ReAct 23.33%; whole set: AutoGen 69.48%, GPT-4 55.18%. NQ (GPT-3.5): AutoGen F1 25.88%, recall 66.65%; the other two bars are 22.79%/62.59% and 15.12%/58.56% (the appendix implies W/O interactive retrieval is about 23.40%/62.60% on the first 500 questions and beats DPR); about 19.4% of questions triggered 'Update Context'. ALFWorld average / best of 3: AutoGen 3-agent 69/77, 2-agent 54/63, ReAct 54/66 (grounding agent +15% on average). OptiGuide F1/recall: multi-agent GPT-4 96/98, single GPT-4 88/78, multi GPT-3.5 83/72, single GPT-3.5 48/32; code 430 to 100 lines; user time 4 min 35 s (SD about 2.5 min) with Code Interpreter vs about 1.5 min; both 8/10 correct; prompt saving ratio netflow 3.14x (0.65), facility 3.14x (0.64), tsp 4.88x (1.71), coffee 3.38x (0.86), diet 3.03x (0.31). Group chat successes /12 (two-agent, group chat, task-based selection): GPT-3.5 8, 9, 7; GPT-4 9, 11, 8; average LLM calls and termination failures: GPT-3.5 9.9/9, 5.3/0, 4/0; GPT-4 6.8/3, 4.5/0, 4/0. MiniWoB++: 52.8% over 49 tasks, 3.6% below RCI.
papers.statistics: Mostly descriptive; OptiGuide saving ratios given as mean (SD); user time SD about 2.5 min. No significance tests or confidence intervals.

papers.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
papers.authors: Yao S, Zhao J, Yu D, Du N, Shafran I, Narasimhan K, Cao Y
papers.aim: To make LLMs think and take actions (use tools) in the same loop.
papers.method: Model writes a thought, takes an action (e.g. search), reads the observation, and repeats.
papers.result: Fewer hallucinations on HotpotQA and FEVER. On ALFWorld and WebShop it beat imitation and RL methods by a large margin (34% and 10% absolute).
papers.tools: PaLM, GPT-3, few-shot prompting, Wikipedia API
papers.gap: Long reasoning chains can still go wrong, and the model does not know when to stop and ask a human.
papers.relation: Basic loop for each of our agents. The thought-action-observation trace is useful as a readable record for the audit trail.
papers.limitations: Depends on prompt examples. Future: fine-tuning on more traces.
papers.methodologyDetail: ReAct changes how a language model is prompted rather than how it is trained. The authors add 'thoughts' (free text) to the normal action space, so the model can write reasoning that updates its context without touching the environment, then choose an action and read the observation. For knowledge tasks (HotpotQA, FEVER) they used a question-only setup and a deliberately simple Wikipedia API with three actions: search[entity] (first 5 sentences or top-5 similar titles), lookup[string] (next sentence with that string) and finish[answer]. They hand-wrote ReAct trajectories for 6 HotpotQA and 3 FEVER training examples and used them as few-shot prompts for a frozen PaLM-540B with greedy decoding. Baselines were made by deleting parts of the same trajectories: Standard (no thoughts or actions), CoT (thoughts only), CoT-SC (21 samples at temperature 0.7, majority vote) and Act (no thoughts). They then combined methods with two rules: if ReAct gave no answer within 7 (HotpotQA) or 5 (FEVER) steps, fall back to CoT-SC; if the CoT-SC majority answer appeared in fewer than half of the samples, switch to ReAct. Best results were 35.1 EM on HotpotQA and 64.6% on FEVER. They manually labelled 200 trajectories to show CoT hallucination (56% of its failures) versus 0% for ReAct. They also fine-tuned PaLM-8B and 62B on 3,000 correct ReAct trajectories (batch 64, 4,000 steps). For ALFWorld they annotated 3 trajectories per task type with sparse thoughts, built 6 prompts per type, and tested on 134 unseen games (71% best vs 45% Act, 37% BUTLER). For WebShop they used one-shot prompts on 500 instructions (40.0% success). For our project, the agreement-based back-off rule is a template for deciding when an agent should act alone, call a tool, or defer to a clinician.
papers.studyDesign: Methods paper with benchmark experiments (retrospective, public benchmarks). Princeton University and Google Research Brain team (USA). No human subjects except authors annotating trajectories and labelling 200 error cases.
papers.datasets: HotpotQA (multi-hop QA over Wikipedia; question-only setup; 6 training cases used as exemplars; 500 random validation questions for GPT-3 experiment; number of PaLM test questions: Not reported in the main text). FEVER (fact verification; labels SUPPORTS, REFUTES, NOT ENOUGH INFO; 3 exemplars). ALFWorld (text household game, 6 task types: Pick, Clean, Heat, Cool, Look, Pick 2; 134 unseen evaluation games; 3 annotated trajectories per task type). WebShop (1.18M real Amazon products, 12k human instructions; evaluation on 500 test instructions; one-shot prompt). Fine-tuning data: 3,000 correct trajectories generated by ReAct (and by each baseline) on HotpotQA. Error analysis: 50 correct and 50 incorrect trajectories each from ReAct and CoT (200 total).
papers.preprocessing: Prompts built by manually writing thought-action-observation trajectories for randomly chosen training cases (6 HotpotQA, 3 FEVER, 3 per ALFWorld task type, 1 WebShop). Baseline prompts made by removing parts of ReAct trajectories (Standard removes all; CoT keeps thoughts only; Act removes thoughts). For ALFWorld, 6 prompts per task type from every permutation of 2 of the 3 trajectories. No train/test split beyond the benchmarks' own splits.
papers.modelDetails: Action space is augmented with language: A_hat = A union L, where a 'thought' changes only the context, not the environment. Knowledge tasks: dense alternation of thought, action, observation. Wikipedia API: search[entity] returns the first 5 sentences of the page or top-5 similar entities; lookup[string] returns the next sentence containing the string; finish[answer] ends the task. Decision tasks: sparse thoughts decided by the model (goal decomposition, subgoal tracking, commonsense on where objects are). Combination rules: ReAct->CoT-SC backs off to CoT-SC if ReAct gives no answer within 7 steps (HotpotQA) or 5 steps (FEVER); CoT-SC->ReAct backs off to ReAct if the majority answer among n CoT-SC samples occurs fewer than n/2 times. CoT-SC uses 21 samples at temperature 0.7. ReAct-IM ablation uses only dense external-feedback thoughts. Greedy decoding for all methods.
papers.training: Prompting: no training. Fine-tuning (HotpotQA): bootstrapped 3,000 correct trajectories; batch size 64; PaLM-8B: ReAct and Act 4,000 steps, Standard and CoT 2,000 steps; PaLM-62B: ReAct and Act 4,000 steps, Standard and CoT 1,000 steps. Learning rate, optimizer and hardware: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: HotpotQA exact match (EM); FEVER accuracy; ALFWorld success rate per task type (average and best of 6 prompts); WebShop average score (percentage of desired attributes covered) and success rate (all requirements met) on 500 instructions. Human error analysis on 200 HotpotQA trajectories. Scaling study over 8B, 62B, 540B for prompting and fine-tuning. GPT-3 replication on 500 HotpotQA validation questions and 134 ALFWorld tasks.
papers.baselines: Standard prompting, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), CoT with self-consistency (CoT-SC), Act-only, ReAct-IM (Inner Monologue style), BUTLER and BUTLER-g (imitation learning, 105 expert trajectories per task type), WebShop IL (1,012 human trajectories) and IL+RL (10,587 instructions), human experts, supervised state of the art.
papers.results: PaLM-540B HotpotQA EM / FEVER Acc: Standard 28.7/57.1; CoT 29.4/56.3; CoT-SC 33.4/60.4; Act 25.7/58.9; ReAct 27.4/60.9; CoT-SC->ReAct 34.2/64.6; ReAct->CoT-SC 35.1/62.0; supervised SoTA 67.5/89.5. Error analysis ReAct vs CoT: true positive 94% vs 86%, false positive 6% vs 14%; failures: reasoning error 47% vs 16%, search error 23% vs -, hallucination 0% vs 56%, label ambiguity 29% vs 28%. ALFWorld success (%) All: Act best of 6 45; ReAct avg 57, best of 6 71; ReAct-IM avg 48, best 53; BUTLER-g 22; BUTLER 37 (ReAct best per task: Pick 92, Clean 58, Heat 96, Cool 86, Look 78, Pick 2 41). Relative gain of ReAct over Act 33% to 90%, average 62%. WebShop score/SR: Act 62.3/30.1; ReAct 66.6/40.0; IL 59.9/29.1; IL+RL 62.4/28.7; human expert 82.1/59.6. GPT-3 vs PaLM-540B: HotpotQA EM 30.8 vs 29.4; ALFWorld 78.4% vs 70.9%. Fine-tuned PaLM-8B ReAct beats all PaLM-62B prompting methods; fine-tuned 62B ReAct beats all 540B prompting methods.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no significance tests or confidence intervals; ALFWorld reported as average and best over 6 prompt permutations).
papers.availability: Project page and GPT-3 code: https://react-lm.github.io/ ; all prompts in Appendix C. PaLM is not publicly available.

papers.title: A survey on large language model based autonomous agents
papers.authors: Wang L, Ma C, Feng X, Zhang Z, Yang H, Zhang J, et al., Wen JR
papers.aim: To review how LLM-based agents are built, used and evaluated.
papers.method: Literature review. They propose a common framework with profile, memory, planning and action modules.
papers.result: A clear taxonomy of agent design, applications (incl. science and medicine) and evaluation methods.
papers.tools: Survey (no experiments)
papers.gap: Safety, evaluation standards, and role reliability are listed as open problems.
papers.relation: Useful to describe our architecture in standard terms in the thesis (each agent = profile + memory + planning + action).
papers.limitations: Moves fast, some parts already outdated. Not medical specific.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a survey, so the method is a structured review rather than an experiment. The authors collected LLM-based autonomous agent papers, mostly published between January 2021 and August 2023, and plotted their cumulative growth by agent type (tool, simulation, general, embodied, game, web and assistant agents) in Figure 1. They did not report a formal search string, databases, or inclusion counts. They organised the literature around three questions. First, construction: they abstracted a unified agent architecture with four modules. The profiling module sets the role of the agent in the prompt, created by handcrafting, LLM generation, or alignment with real datasets. The memory module stores past observations in unified or hybrid structures and supports reading, writing and reflection. The planning module decomposes tasks either without feedback (single-path such as Chain-of-Thought, multi-path such as Tree-of-Thoughts, or external planners such as PDDL solvers) or with feedback from the environment, humans or other models. The action module turns decisions into outputs, using internal knowledge or external tools such as APIs, databases and other models. They also split capability acquisition into fine-tuning (human-annotated, LLM-generated or real-world datasets) and no fine-tuning (prompt engineering and mechanism engineering). Each representative agent is coded against these categories in Table 1. Second, application: papers are grouped into social science, natural science and engineering domains in Table 2. Third, evaluation: methods are grouped into subjective (human annotation, Turing test) and objective (metrics, protocols, benchmarks) strategies in Table 3. Finally, the authors derive six open challenges, including hallucination and knowledge boundary. A PhD student can reuse this four-module taxonomy to specify each agent of a clinical multi-agent system and to choose evaluation metrics, but should add explicit modules for uncertainty, deferral and privacy, which the survey does not cover.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative / taxonomic literature survey by the Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China (Beijing, China). No human participants, no data collection, no prospective or retrospective study.
papers.datasets: No dataset was used. The corpus is published LLM-agent papers; Figure 1 plots the cumulative number of papers from January 2021 to August 2023, split by agent category (tool, simulation, general, embodied, game, web, assistant agents). The paper cites more than 180 references. Inclusion criteria for papers are not formally reported; the authors state they also included some studies that do not explicitly mention LLM agents but are highly related.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (no data processing, no train/validation/test split).
papers.modelDetails: Unified framework: (1) Profiling module writes agent role information (basic information such as age, gender, career; psychology; social relations) into the prompt. Profiles are created by handcrafting, LLM-generation, or dataset alignment. (2) Memory module: structures are unified memory (short-term only) or hybrid memory (short-term plus long-term); formats include natural language, embeddings, databases and structured lists; operations are memory reading, writing and reflection. (3) Planning module: planning without feedback (single-path reasoning such as CoT, multi-path reasoning such as ToT, external planners) and planning with feedback (environmental, human, and model feedback). (4) Action module: action target, action production (via memory recollection or plan following), action space (external tools such as APIs, databases, external models, or internal LLM knowledge), and action impact. Capability acquisition: with fine-tuning (human-annotated, LLM-generated or real-world datasets) or without fine-tuning (prompt engineering and mechanism engineering such as trial-and-error, crowd-sourcing, experience accumulation and self-driven evolution).
papers.training: Not applicable (no model was trained).
papers.evaluation: No experimental evaluation. The survey classifies agent evaluation into: subjective evaluation (human annotation and Turing test) and objective evaluation using metrics (task success metrics such as success rate, reward/score, coverage, accuracy/error rate; human similarity metrics such as coherence, fluency, dialogue similarity, human acceptance rate; efficiency metrics such as development cost and training efficiency), protocols (real-world simulation, social evaluation, multi-task evaluation, software testing) and benchmarks.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (survey).
papers.results: No quantitative results. Main outputs are Table 1 (representative agents mapped to profile, memory, planning, action and capability-acquisition strategies), Table 2 (applications: psychology, political science and economy, social simulation, jurisprudence, research assistant; documentation and data management, experiment assistant, natural science education; civil engineering, computer science and software engineering, industrial automation, robotics and embodied AI), and Table 3 (evaluation strategies per work).
papers.availability: Not available as code. The arXiv paper (2308.11432) is freely available; the authors maintain a related paper list on GitHub (exact link not stated in the text read).

papers.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
papers.authors: Mitchell M, Wu S, Zaldivar A, Barnes P, Vasserman L, Hutchinson B, Spitzer E, Raji ID, Gebru T
papers.aim: To propose a short standard document that comes with every trained model.
papers.method: Defined sections: model details, intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation data, training data, ethical points, caveats. Showed two example cards.
papers.result: Model cards became a widely used reporting practice.
papers.tools: Documentation framework
papers.gap: It is static and voluntary. Nothing checks at runtime that the model is used inside its tested conditions.
papers.relation: Our proposal mentions a model-facts statement for each agent. Model cards give the template. We can extend it so the orchestrator checks it at runtime.
papers.limitations: Not medical. Future: automatic and living documentation.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first set out the problem: trained models are released without standard documentation of where they work and where they fail. They then design a template with nine sections (model details, intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation data, training data, quantitative analyses, ethical considerations, caveats and recommendations), each with guiding questions. A key rule is disaggregated evaluation: results must be broken down by relevant factors (for example demographic or phenotypic groups, instrument type, environment), both one at a time (unitary) and in combination (intersectional), and reported with confidence intervals. To show how this works, they built two cards. For image classification they fine-tuned a convolutional network, pretrained for face recognition, with cross-entropy loss to detect smiling on the CelebA training split. On the CelebA test split they computed four confusion-matrix error rates (FPR, FNR, FDR, FOR) for female vs male, young vs old, and the four age-by-gender intersections, at a 0.5 decision threshold, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. All errors lay between 0.04 and 0.14, but older men had a much higher false discovery rate and men overall had a higher false negative rate. The card therefore recommends use where detecting presence of a smile matters more than absence, and suggests fine-tuning with more images of older men. For text, they documented Perspective API's TOXICITY model using pinned AUC per identity term on a synthetic, intersectional Identity Phrase Templates test set, comparing version 1 and version 5. Version 1 performed poorly on terms like 'gay' and 'lesbian'; version 5 was more balanced after mitigation. To adapt this method, a PhD project can write one card per agent, choose factors such as hospital, scanner field strength, age band, sex and tumour type, report sensitivity, specificity and calibration per factor with bootstrap CIs, and state the deferral threshold and out-of-scope uses.
papers.studyDesign: Conceptual framework paper with two illustrative case studies (retrospective evaluation on public data). Authors from Google and the University of Toronto, USA/Canada. No human participants.
papers.datasets: (1) CelebA (public celebrity face dataset): training split used for training and test split used for evaluation of the smiling classifier; evaluation factors are gender (binary, male/not male) and age group (young/old) as annotated by third-party annotators. Number of images and class counts are not reported in the paper. (2) Identity Phrase Templates test set (Dixon et al.): synthetic, template-based sentences in which identity terms (sexual orientation, gender identity, race) are swapped into template sentences; an intersectional version was used. Size not reported. (3) Perspective API training data: proprietary comments from online forums such as Wikipedia and New York Times with crowdsourced toxicity labels; size not reported.
papers.preprocessing: Not reported. CelebA standard training and test splits were used. Synthetic test sentences were generated from templates.
papers.modelDetails: Model card template sections: (1) Model details (developer, date, version, type, training algorithms, paper, citation, licence, contact); (2) Intended use (primary uses, primary users, out-of-scope uses); (3) Factors (relevant factors such as groups, instrumentation and environment; evaluation factors); (4) Metrics (performance measures, decision thresholds, variation approaches such as confidence intervals); (5) Evaluation data (datasets, motivation, preprocessing); (6) Training data (may mirror evaluation data or give minimal distributional information); (7) Quantitative analyses (unitary and intersectional results); (8) Ethical considerations; (9) Caveats and recommendations. Example 1: CNN pretrained for face recognition, fine-tuned with cross-entropy loss for binary smiling detection; decision threshold 0.5. Example 2: Perspective API TOXICITY CNN predicting the likelihood that a comment is perceived as toxic, defined as 'a rude, disrespectful, or unreasonable comment that is likely to make you leave a discussion'; not intended for fully automated moderation.
papers.training: Smiling classifier: pretrained for face recognition, then fine-tuned with cross-entropy loss on the CelebA training split. Optimizer, learning rate, epochs, batch size and hardware are not reported. TOXICITY model training details are proprietary and not reported.
papers.evaluation: Disaggregated evaluation. Smiling classifier: confusion-matrix metrics (false positive rate, false negative rate, false discovery rate, false omission rate) computed per gender, per age group, and per intersection (age by gender) on the CelebA test split at the 0.5 threshold; 95% confidence intervals by bootstrap resampling. Toxicity: Pinned AUC (threshold-agnostic separability of toxic vs non-toxic comments for each identity group within a background distribution of other groups), reported for TOXICITY v1 and v5.
papers.baselines: No external baselines. Comparison is between subgroups and between two versions of the same model (TOXICITY v1 vs v5).
papers.results: Smiling classifier (CelebA test): all error rates (FPR, FNR, FDR, FOR) in the range 0.04 to 0.14 at threshold 0.5; FDR highest for older men; men in aggregate had higher FNR. Exact per-group values with 95% CIs appear only in the Figure 2 graphs. Toxicity: TOXICITY v1 had low pinned AUC for terms such as 'lesbian', 'gay' and 'homosexual'; TOXICITY v5 showed more equitable pinned AUC across identity terms. Exact values appear only in the Figure 3 graphs.
papers.statistics: 95% confidence intervals by bootstrap resampling for the smiling classifier metrics. No hypothesis tests or p-values.
papers.availability: Not available (no code release). Template described in the paper; Perspective API is a public service.

papers.title: Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing
papers.authors: Raji ID, Smart A, White RN, Mitchell M, Gebru T, Hutchinson B, Smith-Loud J, Theron D, Barnes P
papers.aim: To define how an organisation can audit its own AI system from start to end.
papers.method: SMACTR framework: Scoping, Mapping, Artifact collection, Testing, Reflection, with documents produced at each stage.
papers.result: A practical audit process and list of audit artifacts.
papers.tools: Process / governance framework
papers.gap: Organisational process only, no technical logging design.
papers.relation: Helps us decide what our audit record must hold so a reviewer can rebuild who decided what and why.
papers.limitations: Not tested in hospitals. Future: link to regulation.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors build the framework by borrowing tested practices from regulated industries. From aerospace and medicine they take design checklists; from safety engineering they take Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA), which lists failure modes and ranks them by likelihood and severity; from medical devices they take the design history file. They combine these with responsible-innovation ideas (anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion, responsiveness) and systems thinking. The result is SMACTR, five stages that each leave documents in a 'transparency trail'.
