papers.tools: Open-source LLMs: Qwen1.5-110B-Chat, Qwen1.5-72B-Chat, WizardLM-8x22B, LLaMA-3-70B-Instruct, Mixtral-8x22B-v0.1, dbrx-instruct; GPT-4o as optional aggregator; GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview) as automatic judge; Together Inference Endpoint API; BLEU, Levenshtein (RapidFuzz) and TF-IDF similarity for analysis. Code: https://github.com/togethercomputer/moa.
papers.gap: MoA only improves general chat answer quality. It gives no calibrated confidence, no uncertainty estimate and no rule to stop or defer to a human. It was not tested on medical or imaging tasks, and the structure (number of layers, choice of models) was chosen by hand.
papers.relation: For Objective O1 (multi-agent orchestration), MoA gives a simple and tested pattern for how an orchestrator can combine outputs from several specialised agents: proposers produce candidate answers and an aggregator synthesises them. Our brain-tumour system could use a similar aggregation step for the reports of imaging, pathology and planning agents, but it must add calibrated confidence and a deferral rule to the clinician, which MoA lacks. MoA's finding that diverse proposers help and that a ranker (select one answer) is worse than synthesis is useful when designing the orchestrator.
papers.limitations: Authors' limitation: the final answer cannot start until the last layer is done, so the time to first token (TTFT) is high. Future work: limit the number of layers, try chunk-wise aggregation, and systematically optimise the MoA architecture and widen the layers. Other limits: evaluation relies on GPT-4-based judges; outputs are slightly more verbose (lower FLASK conciseness); cost is higher than a single open model.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first showed 'collaborativeness': when an LLM is given answers from other models, its AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate goes up, even if those answers are weaker than its own. They then built Mixture-of-Agents. Step 1: choose a pool of six open-source chat models (Qwen1.5-110B-Chat, Qwen1.5-72B-Chat, WizardLM-8x22B, LLaMA-3-70B-Instruct, Mixtral-8x22B-v0.1, dbrx-instruct), picked for good past win rate and for diversity. Step 2: in layer 1, each model answers the user prompt independently. Step 3: in layer 2, each model receives the original prompt plus all six layer-1 answers inside a fixed Aggregate-and-Synthesize prompt that asks it to critically judge the answers, accept that some may be wrong, and write one improved answer. Step 4: repeat for layer 3. Step 5: one final aggregator (Qwen1.5-110B-Chat by default, or GPT-4o, or Qwen1.5-72B-Chat with only 2 layers for MoA-Lite) writes the final answer. No training is needed; all calls go through the Together API. Evaluation used AlpacaEval 2.0 (805 instructions, GPT-4 judge, length-controlled win rate against GPT-4 Preview), MT-Bench (GPT-4 scores per turn), FLASK (12 skills) and MATH accuracy. Each MoA configuration was run 3 times. MoA reached 65.1% LC win rate vs 57.5% for GPT-4o, and 65.7% with GPT-4o as aggregator. Ablations showed that synthesis beats choosing one answer with an LLM ranker, that more and more diverse proposers help (61.3% with 6 different models vs 56.7% with 6 samples at temperature 0.7 from one model), and that some models are good proposers but poor aggregators (WizardLM 63.8% vs 52.9%). Cost and TFLOPs analysis placed MoA and MoA-Lite on the Pareto front. To adapt this for a clinical orchestrator, one would replace generic proposers with specialised diagnostic agents, keep the synthesis prompt, and add a calibrated confidence and deferral step that MoA does not include.
papers.studyDesign: Experimental benchmark study of an inference-time method (no training). Authors from Together AI, Duke University, University of Chicago and Stanford University, USA. Uses public benchmarks only; no human participants and no clinical data.
papers.datasets: (1) AlpacaEval 2.0: 805 instructions representing real use cases; each answer is compared with GPT-4 (gpt-4-1106-preview) by a GPT-4-based judge. (2) MT-Bench: multi-turn questions scored by GPT-4 (1st and 2nd turn scores, out of 10). (3) FLASK: fine-grained evaluation with 12 skill-specific scores (robustness, correctness, efficiency, factuality, commonsense, comprehension, insightfulness, completeness, metacognition, readability, conciseness, harmlessness). (4) MATH dataset (Hendrycks et al., 2021) in the appendix for reasoning; number of problems used not reported. No classes, patients or images; inclusion/exclusion criteria not applicable.
papers.preprocessing: No training, so no train/validation/test split. Benchmarks were used as provided. For single-proposer experiments, n answers were sampled from the same model at temperature 0.7. The prompt for each layer is the original user prompt plus the concatenated responses of the previous layer inserted into the Aggregate-and-Synthesize prompt. Other decoding settings (max tokens, temperature for the main runs) are not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Architecture: l layers, each with n LLM agents A(i,1)...A(i,n). Layer output y_i = Aggregate-and-Synthesize prompt applied to [A(i,1)(x_i), ..., A(i,n)(x_i)] + x_1, and x_(i+1) = y_i. The last layer uses only one LLM, whose output is the final answer. Roles: proposers give useful reference answers; aggregators synthesise them. The aggregation prompt tells the model to critically evaluate the given responses, recognise that some may be biased or incorrect, and write one refined, accurate answer. Default MoA: 6 proposers (Qwen1.5-110B-Chat, Qwen1.5-72B-Chat, WizardLM-8x22B, LLaMA-3-70B-Instruct, Mixtral-8x22B-v0.1, dbrx-instruct), the same 6 models in each of 3 layers, and Qwen1.5-110B-Chat as final aggregator. MoA w/ GPT-4o: same, but GPT-4o is the final aggregator. MoA-Lite: same proposers, 2 layers, Qwen1.5-72B-Chat as aggregator. Model selection criteria: past win-rate performance and output diversity. No uncertainty, gating values, thresholds or deferral rules are used; the LLM itself plays the role of the gating network in Mixture-of-Experts.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning. All open-source model inference was run through the Together Inference Endpoint; GPT-4o via OpenAI API. Experiments were run three times and mean +/- standard deviation reported. Cost computed from API prices as of 22 May 2024; latency approximated by TFLOPs (sum over layers of the maximum TFLOPs among proposers in each layer; GPT-4 size assumed 8x220B). Hardware and run time not reported.
papers.evaluation: AlpacaEval 2.0: length-controlled (LC) win rate and raw win rate against GPT-4 Preview (11/06), judged by GPT-4 (LC metric has Spearman 0.98 with human judgements, cited). MT-Bench: GPT-4 scores for turn 1, turn 2 and average, run by the authors. FLASK: 12 skill scores (1-5 scale). MATH: accuracy per layer for different aggregators. Ablations: MoA vs LLM-ranker (aggregator selects one answer), number of proposers n = 1, 2, 3, 6, single- vs multiple-proposer, each model as aggregator vs as proposer (2 layers). Analysis: Spearman correlation between BLEU (3-, 4-, 5-gram), Levenshtein and TF-IDF similarity of each proposal to the aggregated answer and GPT-4 preference scores. Budget analysis: LC win rate vs cost per instance and vs TFLOPs (Pareto front).
papers.baselines: GPT-4 Omni (05/13), GPT-4 Turbo (04/09), GPT-4 Preview (11/06), GPT-4 (03/14 and 06/13), GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 (FLASK), WizardLM 8x22B, Qwen1.5-110B-Chat, Qwen1.5-72B-Chat, Llama 3 70B Instruct, Mixtral 8x22B v0.1, dbrx-instruct, and an LLM-ranker baseline using Qwen1.5-110B-Chat.
papers.results: AlpacaEval 2.0 (LC win / win): MoA w/ GPT-4o 65.7+/-0.7% / 78.7+/-0.2%; MoA 65.1+/-0.6% / 59.8+/-0.3%; MoA-Lite 59.3+/-0.2% / 57.0+/-0.7%; GPT-4 Omni 57.5% / 51.3%; GPT-4 Turbo 55.0% / 46.1%; WizardLM 8x22B 51.3% / 62.3%; GPT-4 Preview 50.0% / 50.0%; Qwen1.5 110B 43.9% / 33.8%; Qwen1.5 72B 36.6% / 26.5%; GPT-4 (03/14) 35.3% / 22.1%; Llama 3 70B 34.4% / 33.2%; Mixtral 8x22B 30.9% / 22.2%. MT-Bench (avg, turn1, turn2): MoA w/ GPT-4o 9.40+/-0.06, 9.49, 9.31; GPT-4 Turbo 9.31, 9.35, 9.28; MoA 9.25+/-0.10, 9.44, 9.07; GPT-4 Preview 9.20; GPT-4 Omni 9.19; MoA-Lite 9.18+/-0.09; Qwen1.5 110B 8.96. Number of proposers (2 layers, Qwen1.5-110B aggregator), multiple vs single proposer: n=6 61.3% vs 56.7%; n=3 58.0% vs 56.1%; n=2 58.8% vs 54.5%; n=1 47.8% vs 47.8%. As aggregator / as proposer: Qwen1.5-110B 61.3% / 56.7%; Qwen1.5-72B 59.3% / 53.3%; LLaMA-3-70B 45.0% / 60.6%; WizardLM 52.9% / 63.8%; Mixtral 48.4% / 54.8%; dbrx 41.5% / 55.1%. MATH accuracy (layer 1, 2, 3): Qwen1.5-110B aggregator 0.500, 0.570, 0.576; WizardLM 0.544, 0.574, 0.580; Llama-3-70B 0.456, 0.584, 0.578; Qwen1.5-72B 0.428, 0.526, 0.552; Mixtral 0.282, 0.534, 0.556; dbrx 0.314, 0.456, 0.522. MoA-Lite beat GPT-4 Turbo by about 4% while being more than twice as cost-effective. FLASK: MoA better than Qwen-110B on robustness, correctness, efficiency, factuality, commonsense, insightfulness, completeness; worse on conciseness.
papers.statistics: Three repeated runs with mean +/- standard deviation for MoA variants. Spearman rank correlation between similarity scores and preference scores (positive; exact values only shown in figures, roughly up to 0.3). No significance tests or confidence intervals reported.
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/togethercomputer/moa. Benchmarks are public. Models are public open-source models or commercial APIs.

papers.title: Robots That Ask For Help: Uncertainty Alignment for Large Language Model Planners
papers.authors: Allen Z. Ren, Anushri Dixit, Alexandra Bodrova, et al.
papers.aim: To make an LLM-based robot planner know when it does not know, so it asks a human for help only when needed, while giving a statistical guarantee on task success.
papers.method: KnowNo turns each planning step into a multiple-choice question: the LLM first generates candidate next steps (A-D plus 'E: an option not listed here'), then its next-token probabilities on the option letters are used as scores. Split conformal prediction on a labelled calibration set (N = 400) picks a score threshold so that the prediction set covers the correct option with a user-chosen probability 1-epsilon. If the set has more than one option, the robot asks the human to choose; a sequence-level extension handles multi-step plans.
papers.result: In simulation (target 1-epsilon = 0.85, 200 trials per method) KnowNo had the smallest deviation from the target success rate and reduced human help by up to 24% versus Simple Set. Hardware multi-step tabletop (epsilon = 0.25, 50 trials): task success 0.74, set size 1.72, step help 0.58, trial help 0.92, versus Simple Set 0.72 / 2.04 / 0.72 / 1.00 and No Help success 0.38. Mobile manipulator (epsilon = 0.15): task success 0.76, set size 2.22, help 0.67 versus Simple Set 0.75 / 2.38 / 0.81 and No Help 0.51. Overall help was reduced by 10-24% compared with baselines.
papers.tools: PaLM-2L (main LLM), PaLM-2L instruction-finetuned, GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003); PyBullet simulator; UR5 arm with suction; two Kuka IIWA 7 arms (bimanual); Google mobile manipulator with RT-1 policy; MDETR and Owl-ViT open-vocabulary detectors; Segment Anything; polylabel; Sequential Quadratic Programming for bimanual trajectories.
papers.gap: The guarantee assumes perception and low-level actions are correct and that the human always gives correct help. It does not model perception (vision-language) uncertainty, action failure, or human error, and it needs an i.i.d. calibration set from the deployment distribution.
papers.relation: Uses conformal prediction so an LLM planner asks a human for help when uncertain, the core pattern for calibrated deferral inside an orchestrator.
papers.limitations: Authors state: the task completion guarantee assumes objects are fully grounded in the LLM text input and that proposed actions are executed successfully; the human must faithfully provide help. Low-level action success on the mobile manipulator was only about 86%, which lowered task success below plan success. Ensemble Set needs 20x inference. GPT-3.5 showed a strong MCQA bias toward options D and E. Future work: include perception and policy uncertainty in calibration, model human error, combine with active preference learning, and modify CP to minimise intervention rate directly.
papers.methodologyDetail: KnowNo wraps a frozen LLM planner (PaLM-2L) with conformal prediction to decide when to ask a human. First the authors define a scenario distribution for each task, for example tabletop scenes with three coloured bowls and three blocks and instructions with attribute, numeric or spatial ambiguity. They sample 400 scenarios and, for each, build a text context from the robot's detector output (MDETR or Owl-ViT), the user instruction and few-shot examples. The LLM is prompted to propose four different next steps (A-D) and the option 'E) an option not listed here' is added. The LLM is then asked which option is correct, and the softmax probability of each option letter is taken as the score. A human labels the correct option for each of the 400 calibration scenarios (about 1.5 hours single-step, 4 hours multi-step). The nonconformity score is 1 minus the score of the true option; the threshold q-hat is the ceil((N+1)(1-epsilon))/N quantile, with epsilon adjusted using a Beta inverse CDF so coverage holds with probability 0.99 (delta = 0.01). At test time, all options with score at least 1 - q-hat form the prediction set. One option means the robot acts; more than one means the robot shows the set (or an LLM-written question) to the human, who picks the right one. For multi-step tasks the sequence score is the minimum step score, calibration is done on whole sequences, and the same threshold is applied step by step. Evaluation used 200 simulated trials per method with epsilon = 0.15 or swept from 0.25 to 0.01, and 50 hardware trials on a UR5 arm and a mobile manipulator, with the Simple Set baseline's epsilon tuned to match KnowNo's plan success so that help rate and set size can be compared fairly. For a clinical orchestrator, the same steps apply: replace robot options with candidate diagnoses or plans, collect about 400 clinician-labelled cases for calibration, and route non-singleton sets to the clinician.
papers.studyDesign: Methods and experimental study (Princeton University and Google DeepMind, USA). Simulation plus physical robot experiments; prospective trials on sampled scenario distributions; no human-subject clinical data.
papers.datasets: No public dataset. Each setting has a hand-designed scenario distribution (Section A7) from which i.i.d. scenarios are sampled. (1) Simulation tabletop rearrangement in PyBullet: three bowls and three blocks (green, yellow, blue); three ambiguity types: Attribute, Numeric, Spatial; single-step, one correct option. (2) Hardware multi-step tabletop rearrangement: UR5 arm sorting toy food (28 toy items in total, three on the table per scenario) by a simulated human preference for healthy food; multi-step with multiple acceptable options. (3) Hardware mobile manipulator in an office kitchen: counter, drawers, recycling/compost/landfill bins; ambiguities from Winograd schemas and unsafe actions (e.g. metal bowl in microwave); single-step, multiple acceptable options. (4) Bimanual setup with two Kuka IIWA 7 arms, ambiguity in arm choice; all instructions ambiguous. Calibration set size N = 400 labelled examples per setting; labelling took about 4 hours (multi-step) and 1.5 hours (single-step).
papers.preprocessing: Robot observation converted to text using an object detector (MDETR for hardware tabletop, Owl-ViT for simulation and bimanual) or an oracle. Few-shot prompt produces four semantically different candidate next steps; option 'E) an option not listed here' is appended post hoc. Augmented context = context + generated options. Calibration/test split: N = 400 calibration scenarios; test: 200 trials per method per setting in simulation, 50 hardware trials (tabletop), 10 trials (bimanual). Scenario distributions were modified to avoid placing look-alike items (e.g. peanut butter and meat patty) together because of detector confusion.
papers.modelDetails: Step 1 Multiple-choice generation: few-shot prompt to LLM produces options A-D; E appended. Step 2 Scoring: the LLM is asked which option is correct; normalised next-token probability f(x)_y of each letter is the confidence score (avoids length bias of sentence probability). Step 3 Conformal calibration: nonconformity score kappa_i = 1 - f(x_i)_{y_i} on calibration data; q-hat = ceil((N+1)(1-epsilon))/N empirical quantile; prediction set C(x) = {y : f(x)_y >= 1 - q-hat}. Dataset-conditional guarantee via Beta inverse CDF with N = 400 and delta = 0.01 (coverage holds with probability 0.99 over the calibration draw). Step 4 Deferral rule: if |C(x)| = 1 execute; if |C(x)| > 1 ask the human, who chooses from the set (or halts if the true option is absent); for 'E' the human gives the action. The prediction set is turned into a natural-language question by heuristics or by prompting the LLM. Multi-step: sequence score = minimum over timesteps of f(x_t)_{y_t}; calibrate at sequence level, then apply the same q-hat causally at each step (Claim 1, Proposition 2). Extension to multiple acceptable options in Sections A3-A4. Example in Fig. 1: threshold 0.21, two options above it, so the robot asks.
papers.training: No model training or fine-tuning; LLMs used off the shelf. Calibration only (N = 400, delta = 0.01). Ensemble Set baseline uses 20 randomised few-shot prompts (20x inference). Low-level control: pick-and-place via inverse kinematics (simulation, UR5), SQP (bimanual), RT-1 policy or scripted policies (mobile manipulator). Hardware and training time: Not reported (beyond 4 h / 1.5 h labelling time).
papers.evaluation: Metrics: plan success rate, task success rate, average prediction set size, human help rate (step-wise and trial-wise), and deviation of empirical success from target 1-epsilon. Simulation: epsilon = 0.15 for the deviation study; epsilon swept 0.25 to 0.01 for KnowNo and 0.6 to 0.01 for Simple/Ensemble Set; 200 trials per method. Hardware: epsilon for Simple Set tuned (0.42 tabletop, 0.24 mobile) to match KnowNo's plan success in simulation before running hardware trials, so help and set size can be compared at equal plan success. Ablation (Table A1) compares MCQA scores with sentence-level raw probability and perplexity.
papers.baselines: Simple Set (cumulative thresholding of the same LLM scores), Ensemble Set (frequency over 20 randomised prompts), Prompt Set (LLM directly outputs a prediction set), Binary (LLM outputs Certain/Uncertain, as in Inner Monologue), No Help (always execute top option); ablations CP with RawProb and CP with Perplexity.
papers.results: Simulation (epsilon = 0.15): KnowNo had the least deviation from target; human help reduced by up to 24% versus Simple Set at some success levels in the most ambiguous settings. Table A1 (epsilon = 0.15): Attribute KnowNo set size 1.18, help 0.18 vs RawProb 1.33/0.32, Perplexity 1.35/0.36; Spatial KnowNo 2.23/0.69 vs 2.50/0.82 and 2.67/0.88; Numeric KnowNo 2.17/0.79 vs 4.06/1.00 and 4.06/1.00. Hardware multi-step tabletop (Table 1): KnowNo 1-epsilon 0.75, plan success 0.76, task success 0.74, set size 1.72, help-step 0.58, help-trial 0.92; Simple Set (1-epsilon 0.58) 0.76, 0.72, 2.04, 0.72, 1.00; No Help plan 0.41, task 0.38; Simple Set at epsilon 0.25 needed 87% step-wise help. Mobile manipulation (Table 2): KnowNo PaLM-2L 1-epsilon 0.85, plan 0.87, task 0.76, set size 2.22, help 0.67; Simple Set 0.76, 0.87, 0.75, 2.38, 0.81; No Help plan 0.62, task 0.51; KnowNo PaLM-2L-IF plan 0.86, set 1.86, help 0.67; KnowNo GPT-3.5 plan 0.87, set 2.50, help 0.86. Bimanual (epsilon = 0.15): 84% plan success with 92% help; 9/10 hardware successes with help in 9/10. Low-level action success about 86% in mobile manipulation; pick-and-place failed once in 50 KnowNo trials.
papers.statistics: Formal coverage guarantees from conformal prediction (marginal and dataset-conditional, delta = 0.01). No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals on the empirical comparisons reported.
papers.availability: Code, prompts and videos: https://robot-help.github.io. Scenario data not released as a dataset.

papers.title: Position: Uncertainty Quantification Needs Reassessment for Large-language Model Agents
papers.authors: Kirchhof M, Kasneci G, Kasneci E
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), Position Paper Track, PMLR 267, Vancouver, Canada
papers.aim: To argue that the usual split of uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic parts does not work for interactive, multi-turn LLM agents. It proposes new research directions for handling uncertainty in agent-user interaction.
papers.method: A position paper built on a critical literature review and small worked examples. It shows with toy cases (a two-Dirac Bernoulli belief, a linear model on quadratic data, a chatbot asking follow-up questions) that common definitions conflict. It then proposes three research avenues: underspecification uncertainty, interactive learning, and output uncertainty, and discusses counter-positions.
papers.result: No new experiments. Key cited evidence: aleatoric and epistemic estimators are almost perfectly correlated, with rank correlations of 0.8 to 0.999 across methods (Mucsanyi et al., 2024); ambiguity appears in 56% of Natural Questions test questions (Min et al., 2020); GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k detects ambiguous questions with only 57% accuracy (50% is chance), and humans rate only 53% of its follow-up questions as helpful (Zhang et al., 2024c); about one arXiv preprint per day in 2024 mentions aleatoric or epistemic uncertainty.
papers.tools: Not applicable (conceptual paper; no models trained or run). Figures reuse an ImageNet-1k deep-ensemble result reproduced with permission from Mucsanyi et al. (2024).
papers.gap: No benchmarks, metrics or methods yet exist for underspecification uncertainty, for deciding which and how many follow-up questions an agent should ask, or for faithful text-based uncertainty outputs. No empirical test of the proposed directions is given.
papers.relation: For O1, it supports designing the orchestrator around the task (defer or not) rather than around a strict aleatoric/epistemic label. It argues that when agents talk to other automated systems, calibrated numbers with a threshold are preferable, while to humans uncertainty should be explained in text. This maps well to our design: numeric calibrated confidence passed between agents and used for the deferral threshold, and a short verbal explanation of competing diagnoses shown to the neurosurgeon. Interactive learning also motivates letting the system ask clinicians for missing information instead of guessing.
papers.limitations: Position paper only: no empirical validation, no domain (e.g. medical) case study, and arguments rely on cited studies and toy examples. Future work named by the authors: research on task- and context-underspecification uncertainty; interactive learning that decides which follow-up questions to ask and when to stop; output uncertainties that list possibilities, explain why, and faithfully reflect internal beliefs; benchmarks and metrics beyond scalar uncertainty (e.g. SelfReflect); datasets for under-represented user groups.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a position paper, so its 'method' is argument rather than experiment. The authors start by listing the main schools of thought on aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in a table. They then test these definitions against three small examples. In the first, a binary classifier's belief is split between theta = 0 and theta = 1. The disagreement view (mutual information) calls this maximum epistemic uncertainty. The axiomatic view of Wimmer et al. calls it near-zero, because only two models remain. The density view says it depends on how much training data lies near x. In the second example, a linear model is fitted to quadratic data on x in [-1, 3]. The leftover model bias counts as aleatoric if aleatoric means 'irreducible within the model class', but as epistemic if a richer model class could remove it. Third, they review additive decompositions such as total entropy = expected entropy + mutual information. They cite evidence that the two parts are almost perfectly correlated in practice (rank correlation 0.8-0.999 on ImageNet-1k ensembles). They then move to chatbots. A conversation x_t grows over time, so an uncertainty that looks irreducible at turn t can become reducible once the agent asks a follow-up question. The label is therefore a subjective modelling choice. From this they propose three research directions. (a) Underspecification uncertainty, both about the task, P(y|x) = integral of P(y|t)P(t|x), and about missing context. (b) Interactive learning: choose follow-up questions, perhaps by expected mutual-information reduction, without asking too many. (c) Output uncertainty: explain the competing answers and why, and do not give only a number. In a counter-position section they agree that numeric calibrated scores remain best for machine-to-machine settings and for threshold-based abstention. For a clinical multi-agent system, the practical recipe is to define uncertainty by its downstream use (deferral), to combine several estimators with veto power, to pass numbers between agents, and to give clinicians a text explanation.
papers.studyDesign: Position paper with narrative literature review and illustrative theoretical examples. Authors at University of Tuebingen (now Apple) and Technical University of Munich, Germany. No data collection; not prospective or retrospective.
papers.datasets: Not applicable. No dataset is used by the authors. Datasets only mentioned through cited work: Natural Questions (56% ambiguous questions), ImageNet-1k (deep ensemble correlation figure).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable as a method. The conceptual framework is: (1) Table 1 lists seven schools of thought, e.g. epistemic as number of possible models, as disagreement (mutual information), as low training density, or as leftover uncertainty; aleatoric as Bayes-optimal risk, as pointwise ground-truth variance, or as practitioner labels. (2) Example 1: a learner whose belief Q(theta) is two Diracs at theta = 0 and theta = 1 is maximal epistemic under the disagreement view but near-zero under the axiomatic view. (3) Example 2: a linear model on quadratic data with x in [-1, 3]; model bias is aleatoric for Bayes-optimality proponents but epistemic for data-uncertainty proponents. (4) Decomposition H(y|x) = E_Q[H(y|theta,x)] + I(y;theta) (Depeweg et al., 2018) is shown not to separate in practice. (5) In chat, uncertainty moves between aleatoric and epistemic as the conversation x_t grows. (6) Task underspecification is written as P(y|x) = integral over tasks t of P(y|t) P(t|x) dt. (7) Practical advice: for abstention, combine several estimators, each with a veto, and use numeric thresholds for machine-to-machine settings.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable (no experiments). The authors recommend future metrics similar to conformal prediction: output possibility sets that are as small as possible but large enough to cover all likely answers.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: No quantitative results of its own. Cited numbers: rank correlation between aleatoric and epistemic estimates 0.8-0.999 (Mucsanyi et al., 2024); 56% of Natural Questions are ambiguous; 57% accuracy of GPT-3.5-Turbo-16k at detecting ambiguity versus 50% chance; 53% of follow-up questions rated helpful; roughly one arXiv paper per day in 2024 using the terms aleatoric or epistemic.
papers.availability: Not available (no code or data; paper is open on arXiv under CC BY 4.0).

papers.title: Uncertainty Quantification and Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.authors: Liu X, Chen T, Da L, Chen C, Lin Z, Wei H
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD '25), Toronto, Canada
papers.aim: To review uncertainty quantification (UQ) and confidence calibration methods for LLMs. It organises them in a new taxonomy by uncertainty dimension and computational cost, and lists benchmarks, metrics, applications and open problems.
papers.method: A narrative survey. It defines four uncertainty dimensions (input, reasoning, parameter, prediction) and separates uncertainty U(x) from confidence C(x, s). It then classifies about 35 methods by dimension, efficiency (single round, multiple rounds, multiple rounds plus external model, fine-tuning) and model access (white-box or black-box), and summarises benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics.
papers.result: No new experiments. Main output is Table 2 (method taxonomy) and Table 3 (benchmarks). Cited numbers: over 30% of answers in medical QA contain factual errors; uncertainty-aware flagging could reduce diagnostic errors by up to 41%; multi-sample UQ costs about $12k per million queries for very large LLMs for at most 0.02 AUROC gain; action-feasibility checks raised robot planning success from about 70% to 80%; LVLMs show 2.4 times higher uncertainty in visual than textual parts, causing 63% of errors in multimodal QA.
papers.tools: Not applicable (survey). Methods reviewed include perplexity, maximum token log-probability, entropy, P(True), SAR, predictive entropy, semantic entropy (NLI-based clustering), kernel language entropy, spectral graph measures (Ecc, Eig, Deg), conformal prediction variants (ConU, LoFreeCP, level-adaptive CP, conformal language modelling), LoRA ensembles, BLoB, BLoRA, SAPLMA, UaIT, CoT-UQ, TouT, TopologyUQ, SPUQ, and LM-Polygraph.
papers.gap: Few methods handle input (ambiguity) uncertainty. Most UQ works on a single output and cannot track uncertainty across multi-step reasoning chains or multi-agent plans. Cross-modal (image plus text) uncertainty is poorly aligned. Evaluation metrics (AUROC, AUARC) do not separate confidently wrong answers from appropriately uncertain ones. Multi-sample methods are costly.
papers.relation: For O1, this survey is the menu of confidence estimators each agent in our orchestrator can use before passing its confidence on. Black-box options (sampling consistency, semantic entropy, conformal prediction such as LoFreeCP and ConU) suit API LLM agents, while white-box ones (token entropy, P(True), LoRA ensembles) suit locally hosted models, which matters for privacy in Sri Lanka. Its 'system-level uncertainty in agents' challenge names the exact gap our PhD addresses: propagating uncertainty across agent hand-offs. Its cross-modality point applies to fusing MRI and report agents.
papers.limitations: Narrative survey; search strategy, inclusion criteria and number of screened papers are not reported. No empirical comparison of methods. Healthcare coverage is short (three cited works). Future directions named: hybrid low-cost UQ that triggers multi-sampling only for high-risk outputs such as medical diagnoses; modular, interpretable uncertainty sources; unified cross-modal uncertainty embeddings; temporally aware uncertainty tracking for agents with structured memory or graph-based tracing; better UQ evaluation beyond binary correctness and LLM-as-a-judge.
papers.methodologyDetail: The survey first separates two ideas. Uncertainty U(x) is a property of the whole predictive distribution for an input, for example its entropy. Confidence C(x, s) is belief in one specific output s, usually the sequence likelihood, which is the product of token probabilities. It then defines calibration as matching confidence to expected correctness, E[f(s|x) | C = c] = c, and ranking performance as separating right from wrong answers (AUROC, AUARC). Next it proposes four dimensions: input (ambiguous prompt), reasoning (multi-step chains), parameter (missing knowledge) and prediction (sampling variation). Each method in Table 2 is labelled by dimension, by cost (single generation, multiple generations, multiple generations plus an extra model such as NLI, or fine-tuning), by access (white-box logits or black-box API) and by whether it gives a confidence score. Section 3 explains each family with its formula. Single-pass scores include perplexity, maximum negative token log-probability and mean or maximum token entropy. Sampling scores include predictive entropy over many outputs, Jaccard consistency and conformal prediction with coverage guarantees. Semantic scores cluster sampled answers by NLI entailment and compute entropy over meanings (semantic entropy) or over a kernel (KLE), or use spectral measures of a similarity graph. Parameter methods add Bayesian or ensemble LoRA adapters. Section 4 lists benchmarks by type and describes the standard protocol: label each answer correct or not with a judge, then measure how well the uncertainty predicts that label. Sections 5-6 cover robotics, transportation and healthcare uses and open problems. For a clinical multi-agent system, a student can follow the survey's map in four steps. First choose the estimator per agent by access type: black-box conformal or semantic-entropy methods for API agents, token entropy or LoRA ensembles for local models. Then calibrate each estimator. Then judge it with AUROC, AUARC and ECE on a labelled validation set. Finally, add a cross-step tracker, which the survey names as an open problem.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative literature survey with a proposed taxonomy. Authors from Arizona State University, University of Chicago and University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA. No data collection.
papers.datasets: No datasets used by the authors. Benchmarks reviewed (Table 3): reading comprehension - TriviaQA, CoQA, RACE, CosmosQA, SQuAD, HotpotQA; reasoning and maths - StrategyQA, HotpotQA, GSM8K, CalibratedMath; factuality - TruthfulQA, FEVER, HaluEval, FActScore; general knowledge - MMLU, GPQA, HellaSwag; consistency and ambiguity - ParaRel (328 paraphrases for 38 relations), AmbigQA, AmbigInst, Abg-SciQA. UQ-specific: MAQA (epistemic), LM-Polygraph, and a conformal prediction benchmark.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Taxonomy. Dimensions: input uncertainty (aleatoric; ambiguous prompts), reasoning uncertainty (mixed; multi-step or retrieval), parameter uncertainty (epistemic; knowledge gaps), prediction uncertainty (mixed; variation across samples). Confidence of a generation: C(x, s) = product over i of p(s_i | s_<i, x) (sequence likelihood); uncertainty U(x) is input-level, e.g. entropy. Calibration is perfect when E[f(s|x) | C(x,s) = c] = c for all c, where f is a correctness function. Single-round methods: perplexity = exp(-(1/N) sum ln p(w_i)); Max(p) = max_i(-ln p(w_i)); token entropy H_i = -sum p_i(w) log p_i(w), with Avg(H) or Max(H); P(True) self-evaluation. Multi-round methods: predictive entropy over samples, SAR, conformal prediction (black-box via frequency, normalised entropy and semantic similarity as nonconformity scores; white-box via logits; conditional CP adapts coverage to input difficulty), Jaccard-based consistency. Multi-round with external model: semantic entropy (NLI clusters, entropy over clusters), kernel language entropy (von Neumann entropy over a semantic kernel), NLI similarity graphs with eccentricity, eigenvalue and degree measures. Parameter UQ: Bayesian LoRA (BLoB, BLoRA), LoRA ensembles, supervised confidence probes, uncertainty-aware instruction tuning. Reasoning UQ: CoT-UQ, TouT (Monte Carlo dropout on Tree-of-Thought steps), TopologyUQ (graph-edit distance over explanation graphs).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Reviewed protocols: UQ is usually evaluated as binary classification of correct versus incorrect answers using a correctness function (LLM-as-a-judge, human labels, or ROUGE/BLEU). Metrics: AUROC (separation of correct and incorrect), AUPRC, AUARC (accuracy-rejection curve, for selective answering), and ECE variants for calibration. Other: aleatoric-only checks with AmbigQA; comparing model variability with human variability; FActScore for long-form generation.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: No quantitative results of its own. Cited values: >30% factual errors in medical QA answers; up to 41% fewer diagnostic errors when uncertain cases are flagged for specialist review; $12k per million queries for multi-sample UQ with at most 0.02 AUROC gain; hybrid proxies could reach 90% of best performance at 10% cost; robot planning success about 70% to 80% with feasibility checks; 2.4x higher visual uncertainty in LVLMs and 63% of multimodal QA errors.
papers.availability: Not available (no code or data released with the survey; preprint free on arXiv).

papers.title: Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Generation
papers.authors: Kuhn L, Gal Y, Farquhar S
papers.aim: To measure the uncertainty of large language model (LLM) answers in free text. The paper treats sentences that mean the same thing as one answer, so uncertainty is measured over meanings, not over exact words.
papers.method: The model samples several answers to the same question. A natural language inference (NLI) model groups answers that entail each other in both directions into meaning clusters. The entropy over these clusters (semantic entropy) is used as the uncertainty score and tested on how well it predicts whether an answer is correct (AUROC).
papers.result: Semantic entropy predicted answer correctness better than all baselines. With OPT-30B on TriviaQA, AUROC was 0.828 for semantic entropy versus 0.802 for length-normalised entropy; on CoQA it was 0.767 versus 0.753. Question-answering accuracy was 50.6% on TriviaQA and 82.3% on CoQA. Wrong answers had more distinct meaning clusters (CoQA 1.77 vs 1.27; TriviaQA 3.89 vs 1.89). The bidirectional entailment clustering was 92.7% (TriviaQA) and 95.3% (CoQA, 95.5% in the main text) accurate against human labels. Best sampling temperature was 0.5.
papers.tools: OPT models (2.7B, 6.7B, 13B, 30B; 1.3B in one ablation) via HuggingFace transformers; DeBERTa-large fine-tuned on MNLI for entailment; Rouge-L for correctness; 80GB NVIDIA A100 GPUs; code at github.com/lorenzkuhn/semantic_uncertainty (MIT licence).
papers.gap: Tested only on short-answer question answering with general-knowledge data. Not tested on long text such as summaries or reports, on medical data, or on how the score should be used to trigger human review.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), semantic entropy gives an unsupervised uncertainty signal for free-text agent outputs (for example, a radiology report draft or a surgical-planning note). The orchestrator could sample several outputs from an agent, cluster them by meaning, and defer to a clinician when semantic entropy is above a calibrated threshold. It needs only sampling access and a small NLI model, which suits a low-resource Sri Lankan setting, but a clinical NLI model and a long-text version would be needed.
papers.limitations: Only question answering with short reference answers was studied. Semantic clustering fails at high temperature (accuracy only 61% at T=1.5) and semantic entropy then falls below length-normalised entropy on CoQA. The method still gives too much weight to unimportant tokens. It does not protect against a model that is deceptive. It needs M samples per input (extra compute). Future work: summarisation and other long outputs, better paraphrase detection, and extending semantic likelihoods to other measures such as mutual information.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors start from the idea that a free-text answer has many surface forms with the same meaning, so normal token-level entropy overstates uncertainty. They use two public English question-answering datasets: about 8,000 CoQA development questions (open-book, with a context paragraph and earlier conversation turns, zero-shot prompt) and 8,000 TriviaQA training questions (closed-book, 10-shot Q:/A: prompt). They use unmodified OPT models of 2.7B, 6.7B, 13B and 30B parameters on 80GB A100 GPUs, with no fine-tuning, ensembling or Bayesian changes. For each question they first produce one 'best' answer with beam search (5 beams) and mark it correct if its Rouge-L with the reference is above 0.3; a human check of 200 answers per dataset showed this rule agreed with people 89% (CoQA) and 96% (TriviaQA) of the time. They then draw M = 10 answers by multinomial sampling at temperature 0.5, cutting text at stop-words such as 'Q:'. Next they cluster the 10 answers by meaning: each pair (question + answer) is passed in both orders to DeBERTa-large fine-tuned on MNLI, and two answers join the same cluster only if both directions are 'entailment'. Each new answer is compared to one member per cluster. Manual labelling of 300 pairs per dataset showed 92.7% and 95.3% clustering accuracy. They sum the sequence probabilities inside each cluster to get a meaning probability and compute semantic entropy as the average negative log of these cluster probabilities. Finally, they rank all questions by this score and compute AUROC for separating correct from wrong answers, comparing with predictive entropy, length-normalised entropy, p(True), lexical similarity and margin probability. With OPT-30B, semantic entropy reached AUROC 0.828 on TriviaQA (vs 0.802) and 0.767 on CoQA (vs 0.753). Ablations over temperature, sample count, sampling method, model size and correctness rule show the gains hold, with 0.5 temperature and about 10 samples being enough. To adapt this, a PhD student could replace the QA tasks with agent report outputs, use a clinical NLI model, and choose a deferral threshold on a labelled calibration set.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological machine-learning study with retrospective experiments on public benchmark datasets. University of Oxford (OATML group, Department of Computer Science), United Kingdom. No human participants except author-made manual labels.
papers.datasets: 1) CoQA (open-book conversational question answering; model answers using a supporting paragraph): development split, about 8,000 questions. 2) TriviaQA (closed-book question answering): a subset of 8,000 questions from the training split, chosen to match CoQA size. Modality: English text. No classes; each question has a reference answer. Extra human-labelled sets: 200 answers per dataset from the 30B model to check the correctness metric; 300 generations per dataset from the 13B model labelled for semantic equivalence; 100 classifications at T=1.5 inspected. No other inclusion or exclusion criteria reported.
papers.preprocessing: No model training, so no train/validation/test split; models are used pre-trained and unmodified. Prompts: CoQA uses zero-shot prompting with the context paragraph, the previous question-answer turns of the conversation, then 'Q: [question] A:'. TriviaQA uses a 10-shot prompt of Q:/A: pairs. Generations are trimmed at stop-words 'Q:', 'Question:', 'QUESTION:' and 'questions:'. Optional length-normalisation of log-probabilities (divide joint log-probability by sequence length). No augmentation.
papers.modelDetails: Step 1 Generation: sample M answers from one LLM given context x using multinomial sampling (generate() with do_sample=True, num_beams=1); default M=10, temperature 0.5. The answer checked for correctness is produced by beam search (num_beams=5, do_sample=True). Step 2 Clustering: bidirectional entailment. For each pair of answers, the question plus answer A and question plus answer B are concatenated and given to DeBERTa-large fine-tuned on MNLI, which outputs entailment, neutral or contradiction. Two answers are in the same meaning class only if entailment holds in both directions. Because equivalence is transitive, each new answer is compared only to one member of each existing class (Algorithm 1); worst case M(M-1)/2 comparisons. Step 3 Entropy: the probability of a meaning class is the sum of the sequence probabilities p(s|x) of its members; semantic entropy SE(x) = -sum over classes of p(c|x) log p(c|x), estimated by Monte Carlo as SE(x) approx -(1/|C|) sum log p(C_i|x). Higher SE means higher uncertainty. No deferral threshold is set; the score is evaluated as a ranking.
papers.training: No training or fine-tuning of the LLM. DeBERTa-large MNLI model used off the shelf. Hardware: 80GB NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Sampling ablations: temperatures 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5; up to 20 samples per question tested on 2.7B, 6.7B and 13B CoQA runs; more than 10 samples gave no significant gain. Training time not reported.
papers.evaluation: Uncertainty is evaluated as predicting whether to trust an answer. Correctness label: answer is correct if Rouge-L with the reference answer is above 0.3. Metric: AUROC of the uncertainty score for separating correct from incorrect answers (1 = perfect, 0.5 = random). Brier score and calibration were not used because probabilities over meanings are not available. Robustness: other correctness criteria (Rouge-L > 0.5, Rouge-1 > 0.3 or > 0.5, exact match). Human check of the Rouge-L rule on 200 answers per dataset. Ablations: model size (1.3B to 30B), number of samples, temperature, multinomial versus beam sampling. No cross-validation or external clinical validation.
papers.baselines: Predictive entropy; length-normalised predictive entropy (single-model version of Malinin and Gales 2020); p(True) (Kadavath et al. 2022, 10-shot prompt with OPT instead of 20-shot with a 52B model); lexical similarity (average pairwise Rouge-L of sampled answers); margin probability (Lin et al. 2022b, appendix); number of distinct semantic clusters.
papers.results: OPT-30B, TriviaQA (Rouge-L > 0.3): semantic entropy AUROC = 0.828, normalised entropy = 0.802, accuracy = 0.506. Rouge-L > 0.5: 0.835 vs 0.810 (accuracy 0.456); Rouge-1 > 0.5: 0.835 vs 0.810 (accuracy 0.457); exact match: 0.828 vs 0.808 (accuracy 0.394). CoQA (Rouge-L > 0.3): semantic entropy = 0.7672, normalised entropy = 0.7533, accuracy = 0.8239; Rouge-L > 0.5: 0.7379 vs 0.7290; Rouge-1 > 0.5: 0.7397 vs 0.7309; exact match: 0.6749 vs 0.6727. Number of distinct answers as uncertainty: AUROC 0.66 (CoQA) and 0.79 (TriviaQA), versus semantic entropy 0.77 and 0.83. Mean distinct meaning clusters, correct vs incorrect: CoQA 1.27 vs 1.77, TriviaQA 1.89 vs 3.89. Sampling: multinomial sampling SE AUROC 0.758 (diversity 0.490) vs multinomial beam sampling 0.735 (diversity 0.258). Margin probability on CoQA with 13B: AUROC 0.54. Accuracy of automatic correctness labels vs human: CoQA 0.89, TriviaQA 0.96. Entailment clustering accuracy: 92.7% TriviaQA, 95.3% CoQA; 61% at T=1.5. Best temperature 0.5. p(True) was much worse than all entropy methods (exact values only in figures). The gap over baselines grew with model size and number of samples.
papers.statistics: Not reported (no formal statistical tests, p-values or confidence intervals; differences described from AUROC values and figures).
papers.availability: Code and hand-labelled semantic equivalence data: https://github.com/lorenzkuhn/semantic_uncertainty (MIT licence). Models: public OPT and DeBERTa-large MNLI on HuggingFace. Datasets: public CoQA and TriviaQA.

papers.title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
papers.authors: Farquhar S, Kossen J, Kuhn L, Gal Y
papers.aim: To detect 'confabulations', a type of LLM hallucination where the model gives wrong and arbitrary answers, using an unsupervised uncertainty score computed over meanings. The score is also used to refuse to answer risky questions and so raise accuracy.
papers.method: For each question, the LLM samples 10 answers, which are clustered by bidirectional entailment (GPT-3.5 or DeBERTa-large-MNLI), and semantic entropy is computed over the clusters. A 'discrete' version uses only cluster counts, so it works with black-box models. For long text (biographies), the paragraph is split into factual claims, questions are generated for each claim, and semantic entropy is averaged over the answers.
papers.result: Averaged over 30 task-model combinations (5 datasets x 6 LLMs), semantic entropy had AUROC 0.790, versus naive entropy 0.691, P(True) 0.698 and supervised embedding regression 0.687. Performance was stable (AUROC 0.78-0.81) across LLaMA 2, Falcon and Mistral from 7B to 70B. On GPT-4 biographies (150 claims, 45 incorrect), discrete semantic entropy had higher AUROC and AURAC than P(True) and self-check baselines; P(True) only did better after more than 20% of claims were rejected.
papers.tools: LLMs: LLaMA 2 Chat (7B, 13B, 70B), Falcon Instruct (7B, 40B), Mistral Instruct (7B), GPT-4 (v.0613) for biographies; entailment: GPT-3.5 (Turbo 1106) with a prompt (main choice) or DeBERTa-large fine-tuned on MNLI (1.5B parameters, used for paragraphs); GPT-4 as automatic correctness judge; logistic regression for the embedding regression baseline. Hardware not reported in the main text.
papers.gap: Does not detect errors where the model is consistently wrong (learned misconceptions, systematic reasoning errors, deception). Long-text version relies on fragile question generation. No clinical or imaging deployment, no study of how users act on the score, and no calibrated threshold for deferral is set.
papers.relation: For O1, this paper is direct evidence that an uncertainty score can drive refusal (deferral): rejecting high-entropy questions raises the accuracy of the remaining answers (AURAC). The orchestrator in the brain-tumour system can use discrete semantic entropy on each LLM agent's output (also for API models with no token probabilities) and route high-entropy outputs to a neuroradiologist or neurosurgeon. The factoid decomposition method can be adapted to check long agent reports claim by claim. It is tested on the biomedical BioASQ set, but not on clinical reports, so local validation in Sri Lanka is still needed.
papers.limitations: Only detects confabulations (arbitrary errors), not systematic errors. Clustering can be too strict in context (for example, an exact date versus only the year treated as different meanings). Evaluation uses fixed reference answers that do not match open conversation. The paragraph method depends on generated questions that sometimes miss aspects of a claim. Needs several samples per input (extra cost). Results are averages without standard errors. Future work: abstractive summarisation, other input variations (rephrasing, counterfactuals), and measures that separate aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors build on their ICLR 2023 semantic entropy idea and test it at scale on modern instruction-tuned LLMs. They take five public free-form QA datasets (BioASQ 2023 Task B, SQuAD 1.1, TriviaQA, SVAMP and NQ-Open) and randomly draw 400 training and 400 test questions from each. They remove context passages so that models must answer from memory, which makes errors more common. Six LLMs are used: LLaMA 2 Chat 7B, 13B and 70B, Falcon Instruct 7B and 40B, and Mistral Instruct 7B. Each question is asked with a one-sentence answer prompt. The model gives one low-temperature (0.1) answer, which GPT-4 marks correct or wrong against the reference, and ten sampled answers (temperature 1, nucleus p = 0.9, top-K = 50) with their token probabilities. The ten answers are clustered: GPT-3.5 Turbo is asked whether answer 1 entails answer 2 and vice versa, and answers that entail each other in both directions join one cluster. Cluster probabilities are the normalised sums of member sequence probabilities, and semantic entropy is the entropy of this cluster distribution. A discrete version uses only the share of answers in each cluster. The score is evaluated with AUROC for flagging wrong answers and with rejection accuracy and AURAC when the most uncertain questions are refused. Over 30 dataset-model pairs, semantic entropy reached AUROC 0.790 versus 0.691 to 0.698 for the baselines, and it stayed better when the supervised baseline faced distribution shift. For long text, GPT-4 wrote biographies of 21 WikiBio people; these were split into 150 claims (45 false, labelled by hand). For each claim six questions were generated, three new answers drawn per question, and discrete semantic entropy computed over the answers plus the claim with DeBERTa entailment, then averaged per claim. This beat P(True) and self-check. A PhD student could reuse this pipeline to score each agent output, set a rejection rate or threshold on a local validation set, and send the most uncertain cases to clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological machine-learning study with retrospective experiments on public question-answering datasets plus a new author-labelled dataset (FactualBio). University of Oxford (OATML group, Department of Computer Science), United Kingdom. No patients involved.
papers.datasets: Sentence-length experiments, 5 public free-form datasets, each with 400 train and 400 test examples randomly sampled from the original split: 1) BioASQ (life-sciences QA, Task B of the 2023 challenge, 11B); 2) SQuAD 1.1 (reading comprehension from Wikipedia; v2.0 unanswerable questions excluded); 3) TriviaQA (trivia QA); 4) SVAMP (elementary-school maths word problems); 5) NQ-Open (real Google Search questions). Context passages were not given to the model, to make questions harder. Paragraph experiments: FactualBio, GPT-4 (v.0613) biographies of 21 individuals randomly sampled from WikiBio, decomposed into 150 factual claims, manually labelled; 45 incorrect and 105 correct. Modality: English text. Semantic entropy itself uses no training data; the train split is only used for supervised baselines and few-shot prompts.
papers.preprocessing: Split: 400 train / 400 test examples per dataset (sampled inside the original train/test split where one existed). Prompt for sentence-length answers: 'Answer the following question in a single brief but complete sentence. Question: {question} Answer:'. A short-phrase variant (answers as short as possible) is reported in the supplement. For FactualBio: paragraph decomposed into factual claims with a GPT-4 prompt; six questions per claim (prompt run twice, three questions each); short answers requested. No augmentation or normalisation.
papers.modelDetails: Step 1: Given input x, sample M = 10 answers from one LLM, varying only the random seed, at temperature 1 with nucleus sampling (p = 0.9) and top-K (K = 50), and record token probabilities. One extra answer at temperature 0.1 is the 'best answer' whose correctness is judged. Step 2: Cluster answers by bidirectional entailment. Two answers share a meaning if each entails the other in the context of the question. Main entailment model: GPT-3.5 Turbo 1106 with the prompt 'Does Possible Answer 1 semantically entail Possible Answer 2? Respond with entailment, contradiction, or neutral.' Alternative: DeBERTa-large-MNLI on question+answer pairs. A new answer is compared with the first member of each cluster; if none match it starts a new cluster. Step 3: Semantic entropy. Cluster probability = sum of the sequence probabilities of its members, normalised so that cluster probabilities sum to 1 (Rao-Blackwellised Monte Carlo estimate); SE(x) = -sum P(Ci|x) log P(Ci|x). Discrete semantic entropy: P(Ci|x) = fraction of the M answers in cluster i (no token probabilities needed). Paragraph version: (1) decompose paragraph into factual claims; (2) generate Q = 6 questions per claim; (3) generate 3 new answers per question with the original LLM; (4) compute discrete semantic entropy over the 3 answers plus the original claim; (5) average over the 6 questions to score the claim. For paragraphs, DeBERTa with a 'non-defeating' rule is used: same meaning if at least one entails the other and neither contradicts. If more than half the answers contain 'not available', 'not provided', 'unknown' or 'unclear', uncertainty is set to maximal. Rejection rule: refuse to answer the X% of inputs with highest entropy; no single fixed threshold is set.
papers.training: Semantic entropy needs no training or fine-tuning. Embedding regression baseline: logistic regression trained on the final hidden state of the LLM using the 400 training examples. P(True) baseline: up to 20 few-shot examples from the training set (fewer when the context window was too small). Number of samples (10 for sentence-length; 3 per question for paragraphs) chosen by supplementary analysis. Optimizer, hardware and run time not reported in the main text.
papers.evaluation: Correctness of the low-temperature answer for sentence-length outputs judged by GPT-4 against the reference answer with a yes/no prompt (checked against human judgement in Supplementary Note 6; short-phrase setting uses SQuAD F1 > 0.5). Metrics: AUROC for predicting that an answer is incorrect; rejection accuracy at X% (accuracy on the most-confident X% of inputs); AURAC (area under the rejection accuracy curve over all cut-offs). Results averaged over 5 held-out test sets for each of 6 models (30 combinations). Out-of-distribution test for embedding regression: trained on one of the four other datasets. FactualBio: AUROC, AURAC and rejection accuracy at 80%, 90%, 95% and 100% on 150 manually labelled claims. No cross-validation and no external clinical validation.
papers.baselines: Naive entropy (length-normalised predictive entropy of token sequences); P(True) (Kadavath et al. 2022, few-shot, up to 20 examples); embedding regression (supervised logistic regression on final hidden state, in-distribution and out-of-distribution); for biographies, an adapted P(True) (prompt run 10 times at temperature 1, fraction of 'yes') and a self-check baseline (asking the model if the claim is likely true).
papers.results: Sentence-length, average over 30 dataset-model combinations: AUROC semantic entropy = 0.790, naive entropy = 0.691, P(True) = 0.698, embedding regression = 0.687. Semantic entropy AUROC range across models = 0.78 to 0.81. Discrete semantic entropy performed similarly to the standard estimator (exact values in figures). Semantic entropy also had higher AURAC than all baselines for all six models (values shown in Fig. 2; per-dataset numbers in the Supplementary Information). Embedding regression dropped when trained on a different dataset (OOD). P(True) improved with model size. FactualBio (GPT-4, 150 claims, 45 false): discrete semantic entropy had higher AUROC and AURAC than P(True) variant and self-check (exact values only in Fig. 3); highest rejection accuracy when 80% or more of claims are answered; P(True) slightly better only when the top 20% are rejected.
papers.statistics: No statistical tests or p-values. The authors report raw averages across held-out datasets without standard errors, arguing that consistency across datasets is a better indicator of variation. Agreement of GPT-4 correctness labels and entailment predictions with human raters is reported in the Supplementary Notes.
papers.availability: Code: github.com/jlko/semantic_uncertainty (short-phrase and sentence-length) and github.com/jlko/long_hallucinations (paragraphs); archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10964366. Data: public datasets accessed through the code; FactualBio released with the code base.

papers.title: Generating with Confidence: Uncertainty Quantification for Black-box Large Language Models
papers.authors: Lin Z, Trivedi S, Sun J
papers.venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), May 2024; arXiv:2305.19187 (first posted 2023)
papers.aim: To measure the uncertainty and confidence of black-box LLM answers, where only the generated text is available (no token probabilities or embeddings). The measures are used for selective generation, where unreliable answers are rejected or sent for further checking.
papers.method: For each question, m answers are sampled from the LLM and pairwise similarity is computed with Jaccard similarity or an NLI model (DeBERTa-large-MNLI). A similarity graph is built and simple dispersion measures are computed: number of semantic sets, sum of graph Laplacian eigenvalues (EigV), degree (Deg) and eccentricity (Ecc). They are tested on how well they rank answers by correctness (AUROC and AUARC) on three QA datasets with four LLMs.
papers.result: Entailment-based measures beat the black-box baselines and often beat the white-box semantic entropy. Example (TriviaQA, LLaMA-13B): confidence AUARC Deg(E) = 88.86 versus semantic entropy 79.15, P(true) 67.27, random 61.18 and oracle 91.24. Selecting the top 50% of answers by Deg(E) raised accuracy from 62% to about 90%. Even m = 3 samples gave good results. After histogram-binning calibration, adaptive calibration error was about 0.02-0.04 (e.g. Ecc(E) on TriviaQA-LLaMA gap 0.026).
papers.tools: LLMs: OPT-13B, LLaMA-13B, LLaMA2 (model size not stated in the main text), gpt-3.5-turbo (0301, via OpenAI API). Similarity: Jaccard; DeBERTa-large-MNLI (microsoft/deberta-large-mnli). Spectral graph methods (graph Laplacian, eigenvectors); UMAP for visualisation; histogram binning for calibration. gpt-3.5-turbo as correctness judge. Hardware: 2x AMD EPYC Milan 7513 CPU, 512 GB RAM, 8x NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Code: github.com/zlin7/UQ-NLG.
papers.gap: Only short-answer question answering was tested. Correctness labels come mostly from GPT, not humans. Uncertainty and confidence are evaluated separately, not combined. No medical or multi-step agent setting, and no formal guarantee on error rates when answers are rejected.
papers.relation: For O1, the orchestrator may use API-based LLM agents (for example, a report-drafting or guideline agent) that give no token probabilities. These black-box measures need only several sampled outputs and a small NLI model, so the orchestrator can score each agent output and defer to clinicians when confidence is low. The per-response confidence (Deg, Ecc) can also pick the best of several agent drafts, and the paper shows that these scores can be calibrated with histogram binning on a 1,000-item calibration set, which supports calibrated deferral thresholds in the PhD framework.
papers.limitations: Evaluation is restricted to QA because reliability labels are hard to get for open conversation. GPT judging improves on Rouge-L but is not perfect (90.9% to 98.0% agreement with humans) and may use its own knowledge. With temperature 0 (greedy decoding) all sampling-based measures fail; at lower temperature (0.5) white-box semantic entropy often does better. The measures reflect the LLM's own posterior, so they cannot catch factual errors learned from training data or overconfidence. Confidence scores are not directly interpretable without calibration. Future work: combine uncertainty and confidence, use human labels, and extend beyond QA.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors want uncertainty scores that work when an LLM is only reachable through an API. They separate uncertainty U(x), which describes how spread out the possible answers to an input are, from confidence C(x, s), which describes one specific answer. They use three public QA datasets: CoQA development (7,983 questions), TriviaQA rc.nocontext validation (9,960) and Natural Questions validation (3,610). Four LLMs are tested: OPT-13B, LLaMA-13B, LLaMA2 and gpt-3.5-turbo, with default sampling settings (temperature 1, or 0.6 with top_p 0.9 for LLaMA2). For each question they sample 20 answers. Every pair of answers is scored for similarity with Jaccard overlap or with DeBERTa-large-MNLI, giving either the entailment probability or one minus the contradiction probability. These scores form a weighted graph with one node per answer. From the graph they compute: the number of semantic sets; EigV, the sum of max(0, 1 - eigenvalue) of the normalised Laplacian, which estimates the number of meanings; Deg, based on how connected each answer is; and Ecc, the distance of each answer from the centre in a spectral embedding. Deg and Ecc also give a confidence per answer. Correctness is judged by gpt-3.5-turbo on a 0-100 scale against the reference (above 70 = correct), with human checks showing 90.9-98.0% agreement. Each experiment is repeated 10 times: 1,000 random questions tune the NLI temperature and eigenvalue cut-off, and the rest are used for testing. They report AUROC and AUARC (mean +/- SD) and adaptive calibration error after 15-bin histogram binning. Entailment-based Deg and Ecc gave the best results, for example AUARC 88.86 versus 79.15 for white-box semantic entropy on TriviaQA-LLaMA, and keeping the top 50% raised accuracy from 62% to about 90%. To adapt this, an orchestrator can sample each agent several times, score agreement with a clinical NLI model, calibrate the confidence on a local labelled set, and defer low-confidence cases to clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological machine-learning study with retrospective experiments on public QA benchmarks. University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (including Carle Illinois College of Medicine) and MIT CSAIL, United States. No patients involved.
papers.datasets: 1) CoQA (open-book conversational QA): development split, 7,983 questions. 2) TriviaQA (closed-book QA): validation split of the rc.nocontext subset, 9,960 de-duplicated questions. 3) Natural Questions (nq, harder closed-book QA): validation split, 3,610 questions. Modality: English text. No classes; each question has a reference answer. Human verification set: 33 samples per dataset and model (OPT, LLaMA, GPT), e.g. 99 pairs for TriviaQA. No other inclusion or exclusion criteria reported.
papers.preprocessing: Split: each experiment repeated 10 times; each time a random subset of 1,000 questions is the calibration set (for choosing hyper-parameters of the uncertainty and confidence measures) and the rest is the test set. Prompts: TriviaQA uses the LLaMA paper prompt ('Answer these questions: Q: In Scotland a bothy/bothie is a? A: House Q: [question] A:'); Natural Questions uses a 5-shot version with 5 random training questions; CoQA uses the context paragraph, earlier Q/A turns and the question (code from Kuhn et al. 2023). NLI input format: '[question] [answer_1] [SEP] [question] [answer_2]'. Default generation configs: temperature 1 and top_p 1 for all models except LLaMA2 (temperature 0.6, top_p 0.9); an ablation uses temperature 0.5. No augmentation.
papers.modelDetails: Step 1: For input x, sample m responses (default m = 20; ablation m = 1, 3, 5, 10, 20). Step 2: Compute pairwise similarity a(sj1, sj2): Jaccard (word-set intersection over union); NLI-entail = softmax probability of entailment; NLI-contra = 1 - probability of contradiction (from DeBERTa-large-MNLI, with an NLI temperature chosen from 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 3, 5, 7). Step 3: Build a symmetric weighted adjacency matrix W with w = (a12 + a21)/2, degree matrix D, and normalised graph Laplacian L = I - D^-1/2 W D^-1/2. Measures: (a) NumSet: number of semantic sets from bidirectional entailment (merge two answers if p_entail > p_contra in both directions); (b) EigV: U = sum over eigenvalues of max(0, 1 - lambda_k), a continuous number of meanings; (c) Deg: U = trace(mI - D)/m^2 (average pairwise distance) and confidence C(x, sj) = D_jj/m; (d) Ecc: embed each response with the k smallest eigenvectors of L, centre them, U = norm of all centred embeddings, C(x, sj) = minus the distance of response j from the centre; eigenvalue cut-off chosen from 0.4 to 0.9. Uncertainty U(x) depends only on the input; confidence C(x, s) is per response. Selective generation: reject inputs or responses with high U or low C. Optional calibration: histogram binning with 15 bins fitted on the first generation of the 1,000 calibration questions.
papers.training: No LLM training. Only hyper-parameters (NLI temperature, eigenvalue threshold) are chosen on the 1,000-question calibration set in each of 10 random runs. Hardware: 2x AMD EPYC Milan 7513 CPU, 512 GB RAM, 8x A6000 GPUs. Generating 20 responses with OPT/LLaMA took 2.5 to 15 hours per dataset (2 to 11 seconds per question; CoQA slowest). Running the NLI model for 20 responses (380 comparisons, worst case) took about 0.8 seconds.
papers.evaluation: Correctness: gpt-3.5-turbo rates each response against the reference from 0 to 100 using a few-shot prompt; scores above 0.7 (70) count as correct; 99.34% of ratings could be parsed. Human check of GPT judgement: accuracy 90.9% (CoQA), 98.0% (TriviaQA, 97 of 99), 95.9% (NQ). Settings: U + expected accuracy (U+EA, expected accuracy = mean correctness of the m responses), C + individual accuracy (C+IA), and U + individual accuracy. Metrics: AUROC for predicting correctness and AUARC (area under the accuracy-rejection curve; random = base accuracy, oracle = upper bound). Calibration: adaptive calibration error (ACE) after histogram binning. All metrics reported as mean +/- standard deviation over 10 random calibration/test splits.
papers.baselines: Black-box: NumSet (number of semantic sets, Kuhn et al. 2023); LexiSim (average Rouge-L between responses). White-box (not for GPT): semantic entropy (SE, Kuhn et al. 2023) and P(true) (Kadavath et al. 2022). Reference lines: Random (base accuracy) and Oracle.
papers.results: Table 1, AUARC for U(x) predicting expected accuracy (mean +/- SD, in %). TriviaQA: LLaMA random 61.18, oracle 87.03, NumSet 78.78, LexiSim 80.32, EigV(E) 85.01, Ecc(E) 84.66, Deg(E) 85.27, SE 79.15, P(true) 64.98; LLaMA2 random 76.24, EigV(E) 93.07, SE 93.99; OPT random 25.75, Deg(E) 52.06, SE 51.11; GPT random 87.42, Ecc(E) 95.21, LexiSim 94.69. CoQA: LLaMA random 62.46, Deg(E) 81.50, SE 78.83; LLaMA2 EigV(E) 90.21, SE 89.29; OPT Deg(E) 73.91, SE 70.75; GPT EigV(E) 88.80, LexiSim 86.60. NQ: LLaMA random 23.63, Deg(E) 41.07, SE 36.03; LLaMA2 EigV(E) 63.58, SE 62.40; OPT Ecc(E) 18.82, SE 18.40; GPT Ecc(E) 75.40, LexiSim 73.40. Table 2, AUARC for C(x, s) predicting individual accuracy: TriviaQA-LLaMA Deg(E) 88.86 +/- 0.05 (oracle 91.24), Ecc(E) 88.17, SE 79.15, P(true) 67.27; TriviaQA-OPT Deg(E) 56.11; CoQA-LLaMA Ecc(E) 84.62, Deg(E) 84.60; CoQA-OPT Ecc(E) 78.14; NQ-LLaMA Deg(E) 46.54; NQ-OPT Deg(E) 21.30; NQ-GPT Ecc(E) 75.43. Rejecting the 50% least confident (Deg(E), LLaMA, TriviaQA) raised accuracy from 62% to about 90%. ACE after calibration (x 10^-2), TriviaQA-LLaMA: Deg(E) 2.37, Ecc(E) 2.60, SE 4.56, P(true) 4.30. NLI-entail similarity was the best choice in general.
papers.statistics: Mean and standard deviation over 10 random calibration/test splits are reported for all metrics. No formal hypothesis tests or p-values. Human-GPT agreement on correctness: 90.9%, 98.0%, 95.9%.
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/zlin7/UQ-NLG. Datasets: public CoQA, TriviaQA and Natural Questions. NLI model: microsoft/deberta-large-mnli on HuggingFace.

papers.title: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
papers.authors: Christopher Mohri, Tatsunori Hashimoto
papers.aim: To give high-probability correctness (factuality) guarantees for any black-box language model output by linking factuality to conformal prediction.
papers.method: The LM output is split into sub-claims by GPT-4, each sub-claim gets a confidence score, and claims below a threshold are removed and the rest merged back into one answer. The threshold is chosen by split conformal prediction on a small human-annotated calibration set so that the final output is fully correct with probability at least 1-alpha. Lower-confidence claims are removed first, so the answer becomes less specific but more reliable (a 'back-off' algorithm).
papers.result: Correctness rose from about 30% to 80% on FActScore, 78% to 93% on Natural Questions, and 75% to 95% on MATH while keeping most sub-claims. With frequency scoring, FActScore factuality went from about 25% to about 80% while keeping about half of the sub-claims; NQ gained about 15% by removing about a quarter of claims; MATH gained about 15% by removing about 10% of claims. Empirical factuality closely tracked the target 1-alpha over 1000 random splits.
papers.tools: GPT-4 as base LM, sub-claim separator, merger, confidence scorer and frequency counter; Python code released (github.com/tatsu-lab/conformal-factual-lm); Google search for manual fact checking.
papers.gap: Guarantee is marginal (on average over inputs and calibration draws), not per-input; it assumes exchangeable data and fails under distribution shift; validated only on 50 examples per dataset and only with GPT-4; utility depends heavily on the quality of the claim scoring function.
papers.relation: Gives distribution-free correctness guarantees on LLM outputs, a basis for calibrated thresholds in the orchestrator's deferral decisions.
papers.limitations: Authors state: coverage is not conditional (one domain or user may differ from the target); it is marginal over the calibration draw, so a small fixed calibration set may deviate (empirical standard deviation about 0.09 with high-probability guarantees over the calibration set); under distribution shift the threshold may lose coverage; guarantees restricted to a prescribed distribution P. Partial-factuality variant gave small gains. Future work: apply conformal methods robust to distribution shift and conditional coverage.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors want an LM answer that is fully correct with probability at least 1-alpha. They take 50 inputs each from FActScore (biographies), Natural Questions (long-form answers) and MATH (step-by-step solutions). GPT-4 writes an answer for each input. A second GPT-4 prompt splits the answer into atomic sub-claims; for MATH each reasoning step is a sub-claim. The authors themselves label every sub-claim as Factual, Subjective, Unverifiable or False after checking with Google; Factual and Subjective count as true. Each sub-claim then gets a confidence score. The best practical scorer is frequency scoring: GPT-4 generates 5 more answers at temperature 1.0 and counts how many of them support the sub-claim, with ties broken by GPT-4's own stated confidence and tiny N(0, 0.001) noise. For a threshold t, the output keeps only sub-claims with score at least t and GPT-4 merges them into fluent text; a very high t gives an empty (abstaining) answer. For each calibration example the score r is the smallest threshold above which every kept claim is true; this needs only claim-level labels. The final threshold is the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n quantile of these r values. At test time, claims below the threshold are dropped. To check the guarantee, each dataset was split in half 1000 times: the threshold was fitted on one half and factuality measured on the other. They also plot factuality against the percent of claims removed, using leave-one-out, to show utility. For a clinical multi-agent system, the same pipeline can filter an LLM-generated radiology or planning summary: split into findings, score them by agreement across samples or agents, calibrate on clinician-checked reports, and send the case to a clinician when too many claims must be removed.
papers.studyDesign: Methods paper with empirical evaluation (Stanford University, USA). Retrospective evaluation on public benchmark questions with author-made factuality annotations.
papers.datasets: Three datasets, first 50 inputs from each: (1) FActScore biography generation (people entities), sub-claims regenerated with the separator S; (2) Natural Questions (simplified training set, real Google queries) answered as long-form text; (3) MATH word problems, where each reasoning step is a sub-claim. GPT-4 outputs were annotated manually by the authors with a 4-way label (Factual, Subjective, Unverifiable, False) verified with Google; Factual and Subjective counted as entailed. Annotation done before experiments.
papers.preprocessing: GPT-4 generates the answer; GPT-4 with a prompt separates it into sub-claims; each sub-claim is scored; ties broken with N(0, 0.001) noise kept consistent across scoring functions. Calibration/test: each dataset randomly split in half 1000 times (threshold fitted on first half, factuality measured on second half); utility curves use leave-one-out evaluation.
papers.modelDetails: Entailment set E(y) = {y' : y' implies y}; output is correct iff reference y* is in E(y). Back-off function F_t(x) = M({c in S(L(x)) : s(c) >= t}), merging all sub-claims with score at least t; F_sup T returns abstention (empty output), so F_t is 'sound'. Score r(x, y*) = inf{t : for all j >= t, y* entails F_j(x)}, which under Assumption 5.1 needs only sub-claim-level entailment labels. Threshold q-hat_alpha = ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n quantile of the calibration scores; output F_q-hat(x). Theorem 4.1: P(correct) >= 1-alpha for alpha in [1/(n+1), 1], and <= 1-alpha+1/(n+1) when nested. Partial factuality (Corollary 5.3): guarantee that at least a fraction a of kept claims are true (tested with a = 0.7 FActScore, 0.9 NQ, 0.8 MATH). Scoring functions: random N(0,1); ordinal (n - j); GPT-4 verbal confidence; frequency scoring (5 alternate samples at temperature 1.0, GPT-4 counts how often each claim appears; ties broken by GPT-4 confidence); oracle (true entailment). Ranking-based variants in Appendix C.
papers.training: No training. GPT-4 used through prompts only. Frequency scoring samples 5 extra outputs at temperature 1.0. Calibration uses half of 50 annotated examples per split. Hardware and time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Empirical factuality versus target 1-alpha over 1000 random half/half splits (frequency scoring; other scorers in Appendix E). Utility = percent of sub-claims removed versus factuality, leave-one-out, across alpha values; standard errors shown. Qualitative examples at alpha = 0.2 (FActScore) and alpha = 0.1 (NQ, MATH).
papers.baselines: Base GPT-4 output without filtering; random scoring; ordinal scoring; GPT-4 confidence scoring; oracle scoring as upper bound.
papers.results: Base GPT-4 factuality: about 25-30% on FActScore, about 75-78% on NQ and MATH. With conformal factuality: 30% to 80% (FActScore), 78% to 93% (NQ), 75% to 95% (MATH) while retaining most claims. Frequency scoring: FActScore about 25% to about 80% keeping about half the claims; NQ +about 15% removing about one quarter; MATH +about 15% removing about 10%; 20-50% gains in correctness overall. At alpha = 0.2 on FActScore most examples had about 50% of claims removed (not just whole-answer abstention). Empirical factuality tracked target closely; extra variation with standard deviation about 0.09 across calibration draws.
papers.statistics: Distribution-free conformal bounds (Theorem 4.1). Standard errors over 1000 random splits. No hypothesis tests reported.
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/tatsu-lab/conformal-factual-lm. Datasets are public (FActScore, Natural Questions, MATH); annotations released with the code (as stated by repository release).

papers.title: The challenge of uncertainty quantification of large language models in medicine
papers.authors: Atf Z, Safavi-Naini SAA, Lewis PR, Mahjoubfar A, Naderi N, Savage TR, Soroush A
papers.aim: To review how uncertainty in large language models (LLMs) used in medicine can be measured, explained and managed. The paper also proposes a conceptual framework that separates epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty and links them to clinical decisions.
papers.method: A narrative (non-systematic) literature review combined with a philosophical discussion of uncertainty. The authors group the sources of uncertainty into data, model, user and context, summarise methods in two thematic tables, and then propose an eight-component conceptual framework. No new model is built and no experiment is run.
papers.result: No quantitative results.
