Depression: 9 cost scenarios, undetermined cost = 1, FP cost in {2, 5, 10}, FN cost in {2, 5, 10}; models were L1 logistic regression, random forest (ntree = 500, mtry = sqrt of predictors) and SVM (RBF kernel, C = 1, gamma = 1/data dimension). Cancer tasks: Lasso logistic regression; cost ratio FP:FN:undetermined = 13.5:8:1 from survey. Chosen thresholds (T1/T2): GBM double 0.27/0.90 (single 0.59); DRA 0.15/0.70 (single 0.65); APR 0.12/0.70 (single 0.28); LAR 0.17/0.71 (single 0.59). After training, model is applied to unlabelled notes; positive/negative are final, undetermined go to abstractors. Failure analysis of FP/FN corrected abstractor errors and retrained models.
papers.training: Lasso regularisation and document-term-matrix sparsity tuned by 10-fold cross-validation with misclassification cost as the metric. Random forest and SVM used default settings (ntree 500; RBF, C = 1, gamma = 1/dimension). Weak supervision label model trained on 1000 notes. Optimizer, hardware and training time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Hold-out test sets (40% of notes for Stanford tasks; 451 labelled notes for depression). Metrics: misclassification cost, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, plus new selective metrics: undetermined rate = (UN + UP)/all predictions; positive undetermined rate = UP/(TP + FN + UP); negative undetermined rate = UN/(TN + FP + UN). Weak label model checked by AUC and metrics at threshold 0.5. GBM model also compared against structured proxies: ICD-10 C71.0-C71.9, C72.9, ICD-9 C191.9; CPT 81287, 81345, 70554, 70555, 78600, 78601, 78605, 78606, 78608, 78609, 78610, 61510; temozolomide or bevacizumab orders. Cost survey: 7 clinician and abstractor responses, 1 outlier removed (n = 6), scenario of 100 notes.
papers.baselines: Single-threshold (non-selective) classifiers of the same model; structured proxy variables for GBM (any GBM-related ICD code, any GBM-related CPT code, GBM-related medication); logistic regression vs random forest vs SVM for depression.
papers.results: Weak supervision depression label model: test AUC 0.87; at 0.5 sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.81, PPV 0.61, NPV 0.97. Depression (FN 2, FP 2): undetermined 0% LR, 4.21% RF, 0% SVM; cost change -2% LR, +5% RF, 0% SVM. FN 5, FP 2: undetermined 37.25% LR, 38.58% RF, 69.40% SVM; cost change 9%, -5%, -22%. FN 10, FP 2: undetermined 78.49% LR, 72.28% RF, 77.61% SVM; cost change -19%, -42%, -25%. GBM (test N = 264): double vs single sensitivity 0.96 vs 0.94, specificity 0.96 vs 0.79, PPV 0.98 vs 0.89, NPV 0.91 vs 0.88, FN 4 vs 10, FP 2 vs 20, predictions 150 vs 264, undetermined rate 0.43 (positive 0.38, negative 0.52), cost 173 vs 350 (-51%). DRA (N = 240): sens 0.93 vs 0.87, spec 0.93 vs 0.92, PPV 0.92 vs 0.90, NPV 0.94 vs 0.90, undetermined 0.09, cost 114 vs 136 (-16%). APR (N = 394): sens 0.91 vs 0.82 (text says 0.81), spec 0.99 vs 0.99, PPV 0.94 vs 0.88, NPV 0.99 vs 0.98, undetermined 0.05, cost 47 vs 72 (-35%). LAR (N = 353): sens 0.91 vs 0.71, spec 1.00 vs 0.99, PPV 0.98 vs 0.94, NPV 0.99 vs 0.94, undetermined 0.10, cost 59 vs 100 (-41%). GBM proxies: ICD sens 0.62, spec 0.46, PPV 0.70, NPV 0.38, cost 1141; CPT 0.36/0.59/0.64/0.32, cost 1337; medication 0.21/0.84/0.71/0.34, cost 1269. Automation 57% to 95% across the 4 cancer outcomes.
papers.statistics: Inter-rater reliability on 172 duplicate-abstracted GBM notes (54 by a physician): Fleiss' kappa 0.869 (P < .001). Non-physician vs physician abstractors: sensitivity 0.98, specificity 1.00, PPV 1.00, NPV 0.90. No confidence intervals or significance tests reported for model comparisons.
papers.availability: Code: Not available. Data: MIMIC-III is public by credentialed access; Stanford data not public, available from corresponding author on reasonable request. Labelling functions and features in supplementary tables S1-S5.

papers.title: Evaluating large language models as agents in the clinic
papers.authors: Mehandru N, Miao BY, Rodriguez Almaraz E, Sushil M, Butte AJ, Alaa A
papers.aim: To argue that LLM-based clinical agents should be judged in high-fidelity simulations of clinical workflows, not only on static exam-style benchmarks, and to propose an evaluation format called AI-SCE (Artificial Intelligence Structured Clinical Examinations).
papers.method: A short Comment (perspective) article with no experiments. It reviews how LLM agents use tools, databases and other agents, and proposes agent-based modelling (ABM) simulations of clinical settings, borrowed from self-driving car testing, plus OSCE-style AI-SCE benchmarks built by interdisciplinary teams that grade both final outputs and intermediate reasoning, tool use and agent interactions.
papers.result: No quantitative results of its own. It cites prior figures: Med-PaLM 2 scored 85% on medical exam questions and GPT-4 scored 86% on USMLE. Main output is a conceptual framework (ABM simulation + AI-SCE evaluation + human evaluator panel + external datasets + post-deployment monitoring + RCTs).
papers.tools: Conceptual only. Mentions GPT-4, ChatGPT, Med-PaLM 2 / MedLM, AMIE, Auto-GPT, generative agents (interactive simulacra), NeMo Guardrails, MIMIC-IV, UCSF Information Commons, federated learning, Epic MyChart integration at UC San Diego Health.
papers.gap: No concrete AI-SCE benchmark, scoring rubric, simulation environment or validation is provided; how to measure simulation fidelity and agreement with human evaluators is left open.
papers.relation: Supports our plan to test the brain-tumour multi-agent orchestrator in simulated tumour-board and pre-operative planning workflows, scoring not only final diagnoses but each agent's intermediate steps, tool calls and deferral decisions, with a clinician panel (OSCE-like rubric from Sri Lankan neurosurgeons and radiologists), ablation of agents, external datasets and post-deployment monitoring. It also names federated learning and de-identified data as ways to build simulations while protecting privacy.
papers.limitations: Perspective piece with no data or experiments. Authors note that clinical tasks often lack perfect agreement with individual human evaluators, so a panel is needed; simulations must be checked against real settings with RCTs; post-deployment monitoring is needed for distribution shift and bias. Future work: build AI-SCE benchmarks with clinicians, computer scientists and researchers; move from static datasets to dynamic simulation environments.
papers.methodologyDetail: This paper is a short Comment, so it gives a method for evaluation rather than an experiment. The authors start from the view that once an LLM can plan, call tools, query records or talk to other agents, it should be treated as an agent, not just a language model. Exam scores such as Med-PaLM 2's 85% or GPT-4's 86% on USMLE then say little about how it will behave in a clinic. Their proposed workflow has four parts. First, define the agent and its environment: which tools it can use (guidelines, EHR databases, calculators, curated software) and which other agents it works with. Second, build a simulated clinical environment using agent-based modelling, as is done for self-driving cars with obstacles, signals and pedestrians. In the clinic the 'obstacles' are patient-physician encounters and hospital processes. Patients and clinicians can be simulated by LLM agents built from real EHR or trial data, ideally from several hospitals and diverse populations. Privacy can be kept with de-identified sets like MIMIC-IV or with federated learning. Third, score the simulation with an AI-SCE, the AI version of an OSCE. Interdisciplinary teams of clinicians, computer scientists and researchers write graded checklists from hard real cases. Scoring covers the final output and every intermediate step: reasoning, tool calls, data curation and agent-to-agent messages. Ablation, meaning adding or removing agents, shows each agent's effect, and the results guide guardrail design. Fourth, keep humans and the real world in the loop. Use a panel of human raters, because single raters disagree on complex tasks. Test on external datasets, monitor after deployment for drift and bias, and run RCTs to check that the simulation matches reality. For a PhD project this can be applied as follows: write OSCE-style rubrics with local neurosurgeons, simulate referral-to-surgery pathways, log each agent's steps and deferrals, and run agent ablations. No numeric settings are given in the paper.
papers.studyDesign: Comment / perspective article. Authors from University of California, Berkeley and University of California San Francisco (USA). Not prospective or retrospective; no participants or data.
papers.datasets: None used. Suggested data sources for building simulations: real-world EHR or clinical-trial data, validated across multiple hospital systems with diverse populations; de-identified datasets such as MIMIC-IV and UCSF Information Commons; federated learning to protect privacy. Mentions existing benchmarks MedQA (USMLE-style) and MedNLI as insufficient.
papers.preprocessing: Not reported (no data processed).
papers.modelDetails: Conceptual framework, step by step: 1) Build LLM agents with access to tools and information (clinical guidelines, EHR databases, clinical calculators, curated clinical software); agents plan, retrieve and run multi-step analyses, and can collaborate in multi-agent settings to check solutions. 2) Use agent-based modelling to simulate the clinical environment (patient-physician interactions, hospital processes); patients and physicians can themselves be simulated as LLM agents built from EHR or trial data. 3) Evaluate with AI-SCE: OSCE-style lists of processes or diagnoses, derived from difficult clinical scenarios or real tasks, created by interdisciplinary teams; go beyond BLEU/ROUGE; draw on multi-turn benchmarks. 4) Grade both outputs and intermediate steps (reasoning, tool use, data curation, interactions with other agents and users), and measure effects of adding or removing agents. 5) Use results to design guardrails. No thresholds, prompts or numeric parameters given.
papers.training: Not reported (no model trained).
papers.evaluation: Proposed, not performed: AI-SCE assessment of simulated agent behaviour; panel of human evaluators; testing on external datasets; post-deployment monitoring for data shift and bias; randomized controlled trials comparing simulation with real-world settings and measuring real-world impact.
papers.baselines: Not applicable. Contrasts the proposal with static NLP benchmarks (MedQA, MedNLI, BLEU, ROUGE) and cites AMIE's OSCE-style comparison against primary care physicians.
papers.results: No original results. Cited values: Med-PaLM 2 = 85% on medical examination questions; GPT-4 = 86% on USMLE.
papers.availability: Not available (no code or data; article is CC BY 4.0).

papers.title: Towards autonomous medical artificial intelligence agents
papers.authors: Ferber D, Hilgers L, Höper C, Kinny-Köster B, Eckardt JN, Egger-Heidrich K, Bill M, Schneider MMK, Clusmann J, Kadric L, Oehme M, Mayrhofer-Schmid M, Oeser A, Wölflein G, Wiest IC, Middeke JM, Iafrate AJ, Truhn D, Jäger D, Kather JN
papers.aim: To test whether an autonomous LLM agent (MIRA) working inside a sandboxed, FHIR-based EHR can manage full emergency department cases (history, tests, diagnosis, treatment, admission) at physician level and safely.
papers.method: MIRA (GPT-4o physician agent with an o1-preview planning tool) talks to an LLM patient agent grounded in real MIMIC-IV histories and calls 11 FHIR-compliant tools with more than 85,000 options to order tests, prescribe drugs, schedule procedures and admit. It was run on 574 curated emergency cases across 8 diagnoses and compared head-to-head with 4 board-certified physicians and a 6-physician mixed-seniority cohort on 311 matched cases, plus safety, admission-decision and bias-perturbation experiments.
papers.result: Diagnostic accuracy 88.9% vs MIMIC-IV labels (n = 574). On 311 matched cases, MIRA scored 87.8% vs 78.1% for board-certified physicians (P < 0.001) and 71.1% for the mixed cohort (P < 0.001). Procedure recall was 53.5% vs 38.3%, and guideline adherence was +35 percentage points vs board-certified physicians. Admission recall was 1.00 for both pneumonia and pulmonary embolism. There were no high-severity drug interactions, renal dosing or allergy errors in 56 audited cases, and 0/933 and 0/880 premature information leaks by the patient agent.
papers.tools: GPT-4o (physician agent, temperature 0.01); o1-preview (Plan reasoning tool); LLM patient agent; LLM-as-judge evaluators (diagnosis, procedure match, guideline adherence, medication standardisers); HAPI-FHIR server in Docker; fhir.resources Python package; jina-embeddings-v3 with a local Qdrant index for retrieval over ICD-9/10 procedures; RxNav, UMLS and openFDA APIs; coding systems ICD, LOINC, OMOP, ATC, NDC, RxNorm, SNOMED-CT; token masking of tool parameters; custom physician GUI; MIMIC-IV v2.2.
papers.gap: Retrospective sandbox simulation only; patient speech derived from structured HPI text; single public dataset with possible training-data contamination; no imaging pixels (only reports and metadata); no explicit uncertainty-based deferral to physicians; no prospective or real-world evaluation; reliability not 100% (for example antibiotic choices).
papers.relation: A flagship design point for how much autonomy an orchestrated clinical agent can have. Its sandboxed FHIR tool layer, enumerated or token-masked tool parameters (to block hallucinated orders), turn limit, separate planning tool and LLM-as-judge validated against physicians are directly reusable for our brain-tumour orchestrator. It also shows what our work must add: calibrated deferral to clinicians, imaging agents for MRI, privacy-preserving federated training, and validation with Sri Lankan neurosurgeons instead of full autonomy.
papers.limitations: Patient interactions were simulated from discharge-summary HPI, so they are more structured than real speech. MIMIC-IV may be in LLM training data, so results may be an upper bound. The physician cohorts come from a German system without an emergency medicine specialty. Recommendations were not 100% reliable, and route of administration had the most prescription errors. There was no literature retrieval tool. Future work: prospective real-world studies, an economic steward sub-agent for cost-aware ordering, physicians supplying live updates, use under physician supervision for bounded tasks (medication reconciliation, lab panels, consult drafts), and better generalisation, safety and governance.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built a closed test world and dropped an LLM agent into it. First they made a benchmark from MIMIC-IV. They kept emergency admissions whose principal diagnosis matched one of 8 conditions (four abdominal, three internal-medicine emergencies, plus pancreatic cancer). From each case they pulled the history of present illness and physical exam from the discharge summary with regular expressions. They then took the first result of every lab, urine and microbiology test within 24 h, mapped each to LOINC or OMOP, and wrote imaging as modality plus region. All mentions of the diagnosis were redacted. Two physicians reviewed 600 random cases and removed 26 that could not be diagnosed from the data, leaving 574. Next they set up a local HAPI-FHIR server in Docker as a sandbox EHR. A patient agent, an LLM given only the history, answers questions in chat. MIRA (GPT-4o, temperature 0.01) starts from the triage complaint and, at each turn, either talks to the patient or calls tools. The 11 tools cover exam, labs (246 codes), urine (28), microbiology (176), radiology, medications with structured dose fields, retrieval-based procedure search over more than 80,000 ICD procedures (jina-embeddings-v3 and Qdrant), procedure requests, an o1-preview Plan tool and Admission. Tool arguments are restricted by token masking, so the agent cannot order things that do not exist. A limit of 20 turns forces the case to close. The same tools were given to 4 board-certified and 6 mixed-seniority physicians through a GUI on 311 matched cases. LLM judges scored diagnosis, procedures, guideline use and medication matching, and each judge was first checked against a blinded physician (94.5-100% agreement). Extra tests covered patient-agent faithfulness (622 rephrasings), leaks (933 cases plus 880 adversarial prompts), safety audits (56 cases, 468 prescriptions), admit-or-discharge decisions on 80 synthetic variants scored by CURB-65 and sPESI, and 6 bias perturbations (480 runs). Statistics used McNemar, Wilcoxon, bootstrap CIs and Holm or Benjamini-Hochberg corrections. MIRA reached 87.8% vs 78.1% diagnostic accuracy. To adapt this, swap the emergency tools for MRI, histopathology and surgical-planning tools, and add an uncertainty gate that defers to a neurosurgeon.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective simulation study with head-to-head comparison against physicians (reader-style study). Institutions: NCT Heidelberg University Hospital, TU Dresden (Else Kroener Fresenius Center), University Hospital Carl Gustav Carus Dresden, NYU Langone, DKTK/DKFZ, and others (Germany, USA). Data: MIMIC-IV (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, 2008-2019). Used under the PhysioNet Credentialed Health Data Agreement.
papers.datasets: MIMIC-IV v2.2 (about 300,000 patients). Benchmark of 574 emergency department admissions across 8 diagnoses: appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis, pancreatitis, pneumonia, urinary tract infection, pulmonary embolism, pancreatic cancer (about 4% of cases). Inclusion: principal ICD-9/10 diagnosis matching the discharge letter, plus a matching emergency admission diagnosis; data from the first 24 h only. Exclusions: incomplete imaging (modality or region unknown, or required imaging missing), missing HPI, physical exam or blood tests. Of 600 randomly reviewed cases checked by 2 physicians against guideline minimum requirements, 26 were excluded (1 pancreatitis, 1 appendicitis, 3 UTI, 6 pneumonia, 15 cholecystitis), leaving 574. A board-certified physician confirmed 90/90 random cases. Matched physician subset: 311 cases (cholecystitis 45, pulmonary embolism 45, UTI 45, diverticulitis 44, appendicitis 43, pancreatitis 42, pneumonia 26, pancreatic cancer 21). Admission/discharge set: 80 synthetic variants from 20 MIMIC-IV templates (pulmonary embolism 40: 20 admit, 20 discharge; pneumonia 40: 18 admit, 22 discharge). Perturbation set: 10 cases per diagnosis x 6 biases = 480 paired runs. Procedures: ICD-coded procedures absent in 293/574 cases, so they were taken from free text.
papers.preprocessing: HPI and admission physical exam extracted from discharge summaries with regular expressions. Admission medications from free text or the ED medication reconciliation table. Earliest result for each lab or microbiology parameter within 24 h after admission (or from a prior encounter within 24 h). Labs mapped to OMOP and LOINC and turned into an LLM-readable table (label, result, reference range). Microbiology grouped per organism with susceptibilities. Radiology modality and region taken by keyword sets. Diagnosis mentions redacted with three underscores. Over 80,000 ICD-9/10 procedure descriptions embedded with jina-embeddings-v3 into a Qdrant index. For pancreatic cancer, an LLM extracted structured prior history (imaging, ERCP, biopsy, planned admissions). Enumerations: 246 lab LOINC codes, 28 urine options, 176 microbiology LOINC codes. No train/test split (no model training; zero-shot agent).
papers.modelDetails: Two-agent loop. 1) Patient agent: an LLM given only the HPI. It is told to stay faithful to it, to ignore post-visit facts (final diagnosis, treatments, imaging findings) and to say it does not know when asked about missing facts. 2) MIRA: GPT-4o (temperature 0.01). It starts from the prompt 'The patient you are now seeing has primary symptoms: {primary_symptom}', taken from the triage chief complaint. At each turn it replies to the patient or calls tools, and calls can run in parallel. The 11 tools are PatientHistory (pancreatic cancer only), PhysicalExaminationRequest, LabRequest, UrineRequest, MicrobiologyRequest, RadiologyRequest, MedicationRequest (dose, unit, period, frequency, route), ProcedureSearch (RAG), ProcedureRequest, Plan (o1-preview reasoning with full history, tool schema and few-shot examples) and Admission (final diagnosis, ends the case). For the disposition experiments, CloseCase and VitalSignsRequest were added. Each '-Request' tool fills FHIR resource fields and posts them to a local HAPI-FHIR server. The server returns FHIR observations built from the real MIMIC-IV data. Type hints and token masking restrict parameters to valid codes, so invalid orders are impossible. Safeguard: a limit of 20 conversation turns, after which the Admission tool is forced. There is no explicit uncertainty or deferral rule.
papers.training: No model training or fine-tuning; off-the-shelf GPT-4o and o1-preview with system prompts and few-shot examples (Supplementary Information 16-18, tool prompts in Supplementary Data Table 44). Each analysis was run once on a prespecified set. Hardware and run time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Ground truth from MIMIC-IV: ICD-10 primary diagnosis, admission physical exam, labs, urine, microbiology and imaging within 24 h, procedures and medications. Diagnosis was judged correct by an LLM Diagnosis Evaluator (few-shot, chain-of-thought), checked against a blinded board-certified physician on 200 cases (96.5% agreement), with no source bias (37 paired cases, McNemar P = 1.00). Test selection was scored as recall and overlap with MIMIC-IV, plus a Tversky distance (alpha = 2 for over-ordering, beta = 1 for misses). Procedures: recall with exact ICD and LLM-judged equivalent matches, on correctly diagnosed cases only (judge vs physician: Cohen's kappa = 1.0). Guideline adherence was scored by an LLM evaluator against WSES, ASCRS, ATS, AJKD and ASH guidelines for 7 diseases (94.5% agreement with the physician on 112 cases and 256 metrics). Medication standardiser: 97.4% item agreement (454/466). Safety: a blinded physician audited 56 cases on 6 domains and 468 prescriptions. Patient agent: 622 rephrased question pairs, 933 cases audited for leaks and 880 adversarial prompts (11 attack types). Reader comparison: 4 board-certified physicians (7-11 years of experience) and a mixed cohort of 6 (4 residents with 0-5 years, plus a radiologist and a haemato-oncologist with 12 and 15 years). Each worked on non-overlapping case subsets through a GUI with the same tools and no turn limit.
papers.baselines: Four board-certified physicians; a mixed-seniority cohort of six physicians; MIMIC-IV documented care as the reference; prior work (Hager et al., MAI-DxO and AMIE) discussed but not rerun.
papers.results: Diagnosis vs MIMIC-IV (n = 574): mean 88.9%, appendicitis 98.6% (146/148), pancreatitis 92.3%, UTI 77.6%, pneumonia 72.4%. Matched set (n = 311): MIRA 87.8% vs board-certified 78.1% (P < 0.001; exact P = 0.000287) vs mixed 71.1% (P < 0.001). Pancreatitis: 95.2% vs 78.6% (P < 0.05) vs 61.9% (P < 0.001). Physical exam requested in 97.1% vs 87.8% vs 88.4% of cases (P < 0.001). Blood test coverage of MIMIC-IV: 51.1% vs 28.3% vs 34.6%. Overall test alignment: 55.3% vs 61.5% vs 62.5%. Tversky distance (lower is closer): microbiology 0.640 vs 0.677 (P = 0.06) vs 0.66; blood 0.607 vs 0.784 vs 0.73 (P < 0.001); radiology 0.508 vs 0.628 (P < 0.001) vs 0.572 (P < 0.01). Home medication reconciliation: recall 95.2%, precision 99.6%. Procedures: laparoscopic appendectomy 124/124 (100%), laparoscopic cholecystectomy 90.6% exact; total recall 100% for appendicitis and 81.2% for cholecystitis; overall 53.5% vs 38.3%; Tversky 0.415 vs 0.556 vs 0.579 (P < 0.0001). Guideline adherence: mean paired difference +35 pp vs board-certified and +36 pp vs mixed (P < 0.001). Safety (56 cases): 0 high-severity drug interactions, renal, allergy, QT or opioid errors; 3 therapeutic duplications judged reasonable. Prescriptions (468): dosing text 99.8%, dose 97.6%, units 98.3%, period 99.6%, frequency 99.1%, route 97.0%. Disposition: admission recall 1.00 for both; specificity 0.86 (0.68-1.00) pneumonia and 0.70 (0.43-0.94) pulmonary embolism; precision 0.86 (0.65-1.00) and 0.77 (0.64-0.95); NPV 1.00; accuracy 0.93 (0.80-1.00) and 0.85 (0.73-0.98). Bias perturbations: pooled risk difference -1.2 pp (-7.5 to 5; anxiety) to -10.0 pp (-17.5 to -2.5; sex), with sex bias P < 0.05 unadjusted and Holm P = 0.129. Patient agent: answer consistency 99.4%, HPI alignment 99.3% and 99.1%; leaks 0/933 (CI 0.0-0.4%) and 0/880; prior-workup disclosure 31/933 (3.3%, 2.3-4.7%).
papers.statistics: Clopper-Pearson exact 95% CIs for leak rates; McNemar's exact test (Fisher's exact when a discordant cell was empty) for paired diagnostic, physical exam, guideline and bias comparisons; paired odds ratios with exact CIs; Holm adjustment within diagnoses; Wilson 95% CIs on accuracy bars; two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with median, IQR and rank-biserial correlation for test selection, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples) for precision, recall and F1; patient-cluster bootstrap (10,000) for disposition metrics; non-parametric paired bootstrap 95% CIs for risk differences. Agreement of LLM judges with the physician: 96.5%, 97.4%, kappa = 1.0 and 94.5%.
papers.availability: Code: https://github.com/Dyke-F/MIRA. Data: MIMIC-IV v2.2 via PhysioNet credentialed access (https://physionet.org/content/mimiciv/2.2/). Source data and supplementary tables published with the article.

papers.title: The role of agentic artificial intelligence in healthcare: a scoping review
papers.authors: Collaco BG, Haider SA, Prabha S, Gomez-Cabello CA, Genovese A, Wood NG, Bagaria SP, Gopala N, Tao C, Forte AJ
papers.aim: To map how agentic AI systems are used in healthcare, and to propose a clear line between AI agents and agentic AI. It also lists the features, limits and open problems of these systems.
papers.method: A scoping review following the Cochrane Handbook and PRISMA-ScR, with a protocol registered on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/JFT2C). Five databases were searched on 15 April 2025. Two reviewers screened 984 records and included 7 studies. Risk of bias was rated with RoB-2 and ROBINS-I.
papers.result: 984 records were found, 89 were read in full, and 7 studies were included (screening finished 29 April 2025). Only 1 was an RCT (SmartText, n = 42, a non-significant effect). The other 6 were experimental, computational or simulation studies with no patients recruited. Reported results: ChatExosome 94.1% accuracy for HCC (87.5% in AFP-negative HCC), an RL VR assistant 87% accuracy, TraumaTracker over 430 trauma reports in about 9 months, and GPT-Plan matching or beating expert planners on 17 patients. Three systems were multi-agent and four were single-agent. None showed adaptation over time or long-term memory. Risk of bias ran from moderate to critical.
papers.tools: Databases: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, Scopus, Google Scholar (first 100 hits). EndNote 21.3 for screening. A Microsoft Excel extraction sheet. RoB-2, ROBINS-I and the ROBVIS visualisation tool. BioRender for figures. The included systems used GPT-4 and other LLMs, BDI agents, PPO-AC reinforcement learning, RAG, and a feature fusion transformer.
papers.gap: Evidence on agentic AI in healthcare is sparse and early. There is 1 RCT, few real-world deployments, and no agreed definition. No system adapts over time or keeps long-term memory. There is no standard evaluation framework covering autonomy, safety, transparency or how much human oversight each autonomy tier needs. Regulation (FDA PCCP, EU AI Act) does not yet cover agentic systems.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), this gives the current baseline of agentic designs in clinical care: single-agent orchestrators such as MultiMedRes versus multi-agent role teams such as GPT-Plan, ProtChat and TraumaTracker. It also gives minimal criteria for calling a system agentic (autonomy, goal-directed behaviour, action initiation). It calls for autonomy tiers with defined human-in-the-loop oversight. That supports our calibrated selective autonomy and deferral-to-clinician design. It also names federated learning, lightweight agents and open-source models as routes for low-resource settings, which match our Sri Lanka setting. None of the 7 studies covered brain tumours or neurosurgical planning, which confirms a gap for our project.
papers.limitations: Only 7 heterogeneous studies were included, so no meta-analysis was done. Only the first 100 of more than 20,000 Google Scholar hits were screened, which may add selection bias. IEEE Xplore and ACM Digital Library were not searched. 14 papers were excluded because the full text was not available. Only English-language peer-reviewed work from 2017 onward was considered. Authors note possible selection and publication bias. Future work: pilot studies in digitally mature domains (radiology, radiation oncology, pathology, emergency medicine), then multi-centre RCTs, standard benchmarks, autonomy-tier classification, latency and compute measures, privacy protection (anonymisation, differential privacy, federated learning) and HIPAA/GDPR compliance.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors ran a scoping review following the Cochrane Handbook and PRISMA-ScR, with a protocol registered on OSF (10.17605/OSF.IO/JFT2C). First they set 3 minimal criteria for a system to count as agentic AI: autonomous operation, goal-directed behaviour, and action initiation or tool invocation (for example sending alerts or calling an API). Long-term memory and multi-agent collaboration raise the 'degree of agency' but were not required. They limited the search to peer-reviewed studies from 2017 onward, the start of the transformer era. On 15 April 2025 they searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, Scopus and Google Scholar through the Mayo Clinic Library. The search combined three blocks: AI and LLM terms (for example GPT-4, ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Deepseek), agent terms (for example 'Agentic AI', 'AI agent', 'multi-agent system', 'tool-using AI', 'memory-enabled AI') and healthcare terms. PubMed used MeSH terms. Google Scholar gave more than 20,000 hits, so only the first 100 by relevance were screened. IEEE Xplore and ACM were not searched. Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts in EndNote 21.3, with a third reviewer for disagreements. Of 984 records, 89 were read in full and 82 were excluded (53 not agentic, 14 full text not available, 4 reviews, 4 not peer-reviewed, 3 non-medical, 3 trial registries, 1 abstract only). That left 7 studies by 29 April 2025. One author extracted data into a pre-built Excel sheet and a second checked it. The sheet covered country, design, domain, system name, task, key findings, agentic features and limitations. Two reviewers rated risk of bias, using RoB-2 for the single RCT and ROBINS-I for the 6 non-randomised studies, plotted with ROBVIS. The studies were too different for a meta-analysis, so the synthesis was narrative. They compared architectures (3 multi-agent, 4 single-agent), outcomes (for example 94.1% HCC accuracy, 87% VR adaptation accuracy) and limitations. They found no adaptation over time or long-term memory in any system. To adapt this for a PhD, reuse the 3-criterion definition and the 7-feature checklist to classify brain-tumour agent systems, and add autonomy-tier and human-oversight fields to the extraction sheet.
papers.studyDesign: Scoping review (secondary research), done at Mayo Clinic, USA. Protocol registered on OSF. Literature searched retrospectively from 2017 to 15 April 2025. The included studies came from Italy (1), USA (2), Saudi Arabia (1) and China (3). They were 1 RCT (NCT03212079), 2 simulation-based experiments, 1 retrospective feasibility study, 2 computational studies and 1 diagnostic accuracy study.
papers.datasets: No primary dataset. The evidence base came from 5 databases: PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, Scopus and Google Scholar (more than 20,000 hits; first 100 by relevance screened). Records identified: 984. Full texts assessed: 89. Excluded at full text: 82 (53 did not meet agentic AI criteria, 4 not peer-reviewed, 3 no medical application, 1 abstract only, 4 reviews, 3 trial registries, 14 full text not available). Included: 7 studies, namely Croatti 2019 TraumaTracker (emergency medicine), Hassoon 2021 SmartText (lifestyle RCT, n = 42 cancer survivors over 3 arms, 4 weeks), Mariselvam 2023 RL virtual assistant (paediatric rehabilitation, Down syndrome), Gu 2025 MultiMedRes (radiology, chest X-ray difference VQA), Huang 2025 ProtChat (protein analysis), Wang 2025 GPT-Plan (radiotherapy planning, 17 patients, lung and cervical cancer), Yang 2025 ChatExosome (HCC from plasma exosome Raman spectra). Inclusion: peer-reviewed observational or interventional studies from 2017 onward on healthcare AI meeting 3 minimal agentic criteria (autonomous operation, goal-directed behaviour, action initiation or tool invocation). Exclusion: rule-based or ML systems without agentic properties, non-medical domains, in vitro or animal studies, abstracts without full text, inaccessible texts, reviews, opinions, letters, editorials, technical notes, preclinical studies, duplicates and anything before 2017.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (no imaging or model data). Review steps: duplicates removed, title and abstract screening, then full-text screening against the criteria in EndNote 21.3. Google Scholar was limited to the first 100 results by relevance. MeSH terms were added for PubMed. No train, validation or test split.
papers.modelDetails: No model was built. The review defines the features used to classify systems: [I] autonomous operation, [II] goal-directed behaviour, [III] adaptability, [IV] action initiation or tool invocation, [V] multi-agent framework, [VI] long-term memory, [VII] retrieval-augmented or advanced reasoning. Features I, II and IV are the minimal criteria for inclusion. Architectures reported in the included studies: TraumaTracker used 2 cooperating BDI agents (Tracker Agent and Alert Generator Agent). SmartText was a single rule-based coaching agent sending up to 3 personalised messages a day. The VR assistant was single-agent RL, with PPO-AC the best algorithm. MultiMedRes was a single GPT-4 learner agent that breaks a question into sub-questions and queries external expert models, deciding itself when to stop. ProtChat was multi-agent (User Proxy, Inference, Evaluation, Visualization and Chat Manager agents) built on GPT-4 plus protein LLMs. GPT-Plan was multi-agent (Dosimetrist, Physicist, TPS_proxy and Human_proxy agents) with retrieval-augmented plan refinement. ChatExosome was single-agent, using a feature fusion transformer classifier plus RAG. No uncertainty or deferral thresholds were reported.
papers.training: Not applicable (no model training in this review). Not reported for the included systems at the level of this review.
papers.evaluation: Two independent reviewers (BC, SH) did the search and screening, with a third reviewer (AG) for disagreements. Data extraction: one author (BC) extracted and a second (SH) checked, using a pre-built Excel sheet (authors, year, country, design, domain, AI system name, clinical task, key findings, features, limitations). A third reviewer (SP) resolved disagreements. Risk of bias: RoB-2 for the 1 RCT and ROBINS-I for the 6 non-randomised studies, rated by 2 reviewers with third-reviewer input. Narrative synthesis only. No meta-analysis because designs, populations and outcomes were too different.
papers.baselines: Not applicable. The review compares agentic AI conceptually with traditional AI, generative AI and AI agents (Fig. 6). Within the included RCT, SmartText was compared with MyCoach (voice-assisted AI coaching) and printed information.
papers.results: Search: 984 records, 89 full texts, 7 included. Designs: 1 RCT and 6 experimental studies with no patient recruitment. Architectures: multi-agent in 3 (TraumaTracker, GPT-Plan, ProtChat) and single-agent in 4 (SmartText, VR assistant, MultiMedRes, ChatExosome). Outcomes: ChatExosome accuracy = 94.1% for HCC versus controls and 87.5% in AFP-negative HCC. RL VR assistant accuracy = 87% for adapting difficulty. TraumaTracker made over 430 trauma reports during about 9 months of deployment. SmartText had a modest, non-significant effect on daily steps versus MyCoach and printed material (n = 42, 4 weeks). MultiMedRes reached state-of-the-art zero-shot DVQA and beat fine-tuned and fully supervised models. GPT-Plan matched expert planners for cervical cancer and beat them for lung cancer (17 patients). Six of 7 systems were not used in real-world settings. None showed adaptive behaviour over time or long-term memory. Risk of bias: RCT had some concerns (participants knew their arm). Croatti 2019 was serious and Mariselvam 2023 critical. The other 4 were moderate.
papers.statistics: No pooled statistics or meta-analysis. Risk of bias was rated with RoB-2 and ROBINS-I and shown with ROBVIS. Reviewer agreement (kappa) was not reported. Disagreements were settled by consensus.
papers.availability: Protocol: OSF, 10.17605/OSF.IO/JFT2C. Extraction sheet and data in the article and supplementary materials. No code (not applicable).

papers.title: A foundational architecture for AI agents in healthcare
papers.authors: Liu F, Niu Y, Zhang Q, Wang K, Dong Z, Wong IN, Cheng L, Li T, Duan L, Li K, Li G, Hou TW, Fok M, Luo H, Chen X, Zhang K, Yin Y
papers.aim: To give a clear conceptual framework for medical AI agents, review their clinical applications, and set out the technical, ethical and regulatory challenges to using them in practice.
papers.method: A narrative (non-systematic) review. The authors searched PubMed, Google Scholar and arXiv for papers up to May 2025 and grouped the findings by theme. They propose a four-part agent architecture (planning, action, reflection, memory) and map it onto clinical uses and evaluation criteria. Full text was read from the Europe PMC open-access XML (PMC12629813); the PDF could not be downloaded.
papers.result: No new quantitative results. The review defines medical AI agents by four components: planning (LLM/VLM reasoning core), action (APIs, device interfaces, software libraries, robotic actuators), reflection (perception of images and vital signs, error analysis) and memory (short-term session context and long-term patient history). It describes a multi-agent clinical workflow (early-warning, diagnosis, treatment, surgical-robotics and real-time monitoring agents) and an 'AI Agent Hospital' system with ED, inpatient-ward and MDT agents. It proposes four evaluation areas: recommendation accuracy, task execution and efficiency, long-term learning and adaptation, and explainability.
papers.tools: Large language models (LLMs) and vision language models (VLMs) as the planning core; examples cited include Med-PaLM 2 and the Agent Hospital simulation (Li et al.). Tool interfaces: EHR/laboratory/imaging APIs, device interfaces (infusion pumps, ventilators, surgical robots), image processing and NLP libraries, robotic actuators. Edge deployment with pruning and quantization.
papers.gap: No quantitative synthesis or systematic appraisal of evidence. Explainability has no standard metric. Long-term learning of agents is hard to evaluate. Regulation (FDA SaMD, EU AI Act) does not yet fit continuously learning, autonomous agents. Legacy hospital IT lacks standard APIs.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), this paper gives a ready reference architecture (planning, action, reflection, memory) that can be mapped onto our brain-tumour orchestrator: an MRI diagnosis agent, a surgical-planning agent and a coordinator. Its idea of priority-based conflict resolution with escalation to human clinicians for complex cases supports our calibrated selective-autonomy design, where the system defers to clinicians when uncertain. Its points on lightweight edge models and privacy also fit the low-resource Sri Lankan setting and our federated learning plan. It gives no deferral rule or calibration method, which our work must add.
papers.limitations: Narrative review with no stated inclusion/exclusion counts, no quality appraisal and no meta-analysis. Mostly conceptual; case examples (e.g. sepsis detection at Johns Hopkins) are described without numbers. Future work named: proactive agents, personalised agents, multi-agent collaboration with consensus and escalation protocols, lightweight edge models, stakeholder-specific explainability benchmarks, longitudinal simulation studies for evaluating adaptation, and AI literacy in medical education.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a narrative review, so the method is a literature synthesis rather than an experiment. Step 1: the authors searched PubMed, Google Scholar and arXiv for work published up to May 2025, using keywords on medical AI agents, enabling technologies (LLMs, VLMs, multimodal models), clinical uses and implementation barriers. They included peer-reviewed articles, reviews, major conference papers and influential preprints; they do not report how many records were screened or included, and there is no PRISMA flow or quality appraisal. Step 2: they grouped the literature by theme and built a four-part agent model. Planning is the reasoning core (LLM or VLM) that combines symptoms, vitals, labs and imaging into differential diagnoses. Action executes decisions through APIs to EHR, lab and imaging systems, device interfaces, software libraries and robotic actuators. Reflection perceives images and signals and evaluates outcomes and errors. Memory is split into short-term session context and long-term patient history. Step 3: they mapped this model onto a patient journey handled by a multi-agent team (early-warning, diagnosis, treatment, surgical-robotics and real-time monitoring agents), then scaled it to an 'AI Agent Hospital' with emergency department, inpatient ward and multidisciplinary-team agents under a central coordinator. Step 4: they proposed four evaluation dimensions: recommendation accuracy against expert clinicians (sensitivity, specificity, accuracy), efficiency (task completion time, success rate, number of steps, cost), long-term learning (through longitudinal simulation) and explainability. Step 5: they listed barriers (legacy IT without standard APIs, cost, clinician trust, latency, context-length limits, bias, privacy) and regulatory gaps between the FDA SaMD approach with pre-approved change plans and the EU AI Act risk tiers. For a PhD project, the reusable parts are the component taxonomy, the multi-agent conflict rule (priority-based decision trees with escalation to clinicians) and the evaluation dimensions, which can be turned into measurable metrics such as deferral rate and task success.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative literature review and conceptual framework paper. Authors from Macau University of Science and Technology, Chinese PLA General Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, Wenzhou Medical University, Peking University and other centres in China and Macau. No patient data; not prospective or retrospective.
papers.datasets: No dataset used. Literature sources: PubMed, Google Scholar and arXiv, articles published up to May 2025, including peer-reviewed articles, reviews, conference proceedings and influential preprints. Number of included papers: Not reported (the reference list has about 133 entries).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (review). Selected literature was thematically synthesised into sections on framework, applications, development, evaluation and ethics.
papers.modelDetails: Proposed framework, not a trained model. (1) Planning: LLM/VLM core that reads EHRs, test results and literature and produces differential diagnoses and workup plans, with external medical knowledge bases for guideline alignment. (2) Action: carries out decisions through four kinds of tools - APIs to EHR, laboratory and imaging systems; hardware interfaces to devices such as infusion pumps, ventilators and surgical robots; software libraries for imaging, NLP and prediction; robotic actuators. (3) Reflection: perceives and interprets images (X-ray, MRI, CT) and physiological signals, evaluates outcomes, analyses errors and uses feedback. (4) Memory: short-term memory holds session context (example given: heart rate 72 bpm, blood pressure 120/80 mmHg); long-term memory holds histories, outcomes and learned patterns. Multi-agent collaboration: hierarchical task decomposition, distributed consensus, dynamic role allocation, standard medical ontologies for communication, priority-based decision trees for conflicting recommendations, and escalation to human clinicians for complex cases. No uncertainty thresholds or numeric deferral rules are given.
papers.training: Not applicable (no model trained).
papers.evaluation: Proposed evaluation criteria for medical AI agents: (1) recommendation accuracy, compared against experienced clinicians using sensitivity, specificity and accuracy; (2) task execution and efficiency: task completion time, success rate, step complexity and economic cost (including licensing cost of closed-source models); (3) long-term learning and adaptation, possibly through longitudinal simulation studies; (4) explainability and transparency, e.g. feature-importance maps or decision trees, with stakeholder-specific benchmarks suggested.
papers.baselines: Not applicable. The paper contrasts human clinicians, traditional single-task medical AI and medical AI agents in a qualitative table (Table 1).
papers.results: No new quantitative results. Table 1 compares autonomy: human clinician full, traditional AI none, AI agent high; learning: traditional AI static, agent continuous; context awareness: traditional AI low to none, agent high via memory. Cited examples: Med-PaLM 2 reached expert-level performance on medical licensing questions (no number given in this review); AI sepsis alerts at Johns Hopkins showed promising sensitivity (no number given).
papers.availability: Not available (review article; no code or data).

papers.title: EvoMDT: a self-evolving multi-agent system for structured clinical decision-making in multi-cancer
papers.authors: Liu Q, Hu Z, Huang T, Niu Y, Zhang X, Ma S, Lin C, Huat GK, Kwon HE, Gao F, Sun X, Ying Z, Qiang G
papers.aim: To build a multi-agent system that copies how a multidisciplinary tumour board (MDT) makes lesion-level cancer decisions, with traceable evidence and safety checks. To test it on public QA benchmarks, real hospital cases in four cancers and a single-blind physician rating.
papers.method: Five LLM agents (Diagnostic, Treatment, Safety, Monitoring, Coordinator) built on DeepSeek V3/R1 reason over a pan-cancer guideline knowledge base with hybrid retrieval. The Coordinator merges agent outputs by confidence-weighted consensus with a safety-first conflict rule, and a self-evolution loop rewrites prompts and workflow after each task. Validation had three layers: six QA benchmarks, 405 retrospective real cases from four Chinese hospitals, and single-blind rating by five oncologists.
papers.result: Benchmark accuracy 0.86 (MedQA), 0.89 (MedQA-Cancer), 0.75 (MedMCQA-Cancer) vs Llama3-70B 0.76/0.76/0.63 and Claude-3 0.79/0.75/0.69. BERTScore 0.66 (MedQARo), 0.63 (MedQuAD), 0.68 (ROND). On 405 real cases semantic similarity 0.62-0.68, ROUGE 0.04-0.06, AI score 6-9 vs 2-3 for baselines. Physician composite score 3.44 (95% CI 3.29-3.59) of 5, within the range of five physicians. Median response time 10.6 min vs 15.8-18.9 min for physicians (all P < 10^-98).
papers.tools: DeepSeek V3 and DeepSeek R1 (foundation LLMs, interchangeable); hybrid retriever BM25 + domain embeddings (weights 0.8 semantic / 0.2 keyword); lightweight medical knowledge graph; ontologies ICD-10/11, TNM-8, SNOMED CT, RxNorm/ATC, CTCAE v5.0, RECIST/iRECIST; DrugBank, Lexicomp, FAERS; BERTScore with BGE-m3 and Qwen3-Embedding; DeepSeek as AI judge; Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.1.0, CUDA 12.1, cuDNN, Hugging Face Transformers, scikit-learn, timm; Ubuntu server with 8 x NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB); EDC system for ratings.
papers.gap: Only four cancer types and retrospective Chinese data; no imaging or raw unstructured notes as direct input; no prospective deployment or patient outcome study; no formal calibration analysis of agent confidence scores; evaluation relies on text similarity and AI judges.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), EvoMDT is a direct template for a brain-tumour care-pathway orchestrator: role-separated agents, JSON message passing with provenance, a coordinator using confidence-weighted consensus and safety-first tie-breaking, and a three-layer validation (benchmarks, real cases, blinded clinician rating). It does not include a deferral rule, so our calibrated selective-autonomy layer would add an explicit 'defer to clinician' path where EvoMDT only weights confidence. Its rubric and ICC-based reader study can be adapted for Sri Lankan neurosurgeon validation.
papers.limitations: Retrospective datasets limited in scale and geography (four tertiary hospitals in China). Site practice and documentation differences remain. No evaluation in other cancers (gastrointestinal non-HCC, gynaecologic, sarcomas, rare tumours). Knowledge base built from published guidelines only; future work to add registry and trial evidence. Response-time gains measured on structured dossiers, not raw records. Interpretability may not capture complex reasoning or ethics. Future work: prospective deployment, patient-outcome studies, trust calibration, multi-modal fusion, human-in-the-loop continual learning, regulatory-grade auditability.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team first built a pan-cancer, lesion-centric knowledge base. Guideline PDFs and web pages (international and Chinese) were split by a deterministic parser into atomic rules: staging rules, therapy steps with dose and schedule, contraindications, and follow-up intervals. Each rule was mapped to ICD-10/11, TNM-8, RxNorm/ATC, CTCAE v5.0 and RECIST/iRECIST, kept its original evidence grade (NCCN, ESMO, ASCO), and carried provenance (source, version, page anchor) and a version hash. Retrieval mixed dense semantic search (weight 0.8) with BM25 keyword search (weight 0.2) and a small knowledge graph of disease-stage-biomarker-therapy and drug-drug links. When sources disagreed, the rule was: safety first, then stronger evidence, then local jurisdiction, then recency. On top of this they ran five DeepSeek V3/R1 agents with role prompts. The Diagnostic agent gives a ranked differential, stage and confidence. The Treatment agent scores options by a weighted utility. The Safety agent checks drug interactions and contraindications and can veto risky plans. The Monitoring agent writes a 0-3, 3-12 and >12 month follow-up plan. Each agent returns JSON with its conclusion, a confidence score and cited evidence. The Coordinator combines them as sum of weight x recommendation x confidence, raises the Safety agent's weight in high-risk cases, scores conflict severity, and resolves trade-offs safety-first while logging what it accepted and rejected. A self-evolution loop edits prompts and workflow after each task. Evaluation had three layers. Layer 1 used MedQA, MedQA-Cancer and MedMCQA-Cancer (accuracy) and MedQuAD, MedQARo and ROND (BERTScore with BGE-m3 and Qwen3-Embedding over 5 seeds). Layer 2 used 405 retrospective cases from four Chinese hospitals (lung 100, breast 100, HCC 105, lymphoma 100), with no imputation of missing fields. Outputs were compared with expert plans using ROUGE, semantic similarity and a DeepSeek judge score, against shuffled-plan and nonsense baselines. Layer 3 had five oncologists (3-25 years of experience), trained for 60 minutes on 5 pilot cases. Blinded to the source, they rated paired EvoMDT and human plans in randomised order on six 1-5 Likert dimensions. Agreement was measured with ICC(2,1), and times were compared with Mann-Whitney U tests with FDR correction.
papers.studyDesign: System development plus multi-layer evaluation: (1) benchmark testing on six public medical QA datasets; (2) multi-centre retrospective study of real-world cases from four tertiary hospitals in China (Peking University Third Hospital; Shanxi Cancer Hospital; Henan Cancer Hospital; First Affiliated Hospital of Fujian Medical University), cases diagnosed/treated October 2023 to March 2025, ethics approved, consent waived; (3) single-blind, randomised, paired physician rating study with five oncologists.
papers.datasets: Public QA benchmarks (filtered for oncology relevance): MedQA (general medical exam MCQ); MedQA-Cancer (cancer-only subset of MedQA); MedMCQA-Cancer (oncology questions from Indian MedMCQA); MedQuAD (about 47,000 QA pairs from NIH sites such as cancer.gov); MedQARo (Romanian cancer case QA, over 100,000 QA pairs); ROND (Radiation Oncology NLP Database). Number of questions used per benchmark: Not reported. Real-world cohort: 405 de-identified patient records with expert MDT treatment plans as ground truth: lung adenocarcinoma n = 100, breast cancer n = 100, hepatocellular carcinoma n = 105, malignant lymphoma n = 100. Unit of analysis is the index lesion at first diagnosis; for multifocal, bilateral or recurrent disease only the primary index lesion was included, others kept as metadata. Knowledge base: international and Chinese guideline catalog (Supplementary Tables 1-2), containing no patient data.
papers.preprocessing: Guideline PDFs/HTML segmented by a deterministic parser into atomic recommendation units (staging rules, therapy steps with dose and schedule, contraindications, surveillance intervals), normalised to ICD-10/11, TNM-8, RxNorm/ATC, CTCAE v5.0, RECIST/iRECIST, cast into machine-readable schemas (indication, line of therapy, biomarker thresholds, organ-function gates, exceptions) with provenance (source, version/year, page/table anchors), version hashes, quarterly update sweeps and hot-fix ingestion. Native evidence grades (NCCN, ESMO, ASCO, Chinese systems) mapped to an internal ordinal scale. Patient records: oncologist-led standardisation into a unified schema (demographics, pathology, stage, lesion descriptors, initial treatment plan); missing or inconsistent variables kept as 'not available' with no imputation. Cases presented as structured standardised case dossiers (demographics, lesion-level staging/biomarkers, organ function, comorbidities). No model training split, as the system is prompt-based: Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Five agents, each a foundation LLM (DeepSeek V3 / R1) with a role prompt (given in Table 2) and retrieval. Diagnostic Agent: Bayesian differential diagnosis P(D|S) = P(S|D)P(D)/P(S), TNM/BCLC/Lugano staging, investigations ranked by yield, calibrated confidence. Treatment Agent: multi-criteria decision analysis U(T) = sum w_i v_i(T) over efficacy, safety, cost, patient factors; pharmacogenomics (CYP450, HLA); sequencing by Markov decision processes. Safety Agent: composite risk R = sum alpha_i R_i + sum beta_j I_j; drug interaction queries to DrugBank, Lexicomp, FAERS; signal detection (PRR, BCPNN, GPS); contraindications graded absolute/major/moderate/minor/theoretical; prioritises safety over efficacy. Monitoring Agent: utility M(t) = sum p_i(t) s_i / c_i over acute (0-3 months), intermediate (3-12 months), long-term (>12 months) phases with RECIST/iRECIST and CTCAE v5.0. Coordinator Agent: weighted consensus D_final = sum w_i D_i C_i (w = domain-relevance weight, C = agent confidence), dynamic weights by case (complexity raises Diagnostic, refractory disease raises Treatment, high risk raises Safety), conflict severity S_conflict = alpha D_semantic + beta R_risk + gamma I_implementation triggering hierarchical safety-first resolution. Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus tolerating f < n/3 faulty agents (n = 5). Agents exchange structured JSON with conclusion, confidence and evidence list with provenance triplets (source ID, anchor, version); Coordinator logs accepted/rejected options, conflicts and tie-break rationale. Retrieval: hybrid with 0.8 semantic and 0.2 keyword (BM25) weight plus knowledge graph; source conflicts resolved by safety first, then higher evidence strength, jurisdiction match, then recency. Self-evolution: after each task the system refines agent prompts and changes workflow structure (add an agent, reorder tasks, switch serial to parallel). Values of alpha, beta, gamma and w_i: Not reported. No explicit abstention/deferral threshold.
papers.training: No model training or fine-tuning; prompt-based system with iterative prompt refinement from expert feedback and development cases, validated by board-certified oncologists. Hardware: Ubuntu server with eight NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs (24 GB each), Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.1.0, CUDA 12.1; fixed random seeds. Optimizer, learning rate, epochs, batch size: Not applicable / Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Layer 1: MCQ benchmarks scored by accuracy; generative benchmarks scored by BERTScore F1 with multilingual encoders BGE-m3 and Qwen3-Embedding, default pooling, resampled over 5 random seeds; metrics normalised for a radar chart. Layer 2: 405 real cases compared to expert plans with ROUGE-1/ROUGE-L recall, semantic (cosine/BERTScore) similarity, and an AI ensemble score (DeepSeek judge, 0-10 scale); planned outcomes also included guideline concordance, weighted plan concordance, evidence traceability and safety-violation rate. Baselines: random (shuffled expert plans within the same cancer) and simple/rule-based (wrong generic advice such as 'take cold medicine'). Layer 3: five board-certified oncologists (3, 7, 12, 18, 25 years experience) had 60-min rubric training and 5 pilot cases (target ICC > 0.70); single-blind paired A/B comparison of EvoMDT vs human MDT plan, stratified block randomisation by cancer type and complexity, randomised case and A/B order; six dimensions on 1-5 Likert (Safety & Ethics, Efficiency, Completeness, Clinical Appropriateness, Evidence Utilization, Patient-Centeredness) using a unified tumour-specific rubric (Table 3); EDC with range checks; response time = wall-clock time from dossier available to complete plan submitted; times < 0.5 min reviewed; outliers by Tukey fences (+/-3 IQR); post-lock missingness < 2%.
papers.baselines: Llama3-70B, Claude-3, Med-PaLM 2 (benchmarks); random shuffled-plan baseline and simple/rule-based wrong-answer baseline (real cases); five human oncologists (physician study).
papers.results: MCQ accuracy: EvoMDT MedQA 0.86, MedQA-Cancer 0.89, MedMCQA-Cancer 0.75; Llama3-70B 0.76/0.76/0.63; Claude-3 0.79/0.75/0.69. Generative BERTScore: EvoMDT MedQARo 0.66, MedQuAD 0.63, ROND 0.68; Claude-3 0.61/0.59/0.65; Med-PaLM 2 0.62/0.63/0.63. Real cases: ROUGE about 0.04-0.06; semantic similarity 0.62-0.68; AI score 6-9 points across breast, liver, lung, lymphoma vs about 2-3 for random and simple baselines. Physician study (n = 405 dossiers): composite mean 3.44 (95% CI 3.29-3.59); Response Completeness and Safety & Ethics 3.68 (95% CI 3.58-3.78), high-score rate (>=4) 63.7%; Clinical Appropriateness, Efficiency, Evidence Utilization, Patient-Centeredness each 3.32 (95% CI 3.23-3.42), high-score rate 43.5%. Physician composite means by cancer ranged 3.01-3.92 (e.g., lung: 3.26, 3.53, 3.68, 3.92, 3.09). Response time median 10.6 min (IQR 9.5-12.0; mean 10.8 +/- 1.7) vs physician medians 15.8-18.9 min (30-40% faster). Composite means across cancers 3.3-3.5, no significant difference.
papers.statistics: Two-sided tests, alpha = 0.05; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (q < 0.05). Mann-Whitney U EvoMDT vs each physician time: all P < 10^-98, rank-biserial r = 0.74-0.85. Kruskal-Wallis across cancers P > 0.10. Chi-square/Fisher for categorical outcomes. ICC(2,1) two-way random, absolute agreement: Safety & Ethics 0.89 (0.85-0.93), Completeness 0.86 (0.82-0.90), Clinical Appropriateness 0.85 (0.81-0.89), Efficiency 0.84 (0.80-0.88), Evidence Utilization 0.83 (0.79-0.87), Patient-Centeredness 0.79 (0.75-0.83). Spearman inter-dimension rho mostly |rho| < 0.10; strongest Evidence x Patient-Centeredness rho = 0.095 (P < 0.05). Sensitivity analyses with site fixed effects and age/stage adjustment (values not reported).
papers.availability: Code: core modules and prompts at https://github.com/KesselZ/EvoMDT. Data: not public; available from corresponding author on reasonable request.

papers.title: A multi-agent approach to neurological clinical reasoning
papers.authors: Sorka M, Gorenshtein A, Aran D, Shelly S
papers.aim: To test how well large language models (LLMs) handle neurology board-exam reasoning, and whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or a five-agent framework improves their accuracy.
papers.method: The authors built a benchmark of 305 Israeli neurology board exam questions and graded each on three complexity dimensions. They tested 10 LLMs as base models and with RAG over a neurology textbook. The three best models were then run inside a five-agent CrewAI system (classifier, interpreter, retriever, synthesiser, validator), and results were checked on 155 neurology questions from MedQA.
papers.result: Base accuracy ranged from 46.8% (DeepSeek-R1-8B, MedLLaMA3) to 90.9% (o1). RAG raised GPT-4o from 80.5% to 87.3% but cut Meditron-70B from 52.9% to 41.2%. The multi-agent system reached 94.6% with o1, 89.3% with GPT-4o and 89.2% with LLaMA 3.3-70B (base 69.5%, p < 0.001). On MedQA neurology, agentic GPT-4o reached 94.8% and LLaMA 3.3-70B 81.3%.
papers.tools: Python 3.11.9; CrewAI 0.95.0 (multi-agent); ChromaDB 0.5.10 (vector store); Ollama 0.4.4 (local models); BAAI bge-large-en-v1.5 embeddings; SaveFile/ReadFile tools; models: OpenAI o1-preview, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA 3.3-70B-Instruct, LLaMA 3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B and -8B, Meditron-70B, OpenBioLLM-70B, MedLLaMA3 v20; knowledge base: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice (8th ed., 2022).
papers.gap: Text-only questions; no images, no real patient records, no uncertainty-based deferral to clinicians. The validator agent did not catch retrieval gaps and often reinforced reasoning errors. No clinician-in-the-loop or prospective clinical testing.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration), this paper gives a concrete, reproducible agent pipeline (complexity classifier, query decomposition, retrieval, synthesis, validator with feedback loop) in a neurology domain that includes neuro-oncology questions. It shows that agent decomposition lifts an open-source 70B model close to frontier-model accuracy, which matters for a low-resource Sri Lankan deployment where local open models may be needed. Its finding that the validator shares the same blind spots supports our design choice of calibrated uncertainty and deferral to clinicians rather than self-validation alone.
papers.limitations: Benchmark excludes questions with visual elements; board-style performance may not transfer to real clinical cases with incomplete information; RAG benefit was dataset-specific (textbook matched board exam better than MedQA); multi-agent computation may be too slow for real-time use; p-values are unadjusted and exploratory. Future work: specialised architectural components, better knowledge integration, multimodal inputs.
papers.methodologyDetail: Step 1, data: the team took 305 four-option MCQs from three Israeli neurology board exams (June 2023 to September 2024), had them professionally translated from Hebrew, and removed questions with images. Two neurologists tagged each question with one of 13 subspecialties and a reasoning type (263 diagnostic, 42 therapeutic). A senior panel checked answers and scored each question L1-L3 on three axes: factual knowledge depth, clinical concept integration and reasoning complexity. For external validation they filtered 155 neurology items out of 1,273 MedQA questions using an LLM and then manual checks. Step 2, base testing: ten LLMs (8B to 70B open models plus OpenAI o1 and GPT-4o) answered every question with the same prompt, temperature 0.7 and top-p 0.9, no tuning. Step 3, RAG: they chunked Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice (8th ed.) into 512-token chunks with 128-token overlap, embedded them with bge-large-en-v1.5 (batch 32, normalised), stored them in ChromaDB 0.5.10 and retrieved the top 60 passages by cosine similarity for each question. Step 4, agents: the three best RAG models (o1, GPT-4o, LLaMA 3.3-70B) were placed in a CrewAI 0.95.0 pipeline of five agents. A classifier labels complexity; an interpreter extracts concepts and writes several search queries; a retriever runs repeated searches and writes passages to files (SaveFile) to avoid context limits; a synthesiser reads the files in chunks (ReadFile) and scores each option; a validator approves the answer or sends it back to the interpreter for another loop. A controller passes JSON between agents. Open models ran locally via Ollama 0.4.4. Step 5, analysis: accuracy with Wilson 95% CIs and F1 were computed overall, per complexity level, per subspecialty and per exam; Fisher's exact tests compared each method to base. The key outcome was LLaMA 3.3-70B rising from 69.5% to 89.2% with agents. Step 6: they manually classified remaining errors into retrieval gaps and four reasoning failure types. To adapt this for brain-tumour support, one could keep the five-role structure but add a calibrated confidence output and a deferral rule, because the validator alone did not catch its own errors.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark (in silico) evaluation study. Technion-Israel Institute of Technology and Rambam Health Care Campus, Haifa, Israel, with Mayo Clinic, USA. No patients involved; uses exam questions.
papers.datasets: (1) Israeli Board Certification Exams in Neurology, June 2023 to September 2024, three exam periods: 305 four-option multiple-choice questions, translated from Hebrew to English; questions with visual elements excluded. 13 subspecialties, most common Neuromuscular (22%), Behavioral and Cognitive Neurology (15%), Movement Disorders (10%). Reasoning type: 263 (86%) diagnostic, 42 (14%) therapeutic. Each question graded L1-L3 on factual knowledge depth (FKD), clinical concept integration (CCI) and reasoning complexity (RC). Pass mark 65%. (2) MedQA (US licensing exam): from 1,273 questions, 155 (12.1%) neurology questions selected by LLM classification then manual validation by two authors.
papers.preprocessing: Professional translation Hebrew to English; removal of image-based questions. Two authors (SS, AG) assigned each question to one of 13 subspecialties (dominant domain if two). Senior neurologist panel validated answers against guidelines and graded complexity. Knowledge base: textbook split by semantic chunking into 512-token chunks with 128-token overlap, embedded with bge-large-en-v1.5 (normalised embeddings, batch size 32). No train/test split, as no model training was done.
papers.modelDetails: Five CrewAI agents with a central controller and JSON data flow. (1) Question Complexity Classifier labels the question as simple fact recall or complex integration; this guides later steps. (2) Question Interpreter breaks the question into key concepts (symptoms, history, findings) and writes optimised search queries per concept (e.g., five queries in the worked example). (3) Research Retrieval Agent queries the RAG store (ChromaDB, cosine similarity, top 60 passages per query) in multiple rounds and saves passages to files with a SaveFile tool to get around token limits. (4) Answer Synthesis Agent reads the question, the decomposed concepts and the stored chunks incrementally with a ReadFile tool and evaluates each option with structured reasoning. (5) Validator Agent checks the answer against medical criteria and knowledge-base consistency; if it fails, it sends feedback to the Question Interpreter for another cycle; if it passes, the answer is final. No numeric confidence or deferral threshold is reported. Sampling: temperature 0.7, top-p 0.9 for all models.
papers.training: No model training or fine-tuning. Inference only with standard prompts (temperature 0.7, top-p 0.9), no model-specific hyperparameter tuning. Open models run locally via Ollama; OpenAI models via API versions o1-preview 2024-12-01-preview and GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini 2024-08-01-preview. Hardware and run time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Three conditions: base model, RAG-enhanced, and agentic framework (agentic only for o1, GPT-4o, LLaMA 3.3-70B). Metrics: accuracy with 95% Wilson score confidence intervals and F1 score. Results also broken down by complexity level (FKD, CCI, RC L1-L3), by 13 subspecialties and by exam period. External validation on 155 MedQA neurology questions. Qualitative error analysis of remaining errors of the best model (retrieval failures vs four reasoning failure types).
papers.baselines: Ten base LLMs without retrieval and with standard RAG: o1, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, LLaMA 3.3-70B, LLaMA 3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-70B, DeepSeek-R1-8B, Meditron-70B, OpenBioLLM-70B, MedLLaMA3 v20.
papers.results: Board exam (n=305), base / RAG / agentic accuracy: o1 90.9% (87.1-93.6), F1 0.952 / 92.2% (88.6-94.7), F1 0.959 / 94.6% (91.6-96.7), F1 0.973. GPT-4o 80.5% (75.9-84.7) / 87.3% (83.0-90.5) / 89.3% (85.2-92.2), F1 0.943. LLaMA 3.3-70B 69.5% (64.1-74.4) / 73.4% (68.2-78.1) / 89.2% (85.2-92.2), F1 0.943. Base and RAG only: DeepSeek-R1-70B 87.7% / 86.7%; GPT-4o-mini 60.7% / 73.4%; OpenBioLLM-70B 65.9% / 68.8%; Meditron-70B 52.9% / 41.2%; LLaMA 3.1-8B 57.5% / 65.9%; DeepSeek-R1-8B 46.8% / 67.9%; MedLLaMA3 46.8% / 54.9%. LLaMA 3.3-70B level-3 questions base / RAG / agent: FKD 57.5% / 70.0% / 87.5%; CCI 66.3% / 70.2% / 90.3%; RC 61.0% / 73.2% / 92.6%. Subspecialty gains for LLaMA agent vs RAG: headache 50% to 100%, neuromuscular 74% to 100%, neuroimmunology 67% to 86%, neuro-ophthalmology 72% to 93%. MedQA neurology (n=155) base / RAG / agent: o1 96.8% / 94.8% / 94.8%; GPT-4o 85.2% / 89.7% / 94.8%; LLaMA 3.3-70B 76.8% / 74.8% / 81.3%. Complexity dimension correlations: FKD-CCI 0.56, FKD-RC 0.51, CCI-RC 0.67.
papers.statistics: Accuracy with 95% CI by Wilson score method. Fisher's exact test (alpha 0.05) for base vs RAG (10 comparisons) and base vs agent (3 comparisons), unadjusted. p-values vs base: RAG o1 0.664, GPT-4o 0.027, LLaMA 3.3-70B 0.326, DeepSeek-R1-70B 0.809, GPT-4o-mini 0.001, OpenBioLLM 0.491, Meditron 0.004, LLaMA 3.1-8B 0.038, DeepSeek-R1-8B <0.001, MedLLaMA3 0.053; Agent o1 0.085, GPT-4o 0.003, LLaMA 3.3-70B <0.001. Pearson correlation between complexity dimensions (0.51-0.67). Inter-rater agreement for classification: Not reported.
papers.availability: Data available as supplementary tables (S1-S3 Files, including the 305-question complexity classification). Code: Not available.

papers.title: CARE-AD: a multi-agent large language model framework for Alzheimer's disease prediction using longitudinal clinical notes
papers.authors: Li R, Wang X, Berlowitz D, Mez J, Lin H, Yu H
papers.aim: To predict Alzheimer's disease (AD) onset up to 10 years before the first diagnosis code by using a team of specialist LLM agents that read longitudinal clinical notes, as a virtual multidisciplinary consultation.
papers.method: A fine-tuned LLaMA 3.1 8B extraction agent finds AD-related symptom sentences in VHA notes and sorts them into five categories, building an age-ordered patient profile. Five specialist agents (primary care, neurology, psychiatry, geriatrics, clinical psychology) on LLaMA 3 70B assess the profile with role prompts, and an AD specialist agent combines them into a yes/no risk prediction. It was tested retrospectively on 1000 AD cases and 3627 matched controls at seven prediction horizons.
papers.result: Accuracy 0.83 at -1 day and 0.53 at -10 years. At -10 years CARE-AD (0.53) beat zero-shot (0.26), chain-of-thought (0.35), self-consistency (0.43) and self-refine (0.45) with the same LLaMA 3 70B, and equalled AutoGen multi-agent only when AutoGen used 12+ calls (0.53). Random forest on structured data reached only 0.40 at -10 years. Extraction agent binary F1 0.81, accuracy 0.93.
papers.tools: LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct fine-tuned with LoRA (Hugging Face PEFT) for extraction; LLaMA 3 70B for specialist and AD specialist agents (zero-shot role prompts); AutoGen framework for baseline; spaCy sentence segmentation; scikit-learn random forest with TF-IDF features; GPT-4 used earlier to create synthetic training sentences; 8 x NVIDIA A6000 (48 GB) GPUs; secure VA VINCI environment.
papers.gap: Single US veteran population (98% male); no prospective or workflow testing; uncertain answers are forced to positive instead of a formal deferral or calibrated confidence; no comparison with larger proprietary LLMs due to privacy rules; modest accuracy at long horizons.
papers.relation: For O1, CARE-AD is a clear pattern for agent hand-off: an extraction agent produces a structured, time-ordered profile, specialist agents each give domain views, and a coordinator (AD specialist) synthesises them. Its ablation shows each specialist adds value (removing the neurologist drops accuracy 0.53 to 0.50), which supports specialist agents (radiology, pathology, neurosurgery) in our brain-tumour orchestrator. It also shows a privacy-driven design (open-weight models run on-premises), useful for Sri Lanka. Its handling of 'uncertain' outputs as positive is a gap our calibrated deferral design can fill.
papers.limitations: VHA data may not generalise (sex imbalance, socioeconomic issues, high PTSD and TBI rates). Minimum 5 years of notes required, which may cause selection bias against low-utilisation patients. Diagnosis date set by first ICD code; true diagnosis may be earlier, inflating -1 day results. Privacy limits stopped testing of GPT-family models. Future work: non-VHA validation, more data sources, public datasets and other LLMs, integration into clinical decision-support workflows.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors used US Veterans Health Administration EHR data from 2000 to 2022. AD cases had at least two AD ICD codes from 2015 to 2022, one given in a specialty clinic, and at least 5 years of prior notes. This gave 17,488 cases. Up to four controls without dementia were matched to each case on age, sex, race/ethnicity, health-care use, Charlson index and deprivation index, giving 64,691 controls. Because the LLM pipeline is zero-shot and costly, they randomly drew 1000 cases and 3627 controls for evaluation. Notes from relevant clinics were split into sentences with spaCy, and short (<3 tokens), numeric-only or long (>125 tokens) sentences were removed. To build the extraction agent, two annotators supervised by two physicians labelled 5112 notes from 76 AD patients (kappa 0.868), giving 11,571 sentences in five symptom classes. Synthetic sentences from MIMIC-III and GPT-4 were added. Two LLaMA 3.1 8B models were fine-tuned with LoRA (PEFT, 8 A6000 GPUs, about 10 h): one for AD-relevant vs not (negatives at 5:1), and one for the five-class label. Labelled sentences were placed on an age timeline to build each patient's profile, cut at seven horizons from 1 day to 10 years before diagnosis. Five LLaMA 3 70B agents (primary care, neurologist, psychiatrist, geriatrician, clinical psychologist) each read the profile with a role prompt and wrote an assessment. An AD specialist agent then combined the five into a final answer, using six calls in total. Any answer that was not a clear 'no risk' was scored as AD-positive. Performance was measured with class-wise precision, recall, F1 and accuracy, with 95% CIs from 5000 stratified bootstrap samples. Comparisons were single-model zero-shot, CoT, self-consistency, self-refine, AutoGen debate (1-3 rounds), leave-one-agent-out ablation, and a TF-IDF random forest on structured codes.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective case-control study using US Veterans Health Administration Corporate Data Warehouse EHR data (2000-2022), IRB approved by VA Bedford Health Care, consent waived. Zero-shot evaluation of a multi-agent LLM system on a random evaluation subset, with single-model, multi-agent conversation, ablation and structured-data baselines.
papers.datasets: VHA CDW cohort: 17,488 AD cases and 64,691 matched controls. AD cases: AD-specific ICD codes between 1 Oct 2015 and 30 Sep 2022, at least two AD diagnoses on separate occasions, one in a specialty clinic (neurology, geriatrics, GeriPACT, mental health, psychology, psychiatry, geriatric psychiatry) by a relevant specialist (identified by Stop Codes); minimum 5-year observation window. Controls: no dementia codes, up to 4 per case matched on age, sex, race/ethnicity, clinical utilisation, Charlson Comorbidity Index and Area Deprivation Index. Evaluation set: 1000 AD cases and 3627 controls (age 79.0 +/- 8.4 vs 78.6 +/- 8.6; male 98.2% vs 98.4%; White 79% vs 80.3%; Black 13.1% vs 11.0%; AD-relevant sentences per year 99 vs 60). Extraction training data: gold standard of 5112 notes from 76 AD patients (not in the evaluation set) giving 11,571 annotated sentences, plus a synthetic dataset (MIMIC-III sentences labelled by LLM, and GPT-4 generated labelled sentences). Five symptom classes: cognitive impairment, notice/concern by others, requiring assistance/functional impairment, physiological changes, neuropsychiatric symptoms (class counts in Supplementary Table 1, not given in main text).
papers.preprocessing: Notes restricted to relevant encounter types (primary care, emergency, home-based primary care, memory clinic, neurology, neuropsychology, geriatrics, psychiatry, psychology, cognitive care nursing, mental health, compensation and pension exams, consultations), from EHR start or study start up to the AD index date. Sentence segmentation with spaCy; removed sentences with fewer than 3 tokens, numeric-only, or more than 125 tokens. Binary classifier negatives sampled from the same 76 patients at a 5:1 negative-to-positive ratio. Classified sentences mapped to patient age and aggregated chronologically into time-stamped profiles. Observation windows end 1 day, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 and 10 years before first AD diagnosis. Random forest baseline: 1000 patients held out, then 90%/10% train/tune split of the rest. No training split for the LLM agents (zero-shot).
papers.modelDetails: Step 1, data extraction agent: two separate LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct models fine-tuned with LoRA for logit-based classification: (a) binary AD-relevant vs not for each sentence; (b) for relevant sentences, five-class symptom category by argmax over logits. Step 2, profile construction: category-labelled sentences ordered by patient age. Step 3, five domain agents on LLaMA 3 70B with structured role prompts (primary care physician for holistic view; neurologist; psychiatrist; geriatrician for daily living and independence; clinical psychologist for behaviour) each give an assessment of the profile. Step 4, AD specialist agent (LLaMA 3 70B) integrates the five assessments with extracted evidence into an AD risk answer. Total six LLM calls per patient, one round, no inter-agent debate. Decision rule: if the AD specialist states no AD risk or symptoms unrelated to AD, the case is negative; all other answers, including uncertainty or 'needs further testing', are counted as AD-positive. No numeric confidence threshold. Prompts in Supplementary Note 5 and agent setup in Supplementary Table 6.
