Reader study: nine board-certified neuropathologists (3 junior < 5 years, 4 intermediate 5-15 years, 2 senior > 15 years) from USA, EU, East Asia, Southeast Asia read 20 FFPE + 20 frozen slides within 90 s each, then optionally re-read untimed; binary diagnosis plus confidence 0/25/50/75/100%; no IHC, genomics or history; Fleiss' kappa and Jaccard index. Heatmaps reviewed by neuropathologists (40 random correct heatmaps; 33 slides scored 1-10 on 12 histologic features).
papers.baselines: Nine foundation models without uncertainty control (CTransPath, Phikon, Lunit, UNI, Virchow2, CONCH, GPFM, mSTAR, CHIEF); end-to-end weakly supervised Swin Transformer; identical model without uncertainty control (ablation); OOD baselines Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensemble; Ciga (AUROC 0.469, excluded).
papers.results: Mayo held-out: PICTURE AUROC 0.998 (95% CI 0.995-1.0); baselines 0.833 (Phikon) up to near PICTURE (Virchow2, UNI). External FFPE: UPenn 0.996 (0.990-1.0) vs UNI 0.976 (P < 0.001), Virchow2 0.995 (P = 0.243 in figure; 0.387 in text); BWH 0.987 (0.961-1.0) vs UNI 0.977 (P = 0.025), Virchow2 0.975 (P = 0.014); Vienna 0.992 (0.982-0.999) vs UNI 0.966, Virchow2 0.964 (both P < 0.001); TVGH 0.992 (0.986-0.998) vs CONCH 0.982 (P = 0.001), Virchow2 0.980 (P < 0.001). Frozen: UPenn 0.958 (0.919-0.988) vs Swin 0.898 (P < 0.001), CONCH 0.946 (P = 0.067); BWH 0.987 (0.956-1.0) vs CONCH 0.987 (P = 0.505), CHIEF 0.971; Vienna 0.982 (0.956-0.997) in text (0.988 in figure) vs UNI 0.966; TVGH 0.924 (0.846-0.985) vs CONCH 0.919 (P = 0.427). Pooled five-fold: PICTURE 0.999, Virchow2 1.000, UNI 0.999, Lunit 0.995, Phikon 0.994, GPFM 0.987, CTransPath 0.950, CONCH 0.959, CHIEF 0.962, mSTAR 0.973. Abstract range across five independent cohorts: AUROC 0.924-0.996; overall 0.989. Mean epistemic uncertainty: frozen GBM 0.070, frozen PCNSL 0.103, FFPE GBM 0.045, FFPE PCNSL 0.048. OOD AUROC 0.919 (0.914-0.923) vs MC dropout 0.666 (0.638-0.695) and deep ensemble 0.554 (0.525-0.584); samples with certainty < 0.5 were 84.7% OOD. Readers: Jaccard 0.56-0.87 (FFPE), 0.49-0.81 (frozen); 113 misdiagnoses, 81 (71.7%) with reported confidence <= 50%. Heatmap features in 40 correct cases: dense tumour 90%, infiltration 77.5%, haemorrhage 72.5%, microvascular proliferation 25%, pseudopalisading necrosis 22.5%. Necrosis classifier AUROC 0.92 (3384 annotated instances).
papers.statistics: 95% CIs by 1000 bootstrap samples; one-sided bootstrap significance tests (N = 1000); DeLong's test; two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (necrosis P = 1.97e-4, nuclear size heterogeneity P = 1.51e-4, cell density P = 1.57e-23; senior/intermediate vs junior P = 0.0128 FFPE, 0.0318 frozen; OOD vs GBM P < 0.001, vs PCNSL P = 0.008); Fleiss' kappa 0.271 (FFPE) and 0.248 (frozen); Jaccard index.
papers.availability: Code and trained models: https://github.com/hms-dbmi/picture. TCGA data from GDC; Vienna pathology data at https://doi.org/10.25493/WQ48-ZGX; other cohorts on request with data use agreements (non-commercial academic use only).

papers.title: Human-AI collaboration in large language model-assisted brain MRI differential diagnosis: a usability study
papers.authors: Kim SH, Wihl J, Schramm S, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether working together with a large language model (LLM) changes the accuracy and speed of brain MRI differential diagnosis by radiology residents. It also looks at where human-LLM interaction goes wrong.
papers.method: A retrospective, single-centre, randomised cross-over usability study. Six radiology residents read 40 difficult brain MRI cases, half with conventional internet search and half with an LLM search engine (PerplexityAI powered by GPT-4). Accuracy, time, confidence, LLM logs (hallucinations, wrong inputs) and questionnaires were analysed.
papers.result: LLM-assisted reading gave higher accuracy: 70/114 (61.4%) vs 53/114 (46.5%) correct, p = 0.033 (chi-square); median numeric score 1 vs 0, p = 0.021; Cohen's h = 0.30. Mixed model beta = 0.150, SE = 0.065, p = 0.021. No change in reading time (7.38 vs 7.17 min, p = 0.64) or confidence (median 3 vs 3, p = 0.50). When the LLM gave the correct diagnosis, readers used it in 82.1% (60/73) of cases. Reader prompts were wrong in 9.2% of cases; LLM hallucinated in 11.5% of cases (5.4% of queries).
papers.tools: PerplexityAI chatbot / search engine with GPT-4 (OpenAI, November 2023); Toggl Track time-tracking software; Radiopaedia.org as reference for hallucination checks; G*Power v3.1 for sample size; Python 3.9.7 for analysis.
papers.gap: Only inexperienced residents and a controlled setting were tested. The LLM was text-only, so readers had to describe images by hand. No uncertainty signal or deferral was given by the LLM, and medical-specific or multimodal LLMs were not tested.
papers.relation: A controlled study of radiologists working with an LLM on brain MRI diagnosis, giving evidence for designing clinician validation steps.
papers.limitations: Readers were residents with little neuroradiology experience (mean 6.3 months), so results may not hold for experts. Controlled setting, not real clinical workload. Gold standard is imperfect for some imaging-only diagnoses. Readers had little training on the LLM tool compared with web search. PerplexityAI mixes search and LLM, and its limits are not studied. A general-purpose LLM (GPT-4) was used. Future work: voice interaction, multimodal LLMs that read images, integration with RIS/PACS, medical-specific LLMs.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team built a reader study to see how people actually use an LLM, not how the LLM performs alone. First, they picked 40 adult brain MRI exams (2016-2023) from their hospital archive. Each case had a focal, uncommon but definite diagnosis, confirmed by histology (17 cases) or by two neuroradiologists using follow-up (23 cases). One radiologist (3 years of experience) drew arrows on the key finding. The 40 cases were split at random into two sets of 20. Six radiology residents (mean 6.3 months of neuroradiology) were split at random into two groups. In a cross-over design, each resident read one set with normal web search and the other set with PerplexityAI running GPT-4, so each case was read equally often with each workflow. Before the LLM session, residents had a 10-15 minute training with 3 practice cases and a sample prompt (age range, sex, symptoms, MRI findings, ask for likely diagnoses). They could prompt freely and could also use web search to check the LLM. For every case they gave up to 3 ranked diagnoses, a 5-point confidence score, and their time was logged with Toggl Track. Cases were removed if the reader knew the case, missed the finding, or solved it without help (12 of 240 responses), leaving 114 per arm. Accuracy was scored as binary (true diagnosis in top 3) and as rank score 0-3. Tests: chi-square, Mann-Whitney U, t-test, Cohen's h, and a mixed-effects model with reader and case as random effects. Three radiologists reviewed all LLM logs against Radiopaedia to count wrong inputs and hallucinations, and a 2x2 table linked LLM correctness to reader correctness. Result: accuracy rose from 46.5% to 61.4% (p = 0.033) with no time cost, but hallucinations (11.5% of cases) and wrong prompts (9.2%) remained. A PhD student can reuse this cross-over design, scoring scheme and log-audit method to validate a multi-agent system with clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective, diagnostic, randomised cross-over usability (reader) study at one institution: Klinikum rechts der Isar, Technical University of Munich, Germany. Reading sessions from 3 November 2023 to 8 July 2024. IRB approved; informed consent waived.
papers.datasets: Local imaging database, Klinikum rechts der Isar. 40 brain MRI exams acquired between 01/01/2016 and 12/31/2023, split at random into two sets of 20. Diagnosis confirmed by histopathology in 17/40 (42.5%) or by agreement of two neuroradiologists with follow-up in 23/40 (57.5%). Inclusion: adult (at least 18 years), focal image finding, confirmed diagnosis, initial diagnosis at time of exam, non-trivial less common conditions (examples: hemangioblastoma, MVNT, PRES, PML, cavernous malformation, idiopathic intracranial hypertension). Key finding marked with arrows by one radiologist with 3 years of experience. Readers: 6 radiology residents (mean 6.3 months neuroradiology experience, range 2-11 months). 240 reader responses in total; 12 excluded (familiar with case n = 1, did not see finding n = 2, could solve without research n = 9), leaving 114 per arm.
papers.preprocessing: No image preprocessing (no AI image model). Arrow annotations added to the key finding on each MRI. Readers received the MRI plus demographic and clinical details. All prompts written in English. Randomisation: 40 cases into two sets of 20; 6 residents into two groups; cross-over so each case was read with both workflows equally often. Training: 10-15 min introduction to the LLM tool using 3 sample cases not in the test set, with a sample prompt (age range, sex, symptoms, MRI findings, request for most likely differential diagnoses).
papers.modelDetails: No model was trained. Tool: PerplexityAI, a retrieval-augmented LLM search engine that reads real-time web content and cites sources, powered by GPT-4. Readers wrote free prompts (no fixed strategy) and could also do conventional web search to check LLM suggestions. Each reader gave up to 3 ranked differential diagnoses per case. No uncertainty estimate or deferral rule was built in; the human reader made the final decision.
papers.training: Not applicable (no model training). Human training: 10-15 minute session with 3 sample cases before the LLM-assisted session. Readers completed cases over 4 sessions.
papers.evaluation: Two accuracy scores: binary (correct if true diagnosis in top 3) and numeric rank score (3 = first, 2 = second, 1 = third, 0 = absent). Interpretation time measured with Toggl Track. Confidence on a 5-point Likert scale. Pre-study survey (demographics, experience, LLM exposure) and post-study questionnaire (clinical applicability, response quality, ease of adoption, overall experience). LLM logs reviewed for number of queries, query type, number of differential diagnoses, number and type of sources. Three radiologists (2, 3 and 8 years of experience) screened logs for incorrect user inputs and hallucinations, comparing with Radiopaedia. A contingency table linked correct LLM suggestion to correct reader answer. Qualitative notes from observers (SHK, SS) were grouped by theme.
papers.baselines: Conventional internet search workflow (same readers, cross-over).
papers.results: Binary accuracy: LLM-assisted 70/114 = 61.4%; conventional 53/114 = 46.5%; p = 0.033. Numeric score median: 1 vs 0; p = 0.021. Mixed-effects model: beta = 0.150, SE = 0.065, z = 2.309, p = 0.021. Cohen's h = 0.30. Time: 7.38 +/- 3.35 min vs 7.17 +/- 3.49 min, p = 0.64. Confidence median 3 vs 3, p = 0.50. LLM logs (113/114 cases; 1 log lost): queries per case 2.12 +/- 1.56; differential diagnoses per case 7.59 +/- 5.23; sources per response 13.0 +/- 12.34; 72.0% of sources were journal articles; 64.2% of queries asked for differential diagnosis, 11.1% sample images, 3.7% image features. Incorrect user input 9.2% of cases (4.3% of queries). Hallucinations 11.5% of cases (5.4% of queries); 9/13 wrong imaging features, 4/13 wrong anatomical associations. Contingency: LLM correct and reader correct 60; LLM correct but reader wrong 13 (17.9%); LLM wrong but reader correct 10 (14.3% of correct readers); both wrong 30. Questionnaire medians: use in practice 4, response quality 4, ease of adoption 4, overall experience 3.5.
papers.statistics: Chi-square test (binary score); Mann-Whitney U test (numeric score and confidence); independent Student's t-test (time); significance p < 0.05. Cohen's h for effect size. Linear mixed-effects model with workflow as fixed effect and participant and case as random effects. Sample size: effect size 0.2, power 80%, alpha 0.05, two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test, minimum 208 responses (G*Power 3.1). No inter-rater agreement reported for the hallucination panel.
papers.availability: Not available (case list in supplementary material; no code or data repository). Preprint on medRxiv: https://doi.org/10.1101/2024.02.05.24302099

papers.title: Clinical implementation of artificial intelligence in neuroradiology with development of a novel workflow-efficient picture archiving and communication system-based automated brain tumor segmentation and radiomic feature extraction
papers.authors: Aboian M, Bousabarah K, Kazarian E, Zeevi T, Holler W, Merkaj S, Cassinelli Petersen G, Bahar R, Subramanian H, Sunku P, Schrickel E, Bhawnani J, Zawalich M, Mahajan A, Malhotra A, Payabvash S, Tocino I, Lin M, Westerhoff M
papers.aim: To build and test a workflow that runs automated brain-tumour segmentation and radiomic feature extraction inside the clinical PACS, so radiologists can check and correct AI output in their normal reading tool and build annotated datasets during routine work.
papers.method: A UNETR model was trained on 1,251 BraTS 2021 FLAIR series to segment the whole tumour plus oedema, and tested on 73 high-grade gliomas from Yale New Haven Health against a neuroradiologist's manual masks. The model was deployed with Docker and NVIDIA Triton inside the Visage 7 PACS, where radiologists can edit the mask; PyRadiomics was embedded in the PACS to extract 106 features, which were checked against a reference implementation outside PACS.
papers.result: Validation mean DSC 0.90 (BraTS hold-out). External test (73 Yale high-grade gliomas): median DSC 0.86, mean DSC 0.81. Total segmentation processing 2.33 s (PACS interaction 0.33 s, pre/post-processing 1.48 s, inference 0.52 s); abstract reports about 4 s on average. Radiomics extraction of 106 features took about 4 s (abstract: 5.8 +/- 0.01 s). With matched PyRadiomics version 3.0, PACS and reference features agreed with zero error; with mismatched versions 17 of 106 features differed by up to 1.4%.
papers.tools: UNETR (UNet Transformer); Visage 7 PACS client (Visage 7-1-18) and Visage AI Accelerator research PACS (Visage Imaging); Docker; NVIDIA Triton inference server; TensorRT; mixed precision; Python API; PyRadiomics v3.0 (reference v3.0.post3.dev0+ge100f1d); HD-BET-style brain extraction (Isensee et al., 2019); OWASP Docker security checklist; NVIDIA TITAN RTX 24 GB GPU, Intel Core i7-6900K 3.20 GHz CPU, 64 GB RAM; DICOM presentation state for saving masks; JSON export.
papers.gap: Only whole-tumour FLAIR segmentation was tested; no uncertainty estimate or flag tells the radiologist when the AI mask may be wrong; no measurement of how much time radiologists save or how often they edit masks; single institution test set; no prospective clinical evaluation.
papers.relation: For O1 (multi-agent orchestration) this is a concrete template for how an imaging/segmentation agent can be plugged into the hospital PACS: the PACS calls a containerised model through an API, the result returns as an editable overlay, and the clinician verifies or corrects it before downstream radiomics. Our framework can reuse this human-in-the-loop hand-off pattern but add a calibrated confidence score so low-confidence masks are routed to the clinician first, which this paper does not do.
papers.limitations: Accuracy assessed only on FLAIR whole-tumour masks. Trained on BraTS but tested on one institution (several hospitals of one health system). Small test set (73 cases); authors say it has been expanded to 430 glioma cases. Only one radiomics tool (PyRadiomics). DSC lower than BraTS 2021 challenge results, partly because the clinical data includes motion-degraded scans. Future work: use stronger models such as nnU-Net, expand training with institutional data, and move toward AI running unsupervised on each eligible study.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team first trained a whole-tumour segmentation model. They took all 1,251 FLAIR series with whole-tumour labels from BraTS 2021 and split them into 1,151 for training and 100 for validation. Each volume was skull-stripped, cropped, reoriented, resampled by trilinear interpolation to 1.5 x 1.5 x 2 spacing, and z-score normalised; this result was cached. A UNETR network (transformer encoder, U-Net decoder) was trained on 128 x 128 x 64 patches; the z axis was resampled from 1 to 2 so the patch fits in a 24 GB NVIDIA TITAN RTX. Training ran for 250 epochs and the checkpoint with best validation mean Dice (0.90) was kept; gains stopped after epoch 170. The model was further trained on internal Yale data. For testing, pre-operative MRI of 73 adults with pathologically proven high-grade glioma was anonymised and copied from the clinical PACS to a research PACS (Visage AI Accelerator). A board-certified neuroradiologist, blinded to grade and outcome, manually drew 3D whole-tumour plus oedema masks as ground truth. The AI reached median Dice 0.86 and mean 0.81. For deployment, the model was packed in a Docker container (following OWASP Docker security rules) and served by NVIDIA Triton with TensorRT and mixed precision. When the radiologist presses a button in Visage 7, a Python API fetches the images, preprocesses them, sends an HTTP request to Triton, runs sliding-window inference with flip test-time augmentation, and returns the mask as an editable overlay. Total time was 2.33 s (0.33 s PACS I/O, 1.48 s pre/post-processing, 0.52 s inference). The radiologist checks or edits the mask, saves it as a DICOM presentation state, and then runs embedded PyRadiomics to get 106 features in JSON (about 4 s). Features matched an external reference exactly once both used PyRadiomics v3.0 (before, 17 features differed by up to 1.4%), and were identical across three repeat runs. To adapt this, one could swap UNETR for nnU-Net, add multi-sequence input, and attach an uncertainty score that decides whether the mask is shown as pre-approved or flagged for review.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective technical development and implementation study at Yale New Haven Health / Yale School of Medicine (New Haven, CT, USA) with Visage Imaging (Berlin, Germany; San Diego, USA). IRB approved; consent waived. Model development on public BraTS 2021 and testing on internal pre-operative MRI of adults with pathologically proven grade 3-4 gliomas.
papers.datasets: (1) BraTS 2021 (RSNA-ASNR-MICCAI): multi-institutional multi-sequence glioma MRI; all 1,251 FLAIR series with whole-tumour labels used; split 1,151 training and 100 validation. (2) Yale New Haven Health internal test set: pre-operative MRI FLAIR of 73 pathologically proven high-grade gliomas (adults, grade 3 and 4); images anonymised and moved from clinical PACS to research PACS; reference standard = manual 3D whole tumour plus surrounding oedema segmentation by one board-certified neuroradiologist blinded to grade and outcome. Inclusion: adults, pathologically proven glioma grade 3/4, pre-operative MRI. Exclusion: Not reported. Data include motion-degraded but clinically relevant scans.
papers.preprocessing: Brain extraction (Isensee et al., 2019); cropping; reorientation; resampling with trilinear interpolation to spacing 1.5 x 1.5 x 2 (reported as cm3 in the paper, z resampled from 1 to 2 to save memory); z-score intensity normalisation. Training on volumetric patches of 128 x 128 x 64 with patch sampling; preprocessing done once per volume and cached. Split: BraTS 1,151 train / 100 validation; external test 73 Yale cases. Test-time augmentation: flipping along each axis. Augmentation during training: Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Architecture: UNETR, a 3D U-Net style network with a transformer encoder instead of convolutional encoder layers; input = single FLAIR volume; output = whole-tumour (tumour + oedema) mask. Patch 128 x 128 x 64 chosen because a 128^3 nnU-Net-style patch at 1 mm isotropic would not fit in 24 GB VRAM. Inference uses sliding window, test-time flipping on each axis, mixed precision and TensorRT. Deployment pipeline: (1) radiologist opens study in Visage 7; (2) viewer content passed to a Python API in a Docker container, which pulls image data from PACS; (3) container preprocesses and sends an HTTP request to NVIDIA Triton; (4) segmentation returned and converted to an overlay in the viewer; (5) radiologist edits the mask with standard PACS tools (with copy/paste of masks across sequences and a quad MPR layout with 3D registration); (6) mask saved as DICOM presentation state; (7) radiologist runs embedded PyRadiomics on the curated mask, output 106 features as JSON. Segmentation and extraction can also be pre-run before the radiologist opens the study. No uncertainty, confidence or deferral rule. Loss function: Not reported.
papers.training: Trained on BraTS 2021 FLAIR (1,151 train, 100 validation) and then further trained on an internal Yale dataset (size not reported). Training stopped after 250 epochs; best model chosen by validation mean DSC (0.90); model stopped improving after epoch 170. Optimizer, learning rate, batch size, loss and scheduler: Not reported. Hardware: NVIDIA TITAN RTX (24 GB), Intel Core i7-6900K @ 3.20 GHz, 64 GB RAM. Training time: Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Segmentation accuracy: Dice similarity coefficient between AI mask and neuroradiologist manual mask on 73 external Yale cases; Figure 2 also shows Jaccard index, positive predictive value, true positive rate and true negative rate (values only in the figure). Timing: processing time per step on the deployment hardware. Radiomics correctness: relative difference of 106 PyRadiomics features extracted inside PACS versus a reference script outside PACS, and repeatability across three separate extraction time points. No cross-validation, no reader study.
papers.baselines: No model baselines. Comparison to published literature and to BraTS 2021 challenge results (qualitative). Radiomics compared with an external PyRadiomics reference implementation.
papers.results: BraTS validation set: best mean DSC = 0.90. Yale test set (n = 73): median DSC = 0.86, mean DSC = 0.81. Timing: total segmentation processing = 2.33 s (PACS image retrieval and storing = 0.33 s; preprocessing and postprocessing = 1.48 s; model inference = 0.52 s); the abstract states segmentation took on average 4 s. Radiomics: 106 features in about 4 s (abstract: 5.8 +/- 0.01 s). Feature agreement: with PyRadiomics v3.0 vs v3.0.post3.dev0, 17 of 106 features differed by up to 1.4%; with matched v3.0 the absolute error = 0; zero error across three time points. Total time for segmentation plus feature extraction below 5 s.
papers.statistics: Descriptive only (median and mean DSC, mean +/- SD time, relative difference). No statistical tests, p-values or confidence intervals reported. Single reader, so no inter-rater agreement.
papers.availability: Code and model: Not available. Raw data: available from the authors on request (data availability statement). BraTS 2021 is public.

papers.title: Evaluating the clinical utility of artificial intelligence assistance and its explanation on the glioma grading task
papers.authors: Jin W, Fatehi M, Guo R, Hamarneh G
papers.aim: To run a phase II clinical user study of AI assistance for glioma grading on MRI. To measure whether AI predictions and heatmap explanations change neurosurgeons' accuracy, trust and willingness to use AI.
papers.method: A 3D VGG-like CNN was trained on BraTS 2020 to classify GBM vs grade II/III glioma, and SmoothGrad was chosen from 16 XAI methods to make heatmaps. In an online pre-post survey, 35 Canadian neurosurgeons each read 25 MRIs alone, then with the AI prediction, then with the heatmap. Accuracy, decision changes, trust and willingness to use AI were analysed with Friedman and Wilcoxon tests.
papers.result: Physician accuracy 82.5 +/- 8.7% alone, 87.7 +/- 7.3% with AI prediction (p = 0.002), 88.5 +/- 7.0% with added explanation (p = 0.35 vs prediction only). AI accuracy 88.0% on the 25-case subset. Trust rose from 5.31 to 6.72 after seeing performance metrics (p = .0004). Mean heatmap quality rating 6.12 +/- 2.92 of 10.
papers.tools: 3D VGG-like CNN (six 3D conv layers + two fully connected layers); SmoothGrad (selected among 16 post-hoc XAI algorithms); online survey with MRI and heatmap videos; SciPy and Pingouin for statistics. Hardware and framework: Not reported.
papers.gap: Heatmaps did not improve accuracy and did not tell clinicians when to trust the AI; no model confidence was shown; small sample (35, no radiologists); simulated task on public retrospective data; binary grading only.
papers.relation: For O1 this informs the clinician-validation interface of the orchestrator. Showing AI predictions improved accuracy, but heatmaps alone did not help clinicians decide when to rely on the AI, and clinicians asked for model confidence. This supports adding calibrated confidence and explicit deferral flags, not only saliency maps. The pre-post read protocol, trust and willingness scales and decision-change analysis can be reused in our Sri Lankan clinician study.
papers.limitations: Authors: only 35 participants, no radiologists enrolled, which blocks multivariate analysis; phase II simulated task on retrospective data; future phase III randomised trial in real clinical settings needed; XAI should be co-designed with clinicians and users need training. Also: data from the medRxiv preprint version, numbers may differ slightly from the journal version; DR+XAI always followed DR+AI so order effects cannot be separated.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors used the public BraTS 2020 set of 369 pre-operative glioma MRIs (76 grade II/III, 293 GBM) with four sequences that were already co-registered, resampled to 1 mm3 and skull-stripped. They made a stratified split of 239 training, 56 validation and 74 test cases, keeping the grade ratio. A 3D VGG-like CNN with six 3D convolution layers and two fully connected layers was trained to output GBM or grade II/III; test accuracy was 90.54%. From 16 post-hoc attribution methods they chose SmoothGrad because it was most faithful to the model. From the test set they sampled 25 cases (7 grade II/III, 18 GBM) so the model's error pattern matched the full test set; the AI scored 88.0% on these. A pilot with 6 residents gave an effect size of 1.3 and a required sample of 13. They then ran a Canada-wide online survey (October 2021 to February 2022). Participants with solo accuracy at or below 0.55 were excluded. Thirty-five neurosurgeons took part. Each first saw the AI's performance metrics, then read 25 MRIs in random order. For each case they gave their own grade, then saw the AI prediction and could revise, then chose whether to view the heatmap video, saw it, gave a final grade and rated how well the heatmap matched their judgment (0-10). Trust and willingness to use AI were rated at baseline, after seeing metrics and after all cases. Because data were not normal, a Friedman test and Bonferroni-corrected Wilcoxon tests were used. Accuracy rose from 82.5% to 87.7% with predictions (p = 0.002) but not further with heatmaps (88.5%, p = 0.35). Decision-change counts showed that heatmaps caused both right and wrong switches. A PhD student can copy this staged read design to compare our system with and without calibrated confidence and deferral flags, using the same trust scales and decision-change analysis.
papers.studyDesign: Phase II pre-post clinical user study (online survey + optional interview), Canada-wide, simulated task on retrospective public MRI. Simon Fraser University and University of British Columbia. Ethics: SFU REB H20-03588. Recruitment October 2021 to February 2022.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2020: 369 pre-operative glioma MRI cases from 19 institutions (incl. TCGA/TCIA), 4 sequences (T1, T1C, T2, FLAIR); 76 grade II/III and 293 GBM, pathology confirmed. Clinical test subset: 25 MRIs (7 grade II/III, 18 GBM) from the hold-out test set, sampled to keep the model's confusion-matrix proportions. Participants: 35 neurosurgeons enrolled (12 attendings, 2 fellows, 21 residents) from 236 contacted (14.8%); 29 completed; 6 dropped out after 2, 3, 3, 3, 8 and 17 cases. Inclusion: MD, consultant or trainee in neurosurgery/radiology/neuroradiology, and solo accuracy above 0.55. Pilot: 6 neurosurgical residents. Demographics: female:male 7:19; age 34.7 +/- 8.2; years in medicine 9.8 +/- 9.1; years in neurosurgery 7.1 +/- 6.5.
papers.preprocessing: BraTS pre-processing: co-registration to the same T1 template, resampling to 1 mm3, skull-stripping. Stratified split 65% train (239 cases), 15% validation (56), 20% hold-out test (74), same grade ratio in each set, no patient overlap. Augmentation and intensity normalisation: Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: 3D VGG-like CNN: six 3D convolutional layers followed by two fully connected layers; input 4-sequence 3D MRI; output GBM vs grade II/III. Explanation: SmoothGrad heatmap chosen from 16 post-hoc feature-attribution methods as the most truthful to the model (evaluation in Supplement S2). Heatmap shown as 3D video overlaid on MRI. No confidence score or deferral rule shown to users.
papers.training: Optimizer, learning rate, epochs, batch size and hardware: Not reported. Accuracies: training 80.28%, validation 92.86%, test 90.54%.
papers.evaluation: Per MRI (randomised order per participant): (1) DR: own grade; (2) DR+AI: AI prediction revealed, updated judgment; (3) asked if they want the explanation (yes/no), shown SmoothGrad heatmap, DR+XAI final judgment; rated heatmap agreement on 0-10 scale. Trust (-5 to 5, rescaled 0-10) and willingness to use AI (0-10) asked at baseline, after seeing AI performance metrics, and after 25 cases. Explanation goals ranked from 15 options. Optional 20-30 min interview analysed qualitatively. Metric: accuracy (also sensitivity, specificity, F1 in supplement); decision agreement and decision change; common language effect size. Pilot-based sample size: effect size 1.3, alpha 5%, power 90%, needed 13.
papers.baselines: Physicians alone (DR) vs physicians + AI prediction (DR+AI) vs physicians + AI prediction + explanation (DR+XAI); AI alone 88.0% on the subset.
papers.results: 2,279 decisions (DR 761, DR+AI 759, DR+XAI 759). Accuracy: DR 82.49 +/- 8.69% (median 84, range 60-100); DR+AI 87.70 +/- 7.33% (median 88, range 68-100); DR+XAI 88.52 +/- 7.02% (median 88, range 72-100). Common language effect size: DR+AI > DR 67.2%; DR+XAI > DR 71.0%; DR+XAI > DR+AI 53.6%. Agreement with AI: 81.0% (615/759) DR, 86.8% (659/759) DR+AI, 87.2% (662/759) DR+XAI. Decision changes with AI prediction: 5.8% (44/759), 81.8% (36/44) correct, 18.2% (8/44) wrong. With explanation: 1.7% (13/759), 69.2% (9/13) correct, 30.8% (4/13) wrong. Trust: baseline 5.31 +/- 2.04, after metrics 6.72 +/- 1.67, after use 6.62 +/- 2.68. Willingness: 4.10 +/- 2.79, 5.07 +/- 2.45, 4.59 +/- 3.16. Need for explanation: 66% (23/35) degree < 0.3, 20% (7/35) > 0.7; 14% never, 9% always. Heatmap quality 6.12 +/- 2.92 (744 ratings). Top explanation goal: build and calibrate trust (selected 18 times).
papers.statistics: Shapiro-Wilk (normality) and Mauchly (sphericity); Friedman test accuracy chi2(2) = 23.53, p < 0.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank with Bonferroni: DR+AI vs DR Z = 9.0, p = 0.002; DR+XAI vs DR Z = 3.0, p = 0.0004; DR+AI vs DR+XAI Z = 15.5, p = 0.35. Trust Friedman chi2(2) = 16.97, p = .0002; baseline vs metrics Z = 4.0, p = .0004; baseline vs use Z = 58.0, p = .025. Willingness chi2(2) = 8.09, p = .018; baseline vs metrics Z = 29.5, p = .012. Spearman trust-willingness 0.70 (p < 0.001). Chi-square need-explanation vs disagreement chi2(1) = 62.7, p < 0.001. Alpha 0.05.
papers.availability: Survey data and analysis code in Supplemental S4 (per preprint). BraTS 2020 is public. Model code: Not available.

papers.title: Deep learning-based postoperative glioblastoma segmentation and extent of resection evaluation: Development, external validation, and model comparison
papers.authors: Cepeda S, Romero R, Luque L, et al.
papers.aim: To build a deep learning model that segments postoperative glioblastoma MRI (residual enhancing tumour, edema, surgical cavity) and classifies extent of resection (EOR) with the RANO-Resect system. It also compares the model with other public segmentation tools on external data.
papers.method: A multi-institutional retrospective cohort of 395 scans (184 patients) was used to train two 3D models, UNETR in MONAI and nnU-Net 3D full-resolution, with 5-fold cross-validation. The models were compared with 7 public algorithms on a 52-scan external cohort, then the best model was tested on a 139-patient independent cohort and BraTS 2020 validation. Residual tumour volumes were turned into RANO-Resect EOR classes by volume thresholds.
papers.result: RH-GlioSeg-nnU-Net was best: median Dice 0.81 (ET), 0.77 (edema), 0.81 (cavity) on the comparison cohort. EOR 2-class accuracy 0.96 and 5-class accuracy 0.85. Image-level residual tumour detection AUC 0.98, precision 0.93. On the independent Oslo cohort: ET Dice 0.48, AUC 0.98, 2-class EOR accuracy 0.84. On BraTS 2020 preoperative validation: mean Dice 0.78 (ET), 0.88 (whole tumour), 0.72 (tumour core).
papers.tools: MONAI (UNETR), nnU-Net v-3D full resolution, dcm2niix, SimpleElastix, SRI24 atlas, SynthStrip, ITK-SNAP 4.0.1, USE-Evaluator; Python 3.9, PyTorch 2.1.1+cu121, TensorFlow 2.10.0/2.13.0, WSL Ubuntu 20.04.4; Intel Core i7, 64 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 3090 24 GB GPU.
papers.gap: Small residual tumours (under 2.69 cm3) are still poorly segmented, and Dice drops to 0.48 on the independent cohort. No uncertainty estimate or deferral is given. Full 5-class EOR could not be tested on the independent cohort. Training data come only from Europe/public sets, not from low-resource settings.
papers.relation: An externally validated postoperative glioblastoma model that represents the surgical-outcome stage of the pathway an orchestrator must cover.
papers.limitations: Postoperative segmentation is hard (blood, air, hemostatic material). Ground truth from manual/semiautomatic segmentation carries inter-observer variability. Independent cohort had only ET labels, so only 2-class EOR could be tested. Model comparisons are not fully fair because models differ in architecture, preprocessing and training data, and some were not built for postoperative scans. Future work: test in other clinical settings, expand open science and federated initiatives such as FL-PoST and BraTS post-treatment challenge.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built a postoperative glioblastoma segmentation tool and tested it against others. They first gathered 395 MRI scans from 184 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients: 3 hospitals (Valladolid, Trondheim, Madrid) and 3 public sets (LUMIERE, Burdenko, IvyGAP). Each scan had T1w, T1ce, T2w and FLAIR; scans with artefacts or missing sequences were dropped. The mix was deliberate: 112 preoperative, 181 early postoperative (within 72 h) and 102 follow-up scans, on the idea that seeing the tumour before and after surgery helps the model learn residual tumour. Images were converted with dcm2niix, registered to the SRI24 atlas, resampled to 1 mm isotropic (SimpleElastix), skull-stripped (SynthStrip), Z-score normalised and set to 240 x 240 x 155. Two neurosurgeons drew three labels in ITK-SNAP (enhancing tumour, edema, cavity), checked by a neuroradiologist, about 35 minutes per patient. They trained two models with 5-fold cross-validation: UNETR in MONAI (input 128 x 128 x 64, hidden size 768, 12 heads, DiceFocal loss, 200 epochs per fold) and nnU-Net 3D full-resolution (Dice + cross-entropy, 1000 epochs per fold, heavy augmentation), each as a 5-fold ensemble without post-processing, on one RTX 3090. Predicted residual volumes were mapped to RANO-Resect classes using fixed thresholds (1 cm3 and 5 cm3), and a 0.1 cm3 cut-off decided whether any residual tumour was present. They ran seven public models and their own two on 52 external scans from two Spanish hospitals and QIN-GBM, scoring with USE-Evaluator (Dice, HD95, ASSD, volume metrics) and EOR accuracy. nnU-Net won (Dice 0.81/0.77/0.81; EOR accuracy 0.96 for 2 classes, 0.85 for 5 classes). The best model was then run on 139 Oslo patients (ET Dice 0.48, AUC 0.98, EOR accuracy 0.84) and on BraTS 2020 (Dice 0.78/0.88/0.72). A student can reuse the pipeline from GitHub as a postoperative agent and add an uncertainty-based deferral step for small residual tumours.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective, multi-institutional model development and external validation study. Training sites: Rio Hortega University Hospital (Valladolid, Spain), St. Olavs University Hospital (Trondheim, Norway), 12 de Octubre University Hospital (Madrid, Spain) plus public LUMIERE, Burdenko GBM Progression and IvyGAP datasets. External: La Princesa University Hospital (Madrid), Albacete University Hospital (Spain), QIN-GBM public dataset; independent: Oslo University Hospital (Norway); BraTS 2020 online validation. Ethics: REK Norway 2016/1791, 397012, 2019/510; CEIm Rio Hortega 21-PI085.
papers.datasets: IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (WHO CNS 2021), MRI sequences T1w, T1ce, T2w, FLAIR. Exclusion: poor image quality from artefacts or missing sequences. Training cohort: 184 patients, 395 scans (112 preoperative, 181 early postoperative within 72 h, 102 follow-up with recurrence by modified RANO). By site: Rio Hortega 57 patients/162 scans; 12 de Octubre 21/63; St Olavs 33/87; LUMIERE 38/38; Burdenko-GBM-Progression 30/30; IvyGAP 5/15. Postoperative EOR in training: 135 GTR / 43 residual tumour; median residual ET 2.55 cm3 (IQR 12.31). Model comparison cohort: 52 early/late postoperative scans (Albacete 21, La Princesa 15, QIN-GBM 16); 23 GTR / 29 residual; median ET 6.08 cm3. Independent validation: Oslo University Hospital, 139 patients early postoperative, 5 GTR / 134 residual, median ET 0.66 cm3, ET labels only. BraTS 2020 validation: 125 preoperative patients. RANO class distribution: Class 2A 61.9% in training, 42.6% in comparison cohort; Class 2B 54% in independent cohort.
papers.preprocessing: DICOM to NIfTI with dcm2niix; co-registration to SRI24 atlas; resampling to 1 mm isotropic with SimpleElastix; skull stripping with SynthStrip; Z-score intensity normalisation; final size 240 x 240 x 155 voxels. Public datasets received only the steps they still needed. Ground truth: 3 labels (1 = contrast-enhancing tumour, T1ce hyperintense but T1w hypointense; 2 = edema/infiltration on T2-FLAIR; 3 = surgical cavity incl. blood, hemostatic material, air; necrosis in preoperative scans) made by 2 neurosurgeons with over 10 years of experience in ITK-SNAP 4.0.1 (active contour + clustering, then manual slice-by-slice correction), approved by a neuroradiologist with over 15 years of experience; about 35 min per patient. Independent cohort labels: semiautomatic plus deep learning pre-segmentation refined by experts. Augmentation: UNETR - random flips, rotations, elastic deformations, intensity changes; nnU-Net - rotations, scaling, Gaussian noise and blur, brightness and contrast, low-resolution simulation, gamma correction, mirroring. Split: 5-fold cross-validation on the training cohort; separate external and independent test sets.
papers.modelDetails: Model 1, RH-GlioSeg-UNETR (MONAI): input resized to 128 x 128 x 64; 4 input channels (T1w, T1ce, T2w, FLAIR) and 4 output channels incl. background; feature size 32; hidden size 768; 12 attention heads; DiceFocal loss; ensemble of 5 fold models with voting; no post-processing. Model 2, RH-GlioSeg-nnU-Net: nnU-Net 3D full-resolution U-Net; Dice + cross-entropy loss; 5-fold ensemble; no post-processing. EOR rule from predicted volumes (RANO-Resect): Class 1 supramaximal = no CE tumour and <= 5 cm3 non-CE tumour; Class 2 maximal = <= 1 cm3 CE tumour (2A complete = no CE tumour plus > 5 cm3 non-CE; 2B near-total = <= 1 cm3 CE); Class 3 submaximal = > 1 cm3 CE (3A subtotal <= 5 cm3; 3B partial > 5 cm3); Class 4 biopsy. Image-level residual tumour detection uses a 0.1 cm3 threshold: below it, a case is treated as no residual tumour. No uncertainty or deferral mechanism.
papers.training: UNETR: 5 folds, 200 epochs per fold. nnU-Net: 5 folds, 1000 epochs per fold. Optimizer, learning rate and batch size not reported in the main text (nnU-Net defaults implied but not stated). Hardware: Intel Core i7, 64 GB RAM, one RTX 3090 24 GB GPU; Python 3.9, PyTorch 2.1.1+cu121. Training time not reported.
papers.evaluation: Internal 5-fold cross-validation; external comparison cohort (52 scans) for head-to-head comparison with 7 public models plus both own models; independent external cohort (139 scans) for the best model; BraTS 2020 online validation (125 cases) for preoperative performance. Segmentation metrics with USE-Evaluator: Dice, IoU, volumetric similarity, absolute volume difference, HD95 (mm), ASSD (mm), precision, sensitivity. Empty masks handled as image-level classification with a 0.1 cm3 threshold (correct classification rate, AUC, precision, sensitivity, specificity). EOR classification: precision, recall, F1, accuracy, AUC for 2 classes (maximal vs submaximal) and 5 classes. Analysis of Dice by quartile of residual ET volume.
papers.baselines: DeepMedic, HD-GLIO, PICTURE nnU-Net, DeepEOR, Raidionics AGU-Net, nnU-Net-CPS, Turin U-Net, plus own RH-GlioSeg-UNETR.
papers.results: Comparison cohort, ET (median +/- 95% bootstrapped CI): RH-GlioSeg-nnU-Net Dice 0.81 +/- 0.04, HD95 3.24 +/- 0.78 mm, ASSD 0.95, IoU 0.68, VS 0.95; HD-GLIO Dice 0.76; PICTURE-nnU-Net 0.73; RH-GlioSeg-UNETR 0.73; nnU-Net-CPS 0.69; DeepMedic 0.65; Raidionics 0.65; DeepEOR 0.23; Turin U-Net 0.05. Edema: RH-GlioSeg-nnU-Net 0.77, RH-GlioSeg-UNETR 0.77, PICTURE 0.74, HD-GLIO 0.70, DeepMedic 0.70, DeepEOR 0.58, Turin 0.15. Cavity: RH-GlioSeg-nnU-Net 0.81, PICTURE 0.77, UNETR 0.75, Turin 0.14. Image-level ET detection: RH-GlioSeg-nnU-Net AUC 0.98, precision 0.93. EOR 2-class accuracy: RH-GlioSeg-nnU-Net 0.96 (precision 0.97, recall 0.96, F1 0.96, AUC 0.96), PICTURE 0.92, HD-GLIO 0.90, nnU-Net-CPS 0.90, UNETR 0.89, Raidionics 0.89, DeepMedic 0.71, DeepEOR 0.50, Turin 0.48. EOR 5-class accuracy: RH-GlioSeg-nnU-Net 0.85 (AUC 0.88), HD-GLIO 0.79, PICTURE 0.64, UNETR 0.62, DeepMedic 0.46, DeepEOR 0.31, Turin 0.29. Independent Oslo cohort (ET): Dice 0.48 +/- 0.04, HD95 11.13 mm, IoU 0.32, precision 0.55, recall 0.53; image-level CCR 0.90, AUC 0.98, sensitivity 0.95, specificity 0.88; 2-class EOR accuracy 0.84. BraTS 2020: mean Dice ET 0.78, whole tumour 0.88, tumour core 0.72. Residual ET below 2.69 cm3 gave lower Dice for all models.
papers.statistics: Medians with 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals for segmentation metrics. No hypothesis tests or p-values between models reported. No inter-rater agreement for the ground truth reported.
papers.availability: Code and preprocessing pipeline: https://github.com/smcch/Postoperative-Glioblastoma-Segmentation (model publicly released). Images are private, available on request from the corresponding author; public parts from LUMIERE, Burdenko, IvyGAP, QIN-GBM (TCIA) and BraTS 2020.

papers.title: Intraoperative artificial intelligence for brain tumor surgery: from tissue diagnosis to real-time surgical guidance
papers.authors: Goff NK, Markert JE, Park M, et al.
papers.aim: To give an overview of state-of-the-art AI models that neurosurgeons can use during brain tumour resection. It covers cryosection, fluorescence, nanopore sequencing and stimulated Raman histology (SRH), and the barriers to clinical use.
papers.method: A narrative (non-systematic) review by the NYU Langone group. Models are grouped into three tasks: lesional vs non-lesional tissue (margins), diagnostic classification (type, grade) and molecular characterisation (WHO 2021). A summary table lists architecture, number of test patients and performance of each key model.
papers.result: Cryosection: LGNet AUROC 0.965 and 0.972 for PCNSL on two external cohorts; CHARM AUROC 0.94 (benign vs tumour), 0.84 (LGG vs HGG), 0.82 (IDH), 0.88/0.90/0.93 for oligodendroglioma/astrocytoma/glioblastoma. 5-ALA hyperspectral ML: 85.7% margin (3-class), 96.1% WHO grade, 93% IDH, 87.3% 10-class tumour type. ICG FL-CNN AUROC 0.945. Nanopore: Sturgeon 45/50 correct retrospectively, 18/25 prospectively (7 abstained); crossNN 96.11% MC and 99.07% MCF in CV, 0.83/0.88 external; ROBIN 90% concordance in under 2 h, high confidence in 76% of cases. SRH: FastGlioma AUROC 0.921 (4-class infiltration), 0.981 normal vs dense vs FLAIR 0.763, contrast 0.718, 5-ALA 0.890; DeepGlioma 91.5% subtype accuracy in under 90 s; RapidLymphoma balanced accuracy 97.81%.
papers.tools: Reviewed models: LGNet (ResNet50), CHARM (ViT), MLP and random forest on 5-ALA hyperspectral data, FL-CNN (EfficientNet-B0) on second-window ICG, Sturgeon, crossNN, NanoDx random forest, ROBIN ensemble, PromethION nanopore sequencer, FastGlioma (ResNet34 foundation model), DeepGlioma (ResNet50/transformer), RapidLymphoma (ResNet50, self-supervised), ELUCIDATE (Mask R-CNN). Figures made in BioRender. Authors used Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.8 for formatting and feedback.
papers.gap: No randomised clinical trials show patient-level benefit. Many models lack external or prospective validation. Few models are multimodal (imaging + pathology + molecular). No FDA-cleared AI device exists for intraoperative neuro-oncology. Human-AI interaction is rarely studied. Costly equipment (SRH, nanopore) limits use outside large hospitals.
papers.relation: Reviews AI tools across the neurosurgical stages of brain-tumour care, which helps define the specialised agents to orchestrate.
papers.limitations: Narrative review with no systematic search, inclusion criteria or quality assessment. The authors' group developed several of the SRH models discussed (possible bias). Future work: randomised trials with endpoints such as extent of resection, diagnostic accuracy, survival and neurological morbidity; systematic comparisons with human-AI interaction; multimodal models; FDA lifecycle and predetermined change control plans.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a narrative review, so the method is a structured reading of the field rather than an experiment. The authors (NYU Langone neurosurgery group led by Orringer, who also built several SRH tools) chose state-of-the-art intraoperative AI models and grouped them by data source and by task. The data sources are four: cryosection (frozen H&E slides, read within about 20 minutes), fluorescence (5-ALA given 3-4 hours before surgery and excited at 405 nm; ICG given 24-48 hours before), nanopore DNA methylation sequencing (100-400 Mb in 60-90 minutes on a PromethION) and stimulated Raman histology (two Raman channels at 2845 and 2930 cm-1 stitched into a virtual H&E image). The tasks are three: tissue vs non-tissue at the margin, tumour type and grade, and molecular class under WHO 2021. For each model they report architecture, number of test patients and the main metric (Table 1), for example CHARM ViT with AUROC 0.94 on 403 test patients, ROBIN ensemble with 90% concordance on 50 cases in under 2 hours, and FastGlioma with AUROC 0.921 on 220 prospective patients. They then discuss barriers: no randomised trials, little external or prospective validation, no FDA-cleared intraoperative neuro-oncology device, workflow inertia, high cost of SRH and nanopore outside large hospitals, and few multimodal models. For a PhD on multi-agent clinical AI, this review can be used as a catalogue of possible intraoperative agents with known inputs, outputs, turnaround times and accuracies. Two designs are directly useful for selective autonomy: Sturgeon returns 'not enough information' instead of a wrong class (7 of 25 prospective cases), and ROBIN combines three classifiers and reports high confidence only when they agree (76% of cases). A student could copy these ideas into an orchestrator that defers to the neuropathologist when agents disagree, and select low-cost modalities suitable for Sri Lanka.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review. Department of Neurosurgery, NYU Langone Health, New York, USA (with UT Austin Dell Medical School and University of Alabama at Birmingham). Not a primary data study; no prospective or retrospective cohort of its own.
papers.datasets: No own dataset. Data of reviewed studies: CHARM trained on 1524 glioma patients from 3 populations, 403 test patients; LGNet 686 test patients; Leclerc et al. 50 biopsies from 10 patients; Black et al. 891 biopsies from 184 patients; FL-CNN 1874 samples from 23 patients; Sturgeon 50 retrospective + 25 prospective surgeries; ROBIN 50 intraoperative cases; FastGlioma 220-patient prospective cohort; DeepGlioma 153 test patients; RapidLymphoma 160 prospective (168 test in table) patients; ELUCIDATE 35 cases in cross-validation; earlier SRH classifier with 13 histological categories.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable for the review itself. Described workflows: cryosection - freeze in cryostat, H&E stain, image, patch, feature extraction; fluorescence - 5-ALA given 3-4 h (ICG 24-48 h) before surgery, excitation at 405 nm, hyperspectral cubes or intensity images; nanopore - DNA extraction and PromethION sequencing, about 100-400 Mb in 60-90 min, 20-40 min data intervals for Sturgeon; SRH - Raman shifts 2845 cm-1 (lipids) and 2930 cm-1 (proteins/nucleic acids), third channel by subtraction, 1000-pixel strips stitched into a virtual H&E whole-slide image, then patched.
papers.modelDetails: Review content, not one model. Key mechanisms: LGNet - ResNet50 classifier of PCNSL vs non-PCNSL on frozen sections. CHARM - context-aware ViT for tumour detection, grade, IDH, 1p/19q, ATRX, TP53, CDKN2A/B, CIC with attention maps. 5-ALA - classical ML and MLPs on 5 fluorophores (2 PpIX states, NADH, lipofuscin, flavins). ROBIN - ensemble of NanoDx random forest, crossNN and Sturgeon; classifiers vote and confidence rises when they agree. Sturgeon - classifies as 'not enough information' rather than guessing (an abstention rule). crossNN - interpretable feature weights across methylation platforms. FastGlioma - SRH foundation model scoring infiltration 0-3. DeepGlioma - molecular status and subtype from SRH in under 90 s. RapidLymphoma - self-supervised learning on SRH patches.
papers.training: Not reported (review). Training details of individual models are not given.
papers.evaluation: Review summarises reported metrics: AUROC, accuracy, balanced accuracy, concordance with final diagnosis, AP50, cross-validation (leave-one-out for early SRH, k-fold for crossNN), external and prospective test sets. Notes that many studies use single-arm non-inferiority simulated trials.
papers.baselines: Reviewed comparisons: pathologists vs LGNet (pathologist + LGNet best); neurosurgeons and white-light AI vs FL-CNN; FLAIR, contrast enhancement and 5-ALA vs FastGlioma; frozen section vs RapidLymphoma; H&E histology vs SRH classifier (non-inferior).
papers.results: Table 1: LGNet AUROC 0.97 (686 test); CHARM tumour segmentation AUROC 0.94 and glioma classification 0.90 (403 test); 5-ALA infiltration MLP accuracy 85.7%, AUROC 0.95 (184 patients); 5-ALA tumour classification random forest accuracy 83.6%, AUROC 0.98; FL-CNN accuracy 89.1%, AUROC 0.945 (23 patients), LGG vs HGG AUROC 0.810, Ki-67 0.688; ROBIN accuracy 90% (50 test), MGMT concordance over 95%, IDH 9/10; FastGlioma AUROC 0.921 (220 test); DeepGlioma accuracy 91.5%, AUROC 0.926 (153 test); RapidLymphoma accuracy 97.8%, AUROC 0.987 (168 test); ELUCIDATE AP50 about 0.85 (35 CV). Early SRH lesional vs non-lesional AUROC 0.984 (LOOCV), paediatric 0.970; 13-class SRH accuracy 94.6%; cell-based SRH subtype accuracy 90.28%; Leclerc 5-ALA pilot 77%. RapidLymphoma non-inferior to frozen section in 25 PCNSL patients. Intraoperative neuropathology reports are ambiguous in about 10-20% of cases.
papers.statistics: Not reported (narrative review; no pooled analysis or tests).
papers.availability: Not available (review; no code or data).

papers.title: FUTURE-AI: international consensus guideline for trustworthy and deployable artificial intelligence in healthcare
papers.authors: Lekadir K, Frangi AF, Porras AR, et al.
papers.aim: To set an international consensus guideline for building and deploying trustworthy AI tools in healthcare. It covers the whole AI lifecycle, from design to deployment and monitoring.
papers.method: A modified Delphi consensus run over 24 months (8 rounds) by the FUTURE-AI Consortium, which grew to 117 experts from 50 countries. Six guiding principles (fairness, universality, traceability, usability, robustness, explainability) plus a general category were defined, and 30 best practices were agreed by surveys, written feedback and online meetings. Each practice is graded as recommended or highly recommended for research and for deployable tools, with practical steps per lifecycle phase.
papers.result: The final guideline has 30 recommendations: fairness 3, universality 4, traceability 6, usability 5, robustness 3, explainability 2, general 7. All were approved with less than 5% disagreement in the final vote. Round 1 produced 55 preliminary recommendations; round 2 (72 experts, >90% agreement threshold) reduced them to 22 with 16 contentious points; round 3 expanded to 30. Practical step tables (Tables 3-6) map each recommendation to design, development, evaluation and deployment phases.
papers.tools: Modified Delphi method; online surveys (5-point importance scale; agree/disagree/neutral/did not understand/no opinion scale); online and email working groups; four online consensus meetings (June 2023); website www.future-ai.eu with a self-assessment checklist.
papers.gap: Recommendations are generic and do not prescribe specific techniques. Liability and who audits remain open. Current regulations block post-release model updates. Domain-specific operationalisation (for example neuro-oncology, multi-agent systems) is not yet worked out. Cost may widen gaps for resource-limited health systems.
papers.relation: A consensus guideline that requires traceability, logging and human oversight, which sets requirements for the orchestrator's audit trail.
papers.limitations: Generic framework, applicability varies by use case; no specific methods imposed. No standard yet exists for some recommendations. Implementation may be costly, especially for small developers and resource-limited systems. Liability and auditing roles not settled. Regulations do not yet allow local adaptation after release. Future work: domain-specific operationalisation, regulatory integration, living framework updated through the website, webinars and workshops.
papers.methodologyDetail: FUTURE-AI was built with a modified Delphi process over 24 months. Step 1: the team reviewed literature on trustworthy, responsible and ethical AI, plus reporting guidelines and EU, FDA and WHO documents, then grouped requirements into six principles that form the acronym FUTURE (fairness, universality, traceability, usability, robustness, explainability). Step 2 (round 1): six working groups of three experts (clinicians, data scientists, engineers) from five EU imaging projects each drafted 6-10 best practices using medical imaging as the use case; after removing overlap they had 55 items. Step 3 (round 2): the consortium grew to 72 experts, who rated every item on a five-level importance scale and could edit, merge or add items. Items with over 90% high agreement were kept and method-specific items with negative feedback were dropped, leaving 22 items and 16 contentious points; a seventh 'general' category was added for privacy, regulation and society. Step 4 (round 3): scope widened from imaging to all healthcare, giving 30 items. Step 5 (round 4): each item was graded as recommended or highly recommended, separately for research prototypes and deployable tools. Step 6 (round 5): manuscript drafting and feedback, adding method examples. Step 7 (round 6): 44 new external experts, chosen for diversity (patients, regulators, Africa, Latin America, Asia), voted agree/disagree/neutral. Step 8 (round 7): four online meetings in June 2023 settled wording. Step 9 (round 8): final vote by 117 experts from 50 countries; all 30 items passed with under 5% disagreement. The output is a phase-by-phase checklist (Tables 3-6). For a PhD orchestrator, the most useful items are: calibrated per-patient uncertainty and implausible-output checks (traceability 3), full logging of inputs, outputs and clinician decisions with anonymised IDs in encrypted logs (traceability 5), human override (usability 2), local validity and recalibration in low-resource settings (universality 1 and 4), and federated learning or differential privacy (general 2). A student can score their system against all 30 items as a compliance table.
papers.studyDesign: International expert consensus study (modified Delphi), 24 months, started 2021. FUTURE-AI Consortium led from Universitat de Barcelona (BCN-AIM) with experts from 50 countries on all continents; origin in five EU projects (EuCanImage, ProCAncer-I, CHAIMELEON, PRIMAGE, INCISIVE; AI4HI network). Funded by EU Horizon 2020 grant 952103 (EuCanImage). Not a patient study.
papers.datasets: No patient data. Participants: round 1, six working groups of 3 experts each (18 experts); rounds 2-5, 72 experts (AI scientists, clinicians, ethicists, social scientists, legal and industry experts); round 6, 44 additional external experts (patient advocates, social scientists, regulators, more from Africa, Latin America and Asia); round 8, final consortium of 117 experts from 50 countries. Literature review of trustworthy AI, reporting guidelines (TRIPOD+AI, CLAIM, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI, PROBAST-AI, CLEAR) and EU, FDA and WHO documents.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable. Consensus process steps: literature review and thematic clustering of trustworthy AI requirements into 6 principles (Table 1); round 1 working groups proposed 6-10 best practices per principle, merged to 55 after removing overlap; round 2 survey kept items with >90% high agreement and discarded those with strong negative feedback (mostly method-specific ones), giving 22 items and 16 contentious points, plus a new general category; round 3 broadened scope from medical imaging to healthcare, giving 30 items; round 4 rated each item for research vs deployable tools; round 5 manuscript feedback; round 6 external feedback from 44 experts; round 7 four online meetings in June 2023; round 8 final online vote.
papers.modelDetails: Not an AI model. The framework structure: Fairness (define bias sources; collect individual and data attributes; evaluate fairness and correct bias). Universality (define clinical settings including low vs high resource; use standards such as SNOMED CT, OMOP, DICOM, FHIR/HL7, IEEE, ISO; evaluate on external/multisite data; evaluate local clinical validity with recalibration or fine-tuning). Traceability (risk management file; documentation such as AI information leaflet, model cards, AI passport; quality control of inputs and outputs with out-of-distribution detection, sanity checks and calibrated uncertainty per patient; periodic auditing, e.g. biannual or annual, with drift detection; logging of user actions, AI inputs, AI outputs, clinical decisions, timestamp, user ID, anonymised patient ID, in encrypted logs; governance with assigned roles and liability). Usability (user requirements; human-AI interaction and oversight with human-in-the-loop checks and ability to overrule AI; training materials; usability evaluation including automation bias; clinical utility and safety, e.g. randomised trial). Robustness (define data variations; train with representative real-world data; stress and repeatability tests). Explainability (define needs with users; evaluate explanations quantitatively and with users). General (stakeholder engagement; privacy and security incl. federated learning, differential privacy, encryption; risk mitigation; evaluation plan; regulatory compliance such as EU AI Act, MDR, FDA SaMD; ethical issues; social and environmental issues). Compliance levels: + recommended, ++ highly recommended, separately for research and deployable tools.
papers.training: Not applicable (no model training). Consensus process lasted 24 months over 8 rounds.
papers.evaluation: Quantitative analysis of voting patterns (consensus and disagreement levels) and qualitative synthesis of free-text feedback by recurring themes. Round 2 voting options: absolutely essential, very important, of average importance, of little importance, not important at all; plus keep/refine wording. Round 6 options: agree, disagree, neutral, did not understand, no opinion. Consensus threshold in round 2: >90% high agreement. Final approval: less than 5% disagreement.
papers.baselines: Compared conceptually with existing guidelines: FAIR data principles, TRIPOD+AI, CLAIM, CONSORT-AI, DECIDE-AI, PROBAST-AI, CLEAR, WHO ethics report, EU High-Level Expert Group checklist.
papers.results: Round 1: 55 preliminary recommendations from 6 groups of 3 experts. Round 2: 72 experts; 22 recommendations retained and 16 contentious points identified; seventh 'general' category added. Round 3: 30 recommendations (6 new general items). Round 6: 44 external experts gave feedback; most non-agreement due to unclear wording. Round 7: 4 online meetings, June 2023; adversarial-attack testing was merged into cybersecurity, and mandatory third-party clinical evaluation was dropped as impractical in resource-limited settings. Round 8: 117 experts, all 30 recommendations approved with <5% disagreement; remaining disagreement was mainly about 'recommended' vs 'highly recommended'. From Table 2, 26 of 30 items are highly recommended (++) for deployable tools and 13 of 30 for research tools.
papers.statistics: Descriptive consensus percentages only (>90% agreement threshold in round 2; <5% disagreement in final vote). No statistical tests.
papers.availability: Guideline and self-assessment checklist at www.future-ai.eu; appendix tables (glossary, stakeholders) online with the BMJ article. No code or data.

papers.title: Intricacies of human-AI interaction in dynamic decision-making for precision oncology
papers.authors: Niraula D, Cuneo KC, Dinov ID, et al.
papers.aim: To study how clinicians change their radiotherapy dose decisions when they see recommendations, outcome estimates and uncertainty from an AI decision-support tool (ARCliDS). The study looks at model-agnostic and model-specific collaborative behaviour.
papers.method: A two-phase within-subject reader study. Clinicians first chose a mid-treatment dose without AI (Unassisted) and then re-chose it after seeing ARCliDS recommendations (AI-assisted), and gave confidence (0-5) and an AI trust score (0-5). Decisions were analysed with matched-pair randomization t-tests, Spearman correlations and intraclass correlation coefficients.
papers.result: 144 evaluations (NSCLC 72 = 9 evaluators x 8 patients; HCC 72 = 8 evaluators x 9 patients). AI changed 41 (57%) NSCLC and 34 (47%) HCC decisions, but distribution-level tests were mostly not significant. Decision adjustment correlated with dissimilarity to AI (NSCLC rho=0.53, HCC rho=0.60, p<0.001). Agreement with AI correlated with AI trust (NSCLC rho=0.59, HCC rho=0.70, p<0.001). Inter-evaluator ICC rose with AI, e.g. NSCLC ICC(C,1) 0.135 to 0.216, HCC ICC(C,1) 0.163 to 0.264.
papers.tools: ARCliDS (model-based deep reinforcement learning, graph neural network radiotherapy environment, ensemble of 5 models for uncertainty); R Shiny, Plotly, reticulate, googlesheets4, shinyapps.io (Standard plan, max 5 instances, 8 GB each), Google Sheets storage; Python with pydicom, dicompylercore, NumPy (float16 arrays), scipy.ndimage.zoom; irr R package for ICC; randomization test code from David C Howell.
papers.gap: No ground truth for the continuous dose decisions; no external validation dataset; small sample; retrospective, simulated setting; no subgroup analysis by experience or specialty; effect of faulty AI not tested.
papers.relation: Studies how clinicians accept or override AI recommendations in oncology depending on AI confidence, which is relevant to logging and using clinician validations.
papers.limitations: Adaptive radiotherapy is not standard practice; patients came from the AI training data, not an external set; 144 evaluations give low inferential power; retrospective setting may differ from prospective behaviour; remarks were optional and uneven (48 total). Future work: prospective randomized study, larger sample, faulty-AI arms, varying explainability, time pressure, stratification by clinician characteristics, per-user online fine-tuning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors tested how clinicians work with ARCliDS, a reinforcement-learning tool that recommends a mid-treatment daily radiotherapy dose. ARCliDS was trained earlier on two retrospective trial cohorts: NSCLC patients from trial NCT01190527 (30 fractions, 13 multi-omics features chosen from 297) and HCC patients from three adaptive SBRT trials (3+2 fractions, 13 features chosen from 110). Its environment predicts TCP and NTCP, and its agent maximises a reward r = tcp(1-ntcp) with bonus points (+2 when tcp>0.70 and ntcp<0.172 for NSCLC, or tcp>0.90 and ntcp<0.25 for HCC; +1 when tcp>0.50 and ntcp<0.50). An ensemble of 5 models gives mean +/- SEM for the dose and outcomes. Cross-validated AUROC was 0.73 (TCP) and 0.79 (NTCP) for NSCLC and 0.74 and 0.68 for HCC. For the study, 8 NSCLC and 9 HCC patients were randomly picked. DICOM CT, structures and dose were converted to float16 NumPy arrays and shown as 2D slices in an R Shiny web app with Plotly viewers, auto-saving to Google Sheets. Each evaluator watched a 10-minute tutorial, then for each patient (random order) entered an unassisted dose (NSCLC 1.5-4 Gy/fx, HCC 1-15 Gy/fx) and confidence 0-5. Next they saw the AI dose, a TCP-NTCP outcome space with error bars and feature distribution plots, then re-entered dose and confidence and answered 4 items that sum to an AI trust score 0-5. They could not go back to the unassisted page. Thirteen clinicians from Moffitt and Michigan completed 17 evaluations, giving 144 paired decisions. Analysis used matched-pair randomization t-tests, Spearman correlations of derived values (adjustment aia-un, dissimilarity ai-un, agreement -|aia-ai|, closeness to standard of care), and McGraw-Wong ICC for inter-reader agreement. A PhD student can reuse this paired design, the 0-5 confidence and trust scales, and the derived quantities to measure clinician validation of a deferring AI.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective, two-phase sequential Human-AI interaction reader study (within-subject, each case: Unassisted then AI-assisted). Two institutions in the USA: Moffitt Cancer Center (Tampa, FL) and Michigan Medicine (University of Michigan). IRB Moffitt MCC# 20750. Two disease modules: NSCLC adaptive radiotherapy and HCC adaptive SBRT.
papers.datasets: (1) NSCLC: UMCC 2007-123 phase II dose-escalation trial NCT01190527; inoperable or unresectable NSCLC, 30 daily fractions (about 50 Gy EQD2 in evaluation phase, up to 92 Gy EQD2 total); endpoints local control (LC) and radiation pneumonitis grade >=2 (RP2); 297 multi-omics features reduced to 13 (cytokines pre-IL4, pre-IL15, slope-IP10; PET radiomics pre-MTV, RD-GLSZM-LZLGE, RD-GLSZM-ZSV; dosimetry tumour gEUD, lung gEUD; SNPs Cxcr1-Rs2234671, Ercc2-Rs238406, Ercc5-Rs1047768; miR-191-5p, miR-20a-5p). Training cohort size: Not reported in this paper (see Niraula et al. 2023). (2) HCC: adaptive arm of trials NCT01519219, NCT01522937, NCT02460835; adaptive SBRT 3+2 fractions with 1-month break; endpoints LC and liver toxicity (>=2 point Child-Pugh rise); 110 features reduced to 13 (sex, age, pre-cirrhosis, pre-ECOG-PS, active lesions, pre-albumin, GTV, Liver-GTV, GTV gEUD, Liver-GTV volume, RD-TGF-beta, RD-CD40L, RD-HGF); 95 of 99 HCC patients had local control. Reader study cases: 8 NSCLC and 9 HCC patients randomly selected from the training data based on imaging availability. Imaging shown: CT, RT structures, 3D dose, cumulative DVH; pre/mid PET for NSCLC; pre-treatment MRI and liver function for HCC. Readers: 20 volunteers, 13 completed, 4 did both modules, 17 completed evaluations (9 NSCLC, 8 HCC); physicians and residents of various specialties.
papers.preprocessing: DICOM CT, RT structure and 3D dose files converted with pydicom and dicompylercore: pixel-to-coordinate transform; select overlapping region between CT and dose; enlarge and interpolate dose to CT resolution with scipy.ndimage.zoom; merge all RT structures into one 3D grid using unique integer values; save as compressed float16 3D NumPy arrays. PET and MRI registered onto CT and RT structures with the same procedure. Cumulative DVH extracted. 2D axial, coronal and sagittal slices shown to reduce rendering time. AI recommendations and outcome estimates precomputed. ARTE validation used 80-20 split, 10-fold stratified shuffle cross-validation.
papers.modelDetails: ARCliDS has two parts. ARTE (artificial radiotherapy environment): radiobiologically constrained transition functions for patient state (graph of multi-omics features, graph neural network based), an RT outcome estimator (TCP and NTCP) and a reward function. ODM (optimal decision maker): agent trained with model-based deep reinforcement learning. Base reward r = tcp(1-ntcp). NSCLC reward: r+2 if tcp>0.70 and ntcp<0.172; r+1 if tcp>0.50 and ntcp<0.50; else r. HCC reward: r+2 if tcp>0.90 and ntcp<0.25; r+1 if tcp>0.50 and ntcp<0.50; else r. Dose range: NSCLC 1.5-4 Gy/fx; HCC 1-15 Gy/fx. Uncertainty: ensemble of 5 models, recommendation shown as mean +/- SEM daily dose plus EQD2; outcome space TCP vs NTCP with SEM error bars, colored by reward, green diamond for recommendation; population feature distribution plots. AI trust score (0-5) from 4 multiple-choice items: outcome reasonableness 1 pt, outcome uncertainty 1 pt, agreement with recommended dose range 2 pts, dose uncertainty 1 pt; only 'Reasonable' or 'Agree' scores points. No automatic deferral rule; the clinician always makes the final decision.
papers.training: ARCliDS modules were trained earlier on the retrospective trial cohorts (details in Niraula et al. 2023, Sci Rep); optimizer, learning rate, epochs and batch size: Not reported in this paper. Reader training: two 10-minute tutorial videos (one per disease), a pre-evaluation information session with demo and Q&A; evaluation designed to take under one hour; study ran a little over five months. Cyber security clearance took about 2 weeks (over 4 months total to reach the application).
papers.evaluation: Each evaluator saw patients in a randomized order; Unassisted phase locked once AI was seen and unassisted decision hidden on the AI page. Outcomes: unassisted decision (un), AI-assisted decision (aia), AI recommendation (ai), confidence (0-5) before and after, AI trust (0-5), free-text remarks. Derived: decision adjustment frequency, adjustment level (aia-un), dissimilarity (ai-un), agreement -|aia-ai|, closeness to standard of care -|d-SOC| with SOC 2 Gy/fx NSCLC and 10 Gy/fx HCC. Two-sided matched-pair randomization t-test on un-aia; Spearman correlations; Pearson for un vs aia; ICC (McGraw and Wong, two-way random effects, Consistency and Absolute agreement, single and average) via irr; toxicity-free local control score TCP(1-NTCP). AI model itself: 80-20 split 10-fold stratified shuffle CV, AUROC for TCP and NTCP; radiobiological self-evaluation of ODM. No external validation.
papers.baselines: Unassisted clinician decisions (Human only) versus AI-assisted decisions (Human + AI); standard of care dose (NSCLC 2 Gy/fx, HCC 10 Gy/fx); retrospective clinical decisions for the ODM self-evaluation.
papers.results: Adjusted decisions: NSCLC 41/72 (57%), HCC 34/72 (47%); 15/17 evaluations (88%) had at least 2 adjustments; NSCLC evaluators #7 and #8 made zero. Adjustment range: NSCLC 0-100% by evaluator, 44-78% by patient; HCC 22-67% by evaluator, 25-75% by patient. Adjustment vs dissimilarity: NSCLC rho=0.53, NSCLC excluding zero-adjusters rho=0.58, HCC rho=0.60 (all p<0.001). Trust vs agreement: 0.59, 0.69, 0.70 (p<0.001). aia confidence vs trust: NSCLC rho=0.14 (p=0.26), NSCLC excl. rho=0.34 (p=0.0094), HCC rho=0.47 (p<0.001). Change in confidence vs trust: HCC rho=0.32 (p=0.0055), NSCLC 0.11 (p=0.37), NSCLC excl. 0.19 (p=0.17). Change in confidence vs adjustment level: NSCLC rho=-0.24 (p=0.045), excl. -0.29 (p=0.028), HCC 0.28 (p=0.017). Confidence vs closeness to SOC: un NSCLC 0.15 (p=0.21), excl. 0.25 (p=0.059), HCC 0.32 (p=0.0056); aia NSCLC 0.092 (p=0.44), excl. 0.29 (p=0.029), HCC 0.48 (p<0.001). ICC unassisted to AI-assisted: NSCLC ICC(C,1) 0.135 [-0.005,0.507] to 0.216 [0.04,0.606]; ICC(A,1) 0.102 to 0.201; ICC(C,9) 0.584 to 0.713; ICC(A,9) 0.504 to 0.694; HCC ICC(C,1) 0.163 to 0.264; ICC(A,1) 0.117 to 0.195; ICC(C,8) 0.608 to 0.742; ICC(A,8) 0.515 to 0.659. NSCLC: 76% of adjustments raised TCP and NTCP; HCC: 74% (25/34) lowered TCP and NTCP. Score change aia-un: NSCLC mean 0.0011 (SD 0.0058); HCC mean 0.0059 (SD 0.0144), median 0.0034. ARTE AUROC: NSCLC TCP 0.73+/-0.15, NTCP 0.79+/-0.17; HCC TCP 0.74+/-0.27, NTCP 0.68+/-0.24. ODM reproduced 36% good / improved 74% bad decisions (NSCLC) and 50% / 30% (HCC). Remarks: 48 total (14, 14, 9, 11).
papers.statistics: Two-sided matched-pair randomization t-test (H0: un-aia=0), mostly not significant; Spearman rank correlation with two-sided p-values and 95% covariance ellipses; Pearson correlation for un vs aia (significant positive but not near 1); ICC with 95% CI and one-sided F-test p-values (e.g. NSCLC ICC(C,1) AI-assisted p=0.004; HCC ICC(C,1) AI-assisted p=0.001).
papers.availability: Evaluator decision source data provided with the paper. Patient clinical data restricted (University of Michigan data sharing application). ARCliDS code is proprietary (Moffitt and University of Michigan). Online tools: https://arclids.shinyapps.io/ARCliDS/, https://arclids.shinyapps.io/Eval_NSCLC_v2/, https://arclids.shinyapps.io/Eval_HCC_v2/.

papers.title: Human-AI interaction and collaboration in radiology: from conceptual frameworks to responsible implementation
papers.authors: Kocak B, Cuocolo R
papers.aim: To give a clear overview of how radiologists and AI interact and collaborate, where collaboration adds value or causes harm, and what is needed for responsible implementation.
papers.method: Narrative review based on targeted, topic-driven literature searches, expert knowledge and backward and forward reference chaining, without a formal systematic search. It builds conceptual models, a workflow taxonomy along an autonomy spectrum and design principles, and summarises evidence on cognitive effects, governance and emerging systems.
papers.result: The review proposes an eight-model workflow taxonomy from human-only reading to standalone AI, including an 'uncertainty-aware delegation and high-confidence filtering' model where AI auto-finalises normal cases and escalates uncertain or positive ones. It summarises evidence such as 'AI as supporting reader' cutting second human reads by up to 87% in more than 280,000 mammograms, prostate MRI AUC rising from 0.882 to 0.916 with AI (61 readers, 360 exams), trainee accuracy falling from about 80% to 20% with incorrect AI, and biased AI lowering clinician accuracy by about 9.1-11.3 percentage points.
papers.tools: Not applicable (review). Mentions vision-language models (e.g. Flamingo-CXR), saliency maps, NLP report-image discrepancy checking, active learning, FDA Predetermined Change Control Plan; figures made in Canva.com; language edited with ChatGPT 5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro.
papers.gap: Most studies evaluate algorithms alone, not the human-AI team in real workflows. Few prospective, multi-institutional studies of team performance, workload, equity and long-term learning. Explanation tools (saliency maps) are unstable; calibrated uncertainty for role arbitration is not yet well tested.
papers.relation: Reviews frameworks for dividing work between radiologists and AI, which guides where the orchestrator should hand control to clinicians.
papers.limitations: Narrative, non-systematic review, so study selection may be biased; no pooled quantitative analysis; workflow diagrams are simplified and focus on narrow task-specific AI. Future work: prospective multi-institutional studies of team performance, workload, equity and training outcomes; uncertainty-aware role arbitration; usable explanations; AI literacy.
papers.methodologyDetail: This is a narrative review, so there is no dataset or model to reproduce. The authors ran targeted, topic-driven literature searches, used their own expert knowledge, and followed references backward and forward. They did not use a formal systematic protocol, quality scoring or meta-analysis. They organised the material in five steps. First, they defined core terms (human-AI interaction, collaboration, team performance, diagnostic complementarity, automation bias, algorithmic aversion, cognitive offloading, trust calibration, physician-in-the-loop) in a table. Second, they built a workflow taxonomy of eight models along an autonomy spectrum, from human-only reading to standalone AI. For each model they listed the human role, the AI role, the output and the autonomy level. The 'uncertainty-aware delegation and high-confidence filtering' model lets the AI auto-finalise normal cases and escalate uncertain or positive ones, while the radiologist audits a sample of auto-finalised cases. Third, they gave six design principles (task allocation, workflow placement, interaction mode, trust calibration, learning and feedback, training and supervision) and a table of advantages and risks for five interaction setups. Fourth, they summarised evidence on cognitive effects using numbers from cited studies, for example trainee accuracy falling from about 80% to 20% with wrong AI, and biased AI lowering accuracy by 9.1-11.3 points. Fifth, they described governance (liability stays with the clinician, interdisciplinary committees, shadow then pilot deployment, drift monitoring, FDA change-control plans, EU AI Act literacy) and a five-step physician-in-the-loop active learning loop. For this PhD, the taxonomy and active learning loop can be used as the design template for when the orchestrator acts alone, when it defers, and how clinician corrections feed recalibration.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (review article) by authors from Basaksehir Cam and Sakura City Hospital, Istanbul, Turkiye and University of Salerno, Italy. No primary data; not prospective or retrospective.
papers.datasets: No dataset used. Cited evidence includes: Lee et al. reader study, 30 radiologists and residents, 120 chest radiographs (60 with malignant nodules); Ng et al. simulation, more than 280,000 mammograms from two countries; prospective 'AI as additional reader' study, tens of thousands of screening exams; Zajac et al. qualitative study, 18 radiologists at 9 sites in Denmark and Kenya; PI-CAI consortium, 61 readers from 53 centres in 17 countries, 360 MRI exams; EuroAIM/EuSoMII survey of 572 ESR members; international survey of 1,041 radiologists; Chinese survey of 6,726 radiologists from 1,143 hospitals; prospective study of 18,680 chest radiographs.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable (review). Not reported.
papers.modelDetails: Conceptual frameworks, not a model. Diagnostic complementarity: human and AI errors only partly overlap, so the team can beat either alone.
