Autonomy spectrum with 8 workflow models: standard of care (human only); concurrent decision support (low); second reader and quality assurance (low to moderate); AI as supporting reader (moderate, AI acts as second reader only when it agrees with reader 1, discordant cases go to human reader 2); AI as additional reader (moderate, safety net on negative-consensus cases, arbitrator reviews flags); AI triage and worklist prioritisation (moderate to high); uncertainty-aware delegation and high-confidence filtering (high, AI auto-finalises normal cases, escalates uncertain or positive cases, radiologist audits a sample of auto-finalised normals); standalone AI reporting (autonomous, not clinically viable). Six design principles: task allocation, workflow placement, mode of interaction, trust calibration, learning and feedback, training and supervision. Physician-in-the-loop active learning loop in 5 steps: use in routine reporting; flag a subset (uncertain or discordant) for feedback; store in feedback set; periodic review, recalibration or retraining; redeploy and monitor drift and safety. No numeric thresholds given.
papers.training: Not applicable (review). Not reported.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable; no formal search protocol, quality appraisal or synthesis method reported. The review recommends phased deployment (shadow deployment, then scoped pilot, then full rollout), continuous post-market surveillance for drift, and evaluation frameworks such as Park et al., ECLAIR and RADAR.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (review).
papers.results: Reported evidence from cited studies: AI supporting reader reduced second human reads by up to 87% while maintaining screening performance; AI additional reader added 0.7-1.6 cancers per 1,000 women screened (83.3% invasive, 47.0% <=10 mm); prostate MRI with AI: AUC 0.882 to 0.916, sensitivity 94.3% to 96.8%, specificity 46.7% to 50.1% at PI-RADS >=3 (3 more true positives, 10 fewer false positives); AI triage cut critical chest radiograph reporting delay from 11.2 to 2.7 days and pneumothorax turnaround from 80.1 to 35.6 min; CTPA pulmonary embolism turnaround 59.9 to 47.6 min; trainee mammography accuracy about 80% with correct AI vs 20% with incorrect AI; biased AI reduced clinician accuracy by about 9.1-11.3 percentage points; saliency map localisation AUPRC 0.024-0.16; reading time 13.3 s vs 14.8 s overall, 10.8 s vs 13.1 s for normal-flag studies, 18.6 s vs 18.4 s for abnormal-flag studies; survey: 47.2% expected more workload, costs 49.5%, legal 43.7%, lack of validation 35.5%; 37% cited lack of trust (aOR 1.77, 95% CI 1.24-2.53, P=0.002 outside Europe); 98% said radiology teams should join AI development, 45% said radiologists should keep full responsibility; 64.8% of Singapore residents and faculty were AI novices, 59.2% said teaching was inadequate.
papers.statistics: No own statistical analysis. Cited: adjusted odds ratio 1.77 (95% CI 1.24-2.53; P=0.002) for lack-of-trust view outside Europe.
papers.availability: Not available (review; no code or data). Open-access article under CC BY-NC 4.0 at dirjournal.org.

papers.title: The rise and potential of large language model based agents: a survey
papers.authors: Zhiheng Xi, Wen-Xiang Chen, Xin Hua Guo et al.
papers.aim: To survey large language model (LLM) based agents: their foundations, a general architecture, applications and open problems.
papers.method: Comprehensive survey: traces the agent concept from philosophy to AI, explains why LLMs suit agents, proposes a general framework (brain, perception, action), and reviews single-agent, multi-agent and human-agent cooperation applications, agent societies and open challenges.
papers.result: Framework: the 'brain' (LLM with memory, knowledge, reasoning and planning), 'perception' (text and multimodal inputs) and 'action' (text output, tool use, embodied actions). Multi-agent systems interact by collaboration, negotiation or competition toward shared goals; key open issues include evaluation, hallucination, security, trustworthiness and scaling agent societies.
papers.tools: Literature survey with taxonomy; public paper list (GitHub WooooDyy/LLM-Agent-Paper-List).
papers.gap: General-purpose survey; little on clinical safety, calibration or regulation.
papers.relation: Gives the conceptual vocabulary for O1: our orchestrator is the 'brain', imaging and pathology models are perception tools, and agent outputs plus deferral are actions within a cooperative human-agent system.
papers.limitations: Fast-moving field; non-systematic selection of works.
papers.methodologyDetail: This large survey explains what LLM-based agents are and how they are built. It proposes a simple three-part design: a 'brain' (the language model, with memory, knowledge, reasoning and planning), 'perception' (taking in text, images or other inputs) and 'action' (writing text, calling tools or acting in an environment). It reviews agents working alone, multiple agents cooperating or debating, and humans working with agents, and discusses evaluation, hallucination, safety and trust. For our PhD it provides the terms and structure for describing the O1 architecture: an orchestrating 'brain' that calls specialised perception tools (MRI and pathology models) and acts only within a human-supervised, deferral-aware workflow.
papers.studyDesign: Survey / review.
papers.datasets: Not applicable (several hundred papers on LLM-based agents).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable. Brain-perception-action framework; single-agent, multi-agent (cooperative and adversarial) and human-agent (instructor-executor and equal-partnership) paradigms.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Discussion of agent evaluation dimensions (utility, sociability, values, ability to evolve).
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Taxonomy and roadmap of LLM-based agents and their open problems.

papers.title: Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making
papers.authors: Paul Hager, Friederike Jungmann, Robbie Holland et al.
papers.aim: To test whether current LLMs can make realistic clinical decisions - gathering information, following guidelines and fitting into workflows - beyond exam-style questions.
papers.method: Curated MIMIC-IV-based dataset of 2,400 real patients with four abdominal pathologies (appendicitis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis) and a framework where LLMs iteratively request history, examination, labs and imaging before diagnosing and treating; a full-information variant (MIMIC-CDM-FI) compared LLMs with 4 clinicians on 80 cases; robustness tests on instructions, information quantity and order.
papers.result: Open LLMs (Llama 2 Chat, OASST, WizardLM, Clinical Camel, Meditron, all 70B) diagnosed significantly worse than physicians (p<0.001, especially cholecystitis and diverticulitis), did not follow diagnostic or treatment guidelines, misinterpreted laboratory results, often ignored instructions, and their accuracy changed with the order and amount of information (ranges up to 18.0%). Conclusion: not ready for autonomous clinical decision-making.
papers.tools: MIMIC-IV, Llama 2 and derivatives, evaluation framework released with the dataset.
papers.gap: Open models only; abdominal pathologies in emergency setting; text-based.
papers.relation: Direct evidence for O1 and O2: an LLM orchestrator must not decide autonomously; it needs structured tool calls, guideline checks, robustness to input order and clinician oversight with deferral.
papers.limitations: Proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4) not tested due to data-use rules; single database.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of exam questions, the authors built a realistic test from 2,400 real emergency patients in the MIMIC-IV database with four abdominal conditions. An LLM receives the patient's story and must decide which examinations, blood tests and scans to request, then give a diagnosis and treatment, as a doctor would. Five leading open 70-billion-parameter models, including medical versions, were tested and compared with four doctors. The models were significantly less accurate than the doctors, ignored diagnostic and treatment guidelines, misread lab results, often failed to follow instructions, and changed their answers depending on the order in which information was given. For our PhD this justifies keeping the LLM orchestrator on a short leash: structured tools, guideline checks, consistent input formatting, calibrated confidence and clinician sign-off.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation and evaluation study with clinician comparison.
papers.datasets: MIMIC-IV-Ext Clinical Decision Making: 2,400 patient cases with appendicitis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis or diverticulitis; full-information subset of 80 cases read by 4 clinicians.
papers.preprocessing: Extraction of history of present illness, physical examination, laboratory results and radiology reports; diagnoses and treatments mapped from records.
papers.modelDetails: Llama 2 Chat (70B), OASST (70B), WizardLM (70B), Clinical Camel (70B), Meditron (70B) acting as autonomous agents that request information step by step.
papers.training: No training (inference with prompts; 20 random seeds for variability).
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy per pathology, guideline adherence for tests and treatment, lab interpretation, instruction following, sensitivity to information order and amount.
papers.baselines: Four practising clinicians.
papers.results: LLMs significantly worse than clinicians (p<0.001); poor guideline adherence and lab interpretation; performance varied by up to 18.0% with information ordering.
papers.statistics: Mean and SD over 20 seeds; significance tests vs clinicians.
papers.availability: Dataset via PhysioNet (MIMIC-IV-Ext-CDM) and code on GitHub.

papers.title: Simulation-Based Evaluation of a Large Language Model-Enabled Clinical Decision Support Platform in Oncology
papers.authors: Lajmi N, Patel M, Obery G, Dorge A, Sharma A, Halligan J, Lo E
papers.aim: PURPOSEA core clinical task is to synthesize fragmented patient data into a coherent summary to support decision making. However, electronic health record (EHR) inefficiencies burden clinicians and contribute to their cognitive overload and burnout.
papers.method: This study evaluated the impact of a large language model (LLM)–enabled clinical decision support (LLM-CDS) platform compared with a simulated EHR (SimEPR) on workflow efficiency and user experience in generating accurate clinical summaries during tumor board preparation and explored its applicability to consultation preparation, referrals, treatment planning, and patient communication.METHODSIn a remote, within-participant simulation, 26 oncologists from the United Kingdom, United States, Spain, and Singapore reviewed synthetic breast cancer cases and created comprehensive summaries for tumor board discussions using both LLM-CDS and SimEPR. LLM-CDS provided editable LLM-generated summaries; SimEPR required manual composition. Time to task completion was recorded. An independent reviewer assessed summary quality based on completeness, correctness, and conciseness. Participants also completed surveys on usability, cognitive load, and feature acceptability.RESULTSLLM-CDS significantly reduced the summary completion time compared with SimEPR (6:55 v 8:47 minutes; P < .001). Summary completeness was rated higher with LLM-CDS (mean score, 3.93 v 3.13), whereas correctness and conciseness were similar. Overall, 87% of participants would recommend LLM-CDS and 96% would anticipate time savings. The system usability scale score for LLM-CDS was 65.7. Although perceived cognitive load was lower with LLM-CDS, the difference was not statistically significant.
papers.result: The LLM summary was the most valued, with 92% finding it useful for the tumor board and consultation preparation.CONCLUSIONThe LLM-CDS platform improved the efficiency and completeness of clinical summarization. Strong user acceptance and anticipated time savings underscore the potential for streamlining a range of oncology workflows.
papers.gap: Synthetic cases and a simulated EHR only; no real patients or live tumour board; summary errors not linked to downstream decisions; no uncertainty shown to users.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Small sample (26), breast cancer only, single session; future work in live workflows and other tumour types.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors ran a remote crossover simulation in which 26 oncologists from four countries prepared tumour-board summaries for synthetic breast cancer cases twice: once with an LLM decision-support platform that drafts an editable summary, and once by writing it manually in a high-fidelity simulated EHR. Ten synthetic cases with realistic disease histories were prepared with an oncologist. Time to task completion was logged, an independent reviewer scored each summary for completeness, correctness and conciseness, and participants completed the System Usability Scale, a cognitive-load questionnaire and feature-acceptability questions. The design shows how a human-in-the-loop tool can be evaluated for workload and usability before live deployment.
papers.studyDesign: Remote within-participant simulation study (crossover); 26 oncologists from the UK, USA, Spain and Singapore, academic and community settings.
papers.datasets: 10 synthetic breast cancer cases of varying complexity in a high-fidelity simulated EHR (SimEPR); 26 participants each used both systems.
papers.preprocessing: Synthetic cases built with a board-certified oncologist; each participant used both systems.
papers.modelDetails: LLM-enabled clinical decision support platform giving editable LLM-generated patient summaries, compared with manual summary writing in a simulated EHR.
papers.training: No model training; LLM used as delivered by the platform.
papers.evaluation: Time to complete a tumour-board summary; independent reviewer rated completeness, correctness and conciseness; SUS, cognitive load and acceptability surveys.
papers.baselines: Manual summarisation in the simulated EHR.
papers.results: Summary time 6:55 vs 8:47 min (P<.001); completeness 3.93 vs 3.13; correctness and conciseness similar; SUS 65.7; 87% would recommend; lower cognitive load not significant.
papers.statistics: Paired comparisons of time and quality scores; P values reported.

papers.title: Large language model (ChatGPT) as a support tool for breast tumor board
papers.authors: Sorin V, Klang E, Sklair-Levy M, Cohen I, Zippel DB, Balint Lahat N, Konen E, Barash Y
papers.aim: Large language models (LLM) such as ChatGPT have gained public and scientific attention. The aim of this study is to evaluate ChatGPT as a support tool for breast tumor board decisions making.
papers.method: We inserted into ChatGPT-3.5 clinical information of ten consecutive patients presented in a breast tumor board in our institution. We asked the chatbot to recommend management. The results generated by ChatGPT were compared to the final recommendations of the tumor board. They were also graded independently by two senior radiologists. Grading scores were between 1–5 (1 = completely disagree, 5 = completely agree), and in three different categories: summarization, recommendation, and explanation. The mean age was 49.4, 8/10 (80%) of patients had invasive ductal carcinoma, one patient (1/10, 10%) had a ductal carcinoma in-situ and one patient (1/10, 10%) had a phyllodes tumor with atypia. In seven out of ten cases (70%), ChatGPT’s recommendations were similar to the tumor board’s decisions. Mean scores while grading the chatbot’s summarization, recommendation and explanation by the first reviewer were 3.7, 4.3, and 4.6 respectively. Mean values for the second reviewer were 4.3, 4.0, and 4.3, respectively.
papers.result: In this proof-of-concept study, we present initial results on the use of an LLM as a decision support tool in a breast tumor board. Given the significant advancements, it is warranted for clinicians to be familiar with the potential benefits and harms of the technology.
papers.gap: Only 10 cases, a general chatbot, no confidence or abstention, no prospective use.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Very small sample, single centre; data-privacy and liability issues; larger studies needed.
papers.methodologyDetail: Researchers took ten consecutive breast cancer patients from one institution's tumour board, extracted their clinic notes, imaging, surgical and pathology reports, and wrote structured English vignettes while blinded to the board's decision. Each vignette was given to ChatGPT-3.5, which was asked to recommend management. The model's answers were compared with the board's final recommendation and graded independently by two senior radiologists on a five-point scale for summarisation, recommendation and explanation. The study is a small feasibility test of an LLM as a tumour-board aid, without uncertainty estimates or deferral.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-centre proof-of-concept study at Chaim Sheba Medical Center, Israel; IRB-approved with waiver of consent.
papers.datasets: 10 consecutive women with breast cancer presented at the breast tumour board in January 2023 (8 invasive ductal carcinoma, 1 DCIS, 1 phyllodes tumour).
papers.preprocessing: Clinical notes, imaging, surgery and pathology reports summarised into English vignettes by a researcher blinded to the board decision.
papers.modelDetails: ChatGPT-3.5 prompted with each vignette to recommend management.
papers.training: No training; zero-shot prompting.
papers.evaluation: Agreement with the final tumour-board recommendation; two senior radiologists graded summarisation, recommendation and explanation on a 1-5 scale.
papers.baselines: Tumour-board decisions as reference.
papers.results: Recommendations matched the board in 7/10 cases; reviewer mean scores 3.7/4.3/4.6 and 4.3/4.0/4.3 for summarisation, recommendation and explanation.

papers.title: Clinical decision support in hematological malignancies using a case-grounded AI agent
papers.authors: Zoller J, Kalz M, Wu X, Cuntz S, Kruk L, Kehl N, Michel JJ, Funk C, Richter S, Tix T, et al.
papers.aim: Multidisciplinary tumor boards integrate longitudinal treatment histories, molecular profiling and rapidly evolving evidence to guide decisions in hematological malignancies, yet access to this level of subspecialty deliberation is increasingly uneven. Here we develop HemaGuide, a locally deployable, modular large language model agent that converts unstructured clinical documents into structured case representations, autonomously routes cases to specialized decision modes (‘guideline’, ‘advanced’ and ‘molecular’) and grounds recommendations in disease-specific guideline flowcharts and a clinical decision memory of >2,000 real-world tumor board cases.
papers.method: In expert-blinded benchmarking on 45 high-complexity cases across six foundation models, HemaGuide substantially improved concordance with tumor board decisions. A systematic ablation study across 11 layers confirmed that performance gains were routing-type-dependent, with no single component sufficient across case types. Automated classification of 70 clinically relevant missense variants showed high concordance with expert standards; no oncogenic variant was downgraded to benign and the whole workflow was completed under real-time conditions on commodity hardware with a median latency of 39 s rather than the hours typically required for manual molecular board workflows. In a simulated practice study, agent-assisted resident physicians achieved near-senior concordance and partially outperformed senior physicians in their subspecialty. External validation on 555 independent cases from a second academic center yielded 81.8% concordance across 47 entities, and a prospective 1-month silent trial on 64 consecutive, unselected cases achieved 82.8% concordance.
papers.result: Hallucinations occurred in 2 of 664 evaluated cases (0.3%). Together these data provide evidence that locally deployable, case-grounded large language model agents can deliver auditable clinical decision support across hematological malignancies, with concordance maintained across institutions and under real-time conditions on commodity hardware.
papers.gap: Routing is by case type, not by calibrated uncertainty; no explicit deferral to clinicians when the agent is unsure; haematology rather than imaging.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Silent trial only (no effect on decisions); documents ingested manually; concordance with boards is not a gold standard.
papers.methodologyDetail: HemaGuide turns routine tumour-board documents into a structured case, enriches it, and routes it to one of three decision modes, each grounded in disease-specific guideline flowcharts and in a memory of more than 2,000 previous real-world board cases. The authors benchmarked it with six foundation models on 45 hard cases scored blind by experts, ran an 11-layer ablation showing that gains depended on routing type, tested automated variant classification, and ran a simulated practice study with residents and seniors. They then validated it externally on 555 cases from another centre and ran a one-month prospective silent trial on 64 consecutive cases, measuring concordance, latency and hallucinations. It is a strong template for staged validation of an auditable, routed clinical agent.
papers.studyDesign: Development and multi-level validation of a locally deployable LLM agent (HemaGuide) for haematology tumour boards: expert-blinded benchmarking, ablation, simulated practice study, external validation at a second academic centre and a 1-month prospective silent trial.
papers.datasets: Clinical case memory of >2,000 real tumour-board cases; 45 high-complexity benchmark cases; 70 missense variants; 555 external cases from a second centre (47 entities); 64 consecutive prospective cases.
papers.preprocessing: Unstructured tumour-board documents converted into a semi-structured case representation with nine clinical sections plus optional molecular layers.
papers.modelDetails: Modular agent with a swappable LLM backbone: case extraction, enrichment and autonomous routing to 'guideline', 'advanced' or 'molecular' decision modes, grounded in guideline flowcharts and retrieval from the case memory, producing an auditable recommendation.
papers.training: No fine-tuning; retrieval-grounded prompting across six foundation models; runs on commodity hardware.
papers.evaluation: Concordance with tumour-board decisions judged by blinded experts; variant classification concordance; latency; hallucination rate; ablation over 11 layers.
papers.baselines: Plain foundation models without the agent layers; resident and senior physicians in the simulated practice study.
papers.results: External concordance 81.8% (555 cases); prospective silent trial 82.8% (64 cases); no oncogenic variant downgraded to benign; median latency 39 s; hallucinations in 2/664 cases (0.3%); assisted residents near senior level.

papers.title: When AI joins the table: evaluating large language model performance in soft tissue sarcoma tumor board decisions
papers.authors: Dehdab R, Afat S, Mankertz F, Brendel JM, Maalouf N, Werner S, Brendlin A, Herrmann J, Nikolaou K, Kloker LD, et al.
papers.venue: Journal of cancer research and clinical oncology
papers.aim: ObjectivesMultidisciplinary tumor boards (MDTs) are critical for the personalized management of soft tissue sarcomas (STS), but they are limited by time, costs, and resource demands. With recent advances in large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, there is growing interest in evaluating their potential role in augmenting MDT workflows.
papers.method: This study aimed to assess the clinical performance of ChatGPT-4o in real-world STS cases using predefined evaluation criteria, comparing its treatment suggestions with expert MDT decisions.Materials and methodsThis retrospective study included 152 patients presented to the multidisciplinary sarcoma tumor board. ChatGPT-4o was prompted to generate guideline-based treatment recommendations based on anonymized tumor board registration letters. Outputs were scored by blinded expert reviewers using a five-domain framework: diagnostic modalities, therapeutic modalities, treatment sequencing/timing, chemotherapy regimen, and clinical contextualization. Descriptive statistics and non-parametric ANOVA with post hoc tests assessed performance, including subgroup analysis by sarcoma subtype.ResultsChatGPT-4o scores were significantly lower than the maximum achievable value of 1.0 across all five criteria (all p < 0.0001). Among individual domains, clinical contextualization significantly outperformed all other criteria in pairwise comparisons (all p < 0.05). No significant performance differences were observed across sarcoma subtypes (H = 19.74, p = 0.138).ConclusionsChatGPT-4o demonstrated substantial expert-rated performance in generating tumor board recommendations for soft tissue sarcoma cases, particularly excelling in personalized contextualization.
papers.result: Discrepancies in treatment sequencing and chemotherapy selection highlight the need for expert oversight. These findings support the feasibility of LLM integration into oncology workflows, warranting further refinement toward safe, supportive clinical use.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00432-026-06432-w.
papers.gap: No confidence estimate or abstention; single LLM; compared with board decisions rather than outcomes.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single centre, retrospective; text-only letters; need for expert oversight and multicentre validation.
papers.methodologyDetail: From all sarcoma tumour-board cases in one year, the team randomly selected cases, excluded GIST and bone sarcomas and incomplete records, kept 13 cases to develop the prompt, and evaluated ChatGPT-4o on 138 patients. The anonymised registration letter was given to the model, which proposed guideline-based management. Blinded experts scored each output in five predefined domains, scores were normalised, and non-parametric tests compared domains and subtypes. The study shows a structured scoring framework for comparing LLM recommendations with a multidisciplinary board.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-centre study at the Sarcoma Center, University Hospital Tübingen; IRB-approved, consent waived.
papers.datasets: 200 cases randomly drawn from 1,901 sarcoma tumour-board cases in 2024; after exclusions 152 soft tissue sarcoma cases, 13 used for prompt development and 138 analysed.
papers.preprocessing: Anonymised tumour-board registration letters used as input.
papers.modelDetails: ChatGPT-4o prompted to produce guideline-based treatment recommendations.
papers.training: No training; prompt developed on 13 held-out cases.
papers.evaluation: Blinded expert scoring in five domains (diagnostics, therapy, sequencing/timing, chemotherapy regimen, clinical contextualisation), normalised to 0-1.
papers.baselines: Expert tumour-board decisions.
papers.results: Scores significantly below the maximum in all five domains (P<0.0001); contextualisation best; no difference across sarcoma subtypes (H=19.74, P=0.138); errors mainly in sequencing and chemotherapy choice.
papers.statistics: Shapiro-Wilk, one-sample tests, Kruskal-Wallis with post hoc tests; no sample-size calculation.

papers.title: A prospective pragmatic evaluation of automatic trial matching tools in a molecular tumor board
papers.authors: Gueguen L, Olgiati L, Brutti-Mairesse C, Sans A, Le Texier V, Verlingue L
papers.aim: Publicly available trial matching tools can improve the access to therapeutic innovations, but errors may expose to over-solicitation and disappointment. We performed a pragmatic non-interventional prospective evaluation on sequential patients at the Molecular Tumor Board of Centre Leon Berard.
papers.method: During 10 weeks in 2024, we analysed 157 patients with four clinical trial matching tools from the 19 screened: Klineo, ScreenAct, Trialing and DigitalECMT. Each patient had 2.19 trials proposed on average, and 38% had no trials suggested. The mean performances were precision = 0.33, recall = 0.32, AP@3 = 0.45, and NDCG@3 = 0.34. Using all the tools can increase to 26% the clinical trial options. The most frequent error concerned the type of gene variants required by the selection criteria.
papers.result: We showed that using a Large Language Model on the patients’ molecular reports could improve the performance by up to 5%. We recommend that experts supervise the results and we advocate for improved technologies.
papers.gap: No confidence or deferral; tools are black boxes; molecular criteria remain the main error source.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single centre, short period; tools change over time; expert supervision recommended.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors reviewed 19 publicly available clinical-trial matching tools, selected four on availability, relevance to molecular boards, usability and preliminary performance, and ran them prospectively for every patient presented at their molecular tumour board for ten weeks. Experts judged each proposed trial against the patient's record, giving precision, recall and ranking metrics, and analysed which eligibility criteria caused errors. They then tested whether passing the molecular report through an LLM improved matching. It is an example of a prospective, pragmatic evaluation of decision-support tools inside a real board workflow.
papers.studyDesign: Pragmatic, non-interventional prospective evaluation at the Molecular Tumor Board of Centre Léon Bérard, France, over 10 weeks in 2024.
papers.datasets: 157 consecutive patients; 19 trial-matching tools screened and 4 evaluated (Klineo, ScreenAct, Trialing, DigitalECMT).
papers.preprocessing: Patient characteristics, molecular alterations and treatment history taken from full electronic health records and entered into each tool.
papers.modelDetails: Commercial trial-matching tools; an LLM applied to molecular reports as an improvement test.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Human expert assessment of proposed trials: precision, recall, AP@3, NDCG@3; error analysis by selection criterion.
papers.baselines: The four tools compared with each other and combined.
papers.results: Mean 2.19 trials per patient, 38% with none; precision 0.33, recall 0.32, AP@3 0.45, NDCG@3 0.34; combining tools increased options by 26%; LLM on molecular reports improved performance by up to 5%.

papers.title: Clinical evaluation of large language model recommendations in melanoma: comparison with multidisciplinary tumor board decisions in a real-world cohort
papers.authors: Babic B, Umihanic S, Osmanovic H, Selak N, Sehic-Kozica E, Moranjkic L, Marijanovic I, Karaga M, Jalovcic Suljevic A, Umihanic S, et al.
papers.aim: BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) are increasingly being studied as potentially valuable support tools in oncology practice including clinical decision support. Yet, their real-world utility in melanoma treatment decision-making is still not sufficiently considered, especially in resource-limited settings.
papers.method: Accordingly, this study evaluated the performance of four LLMs against real-world treatment decisions of a melanoma multidisciplinary tumor board (MDT).MethodsThis retrospective single-center study included 151 consecutive patients with newly diagnosed cutaneous melanoma discussed at the MDT at the University Clinical Center Tuzla, Bosnia and Herzegovina, between 2020 and 2024. Melanoma treatment recommendations generated by four LLMs, ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-5 Thinking, Gemini 2.5 Pro and DeepSeek-V3.2, were evaluated by four board-certified oncologists against the actual MDT treatment decisions. Additionally, the LLM-generated recommendations were also rated across five pre-specified domains: clarity, clinical applicability, coverage, explanation and support with evidence, and guideline concordance.ResultsIn this study, inter-rater reliability was acceptable to good, supporting the consistency of expert evaluation. ChatGPT-5 Thinking showed the strongest and most consistent overall performance, followed by ChatGPT-4o, while Gemini 2.5 Pro and DeepSeek-V3.2 were rated less favorably. Differences between LLMs were statistically significant across all evaluated domains.
papers.result: Performance differences appeared most clinically relevant in more complex scenarios, particularly when consideration of adjuvant or systemic treatment strategies was required.ConclusionThe findings of this study suggest that selected LLMs may have a supportive role in everyday melanoma MDT practice particularly in oncology centers with limited resources. However, the current results do not support the use of LLM-generated recommendations as independent treatment decisions, and further prospective studies are required before LLM-assisted treatment recommendations can be safely integrated into the MDT workflow.
papers.gap: No confidence or abstention; pragmatic chat use without logging of retrieved evidence; no prospective effect on decisions.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Retrospective, single centre; model versions change; results do not support autonomous use.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors took 151 consecutive newly diagnosed melanoma patients presented to one tumour board in a resource-limited centre and extracted their clinical and pathological variables and the board's final consensus decision. Four public LLMs were given the guidelines for the relevant year as uploaded PDFs, instructed to act like a tumour board, and then prompted case by case through their ordinary web interfaces, reflecting a pragmatic clinician-facing use. Each model's recommendation was compared with the board decision, with attention to which treatment modalities and which case complexities caused disagreement.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-centre cohort study, University Clinical Center Tuzla, Bosnia and Herzegovina (2020-2024); a resource-limited setting.
papers.datasets: 151 consecutive treatment-naive adults with histologically confirmed cutaneous melanoma discussed at the melanoma MDT; demographic, histopathological, BRAF, SLNB and AJCC stage variables extracted.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusions: age <18, recurrence, multiple primaries, trial participation, incomplete data; MDT consensus recommendation taken from the official record.
papers.modelDetails: Four LLMs via public web interfaces (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-5 Thinking, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-V3.2), with NCCN and ESMO guidelines for the year of diagnosis uploaded as PDFs (not a formal RAG pipeline).
papers.training: No API, fine-tuning or custom generation parameters; standard settings.
papers.evaluation: Concordance of each LLM's recommendation with the MDT decision by treatment modality, with focus on complex adjuvant and systemic cases.
papers.baselines: MDT decisions; comparison among the four LLMs.
papers.results: Selected LLMs showed useful concordance with the MDT; differences were largest in complex cases needing adjuvant or systemic treatment decisions.
papers.statistics: Concordance rates and comparisons between models.

papers.title: Large language model processing capabilities of ChatGPT 4.0 to generate molecular tumor board recommendations-a critical evaluation on real world data
papers.authors: Schmutz M, Sommer S, Sander J, Graumann D, Raffler J, Soto-Rey I, Sheikhalishahi S, Schmidt L, Unkelbach LP, Ortak L, et al.
papers.aim: AbstractBackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT 4.0 hold promise for enhancing clinical decision-making in precision oncology, particularly within molecular tumor boards (MTBs). This study assesses ChatGPT 4.0’s performance in generating therapy recommendations for complex real-world cancer cases compared to expert human MTB (hMTB) teams.MethodsWe retrospectively analyzed 20 anonymized MTB cases from the Comprehensive Cancer Center Augsburg (CCCA), covering breast cancer (n = 3), glioblastoma (n = 3), colorectal cancer (n = 2), and rare tumors.
papers.method: ChatGPT 4.0 recommendations were evaluated against hMTB outputs using metrics including recommendation type (therapeutic/diagnostic), information density (IDM), consistency, quality (level of evidence [LoE]), and efficiency. Each case was prompted thrice to evaluate variability (Fleiss’ Kappa).ResultsChatGPT 4.0 generated more therapeutic recommendations per case than hMTB (median 3 vs 1, P = .005), with comparable diagnostic suggestions (median 1 vs 2, P = .501). Therapeutic scope from ChatGPT 4.0 included off-label and clinical trial options. IDM scores indicated similar content depth between ChatGPT 4.0 (median 0.67) and hMTB (median 0.75; P = .084). Moderate consistency was observed across replicate runs (median Fleiss’ Kappa = 0.51). ChatGPT 4.0 occasionally utilized lower-level or preclinical evidence more frequently (P = .0019). Efficiency favored ChatGPT 4.0 significantly (median 15.2 vs 34.7 minutes; P < .001).ConclusionIncorporating ChatGPT 4.0 into MTB workflows enhances efficiency and provides relevant recommendations, especially in guideline-supported cases.
papers.result: However, variability in evidence prioritization highlights the need for ongoing human oversight. A hybrid approach, integrating human expertise with LLM support, may optimize precision oncology decision-making.
papers.gap: Variability between runs and reliance on weaker evidence; no mechanism to express uncertainty or defer.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Small sample, single centre, retrospective; hybrid human-LLM approach recommended.
papers.methodologyDetail: Twenty consecutive real molecular tumour board cases were anonymised and given to ChatGPT 4.0 three times each. The authors compared the model's recommendations with those of the human board on the type and number of recommendations, a structured information-density metric, the level of evidence behind each recommendation and the time required, and used Fleiss' kappa across the three runs to measure consistency. The study highlights run-to-run variability as a reliability problem for language-model decision support.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective comparison at the Comprehensive Cancer Center Augsburg, Germany.
papers.datasets: 20 consecutive anonymised molecular tumour board cases (June-August 2021): breast, glioblastoma, colorectal and rare tumours; 39 SNVs; mostly AmpliSeq Focus panel.
papers.preprocessing: Anonymised molecular reports and clinical summaries used as prompts; each case prompted three times.
papers.modelDetails: ChatGPT 4.0 generating therapy recommendations.
papers.training: No training; zero-shot prompting.
papers.evaluation: Recommendation type, information density, consistency across runs (Fleiss' kappa), level of evidence and time taken versus the human MTB.
papers.baselines: Human molecular tumour board recommendations.
papers.results: More therapeutic recommendations per case (median 3 vs 1, P=.005); similar information density (0.67 vs 0.75); moderate run-to-run consistency (kappa 0.51); more low-level evidence (P=.0019); faster (15.2 vs 34.7 min, P<.001).

papers.title: Improving diagnostic accuracy in preoperative glioma classification: performance of knowledge-enhanced large language models compared with radiologists
papers.authors: Li S, Fang X, Jin Y, Deng Y, Hu W, Wu B, Zhou X, Wang G, Li K, Yue Q
papers.aim: Accurate preoperative MRI classification of gliomas is essential but challenging due to complex radiological features and inter-observer variability. This study evaluated three large language models (LLMs) for VASARI-based glioma classification compared to radiologist interpretations.
papers.method: We retrospectively analyzed 150 histopathologically confirmed gliomas (43 circumscribed astrocytic, 53 high-grade diffuse, 54 low-grade diffuse gliomas) using standardized MRI protocols. Three radiologists extracted VASARI features, while three LLMs (GPT-4, Claude3.5-Sonnet, Claude3.0-Opus) analyzed these features using standard input-output or knowledge-enhanced prompting incorporating diagnostic guidelines. Knowledge-enhanced prompting consistently outperformed standard prompting, improving diagnostic consistency (intra-model agreement: Sonnet κ = 0.91, Opus κ = 0.92, GPT-4 κ = 0.72). For diffuse versus circumscribed classification, senior radiologists (AUC = 0.88) and Claude3.5-Sonnet with knowledge-enhanced prompting (AUC = 0.84) performed similarly (p > 0.05).
papers.result: LLM assistance significantly improved junior radiologists’ performance, with AUC increases from 0.77 to 0.83 (p = 0.026). Knowledge-enhanced LLMs demonstrate diagnostic performance comparable to experienced radiologists and improve junior accuracy, suggesting potential as decision-support tools requiring radiologist oversight.
papers.gap: LLM reasons from radiologist-extracted features, not images; no calibrated confidence; single centre.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; feature extraction is manual; radiologist oversight required.
papers.methodologyDetail: In phase one, three neuroradiologists independently scored VASARI imaging features for 150 confirmed gliomas, and three LLMs classified each case from these features using either plain or guideline-enhanced prompts, three times per case, giving 54 assessments per case. Performance was measured against histopathology and consistency with kappa statistics, and errors were categorised. In phase two, three further radiologists read the same cases with and without the best LLM configuration, with randomised order and a one-month washout. The design is a useful template for a paired reader study of AI assistance in glioma diagnosis.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective two-phase study: LLM diagnostic performance, then paired reader study with and without LLM assistance; China.
papers.datasets: 150 histopathologically confirmed gliomas (43 circumscribed astrocytic, 53 high-grade diffuse, 54 low-grade diffuse) on standardised MRI; mean age 31 years.
papers.preprocessing: Three radiologists (3, 7 and 20 years' experience) extracted VASARI features; features used as LLM input.
papers.modelDetails: GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Claude 3.0 Opus with standard input-output prompting or knowledge-enhanced prompting with diagnostic guidelines; three runs per case, majority vote.
papers.training: No training; prompting only.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and AUC against histopathology; intra- and inter-model kappa; error-type analysis; Phase 2 compared three radiologists with and without LLM support after a one-month washout.
papers.baselines: Radiologists of different experience; standard prompting.
papers.results: Knowledge-enhanced prompting improved consistency (Sonnet kappa 0.91) and accuracy, comparable to experienced radiologists; LLM assistance raised junior radiologists' AUC from 0.77 to 0.83 (p=0.026).
papers.statistics: Fleiss and Cohen kappa with 95% CI; AUC comparisons in R 4.2.0.

papers.title: Large language models as decision aids in neuro-oncology: a review of shared decision-making applications
papers.authors: Lawson McLean A, Wu Y, Lawson McLean AC, Hristidis V
papers.venue: Journal of cancer research and clinical oncology
papers.aim: Shared decision-making (SDM) is crucial in neuro-oncology, fostering collaborations between patients and healthcare professionals to navigate treatment options. However, the complexity of neuro-oncological conditions and the cognitive and emotional burdens on patients present significant barriers to achieving effective SDM.
papers.method: This discussion explores the potential of large language models (LLMs) such as OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Bard to overcome these barriers, offering a means to enhance patient understanding and engagement in their care. LLMs, by providing accessible, personalized information, could support but not supplant the critical insights of healthcare professionals. The hypothesis suggests that patients, better informed through LLMs, may participate more actively in their treatment choices. Integrating LLMs into neuro-oncology requires navigating ethical considerations, including safeguarding patient data and ensuring informed consent, alongside the judicious use of AI technologies. Future efforts should focus on establishing ethical guidelines, adapting healthcare workflows, promoting patient-oriented research, and developing training programs for clinicians on the use of LLMs.
papers.result: Continuous evaluation of LLM applications will be vital to maintain their effectiveness and alignment with patient needs. Ultimately, this exploration contends that the thoughtful integration of LLMs into SDM processes could significantly enhance patient involvement and strengthen the patient-physician relationship in neuro-oncology care.
papers.gap: No empirical evaluation; no reliability or uncertainty assessment of LLM information.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Conceptual only; needs patient-oriented empirical studies.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors review the barriers to shared decision-making in neuro-oncology, such as disease complexity, urgency of decisions and patients' cognitive burden, and discuss how large language models could provide accessible, personalised information to patients. They examine ethical issues including data protection and informed consent and propose directions for research and implementation. It frames LLMs as support tools that must stay under clinician oversight.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review / discussion paper.
papers.datasets: No dataset; literature on shared decision-making and LLMs in neuro-oncology.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Conceptual analysis of LLMs (ChatGPT, Bard) as patient-facing aids for shared decision-making.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Argues LLMs can improve patient understanding and engagement but must support, not replace, clinicians; calls for ethical guidelines, workflow adaptation, patient-oriented research and clinician training.

papers.title: Large language models as a diagnostic support tool in neuropathology
papers.authors: Hewitt KJ, Wiest IC, Carrero ZI, Bejan L, Millner TO, Brandner S, Kather JN
papers.venue: The journal of pathology. Clinical research
papers.aim: AbstractThe WHO guidelines for classifying central nervous system (CNS) tumours are changing considerably with each release. The classification of CNS tumours is uniquely complex among most other solid tumours as it incorporates not just morphology, but also genetic and epigenetic features.
papers.method: Keeping current with these changes across medical fields can be challenging, even for clinical specialists. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated their ability to parse and process complex medical text, but their utility in neuro‐oncology has not been systematically tested. We hypothesised that LLMs can effectively diagnose neuro‐oncology cases from free‐text histopathology reports according to the latest WHO guidelines. To test this hypothesis, we evaluated the performance of ChatGPT‐4o, Claude‐3.5‐sonnet, and Llama3 across 30 challenging neuropathology cases, which each presented a complex mix of morphological and genetic information relevant to the diagnosis. Furthermore, we integrated these models with the latest WHO guidelines through Retrieval‐Augmented Generation (RAG) and again assessed their diagnostic accuracy.
papers.result: Our data show that LLMs equipped with RAG, but not without RAG, can accurately diagnose the neuropathological tumour subtype in 90% of the tested cases. This study lays the groundwork for a new generation of computational tools that can assist neuropathologists in their daily reporting practice.
papers.gap: Text descriptions, not slides; artificial cases; no confidence or abstention.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Small set of three tumour types; needs testing on real reporting workflow.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors created 30 realistic neuropathology report descriptions based on real UCLH cases and asked three LLMs to give the WHO 2021 integrated diagnosis, first without help and then with retrieval of the relevant WHO classification chapters. Experts held the answers to clinical reporting standards, so near-misses counted as wrong. The comparison isolates the value of grounding a model in the current classification, which matters because CNS tumour criteria change with each edition.
papers.studyDesign: Experimental comparison of zero-shot and retrieval-augmented LLMs on artificial neuropathology cases; Dresden and UCL Queen Square.
papers.datasets: 30 artificial cases (10 astrocytoma, 10 oligodendroglioma, 10 glioblastoma) built from real pseudonymised UCLH reports, keeping morphology, immunohistochemistry and molecular results.
papers.preprocessing: Descriptions rephrased while keeping varied writing styles and errors; WHO CNS5 adult-type diffuse glioma chapters collated as plain text for retrieval.
papers.modelDetails: ChatGPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet and Llama3-70b (groq) in zero-shot mode and with retrieval-augmented generation over the WHO 2021 criteria.
papers.training: No training; prompting and RAG only.
papers.evaluation: Expert neuropathologists judged whether the integrated diagnosis met clinical reporting standards.
papers.baselines: Zero-shot versions of the same models.
papers.results: Zero-shot models often failed (e.g. astrocytoma correct 6/10 Claude, 1/10 GPT, 0/10 Llama); with RAG the correct subtype was reached in 90% of cases.

papers.title: Validity of evidence-based recommendations by a large language model for interdisciplinary board decisions in neurooncology: An explorative study and critical evaluation
papers.authors: Goldberg M, Eisenkolb VM, Aftahy AK, Negwer C, Meyer HS, Gempt J, Meyer B, Wagner A
papers.aim: ObjectivesThis study aims to evaluate the stylistic and structural equivalence of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-generated summaries, particularly those by Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, compared to traditional human-generated case summaries in neuro-oncological board decisions. The primary goal is to explore the stylistic alignment between AI-generated and human-authored summaries from board meeting audio recordings.MethodsThe study compares 30 traditional human-generated case summaries with 30 AI-generated summaries based on board meeting audio recordings.
papers.method: Two expert raters, blinded to the source of the summaries, evaluated a total of 60 cases. A Likert scale was used to assess the plausibility, linguistic style, evidence adherence, and reference accuracy of the summaries.ResultsThe results indicated that both LLM-generated and human-reviewed summaries demonstrated consistently high performance across all criteria evaluated. The general plausibility ratings were comparable (LLM: 4.7, Human: 4.73, P = .959). Linguistic style ratings also showed similarity (LLM: 4.87, Human: 4.97, P = .512). In terms of adherence to evidence, the means were close (LLM: 4.8, Human: 4.87, P = .541). Reference accuracy was slightly higher for AI-generated summaries (LLM: 4.97, Human: 4.9, P = .664). These findings were consistent with the results from Rater 2, and statistical analysis using Kendall's tau showed no significant differences between methods (P > .05).ConclusionThe study finds that LLM-generated summaries can effectively emulate the style and structure of human-authored ones, indicating their promise as an additional tool in neuro-oncology.
papers.result: These AI models can enhance documentation quality and serve as valuable support in clinical settings. While further research is necessary to explore broader applications, LLMs offer exciting potential as a complement to traditional decision-making processes.
papers.gap: Assesses style and plausibility rather than decision correctness; no uncertainty or deferral; different cases in the two groups.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Small, single centre, two raters; German-language workflow.
papers.methodologyDetail: Transcripts of real neuro-oncology board presentations, stripped of identifiers and of the final decision, were given to ChatGPT o1 to produce a case summary and evidence-based recommendation. Two experienced raters, blinded to the source, scored these alongside 30 previous human-written summaries on plausibility, style, evidence adherence and reference accuracy, and the groups were compared with non-parametric tests. The work explores LLMs as documentation support for brain-tumour boards.
papers.studyDesign: Explorative blinded comparison at a German university neuro-oncology board (Technical University of Munich).
papers.datasets: 60 case summaries: 30 human-written board summaries (Aug-Sep 2024) and 30 LLM summaries generated from anonymised audio transcripts of five board meetings (Oct-Dec 2024).
papers.preprocessing: Audio recordings transcribed and censored; transcripts contained patient histories without the consensus decision.
papers.modelDetails: ChatGPT o1 via the German web interface, prompted in German without prior instructions.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Two blinded expert raters scored plausibility, linguistic style, evidence adherence and reference accuracy on 1-5 Likert scales.
papers.baselines: Human-written tumour-board summaries.
papers.results: Both sources scored highly with no significant differences (e.g. plausibility 4.7 vs 4.73, P=.959; style 4.87 vs 4.97).
papers.statistics: Mann-Whitney U tests; Kendall's tau for inter-rater agreement.
papers.availability: Prompts and outputs appended in the paper.

papers.title: Assessing ChatGPT-4 as a clinical decision support tool in neuro-oncology radiotherapy: a prospective comparative study
papers.authors: Tini P, Novi F, Donnini F, Perrella A, Bagnacci G, Mazzei MA, Minniti G
papers.aim: Background and purposeLarge language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT-4 have shown potential for medical decision support, but their reliability in specialized fields remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate ChatGPT-4’s performance as a clinical decision support tool in neuro-oncology radiotherapy by comparing its treatment recommendations for patients with central nervous system tumors against a multidisciplinary tumor board’s decisions, an independent specialist’s opinion, and published guidelines.Materials and methodsWe prospectively collected 101 neuro-oncology cases (May 2024–May 2025) presented at a tertiary-care tumor board.
papers.method: Key case details were entered into ChatGPT-4 with a standardized query asking whether to recommend radiotherapy and, if so, the target volumes and dose. The AI’s recommendations were recorded and compared to the tumor board’s consensus, a blinded radiation oncologist’s recommendation, and ESMO guideline indications when applicable. Concordance rates (percentage agreement) and Cohen’s kappa were calculated. Sensitivity and specificity were assessed using the reference decisions as ground truth. McNemar’s test was used to evaluate any bias in discordant recommendations.ResultsChatGPT-4 matched the tumor board’s radiotherapy recommendations in 76% of cases (κ = 0.61). Agreement with the independent specialist was 79% (κ = 0.58). In 61 low-complexity cases with clear guidelines, ChatGPT-4 concurred with guideline-based indications in 76.7% of cases, missing some recommended treatments (sensitivity 73%, specificity 100%). In intermediate-complexity scenarios, concordance with the tumor board was 70.8%, with most discrepancies due to the AI recommending treatment that experts did not (sensitivity 85.7%, specificity 64.7%). In high-complexity cases, agreement was 90.9% (sensitivity 100%, specificity 83.3%). Overall, ChatGPT-4 showed an overtreatment bias, more often recommending radiotherapy when the human experts chose observation (p < 0.05 for AI vs. tumor board discordances). Its overall agreement (76%) was lower than that of the human specialist (90%).ConclusionChatGPT-4 can reproduce many expert radiotherapy decisions in neuro-oncology, reflecting substantial absorption of standard clinical practice.
papers.result: However, it cannot substitute for human judgment: the AI omitted some indicated treatments in straightforward cases and suggested unnecessary therapy in some borderline cases, indicating a lack of nuanced clinical reasoning. Careful human oversight is essential if such models are to be used for clinical decision support.
papers.gap: No confidence estimate to flag the borderline cases where it erred; single LLM; text input only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single centre; adult cases only; human oversight essential.
papers.methodologyDetail: For every CNS tumour case discussed for post-operative radiotherapy over one year, the investigators entered the key details into ChatGPT-4 using a fixed question about whether, where and at what dose to irradiate. The answers were compared with the board's consensus, an independent blinded radiation oncologist and guideline recommendations, overall and by pre-defined case complexity, using kappa and McNemar's test. The prospective design and complexity stratification show where an LLM fails in neuro-oncology decisions.
papers.studyDesign: Single-institution prospective observational study, University of Siena, Italy (May 2024-May 2025).
papers.datasets: 101 consecutive CNS tumour cases considered for post-operative radiotherapy: 52 glioblastoma, 24 meningioma, 15 low-grade glioma, 10 rare tumours; no exclusions.
papers.preprocessing: Cases classified a priori as low, intermediate or high complexity by availability of guidelines; key case details entered in a standardised query.
papers.modelDetails: ChatGPT-4 asked whether to recommend radiotherapy and, if so, the target volumes and dose.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Concordance and kappa with the tumour-board consensus, a blinded radiation oncologist and guidelines; sensitivity and specificity for indicated radiotherapy; analysis by complexity.
papers.baselines: Tumour-board decision (also the treatment delivered) and an independent specialist.
papers.results: Agreement with the board 76% (kappa 0.606) and with the specialist 79% (kappa 0.583); omitted indicated treatment in some straightforward cases and suggested unnecessary therapy in some borderline cases.
papers.statistics: Concordance, Cohen's kappa, McNemar's test for direction of disagreement, paired comparison with the specialist.

papers.title: PHO-Agents: A Large Language Model-Powered Multi-Agent System for Predicting Health Outcomes
papers.authors: Shi D, Shugg T, Eadon MT, Su J, Chen Y, Song Q
papers.venue: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
papers.aim: Objective:Predicting health outcomes from electronic health records (EHRs) is challenging because traditional models rely on structured data and often ignore external medical knowledge. We propose an approach that integrates structured EHR with text‑based clinical evidence to improve prediction and interpretability.Methods:We introduce PHO-Agents, a multi-agent system powered by large language models (LLMs) for health outcome prediction.
papers.method: Structured EHR sequences are encoded to produce attention-based representations and initial logits, which are converted into patient summaries by a data agent. A retrieval agent gathers relevant clinical guidelines. Research and practical doctor agents independently assess the patient, and a leader agent synthesizes their analyses. Outputs from the EHR-based model and the LLM agents are fused to generate final predictions and explanation reports. PHO-Agents was evaluated on three real-world cohorts: acute kidney injury (AKI) patients (in-hospital mortality), chronic kidney disease patients (AKI onset within two years), and cancer patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (immune-related adverse events within one year).Results:PHO-Agents outperformed single-agent and multi-agent LLM baselines across all cohorts. In the AKI mortality task, it achieved a PR-AUC of 90.20 ± 2.07, compared with 56.46 ± 2.98 for the best single-agent baseline. Similar gains were observed in the ICI and CKD cohorts.
papers.result: Ablation studies showed that both multi-agent reasoning and logit-level fusion contributed to performance improvements, and case analyses demonstrated clinically consistent explanations.Conclusion:PHO-Agents integrates longitudinal EHR modeling with collaborative LLM reasoning, improving predictive performance, interpretability, and robustness across diverse clinical tasks. This hybrid approach offers a trustworthy strategy for real-world clinical decision support.
papers.gap: No calibrated uncertainty passed between components; no deferral; tabular EHR, not imaging.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: PHO-Agents combines a conventional interpretable EHR model with language-model agents. The EHR model encodes each patient's visit history and gives an initial risk; a data agent summarises the patient; a retrieval agent fetches relevant guidelines; two doctor agents with different perspectives assess the case; and the final prediction fuses the model's logits with the agents' judgement. It was evaluated on mortality, AKI and immunotherapy cohorts from two health systems against single- and multi-agent baselines with ablations. It shows how a specialist model's output can be passed to, and combined with, reasoning agents.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and evaluation on three EHR cohorts from MIMIC-IV and University of Florida Health (IRB202600454).
papers.datasets: Adult cohorts: AKI ICU patients (in-hospital mortality), CKD patients (future AKI risk) and an immune checkpoint inhibitor oncology cohort; patients with missing key fields excluded.
papers.preprocessing: Structured longitudinal EHR sequences encoded per visit; observation windows from index diagnosis or treatment dates.
papers.modelDetails: RETAIN model produces attention-based representations and logits; a data agent turns these into patient summaries; a retrieval agent (MedCPT) gathers guidelines; research and practical doctor agents assess the patient and an aggregator fuses outputs with logit-level fusion; Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct engine.
papers.training: Run on two NVIDIA L4 GPUs; Python 3.9, PyTorch 2.3; settings per cohort in the paper.
papers.evaluation: Outcome prediction metrics (AUROC, AUPRC and related) on each cohort; ablations; qualitative case analyses.
papers.baselines: Zero-shot, few-shot and self-consistency single agents; multi-agent LLM baselines; EHR-only models.
papers.results: PHO-Agents improved prediction over single- and multi-agent baselines; both multi-agent reasoning and logit fusion contributed in ablations; explanations judged clinically consistent.

papers.title: An Agentic LLM Framework for Autonomous Surgical Continuum Monitoring: ReAct-Driven Tool-Use Agents for Presurgical, Intraoperative, and Postsurgical Cardiopulmonary Care
papers.authors: Pylarinou C, Gortzis L, Leivaditis V, Liolis E, Antzoulas A, Papadoulas S, Nikolakopoulos K, Panagiotopoulos I, Mitsos S, Tomos P, et al.
papers.aim: Background: Rule-based multi-agent system (MAS) architectures for healthcare coordination rely on hardcoded decision trees that cannot generalise to novel clinical scenarios or self-correct reasoning errors. These limitations are acute in surgical continuum care, where patients traverse presurgical risk stratification, intraoperative monitoring, postsurgical ICU, ward care, and remote rehabilitation over days to weeks—a complexity no fixed-policy agent architecture can address without prohibitive rule engineering.
papers.method: Objective: We present the first agentic large language model (LLM) framework for autonomous end-to-end surgical continuum monitoring, superseding the prior rule-based MAS Digital Twin. Six ReAct-driven tool-use agents replace fixed-policy agents with dynamic reasoning, multi-hop evidence retrieval, and Reflexion self-correction while maintaining mandatory confidence-gated Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) gating at every care-pathway-modifying decision. Methods: The framework is grounded in the ReAct paradigm and Reflexion self-evaluation, embedded within the DETER Digital Twin state engine S(t). Each agent is specified by a ReAct loop signature, a ten-function clinical tool registry, and confidence-gated HITL escalation logic. Inter-agent coordination replaces the rule-based Priority Queue Manager with an LLM-mediated Coordination Supervisor Agent reasoning over competing resource requests.
papers.result: Results: The framework delivers: (i) six formally specified ReAct-loop agents with explicit tool registries and authorisation boundaries; (ii) a confidence-gated HITL architecture that reduces alert fatigue while preserving safety for ambiguous clinical scenarios; (iii) an extended conflict resolution function P(p,t,context) incorporating surgical phase and DETER deterioration trajectory gradient; (iv) Reflexion self-correction with a formal N_max = 2 termination condition and Clinical Factuality Verification Layer; and (v) a multi-phase Digital Twin state engine extending S(t) to the full surgical continuum. Conclusions: The proposed framework represents a fundamental architectural departure from rule-based clinical AI—from hardcoded policies to dynamic reasoning, from static retrieval to multi-hop tool-use chains, and from fixed escalation thresholds to confidence-gated self-evaluation—providing a formally specified, clinically deployable foundation for next-generation autonomous surgical care coordination.
papers.gap: Confidence gating is not shown to be calibrated; no quantitative evaluation on real patients reported.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Framework-level work; clinical validation still needed.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper replaces fixed-rule agents in a surgical digital twin with six language-model agents that reason and act through ReAct loops, each allowed to call only listed tools such as risk-score calculators, FHIR read/write functions and a resource-allocation evaluator. Every agent must call a human-in-the-loop escalation tool for consequential actions, packaging its reasoning and evidence for a clinician's signed approval, and every step is written to an immutable audit log. Confidence gating decides which outputs need escalation. Its tool registry, authorisation boundaries and audit fields are a close design reference for this study's orchestrator.
papers.studyDesign: System design and specification study (framework paper) for cardiopulmonary surgical-continuum monitoring, Greece/Germany; extends a previous rule-based multi-agent digital twin.
papers.datasets: No new patient cohort reported in the extracted text; agents operate on FHIR R4 resources (Patient, Observation, Condition, MedicationRequest).
papers.preprocessing: Patient data accessed as FHIR bundles with defined time windows.
papers.modelDetails: Six ReAct-loop LLM agents with explicit tool registries and authorisation boundaries (e.g. EuroSCORE/STS risk calculation, examination-order evaluation, priority-based conflict resolution, agent health monitoring), a mandatory HITL_escalate tool that needs a clinician digital signature, and an immutable audit_log of reasoning chain, tools, evidence, action and HITL outcome.
papers.training: No model training; default priority weights w = (0.40, 0.15, 0.20, 0.15, 0.10) for competing patients.
papers.evaluation: Formal specification and scenario-based demonstration of confidence-gated escalation and alert reduction.
papers.baselines: Prior rule-based multi-agent digital twin.
papers.results: Delivers six formally specified agents, a confidence-gated HITL architecture intended to reduce alert fatigue while keeping safety for ambiguous cases, and a full audit trail.

papers.title: A self-correcting Agentic Graph RAG for clinical decision support in hepatology
papers.authors: Hu Y, Xuan W, Zhou Q, Li Z, Li Y, Hu J, Fang F
papers.aim: IntroductionClinical decision-making in hepatology is currently challenged by the rapid expansion of medical knowledge and the limitations of Large Language Models (LLMs), specifically their unreliability and tendency to hallucinate. Furthermore, standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigms often fail to effectively leverage complex medical knowledge structures.MethodsTo address these issues, we propose an Agentic Graph RAG framework built upon a clinically-verified hepatology knowledge graph.
papers.method: Our approach utilizes a state-driven agentic system employing a self-correcting “retrieve-evaluate-refine” loop. Within this workflow, agents dynamically generate, semantically validate, assess, and iteratively optimize graph search strategies to construct a comprehensive and accurate context, which is then used by an LLM to generate reliable responses.ResultsThe framework was evaluated on a custom dataset of clinical questions. It significantly outperformed baseline models (including GPT-4, standard RAG, and Graph RAG) across all evaluation metrics.
papers.result: Specifically, our model achieved superior scores in faithfulness (0.94), context recall (0.92), and answer relevancy (0.91).DiscussionThis agentic approach effectively mitigates LLM hallucinations and provides accurate, interpretable answers. These findings demonstrate the framework's potential as a robust, next-generation intelligent clinical decision support tool for hepatology.
papers.gap: Small question set; automatic metrics rather than clinician outcomes; no uncertainty output.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: A liver-disease knowledge graph is combined with an agent that turns a clinical question into graph queries, checks whether the retrieved evidence is sufficient and, if not, rewrites the query in a loop before answering from verified facts. Thirty questions of three difficulty types were written and validated by experts, and the system was compared with plain and retrieval-based baselines using faithfulness, recall and relevancy scores. Self-correction through evidence evaluation is the transferable idea.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with expert-built evaluation set; hepatology knowledge-graph question answering, China.
papers.datasets: Liver disease knowledge graph; 30 expert-written clinical questions (10 simple factual, 10 multi-hop, 10 ambiguous/colloquial) with gold answers validated blind by a third expert.
papers.preprocessing: Questions and answers validated by consensus.
papers.modelDetails: State-driven agentic Graph RAG with a self-correcting retrieve-evaluate-refine loop that generates, validates and refines graph queries before synthesising an answer; GPT-4-1106-preview backbone.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: RAGAS-style metrics: faithfulness, context recall, answer relevancy; qualitative analysis of the correction loop.
papers.baselines: Standard LLM, vector RAG and non-agentic graph RAG with the same backbone.
papers.results: Faithfulness 0.94, context recall 0.92, answer relevancy 0.91, better than baselines.

papers.title: Answering real-world clinical questions using large language model, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic systems
papers.authors: Low YS, Jackson ML, Hyde RJ, Brown RE, Sanghavi NM, Baldwin JD, Pike CW, Muralidharan J, Hui G, Alexander N, et al.
papers.aim: ObjectiveThe practice of evidence-based medicine can be challenging when relevant data are lacking or difficult to contextualize for a specific patient. Large language models (LLMs) could potentially address both challenges by summarizing published literature or generating new studies using real-world data.Materials and MethodsWe submitted 50 clinical questions to five LLM-based systems: OpenEvidence, which uses an LLM for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG); ChatRWD, which uses an LLM as an interface to a data extraction and analysis pipeline; and three general-purpose LLMs (ChatGPT-4, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro).
papers.method: Nine independent physicians evaluated the answers for relevance, quality of supporting evidence, and actionability (i.e., sufficient to justify or change clinical practice).ResultsGeneral-purpose LLMs rarely produced relevant, evidence-based answers (2–10% of questions). In contrast, RAG-based and agentic LLM systems, respectively, produced relevant, evidence-based answers for 24% (OpenEvidence) to 58% (ChatRWD) of questions. OpenEvidence produced actionable results for 48% of questions with existing evidence, compared to 37% for ChatRWD and <5% for the general-purpose LLMs.
papers.result: ChatRWD provided actionable results for 52% of questions that lacked existing literature compared to <10% for other LLMs.DiscussionSpecial-purpose LLM systems greatly outperformed general-purpose LLMs in producing answers to clinical questions. Retrieval-augmented generation-based LLM (OpenEvidence) performed well when existing data were available, while only the agentic ChatRWD was able to provide actionable answers when preexisting studies were lacking.ConclusionSynergistic systems combining RAG-based evidence summarization and agentic generation of novel evidence could improve the availability of pertinent evidence for patient care.
papers.gap: No uncertainty communication; evaluation of answers, not patient outcomes.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Question set selected for cohort designs; vendor involvement.
papers.methodologyDetail: Fifty real clinical questions were sent to three general chatbots, a literature RAG system and an agentic system that designs and runs an observational study on real-world data. Citations were checked for hallucinations and the agent's generated cohort code was audited, and nine physicians graded every answer for relevance, evidence quality and actionability. The comparison shows the gain from grounding answers in retrieved or newly generated evidence.
papers.studyDesign: Comparative evaluation of five LLM-based systems by blinded physicians (Atropos Health and academic centres).
papers.datasets: 50 clinical questions from physicians' evidence requests, all answerable by a cohort study with full PICO and an active comparator; novel questions oversampled.
papers.preprocessing: Novelty judged by three reviewers searching the literature.
papers.modelDetails: OpenEvidence (RAG over literature), ChatRWD (agentic LLM interface to a real-world-data study pipeline), and ChatGPT-4, Claude 3 Opus and Gemini 1.5 Pro.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Nine physicians rated relevance, quality of supporting evidence and actionability; citations checked for hallucination; ChatRWD cohort code reviewed by informaticians.
papers.baselines: General-purpose LLMs.
papers.results: Answers produced for 86% (OpenEvidence) and 94% (ChatRWD) vs 58-78%; relevant evidence-based answers 24% and 58% vs 2-10% (p<0.0001); ChatRWD actionable for 52% of questions without existing literature vs <10%.

papers.title: DxDirector: an agentic large language model driving the full-process clinical diagnosis
papers.authors: Xu S, Huang X, Wei Z, Pang L, Shen H, Cheng X
papers.aim: Clinical diagnosis in the real world often begins with ambiguous patient complaints that require iterative reasoning and testing. While large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist with specific medical queries, they currently lack the ability to autonomously drive this entire diagnostic workflow, limiting their potential to significantly alleviate physician workload.
papers.method: Here we present DxDirector-7B, an agentic LLM designed to navigate the full diagnostic process through advanced slow thinking capabilities. Unlike existing assistants, our model autonomously determines optimal diagnostic strategies, requesting physician intervention only for necessary clinical operations. In evaluations spanning rare diseases and complex real-world cases, DxDirector-7B achieves superior diagnostic accuracy compared to state-of-the-art medical and general-purpose LLMs with significantly larger parameters.
papers.result: Crucially, it drastically reduces physician involvement while maintaining a robust safety and accountability framework for high-risk conditions.
