These results demonstrate a paradigm shift where AI effectively leads clinical reasoning, offering a scalable solution to enhance diagnostic efficiency and accessibility.
papers.gap: When to involve the physician is learned from data, not set by calibrated risk; simulated environment.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single hospital source; not prospectively deployed.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built training data that turns real diagnostic records into step-by-step reasoning from a chief complaint to a final diagnosis, had experts check samples, and instruction-tuned a 7-billion-parameter model to drive the whole process. In evaluation, two GPT-4o agents replayed the recorded behaviour of patients and specialists, so the model had to ask for tests and examinations as in a real admission without touching real patients. Accuracy and physician involvement were compared with larger models. It illustrates an agent that decides when to involve the clinician.
papers.studyDesign: Model development and evaluation in a simulated full-process diagnostic environment built from real inpatient records, Peking University Third Hospital (IRB approved, consent obtained).
papers.datasets: Real-world complex inpatient cases from a Grade 3A hospital plus rare-disease benchmarks; instruction-response training pairs built from clinical data and reviewed by experts.
papers.preprocessing: PII and locations removed; patient and specialist actions from records replayed by two GPT-4o agents.
papers.modelDetails: DxDirector-7B, a 7B agentic LLM with slow-thinking reasoning that starts from a vague chief complaint, chooses diagnostic steps and requests physician operations only when needed.
papers.training: Instruction tuning on constructed multi-step diagnostic reasoning data (details in supplement).
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy, amount of physician involvement and safety for high-risk conditions, reviewed by medical experts.
papers.baselines: State-of-the-art medical LLMs and larger commercial general-purpose LLMs.
papers.results: Higher diagnostic accuracy than larger models while greatly reducing physician involvement, with a safety and accountability framework for high-risk conditions.

papers.title: MoMA: a mixture-of-multimodal-agents architecture for enhancing clinical prediction modelling
papers.authors: Gao J, Rahman M, Caskey J, Oguss M, O'Rourke A, Brown R, Stey A, Mayampurath A, Churpek MM, Chen G, et al.
papers.aim: Multimodal electronic health record (EHR) data provide richer, complementary insights into patient health compared to single-modality data. However, effectively integrating diverse data modalities for clinical prediction modeling remains challenging due to the substantial data requirements.
papers.method: We introduce a novel architecture, Mixture-of-Multimodal-Agents (MoMA), designed to leverage multiple large language model (LLM) agents for clinical prediction tasks using multimodal EHR data. MoMA employs specialized LLM agents (“specialist agents”) to convert non-textual modalities, such as medical images and laboratory results, into structured textual summaries.
papers.result: These summaries, together with clinical notes, are combined by another LLM (“aggregator agent”) to generate a unified multimodal summary, which is then used by a third LLM (“predictor agent”) to produce clinical predictions. Evaluating MoMA with different modality combinations and prediction settings, MoMA outperforms existing methods on three prediction tasks using private datasets, highlighting its enhanced accuracy and flexibility across various tasks.
papers.gap: Uncertainty of each specialist summary is not passed on; text summaries can lose image detail.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Single health system; private data; three tasks only.
papers.methodologyDetail: MoMA handles multimodal clinical prediction by turning each non-text modality into a text summary with a specialist agent, for example a medical vision-language model describing a chest radiograph. An aggregator agent merges these summaries with the clinical notes into one patient summary, and a predictor agent produces the prediction. The design was compared with learned cross-attention and mixture-of-experts fusion on three tasks using hospital data. It shows a text-based alternative to feature fusion that needs less paired training data.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective model development and evaluation on private multimodal EHR data from University of Wisconsin Hospitals and Clinics; reported to TRIPOD-LLM.
papers.datasets: Three tasks: chest trauma severity (multiclass), joint chest and spine trauma severity (multitask), unhealthy alcohol use screening (binary); inputs are clinical notes plus chest radiographs or laboratory results.
papers.preprocessing: Non-text modalities converted to text summaries by specialist agents before fusion.
papers.modelDetails: Mixture-of-Multimodal-Agents: specialist agents (e.g. LLaVA-Med v1.5 for radiographs, an LLM for labs) write structured summaries; an aggregator LLM merges them with notes; a predictor LLM outputs the class.
papers.training: Predictor fine-tuned for each task (details in methods); specialist agents used off the shelf.
papers.evaluation: Classification metrics (accuracy, F1, AUROC) on held-out sets.
papers.baselines: Cross-attention fusion, Mixture-of-Experts fusion and single-modality models.
papers.results: MoMA outperformed the fusion baselines on all three tasks.
papers.statistics: Comparisons with confidence intervals reported in the paper.

papers.title: Orchestrated multi agents sustain accuracy under clinical-scale workloads compared to a single agent
papers.authors: Klang E, Omar M, Raut G, Agbareia R, Timsina P, Freeman R, Gavin N, Stump L, Charney AW, Glicksberg BS, et al.
papers.venue: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
papers.aim: We tested state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) in two configurations for clinical-scale workloads: a single agent handling heterogeneous tasks versus an orchestrated multi-agent system assigning each task to a dedicated worker. Across retrieval, extraction, and dosing calculations, we varied batch sizes from 5 to 80 to simulate clinical traffic.
papers.method: Multi-agent runs maintained high accuracy under load (pooled accuracy 90.6% at 5 tasks, 65.3% at 80) while single-agent accuracy fell sharply (73.1% to 16.6%), with significant differences beyond 10 tasks (FDR-adjusted p < 0.01). Multi-agent execution reduced token usage up to 65-fold and limited latency growth compared with single-agent runs.
papers.result: The design’s isolation of tasks prevented context interference and preserved performance across four diverse LLM checkpoints. This is the first evaluation of LLM agent architectures under sustained, mixed-task clinical workloads, showing that lightweight orchestration can deliver accuracy, efficiency, and auditability at operational scale.
papers.gap: Synthetic task mix; no uncertainty or human escalation.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; exact-match scoring; text tasks only.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study compared one language-model agent handling a mixed batch of clinical tasks with an orchestrator that hands each task to its own worker agent equipped with a single tool. Tasks were literature retrieval, data extraction from discharge notes and dose calculations, with batch size raised from 5 to 80 to mimic clinical load. Accuracy, latency and tokens were compared across four models with corrected statistical tests. Isolating tasks in dedicated agents prevented context interference, supporting the orchestrated design used in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Controlled in-silico experiment, Mount Sinai (preprint).
papers.datasets: Retrieval: FAISS index of 234,650 PubMed oncology records (2020-2025); extraction: 331,793 EHR discharge summaries; calculation: 20 dosing templates; batches of 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 tasks, ten batches per model-topology.
papers.preprocessing: Exact-match ground truth after case and whitespace normalisation.
papers.modelDetails: Single agent receiving the whole batch (up to 10xN turns) versus an orchestrator that dispatches each task to a dedicated worker using one tool (k-NN retriever, sandboxed calculator, note fetcher) and merges replies; four instruction-tuned LLMs.
papers.training: Random seed 42; no training.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, latency and token use by batch size.
papers.baselines: Single-agent topology.
papers.results: Multi-agent accuracy 90.6% at 5 tasks and 65.3% at 80 vs single agent 73.1% to 16.6%; significant beyond 10 tasks (FDR p<0.01); up to 65-fold fewer tokens.
papers.statistics: Welch t-tests for accuracy; Wilcoxon rank-sum for latency and tokens; Benjamini-Hochberg correction; R 4.3.
papers.availability: Code and logs in the supplement.

papers.title: A multi-agent large language model (LLM) platform for structured medical anamnesis in outpatient care
papers.authors: Zaitseva E, Ochotnicky S, Fandakova M, Levashenko V, Rabcan J
papers.aim: IntroductionMedical anamnesis is fundamental to clinical decision-making, yet outpatient consultations often provide limited time for systematic information collection. This study investigates whether structured anamnesis acquisition can be redistributed to a pre-consultation phase using a framework-driven large language model (LLM) platform.MethodsWe developed Symptio, a proof-of-concept multi-agent LLM platform that operationalises the SOCRATES, Review of Systems, and SAMPLE frameworks as machine-interpretable constraints within a human-in-the-loop workflow.
papers.method: The system was evaluated in 100 simulated outpatient scenarios. Generated anamneses were compared with reference-standard representations using structural agreement and field-level performance metrics.ResultsFull structural agreement across all three frameworks was achieved in 87% of scenarios. Framework-specific agreement reached 96% for SOCRATES, 88% for Review of Systems, and 93% for SAMPLE. Micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score were 99.04%, 98.54%, and 98.79%, respectively. Although no high-severity errors were identified, 58 field-level discrepancies, including 28 medium-severity errors, were observed, supporting the need for physician review of all outputs.DiscussionThe findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of acquiring structured anamnesis in a framework-driven manner within a process-oriented multi-agent LLM architecture under controlled conditions.
papers.result: The proposed approach enables the relocation of routine information collection to a pre-consultation phase while preserving physician authority through human-in-the-loop validation. Further studies are required to evaluate clinical safety, workflow impact, and effectiveness in real-world settings.
papers.gap: Simulated patients only; no uncertainty flags for incomplete histories.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Proof of concept; clinical evaluation required.
papers.methodologyDetail: Symptio moves routine history-taking to the waiting period before an outpatient visit. A chain of narrowly scoped LLM agents collects the patient's answers, structures them and checks them, and the physician then reviews and confirms the result, so authority stays with the clinician. The system was tested on 100 simulated scenarios against reference structured anamneses. It exemplifies separation of concerns between agents to limit generative errors.
papers.studyDesign: Proof-of-concept system development and simulation evaluation (Slovakia).
papers.datasets: 100 simulated outpatient scenarios with reference-standard structured anamneses.
papers.preprocessing: Patients enter information during pre-consultation waiting time; outputs mapped to a structured schema.
papers.modelDetails: Symptio: role-specialised sequential LLM agents, each performing one narrow transformation (collection, structuring, validation), with physician review before use.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Structural agreement with the reference representation and field-level precision/recall.
papers.baselines: Reference-standard anamneses.
papers.results: High structural agreement and field-level performance in simulated scenarios (details in paper).

papers.title: Enhancing Diagnostic Accuracy through Multi-Agent Conversations: Using Large Language Models to Mitigate Cognitive Bias
papers.authors: Yu He Ke, Rui Yang, Sui An Lie, Taylor Xin Yi Lim, Hairil Rizal Abdullah, Daniel Shu Wei Ting, Nan Liu
papers.aim: Background: Cognitive biases in clinical decision-making significantly contribute to errors in diagnosis and suboptimal patient outcomes. Addressing these biases presents a formidable challenge in the medical field.
papers.method: Objective: This study explores the role of large language models (LLMs) in mitigating these biases through the utilization of a multi-agent framework. We simulate the clinical decision-making processes through multi-agent conversation and evaluate its efficacy in improving diagnostic accuracy. Methods: A total of 16 published and unpublished case reports where cognitive biases have resulted in misdiagnoses were identified from the literature. In the multi-agent framework, we leveraged GPT-4 to facilitate interactions among four simulated agents to replicate clinical team dynamics. Each agent has a distinct role: 1) To make the final diagnosis after considering the discussions, 2) The devil's advocate and correct confirmation and anchoring bias, 3) The tutor and facilitator of the discussion to reduce premature closure bias, and 4) To record and summarize the findings. A total of 80 simulations were evaluated for the accuracy of initial diagnosis, top differential diagnosis and final two differential diagnoses. Results: In a total of 80 responses evaluating both initial and final diagnoses, the initial diagnosis had an accuracy of 0% (0/80), but following multi-agent discussions, the accuracy for the top differential diagnosis increased to 71.3% (57/80), and for the final two differential diagnoses, to 80.0% (64/80).
papers.result: Conclusions: The framework demonstrated an ability to re-evaluate and correct misconceptions, even in scenarios with misleading initial investigations. The LLM-driven multi-agent conversation framework shows promise in enhancing diagnostic accuracy in diagnostically challenging medical scenarios.
papers.gap: Few cases; no calibrated uncertainty; vignettes not real workflow.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Small sample, single model; publication bias of case reports.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched PubMed for case reports where a misdiagnosis was attributed to cognitive bias, selected 16 scenarios, and ran each through a multi-agent conversation with GPT-4. One agent proposed an initial diagnosis and others played roles designed to challenge it, after which a final diagnosis was given; initial and final answers were compared with the true diagnosis. It shows structured disagreement between agents as a way to reduce anchoring.
papers.studyDesign: Simulation study using published case reports of misdiagnosis due to cognitive bias; Singapore (no patient data, IRB not required).
papers.datasets: 162 PubMed case reports screened, 37 eligible, 15 selected plus one clinician-derived scenario; 80 framework responses.
papers.preprocessing: Two clinically trained reviewers screened reports independently; rare diseases excluded.
papers.modelDetails: GPT-4 Turbo multi-agent conversation: a first-responder agent gives an initial diagnosis; devil's advocate, tutor and facilitator agents challenge it to counter anchoring and confirmation bias; final diagnosis after discussion.
papers.training: No training; API prompting.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy of initial versus final diagnosis, top-2 differential accuracy.
papers.baselines: Initial single-agent diagnosis; human misdiagnosis in the original reports.
papers.results: Final diagnoses after multi-agent discussion were more accurate than initial ones, including correction of misconceptions in cases with misleading initial investigations.

papers.title: MedCollab: IBIS-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration with Hierarchical Disease Relation Chains for Clinical Diagnosis
papers.authors: Yuqi Zhan, Xinyue Wu, Tianyu Lin, Yutong Bao, Xiaoyu Wang, Weihao Cheng, Huangwei Chen, Feiwei Qin, Zhu Zhu
papers.aim: Clinical diagnosis is a gradual process of evidence integration, in which physicians move from symptoms and medical history to examinations, competing hypotheses, disease relations, and treatment decisions. Large language models have advanced medical text understanding and generation.
papers.method: Yet their clinical use remains limited by weak evidence grounding, opaque reasoning, and inconsistent links among differential diagnosis, final diagnosis, diagnostic basis, and treatment planning. We introduce MedCollab, a multi-agent framework for full-cycle clinical diagnosis and report generation. MedCollab coordinates specialist and examination agents according to patient records. It structures agent deliberation with an Issue-Based Information System (IBIS) protocol, so that each diagnostic position is supported by patient-specific evidence and medical knowledge. It also builds Hierarchical Disease Relation Chains (HDRC) to connect accepted hypotheses through progression, complication, and comorbidity relations. During multi-round deliberation, a verifier-guided consensus module evaluates evidence support, medical plausibility, and logical conflicts. It then adjusts agent contributions and filters unsupported reasoning.
papers.result: Experiments on ClinicalBench and MIMIC-IV show that MedCollab outperforms leading LLMs and medical multi-agent baselines in diagnostic accuracy, evidence consistency, and clinical reasoning quality. These results indicate that structured and auditable collaboration can produce more faithful and clinically coherent diagnostic reports.
papers.gap: Reasoning-quality weights are heuristic, not calibrated; text only; no clinician deferral.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; LLM-assisted data reformatting; benchmark rather than live use.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedCollab sends each case to the relevant specialist and examination agents, then structures their discussion as issues, positions and arguments scored by evidence and knowledge, links diagnoses through disease relation chains, and lets a general-practitioner agent audit the logic and weight each agent's vote by reasoning quality before producing a diagnosis and treatment plan. It was tested on two text case benchmarks against single LLMs and other multi-agent systems. Evidence-weighted voting is an alternative to simple majority consensus.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark evaluation of a multi-agent diagnostic framework (preprint), China.
papers.datasets: ClinicalBench (1,500 bilingual English-Chinese cases) and 983 curated MIMIC-IV cases reformatted to the same schema; a sample reviewed by clinicians.
papers.preprocessing: MIMIC-IV records mapped to a standard case schema with DeepSeek-V4-Pro and audited.
papers.modelDetails: MedCollab: specialist and examination agents coordinated by patient record; deliberation structured with Issue-Based Information System (issue, position, argument) and hierarchical disease relation chains; a GP agent audits logic and weights votes by reasoning quality; RAG over a medical knowledge base; treatment plan generation.
papers.training: No training; prompting with LLM backbones.
papers.evaluation: Primary diagnosis accuracy (ACC), CDR, entity-F1 for factual consistency, department classification accuracy, reasoning-quality scores.
papers.baselines: Leading LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini-3-Flash, Qwen3, GLM-4.7, HuatuoGPT-o1) and multi-agent systems (MedLA, ClinicalAgent, MEDDxAgent).
papers.results: ACC 76.9% (ClinicalBench) and 57.7% (MIMIC-IV) vs best baseline 68.7% and 55.0%; CDR 72.4/48.3.

papers.title: MedRoute: RL-Based Dynamic Specialist Routing in Multi-Agent Medical Diagnosis
papers.authors: Ashmal Vayani, Parth Parag Kulkarni, Joseph Fioresi, Song Wang, Mubarak Shah
papers.aim: Medical diagnosis using Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) has gained increasing attention due to capability of these models in providing precise diagnoses. These models generally combine medical questions with visual inputs to generate diagnoses or treatments.
papers.method: However, they are often overly general and unsuitable under the wide range of medical conditions in real-world healthcare. In clinical practice, diagnosis is performed by multiple specialists, each contributing domain-specific expertise. To emulate this process, a potential solution is to deploy a dynamic multi-agent LMM framework, where each agent functions as a medical specialist. Current approaches in this emerging area, typically relying on static or predefined selection of various specialists, cannot be adapted to the changing practical scenario. In this paper, we propose MedRoute, a flexible and dynamic multi-agent framework that comprises of a collaborative system of specialist LMM agents. Furthermore, we add a General Practitioner with an RL-trained router for dynamic specialist selection, and a Moderator that produces the final decision. In this way, our framework closely mirrors real clinical workflows. Extensive evaluations on text and image-based medical datasets demonstrate improved diagnostic accuracy, outperforming the state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.result: Our work lays a strong foundation for future research. Code and models are available at https://github.com/UCF-CRCV/MedRoute/.
papers.gap: Routing ignores calibrated confidence and clinician escalation; QA benchmarks only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; benchmark questions not clinical workflows.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedRoute imitates referral: a general-practitioner agent reads the question and image and an RL-trained router chooses which specialist agents to consult, from a pool built from the data. Specialists contribute in sequence and a moderator decides. The router learns which specialists improve accuracy. Learned routing is an alternative to fixed rules, but here it optimises accuracy rather than safety or uncertainty.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with reinforcement-learning routing, evaluated on public medical QA and VQA benchmarks (UCF, preprint).
papers.datasets: MedQA, PubMedQA (text); PMC-VQA, DeepLesion (4,736 single-answer samples) and PathVQA (image-text); router trained on small samples of training splits.
papers.preprocessing: Specialist pool built by asking GPT-4.1-mini for 3-7 specialists per question and keeping the most frequent top-k.
papers.modelDetails: General Practitioner LMM with an RL-trained router selects specialist LMM agents dynamically; specialists answer sequentially; a Moderator produces the final decision.
papers.training: Router optimised with reinforcement learning in PyTorch on one GPU node.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on each benchmark.
papers.baselines: Single LMMs and static multi-agent frameworks (e.g. MDAgents-style fixed selection).
papers.results: Improved accuracy over static and single-agent baselines across text and image datasets; code released.

papers.title: MedCoAct: Confidence-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Complete Clinical Decision
papers.authors: Hongjie Zheng, Zesheng Shi, Ping Yi
papers.aim: Autonomous agents utilizing Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in isolated medical tasks like diagnosis and image analysis, but struggle with integrated clinical workflows that connect diagnostic reasoning and medication decisions. We identify a core limitation: existing medical AI systems process tasks in isolation without the cross-validation and knowledge integration found in clinical teams, reducing their effectiveness in real-world healthcare scenarios.
papers.method: To transform the isolation paradigm into a collaborative approach, we propose MedCoAct, a confidence-aware multi-agent framework that simulates clinical collaboration by integrating specialized doctor and pharmacist agents, and present a benchmark, DrugCareQA, to evaluate medical AI capabilities in integrated diagnosis and treatment workflows.
papers.result: Our results demonstrate that MedCoAct achieves 67.58\% diagnostic accuracy and 67.58\% medication recommendation accuracy, outperforming single agent framework by 7.04\% and 7.08\% respectively. This collaborative approach generalizes well across diverse medical domains, proving especially effective for telemedicine consultations and routine clinical scenarios, while providing interpretable decision-making pathways.
papers.gap: Self-reported LLM confidence is not calibrated; no human escalation.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedCoAct pairs a doctor agent and a pharmacist agent so that diagnosis and medication are decided together. Each agent reports a confidence, and low-confidence outputs trigger reflection and cross-checking by the other agent to stop hallucinated information propagating. The authors built a 2,700-case benchmark for joint diagnosis and prescription and compared against a single agent. It is an example of confidence used to trigger review between agents, though the confidence is self-reported.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with a new benchmark (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, preprint).
papers.datasets: DrugCareQA: 2,700 consultation cases covering integrated diagnosis and medication selection.
papers.preprocessing: Cases built with standard diagnosis and prescription answers.
papers.modelDetails: MedCoAct: doctor and pharmacist agents with tools and confidence-aware reflection; low confidence triggers cross-validation and revision between the agents.
papers.training: No training; LLM prompting.
papers.evaluation: Top-1 and top-3 diagnostic accuracy; drug prescription accuracy.
papers.baselines: Single-agent framework and other agent systems.
papers.results: Diagnostic accuracy 67.58% and medication accuracy 67.58%, +7.04 and +7.08 points over the single agent.

papers.title: MACD: Multi-Agent Clinical Diagnosis with Self-Learned Knowledge for LLM
papers.authors: Wenliang Li, Rui Yan, Xu Zhang, Li Chen, Hongji Zhu, Jing Zhao, Junjun Li, Mengru Li, Wei Cao, Zihang Jiang, et al.
papers.aim: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in supporting medical diagnosis, with prompting-based methods offering a flexible and deployable means of capability enhancement. However, existing prompt engineering and multi-agent approaches often focus on optimizing single inferences, paying less attention to the accumulation of reusable experience from clinical practice, constraining their real-world applicability.
papers.method: To address this, this study proposes a novel Multi-Agent Clinical Diagnosis (MACD) framework, which allows LLMs to self-learn clinical knowledge via a multi-agent pipeline that summarizes, refines, and applies diagnostic insights, mirroring the professional development of human physicians. We further extend it to a MACD-human collaborative workflow, where multiple LLM-based diagnostician agents engage in iterative consultations, supported by a judge agent and human oversight for cases where agreement is not reached. The MIMIC-MACD cohort comprising 4,390 real-world patient cases across seven diseases is constructed, including 1,314 cases for knowledge learning and 3,076 held-out cases for evaluation. Across diverse open-weight LLMs, MACD significantly improves primary diagnostic accuracy, achieving an average improvement of 11.6 percentage points over established authoritative knowledge, while narrowing the performance gap between open-weight models and state-of-the-art LLMs.
papers.result: Furthermore, the MACD-human workflow yields an 18.3-percentage-point improvement over physician-only diagnosis on text-only vignettes, demonstrating the synergistic potential of human-AI collaboration. This work thus presents a scalable self-learning paradigm that bridges the gap between the intrinsic knowledge of LLMs and the demands of real-world clinical practice, advancing towards a reliable, interpretable, and deployable AI-assisted diagnosis.
papers.gap: Text records only; no uncertainty or deferral; learned knowledge could encode biases.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: MACD lets language-model agents learn diagnostic knowledge from cases they solve correctly: one agent summarises cases, another refines the accumulated knowledge, and a diagnostician applies it to new cases. Data from MIMIC-IV covering seven abdominal and chest diseases were split so that knowledge came only from successful reasoning, then the approach was compared with standard prompting and with physicians, including a combined human-AI workflow. It shows a way to transfer expertise to lower-resource settings without retraining.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective method development and human-AI evaluation on MIMIC-IV (USTC, preprint); includes a physician comparison.
papers.datasets: MIMIC-MACD: 4,390 cases, 2,400 abdominal (appendicitis 957, cholecystitis 648, diverticulitis 257, pancreatitis 538) and 1,990 chest (pneumonia 1,024, PE 852, pericarditis 114); HPI, examination, labs and radiology reports.
papers.preprocessing: Success-driven sampling splits data into a Learning Set and a Test Set so knowledge is learned only from correct reasoning.
papers.modelDetails: Multi-Agent Clinical Diagnosis: agents summarise cases, refine and apply self-learned diagnostic knowledge; base diagnosticians include Llama-3.1-8B and others; an MACD-human workflow adds physicians.
papers.training: No weight training; knowledge learned as text and refined iteratively.
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy versus guideline prompting and physicians.
papers.baselines: Standard and guideline-based prompting; physicians alone.
papers.results: Improved accuracy over prompting baselines; MACD-human workflow +18.3 percentage points over physician-only diagnosis on text vignettes.

papers.title: Empowering Medical Multi-Agents with Clinical Consultation Flow for Dynamic Diagnosis
papers.authors: Sihan Wang, Suiyang Jiang, Yibo Gao, Boming Wang, Shangqi Gao, Xiahai Zhuang
papers.aim: Traditional AI-based healthcare systems often rely on single-modal data, limiting diagnostic accuracy due to incomplete information. However, recent advancements in foundation models show promising potential for enhancing diagnosis combining multi-modal information.
papers.method: While these models excel in static tasks, they struggle with dynamic diagnosis, failing to manage multi-turn interactions and often making premature diagnostic decisions due to insufficient persistence in information collection.To address this, we propose a multi-agent framework inspired by consultation flow and reinforcement learning (RL) to simulate the entire consultation process, integrating multiple clinical information for effective diagnosis. Our approach incorporates a hierarchical action set, structured from clinic consultation flow and medical textbook, to effectively guide the decision-making process. This strategy improves agent interactions, enabling them to adapt and optimize actions based on the dynamic state.
papers.result: We evaluated our framework on a public dynamic diagnosis benchmark. The proposed framework evidentially improves the baseline methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing foundation model-based methods.
papers.gap: Simulated patients; no calibrated confidence or clinician handover.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: Diagnosis is framed as a multi-turn game between a doctor agent, a simulated patient and an examiner that returns test results. The doctor agent's possible actions are organised hierarchically following real consultation flow, and reinforcement learning teaches it to keep collecting information rather than diagnosing too early. The approach was evaluated on a public dynamic diagnosis benchmark.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on a public dynamic-diagnosis benchmark (Fudan University).
papers.datasets: Public multi-turn dynamic diagnosis benchmark (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Hierarchical action set derived from clinical consultation flow and a medical textbook.
papers.modelDetails: Doctor, patient and examiner agents in a partially observable Markov game; the doctor agent chooses actions from the hierarchical set and is optimised with reinforcement learning to avoid premature diagnosis.
papers.training: RL training of the doctor policy (settings in paper).
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy and interaction efficiency on the benchmark.
papers.baselines: Foundation models and prior agent methods.
papers.results: Improved over baselines and reached state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark.

papers.title: A Structured Debate-Mixture-of-Agents Framework for Complex Clinical Diagnostic Decision Support
papers.authors: Chang Xia, Leilei Ouyang, Huimin Wang, Yong Zhao, Kang Li
papers.aim: Large language models (LLMs) show potential for medical tasks, but their single-turn question-answer format does not reflect how clinical diagnosis is performed in practice. As a result, they remain limited in complex diagnostic settings.
papers.method: We developed Debate-Mixture-of-Agents (DMoA), a novel multi-agent framework that structures role-based interaction to support iterative diagnostic reasoning. Base models and DMoA were evaluated on 297 rare disease cases and 1,719 challenging cases. Across both datasets, DMoA improved most likely diagnosis accuracy by 10.21 percentage points and safety rate by 11.36 percentage points over GPT-4o baseline. Ablation experiments showed that the gains were not simply due to the use of more models or longer outputs, but also reflected the contribution of the structured workflow. Further analyses examined how framework design, base model choice, and token budget affected performance.
papers.result: DMoA performed better with a 4*2 structure, stronger base models, and a larger token budget. These findings demonstrate the potential of DMoA for clinical tasks and suggest further investigation of multi-agent frameworks.
papers.gap: No calibrated uncertainty; no clinician escalation; case-report text only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Preprint; reference diagnoses from published cases.
papers.methodologyDetail: DMoA organises diagnosis as a structured debate: in each Debater a Presenter proposes a diagnostic direction and a Rebutter critiques it, the Presenter revises, and an Aggregator combines the revised hypotheses from several Debaters. It was evaluated on 2,016 rare and challenging cases for most-likely and top-three diagnoses and a safety rate, with ablations showing that the structured workflow, not just more compute, drove the improvement. Fixed role topology contrasts with open-ended agent chat.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective benchmark study with ablations, reliability, error and cost analyses (IEEE JBHI submission, preprint).
papers.datasets: Clinical case dataset of Li et al.: 297 rare-disease cases (297 diseases, 33 categories) and 1,719 challenging cases (32 specialties); supplementary clinical knowledge questions.
papers.preprocessing: Structured or semi-structured case text; reference diagnoses extracted from the case reports; an Information Editor tool helps prepare inputs.
papers.modelDetails: Debate-Mixture-of-Agents: fixed role topology of Debaters (each a Presenter and a Rebutter that generate, rebut and revise hypotheses) feeding an Aggregator that integrates revised hypotheses into the final diagnosis; best with 4x2 structure.
papers.training: No training; varied base models and token budgets.
papers.evaluation: Most-likely-diagnosis accuracy, top-3 accuracy, safety rate, reliability and cost.
papers.baselines: GPT-4o and other base models alone; ablations with more models or longer outputs.
papers.results: Across both datasets DMoA improved most-likely-diagnosis accuracy by 10.21 points and safety rate by 11.36 points over GPT-4o; gains not explained by more models or tokens alone.

papers.title: From Analytics to Tumor Boards: An Evidence-Linked Multi-Agent Workflow for Oncology Feature Extraction
papers.authors: Daniel Kang, Michelle Hu, Soorya Ram Shimgekar, Shayan Vassef, Yufan Wang, Anit Kumar Sahu, Munmun De Choudhury, Vedant Das Swain, Christian Poellabauer, Li Yan Khor, et al.
papers.aim: Clinically relevant oncology information is distributed across heterogeneous, longitudinal documentation, creating substantial abstraction burden and requiring accurate attribution across specimens, tumors, biomarkers, and time points, while manual cancer-registry abstraction can require 27.2 minutes per case, highlighting the need for scalable methods that preserve clinical context while converting documentation into structured data. We evaluate an oncology information-extraction workflow in which OncoLens supplies multi-source, oncology-aware document selection, aggregation, and normalization from integrated EHRs, while the NimbleMind Multi-Agent System (nMAS) is a configurable oncology information-extraction workflow that extracts clinically relevant structured fields from fragmented oncology documentation.
papers.method: The extraction task uses a clinician-informed schema of 328 attributes spanning report metadata, diagnosis, staging, and cancer-type-specific information. nMAS separates clinician-defined field specifications from model execution and combines complexity-aware extraction, report-level consolidation, and source-grounded validation. The retrospective evaluation included 230 de-identified oncology documents from 40 patients and 418 clinician-reviewed document-field pairs containing 1,126 non-empty reference values.
papers.result: Evaluation focused on fields identified by clinicians as present in the source documents rather than exhaustively annotating all 328 schema fields. nMAS achieved a rank-weighted value-level precision of 82.6%, recall of 87.5%, and F1 of 85.0%, compared with an F1 of 66.4% for an independently implemented UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 comparator. These findings support the feasibility of using a configurable, source-grounded extraction workflow to convert fragmented oncology documentation into reusable structured data.
papers.gap: Small single-site set; no uncertainty score per field.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Evaluated only on fields present; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: Manual cancer-registry abstraction can take about 27 minutes per case. This workflow splits a 328-field oncology schema across specialised agents that extract values from heterogeneous reports and attach the supporting text to every value, so a clinician can verify each one before a tumour board. It was evaluated on 230 documents from 40 patients against clinician review. Evidence linking is a practical form of the audit trail this study requires.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective evaluation of an evidence-linked multi-agent extraction workflow (ML4H 2026 submission).
papers.datasets: 230 de-identified oncology documents from 40 patients (pathology, radiology, cytology, clinical notes) from one academic medical centre; clinician-informed schema of 328 attributes.
papers.preprocessing: Direct identifiers replaced by placeholders; evaluation restricted to fields clinicians identified as present.
papers.modelDetails: nMAS: separates clinician-defined fields across specialised agents, links each extracted value to its source evidence, and normalises values for tumour-board use.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Rank-weighted value-level precision and related extraction metrics on clinician-reviewed fields.
papers.baselines: Single-pass LLM extraction.
papers.results: High rank-weighted value-level precision on present fields (exact figures in paper); evidence links support review.

papers.title: CoMMa: Contribution-Aware Medical Multi-Agents for Decentralized Oncology Decision Support
papers.authors: Yichen Wu, Kailong Fan, Sangjoon Park, Yuhan Liu, Zhiyi Shi, Sekeun Kim, Dania Daye, Hana Farzaneh, Xiang Li, Raul Uppot, et al.
papers.aim: Recent multi-agent frameworks have shown promise for oncology decision support, yet most assume centralized data access and rely on prompt-based assignment, limiting their applicability in privacy-sensitive clinical settings. We propose Contribution-Aware Medical Multi-Agents (CoMMa), a decentralized LLM-agent framework where specialists operate on partitioned clinical data streams.
papers.method: Unlike prior approaches that share inputs across agents, CoMMa enforces data decentralization to include stronger role specialization and further enhances this via agent-specific finetuning. To enable reliable and interpretable coordination, we introduce a contribution-aware aggregation mechanism that replaces stochastic, narrative-based reasoning with deterministic embedding projections to approximate each agent's marginal utility.
papers.result: This yields explicit credit assignment over agents, providing a stable and interpretable decision pathway aligned with clinical requirements. We evaluate CoMMa on multiple oncology benchmarks, including real-world multidisciplinary tumor board datasets from large academic hospitals in North America and East Asia, as well as public datasets, demonstrating strong performance and generalization across heterogeneous clinical settings.
papers.gap: Attribution is not uncertainty; no deferral to clinicians.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: CoMMa keeps each type of patient evidence separate and assigns it to a specialist agent, as in a decentralised setting where data cannot be pooled. Each specialist is a frozen language-model encoder with a small trainable head, the specialists exchange information, and a gating network trained with a Shapley-based estimate decides how much each contributes to the final prediction for that patient. The result is an explicit credit assignment over agents rather than narrative consensus.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on oncology benchmarks (Harvard/MGH, preprint).
papers.datasets: Multiple oncology decision benchmarks with partitioned evidence streams (imaging findings, labs, staging, history).
papers.preprocessing: Patient evidence partitioned into separate streams, each given to one specialist.
papers.modelDetails: CoMMa: each stream encoded by a frozen open-source LLM plus a trainable specialty projection; cross-agent collaborative reasoning; contribution-aware aggregation with a sample-specific fusion gate regularised by a Shapley contribution estimator.
papers.training: Agent-specific fine-tuning of projection modules.
papers.evaluation: Prediction accuracy and stability; agent-level attribution.
papers.baselines: Single-agent and role-play multi-agent LLM frameworks.
papers.results: Outperformed single- and role-play multi-agent baselines with stable, interpretable agent contributions.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Intelligence for Multidisciplinary Decision-Making in Gastrointestinal Oncology
papers.authors: Rongzhao Zhang, Junqiao Wang, Shuyun Yang, Mouxiao Bian, Chihao Zhang, Dongyang Wang, Qiujuan Yan, Yun Zhong, Yuwei Bai, Guanxu Zhu, et al.
papers.aim: Multimodal clinical reasoning in the field of gastrointestinal (GI) oncology necessitates the integrated interpretation of endoscopic imagery, radiological data, and biochemical markers. Despite the evident potential exhibited by Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), they frequently encounter challenges such as context dilution and hallucination when confronted with intricate, heterogeneous medical histories.
papers.method: In order to address these limitations, a hierarchical Multi-Agent Framework is proposed, which emulates the collaborative workflow of a human Multidisciplinary Team (MDT). The system attained a composite expert evaluation score of 4.60/5.00, thereby demonstrating a substantial improvement over the monolithic baseline.
papers.result: It is noteworthy that the agent-based architecture yielded the most substantial enhancements in reasoning logic and medical accuracy. The findings indicate that mimetic, agent-based collaboration provides a scalable, interpretable, and clinically robust paradigm for automated decision support in oncology.
papers.gap: No calibrated confidence or deferral; expert scoring only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: Each modality of a gastrointestinal oncology case is handled by its own agent, which extracts structured findings into a shared evidence container; conflicts between modalities are detected, and a core agent writes the MDT report. Compared with one model reading all inputs concatenated, with the same fine-tuning, the multi-agent design avoided context dilution and was rated better by experts. It supports modality-specific agents feeding a coordinating agent.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and expert evaluation of a hierarchical multi-agent MDT system for GI oncology (Shanghai hospitals, preprint).
papers.datasets: GI oncology cases with EMR text, 5-10 endoscopic frames per case, radiology reports and laboratory results, with target MDT diagnostic reports.
papers.preprocessing: Inputs split by modality; cross-modal conflict detection before final reasoning.
papers.modelDetails: Specialist agents for text, endoscopy, radiology and laboratory (Qwen-3 32B; Intern S1 Mini for endoscopy) write to an evidence container; an MDT-Core agent produces the standardised report.
papers.training: Supervised fine-tuning on the training set (same for baseline).
papers.evaluation: Expert panel scoring of reasoning logic, medical accuracy and other dimensions.
papers.baselines: Single-agent Qwen-3 32B with concatenated inputs and identical fine-tuning; real-world clinical benchmarks.
papers.results: Substantial improvements over the single agent across all dimensions, largest in reasoning logic and medical accuracy.

papers.title: MTBBench: A Multimodal Sequential Clinical Decision-Making Benchmark in Oncology
papers.authors: Kiril Vasilev, Alexandre Misrahi, Eeshaan Jain, Phil F Cheng, Petros Liakopoulos, Olivier Michielin, Michael Moor, Charlotte Bunne
papers.aim: Multimodal Large Language Models (LLMs) hold promise for biomedical reasoning, but current benchmarks fail to capture the complexity of real-world clinical workflows. Existing evaluations primarily assess unimodal, decontextualized question-answering, overlooking multi-agent decision-making environments such as Molecular Tumor Boards (MTBs).
papers.method: MTBs bring together diverse experts in oncology, where diagnostic and prognostic tasks require integrating heterogeneous data and evolving insights over time. Current benchmarks lack this longitudinal and multimodal complexity. We introduce MTBBench, an agentic benchmark simulating MTB-style decision-making through clinically challenging, multimodal, and longitudinal oncology questions. Ground truth annotations are validated by clinicians via a co-developed app, ensuring clinical relevance. We benchmark multiple open and closed-source LLMs and show that, even at scale, they lack reliability -- frequently hallucinating, struggling with reasoning from time-resolved data, and failing to reconcile conflicting evidence or different modalities.
papers.result: To address these limitations, MTBBench goes beyond benchmarking by providing an agentic framework with foundation model-based tools that enhance multi-modal and longitudinal reasoning, leading to task-level performance gains of up to 9.0% and 11.2%, respectively. Overall, MTBBench offers a challenging and realistic testbed for advancing multimodal LLM reasoning, reliability, and tool-use with a focus on MTB environments in precision oncology.
papers.gap: Measures answer accuracy, not calibrated confidence or deferral; oncology broadly, not neuro-oncology.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: MTBBench simulates a molecular tumour board: an agent receives a patient's history as a sequence of clinical events with pathology images, immunohistochemistry, blood results and genomics, and must answer clinically validated questions about diagnosis, prognosis and biomarkers. The authors benchmarked many models, analysed their failure modes, and showed that giving agents foundation-model tools for each modality improves multimodal and longitudinal reasoning. It is a relevant benchmark design for longitudinal brain-tumour cases.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation and evaluation of LLM agents for molecular tumour board decisions (ETH Zürich, EPFL, HUG; NeurIPS 2025).
papers.datasets: MTBBench: multimodal, longitudinal oncology questions built from patient data (H&E, IHC, haematology, genomics, temporally ordered clinical events); ground truth validated by clinicians through a co-developed app.
papers.preprocessing: Patient histories presented as time-ordered events with multimodal attachments; multiple-choice and true/false question formats.
papers.modelDetails: Open and closed LLMs/VLMs evaluated as agents; an agentic framework adds foundation-model tools for pathology, IHC and text and access to knowledge bases.
papers.training: No training of the benchmarked models.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on diagnosis, prognosis (e.g. 2-year recurrence) and biomarker questions; analysis of hallucination, temporal reasoning and conflicting evidence.
papers.baselines: LLMs without tools.
papers.results: Models at scale lacked reliability (hallucinations, poor time-resolved reasoning, failure to reconcile conflicting modalities); the tool-based agent framework improved task performance by up to 9.0% (multimodal) and 11.2% (longitudinal).
papers.availability: Benchmark on GitHub (bunnelab/MTBBench) and Hugging Face.

papers.title: TumorBoard: Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent Decision Support for Longitudinal Neuro-Oncology
papers.authors: Yantong Liu, Zheyu Zhang, Runpeng Liu, Mu Xitang, Seong-Yoon Shin, Hyun-Ae Lee
papers.aim: Neuro-oncology decisions require coordinated interpretation of serial MRI, pathology, molecular markers, treatment history, performance status, and evolving guidelines. We present TumorBoard, a multi-agent decision-support system built around a shared longitudinal case state and an auditable claim-evidence ledger.
papers.method: Specialist agents for radiology, neuropathology, molecular diagnosis, guidelines, and therapy planning produce atomic claims with provenance. An adversarial critic exposes contradictions, and a safety governor releases, qualifies, or defers recommendations according to evidence sufficiency and temporal validity. On a 360-case hidden benchmark at a matched token budget, TumorBoard achieved an action F1 of 0.772 and evidence entailment of 0.914. It exceeded the strongest typed-council baseline by 3.1 percentage points (95% CI: 1.6 to 4.7, adjusted p = 0.0012), while recommendation-to-evidence coverage reached 0.927. Under evidence deletion, the system deferred 84.2% of unsafe cases and limited harmful recommendations to 5.8%.
papers.result: The safety governor reduced harmful release by 7.8 percentage points at a false-deferral cost of 4.3 percentage points. Ablation studies of the ledger, critic, and governor produced the predicted failure patterns, establishing structured coordination as the source of the measured multi-agent advantage.
papers.gap: Deferral based on evidence sufficiency rules rather than calibrated model uncertainty; no imaging models; synthetic benchmark.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: TumorBoard keeps one shared, time-stamped state for each brain-tumour patient. Specialist agents add small factual claims, each linked to its source evidence, to a ledger; a critic agent looks for contradictions; and a safety governor decides whether a recommendation is released, released with qualification, or deferred because evidence is insufficient or out of date. On a 360-case benchmark built by clinicians it beat several budget-matched agent designs, and ablations showed that the ledger, critic and governor each produced the expected benefit. It is the closest published design to this study's orchestrator and audit trail.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with a 360-case hidden benchmark built by clinical authors; perturbation, ablation and expert-rating studies (Kunsan National University, preprint).
papers.datasets: Longitudinal neuro-oncology case packets (serial MRI, pathology, molecular markers, treatment history, performance status, guideline versions); 360-case hidden test set balanced for common and difficult states, incomplete cases included.
papers.preprocessing: Two-pass case construction: one clinical author builds the chronological packet, a second independently creates the action graph and decisive evidence; disagreements adjudicated before model runs.
papers.modelDetails: Specialist agents (radiology, neuropathology, molecular diagnosis, guidelines, therapy planning) write atomic claims with provenance to a shared case state and claim-evidence ledger; an adversarial critic exposes contradictions; a safety governor releases, qualifies or defers recommendations by evidence sufficiency and temporal validity.
papers.training: No training; matched token budget across systems.
papers.evaluation: Action-graph F1, evidence entailment, recommendation-to-evidence coverage, harmful-release and deferral rates; robustness to evidence deletion, conflict, guideline version shift, role corruption and prompt injection.
papers.baselines: Direct LLM, RAG agent, plan-critique, free-chat council and typed council (budget-matched).
papers.results: Action F1 0.772 (95% CI 0.754-0.790), entailment 0.914, harmful release 0.039 vs 0.068 for the typed council; gain over best baseline 0.031 (Holm p=0.0012); governor reduced harmful release by 7.8 points at 4.3 points false deferral; 14,220 tokens and 21.8 s per case.
papers.statistics: Paired case-level bootstrap CIs; mixed-effects ordinal models for expert ratings; exact paired tests; weighted kappa/ICC; Holm correction.
papers.availability: All prompts, retrieved passages, messages, ledger states and outputs retained for audit.

papers.title: OMGs: A multi-agent system supporting MDT decision-making across the ovarian tumour care continuum
papers.authors: Yangyang Zhang, Zilong Wang, Jianbo Xu, Yongqi Chen, Chu Han, Zhihao Zhang, Shuai Liu, Hui Li, Huiping Zhang, Ziqi Liu, et al.
papers.aim: Ovarian tumour management has increasingly relied on multidisciplinary tumour board (MDT) deliberation to address treatment complexity and disease heterogeneity. However, most patients worldwide lack access to timely expert consensus, particularly in resource-constrained centres where MDT resources are scarce or unavailable.
papers.method: Here we present OMGs (Ovarian tumour Multidisciplinary intelligent aGent System), a multi-agent AI framework where domain-specific agents deliberate collaboratively to integrate multidisciplinary evidence and generate MDT-style recommendations with transparent rationales. To systematically evaluate MDT recommendation quality, we developed SPEAR (Safety, Personalization, Evidence, Actionability, Robustness) and validated OMGs across diverse clinical scenarios spanning the care continuum. In multicentre re-evaluation, OMGs achieved performance comparable to expert MDT consensus ($4.45 \pm 0.30$ versus $4.53 \pm 0.23$), with higher Evidence scores (4.57 versus 3.92). In prospective multicentre evaluation (59 patients), OMGs demonstrated high concordance with routine MDT decisions.
papers.result: Critically, in paired human-AI studies, OMGs most substantially enhanced clinicians' recommendations in Evidence and Robustness, the dimensions most compromised when multidisciplinary expertise is unavailable. These findings suggest that multi-agent deliberative systems can achieve performance comparable to expert MDT consensus, with potential to expand access to specialized oncology expertise in resource-limited settings.
papers.gap: No calibrated uncertainty or explicit deferral; gynaecologic oncology.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: OMGs reproduces an ovarian tumour board with five specialist agents coordinated by an orchestrator and supported by services for data extraction, evidence retrieval and provenance. It was evaluated on multicentre retrospective and prospective cohorts by expert raters using a five-dimension scale with a safety gate, and in paired studies where clinicians made recommendations with and without the system. It shows a staged evaluation including prospective cohorts and human-AI comparison.
papers.studyDesign: Multicentre retrospective and prospective evaluation with paired human-AI studies; five tertiary hospitals in Shanghai, Jiangsu and Zhejiang; IRB approvals at all centres.
papers.datasets: Retrospective and prospective ovarian tumour cohorts with demographics, pathology, imaging, labs, molecular and genetic profiles, treatment and follow-up.
papers.preprocessing: De-identified data; agent servers extract data, assemble context and track provenance.
papers.modelDetails: OMGs: an orchestrator coordinates five specialty LLM agents (chair, oncologist, radiologist, pathologist, nuclear medicine) through structured MDT deliberation, with evidence retrieval and provenance tracking.
papers.training: No training reported.
papers.evaluation: Five SPEAR dimension scores and a safety-gated overall score from three senior gynaecologic oncologists; paired human-AI studies.
papers.baselines: Clinician recommendations without AI; single-agent LLMs.
papers.results: OMGs enhanced clinicians' recommendations most in Evidence and Robustness, the dimensions weakest when multidisciplinary expertise is lacking.
papers.statistics: Pre-specified endpoints, two-sided alpha 0.05; ICC(2,k) for inter-rater agreement.

papers.title: SurvAgent: Hierarchical CoT-Enhanced Case Banking and Dichotomy-Based Multi-Agent System for Multimodal Survival Prediction
papers.authors: Guolin Huang, Wenting Chen, Jiaqi Yang, Xinheng Lyu, Xiaoling Luo, Sen Yang, Xiaohan Xing, Linlin Shen
papers.aim: Survival analysis is critical for cancer prognosis and treatment planning, yet existing methods lack the transparency essential for clinical adoption. While recent pathology agents have demonstrated explainability in diagnostic tasks, they face three limitations for survival prediction: inability to integrate multimodal data, ineffective region-of-interest exploration, and failure to leverage experiential learning from historical cases.
papers.method: We introduce SurvAgent, the first hierarchical chain-of-thought (CoT)-enhanced multi-agent system for multimodal survival prediction. SurvAgent consists of two stages: (1) WSI-Gene CoT-Enhanced Case Bank Construction employs hierarchical analysis through Low-Magnification Screening, Cross-Modal Similarity-Aware Patch Mining, and Confidence-Aware Patch Mining for pathology images, while Gene-Stratified analysis processes six functional gene categories.
papers.result: Both generate structured reports with CoT reasoning, storing complete analytical processes for experiential learning. (2) Dichotomy-Based Multi-Expert Agent Inference retrieves similar cases via RAG and integrates multimodal reports with expert predictions through progressive interval refinement. Extensive experiments on five TCGA cohorts demonstrate SurvAgent's superority over conventional methods, proprietary MLLMs, and medical agents, establishing a new paradigm for explainable AI-driven survival prediction in precision oncology.
papers.gap: Survival prediction, not diagnosis; no deferral; no clinician evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: SurvAgent first builds a bank of analysed historical cases: a pathology agent explores each slide at increasing magnification, including low-confidence patches, and writes structured reports with reasoning, while a genomics agent summarises gene groups. For a new case it retrieves similar cases and uses expert agents to reason about survival, producing a prediction with an explanation. It shows agents using case memory and confidence-guided exploration in pathology.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on five public cancer survival datasets (preprint).
papers.datasets: Five TCGA-type cohorts with whole-slide images and genomic data and survival times.
papers.preprocessing: WSIs analysed hierarchically at x2.5, x10 and x20; genes grouped into six functional categories.
papers.modelDetails: SurvAgent: case bank built by a PathAgent (low-magnification screening, similarity-aware and confidence-aware patch mining, checklist reports, chain-of-thought with self-critique) and a GenAgent; at inference similar cases are retrieved and dichotomy-based multi-expert agents predict survival.
papers.training: Not detailed in extract.
papers.evaluation: Concordance index; interpretability of reports.
papers.baselines: Multimodal survival models (e.g. MCAT, pathomic fusion) and pathology agents.
papers.results: Best C-index across all five datasets with interpretable multimodal reports.

papers.title: Demo: Healthcare Agent Orchestrator (HAO) for Patient Summarization in Molecular Tumor Boards
papers.authors: Matthias Blondeel, Noel Codella, Sam Preston, Hao Qiu, Leonardo Schettini, Frank Tuan, Wen-wai Yim, Smitha Saligrama, Mert Öz, Shrey Jain, et al.
papers.aim: Molecular Tumor Boards (MTBs) are multidisciplinary forums where oncology specialists collaboratively assess complex patient cases to determine optimal treatment strategies. A central element of this process is the patient summary, typically compiled by a medical oncologist, radiation oncologist, or surgeon, or their trained medical assistant, who distills heterogeneous medical records into a concise narrative to facilitate discussion.
papers.method: This manual approach is often labor-intensive, subjective, and prone to omissions of critical information. To address these limitations, we introduce the Healthcare Agent Orchestrator (HAO), a Large Language Model (LLM)-driven AI agent that coordinates a multi-agent clinical workflow to generate accurate and comprehensive patient summaries for MTBs. Evaluating predicted patient summaries against ground truth presents additional challenges due to stylistic variation, ordering, synonym usage, and phrasing differences, which complicate the measurement of both succinctness and completeness. To overcome these evaluation hurdles, we propose TBFact, a ``model-as-a-judge'' framework designed to assess the comprehensiveness and succinctness of generated summaries. Using a benchmark dataset derived from de-identified tumor board discussions, we applied TBFact to evaluate our Patient History agent. Results show that the agent captured 94% of high-importance information (including partial entailments) and achieved a TBFact recall of 0.84 under strict entailment criteria.
papers.result: We further demonstrate that TBFact enables a data-free evaluation framework that institutions can deploy locally without sharing sensitive clinical data. Together, HAO and TBFact establish a robust foundation for delivering reliable and scalable support to MTBs.
papers.gap: Recall only, no assessment of decisions; no uncertainty flags.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Proprietary data from one partner; LLM-based judging.
papers.methodologyDetail: For molecular tumour boards, the PatientHistory agent compiles a patient's records into a timeline and summary in which every statement cites its source. The team evaluated it on 71 real board patients by breaking reference summaries into facts and checking, with an LLM judge, whether each important fact appeared in the agent's summary, a method they propose for local, data-free evaluation. Specialised prompts that prioritise biomarkers, treatment lines and imaging status improved recall. Citation-backed summaries are relevant to the audit trail.
papers.studyDesign: System demonstration with retrospective evaluation on a proprietary corpus (Microsoft Health and Life Sciences, preprint).
papers.datasets: TB-Bench: de-identified longitudinal materials for 71 oncology patients discussed at molecular tumour boards (board transcripts, EHR exports with imaging, biomarkers, diagnoses, medications, procedures, social history, clinician summaries).
papers.preprocessing: Reference summaries standardised by LLM into a narrative plus timeline; evaluation restricted to dataset-verifiable facts.
papers.modelDetails: Healthcare Agent Orchestrator coordinating agents; the PatientHistory agent builds a citation-backed clinical timeline and summary using Universal Abstraction prompt templates.
papers.training: No training; generic vs specialised prompting.
papers.evaluation: TBFact: fact-level recall of high-importance and all facts under strict and partial entailment, a data-free evaluation framework deployable locally.
papers.baselines: Generic prompting baseline.
papers.results: Specialised prompting gave TBFact recall 0.84 for high-importance facts (0.71 all) vs 0.66 and 0.56 generic; 94% of high-importance information included with partial credit.
papers.availability: Orchestrator code released by Microsoft (open source); TB-Bench proprietary.

papers.title: Multi-Agent AI System for Radiology Report Structuring and Quality Assurance with Independent Radiologist Evaluation
papers.authors: Iryna Hartsock, Cesar Lam, Christopher Otteni, Aliya Qayyum, Robert Gatenby, Cyrillo Araujo, Ghulam Rasool
papers.aim: Purpose: To develop and evaluate a locally deployed multi-agent AI system for radiology report structuring and quality assurance. Materials and Methods: This retrospective study included 638 radiology reports from CT examinations of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis dictated by 15 board-certified radiologists in 2023 and 2024.
papers.method: A multi-agent AI pipeline was developed to perform report structuring and quality assurance (QA). The system structured the report into standardized anatomical sections at the sentence level using regex rules and local large language models. It also detected mismatches between the Findings and Impression sections, or within sections; gender-anatomy conflicts; and undocumented communication of critical findings. Two board-certified radiologists independently evaluated a 45-report subset. Results: The multi-agent system structured the Findings sections of all reports (22,270 sentences) into a predefined anatomical format while retaining the original report content. The system flagged 90 (14.1%) reports, most commonly for section mismatches (80 reports, 12.5%). In the radiologist evaluation, both reviewers agreed that 31 (69%) were correctly restructured, 2 reports (4%) were incorrectly restructured, and disagreed on the remaining 12 reports (27%). Both reviewers agreed that no clinically important information was omitted and no fabricated content was introduced. Overall QA performance was rated as "excellent" or "good" in 84% of the evaluated reports, with the remaining reports rated as "fair". Conclusion: A locally deployed multi-agent AI system combined radiology report structuring and quality assurance within a single workflow.
papers.result: The system demonstrated favorable performance in radiologist evaluation. Such systems may support standardization of reporting and quality assurance in radiology practice.
papers.gap: Escalation by rule failure rather than calibrated confidence; report text only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: Radiology reports were split into sentences and passed through a cascade: cheap rules first, then a local LLM, then a reasoning model only for sentences that remained ambiguous, to sort findings into standard anatomical sections; further agents performed quality checks. Independent radiologists judged the output. Escalating hard items to a more capable component is a simple example of tiered routing, and all processing stayed inside the hospital.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and independent radiologist evaluation, Moffitt Cancer Center; IRB approved, consent waived; models run locally behind the firewall.
papers.datasets: 638 CT chest/abdomen/pelvis reports by 15 radiologists (2023-2024), 146-1,594 words; 22,270 sentences.
papers.preprocessing: Findings extracted by rule-based section detection; custom sentence segmentation; follow-up fragments merged with preceding sentences.
papers.modelDetails: Cascade of agents: Agent 1 regex rules, Agent 2 LLaMA 3, Agent 3 DeepSeek-R1 for harder sentences, assigning sentences to standardised anatomical sections; separate QA agents check report quality.
papers.training: No training; local open models.
papers.evaluation: Share of sentences classified at each stage; radiologist evaluation of structuring accuracy and QA findings.
papers.baselines: Radiologist reference.
papers.results: Regex classified 83.0% of sentences, LLaMA 3 12.3%, DeepSeek-R1 4.7%; <0.04% unclassified (headers); favourable radiologist ratings.

papers.title: MARCH: Multi-Agent Radiology Clinical Hierarchy for CT Report Generation
papers.authors: Yi Lin, Yihao Ding, Yonghui Wu, Yifan Peng
papers.aim: Automated 3D radiology report generation often suffers from clinical hallucinations and a lack of the iterative verification found in human practice. While recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced the field, they typically operate as monolithic "black-box" systems without the collaborative oversight characteristic of clinical workflows.
papers.method: To address these challenges, we propose MARCH (Multi-Agent Radiology Clinical Hierarchy), a multi-agent framework that emulates the professional hierarchy of radiology departments and assigns specialized roles to distinct agents. MARCH utilizes a Resident Agent for initial drafting with multi-scale CT feature extraction, multiple Fellow Agents for retrieval-augmented revision, and an Attending Agent that orchestrates an iterative, stance-based consensus discourse to resolve diagnostic discrepancies.
papers.result: On the RadGenome-ChestCT dataset, MARCH significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both clinical fidelity and linguistic accuracy. Our work demonstrates that modeling human-like organizational structures enhances the reliability of AI in high-stakes medical domains.
papers.gap: No uncertainty passed to a human; consensus may hide disagreement; chest CT only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: MARCH mirrors a radiology department hierarchy for chest CT reporting. A resident agent trained on paired CTs and reports writes a draft using region-level features; a retrieval agent finds similar previous cases; fellow agents revise the draft with that evidence; and an attending agent resolves disagreements through a structured consensus discussion. It was trained and tested on a large public CT dataset with language and clinical-accuracy metrics.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on a public chest CT report dataset (Weill Cornell, preprint).
papers.datasets: RadGenome-ChestCT: 25,692 chest CT scans from 21,304 patients with reports; official split 24,128 train / 1,564 test.
papers.preprocessing: CT partitioned into ten anatomical subregions with the SAT segmentation model.
papers.modelDetails: Resident Agent (frozen RadFM ViT3D + LLaMA-2-Chat-7B with LoRA) drafts the report; Retrieval Agent finds similar cases (image-image, image-text, logits-based over 18 abnormalities); Fellow Agents (GPT-4.1) revise; Attending Agent (GPT-4o) runs stance-based consensus.
papers.training: AdamW, lr 1e-5, batch 1, 10 epochs (~40 h) on one H100; temperature 0 for LLM agents.
papers.evaluation: BLEU, ROUGE-L, METEOR and clinical efficacy precision/recall/F1 over 18 abnormalities via RadBERT.
papers.baselines: R2GenPT and other 3D report-generation models.
papers.results: Significantly better clinical fidelity and linguistic scores than state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: A Multimodal Multi-Agent Framework for Radiology Report Generation
papers.authors: Ziruo Yi, Ting Xiao, Mark V. Albert
papers.aim: Radiology report generation (RRG) aims to automatically produce diagnostic reports from medical images, with the potential to enhance clinical workflows and reduce radiologists' workload. While recent approaches leveraging multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) have achieved strong results, they continue to face challenges such as factual inconsistency, hallucination, and cross-modal misalignment.
papers.method: We propose a multimodal multi-agent framework for RRG that aligns with the stepwise clinical reasoning workflow, where task-specific agents handle retrieval, draft generation, visual analysis, refinement, and synthesis.
papers.result: Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms a strong baseline in both automatic metrics and LLM-based evaluations, producing more accurate, structured, and interpretable reports. This work highlights the potential of clinically aligned multi-agent frameworks to support explainable and trustworthy clinical AI applications.
papers.gap: No clinician evaluation or uncertainty; X-ray only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: Report generation is split into five steps handled by separate agents: retrieve similar prior reports, draft from them, extract key findings, describe the image directly with a vision-language model, and synthesise a final report. Separating retrieval from direct image reading reduces copying of irrelevant text. Evaluated against a single-model baseline with automatic and LLM-judged metrics.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on chest X-ray report generation (University of North Texas, preprint).
papers.datasets: Public chest X-ray report dataset (MIMIC-CXR style) with image-report pairs.
papers.preprocessing: Image and report embeddings for CLIP-style cross-modal retrieval.
papers.modelDetails: Five agents in sequence: Retrieval (top-k similar reports), Draft, Refiner (key findings), Vision (image description by a VLM) and Synthesis (final report), communicating through structured intermediate outputs.
papers.training: No training beyond retrieval embeddings.
papers.evaluation: Automatic NLG metrics and LLM-based evaluation of accuracy, structure and interpretability.
papers.baselines: Strong single-model RAG baseline.
papers.results: Outperformed the baseline on automatic metrics and LLM-based evaluation, with more accurate and structured reports.

papers.title: How Well Can Modern LLMs Act as Agent Cores in Radiology Environments?
papers.authors: Qiaoyu Zheng, Chaoyi Wu, Weike Zhao, Pengcheng Qiu, Lisong Dai, Ya Zhang, Yanfeng Wang, Weidi Xie
papers.aim: Radiology, with its heterogeneous modalities, anatomies, and evolving protocols, is a natural yet high-stakes testbed for agentic AI. As LLMs grow more capable and tool ecosystems such as MCP and Agent Skills more complex, their capability boundaries in radiology remain unclear.
