papers.method: We introduce RadA-BenchPlat, a two-layer benchmark spanning idealized reasoning and real-world execution: a synthetic layer with 2.2k clinician-verified records, 24.2k QA pairs, and 10 tool categories under diverse availability settings; and a real-environment layer pairing 165 2D/3D cases with executable tools for grounding, diagnosis, and report generation. We find that high completion rates under idealized settings do not carry over to real environments, where the best agents trail their upper bound by approximately 15% and drop to 0.327 on long-chain tasks. Prompting strategies (few-shot exemplars, multi-agent coordination) and AutoTB (on-the-fly synthesis of missing tools) mitigate execution drift and breakdowns in difficult scenarios, lifting execution success to 94.5%, yet remain not fully reliable.
papers.result: Overall, our findings suggest that radiology agents are no longer limited to conceptual demonstrations, but are beginning to show potential for real-world applications. Project repository: https://github.com/MAGIC-AI4Med/RadABench
papers.gap: No measure of agent confidence or safe handover; mostly synthetic records.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: The benchmark separates two questions: how well an LLM plans and reasons when tools are perfect, using a large synthetic set of radiologist-checked records and simulated tools, and how well agents perform with real, imperfect tools on 165 real 2D and 3D cases for grounding, diagnosis and report generation. Many recent models were compared by task difficulty. The gap between idealised and real performance highlights tool failure and long chains as the main weaknesses of radiology agents.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study of LLMs as agent cores in radiology (Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Renmin Hospital, preprint).
papers.datasets: RadA-BenchPlat synthetic layer: 2,200 clinician-verified patient records over 22 anatomy-modality combinations, 24.2k QA pairs and 10 tool categories; real-environment layer: 165 2D/3D cases (e.g. Chest ImaGenome, RadGenome-MRI) with executable tools.
papers.preprocessing: Records generated by GPT-4 from templates and polished for over a month by a radiologist (97.32% information-valid, 96.73% clinically consistent); 550 records reviewed by three further clinicians.
papers.modelDetails: LLM agent cores (DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-235B, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, Gemini-3.0-Pro, GPT-5.2, GPT-4o, o3) planning and calling tools for grounding, diagnosis and report generation under varied tool availability.
papers.training: No training; prompting strategies compared.
papers.evaluation: Task completion by difficulty; Dice/Jaccard for grounding; accuracy for diagnosis; RadGraph F1, RaTE, LLM and human ratings for reports.
papers.baselines: Upper-bound idealised tools versus real tools.
papers.results: Completion falls with difficulty (Claude-Sonnet-4.5 0.691 regular to 0.327 high); real-environment agents trail their idealised upper bound by about 15%.

papers.title: AgentRx: A Benchmark Study of LLM Agents for Multimodal Clinical Prediction Tasks
papers.authors: Baraa Al Jorf, Farah E. Shamout
papers.aim: Building effective clinical decision support systems requires the synthesis of complex heterogeneous multimodal data. Such modalities include temporal electronic health records data, medical images, radiology reports, and clinical notes.
papers.method: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have shown impressive performance in various healthcare tasks, especially those involving textual modalities. Considering the fragmentation of healthcare data across hospital systems, collaborative agent frameworks present a promising direction to mitigate data sharing challenges. However, the effectiveness of LLM agents for multimodal clinical risk prediction remains largely unexamined. In this work, we conduct a systematic evaluation of LLM-based agents for clinical prediction tasks using large-scale real-world data. We assess performance in unimodal and multimodal settings and quantify performance gaps between single agent and multi-agent systems. Our findings highlight that single agent frameworks outperform naive multi-agent systems, are better at handling multimodal data, and are better calibrated.
papers.result: This underscores a critical need for improving multi-agent collaboration to better handle heterogeneous inputs. By open-sourcing our code and evaluation framework, this work offers a new benchmark to support future developments relating to agentic systems in healthcare.
papers.gap: No uncertainty or deferral; ICU prediction rather than diagnosis.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: AgentRx builds a large multimodal benchmark from MIMIC data, aligning a patient summary, ICU time series, chest radiograph and radiology reports per encounter, and tests whether LLM agents, alone or as a team of modality-specific agents, can predict mortality and length of stay. Four comparable-size vision-language backbones were used and compared with trained multimodal models. The negative finding is important: agent collaboration did not automatically handle heterogeneous data well.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study (CHIL 2026, PMLR) of single and multi-agent LLM systems for multimodal clinical risk prediction, NYU Abu Dhabi.
papers.datasets: MIMIC-IV EHR time series, MIMIC-CXR images, MIMIC-IV-Note radiology reports and patient summaries; mortality task 17,773 train / 4,925 test encounters (CXR subset 4,259/1,174); length-of-stay task of similar size.
papers.preprocessing: Modalities aligned per encounter; images 224x224; EHR serialised for LLM input.
papers.modelDetails: Single-agent and multi-agent (modality-specific agents with collaboration) frameworks with four ~7-8B VLM backbones: Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, LLaVA-Med-v1.5.
papers.training: Batch size 3-4 (16 for supervised models, 1 for LLaVA-Med); supervised multimodal baselines trained.
papers.evaluation: AUROC, AUPRC and related metrics for in-hospital mortality and length of stay, unimodal and multimodal.
papers.baselines: Supervised multimodal fusion models; single-agent LLMs.
papers.results: LLM agents lagged supervised models on multimodal prediction, and multi-agent collaboration did not reliably close the gap, showing a need for better collaboration over heterogeneous inputs.

papers.title: Safeguarding Agentic AI in Radiology Workflows: A Multimodel Evaluation of Rule-based and Large Language Model-based Verification
papers.authors: Semil Eminovic, Robin Schmidt, Bogdan Levita, Maximilian Lindholz, Tobias Penzkofer, Jawed Nawabi
papers.aim: Purpose: To estimate how often tool-using large language model (LLM) agents record clinically relevant false or unsupported information in simulated radiology documentation and how much safeguards applied before each action reduce these errors. Materials and Methods: In this simulation study (October 2026), 48 synthetic, radiologist-reviewed base scenarios covered finding communication, tumor board preparation and follow-up management.
papers.method: Forty-three also had a misleading-information variant (91 variants). Six LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B) completed each variant with permissions only, deterministic rules, and rules plus a locally run LLM checker (1638 episodes). The primary outcome was at least one executed high-severity violation per episode. Risk differences were estimated per agent at base-scenario level and, exploratorily, pooled across agents, with analyses of document access and blocks. Results: With permissions only, 7.3%-27.1% of episodes had a high-severity violation (pooled across agents, 19.4%). Pooled, it was 16.7% with rules (-2.8 percentage points; 95% CI: -6.1, 0.5) and 13.2% with rules plus the LLM checker (-6.2; 95% CI: -9.5, -3.0). Adding the LLM checker to rules changed it by -3.5 (95% CI: -6.3, -0.7). No difference between agents was detected (P = .43), and task success did not decrease detectably. In misleading variants, agents opened the altered document in 83% of episodes regardless of error, and 58% of erroneous statements cited it. Most blocked actions (64%-68%) would not have caused a violation and were returned for revision.
papers.result: Conclusion: Layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors. Errors after misleading information reflected misjudged rather than missed information.
papers.gap: Verification is rule- and LLM-based, not calibrated uncertainty; synthetic data.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Simulated environment; future model versions may differ.
papers.methodologyDetail: Six LLM agents were asked to write radiology documentation in a simulated information system; in some scenarios an external document contained misleading information. Every action that would change the record had to pass a safety gate configured with permissions only, deterministic rules, or rules plus an LLM checker. A separate evaluator scored every executed statement against a hidden reference. Results quantify how often agents record false information and how much layered verification helps, which informs the safeguards around the orchestrator in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Controlled computational study in a simulated radiology information environment with synthetic patients (Charité Berlin); protocol, scenarios and analysis fixed in advance; reported to TRIPOD-LLM and CLAIM.
papers.datasets: 48 synthetic base scenarios in three documentation modules; 48 clean and 43 misleading-information variants (91 variants); six agents; 1,638 episodes.
papers.preprocessing: Reference standard stored separately and hidden from the agent and checker.
papers.modelDetails: Tool-using LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B) with read-only tools; each state-changing action passes a safeguard gate: permissions only, plus deterministic rules, plus an LLM checker; blocked actions can be revised twice within 40 tool calls.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Proportion of episodes with a high-severity error, task success, justified vs unnecessary blocks, scored by a deterministic evaluator.
papers.baselines: Permissions-only configuration.
papers.results: With permissions only, high-severity errors in 7.3% (Claude Sonnet 5.5) to 27.1% (GLM-5.3) of episodes; average 14.9% clean and 25.0% with misleading information; task success 49.0-77.1%; layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors.
papers.statistics: Within-scenario risk differences with stratified t-intervals (Satterthwaite) and cluster bootstrap; no hypothesis tests.

papers.title: Autonomous Artificial Intelligence Agents for Clinical Decision Making in Oncology
papers.authors: Dyke Ferber, Omar S. M. El Nahhas, Georg Wölflein, Isabella C. Wiest, Jan Clusmann, Marie-Elisabeth Leßman, Sebastian Foersch, Jacqueline Lammert, Maximilian Tschochohei, Dirk Jäger, et al.
papers.aim: Multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) systems have the potential to enhance clinical decision-making by interpreting various types of medical data. However, the effectiveness of these models across all medical fields is uncertain.
papers.method: Each discipline presents unique challenges that need to be addressed for optimal performance. This complexity is further increased when attempting to integrate different fields into a single model. Here, we introduce an alternative approach to multimodal medical AI that utilizes the generalist capabilities of a large language model (LLM) as a central reasoning engine. This engine autonomously coordinates and deploys a set of specialized medical AI tools. These tools include text, radiology and histopathology image interpretation, genomic data processing, web searches, and document retrieval from medical guidelines. We validate our system across a series of clinical oncology scenarios that closely resemble typical patient care workflows. We show that the system has a high capability in employing appropriate tools (97%), drawing correct conclusions (93.6%), and providing complete (94%), and helpful (89.2%) recommendations for individual patient cases while consistently referencing relevant literature (82.5%) upon instruction. This work provides evidence that LLMs can effectively plan and execute domain-specific models to retrieve or synthesize new information when used as autonomous agents. This enables them to function as specialist, patient-tailored clinical assistants.
papers.result: It also simplifies regulatory compliance by allowing each component tool to be individually validated and approved. We believe, that our work can serve as a proof-of-concept for more advanced LLM-agents in the medical domain.
papers.gap: Only 20 cases; no uncertainty or deferral; tool errors can propagate silently.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: An LLM agent was given a set of validated specialist tools and a retrieval system over oncology guidelines and asked to work through 20 realistic multimodal cancer cases, deciding which tool to call, combining results and citing evidence. Clinicians assessed tool use, conclusions and recommendations against GPT-4 alone. The authors argue that validating each tool separately simplifies regulation, a principle relevant to separately validated agents in this framework.
papers.studyDesign: Preprint version of the autonomous oncology agent study (Heidelberg, Dresden, TUM and others), later published in Nature Cancer.
papers.datasets: Knowledge base of about 6,800 documents from MDCalc, UpToDate, MEDITRON guidelines, ASCO, ESMO and Onkopedia; 20 realistic multimodal patient cases (histology, radiology, genomics, clinical history).
papers.preprocessing: Guideline documents keyword-filtered and embedded for retrieval.
papers.modelDetails: GPT-4 as central agent calling tools: vision transformers predicting mutations from histology, MedSAM for radiology segmentation, OncoKB, PubMed search and guideline retrieval.
papers.training: No LLM training; tools are pre-trained models.
papers.evaluation: Correct tool use, correctness of conclusions and completeness of recommendations, citation of guidelines, judged by clinicians.
papers.baselines: GPT-4 without tools.
papers.results: Decision accuracy rose from about 30% (GPT-4 alone) to about 87% with tools; most tool calls correct; most answers cited guidelines.

papers.title: MedOpenClaw and MedFlowBench: Auditing Medical Agents in Full-Study Workflows
papers.authors: Weixiang Shen, Chengzhi Shen, Yanzhu Hu, Che Liu, Junde Wu, Jiayuan Zhu, Xiao Han, Zongyue Li, Jingpei Wu, Min Xu, et al.
papers.aim: Medical imaging benchmarks often evaluate VLMs on pre-selected 2D images, slices, crops, or patches, making evaluation closer to visual recognition. Real clinical workflows impose a different burden: readers must search through complete studies, operate imaging software, navigate across slices and magnifications, and document visual evidence that can be audited.
papers.method: We argue that this evidence-producing workflow is a critical missing evaluation axis for medical imaging agents. To study it, we introduce MedFlowBench, a full-study benchmark for VLM agents, together with MedOpenClaw, a controlled and replayable runtime in which agents operate medical imaging viewers such as 3D Slicer and QuPath. In each episode, an agent inspects a complete radiology study or whole-slide pathology image, returns a task answer, and submits structured evidence, including key slices, coordinates, regions of interest, or lesion-state fields. This evidence is automatically checked against withheld masks, annotations, and labels. Across evaluated models, final answer-only scoring gives an overly optimistic picture: when answers must also be supported by correct evidence, performance drops substantially on complex workflows. We further find that adding image-analysis tools does not by itself solve the problem.
papers.result: Tools help when they make a complex procedure simple and reliable, but agents still struggle when they must choose inputs, manage viewer state, and verify intermediate outputs over multiple steps. MedFlowBench exposes whether medical imaging agents can produce auditable evidence from complete studies, rather than plausible answers from selected images.
papers.gap: No uncertainty or deferral measure; agents not clinically validated.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of answering questions about pre-cropped images, agents in MedOpenClaw must open complete studies in real imaging software, navigate them, find the lesion and record auditable visual evidence. The benchmark covers brain MRI, longitudinal MRI, PET/CT and pathology slides and scores both answers and the evidence produced. It shows that brain-tumour localisation is within reach of frontier models but that longitudinal reasoning and verification remain weak.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark and runtime development for full-study imaging agents (TUM, LMU, Imperial, Oxford, NVIDIA and others, preprint).
papers.datasets: Full imaging studies from public sets including UCSF-PDGM (brain MRI), longitudinal MRI, NSCLC-Radiogenomics (PET/CT), BRACS and CAMELYON17 (pathology).
papers.preprocessing: Complete volumes or slides loaded in viewers; tasks defined with evidence requirements.
papers.modelDetails: MedOpenClaw: a controlled, replayable runtime in which VLM agents operate 3D Slicer and QuPath (navigate slices and magnifications, measure, annotate); MedFlowBench tasks in radiology and pathology tracks.
papers.training: No training; evaluated general and medical VLMs (GPT-5.x, Gemini 3.x, Claude, Qwen3.5) and baselines M3D and RadFM.
papers.evaluation: Task accuracy, strict evidence-grounded accuracy and localisation, under MCQ or structured-answer protocols.
papers.baselines: Direct VLM answering on pre-selected images.
papers.results: Brain MRI easiest (Gemini 3.1 Pro task 0.73, strict 0.73, localisation 0.96); performance dropped sharply for longitudinal comparison and small lesions (e.g. lung PET/CT); tools help when they simplify procedures, but agents struggle to choose inputs, manage viewer state and verify intermediate results.
papers.availability: Runtime and benchmark released; dataset licences listed.

papers.title: A Modular Agent for Reliable and Auditable Spatial Relation Verification in CT Scans
papers.authors: Simon Vincent Abel, Heiko Hillenhagen, Michael Götz, Timo Ropinski, Ayhan Can Erdur, Daniel Santak Wolf
papers.venue: Published at the MICCAI 2026 Agentic AI for Medicine Workshop
papers.aim: Reliable spatial understanding is an important prerequisite for future medical vision-language systems that aim to support radiological report generation and structured image understanding. While modern vision-language models (VLMs) show promising performance on many medical imaging tasks, recent evidence suggests they remain weak in controlled spatial reasoning and often fail to reliably ground spatial relations in image evidence.
papers.method: Given that radiological reasoning hinges on understanding the relative positions of anatomical structures and findings, this spatial weakness poses risks to diagnostic accuracy. We present a modular medical imaging agent for binary spatial relation verification in axial CT slices. Instead of directly predicting spatial answers end-to-end, the system decomposes the task into explicit stages: language parsing, anatomical localization, and deterministic geometric verification. Natural-language queries are converted into structured relation tuples, queried organs are localized with a YOLO-based detector, and the final spatial decision is computed from object centers using deterministic geometric rules. We evaluate the approach on the held-out MIRP spatial QA benchmark and compare it against representative end-to-end VLM baselines.
papers.result: The best-performing hybrid configuration reaches 94.1% accuracy and 94.2% F1, outperforming direct Qwen2-VL prompting by 42.5 percentage points in accuracy, while preserving interpretable intermediate representations and auditable reasoning stages. The results suggest that explicit modular spatial verification can serve as a promising building block for future report-oriented medical imaging agents.
papers.gap: Single 2D task; detector errors not expressed as uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: The agent keeps a normal question-answer interface but, instead of letting the vision-language model guess spatial relations, it routes the question to a detector that finds the anatomical structures and a geometry module that computes the relation, so each answer is traceable to detections and rules. Compared directly with the same models answering end to end, the modular design was far more accurate. It supports delegating verifiable sub-tasks to specialised, auditable components.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and controlled comparison (Ulm University and TUM; MICCAI 2026 Agentic AI workshop).
papers.datasets: MIRP RQ1 benchmark of axial CT slices with binary spatial-relation questions; held-out test set of 938 image-question pairs; anatomical detector trained on the training cohort plus AMOS and BTCV (61 classes, 421,023 instances).
papers.preprocessing: Segmentation-derived bounding boxes; strict patient-level separation between detector training and test.
papers.modelDetails: Hybrid agent: a VLM controller (MedGemma 4B or Qwen2-VL 7B, orchestrated with LangChain) extracts the spatial query and routes it to a pathway where a YOLO detector localises structures and deterministic geometry computes the answer.
papers.training: Detector trained on the training cohort (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Accuracy and F1 on binary spatial questions.
papers.baselines: Direct end-to-end VLM prompting with the same interface.
papers.results: Best hybrid configuration 94.1% accuracy and 94.2% F1, 42.5 points more accurate than direct Qwen2-VL prompting.

papers.title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Uncertainty-Aware and Abstention-Enabled Acute Ischemic Stroke Imaging Decisions
papers.authors: Md Rashadul Islam
papers.aim: Artificial intelligence models have shown strong potential in acute ischemic stroke imaging, particularly for lesion detection and segmentation using computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. However, most existing approaches operate as black box predictors, producing deterministic outputs without explicit uncertainty awareness or structured mechanisms to abstain under ambiguous conditions.
papers.method: This limitation raises serious safety and trust concerns in high risk emergency radiology settings. In this paper, we propose an explainable agentic AI framework for uncertainty aware and abstention enabled decision support in acute ischemic stroke imaging. The framework follows a modular agentic pipeline in which a perception agent performs lesion aware image analysis, an uncertainty estimation agent computes slice level predictive reliability, and a decision agent determines whether to issue a prediction or abstain based on predefined uncertainty thresholds. Unlike prior stroke imaging systems that primarily focus on improving segmentation or classification accuracy, the proposed framework explicitly prioritizes clinical safety, transparency, and clinician aligned decision behavior. Qualitative and case based analyses across representative stroke imaging scenarios demonstrate that uncertainty driven abstention naturally emerges in diagnostically ambiguous regions and low information slices.
papers.result: The framework further integrates visual explanation mechanisms to support both predictive and abstention decisions, addressing a key limitation of existing uncertainty aware medical imaging systems. Rather than introducing a new performance benchmark, this work presents agentic control, uncertainty awareness, and selective abstention as essential design principles for developing safe and trustworthy medical imaging AI systems.
papers.gap: Fixed thresholds, no calibration analysis or clinician evaluation; no quantitative results.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: The framework separates perception, uncertainty estimation and decision into distinct agents for stroke imaging: one agent analyses lesions, another estimates how reliable each slice prediction is, and a decision agent applies a safety policy that can abstain, with visual explanations for both outcomes. The evaluation is qualitative, showing where abstention occurs. It illustrates the design principle of this study but without quantitative validation.
papers.studyDesign: Conceptual framework with qualitative case-based evaluation (Daffodil International University, Bangladesh, preprint).
papers.datasets: Representative acute ischaemic stroke CT/MRI slices (public data; no new cohort reported).
papers.preprocessing: Slice-wise analysis.
papers.modelDetails: Perception agent for lesion-aware analysis; uncertainty estimation agent computing slice-level predictive reliability; decision agent applying a safety policy that predicts or abstains by predefined uncertainty thresholds; explainability module for both predictions and abstentions.
papers.training: Not reported in detail.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative and behavioural evaluation of uncertainty and abstention patterns.
papers.baselines: None quantitative.
papers.results: Abstention arose in diagnostically ambiguous regions and low-information slices; no new performance benchmark claimed.

papers.title: WSI-Agents: A Collaborative Multi-Agent System for Multi-Modal Whole Slide Image Analysis
papers.authors: Xinheng Lyu, Yuci Liang, Wenting Chen, Meidan Ding, Jiaqi Yang, Guolin Huang, Daokun Zhang, Xiangjian He, Linlin Shen
papers.aim: Whole slide images (WSIs) are vital in digital pathology, enabling gigapixel tissue analysis across various pathological tasks. While recent advancements in multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) allow multi-task WSI analysis through natural language, they often underperform compared to task-specific models.
papers.method: Collaborative multi-agent systems have emerged as a promising solution to balance versatility and accuracy in healthcare, yet their potential remains underexplored in pathology-specific domains. To address these issues, we propose WSI-Agents, a novel collaborative multi-agent system for multi-modal WSI analysis.
papers.result: WSI-Agents integrates specialized functional agents with robust task allocation and verification mechanisms to enhance both task-specific accuracy and multi-task versatility through three components: (1) a task allocation module assigning tasks to expert agents using a model zoo of patch and WSI level MLLMs, (2) a verification mechanism ensuring accuracy through internal consistency checks and external validation using pathology knowledge bases and domain-specific models, and (3) a summary module synthesizing the final summary with visual interpretation maps. Extensive experiments on multi-modal WSI benchmarks show WSI-Agents's superiority to current WSI MLLMs and medical agent frameworks across diverse tasks.
papers.gap: Verification scores not calibrated; no clinician handover.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: WSI-Agents answers questions about whole-slide images by first deciding what kind of task a question is and which specialised pathology model should answer it, then checking the preliminary answers with verification steps based on consistency and external knowledge before summarising. It balances the versatility of general models with the accuracy of task-specific ones, which is the same trade-off as the Pathology Agent in this framework.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and benchmark evaluation (Shenzhen University and partners, preprint).
papers.datasets: Multi-modal WSI benchmarks with WSIs paired with questions and reports (e.g. WSI-VQA and report generation sets).
papers.preprocessing: WSIs processed by pathology feature encoders.
papers.modelDetails: WSI-Agents: a task agent classifies the question and allocates specialised expert agents; verification mechanisms (internal consistency and external knowledge checks) assess answers; a summary module produces the final response.
papers.training: Expert agents are existing pathology MLLMs and task-specific models.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on WSI VQA, report generation metrics and multi-task performance.
papers.baselines: Single pathology MLLMs and task-specific models.
papers.results: Outperformed current WSI MLLMs and medical agent frameworks across tasks.

papers.title: LungNoduleAgent: A Collaborative Multi-Agent System for Precision Diagnosis of Lung Nodules
papers.authors: Cheng Yang, Hui Jin, Xinlei Yu, Zhipeng Wang, Yaoqun Liu, Fenglei Fan, Dajiang Lei, Gangyong Jia, Changmiao Wang, Ruiquan Ge
papers.aim: Diagnosing lung cancer typically involves physicians identifying lung nodules in Computed tomography (CT) scans and generating diagnostic reports based on their morphological features and medical expertise. Although advancements have been made in using multimodal large language models for analyzing lung CT scans, challenges remain in accurately describing nodule morphology and incorporating medical expertise.
papers.method: These limitations affect the reliability and effectiveness of these models in clinical settings. Collaborative multi-agent systems offer a promising strategy for achieving a balance between generality and precision in medical applications, yet their potential in pathology has not been thoroughly explored. To bridge these gaps, we introduce LungNoduleAgent, an innovative collaborative multi-agent system specifically designed for analyzing lung CT scans. LungNoduleAgent streamlines the diagnostic process into sequential components, improving precision in describing nodules and grading malignancy through three primary modules. The first module, the Nodule Spotter, coordinates clinical detection models to accurately identify nodules. The second module, the Radiologist, integrates localized image description techniques to produce comprehensive CT reports. Finally, the Doctor Agent System performs malignancy reasoning by using images and CT reports, supported by a pathology knowledge base and a multi-agent system framework. Extensive testing on two private datasets and the public LIDC-IDRI dataset indicates that LungNoduleAgent surpasses mainstream vision-language models, agent systems, and advanced expert models.
papers.result: These results highlight the importance of region-level semantic alignment and multi-agent collaboration in diagnosing nodules. LungNoduleAgent stands out as a promising foundational tool for supporting clinical analyses of lung nodules.
papers.gap: Class scores not calibrated; no deferral; 2D slices.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: LungNoduleAgent works in three stages: several detection models propose nodule masks that are clustered and validated by a panel of vision-language judges; a simulated radiologist writes a local report for each nodule from global and close-up features; and a doctor-agent system retrieves knowledge from a medical knowledge graph and discusses the case to give a malignancy diagnosis with reasons. Generated descriptions were checked with attribute-level yes/no questions, including negative questions that catch fabricated details.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on private and public lung CT data (Hangzhou Dianzi University and partners, preprint).
papers.datasets: Two private sets of 1,616 and 386 axial lung CT slices (512x512) with nodule boxes, morphology and malignancy class (pre-invasive, minimally invasive, invasive adenocarcinoma); LIDC-IDRI (1,018 scans) with masks, attributes and malignancy ratings 1-5.
papers.preprocessing: CT volume split into slices; attribute-level yes/no questions (positive and negative) built from annotations to verify generated reports.
papers.modelDetails: Nodule Spotter (mixture of detection foundation models, mask clustering, VLM judging panel), Simulated Radiologist (local CT report generation with gated cross-attention of global and focal features), Doctor Agent System (knowledge-graph retrieval, multi-agent discussion, final diagnosis with class scores).
papers.training: Training details per module in the paper.
papers.evaluation: Detection metrics, attribute QA accuracy (Pos/Neg QA), malignancy classification accuracy.
papers.baselines: General and medical MLLMs and prior nodule analysis models.
papers.results: Outperformed baselines in nodule description and diagnosis; region-level alignment and multi-agent collaboration both contributed.

papers.title: Evidence-based diagnostic reasoning with multi-agent copilot for human pathology
papers.authors: Luca L. Weishaupt, Chengkuan Chen, Drew F. K. Williamson, Richard J. Chen, Guillaume Jaume, Tong Ding, Bowen Chen, Anurag Vaidya, Long Phi Le, Guillaume Jaume, et al.
papers.aim: Pathology is experiencing rapid digital transformation driven by whole-slide imaging and artificial intelligence (AI). While deep learning-based computational pathology has achieved notable success, traditional models primarily focus on image analysis without integrating natural language instruction or rich, text-based context.
papers.method: Current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in computational pathology face limitations, including insufficient training data, inadequate support and evaluation for multi-image understanding, and a lack of autonomous, diagnostic reasoning capabilities. To address these limitations, we introduce PathChat+, a new MLLM specifically designed for human pathology, trained on over 1 million diverse, pathology-specific instruction samples and nearly 5.5 million question answer turns.
papers.result: Extensive evaluations across diverse pathology benchmarks demonstrated that PathChat+ substantially outperforms the prior PathChat copilot, as well as both state-of-the-art (SOTA) general-purpose and other pathology-specific models. Furthermore, we present SlideSeek, a reasoning-enabled multi-agent AI system leveraging PathChat+ to autonomously evaluate gigapixel whole-slide images (WSIs) through iterative, hierarchical diagnostic reasoning, reaching high accuracy on DDxBench, a challenging open-ended differential diagnosis benchmark, while also capable of generating visually grounded, humanly-interpretable summary reports.
papers.gap: No calibrated confidence or defer-to-pathologist mechanism; brain tumours not specific.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built PathChat+, a pathology assistant model, and SlideSeek, a multi-agent system that explores a whole slide like a pathologist, zooming and collecting regional evidence before reasoning to a diagnosis with an explanation. Evaluation covered region-level question answering, classification and captioning benchmarks and a new 150-slide diagnostic benchmark with many rare diagnoses, with bootstrap intervals and permutation tests. It shows agentic navigation of gigapixel slides with evidence collection.
papers.studyDesign: Model and agent development with ROI-level and slide-level benchmarking (Brigham and Women's / MGH / Harvard, preprint).
papers.datasets: ROI benchmarks: PathMMU (validation 710 Q&A, test 9,677 Q&A; expert-level subset 1,156), PathBenchQA, BRACS, UniToPatho, HiCervix; slide-level DDxBench: 150 H&E WSIs from BWH archives with report-derived diagnoses verified by a pathologist, 55 categories (14 common, 41 rare) across 19 tissues.
papers.preprocessing: Diagnoses mapped to OncoTree codes; rarity defined as <6 per 100,000 per year.
papers.modelDetails: PathChat+ multimodal pathology copilot and SlideSeek multi-agent system that navigates WSIs, gathers evidence across magnifications and reasons to an evidence-based diagnosis.
papers.training: PathChat+ trained on large pathology instruction data (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: VQA accuracy, classification accuracy, captioning, slide-level diagnostic accuracy for common and rare diseases.
papers.baselines: Prior PathChat, state-of-the-art general and pathology MLLMs.
papers.results: PathChat+ substantially outperformed PathChat and general and pathology-specific models across benchmarks.
papers.statistics: 95% CIs by bootstrap (1,000 replicates); two-sided paired permutation tests (1,000 permutations).

papers.title: Trust but Verify:Evidence-Linked Multi-Agent Clinical Information Extraction in Pathology
papers.authors: Yufan Wang, Anit Kumar Sahu, Yan Fei Ng, Daniel Kang, Shayan Vassef, Soorya Ram Shimgekar, Koustuv Saha, Piyum Zonooz, Navin Kumar, Chee Leong Cheng, et al.
papers.aim: Clinical feature extraction from pathology reports is challenging because relevant evidence may be distributed across coded and narrative fields and depend on specimen attribution, negation, ancillary findings, and diagnostic context. We retrospectively evaluated the NimbleMind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), a configurable workflow that separates clinician-defined field specifications from extraction models and returns report-level predictions with source-linked evidence.
papers.method: The study included 54 dummy gastric biopsy pathology reports from Singapore and four binary target fields, yielding 216 feature-case decisions. nMAS correctly classified 213 of 216 decisions (98.61\%), and all evidence spans associated with correct predictions occurred verbatim in the corresponding source reports. All three errors occurred in the two context-dependent \textit{H. pylori}-related fields requiring negation handling or diagnostic attribution. A single-model UMA-style comparator produced the similar label-level performance and error pattern.
papers.result: These findings do not demonstrate predictive superiority for the multi-agent architecture.Rather, the contribution of nMAS lies in workflow integration and traceability through configurable field specifications, complexity-based routing, report-level aggregation, and source-text validation within a clinician-reviewable workflow. Larger multi-institutional studies should assess generalizability, semantic evidence quality, adaptation effort, and clinician verification time.
papers.gap: Tiny pilot; no uncertainty output.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: The workflow lets clinicians define the fields they need and returns, for each field, a prediction plus the exact text in the report that supports it. On 54 gastric biopsy reports it was compared with an independent extraction system; both made the same three errors, so the authors argue the value lies in traceability and workflow integration rather than accuracy. Source-linked evidence is a practical way to make agent outputs auditable.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective pilot technical evaluation of an evidence-linked multi-agent extraction workflow (Nimblemind with Singapore General Hospital, preprint).
papers.datasets: 54 dummy gastric biopsy pathology reports (2022) from a tertiary system in Singapore; four binary target fields chosen with four clinicians; 216 feature-case decisions.
papers.preprocessing: Identifiers replaced with dummy placeholders; full report records (coded and narrative fields) processed.
papers.modelDetails: nMAS: configurable workflow separating clinician-defined field specifications from extraction models; returns predictions with verbatim source-linked evidence spans.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 per field against two reviewers (Cohen's kappa 0.975); evidence-span verification.
papers.baselines: External UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 comparator.
papers.results: 213/216 correct (98.61%); biopsy fields 100%, H. pylori positivity 98.15%, H. pylori gastritis 96.30%; all evidence spans for correct predictions verbatim in source; comparator identical at label level.

papers.title: The Optimization Paradox in Clinical AI Multi-Agent Systems
papers.authors: Suhana Bedi, Iddah Mlauzi, Daniel Shin, Sanmi Koyejo, Nigam H. Shah
papers.aim: Multi-agent artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in clinical settings, yet the relationship between component-level optimization and system-wide performance remains poorly understood. We evaluated this relationship using 2,400 real patient cases from the MIMIC-CDM dataset across four abdominal pathologies (appendicitis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis), decomposing clinical diagnosis into information gathering, interpretation, and differential diagnosis.
papers.method: We evaluated single agent systems (one model performing all tasks) against multi-agent systems (specialized models for each task) using comprehensive metrics spanning diagnostic outcomes, process adherence, and cost efficiency. Our results reveal a paradox: while multi-agent systems generally outperformed single agents, the component-optimized or Best of Breed system with superior components and excellent process metrics (85.5% information accuracy) significantly underperformed in diagnostic accuracy (67.7% vs. 77.4% for a top multi-agent system).
papers.result: This finding underscores that successful integration of AI in healthcare requires not just component level optimization but also attention to information flow and compatibility between agents. Our findings highlight the need for end to end system validation rather than relying on component metrics alone.
papers.gap: No uncertainty passed between steps; text cases.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors split clinical diagnosis into three steps and built systems either with one model doing everything or with a specialised model per step, including one assembled from the best model for each step. Evaluated on 2,400 real cases with outcome, process and cost metrics, the component-optimised system did worse overall, showing that information flow and compatibility between agents matter. End-to-end validation of the whole chain is therefore required.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective comparative evaluation on MIMIC-CDM (Stanford, preprint).
papers.datasets: 2,400 real patient cases with appendicitis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis or diverticulitis (MIMIC-CDM).
papers.preprocessing: Diagnosis decomposed into information gathering, interpretation and differential diagnosis.
papers.modelDetails: Single-agent systems (one model for all steps) vs multi-agent systems (specialised models per step), including a best-of-breed system assembled from top components.
papers.training: No training; various LLMs.
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy, process adherence (information accuracy) and cost efficiency.
papers.baselines: Single-agent systems.
papers.results: Multi-agent systems generally outperformed single agents, but the best-of-breed system with 85.5% information accuracy had lower diagnostic accuracy (67.7%) than a top multi-agent system (77.4%).

papers.title: RadFabric: Agentic AI System with Reasoning Capability for Radiology
papers.authors: Wenting Chen, Yi Dong, Zhaojun Ding, Yucheng Shi, Yifan Zhou, Fang Zeng, Yijun Luo, Tianyu Lin, Yihang Su, Yichen Wu, et al.
papers.aim: Chest X ray (CXR) imaging remains a critical diagnostic tool for thoracic conditions, but current automated systems face limitations in pathology coverage, diagnostic accuracy, and integration of visual and textual reasoning. To address these gaps, we propose RadFabric, a multi agent, multimodal reasoning framework that unifies visual and textual analysis for comprehensive CXR interpretation.
papers.method: RadFabric is built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling modularity, interoperability, and scalability for seamless integration of new diagnostic agents. The system employs specialized CXR agents for pathology detection, an Anatomical Interpretation Agent to map visual findings to precise anatomical structures, and a Reasoning Agent powered by large multimodal reasoning models to synthesize visual, anatomical, and clinical data into transparent and evidence based diagnoses.
papers.result: RadFabric achieves significant performance improvements, with near-perfect detection of challenging pathologies like fractures (1.000 accuracy) and superior overall diagnostic accuracy (0.799) compared to traditional systems (0.229 to 0.527). By integrating cross modal feature alignment and preference-driven reasoning, RadFabric advances AI-driven radiology toward transparent, anatomically precise, and clinically actionable CXR analysis.
papers.gap: Aggregation does not use calibrated confidence; no clinician deferral; CXR only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: RadFabric connects several chest X-ray classifiers and report-generation models through a standard tool protocol, then a reasoning agent reads all their scores and texts and reconciles them, catching findings that one model misses or misattributes. Case examples show classifiers detecting opacities that report generators omit. The reasoning agent can be further trained with reinforcement learning. It is an example of aggregating heterogeneous specialist outputs, though without calibrated uncertainty.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on chest X-ray data (CityU HK, MGH, CUHK and others, preprint).
papers.datasets: Public chest X-ray datasets with multi-label pathology annotations (e.g. MIMIC-CXR/CheXpert-style labels including lung opacity, pneumonia, fractures).
papers.preprocessing: Not detailed in extract.
papers.modelDetails: RadFabric: built on the Model Context Protocol; multiple CXR classification agents and report-generation models (e.g. CAMMAL, CheXagent) feed a reasoning agent that reconciles their outputs; reasoning agent optionally trained with GRPO.
papers.training: Reasoning agent trained with GRPO reinforcement learning (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Per-pathology detection accuracy and overall diagnostic performance.
papers.baselines: Individual CXR agents and report generators; prior systems.
papers.results: Near-perfect fracture detection (1.000 accuracy) and better overall diagnosis than baselines; trained reasoning agent improved further.

papers.title: Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents
papers.authors: Frederik Hauke, Patrick Wienholt, Christiane Kuhl, Dyke Ferber, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Sven Nebelung, Daniel Truhn
papers.aim: Machine learning models for medical image analysis typically lack a reliable measure of confidence, limiting their use in ambiguous or atypical cases. Here we show that Monte Carlo dropout, applied to a multi-task chest-radiograph classifier (eight thoracic findings, 137,593 training images), provides an epistemic uncertainty signal that tracks generalisation across training-set scales and flags confident yet error-prone predictions.
papers.method: Adding this signal to the point prediction raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 ($Δ$AUROC +0.023, 95% CI [+0.014, +0.033]).
papers.result: In a controlled 2x2 factorial experiment, a clinical-decision-support agent exploited this uncertainty only when it was delivered as a binary error-risk flag rather than as raw scores, cutting confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%. Epistemic uncertainty estimation thus carries decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its value for downstream agents depends on how it is communicated.
papers.gap: Chest X-ray only; agent simulated; no human clinicians.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: A chest-radiograph classifier was trained at ten data scales with Monte Carlo dropout to show that its epistemic uncertainty tracks overfitting and flags confident errors. In a factorial experiment, a language-model decision-support agent received the classifier's outputs either with or without uncertainty, presented either as raw numbers or as a simple 'high error risk' flag. Only the flag changed the agent's behaviour, halving confident misdiagnoses. This directly informs how uncertainty should be communicated between agents in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective experimental study with a 2x2 factorial agent experiment (RWTH Aachen, Heidelberg, Dresden; preprint).
papers.datasets: TAIX-Ray Thorax public cohort: 137,593 training, 34,860 validation, 42,928 test radiographs (patient-stratified); ordinal grades for eight findings (heart size, congestion, effusion, opacities, atelectasis left/right).
papers.preprocessing: Grades binarised at >0 for training, raw grades kept; centre-cropped 448x448, z-normalised; augmentations: random crop, vertical flip, axis transposition.
papers.modelDetails: DINOv2 ViT-S/14 (~21M parameters) fine-tuned with a linear head; Monte Carlo dropout for epistemic uncertainty; an LLM clinical-decision-support agent receives predictions with uncertainty as raw scores or as a binary error-risk flag.
papers.training: Per-class BCE; AdamW, lr 1e-6, weight decay 1e-2; FP16; ten training-set fractions for scaling analysis.
papers.evaluation: Error-detection AUROC; relation of uncertainty to validation loss; agent confident-misdiagnosis rate across 2x2 conditions.
papers.baselines: Point prediction alone; raw uncertainty scores.
papers.results: Uncertainty raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 (+0.023, 95% CI +0.014 to +0.033); the agent used uncertainty only as a binary error-risk flag, cutting confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%.

papers.title: Why Specialist Models Still Matter: A Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Paradigm for Medical Artificial Intelligence
papers.authors: Yanan Wang, Shuaicong Hu, Jian Liu, Guohui Zhou, Aiguo Wang, Cuiwei Yang
papers.aim: The impressive performance of generalist large language models (LLMs) such as GPT and Claude in healthcare raises a critical question: will domain-specific medical specialist models become obsolete? We argue that the future of medical artificial intelligence (AI) lies not in building monolithic medical foundation models, nor in replacing human expertise, but in orchestrating collaboration among generalist LLMs, domain-specific specialist models, and clinicians.
papers.method: We propose HetMedAgent, a heterogeneous medical multi-agent framework that enables conflict-aware evidence fusion, uncertainty-based clinician intervention triggering, and adaptive threshold calibration.
papers.result: Experiments on three real-world clinical decision-making tasks demonstrate that the synergy between generalist LLMs and domain-specific specialist models significantly outperforms using either type of model alone, validating the irreplaceable value of specialist models in modality-specific analysis. HetMedAgent represents a shift from building medical LLMs or foundation models to multi-agent collaboration, achieving a balance between general reasoning capabilities and domain-specific precision.
papers.gap: Confidence calibration and clinician workload not rigorously measured; cardiology rather than neuro-oncology.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: HetMedAgent argues that generalist LLMs should coordinate rather than replace specialist models. An orchestrator sends each data type to a trained specialist that reports findings with a confidence; conflicting findings are weighted; a reasoning agent integrates them with clinical information; and when the overall decision is uncertain, a clinician is asked to intervene, with thresholds adjusted adaptively. It was compared with medical LLMs and multi-agent frameworks on three tasks. Its structure is very close to this study's design, though calibration is not deeply evaluated.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on three real-world clinical decision tasks (preprint, China).
papers.datasets: Three clinical decision datasets with multimodal data including echocardiography and ECG plus clinical information (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Modality-specific data dispatched to specialist models.
papers.modelDetails: HetMedAgent: an orchestrator dispatches each modality to specialist models (transformer-based ECHO and ECG models) that return findings with generation confidence; conflict-aware weighting; a reasoning LLM integrates evidence; decision uncertainty triggers clinician intervention; adaptive threshold calibration.
papers.training: Specialist models trained per modality (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: AUROC and F1 for each task; BERTScore and conflict scores for specialist outputs; with and without clinician intervention.
papers.baselines: Medical LLMs (PMC-LLaMA, Meditron, BioMistral, others) and multi-agent systems (MedAgents, AgentClinic, AutoGen, MetaGPT).
papers.results: Without clinician: AUROC 0.866/0.801/0.727 vs best multi-agent 0.823/0.751/0.692; generalist-specialist synergy beat either alone; transformer specialists had best BERTScore and lowest conflict.

papers.title: Trustworthy Agents for Electronic Health Records through Confidence Estimation
papers.authors: Yongwoo Song, Minbyul Jeong, Mujeen Sung
papers.aim: Large language models (LLMs) show promise for extracting information from Electronic Health Records (EHR) and supporting clinical decisions. However, deployment in clinical settings faces challenges due to hallucination risks.
papers.method: We propose Hallucination Controlled Accuracy at k% (HCAcc@k%), a novel metric quantifying the accuracy-reliability trade-off at varying confidence thresholds. We introduce TrustEHRAgent, a confidence-aware agent incorporating stepwise confidence estimation for clinical question answering. Experiments on MIMIC-III and eICU datasets show TrustEHRAgent outperforms baselines under strict reliability constraints, achieving improvements of 44.23%p and 25.34%p at HCAcc@70% while baseline methods fail at these thresholds.
papers.result: These results highlight limitations of traditional accuracy metrics in evaluating healthcare AI agents. Our work contributes to developing trustworthy clinical agents that deliver accurate information or transparently express uncertainty when confidence is low.
papers.gap: Confidence not checked for calibration; EHR text tasks only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors propose measuring an agent's accuracy only on answers it is confident about, at a series of confidence thresholds, which rewards agents that know when to abstain. Their agent estimates confidence at each step of querying an EHR database and combines these into an answer confidence. On two ICU databases it maintained useful accuracy at strict thresholds where baselines did not. HCAcc@k% is a variant of the selective-risk measures used in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Method and metric development on EHR question answering (Kyung Hee University and Upstage AI, preprint).
papers.datasets: MIMIC-III and eICU EHR question-answering benchmarks.
papers.preprocessing: Questions over structured EHR databases.
papers.modelDetails: TrustEHRAgent: a confidence-aware LLM agent with step-wise confidence estimation during multi-step EHR querying and answering; new metric HCAcc@k% (hallucination-controlled accuracy at k% confidence threshold).
papers.training: No training reported.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy and HCAcc@k% at varying thresholds.
papers.baselines: Baseline EHR agents without confidence estimation.
papers.results: TrustEHRAgent beat baselines by up to 25.34 points at HCAcc@70%, where baselines failed completely.

papers.title: CRC-Router: Risk-Constrained Routing for Medical Agentic AI Systems
papers.authors: Xueyang Li, Mingze Jiang, Gelei Xu, Jun Xia, Ching-Hao Chiu, Mengzhao Jia, Danny Z. Chen, Yiyu Shi
papers.aim: Agentic AI systems are increasingly being explored in medical imaging to improve throughput and reduce clinician workload; however, safe deployment remains challenging because autonomous errors may propagate into downstream clinical decisions. A central requirement is therefore not only strong predictive performance, but also a reliable routing mechanism that determines when the system should proceed autonomously and when a case should be escalated for further review.
papers.method: To address this gap, we propose CRC-Router, a risk-constrained, uncertainty-aware routing module that is applicable to both conventional medical prediction models and agentic medical AI systems. CRC-Router combines multiple complementary uncertainty signals with the predictive score to construct a per-finding routing feature vector, maps this vector to an estimated wrong-accept risk using a lightweight per-finding risk model, and then applies Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to calibrate acceptance thresholds under a user-specified risk target. Instantiated on chest X-ray multi-finding triage using the NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset, CRC-Router achieves the strongest empirical risk--coverage trade-off among the evaluated baselines, both as a standalone routing layer and as a plug-in module integrated with the state-of-the-art MedRAX agent.
papers.result: These results demonstrate both the effectiveness of CRC-Router in selective medical automation and its modular, model-agnostic compatibility with existing predictive and agentic medical pipelines. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/XLIAaron/CRC-Router
papers.gap: Uniform risk target per finding, no asymmetric clinical costs or clinician capacity; single step, not a chain of agents.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: One public dataset; marginal guarantees; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: CRC-Router decides, for each finding on a chest radiograph, whether to accept the model's prediction or escalate it. It combines the ensemble's score, its disagreement, its aleatoric uncertainty and an out-of-distribution distance into a feature vector, trains a small model to predict the risk of wrongly accepting, and then uses conformal risk control on a held-out calibration set to set thresholds that keep accepted errors below 5%. It was compared with standard selective-prediction methods at matched coverage and plugged into an existing agent. This is the closest published analogue to the escalation rule of this study, though for single-step chest X-ray findings and without clinical cost weighting.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and retrospective evaluation, standalone and as a plug-in to an agent (University of Notre Dame, preprint).
papers.datasets: NIH ChestX-ray14: 112,120 frontal CXRs, 14 labels; patient-level split 0.5 train / 0.25 calibration / 0.25 test, calibration split equally into risk-model training and CRC calibration.
papers.preprocessing: 24 handcrafted radiomics features (intensity, GLCM texture, histogram) for a Mahalanobis out-of-distribution score.
papers.modelDetails: Committee of five multi-label CNNs (RegNetY-1.6, ResNet-50d, RexNet-150, EfficientNetV2-B3, DenseNet-121) gives predictive scores and epistemic/aleatoric uncertainty; a per-finding routing feature vector feeds a small MLP risk model estimating wrong-accept risk; Conformal Risk Control calibrates per-finding accept/escalate thresholds at target risk alpha = 5%; also integrated with the MedRAX agent.
papers.training: Classifiers: lr 1e-4, batch 24, early stopping (patience 10, max 60 epochs); risk-model architectures chosen by grid search with 5-fold CV AUROC.
papers.evaluation: Per-finding wrong-accept risk, coverage and risk-coverage trade-off at matched ~91% macro coverage.
papers.baselines: Max-probability thresholding, MCD mutual information (ensemble disagreement), conformal prediction, accept-all.
papers.results: Strongest risk-coverage trade-off among baselines, meeting the 5% risk target on more findings, both standalone and with MedRAX.
papers.statistics: Per-disease risk with target checks; risk-coverage curves.

papers.title: Auditing medical multi-agent AI reveals risks of false consensus
papers.authors: Yinghao Zhu, Lei Gu, Zixiang Wang, Haoran Sang, Dehao Sui, Wen Tang, Lan Mi, Yasha Wang, Junyi Gao, Liang Yao, et al.
papers.aim: Large language models are increasingly being assembled into medical multi-agent systems that emulate multidisciplinary consultation through specialist roles, peer review and consensus formation. In clinical decision support, however, apparent consensus is not enough.
papers.method: Clinicians also need to know whether agents checked the evidence, addressed disagreement and kept uncertainty visible. Current evaluations largely score final accuracy, leaving the safety of the collaborative process untested. Here we introduce MedAgentAudit, a clinically grounded workflow audit framework for diagnosing and quantifying collaborative failure modes in medical multi-agent systems. From 3,600 execution logs, we derive an expert-validated taxonomy of ten recurrent failures spanning task comprehension, collaborative discussion, and synthesis and decision-making. We then deploy an expert-validated automated auditor as non-interventional probes across 14,400 cases, covering six multi-agent architectures, six medical text and vision datasets, and four large language model settings per modality. Across systems, collaboration yields uneven accuracy gains and frequent process failures. Unsupported observations affect 16.63% of cases and propagate downstream. In discussion, agents repeat initial views in 98.42% of cases rather than re-examining evidence, and fail to activate specialist reasoning in 42.73%.
papers.result: During synthesis, final answers often substitute authority or majority count for evidence checking, showing authority bias in 28.76% (rising from 35.30% to 68.75% across rounds), self-contradiction in 18.53%, contradiction neglect in 5.48% and minority suppression in 5.11%. MedAgentAudit reframes medical AI evaluation from output scoring to process-level safety and accountability, providing a practical foundation for transparent, auditable and clinician-supervised agentic systems in medicine.
papers.gap: Audits LLM discussion systems, not systems with calibrated perception agents; no fix proposed beyond auditing.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors compared six medical multi-agent systems with single models, then open-coded hundreds of interaction logs to build a taxonomy of how collaboration fails, validated it with experts, and built an automated auditor that observes each stage of the collaboration without changing it. Running the auditor over 14,400 cases quantified failures such as unsupported claims, false consensus and authority bias. It argues for process-level audit, which this study implements through its audit trail and evidence requirements.
papers.studyDesign: Three-phase empirical audit study (Peking University, HKU, Edinburgh and others, preprint).
papers.datasets: Six datasets (MedQA, PubMedQA, MedXpertQA; PathVQA, VQA-RAD, SLAKE), four LLM settings per modality, six multi-agent systems; 3,600 interaction logs sampled for taxonomy (720 open-coded); audit over 14,400 cases.
papers.preprocessing: Stratified sampling of logs; double-blind expert validation of the taxonomy.
papers.modelDetails: MedAgentAudit: a taxonomy of ten collaboration failure modes and an automated auditor inserted as non-interventional probes at predefined interaction steps (input, independent analysis, consensus synthesis, final decision).
papers.training: No training; auditor reliability checked against humans.
papers.evaluation: MAS accuracy vs matched single-LLM baselines; prevalence of each failure mode and its evolution over rounds.
papers.baselines: Single-LLM baselines.
papers.results: Collaboration gave uneven accuracy gains; unsupported observations in 16.63% of cases; agents repeated initial views in 98.42%; specialist reasoning not activated in 42.73%; authority bias 28.76% (rising 35.30% to 68.75% across rounds); self-contradiction 18.53%; contradiction neglect 5.48%; minority suppression 5.11%.
papers.statistics: Human-AI agreement for the auditor; prevalence statistics.

papers.title: MedTRACE: Tool-Augmented Multimodal Clinical Reasoning Agents for Evidence-Grounded Decision-Making
papers.authors: Ji Lu, Lifei Liu, Haoran Yu, Xianglong Wang, Yiru Fang, Kuo Yang, Huiran Duan, Jianping Gou
papers.aim: Multimodal clinical decision-making requires reliable reasoning over heterogeneous evidence from electronic health records, medical images, and physiological signals. Existing models typically map these inputs directly to diagnoses without explicitly assessing evidence sufficiency, tool-use requirements, or diagnostic uncertainty.
papers.method: This paper presents MedTRACE, a tool-augmented multimodal clinical reasoning agent for evidence-grounded decision-making. MedTRACE uses modality-specific encoders to construct a unified patient-state representation and performs an iterative loop of hypothesis formation, toolaware deliberation, and evidence verification. It dynamically invokes visual grounding, evidence retrieval, and structured parsing tools to locate diagnosis-relevant regions, retrieve clinical knowledge and similar cases, and extract structured findings. The acquired evidence enters an evidence memory, where a consistency verifier confirms or revises the current hypothesis. MedTRACE outputs a diagnosis together with supporting evidence, an auditable reasoning trace, and calibrated confidence. Experiments on multiple multimodal clinical diagnosis benchmarks show that MedTRACE improves diagnostic accuracy by 5.4% and AUROC by 4.7 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
papers.result: It also improves evidenceselection F1 by 8.2 percentage points and visual-grounding IoU by 6.5 percentage points, reduces expected calibration error by 31.6%, and decreases unsupported diagnostic errors by 27.8%. These results demonstrate that active evidence acquisition and verification improve the accuracy, interpretability, and reliability of multimodal clinical decisionmaking.
papers.gap: Single agent rather than a pathway of specialist agents; no clinician evaluation of review decisions.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedTRACE encodes text, images and signals into one patient state, then reasons in a loop: it proposes hypotheses, decides whether a tool is needed (grounding, retrieval, parsing), checks the evidence the tool returns, and stores verified findings in memory. The output includes the diagnosis, the evidence, a trace of every action and a calibrated confidence used to decide whether a human should review the case. It combines several elements of this study's design (audit trace, evidence verification, calibrated escalation) in one agent.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and retrospective evaluation on public multimodal datasets (preprint).
papers.datasets: MIMIC-IV linked with MIMIC-CXR (EHR-image diagnosis); MIMIC-CXR, Chest ImaGenome and VinDr-CXR (image-text reasoning and grounding); MIMIC-IV-ECG and PTB-XL (signal reasoning); official or patient-disjoint 70/10/20 splits.
papers.preprocessing: Images 224x224; text truncated to 512 tokens; ECG standardised to 10 s at 500 Hz; test cases excluded from retrieval index.
papers.modelDetails: MedTRACE: BioClinicalBERT, BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16 and CSFM ECG encoders projected to a 768-d patient state with masked attention for missing modalities; Qwen2.5-VL-7B reasoning agent with LoRA runs hypothesis formation, tool-aware deliberation and evidence verification using BiomedParse grounding, MedCPT retrieval and scispaCy parsing; outputs diagnosis, evidence, auditable action trace and calibrated confidence that decides human review.
papers.training: Max 4 reasoning rounds and 3 tool calls; 20 epochs AdamW (lr 2e-5 pretrained, 1e-4 new modules), batch 16, weight decay 0.01, 5% warm-up, grad clip 1.0; LoRA r=16, alpha=32, dropout 0.05.
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic metrics, evidence-selection F1, visual-grounding IoU, expected calibration error, tool-use efficiency.
papers.baselines: Multimodal fusion models and medical agent baselines.
papers.results: Improved diagnosis; evidence-selection F1 +8.2 points; grounding IoU +6.5 points; ECE reduced by 31.6%.

papers.title: DynamiCare: A Dynamic Multi-Agent Framework for Interactive and Open-Ended Medical Decision-Making
papers.authors: Tianqi Shang, Weiqing He, Charles Zheng, Lingyao Li, Li Shen, Bingxin Zhao
papers.aim: The rise of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled the development of specialized AI agents with domain-specific reasoning and interaction capabilities, particularly in healthcare. While recent frameworks simulate medical decision-making, they largely focus on single-turn tasks where a doctor agent receives full case information upfront -- diverging from the real-world diagnostic process, which is inherently uncertain, interactive, and iterative.
papers.method: In this paper, we introduce MIMIC-Patient, a structured dataset built from the MIMIC-III electronic health records (EHRs), designed to support dynamic, patient-level simulations.
papers.result: Building on this, we propose DynamiCare, a novel dynamic multi-agent framework that models clinical diagnosis as a multi-round, interactive loop, where a team of specialist agents iteratively queries the patient system, integrates new information, and dynamically adapts its composition and strategy. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of DynamiCare through extensive experiments, establishing the first benchmark for dynamic clinical decision-making with LLM-powered agents.
papers.gap: No calibrated uncertainty or clinician escalation; text EHR only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: DynamiCare treats diagnosis as an open-ended, multi-round loop in which a team of specialist agents asks a simulated patient for information, and the team composition changes as evidence accumulates. The authors also built MIMIC-Patient so such interactive diagnosis can be evaluated on real EHR content. It reflects the sequential, information-gathering nature of diagnosis.
papers.studyDesign: Dataset construction and method development on EHR-derived patient cases (University of Pennsylvania, preprint).
papers.datasets: MIMIC-Patient: structured dataset built from MIMIC-III EHRs to support dynamic, patient-level simulation.
papers.preprocessing: EHRs converted into structured patient profiles revealed progressively during interaction.
papers.modelDetails: DynamiCare: a dynamic team of specialist LLM agents that is assembled and adjusted over multiple rounds, querying a simulated patient system and converging on a diagnosis.
papers.training: No training reported.
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy and interaction efficiency on MIMIC-Patient.
papers.baselines: Static multi-agent and single-agent frameworks.
papers.results: Demonstrated feasibility and effectiveness of dynamic team formation as a benchmark baseline.
papers.availability: Dataset and code described as released.

papers.title: MedAgentBoard: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Collaboration with Conventional Methods for Diverse Medical Tasks
papers.authors: Yinghao Zhu, Ziyi He, Haoran Hu, Xiaochen Zheng, Xichen Zhang, Zixiang Wang, Junyi Gao, Liantao Ma, Lequan Yu
papers.aim: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has stimulated interest in multi-agent collaboration for addressing complex medical tasks. However, the practical advantages of multi-agent collaboration approaches remain insufficiently understood.
papers.method: Existing evaluations often lack generalizability, failing to cover diverse tasks reflective of real-world clinical practice, and frequently omit rigorous comparisons against both single-LLM-based and established conventional methods. To address this critical gap, we introduce MedAgentBoard, a comprehensive benchmark for the systematic evaluation of multi-agent collaboration, single-LLM, and conventional approaches. MedAgentBoard encompasses four diverse medical task categories: (1) medical (visual) question answering, (2) lay summary generation, (3) structured Electronic Health Record (EHR) predictive modeling, and (4) clinical workflow automation, across text, medical images, and structured EHR data. Our extensive experiments reveal a nuanced landscape: while multi-agent collaboration demonstrates benefits in specific scenarios, such as enhancing task completeness in clinical workflow automation, it does not consistently outperform advanced single LLMs (e.g., in textual medical QA) or, critically, specialized conventional methods that generally maintain better performance in tasks like medical VQA and EHR-based prediction. MedAgentBoard offers a vital resource and actionable insights, emphasizing the necessity of a task-specific, evidence-based approach to selecting and developing AI solutions in medicine.
papers.result: It underscores that the inherent complexity and overhead of multi-agent collaboration must be carefully weighed against tangible performance gains. All code, datasets, detailed prompts, and experimental results are open-sourced at https://medagentboard.netlify.app/.
papers.gap: No uncertainty or deferral evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Benchmark tasks; LLM judging for free-form.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedAgentBoard evaluates medical multi-agent systems fairly against strong single-model prompting and against conventional fine-tuned models on a broad set of tasks, from exam questions and image questions to EHR prediction and clinical data workflows. It found that multi-agent collaboration is not uniformly better and is often beaten by simpler or conventional methods. This supports the choice in this study to use conventional specialist models for perception and reserve agent coordination for routing and escalation.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study comparing multi-agent, single-LLM and conventional methods across medical task types (Peking University, HKU, Edinburgh, ETH; preprint).
papers.datasets: Medical QA (MedQA, PubMedQA multiple-choice and free-form), medical VQA (PathVQA, VQA-RAD), lay summary generation, EHR predictive modelling and clinical workflow automation tasks (data extraction, statistics, visualisation, reporting).
papers.preprocessing: Repeated evaluations with standard deviations; free-form answers judged by LLM.
papers.modelDetails: Conventional fine-tuned models (BioLinkBERT, GatorTron, M3AE, BiomedGPT, MUMC, LLaVA-Med, Med-Flamingo); single LLM/VLM prompting (zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, self-consistency); multi-agent frameworks (MedAgents, ReConcile, MDAgents, ColaCare).
papers.training: Conventional models fine-tuned; LLMs prompted.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy for MC; LLM-as-judge for free-form; task-specific metrics for prediction and workflow tasks.
papers.baselines: All three method families compared with each other.
papers.results: Multi-agent collaboration helped only in some settings (e.g. MedQA CoT-SC 89.90% vs MedAgents 85.25%; VQA-RAD MedAgents 77.10% vs conventional M3AE 89.05%); conventional methods often best on VQA and prediction; complexity and overhead must be weighed against gains.
papers.availability: All code, data and prompts released.

papers.title: Agentic Large Language Models for Training-Free Neuro-Radiological Image Analysis
papers.authors: Ayhan Can Erdur, Daniel Scholz, Jiazhen Pan, Benedikt Wiestler, Daniel Rueckert, Jan C. Peeken
papers.aim: State-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) show high performance in general visual question answering. However, a fundamental limitation remains: current architectures lack the native 3D spatial reasoning required to directly analyze volumetric medical imaging, such as CT or MRI.
