papers.method: Emerging agentic AI offers a new solution, eliminating the need for intrinsic 3D processing by enabling LLMs to orchestrate and leverage specialized external tools. Yet, the feasibility of such agentic frameworks in complex, multi-step radiological workflows remains underexplored. In this work, we present a training-free agentic pipeline for automated brain MRI analysis. Validating our methodology on several LLMs (GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.6) with off-the-shelf domain-specific tools, our system autonomously executes complex end-to-end workflows, including preprocessing (skull stripping, registration), pathology segmentation (glioma, meningioma, metastases), and volumetric reasoning. We evaluate our framework across increasingly complex radiological tasks, from single-scan tumor and anatomy analysis to longitudinal response assessment requiring multi-timepoint comparisons. We analyze the impact of architectural design by comparing single-agent models against multi-agent "domain-expert" collaborations.
papers.result: To support rigorous evaluation of future agentic systems, we release a benchmark dataset of image-prompt-answer tuples derived from public data. Our results demonstrate that agentic AI can solve highly neuro-radiological image analysis tasks through tool use without the need for training or fine-tuning.
papers.gap: No uncertainty from the segmentation tools is passed to the LLM; no clinician escalation.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: Because language models cannot read 3D MRI natively, this agent answers clinical questions about brain MRI by planning and calling local specialised tools: skull stripping, registration, BraTS-winning segmentation models, anatomical parcellation, lesion matching across time points and radiomics. Only text and file pointers reach the LLM. The authors built a benchmark of single-time-point, longitudinal and RANO-assessment questions with expected tool plans and compared architectures and models. It directly shows how an orchestrator can drive brain-tumour segmentation tools, as in this study's MRI agent.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and benchmark creation for agentic brain MRI analysis (TUM, Imperial; preprint).
papers.datasets: Multicentre brain MRI cohort: pre-operative glioma (20), post-operative glioma (42), metastasis (24) and others, with longitudinal subsets (30 LUMIERE patients with expert RANO ratings); Task 1 single-timepoint: 50 patients, 150 cases, 769 queries; Task 2.1 longitudinal: 25 patients, 75 cases, 809 queries; Task 2.2 RANO: 30 queries.
papers.preprocessing: Questions paired with expected tool-call plans and keyword-value answers.
papers.modelDetails: LLM agent (OpenAI Agents SDK, temperature 0) orchestrating 24 local tools: SynthStrip, ANTsPy registration, BraTS winner models via BraTS Orchestrator (glioma, metastases, meningioma, paediatric), SynthSeg, Panoptica lesion matching, PyRadiomics, atlas localisation, RAG; single-agent, agents-as-tools and handoff architectures; imaging never leaves local environment.
papers.training: Training-free.
papers.evaluation: Answer correctness of keyword-value outputs, tool-plan correctness, number of actions, RANO agreement.
papers.baselines: Different LLMs and agent architectures.
papers.results: Agentic LLMs could perform neuro-radiological 3D analysis without training, but accuracy fell with workflow complexity, especially longitudinal tasks; benchmark released.
papers.availability: Benchmark dataset of image-prompt-answer tuples released from public data.

papers.title: Agentic Automation of BT-RADS Scoring: End-to-End Multi-Agent System for Standardized Brain Tumor Follow-up Assessment
papers.authors: Mohamed Sobhi Jabal, Jikai Zhang, Dominic LaBella, Jessica L. Houk, Dylan Zhang, Jeffrey D. Rudie, Kirti Magudia, Maciej A. Mazurowski, Evan Calabrese
papers.aim: The Brain Tumor Reporting and Data System (BT-RADS) standardizes post-treatment MRI response assessment in patients with diffuse gliomas but requires complex integration of imaging trends, medication effects, and radiation timing. This study evaluates an end-to-end multi-agent large language model (LLM) and convolutional neural network (CNN) system for automated BT-RADS classification.
papers.method: A multi-agent LLM system combined with automated CNN-based tumor segmentation was retrospectively evaluated on 509 consecutive post-treatment glioma MRI examinations from a single high-volume center. An extractor agent identified clinical variables (steroid status, bevacizumab status, radiation date) from unstructured clinical notes, while a scorer agent applied BT-RADS decision logic integrating extracted variables with volumetric measurements. Expert reference standard classifications were established by an independent board-certified neuroradiologist. Of 509 examinations, 492 met inclusion criteria. The system achieved 374/492 (76.0%; 95% CI, 72.1%-79.6%) accuracy versus 283/492 (57.5%; 95% CI, 53.1%-61.8%) for initial clinical assessments (+18.5 percentage points; P<.001). Context-dependent categories showed high sensitivity (BT-1b 100%, BT-1a 92.7%, BT-3a 87.5%), while threshold-dependent categories showed moderate sensitivity (BT-3c 74.8%, BT-2 69.2%, BT-4 69.3%, BT-3b 57.1%).
papers.result: For BT-4, positive predictive value was 92.9%. The multi-agent LLM system achieved higher BT-RADS classification agreement with expert reference standard compared to initial clinical scoring, with high accuracy for context-dependent scores and high positive predictive value for BT-4 detection.
papers.gap: No uncertainty or escalation of borderline volume-threshold cases; single centre.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; reference from one neuroradiologist; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: The system combines a validated nnU-Net that measures tumour compartment volumes on baseline and follow-up MRI with three LLM agents: an orchestrator, an extractor that reads clinical notes for steroid use, bevacizumab and radiation dates, and a scorer that applies BT-RADS rules. On nearly 500 consecutive follow-up scans it agreed with an expert neuroradiologist more often than the original clinical reports, and errors were traced to their source. It is a direct brain-tumour example of combining segmentation with agents for follow-up assessment, relevant to this study's Follow-up Agent.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-institution evaluation, Duke University Medical Center; IRB approved, consent waived.
papers.datasets: 509 consecutive post-treatment glioma MRI examinations; 492 evaluable (9 without suitable baseline, 8 segmentation QA failures); mean age 57.1; median interval 63 days.
papers.preprocessing: Free-text clinical notes for medication and treatment history; nnU-Net segmentation of enhancing tumour, non-enhancing tumour, oedema and cavity; percentage change in FLAIR and enhancement volumes.
papers.modelDetails: Orchestrator, extractor (steroid, bevacizumab, radiation dates from notes) and scorer agents applying BT-RADS decision logic to extracted variables plus volumetrics.
papers.training: Segmentation network previously trained and validated; LLM agents not trained.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy vs an independent neuroradiologist reference; per-category sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV; kappa; root-cause and ceiling analyses.
papers.baselines: Initial clinical BT-RADS assessments in reports.
papers.results: Accuracy 374/492 (76.0%, 95% CI 72.1-79.6) vs 57.5% for initial clinical scoring (P<.001); BT-1b 100%, BT-1a 92.7%, BT-3a 87.5% sensitivity; threshold categories lower; BT-4 PPV 92.9%.
papers.statistics: Wilson 95% CIs; McNemar with continuity correction; unweighted and quadratic-weighted kappa; diagnostic metrics; error root-cause analysis.

papers.title: ReclAIm: A Multi-Agent Framework for Monitoring and Correcting Performance Decline in Medical Imaging AI
papers.authors: Eleftherios Tzanis, Michail E. Klontzas
papers.aim: Purpose: To develop and evaluate a multi-agent framework (ReclAIm) for automated monitoring, detection, and correction of performance decline in medical image classification models. Materials and Methods: ReclAIm is a large language model-based multi-agent system that operates through natural language interaction.
papers.method: A master agent coordinating three task-specific agents performed performance evaluation and triggered fine-tuning when substantial performance declines were detected. The fine-tuning workflow incorporated data augmentation, class imbalance handling, and a parameter-anchoring regularization strategy to limit catastrophic forgetting. The system was benchmarked using multiple imaging datasets, including brain MRI, chest CT, and chest radiography, partitioned into model development, inference (performance monitoring), and fine-tuning subsets (60%:20%:20%). Results: ReclAIm successfully orchestrated training, evaluation, and performance monitoring across all datasets. Performance discrepancies between test and inference data were detected in 8 of 18 models, prompting fine-tuning workflows that reduced performance gaps.
papers.result: In cases with declines of up to 40.6% (cardiomegaly dataset, InceptionV3), fine-tuning restored performance metrics to within 2% of baseline values. Conclusion: ReclAIm provides a prototype framework for automated monitoring and targeted fine-tuning of medical image classification models, with a natural language interface designed to support accessibility in research and potential clinical applications.
papers.gap: Monitoring uses labelled data; no uncertainty-based early warning; fine-tuning changes models and therefore escalation behaviour.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: ReclAIm uses a master language-model agent and three tool-using agents to train image classifiers, monitor their performance on incoming data and, when performance drops substantially, run a controlled fine-tuning workflow with anti-forgetting regularisation. It was demonstrated on five public datasets including brain-tumour MRI. Automated monitoring after deployment is relevant to keeping the calibration of this study's agents under review.
papers.studyDesign: Technical development study using public datasets (University of Crete, Karolinska; preprint); no ethics approval required.
papers.datasets: Five public datasets: brain tumour CE-T1 MRI (3,064 2D slices from 233 patients: meningioma, glioma, pituitary), COVID-19 chest CT (4,173 slices, 210 patients), NoduleMNIST3D (1,633 CT volumes), PneumoniaMNIST (5,645 radiographs), and a cardiomegaly set for temporal drift; split 60/20/20 into development, inference (monitoring) and fine-tuning subsets.
papers.preprocessing: Data augmentation and class-imbalance handling within fine-tuning.
papers.modelDetails: LLM-based master agent (smolagents) orchestrating three task-specific agents with strictly defined Python tools for training, evaluation and monitoring; fine-tuning triggered on substantial decline with parameter-anchoring regularisation against catastrophic forgetting; 18 models (e.g. InceptionV3).
papers.training: Details per model in supplement.
papers.evaluation: Detection of performance discrepancy between test and inference data; recovery after fine-tuning.
papers.baselines: Original model performance.
papers.results: Declines detected in 8 of 18 models; for declines up to 40.6% (cardiomegaly, InceptionV3) fine-tuning restored metrics to within 2% of baseline.

papers.title: Meissa: Multi-modal Medical Agentic Intelligence
papers.authors: Yixiong Chen, Xinyi Bai, Yue Pan, Zongwei Zhou, Alan Yuille
papers.aim: Multi-modal large language models (MM-LLMs) have shown strong performance in medical image understanding and clinical reasoning. Recent medical agent systems extend them with tool use and multi-agent collaboration, enabling complex decision-making.
papers.method: However, these systems rely almost entirely on frontier models (e.g., GPT), whose API-based deployment incurs high cost, high latency, and privacy risks that conflict with on-premise clinical requirements. We present Meissa, a lightweight 4B-parameter medical MM-LLM that brings agentic capability offline. Instead of imitating static answers, Meissa learns both when to engage external interaction (strategy selection) and how to execute multi-step interaction (strategy execution) by distilling structured trajectories from frontier models. Specifically, we propose: (1) Unified trajectory modeling: trajectories (reasoning and action traces) are represented within a single state-action-observation formalism, allowing one model to generalize across heterogeneous medical environments. (2) Three-tier stratified supervision: the model's own errors trigger progressive escalation from direct reasoning to tool-augmented and multi-agent interaction, explicitly learning difficulty-aware strategy selection. (3) Prospective-retrospective supervision: pairing exploratory forward traces with hindsight-rationalized execution traces enables stable learning of effective interaction policies. Trained on 40K curated trajectories, Meissa matches or exceeds proprietary frontier agents in 10 of 16 evaluation settings across 13 medical benchmarks spanning radiology, pathology, and clinical reasoning.
papers.result: Using over 25x fewer parameters than typical frontier models like Gemini-3, Meissa operates fully offline with 22x lower end-to-end latency compared to API-based deployment. Data, models, and environments are released at https://github.com/Schuture/Meissa.
papers.gap: Learns when to act from teacher traces, not calibrated uncertainty; no clinician handover.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: Meissa distils the behaviour of large, API-based medical agent systems into a small model that runs on hospital hardware. Its training data are full reasoning and action traces, and the model learns both when to call tools or other agents and how to carry out multi-step interactions. Evaluated on 13 benchmarks including out-of-distribution sets, it approached frontier systems at much lower cost and latency. Offline operation matters for privacy in Sri Lankan hospitals.
papers.studyDesign: Model development by agentic behaviour distillation, evaluated on 13 benchmarks (Johns Hopkins, Cornell; preprint).
papers.datasets: About 40K training queries with trajectories from frontier agent systems; 13 benchmarks across four domains, five out-of-distribution (ChestAgentBench, OmniMed, MedXpertQA, NEJM, NEJM Ext.); 8-gram decontamination and disjoint DICOM hashing.
papers.preprocessing: Trajectories stratified (minimal traces, stronger reasoning, full agentic traces) and cleaned with prospective-retrospective supervision.
papers.modelDetails: Meissa: a 4B-parameter multimodal LLM (Qwen3-VL-4B base) trained to decide interaction depth (direct answer, single tool, tool chains, multi-agent debate, clinical simulation) and to execute multi-step interactions offline.
papers.training: LLaMA-Factory LoRA rank 32, lr 5e-5, 3 epochs (~239M tokens, ~12 GPU-hours) on 8 A6000 GPUs; vLLM inference; mean of 3 seeds.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy (exact match or soft match with synonym normalisation) across benchmarks; latency.
papers.baselines: GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-3-flash; MedRAX, Ophiuchus, MDAgents, AgentClinic; base and answer-only SFT models.
papers.results: Competitive with frontier agent systems using over 25x fewer parameters, fully offline with 22x lower end-to-end latency than API-based systems.

papers.title: ABRA: Agent Benchmark for Radiology Applications
papers.authors: Bulat Maksudov, Vladislav Kurenkov, Kathleen M. Curran, Alessandra Mileo
papers.aim: Existing medical-agent benchmarks deliver imaging as pre-selected samples, never as an environment the agent must navigate. We introduce ABRA, a radiology-agent benchmark in which the agent operates an OHIF viewer and an Orthanc DICOM server through twenty-one function-calling tools that span slice navigation, windowing, series selection, pixel-coordinate annotation, and structured reporting.
papers.method: ABRA contains 655 programmatically generated tasks across three difficulty tiers and eight types (viewer control, metadata QA, vision probe, annotation, longitudinal comparison, BI-RADS reporting, and oracle variants of annotation and BI-RADS reporting), drawn from LIDC-IDRI, Duke Breast Cancer MRI, and NLST New-Lesion LongCT. Each episode is scored along Planning, Execution, and Outcome (Bluethgen et al., 2025) by task-type-specific automatic scorers.
papers.result: Ten current models, five closed-weight and five open-weight, reach at least 89% Execution on real annotation but only 0-25% Outcome; on the paired oracle variant where a simulated detector supplies the finding, Outcome on the same task reaches 69-100% across the models evaluated, localising the bottleneck to perception rather than tool orchestration. Code, task generators, and scorers are released at https://github.com/Luab/ABRA
papers.gap: No uncertainty or escalation; thoracic and breast imaging only.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Small patient numbers; automatic scoring; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: ABRA puts agents inside a real radiology workstation (OHIF viewer and Orthanc server) where they must find series, scroll, window, annotate and report, rather than answer questions about pre-selected images. Tasks span viewer control, metadata, annotation, longitudinal comparison and BI-RADS reporting, and are scored automatically on planning, execution and outcome. Models executed tool calls well but rarely achieved correct outcomes. It uses the same Orthanc infrastructure planned for this study's registry.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation and evaluation of radiology agents operating real viewer software (Dublin City University, UCD; preprint).
papers.datasets: 655 programmatically generated tasks from LIDC-IDRI (10 patients, 20 studies, 142 series; consensus nodule masks), Duke Breast Cancer MRI (50 patients) and NLST New-Lesion LongCT (121 patients, 246 studies); eight task types over three difficulty tiers.
papers.preprocessing: LIDC-IDRI multi-reader contours combined by 50% volumetric majority vote to give 22 reference nodules.
papers.modelDetails: Agents operate an OHIF viewer and Orthanc DICOM server through 21 function-calling tools (slice navigation, windowing, series selection, pixel annotation, structured reporting); ten closed and open models evaluated.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Automatic scorers for Planning, Execution and Outcome; composite S = 0.20P + 0.30E + 0.50O.
papers.baselines: Oracle variants of annotation and BI-RADS tasks.
papers.results: Models reached at least 89% Execution on real annotation but only 0-25% Outcome; oracle variants much higher, showing perception rather than tool use is the bottleneck.

papers.title: ReflecTool: Towards Reflection-Aware Tool-Augmented Clinical Agents
papers.authors: Yusheng Liao, Shuyang Jiang, Yanfeng Wang, Yu Wang
papers.aim: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promising potential in the medical domain, assisting with tasks like clinical note generation and patient communication. However, current LLMs are limited to text-based communication, hindering their ability to interact with diverse forms of information in clinical environments.
papers.method: Despite clinical agents succeeding in diverse signal interaction, they are oriented to a single clinical scenario and hence fail for broader applications. To evaluate clinical agents holistically, we propose ClinicalAgent Bench~(CAB), a comprehensive medical agent benchmark consisting of 18 tasks across five key realistic clinical dimensions. Building on this, we introduce ReflecTool, a novel framework that excels at utilizing domain-specific tools within two stages. The first optimization stage progressively enlarges a long-term memory by saving successful solving processes and tool-wise experience of agents in a tiny pre-defined training set.
papers.result: In the following inference stage, ReflecTool can search for supportive successful demonstrations from already built long-term memory to guide the tool selection strategy, and a verifier improves the tool usage according to the tool-wise experience with two verification methods--iterative refinement and candidate selection. Extensive experiments on ClinicalAgent Benchmark demonstrate that ReflecTool surpasses the pure LLMs with more than 10 points and the well-established agent-based methods with 3 points, highlighting its adaptability and effectiveness in solving complex clinical tasks.
papers.gap: No calibrated confidence or human escalation.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: ReflecTool first lets an agent attempt clinical tasks with a range of tools and reflect on what worked, storing successful solution traces and tool-specific advice in long-term memory. When solving new tasks, it retrieves similar successful cases and uses the stored advice to choose and check tools. The accompanying benchmark covers 18 clinical tasks across five capability dimensions. Learning from successful tool use is relevant to improving agent reliability without retraining.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark and method development (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Fudan, Shanghai AI Lab).
papers.datasets: ClinicalAgent Bench (CAB): 18 tasks across five dimensions (knowledge and reasoning, multimodal, numerical analysis, data understanding, trustworthiness).
papers.preprocessing: A small proportion of samples used in the optimisation stage to build memory.
papers.modelDetails: ReflecTool: a clinical toolbox plus two stages; optimisation stage solves sample problems with tools, self-reflects, compares successful and failed trajectories and stores successful ones and tool-wise suggestions in long-term memory; inference stage retrieves similar successful cases to guide tool selection with tool-wise reflection.
papers.training: No fine-tuning of the LLM.
papers.evaluation: Task-specific metrics across the 18 CAB tasks.
papers.baselines: Pure LLMs and existing agents (MedAgent, MMedAgent, MedRAG, AgentMD, EHRAgent, CTAgent and others).
papers.results: Outperformed pure LLMs and prior agent methods across CAB dimensions.

papers.title: OPGAgent: An Agent for Auditable Dental Panoramic X-ray Interpretation
papers.authors: Zhaolin Yu, Litao Yang, Ben Babicka, Ming Hu, Jing Hao, Anthony Huang, James Huang, Yueming Jin, Jiasong Wu, Zongyuan Ge
papers.aim: Orthopantomograms (OPGs) are the standard panoramic radiograph in dentistry, used for full-arch screening across multiple diagnostic tasks. While Vision Language Models (VLMs) now allow multi-task OPG analysis through natural language, they underperform task-specific models on most individual tasks.
papers.method: Agentic systems that orchestrate specialized tools offer a path to both versatility and accuracy, this approach remains unexplored in the field of dental imaging. To address this gap, we propose OPGAgent, a multi-tool agentic system for auditable OPG interpretation. OPGAgent coordinates specialized perception modules with a consensus mechanism through three components: (1) a Hierarchical Evidence Gathering module that decomposes OPG analysis into global, quadrant, and tooth-level phases with dynamically invoking tools, (2) a Specialized Toolbox encapsulating spatial, detection, utility, and expert zoos, and (3) a Consensus Subagent that resolves conflicts through anatomical constraints. We further propose OPG-Bench, a structured-report protocol based on (Location, Field, Value) triples derived from real clinical reports, which enables a comprehensive review of findings and hallucinations, extending beyond the limitations of VQA indicators.
papers.result: On our OPG-Bench and the public MMOral-OPG benchmark, OPGAgent outperforms current dental VLMs and medical agent frameworks across both structured-report and VQA evaluation. Code will be released upon acceptance.
papers.gap: No uncertainty or escalation; dental domain.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.limitations: Reference reports may miss incidental findings; preprint.
papers.methodologyDetail: OPGAgent interprets dental panoramic radiographs by coordinating specialised tools and assembling their outputs into an auditable structured report, where each finding traces back to a tool result. On over a thousand real radiographs it was compared with general and dental vision-language models and with another agent framework configured with the same tools, using a shared parser so formatting did not bias results. It shows that tool orchestration reduced false positives substantially.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on a new dental benchmark and a public benchmark (Monash and partners, preprint).
papers.datasets: OPG-Bench: 1,009 anonymised orthopantomograms from multiple clinics (patients >=16 years) with clinical and structured reports, 5,219 VQA pairs; public MMOral-OPG benchmark.
papers.preprocessing: Ground truth from real clinical reports with manual spot-checks; shared Parser Agent converts all models' reports to a structured format.
papers.modelDetails: OPGAgent: multi-tool agentic system coordinating specialised dental detection, segmentation and classification tools to produce auditable structured reports and answer questions.
papers.training: Prompting with temperature 0.3; tools pre-trained.
papers.evaluation: Triple-based protocol: exact-match, detection, localisation and classification precision/recall/F1, false positives per case, composite score; VQA accuracy.
papers.baselines: General VLMs (Gemini-3, GPT-5.2, Qwen3-VL, Kimi), dental VLMs (DentalGPT, OralGPT-Omni), MedAgent-Pro with the same LLM and tools.
papers.results: Exact-match F1 42.3% and score 49.7%, above Gemini-3-Flash; precision 43.1% with 4.89 false positives per case vs 10.58; best VQA accuracy (62.53% on MMOral-OPG).

papers.title: SOLVE-Med: Specialized Orchestration for Leading Vertical Experts across Medical Specialties
papers.authors: Roberta Di Marino, Giovanni Dioguardi, Antonio Romano, Giuseppe Riccio, Mariano Barone, Marco Postiglione, Flora Amato, Vincenzo Moscato
papers.venue: 28th European Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 25-30 October 2025, Bologna, Italy
papers.aim: Medical question answering systems face deployment challenges including hallucinations, bias, computational demands, privacy concerns, and the need for specialized expertise across diverse domains. Here, we present SOLVE-Med, a multi-agent architecture combining domain-specialized small language models for complex medical queries.
papers.method: The system employs a Router Agent for dynamic specialist selection, ten specialized models (1B parameters each) fine-tuned on specific medical domains, and an Orchestrator Agent that synthesizes responses.
papers.result: Evaluated on Italian medical forum data across ten specialties, SOLVE-Med achieves superior performance with ROUGE-1 of 0.301 and BERTScore F1 of 0.697, outperforming standalone models up to 14B parameters while enabling local deployment. Our code is publicly available on GitHub: https://github.com/PRAISELab-PicusLab/SOLVE-Med.
papers.gap: Lexical metrics only; no clinical safety or uncertainty assessment.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: SOLVE-Med replaces one large model with ten small domain specialists, a router that picks the most relevant specialists for each question, and an orchestrator that merges their answers. All components were fine-tuned on Italian forum data and can run locally. Text-similarity metrics showed it beat larger single models. It illustrates routing to specialised small models for privacy and cost.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation (University of Naples Federico II; ECAI 2025).
papers.datasets: About 700,000 Italian medical-forum question-answer pairs with 102 platform categories, regrouped into ten specialties for router and specialist training.
papers.preprocessing: Fine-grained labels manually consolidated for semantic consistency.
papers.modelDetails: SOLVE-Med: a Router Agent classifies the question and selects specialists; ten 1B-parameter specialist small language models fine-tuned per domain; an Orchestrator Agent synthesises their answers.
papers.training: Unsloth with LoRA parameter-efficient fine-tuning for specialists and orchestrator.
papers.evaluation: ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR and BERTScore against forum answers; router classifier analysis.
papers.baselines: Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Velvet-14B standalone.
papers.results: Top-3 configuration ROUGE-1 0.301 and BERTScore F1 0.697, outperforming standalone models up to 14B parameters while allowing local deployment.

papers.title: Polaris: A Safety-focused LLM Constellation Architecture for Healthcare
papers.authors: Subhabrata Mukherjee, Paul Gamble, Markel Sanz Ausin, Neel Kant, Kriti Aggarwal, Neha Manjunath, Debajyoti Datta, Zhengliang Liu, Jiayuan Ding, Sophia Busacca, et al.
papers.aim: We develop Polaris, the first safety-focused LLM constellation for real-time patient-AI healthcare conversations. Unlike prior LLM works in healthcare focusing on tasks like question answering, our work specifically focuses on long multi-turn voice conversations.
papers.method: Our one-trillion parameter constellation system is composed of several multibillion parameter LLMs as co-operative agents: a stateful primary agent that focuses on driving an engaging conversation and several specialist support agents focused on healthcare tasks performed by nurses to increase safety and reduce hallucinations. We develop a sophisticated training protocol for iterative co-training of the agents that optimize for diverse objectives. We train our models on proprietary data, clinical care plans, healthcare regulatory documents, medical manuals, and other medical reasoning documents. We align our models to speak like medical professionals, using organic healthcare conversations and simulated ones between patient actors and experienced nurses. This allows our system to express unique capabilities such as rapport building, trust building, empathy and bedside manner. Finally, we present the first comprehensive clinician evaluation of an LLM system for healthcare. We recruited over 1100 U.S. licensed nurses and over 130 U.S. licensed physicians to perform end-to-end conversational evaluations of our system by posing as patients and rating the system on several measures.
papers.result: We demonstrate Polaris performs on par with human nurses on aggregate across dimensions such as medical safety, clinical readiness, conversational quality, and bedside manner. Additionally, we conduct a challenging task-based evaluation of the individual specialist support agents, where we demonstrate our LLM agents significantly outperform a much larger general-purpose LLM (GPT-4) as well as from its own medium-size class (LLaMA-2 70B).
papers.gap: Escalation detection not evaluated for calibration; non-diagnostic, patient-facing tasks.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: Polaris pairs a conversational primary agent with many smaller specialist agents that each check one aspect of safety, such as medication doses, lab values, nutrition advice, privacy, and whether a human should intervene. All agents were co-trained on nurse-patient dialogues with reinforcement learning from human feedback, then evaluated by patient actors and clinicians against nurses and general LLMs. A dedicated human-intervention specialist is an explicit escalation component.
papers.studyDesign: System development and evaluation against nurses and LLMs (Hippocratic AI, preprint).
papers.datasets: Simulated dialogues between registered nurses and patient actors, augmented with multi-hop reasoning instructions; evaluation by patient-actors and U.S. licensed nurses and physicians.
papers.preprocessing: Instruction, conversation and agent tuning data constructed from healthcare dialogues.
papers.modelDetails: Polaris: about one-trillion-parameter constellation of multibillion-parameter LLM agents: a stateful primary conversational agent plus specialist support agents (checklist, privacy, medication, labs and vitals, hospital policy, clinical nutrition, EHR summary, human-intervention detector).
papers.training: Iterative co-training with pre-training, instruction tuning, conversation tuning, agent tuning and RLHF; specialist models 2-5 epochs, int8 or bf16 inference.
papers.evaluation: Subjective patient-actor surveys and clinical-capability validation (medication, labs, diet, policy, privacy) against nurses, GPT-4 and LLaMA-2 70B.
papers.baselines: U.S. licensed nurses, GPT-4, LLaMA-2 70B Chat.
papers.results: On par with human nurses on aggregate across medical safety, clinical readiness, conversational quality and bedside manner; specialist agents outperformed general LLMs on targeted tasks.

papers.title: Toward Trustworthy Large Language Model Agents in Healthcare
papers.authors: Hadi Hasan, Safaa Salman, Adam Tai Abou Dargham, Ammar Mohanna, Ali Chehab
papers.aim: Healthcare appointment scheduling remains a persistent operational bottleneck, driven by manual coordination, fragmented legacy systems, and high administrative overhead. These inefficiencies constrain provider availability and degrade patient access to care.
papers.method: This paper presents CareConnect, a safety-first conversational agent for healthcare logistics automation that leverages large language model (LLM) function calling, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and layered deterministic safety guardrails. The system orchestrates eight domain-specific tools to support appointment booking, modification, cancellation, and facility information retrieval, while enforcing strict scope constraints that prohibit medical advice or diagnosis. Safety-critical situations are handled through deterministic short-circuit mechanisms for emergency detection and medical intent refusal. We evaluate CareConnect on a comprehensive benchmark of 680 task-oriented scenarios spanning end-to-end workflows, multi-turn interactions, and edge cases. Experimental results demonstrate a 91.8% task completion rate with a median per-request latency of 2.2 seconds, 96.0% safety compliance on the dedicated safety-critical evaluation subset, and an average operational cost of $0.0324 per appointment, yielding a significant cost reduction compared to manual human scheduling.
papers.result: These findings show that carefully scoped and rigorously safeguarded LLM-based agents can reliably automate complex healthcare operational workflows while maintaining safety guarantees and achieving substantial cost efficiency. The source code and system implementation are publicly available at https://github.com/Hadi-Hsn/CareConnect.
papers.gap: Administrative, not diagnostic; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: CareConnect automates appointment logistics with an LLM agent that calls booking tools, but places a deterministic safety filter before the model so emergencies and medical questions are handled by fixed rules and never by the LLM. It was tested on 680 scripted scenarios. It shows layered deterministic guardrails around an agent, similar to the mandatory-escalation list in this study.
papers.studyDesign: System development with a scenario benchmark (American University of Beirut, preprint).
papers.datasets: 680 task-oriented test scenarios across standard workflows (160), modifications (130), information retrieval (130), safety compliance (150) and edge cases (110).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: CareConnect: GPT-4o orchestrator with function calling over eight scheduling tools, a deterministic pre-LLM intent classifier that short-circuits emergencies and refuses medical advice, a RAG pipeline for facility information; up to ten reasoning cycles per request.
papers.training: No training.
papers.evaluation: Task completion rate by category; safety compliance.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (functional evaluation).
papers.results: Overall 91.8% (624/680); safety compliance 96.0%; modifications 88.5%; information retrieval 92.3%; edge cases 90.9%.

papers.title: A Comprehensive Survey on the Trustworthiness of Large Language Models in Healthcare
papers.authors: Manar Aljohani, Jun Hou, Sindhura Kommu, Xuan Wang
papers.aim: The application of large language models (LLMs) in healthcare holds significant promise for enhancing clinical decision-making, medical research, and patient care. However, their integration into real-world clinical settings raises critical concerns around trustworthiness, particularly around dimensions of truthfulness, privacy, safety, robustness, fairness, and explainability.
papers.method: These dimensions are essential for ensuring that LLMs generate reliable, unbiased, and ethically sound outputs. While researchers have recently begun developing benchmarks and evaluation frameworks to assess LLM trustworthiness, the trustworthiness of LLMs in healthcare remains underexplored, lacking a systematic review that provides a comprehensive understanding and future insights. This survey addresses that gap by providing a comprehensive review of current methodologies and solutions aimed at mitigating risks across key trust dimensions. We analyze how each dimension affects the reliability and ethical deployment of healthcare LLMs, synthesize ongoing research efforts, and identify critical gaps in existing approaches.
papers.result: We also identify emerging challenges posed by evolving paradigms, such as multi-agent collaboration, multi-modal reasoning, and the development of small open-source medical models. Our goal is to guide future research toward more trustworthy, transparent, and clinically viable LLMs.
papers.gap: Descriptive; no empirical comparison.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: The survey organises research on trustworthy healthcare LLMs into six dimensions and, for each, lists benchmarks, mitigation techniques and evaluation methods, then highlights open challenges created by multi-agent and multimodal systems. It is a useful map of methods for the trust and safety requirements of this framework.
papers.studyDesign: Comprehensive literature survey (Virginia Tech, preprint).
papers.datasets: Literature on trustworthiness of healthcare LLMs, with datasets catalogued by dimension (e.g. Med-HALT, PubHealthTab, HEALTHVER, SecureSQL, Med-harm).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Taxonomy of six trust dimensions (truthfulness, privacy, safety, robustness, fairness, explainability) with benchmarks, mitigation and evaluation methods for each.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Maps methods per dimension (e.g. semantic entropy for hallucination detection, federated learning and differential privacy for privacy) and identifies gaps, including multi-agent collaboration, multimodal reasoning and small open-source medical models.

papers.title: MedGuards: Multi-Agent System for Reliable Medical Error Detection and Correction
papers.authors: Congbo Ma, Hu Wang, Yichun Zhang, Farah E. Shamout
papers.aim: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in healthcare settings, accurate error detection and correction in generated or existing text becomes critical, as even minor mistakes can pose risks to patient safety. Existing methods for error detection and correction, including automated checks and heuristic-based approaches, do not generalize well across unseen datasets.
papers.method: In this paper, we propose MedGuards as a medical safety guardrail, which is a new framework that treats medical error detection and correction as a multi-agent in-context learning task. Specialized agents separately detect, localize, and correct errors, while a confidence-guided arbitration mechanism resolves disagreements using reasoning traces and confidence scores. This design enhances interpretability, robustness, and adaptability, without requiring additional training of the base LLMs. Additionally, we introduce the Keyword-Prioritized Correction Score (KPCS), a new evaluation metric that considers whether critical keywords within the reference text are generated correctly, providing a more comprehensive assessment than conventional metrics. Experiments across four multilingual medical datasets consisting of clinical notes demonstrate significant improvements by the proposed framework across several metrics and models.
papers.result: Our aim is to enable safer deployment of LLMs in real-world healthcare applications. For reproducibility, we make our code publicly available at https://github.com/congboma/MedGuards.
papers.gap: Text errors only; no imaging; no calibrated confidence.
papers.relation: Informs the multi-agent architecture (O1): how specialised AI components and agents are orchestrated, pass uncertainty between steps and keep an auditable record across the brain-tumour pathway.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedGuards uses several cooperating agents to find, verify and correct medical errors in generated or existing clinical text, acting as a safety layer before text is used. It is relevant as a post-hoc check on agent outputs, complementary to calibrated escalation.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and benchmark evaluation (NYU Abu Dhabi, Khalifa University, preprint).
papers.datasets: Medical error detection and correction benchmarks of clinical text (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Clinical texts with injected or real errors.
papers.modelDetails: MedGuards: a multi-agent guardrail that treats medical error detection and correction as a multi-agent interaction among detection, verification and correction agents.
papers.training: No training reported.
papers.evaluation: Error detection accuracy, error localisation and correction quality.
papers.baselines: Single LLMs and prior error-correction systems.
papers.results: Improved detection and correction over single-model baselines.

heading: O2 - Calibrated uncertainty and escalation (when to defer to the clinician)

papers.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
papers.authors: Guo C, Pleiss G, Sun Y, Weinberger KQ
papers.aim: To check if the confidence scores of modern deep networks match their real accuracy.
papers.method: Measured calibration with ECE and reliability diagrams on many networks and datasets. Compared post-hoc fixes.
papers.result: Modern deep networks are over-confident. Depth, width, batch norm and less weight decay make it worse. Temperature scaling (one parameter) fixes most of it.
papers.tools: ResNet, DenseNet, Wide-ResNet; CIFAR, ImageNet, text datasets
papers.gap: Only tested on the same distribution as training.
papers.relation: Every agent in our system must be calibrated before we use its confidence for escalation. Temperature scaling is our first baseline.
papers.limitations: Calibration breaks when data shifts (new hospital). Future: shift-robust calibration.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first measure calibration as the gap between confidence and accuracy. Test predictions are put into 15 equal-width confidence bins; for each bin they compare mean confidence with accuracy, and ECE is the weighted average gap (MCE is the largest gap). They then train modern networks (ResNets, Wide ResNets, DenseNets) and older LeNet-5 on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, SVHN, Birds, Cars and four text datasets, keeping the original papers' training recipes. Experiments on CIFAR-100 that vary depth, width, Batch Normalization and weight decay show that the changes that raise accuracy (more depth and width, BatchNorm, less weight decay) also make networks over-confident, and that NLL over-fits even when accuracy keeps improving. Next, they hold out a validation set (for example 5,000 images for CIFAR) and fit six post-hoc calibration methods on the network's logits. Temperature scaling divides all logits by one learned value T before the softmax, chosen to minimise NLL on the validation set. Across 17 model-dataset pairs it gives the lowest or near-lowest ECE, for example CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 from 16.53% to 1.26%, and it never changes accuracy. Matrix scaling over-fits with many classes. For our PhD this is the first calibration step for every agent: fit T on a hospital validation split, check ECE with 15 bins, then use the calibrated confidence in the escalation rule.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical study on public image and text classification benchmarks. First shows how modern network design affects calibration, then compares post-hoc calibration methods fitted on a held-out validation set.
papers.datasets: Image: Caltech-UCSD Birds (200 classes; 5,994/2,897/2,897 train/val/test), Stanford Cars (196 classes; 8,041/4,020/4,020), ImageNet 2012 (1,000 classes; 1.3M/25,000/25,000), CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (32x32; 45,000/5,000/10,000), SVHN (598,388/6,000/26,032). Text: 20 News (20 classes; 9,034/2,259/7,528), Reuters (8 classes; 4,388/1,097/2,189), Stanford Sentiment Treebank binary and fine-grained.
papers.preprocessing: Data preprocessing, training procedures and hyper-parameters as in each original architecture paper. Birds and Cars networks fine-tuned from ImageNet. A separate validation split is kept only for fitting the calibration method.
papers.modelDetails: Models: ResNet (50, 110, 152), ResNet with stochastic depth, Wide ResNet-32, DenseNet-40/161, LeNet-5, DAN (text) and TreeLSTM (SST). Calibration methods compared: histogram binning, isotonic regression, Bayesian Binning into Quantiles (BBQ), and Platt-scaling variants: matrix scaling (W z + b), vector scaling (diagonal W) and temperature scaling (softmax(z/T), one scalar T > 0 fitted by minimising NLL on the validation set). Temperature scaling does not change the predicted class, so accuracy is unchanged.
papers.training: Networks trained with the settings of their original papers. Calibration parameters (T, W, b, bins) fitted on the validation split by NLL. Also studied how depth, width, Batch Normalization and weight decay (10^-5 to 10^-2) change calibration on CIFAR-100.
papers.evaluation: Expected Calibration Error (ECE) with M = 15 equal-width confidence bins as the main metric; Maximum Calibration Error (MCE); negative log-likelihood (NLL); reliability diagrams; test error.
papers.baselines: Uncalibrated network vs histogram binning, isotonic regression, BBQ, temperature scaling, vector scaling and matrix scaling.
papers.results: ECE (%) before -> after temperature scaling: CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 16.53 -> 1.26; CIFAR-100 Wide ResNet-32 15.0 -> 2.32; CIFAR-100 DenseNet-40 10.37 -> 1.18; Birds ResNet-50 9.19 -> 1.85; ImageNet DenseNet-161 6.28 -> 1.99; ImageNet ResNet-152 5.48 -> 1.86; CIFAR-10 ResNet-110 4.6 -> 0.83; 20 News DAN 8.02 -> 4.11. Matrix scaling made calibration worse with many classes (CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 25.49%). Deeper and wider networks and Batch Normalization increased miscalibration; more weight decay reduced it.
papers.statistics: Not reported (single runs; no confidence intervals or significance tests).

papers.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
papers.authors: Gal Y, Ghahramani Z
papers.aim: To get model uncertainty from normal deep networks without changing them much.
papers.method: Showed dropout training is approximate Bayesian inference. Keep dropout on at test time and run many forward passes (MC dropout).
papers.result: Better predictive log-likelihood and RMSE on regression tasks, and useful uncertainty in classification and RL.
papers.tools: Dropout networks, Bayesian approximation
papers.gap: Uncertainty quality depends on dropout rate, and is often still too low.
papers.relation: Cheap way to get epistemic uncertainty for our MRI segmentation and classification agents on modest hardware.
papers.limitations: Several forward passes needed, so slower at inference. Future: better approximations.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors prove that minimising the usual dropout training loss with L2 weight decay is the same as variational inference in a deep Gaussian process, so a dropout network already holds an approximate posterior over weights. At test time they keep dropout on and run the network T times; the mean of the outputs is the prediction and their spread is the model uncertainty. For regression they add the inverse precision tau^-1, where tau comes from the prior length-scale, dropout rate and weight decay. They test this on the Mauna Loa CO2 series with 4-5 layer networks of 1,024 units (ReLU or TanH, dropout 0.1-0.2), training on the first part and predicting the rest: normal dropout gives a confident wrong value far from the data, while MC dropout widens its uncertainty. On rotated MNIST digits, 100 passes show that a digit can be classed as 5 while the spread of outputs is very large, so uncertainty flags the error. For a fair numeric test they copy the 10-dataset UCI protocol (20 random splits, 50-unit network, dropout 0.05 or 0.005, tau chosen by Bayesian optimisation, Adam, batch 32) and beat VI and PBP on RMSE and log-likelihood on 9 of 10 datasets. For our PhD, MC dropout is the cheapest way to get an uncertainty value from an existing segmentation or classification agent without retraining.
papers.studyDesign: Theory plus benchmark experiments. Shows that a network trained with dropout is an approximate Bayesian model (a deep Gaussian process), then tests the uncertainty it gives on regression, classification and reinforcement learning tasks.
papers.datasets: Regression: Mauna Loa CO2 (about 200 points, extrapolation) and reconstructed solar irradiance (interpolation). Classification: MNIST (rotated digit test). Predictive performance: 10 UCI regression sets - Boston Housing (N=506, 13 inputs), Concrete (1,030, 8), Energy (768, 8), Kin8nm (8,192, 8), Naval (11,934, 16), Power Plant (9,568, 4), Protein (45,730, 9), Wine Red (1,599, 11), Yacht (308, 6), Year MSD (515,345, 90).
papers.preprocessing: CO2 and solar data centred and normalised; model trained on the left part of the series and tested on all of it (extrapolation). UCI: set-up of Hernandez-Lobato and Adams (2015), averaged over 20 random train/test splits (5 for Protein, 1 for Year).
papers.modelDetails: MC dropout: keep dropout switched on at test time, run T stochastic forward passes, and use the mean as the prediction and the variance (plus inverse model precision tau^-1) as predictive uncertainty. Dropout probability and weight decay correspond to a prior length-scale and model precision. CO2: 4 or 5 hidden layers of 1,024 units, ReLU or TanH, dropout 0.1 or 0.2. UCI: one hidden layer of 50 units, dropout 0.05 or 0.005. MNIST: LeNet with dropout; 100 forward passes shown.
papers.training: UCI: prior length-scale 10^-2; tau found by Bayesian optimisation over validation log-likelihood (40 iterations, then 10x more iterations for the final model); mini-batch 32; Adam optimiser. CO2 plots used T = 1,000 passes; T = 10 already gives a reasonable estimate.
papers.evaluation: Test RMSE and test predictive log-likelihood (mean and standard error over splits); qualitative uncertainty plots far from the training data; softmax input/output spread for rotated MNIST digits.
papers.baselines: Variational inference for Bayesian NNs (VI, Graves 2011), Probabilistic Back-propagation (PBP), standard dropout with weight averaging, Gaussian process with squared-exponential kernel.
papers.results: Test RMSE (VI / PBP / MC dropout): Boston 4.32 / 3.01 / 2.97; Concrete 7.19 / 5.67 / 5.23; Energy 2.65 / 1.80 / 1.66; Protein 4.84 / 4.73 / 4.36; Yacht 6.89 / 1.02 / 1.11. Test log-likelihood: Boston -2.90 / -2.57 / -2.46; Concrete -3.39 / -3.16 / -3.04; Protein -2.99 / -2.97 / -2.89. Dropout was best on all datasets except Yacht RMSE. Boston median RMSE 2.68 (IQR 2.45-3.35). On CO2, standard dropout predicted a far-away point confidently, while MC dropout showed large uncertainty there.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- standard error over 20 random splits; medians and IQR reported for Boston. No hypothesis tests.

papers.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
papers.authors: Lakshminarayanan B, Pritzel A, Blundell C
papers.aim: To give a simple, non-Bayesian way to estimate predictive uncertainty.
papers.method: Train several networks with different random starts, using proper scoring rules (and optional adversarial training), then average.
papers.result: Well-calibrated predictions and higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution samples, often better than MC dropout.
papers.tools: Deep ensembles, MNIST, SVHN, ImageNet
papers.gap: Training and running many models costs a lot.
papers.relation: Strong UQ baseline to compare with MC dropout for our agents. Cost matters in low-resource hospitals.
papers.limitations: Compute and memory cost. Future: lighter ensembles.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of a Bayesian network, the authors train several ordinary networks and average them. Each of M networks (default 5) is trained from a different random start on the whole training set and outputs a full predictive distribution - for regression a mean and a variance, trained with Gaussian negative log-likelihood, so the network learns its own noise level. Optionally each training batch is extended with adversarial examples made by the fast gradient sign method with step 1% of the input range, which smooths the predictive distribution. At test time the M outputs are combined as an equal-weight mixture; its spread shows where the members disagree. They evaluate on the 10-dataset UCI benchmark against PBP and MC dropout (best NLL on most sets, e.g. Energy 1.38 vs 1.99), on MNIST (3x200 MLP) and SVHN (VGG-style net), where the ensemble beats MC dropout with the same number of samples on error, NLL and Brier score, and on ImageNet with an Inception network. Finally, a model trained on MNIST is tested on NotMNIST letters: the ensemble's entropy rises clearly on these unseen classes, so its uncertainty can flag inputs outside its training data. For our PhD, a 5-member ensemble per imaging agent is a simple, strong source of uncertainty for escalation, at 5x the training cost.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with benchmark experiments on regression, image classification and out-of-distribution detection.
papers.datasets: 10 UCI regression sets (Boston, Concrete, Energy, Kin8nm, Naval, Power Plant, Protein, Wine, Yacht, Year MSD; same splits as PBP); MNIST; SVHN; ImageNet ILSVRC-2012; NotMNIST test split as unseen classes for out-of-distribution testing.
papers.preprocessing: UCI: protocol of Hernandez-Lobato and Adams (2015). Each ensemble member trained on the full training set (no bagging - bagging made results worse because a bootstrap sample only has about 63% unique points). Diversity comes from random initialisation and random shuffling.
papers.modelDetails: Train M networks independently. Each network outputs a predictive distribution (mean and variance for regression, softmax for classification) and is trained with a proper scoring rule (NLL or Brier). Optional adversarial training with the fast gradient sign method, epsilon = 1% of the input range. Prediction = uniform mixture of the M members; for regression the mixture mean and variance are combined into one Gaussian. Recommended default M = 5. MNIST: MLP with 3 hidden layers of 200 units, ReLU, batch normalisation. SVHN: VGG-style convolutional network. ImageNet: Inception network.
papers.training: Defaults M = 5 networks and adversarial epsilon = 1% of input range (for example 2.55 for 0-255 images). MC-dropout comparison used dropout 0.1 after each non-linearity (0.5 performed worse). Networks trained in parallel.
papers.evaluation: Regression: test RMSE and NLL over 20 splits. Classification: error, NLL and Brier score as ensemble size M grows; ImageNet single-crop accuracy and calibration; predictive entropy on known (MNIST) vs unknown (NotMNIST) classes.
papers.baselines: Probabilistic Back-propagation (PBP), MC dropout (same number of samples M), ensembles without adversarial training, ensembles with random-direction perturbation.
papers.results: UCI NLL (PBP / MC-dropout / Deep Ensembles): Boston 2.57 / 2.46 / 2.41; Energy 2.04 / 1.99 / 1.38; Naval -3.73 / -3.80 / -5.63; Protein 2.97 / 2.89 / 2.83; Yacht 1.63 / 1.55 / 1.18. RMSE sometimes slightly worse (Boston 3.01 / 2.97 / 3.28) because the method optimises NLL. On MNIST and SVHN, ensembles beat MC-dropout on error, NLL and Brier score at every M; adversarial training helped on MNIST and on SVHN only at M = 1. On ImageNet both accuracy and uncertainty quality improved as M increased. Ensembles gave higher predictive entropy on unseen NotMNIST letters than on MNIST digits.
papers.statistics: Mean +/- standard deviation over splits; no hypothesis tests.
papers.availability: Not available (no official code link in the paper).

papers.title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
papers.authors: Geifman Y, El-Yaniv R
papers.aim: To let a network refuse to predict on uncertain inputs while guaranteeing a chosen error rate.
papers.method: Selection with Guaranteed Risk (SGR): pick a confidence threshold on held-out data so the error on accepted cases stays under a target, with high probability. Tested softmax response and MC dropout.
papers.result: On ImageNet they could guarantee 2% top-5 error while still covering about 60% of images.
papers.tools: VGG / ResNet, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet
papers.gap: Single model, single decision, same cost for every mistake.
papers.relation: The risk-coverage trade-off is basically our escalation threshold. We need to extend it to asymmetric error cost and to a chain of agents.
papers.limitations: Guarantee assumes test data like calibration data. Future: training models for selection.
papers.methodologyDetail: The method takes any trained network and adds a reject option with a guaranteed error rate. First a confidence score is chosen for each input: the maximum softmax probability (SR) or the variance of MC-dropout outputs. A labelled hold-out set is sorted by this score. The SGR algorithm then runs a binary search over thresholds: for a candidate threshold it keeps only cases above it, counts their errors, and computes the tightest binomial upper bound on the true error of the kept cases at confidence delta divided by the number of search steps. It moves the threshold until the bound just meets the target risk r* set by the user, so the final rule is: answer if confidence >= theta, otherwise abstain. The authors test this on CIFAR-10/100 with a VGG-16 trained with augmentation and dropout (93.54% accuracy on CIFAR-10) and on ImageNet with VGG-16 and ResNet-50, using one half of the validation data to set theta and the other half to check the guarantee, with delta = 0.001. On CIFAR-10 a 1% error target is met with 78.6% of images answered; on ImageNet top-5 a 2% target keeps 53.5% coverage, and the measured test error never exceeded the bound. For our PhD this is the template for the escalation threshold: a clinician sets the acceptable error (for example 2% wrong tumour grades), the threshold is fitted on a local validation set, and every case below it is referred to the clinician.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with risk-control experiments on image classification benchmarks. A trained classifier is wrapped with a reject option whose error rate is guaranteed with high probability.
papers.datasets: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (half of the 10,000-image validation set, about 5,000 images, used to fit the selector; the other half, about 5,000, used for testing), ImageNet ILSVRC (about 25,000 images to fit and 25,000 to test), top-1 and top-5 tasks.
papers.preprocessing: CIFAR: data augmentation with horizontal flips, vertical and horizontal shifts and rotations. The validation set is randomly split in two equal halves: one to run the selection algorithm, one to test the guaranteed risk.
papers.modelDetails: Selective classifier (f, g): f predicts, g decides to answer or say 'don't know'. Two confidence-rate functions: softmax response (SR, the maximum softmax probability) and MC-dropout variance. The SGR algorithm (Selection with Guaranteed Risk) sorts samples by confidence and does a binary search over the threshold theta; for each candidate it computes a tight binomial upper bound on the selective risk (Gascuel and Caraux) with confidence delta / ceil(log2 m), and keeps the lowest-coverage-loss threshold whose bound is below the target risk r*. Networks: VGG-16 with heavy dropout (CIFAR), pre-trained VGG-16 and ResNet-50 (ImageNet).
papers.training: CIFAR-10 VGG-16: SGD, momentum 0.9, initial learning rate 0.1, weight decay 0.0005, learning rate halved every 25 epochs, 250 epochs; validation accuracy 93.54%. Same recipe for CIFAR-100. Confidence level delta = 0.001 for all SGR runs.
papers.evaluation: Risk-coverage curves; for each target risk r*: train/test selective risk, train/test coverage and the risk bound b*.
papers.baselines: SR vs MC-dropout as the confidence function; full-coverage classifier (no rejection).
papers.results: CIFAR-10 (delta 0.001): target 1% error -> test risk 0.92% at 78.6% coverage (bound 0.99%); target 2% -> 1.49% at 84.7%; target 6% -> 5.72% at 97.8%. CIFAR-100: target 2% -> test risk 1.87% at 21.3% coverage. ImageNet VGG-16 top-1: target 10% -> test risk 9.48% at 59.5% coverage; target 25% -> 24.45% at 91.2%. ImageNet VGG-16 top-5: target 2% -> 1.79% at 53.5% coverage. ResNet-50 top-1: target 10% -> 9.88% at 65.0%. The test risk never exceeded the bound. SR was clearly better than MC-dropout on ImageNet (top-1 at 60% coverage: about 10% vs more than 20% error).
papers.statistics: High-probability guarantee: P(selective risk > b*) < delta = 0.001 (numerical binomial bound with union bound over log2 m search steps). No Bonferroni correction across table rows.

papers.title: Consistent Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert
papers.authors: Mozannar H, Sontag D
papers.aim: To train a classifier and a 'defer to the expert' decision together, with a sound loss.
papers.method: Adds an extra 'defer' class and a consistent surrogate loss based on cross-entropy, taking expert accuracy into account.
papers.result: Beat confidence-based and earlier L2D baselines on CIFAR-10 with synthetic experts, CIFAR-100, CheXpert and hate-speech data.
papers.tools: Surrogate loss, WideResNet, CheXpert
papers.gap: Needs expert labels on training data. Does not limit how many cases go to the expert.
papers.relation: Core method for O2. We need to add the limit of clinician review time and the clinical cost of each error type.
papers.limitations: One expert, one decision. Future: multiple experts and budget constraints.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors frame deferral as cost-sensitive learning: for each training case the cost of predicting class j is the classifier's error, and the cost of the extra 'defer' class is the expert's error on that case (known from the expert's recorded label). They add one output unit to an ordinary network, so it has K class outputs plus a defer output, and train it with a new surrogate loss that reduces to cross-entropy when the expert is ignored and is proven consistent, so with enough data it learns the best possible rule for when to hand a case to the expert. At test time the case goes to the expert when the defer output is the largest. They test it with a WideResNet-28 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 using simulated experts that are perfect on only some classes, on CIFAR10H with 50 real human labels per image when expert labels exist for only part of the data, on hate-speech text and on chest X-rays. The joint training beats the common approach of training the model alone and then comparing its confidence with the expert's (+6.39 points on synthetic data). For our PhD this is the core learning-to-defer recipe: each agent gets a 'refer to clinician' output trained on recorded clinician decisions, and our work adds limits on clinician time and different costs for different clinical errors.
papers.studyDesign: Theory (consistent surrogate loss and generalisation bound) plus experiments with synthetic and real human experts on image, text and chest X-ray classification.
papers.datasets: Synthetic mixture data (logistic regression test); CIFAR-10 (50,000 train / 10,000 test, 32x32, 10 classes); CIFAR-100; CIFAR10H (50 crowdworker labels for each of the 10,000 CIFAR-10 test images, used as a real human expert with limited labels); hate speech and offensive language tweets; chest X-rays with synthetic experts.
papers.preprocessing: Synthetic expert k: perfect on the first k classes, uniform random on the rest (CIFAR-100 expert correct with probability 0.94 on its classes). CIFAR-10 model deliberately trained without augmentation to leave room for the expert. Limited-expert setting: only part of the data has expert labels; missing expert labels imputed.
papers.modelDetails: Learn a classifier h and a rejector r together. One network with K+1 outputs: the first K are class scores, the extra unit is the 'defer' score. Trained with the proposed surrogate loss L_CE^alpha, a cost-sensitive generalisation of cross-entropy that is consistent (minimising it gives the Bayes-optimal defer rule). alpha in {0, 0.5, 1} weights how much the model still fits the true label on deferred cases. Defer when the defer score is larger than every class score.
papers.training: CIFAR-10: WideResNet-28, SGD with momentum, cosine annealing learning rate, 200 epochs; plain model 90.47% test accuracy. CIFAR-100: WideResNet-28 with random crops and flips, 79.28% accuracy.
papers.evaluation: System accuracy (model + expert), coverage (share of cases the model handles), classifier accuracy on non-deferred cases; difference vs baselines with 95% confidence intervals; varying expert competence k and training-set size.
papers.baselines: Confidence baseline (Raghu et al. 2019: defer if expert confidence > model confidence), learned oracle rejector, mixture-of-experts loss (Madras et al. 2018).
papers.results: Synthetic data: L_CE (alpha=0) beat the confidence baseline by 6.39 accuracy points (95% CI 3.71-9.06), matched the oracle (+0.22, CI -1.71 to 2.15) and beat mixture-of-experts by 2.01 (CI 0.14-4.06). CIFAR-100: +1.60 points over the confidence baseline on average for 30 <= k <= 90. CIFAR10H with limited expert labels: L_CE impute system accuracy 96.29 +/- 0.25% at 51.67% coverage (classifier accuracy 99.2% on kept cases); L_CE 2-step 96.03% at 60.81% coverage.
papers.statistics: 95% confidence intervals for accuracy differences; mean +/- standard deviation over repeated runs.

papers.title: Predict Responsibly: Improving Fairness and Accuracy by Learning to Defer
papers.authors: Madras D, Pitassi T, Zemel R
papers.aim: To show that a model should defer by thinking about who will receive the case, not only its own confidence.
papers.method: Learning-to-defer model that is trained with the downstream decision maker in mind, compared with simple reject option.
papers.result: Better accuracy and fairness of the whole system on COMPAS and Heritage Health data.
papers.tools: Neural networks, fairness metrics
papers.gap: Decision makers were simulated.
papers.relation: Supports our idea that deferral depends on the clinician (radiologist, pathologist, neurosurgeon) who will review it.
papers.limitations: Not tested in medicine. Future: real human decision makers.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors model a decision pipeline where an automated model can either decide or pass the case to a human decision-maker who has extra information but may be biased or inconsistent. Classic rejection learning passes a case whenever the model is unsure, using a fixed cost per pass, and ignores who receives the case. Learning to defer adds the decision-maker's prediction into the training loss: on each training case, passing costs whatever error the decision-maker would make, so the model learns to keep the cases where the human is weak or biased and pass the cases where the human is strong. A fairness term can be added so the whole system treats groups (race in COMPAS, age in Health) more equally. Because real joint human-model data is rare, they simulate the human with a second two-layer network trained with extra features, and test three humans: very accurate, biased and inconsistent. Sweeping the pass penalty and fairness weight traces accuracy-fairness curves; the deferring model dominates rejection learning in every scenario. For our PhD this shows that the escalation rule must be learned with respect to the specific clinician who will review the case (radiologist, pathologist, neurosurgeon), not only from the model's own confidence.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with semi-synthetic experiments: real datasets, and a simulated downstream decision-maker (DM) trained under different conditions with extra information the model does not see.
papers.datasets: COMPAS (predict a defendant's recidivism without discriminating by race) and Heritage Health (predict a patient's Charlson comorbidity index without discriminating by age).
papers.preprocessing: Simulated DMs are separate classifiers given extra information in training: violent recidivism for COMPAS, primary condition group for Health. Three DM scenarios: highly accurate DM, biased DM, inconsistent DM (random errors on subgroups).
papers.modelDetails: Two-stage system: model either predicts or says 'pass' and the DM decides. Rejection learning uses a fixed penalty gamma_reject for each pass. Learning to defer instead includes the DM's own prediction in the loss, so the pass decision adapts to where the DM is accurate or biased. Two versions: post-hoc (pass decision from model outputs) and end-to-end (pass network also sees the input X). A fairness regulariser alpha_fair penalises disparate impact between groups. All models and DMs are fully-connected two-layer neural networks.
papers.training: Hyper-parameter sweeps over gamma_reject / gamma_defer and alpha_fair; further details in the appendix (not reported in the main text).
papers.evaluation: System accuracy against fairness (disparate impact between subgroups) and against deferral rate, for each DM scenario.
papers.baselines: Binary classifier optimised for accuracy only; binary classifier with fairness penalty; fair rejection learning; DM alone.
papers.results: Results are given as accuracy-fairness and accuracy-deferral curves (no single summary numbers in the main text). Learning to defer gave higher system accuracy and lower unfairness than rejection learning in all three DM scenarios, including with biased and inconsistent DMs; with an inconsistent DM, only the end-to-end deferring model adapted, because the post-hoc model cannot see X.

papers.title: The Algorithmic Automation Problem: Prediction, Triage, and Human Effort
papers.authors: Raghu M, Blumer K, Corrado G, Kleinberg J, Obermeyer Z, Mullainathan S
papers.aim: To decide which cases an algorithm should handle and which should go to humans, to use human effort well.
papers.method: Triage using predicted human error / disagreement plus model uncertainty. Tested on medical data like diabetic retinopathy grading.
papers.result: Mixing algorithm and human by triage did better than full automation or full human review.
papers.tools: Deep learning, uncertainty estimation, triage
papers.gap: Workflow and time cost of humans not modelled in detail.
papers.relation: Our case: specialist time is the scarcest thing. This paper frames the problem in the same way.
papers.limitations: Preprint, retrospective only. Future: prospective test.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors ask how to split cases between an algorithm and doctors when the algorithm is better on average. They train a CNN on a large fundus photograph set to predict the 5 diabetic retinopathy grades, using the spread of doctor grades as a soft target, and turn its output into a referable / non-referable decision (grade 3 or more). On a small adjudicated test set with many doctor grades per image, they show that per-image errors of doctors and algorithm vary a lot: on some images doctors are more reliable, on others the model is. They then train two more networks to predict, for each image, the chance that the model is wrong and the chance that a doctor is wrong (the latter learned from how much doctors disagree). Images are ranked by this triage score; the easiest share is automated and the remaining images get the available doctor time. Error falls from about 5.5% (doctors) and 4% (full automation) to about 3.5% with triage. For our PhD this supports routing per case on both AI error risk and clinician error risk, and treating clinician review time as a fixed budget in the escalation policy.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective study on a real medical imaging task (diabetic retinopathy grading from fundus photographs), comparing full automation, human-only review and optimal triage between algorithm and doctors.
papers.datasets: Large fundus photograph training set, each image sparsely graded by 1-3 doctors on the 5-point diabetic retinopathy (DR) scale; a smaller gold-standard evaluation set where each image has many individual doctor grades plus a single adjudicated grade (from doctor discussion) used as ground truth; a second dataset in the appendix with the same findings.
papers.preprocessing: DR graded as 5 classes for training; for triage the task is binary: referable DR (grade >= 3) vs non-referable. Multiple doctor grades per image are aggregated and thresholded.
papers.modelDetails: A convolutional neural network outputs a distribution over the 5 DR grades, trained with the empirical distribution of doctor grades as target. Two auxiliary networks predict, per image, (i) the algorithm's error probability Pr[M_i] and (ii) the human error probability Pr[H_i] (built on direct prediction of doctor disagreement). A triage score from these ranks images; the top alpha*N go to the algorithm and the rest share the human effort budget B = cN equally.
papers.training: Model development details given in the paper's appendix (not in the main text).
papers.evaluation: Error rate against the adjudicated grade for: doctors alone, full automation (alpha = 1), equal human coverage (alpha = 0), and triage at intermediate alpha.
papers.baselines: Full automation; equal human effort on all instances; individual doctors.
papers.results: Doctors alone about 5.5% error; full automation about 4%; automation with optimal triage about 3.5%. Human and algorithm error differ strongly from image to image, and this difference is partly predictable, which is why triage beats full automation even though the algorithm is better on average.
papers.statistics: Not reported as formal tests in the main text.

papers.title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification
papers.authors: Angelopoulos AN, Bates S
papers.aim: To explain conformal prediction in a practical way.
papers.method: Tutorial with code: split conformal, adaptive sets, conformal risk control, examples on images and medicine.
papers.result: Shows how to turn any model output into prediction sets with a guaranteed coverage.
papers.tools: Conformal prediction, Python examples
papers.gap: Guarantee needs exchangeable data, which is not true across hospitals.
papers.relation: For tumour type we can give a set of likely classes with a coverage guarantee. A large set = escalate. Works with small calibration sets.
papers.limitations: Coverage only on average, not per patient. Future: shift-aware conformal.
papers.methodologyDetail: Conformal prediction turns any model's heuristic confidence into a set of answers that contains the truth with a user-chosen probability, for example 90%. The recipe needs only a labelled calibration set the model has not seen. For each calibration case a score measures how wrong the model is on the true answer (for classification, one minus the softmax probability of the true class). The (n+1)(1-alpha)/n quantile of these scores becomes a threshold; for a new case every label scoring below the threshold goes into the prediction set. If calibration and new cases come from the same distribution, the set contains the true label at least 1-alpha of the time, whatever the model. The guide then shows better scores (APS, which adds sorted softmax probabilities until the true class, giving larger sets for hard inputs), conformalised quantile regression for continuous outputs, group-wise and class-wise calibration, risk control for losses other than coverage, and weighting for distribution shift, and explains how to test an implementation by repeating calibration on 100+ random splits. For our PhD, the set size from conformal prediction is a direct escalation signal: if the set for a tumour grade or diagnosis has more than one label at the chosen error level, the case goes to the clinician.
papers.studyDesign: Tutorial / methods guide with worked examples and Python pseudocode. No new clinical study.
papers.datasets: Worked examples on ImageNet classification (prediction sets), regression with quantile regression, and other examples (tumour segmentation, time series, outliers) in later sections.
papers.preprocessing: Split conformal prediction: keep a calibration set of n labelled examples that the model never trained on; the model itself is trained on separate data.
papers.modelDetails: Any pre-trained model f.
