papers.modelDetails: Learning-to-defer with a human performance model, adapted to a specific individual by two fine-tuning algorithms.
papers.training: Fine-tuning on k samples from the target individual (details in appendix).
papers.evaluation: Human-model accuracy, system accuracy, average trip duration.
papers.baselines: No fine-tuning; known-mean and ideal oracles.
papers.results: Fine-tuning reduced average trip time by 30 s (oracle 2 min 30 s) and improved human-model accuracy for synthetic experts, but did not consistently improve system accuracy with real annotators.

papers.title: Why Ask One When You Can Ask $k$? Learning-to-Defer to the Top-$k$ Experts
papers.authors: Yannis Montreuil, Axel Carlier, Lai Xing Ng, Wei Tsang Ooi
papers.aim: Existing Learning-to-Defer (L2D) frameworks are limited to single-expert deferral, forcing each query to rely on only one expert and preventing the use of collective expertise. We introduce the first framework for Top-$k$ Learning-to-Defer, which allocates queries to the $k$ most cost-effective entities.
papers.method: Our formulation unifies and strictly generalizes prior approaches, including the one-stage and two-stage regimes, selective prediction, and classical cascades. In particular, it recovers the usual Top-1 deferral rule as a special case while enabling principled collaboration with multiple experts when $k>1$. We further propose Top-$k(x)$ Learning-to-Defer, an adaptive variant that learns the optimal number of experts per query based on input difficulty, expert quality, and consultation cost. To enable practical learning, we develop a novel surrogate loss that is Bayes-consistent, $\mathcal{H}_h$-consistent in the one-stage setting, and $(\mathcal{H}_r,\mathcal{H}_g)$-consistent in the two-stage setting.
papers.result: Crucially, this surrogate is independent of $k$, allowing a single policy to be learned once and deployed flexibly across $k$. Experiments across both regimes show that Top-$k$ and Top-$k(x)$ deliver superior accuracy-cost trade-offs, opening a new direction for multi-expert deferral in L2D.
papers.gap: Simulated experts and non-medical data; no calibration of expert costs.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of deferring each case to one expert, the method chooses the k most cost-effective experts and aggregates them, or learns how many experts a case needs. It comes with consistency proofs and shows better accuracy for a given budget on standard datasets. In clinical terms it formalises when a case needs one versus several reviewers, relevant to multidisciplinary escalation.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical and empirical machine-learning study (NUS, Toulouse, A*STAR; ICLR 2026).
papers.datasets: California Housing (two-stage regression), CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and SVHN (classification) with simulated experts and query costs.
papers.preprocessing: Standard splits.
papers.modelDetails: Top-k Learning-to-Defer: allocates each query to the k most cost-effective entities (model or experts) with a k-independent consistent surrogate; Top-k(x) learns the number of experts per query from input difficulty, expert quality and cost; unifies one-stage and two-stage L2D, selective prediction and cascades.
papers.training: Details in appendix.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy or RMSE vs expected budget and expected number of queried entities.
papers.baselines: One-stage and two-stage single-expert L2D methods (Mozannar & Sontag; Mao et al.; Narasimhan et al.).
papers.results: Top-k and Top-k(x) consistently outperformed single-expert deferral, with better accuracy-cost trade-offs.

papers.title: Learning to Complement and to Defer to Multiple Users
papers.authors: Zheng Zhang, Wenjie Ai, Kevin Wells, David Rosewarne, Thanh-Toan Do, Gustavo Carneiro
papers.aim: With the development of Human-AI Collaboration in Classification (HAI-CC), integrating users and AI predictions becomes challenging due to the complex decision-making process. This process has three options: 1) AI autonomously classifies, 2) learning to complement, where AI collaborates with users, and 3) learning to defer, where AI defers to users.
papers.method: Despite their interconnected nature, these options have been studied in isolation rather than as components of a unified system. In this paper, we address this weakness with the novel HAI-CC methodology, called Learning to Complement and to Defer to Multiple Users (LECODU). LECODU not only combines learning to complement and learning to defer strategies, but it also incorporates an estimation of the optimal number of users to engage in the decision process. The training of LECODU maximises classification accuracy and minimises collaboration costs associated with user involvement.
papers.result: Comprehensive evaluations across real-world and synthesized datasets demonstrate LECODU's superior performance compared to state-of-the-art HAI-CC methods. Remarkably, even when relying on unreliable users with high rates of label noise, LECODU exhibits significant improvement over both human decision-makers alone and AI alone.
papers.gap: Uniform user cost; no asymmetric error costs or calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: LECODU unifies three options for each case: let the AI decide, combine the AI with one or more humans, or defer fully to humans, and learns which option to use while charging a cost for each human involved. Training uses consensus labels estimated from noisy multi-rater data. Tested on natural images and a colon pathology dataset with real pathologist labels, it reduced human workload while keeping accuracy. This is a cost-aware deferral formulation close to O2.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with real multi-rater datasets (University of Surrey, Royal Wolverhampton NHS, Monash; ECCV-style paper).
papers.datasets: CIFAR-10N (train) and CIFAR-10H (test, ~51 human labels per image, up to three users per case); CIFAR10-IDN with synthetic instance-dependent noise 0.2-0.5; Chaoyang colon pathology patches (6,160, three pathologist labels, 4 classes).
papers.preprocessing: Consensus labels and quality scores from CROWDLAB; samples with quality >0.5 kept.
papers.modelDetails: LECODU: a Human-AI Selection Module predicts a distribution over collaboration scenarios (AI alone, AI complemented by one or more users, defer to users) and a Collaboration Module combines AI and user predictions; trained to maximise accuracy and minimise user-involvement cost.
papers.training: Pre-trained learning-with-noisy-labels AI model; selection module trained with cost penalty.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy vs number of users involved (collaboration cost).
papers.baselines: State-of-the-art human-AI collaboration methods (learning to complement, learning to defer, LECOMH).
papers.results: Higher accuracy than prior methods at equal or lower user involvement; often matched multi-user accuracy with fewer users.

papers.title: Realizable $H$-Consistent and Bayes-Consistent Loss Functions for Learning to Defer
papers.authors: Anqi Mao, Mehryar Mohri, Yutao Zhong
papers.aim: We present a comprehensive study of surrogate loss functions for learning to defer. We introduce a broad family of surrogate losses, parameterized by a non-increasing function $Ψ$, and establish their realizable $H$-consistency under mild conditions.
papers.method: For cost functions based on classification error, we further show that these losses admit $H$-consistency bounds when the hypothesis set is symmetric and complete, a property satisfied by common neural network and linear function hypothesis sets. Our results also resolve an open question raised in previous work (Mozannar et al., 2023) by proving the realizable $H$-consistency and Bayes-consistency of a specific surrogate loss. Furthermore, we identify choices of $Ψ$ that lead to $H$-consistent surrogate losses for any general cost function, thus achieving Bayes-consistency, realizable $H$-consistency, and $H$-consistency bounds simultaneously.
papers.result: We also investigate the relationship between $H$-consistency bounds and realizable $H$-consistency in learning to defer, highlighting key differences from standard classification. Finally, we empirically evaluate our proposed surrogate losses and compare them with existing baselines.
papers.gap: No medical evaluation; uniform costs.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper studies which training losses guarantee that learning a predictor and a defer decision together converges to the best possible policy, both in idealised and realistic hypothesis classes. It proposes a broad family of such losses with proofs and confirms them empirically. It provides theoretical grounding for training a deferral model jointly with a classifier.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical learning-theory paper with experiments (NYU Courant, Google Research).
papers.datasets: Standard benchmarks with simulated experts (e.g. CIFAR-10, SVHN) for empirical validation.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: A family of surrogate losses for learning to defer parameterised by a non-increasing function, proven realizable H-consistent and, for classification-error costs, H-consistent and Bayes-consistent.
papers.training: Standard training of predictor and rejector with the surrogate.
papers.evaluation: System accuracy; theoretical bounds.
papers.baselines: Earlier L2D surrogates (Mozannar & Sontag, Verma & Nalisnick, realizable surrogate).
papers.results: New losses matched or improved prior surrogates and resolved an open question on realizable consistency.

papers.title: In Defense of Softmax Parametrization for Calibrated and Consistent Learning to Defer
papers.authors: Yuzhou Cao, Hussein Mozannar, Lei Feng, Hongxin Wei, Bo An
papers.aim: Enabling machine learning classifiers to defer their decision to a downstream expert when the expert is more accurate will ensure improved safety and performance. This objective can be achieved with the learning-to-defer framework which aims to jointly learn how to classify and how to defer to the expert.
papers.method: In recent studies, it has been theoretically shown that popular estimators for learning to defer parameterized with softmax provide unbounded estimates for the likelihood of deferring which makes them uncalibrated. However, it remains unknown whether this is due to the widely used softmax parameterization and if we can find a softmax-based estimator that is both statistically consistent and possesses a valid probability estimator. In this work, we first show that the cause of the miscalibrated and unbounded estimator in prior literature is due to the symmetric nature of the surrogate losses used and not due to softmax.
papers.result: We then propose a novel statistically consistent asymmetric softmax-based surrogate loss that can produce valid estimates without the issue of unboundedness. We further analyze the non-asymptotic properties of our method and empirically validate its performance and calibration on benchmark datasets.
papers.gap: Uniform error costs; non-medical benchmarks.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors show why softmax-based learning-to-defer estimators had produced invalid deferral probabilities and propose an asymmetric softmax loss that is both consistent and calibrated. On synthetic and real human experts it gave lower error under deferral budgets and higher coverage. Calibrated estimates of whether to defer are exactly what a budget-limited escalation policy needs.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical and empirical machine-learning study (NTU Singapore, MIT, SUSTech; NeurIPS 2023).
papers.datasets: CIFAR-100 with synthetic experts (correct on first k in {20,40,60} classes with p=94% or 75%); real experts: CIFAR-10H, HateSpeech, ImageNet-16H; 5 trials.
papers.preprocessing: Standard splits.
papers.modelDetails: Analysis showing that unbounded deferral-probability estimates come from symmetric softmax surrogates, and a new statistically consistent asymmetric softmax surrogate (A-SM) giving valid, bounded probability estimates of deferral.
papers.training: Details in appendix F.
papers.evaluation: System error, coverage, ECE of the deferral estimate, budgeted error at 10/20/30% deferral budgets.
papers.baselines: Symmetric softmax (S-SM), one-vs-all (S-OvA), asymmetric OvA (A-OvA).
papers.results: A-SM matched or beat baselines in error with much higher coverage (e.g. 98.16% vs 77.72% for S-SM at k=20, p=94%), competitive ECE and best budgeted error.
papers.statistics: Mean and standard error over 5 trials; t-tests at 5%.

papers.title: A Unifying Post-Processing Framework for Multi-Objective Learn-to-Defer Problems
papers.authors: Mohammad-Amin Charusaie, Samira Samadi
papers.aim: Learn-to-Defer is a paradigm that enables learning algorithms to work not in isolation but as a team with human experts. In this paradigm, we permit the system to defer a subset of its tasks to the expert.
papers.method: Although there are currently systems that follow this paradigm and are designed to optimize the accuracy of the final human-AI team, the general methodology for developing such systems under a set of constraints (e.g., algorithmic fairness, expert intervention budget, defer of anomaly, etc.) remains largely unexplored. In this paper, using a $d$-dimensional generalization to the fundamental lemma of Neyman and Pearson (d-GNP), we obtain the Bayes optimal solution for learn-to-defer systems under various constraints.
papers.result: Furthermore, we design a generalizable algorithm to estimate that solution and apply this algorithm to the COMPAS and ACSIncome datasets. Our algorithm shows improvements in terms of constraint violation over a set of baselines.
papers.gap: Non-medical datasets; constraint levels assumed.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper derives the optimal way to decide between predicting and deferring when several constraints must hold at once, such as a limit on how many cases go to the expert, limits on particular error types, or fairness. A post-processing algorithm applies this to trained scores. Constraints on expert budget and on specific error types map directly to clinician capacity and asymmetric clinical costs in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical and empirical study (Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems; NeurIPS 2024).
papers.datasets: COMPAS (7,214 defendants, 1,000 real human assessments) and ACSIncome.
papers.preprocessing: Standard preprocessing; 10 random seeds.
papers.modelDetails: d-GNP: a d-dimensional generalisation of the Neyman-Pearson lemma giving the Bayes-optimal learn-to-defer solution under multiple constraints (fairness, expert-intervention budget, anomaly deferral, error-type limits), with a post-processing estimation algorithm.
papers.training: One-layer feed-forward networks for classifier and rejector scores.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy vs constraint violation (demographic parity, TPR/TNR constraints).
papers.baselines: Madras et al. (2018) regularised L2D; Mozannar et al. (2020) with threshold shifting.
papers.results: Lower constraint violation at comparable accuracy than baselines.

papers.title: Coverage-Constrained Human-AI Cooperation with Multiple Experts
papers.authors: Zheng Zhang, Cuong Nguyen, Kevin Wells, Thanh-Toan Do, David Rosewarne, Gustavo Carneiro
papers.aim: Human-AI cooperative classification (HAI-CC) approaches aim to develop hybrid intelligent systems that enhance decision-making in various high-stakes real-world scenarios by leveraging both human expertise and AI capabilities. Current HAI-CC methods primarily focus on learning-to-defer (L2D), where decisions are deferred to human experts, and learning-to-complement (L2C), where AI and human experts make predictions cooperatively.
papers.method: However, a notable research gap remains in effectively exploring both L2D and L2C under diverse expert knowledge to improve decision-making, particularly when constrained by the cooperation cost required to achieve a target probability for AI-only selection (i.e., coverage). In this paper, we address this research gap by proposing the Coverage-constrained Learning to Defer and Complement with Specific Experts (CL2DC) method. CL2DC makes final decisions through either AI prediction alone or by deferring to or complementing a specific expert, depending on the input data. Furthermore, we propose a coverage-constrained optimisation to control the cooperation cost, ensuring it approximates a target probability for AI-only selection. This approach enables an effective assessment of system performance within a specified budget.
papers.result: Also, CL2DC is designed to address scenarios where training sets contain multiple noisy-label annotations without any clean-label references. Comprehensive evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that CL2DC achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art HAI-CC methods.
papers.gap: Coverage constraint but no asymmetric error costs; limited medical evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: CL2DC chooses, for each case, between the AI alone, a specific human expert, or the AI combined with that expert, while guaranteeing that a chosen fraction of cases is handled by the AI alone. It learns from data with several noisy expert labels and no clean ground truth. Specifying the AI-only coverage in advance corresponds to setting a clinician workload target in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with multi-rater datasets (University of Surrey, Monash, Royal Wolverhampton NHS; preprint).
papers.datasets: Multi-rater noisy-label datasets including CIFAR-10H/CIFAR-10N-style sets and medical images (e.g. Chaoyang colon pathology) with several expert labels and no clean labels.
papers.preprocessing: Training sets with multiple noisy expert annotations.
papers.modelDetails: CL2DC: an AI classifier, a gating model choosing AI alone, defer to one of M experts, or AI plus one expert (complement), and a complementary aggregation module; trained with a coverage constraint so a target fraction of cases is handled by AI alone.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy at fixed coverage levels; cooperation cost.
papers.baselines: State-of-the-art human-AI cooperative classification methods (L2D, L2C, LECODU).
papers.results: Outperformed baselines at matched coverage across datasets.

papers.title: Reliable uncertainty quantification for 2D/3D anatomical landmark localization using multi-output conformal prediction
papers.authors: Jef Jonkers, Frank Coopman, Luc Duchateau, Glenn Van Wallendael, Sofie Van Hoecke
papers.aim: Automatic anatomical landmark localization in medical imaging requires not just accurate predictions but reliable uncertainty quantification for effective clinical decision support. Current uncertainty quantification approaches often fall short, particularly when combined with normality assumptions, systematically underestimating total predictive uncertainty.
papers.method: This paper introduces conformal prediction as a framework for reliable uncertainty quantification in anatomical landmark localization, addressing a critical gap in automatic landmark localization. We present two novel approaches guaranteeing finite-sample validity for multi-output prediction: Multi-output Regression-as-Classification Conformal Prediction (M-R2CCP) and its variant Multi-output Regression to Classification Conformal Prediction set to Region (M-R2C2R). Unlike conventional methods that produce axis-aligned hyperrectangular or ellipsoidal regions, our approaches generate flexible, non-convex prediction regions that better capture the underlying uncertainty structure of landmark predictions. Through extensive empirical evaluation across multiple 2D and 3D datasets, we demonstrate that our methods consistently outperform existing multi-output conformal prediction approaches in both validity and efficiency.
papers.result: This work represents a significant advancement in reliable uncertainty estimation for anatomical landmark localization, providing clinicians with trustworthy confidence measures for their diagnoses. While developed for medical imaging, these methods show promise for broader applications in multi-output regression problems.
papers.gap: Marginal guarantees; small datasets; not brain anatomy.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: Landmark predictions are wrapped with conformal prediction so that each landmark comes with a region guaranteed to contain the true position with a chosen probability. Several conformal variants were tested on top of two landmark models in 2D and 3D datasets, using a separate calibration set. Normal-distribution assumptions under-covered, while conformal regions met their targets. This is relevant to giving guaranteed uncertainty regions around anatomical structures in surgical planning.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study with three landmark datasets (Ghent University, preprint).
papers.datasets: ISBI 2015 cephalometric challenge (400 radiographs, 19 landmarks; four folds: two train, one calibration, one test; junior annotator labels); private Canine Hip Dysplasia set (472 radiographs: 207 train, 103 calibration, 162 test; 12 landmarks); a 3D mandibular molar landmark dataset.
papers.preprocessing: Standard splits with a dedicated calibration set.
papers.modelDetails: Model-agnostic multi-output conformal prediction for landmark regions (including M-R2CCP and M-R2C2R methods), applied to SpatialConfigurationNet with learned aleatoric uncertainty and a one-hot heatmap classification approach (2D UNet with ResNet-34; 3D UNet with EfficientNet-B0 and MedicalNet weights).
papers.training: SCN trained as in Payer et al. (2020); other settings in paper.
papers.evaluation: Empirical coverage at nominal levels and size of prediction regions.
papers.baselines: Normality-based uncertainty (Gaussian) and other UQ methods.
papers.results: Conformal regions achieved valid coverage where normality-based methods systematically underestimated total uncertainty, with informative region sizes in 2D and 3D.

papers.title: Federated Conformal Predictors for Distributed Uncertainty Quantification
papers.authors: Charles Lu, Yaodong Yu, Sai Praneeth Karimireddy, Michael I. Jordan, Ramesh Raskar
papers.aim: Conformal prediction is emerging as a popular paradigm for providing rigorous uncertainty quantification in machine learning since it can be easily applied as a post-processing step to already trained models. In this paper, we extend conformal prediction to the federated learning setting.
papers.method: The main challenge we face is data heterogeneity across the clients - this violates the fundamental tenet of exchangeability required for conformal prediction. We propose a weaker notion of partial exchangeability, better suited to the FL setting, and use it to develop the Federated Conformal Prediction (FCP) framework. We show FCP enjoys rigorous theoretical guarantees and excellent empirical performance on several computer vision and medical imaging datasets.
papers.result: Our results demonstrate a practical approach to incorporating meaningful uncertainty quantification in distributed and heterogeneous environments. We provide code used in our experiments https://github.com/clu5/federated-conformal.
papers.gap: Coverage only on average across sites; per-site guarantees weaker; 2D benchmarks.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: FCP extends conformal prediction to federated learning: each hospital computes calibration scores locally and shares only a compressed summary, from which a global threshold is estimated with a guarantee that holds under a weaker form of exchangeability suited to heterogeneous sites. Tested on vision and medical datasets with deliberately heterogeneous clients. It offers a way to calibrate escalation thresholds across hospitals without sharing data.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological and empirical study (MIT, UC Berkeley; ICML 2023).
papers.datasets: FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and MedMNIST (DermaMNIST, PathMNIST, TissueMNIST) partitioned by class across clients; Fitzpatrick17K (114 skin conditions in 3 categories) partitioned by disease category or skin type.
papers.preprocessing: Clients created with label or skin-type heterogeneity.
papers.modelDetails: Federated Conformal Prediction (FCP): train a federated model (e.g. TCT), compute conformal scores on each client's validation data, send sketches of scores, estimate the global quantile by distributed quantile estimation; theory based on partial exchangeability.
papers.training: Federated optimisation details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Empirical coverage and set size; selective classification on skin lesions; ablations of score function and quantile method.
papers.baselines: Local conformal prediction and centralised conformal prediction.
papers.results: FCP achieved coverage close to the target with set sizes similar to centralised conformal prediction under heterogeneity, and supported selective classification.

papers.title: Empirical Validation of Conformal Prediction for Trustworthy Skin Lesions Classification
papers.authors: Jamil Fayyad, Shadi Alijani, Homayoun Najjaran
papers.aim: Background and objective: Uncertainty quantification is a pivotal field that contributes to realizing reliable and robust systems. It becomes instrumental in fortifying safe decisions by providing complementary information, particularly within high-risk applications. existing studies have explored various methods that often operate under specific assumptions or necessitate substantial modifications to the network architecture to effectively account for uncertainties.
papers.method: The objective of this paper is to study Conformal Prediction, an emerging distribution-free uncertainty quantification technique, and provide a comprehensive understanding of the advantages and limitations inherent in various methods within the medical imaging field. Methods: In this study, we developed Conformal Prediction, Monte Carlo Dropout, and Evidential Deep Learning approaches to assess uncertainty quantification in deep neural networks. The effectiveness of these methods is evaluated using three public medical imaging datasets focused on detecting pigmented skin lesions and blood cell types. Results: The experimental results demonstrate a significant enhancement in uncertainty quantification with the utilization of the Conformal Prediction method, surpassing the performance of the other two methods. Furthermore, the results present insights into the effectiveness of each uncertainty method in handling Out-of-Distribution samples from domain-shifted datasets.
papers.result: Our code is available at: Conclusions: Our conclusion highlights a robust and consistent performance of conformal prediction across diverse testing conditions. This positions it as the preferred choice for decision-making in safety-critical applications.
papers.gap: Classification only; no decision or deferral evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors applied conformal prediction, Monte Carlo dropout and evidential learning to skin-lesion and blood-cell classifiers and compared how well each quantified uncertainty when test data were clean, noisy or shifted. Conformal prediction kept its coverage most consistently. It is an empirical argument for conformal methods in medical imaging.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical comparison study (University of British Columbia, University of Victoria; preprint).
papers.datasets: HAM10000 (>10,000 images, 7 classes), Dermofit (~1,200 images, 7 classes) and a blood-cell microscopy set (~17,000 images, 8 classes); split 50/20/30 with a reserved calibration portion.
papers.preprocessing: Class balancing by augmentation (flips, rotations, crops).
papers.modelDetails: Conformal prediction (several score functions) compared with Monte Carlo dropout and evidential deep learning on CNN classifiers.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Coverage, set size, accuracy under in-distribution, noisy and shifted test conditions.
papers.baselines: MC dropout, evidential deep learning.
papers.results: Conformal prediction gave robust and consistent coverage across testing conditions, whereas the other methods were less reliable under shift.

papers.title: Robust Conformal Volume Estimation in 3D Medical Images
papers.authors: Benjamin Lambert, Florence Forbes, Senan Doyle, Michel Dojat
papers.aim: Volumetry is one of the principal downstream applications of 3D medical image segmentation, for example, to detect abnormal tissue growth or for surgery planning. Conformal Prediction is a promising framework for uncertainty quantification, providing calibrated predictive intervals associated with automatic volume measurements.
papers.method: However, this methodology is based on the hypothesis that calibration and test samples are exchangeable, an assumption that is in practice often violated in medical image applications. A weighted formulation of Conformal Prediction can be framed to mitigate this issue, but its empirical investigation in the medical domain is still lacking. A potential reason is that it relies on the estimation of the density ratio between the calibration and test distributions, which is likely to be intractable in scenarios involving high-dimensional data. To circumvent this, we propose an efficient approach for density ratio estimation relying on the compressed latent representations generated by the segmentation model.
papers.result: Our experiments demonstrate the efficiency of our approach to reduce the coverage error in the presence of covariate shifts, in both synthetic and real-world settings. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/benolmbrt/wcp_miccai
papers.gap: Volume only, not voxel-level or decision-level; shift types limited.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Density-ratio estimates can be unstable with few calibration cases.
papers.methodologyDetail: Conformal prediction gives a volume interval around a segmented tumour, but its guarantee breaks when test scans differ from calibration scans. The authors weight calibration samples by how similar they are to the test case, estimating that similarity cheaply from the segmentation network's internal features, and tested it on synthetic shifts and on glioblastoma versus meningioma shift in BraTS. It is directly relevant to keeping tumour-volume uncertainty valid on Sri Lankan scans that differ from training data.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study with synthetic and real brain-tumour experiments (Univ. Grenoble Alpes, Inria, Pixyl; MICCAI 2024).
papers.datasets: Synthetic: 4,000 32x32x32 volumes of spheres; 3,000 high-SNR in-distribution (1,000 train, 1,000 calibration, 1,000 ID test) and 1,000 low-SNR shifted test. Real: BraTS 2023 glioblastoma and meningioma subjects (T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR) with necrosis, oedema and enhancing labels.
papers.preprocessing: Calibration and test drawn from different distributions to create covariate shift (SNR in synthetic data; tumour type in real data).
papers.modelDetails: Weighted conformal prediction for volume prediction intervals, with density-ratio estimation computed from the segmentation model's compressed latent representations.
papers.training: Segmentation network trained per experiment (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Coverage error of volume prediction intervals and interval width under shift.
papers.baselines: Standard split conformal prediction.
papers.results: Reduced coverage error under covariate shift in both synthetic and real brain-tumour settings while keeping useful interval widths.

papers.title: A conformalized learning of a prediction set with applications to medical imaging classification
papers.authors: Roy Hirsch, Jacob Goldberger
papers.aim: Medical imaging classifiers can achieve high predictive accuracy, but quantifying their uncertainty remains an unresolved challenge, which prevents their deployment in medical clinics. We present an algorithm that can modify any classifier to produce a prediction set containing the true label with a user-specified probability, such as 90%.
papers.method: We train a network to predict an instance-based version of the Conformal Prediction threshold. The threshold is then conformalized to ensure the required coverage.
papers.result: We applied the proposed algorithm to several standard medical imaging classification datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms current approaches in terms of smaller average size of the prediction set while maintaining the desired coverage.
papers.gap: Classification only; no deferral or clinical study.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: Most conformal classifiers use one threshold for all cases. Here a small network learns a case-specific threshold and conformal calibration then adjusts it so the coverage guarantee still holds, producing tighter sets of candidate diagnoses. Smaller sets mean fewer options for the clinician to check while keeping the guarantee.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on medical image classification datasets (Bar-Ilan University).
papers.datasets: Several standard medical imaging classification datasets (MedMNIST-type collections).
papers.preprocessing: Standard train/validation/calibration/test splits.
papers.modelDetails: A network predicts an instance-specific conformal threshold (rather than a single global threshold as in APS/RAPS); the learned threshold is then conformalised to guarantee coverage.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Empirical coverage at a target (e.g. 90%) and average prediction-set size.
papers.baselines: APS, RAPS and other conformal methods.
papers.results: Smaller average prediction sets than current approaches while maintaining the required coverage.

papers.title: Three Applications of Conformal Prediction for Rating Breast Density in Mammography
papers.authors: Charles Lu, Ken Chang, Praveer Singh, Jayashree Kalpathy-Cramer
papers.aim: Breast cancer is the most common cancers and early detection from mammography screening is crucial in improving patient outcomes. Assessing mammographic breast density is clinically important as the denser breasts have higher risk and are more likely to occlude tumors.
papers.method: Manual assessment by experts is both time-consuming and subject to inter-rater variability. As such, there has been increased interest in the development of deep learning methods for mammographic breast density assessment. Despite deep learning having demonstrated impressive performance in several prediction tasks for applications in mammography, clinical deployment of deep learning systems in still relatively rare; historically, mammography Computer-Aided Diagnoses (CAD) have over-promised and failed to deliver. This is in part due to the inability to intuitively quantify uncertainty of the algorithm for the clinician, which would greatly enhance usability. Conformal prediction is well suited to increase reliably and trust in deep learning tools but they lack realistic evaluations on medical datasets.
papers.result: In this paper, we present a detailed analysis of three possible applications of conformal prediction applied to medical imaging tasks: distribution shift characterization, prediction quality improvement, and subgroup fairness analysis. Our results show the potential of distribution-free uncertainty quantification techniques to enhance trust on AI algorithms and expedite their translation to usage.
papers.gap: Ordinal task with inter-rater variability; no workload or outcome evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: A breast-density model was trained on a large multi-site screening trial and tested internally and on an external hospital set. Conformal prediction sets were used in three ways: as a signal that incoming data had shifted, as calibrated uncertainty for each case, and as a basis for sending ambiguous cases to a radiologist. It illustrates conformal sets as an operational monitoring and triage tool.
papers.studyDesign: Applied methodological study with internal and external data (MGH / Harvard; ICML workshop preprint).
papers.datasets: DMIST: 108,230 mammograms from 33 sites read by 92 radiologists (60/10/30 split); external MGH set of 8,603 mammograms (IRB approved); BI-RADS density in four categories.
papers.preprocessing: Largest connected component kept to remove burnt-in artefacts; intensities scaled to [0,1]; vertical flip augmentation; ImageNet initialisation; class-weighted cross-entropy.
papers.modelDetails: Deep breast-density classifier with conformal prediction sets used for three applications: detecting distribution shift, quantifying uncertainty under shift, and identifying cases for review or abstention.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Linearly weighted Cohen's kappa; coverage and set size internally and externally.
papers.baselines: Softmax confidence.
papers.results: Conformal set size increased under distribution shift and flagged uncertain cases, demonstrating practical uses for monitoring and selective review.

papers.title: Quantifying Volumetric Risk: Class-Aware Asymmetric Weighted Conformal Prediction for 3D Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Shadi Alijani, Fereshteh Aghaee Meibodi, Homayoun Najjaran
papers.aim: Reliable volumetric segmentation is critical for clinical diagnostics, yet foundation models such as MedSAM remain deterministic and lack calibrated uncertainty under distribution shift. Existing conformal prediction methods offer statistical guarantees but are frequently applied in 2D and assume symmetric error distributions, so they do not capture the class-specific biases that arise in 3D multi-class segmentation.
papers.method: We propose Class-Aware Asymmetric Weighted Conformal Prediction (CA-WCP), which combines latent-space density-ratio weighting for covariate shift with directional quantiles for the lower and upper volume bounds, and scales each bound by a class-specific asymmetry factor derived from validation-set false-positive and false-negative rates. We prove that CA-WCP retains the weighted-exchangeability marginal coverage guarantee for every class, and we evaluate it on 3D brain tumor segmentation (BraTS 2020) and on a synthetic multi-organ CT benchmark constructed under covariate shift.
papers.result: On both benchmarks the 95\% Clopper--Pearson interval for the observed coverage of CA-WCP contains the nominal 90\% level for every semantic class, while interval width is reduced by 8--14\% relative to symmetric weighted conformal prediction. We further encode the calibrated intervals into structured prompts for a multimodal large language model to produce uncertainty-conditioned radiology reports, linking distribution-shift-aware uncertainty quantification to interpretable clinical communication.
papers.gap: Volumes only; small calibration sets; no clinical decision link.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The method produces lower and upper volume estimates for each tumour subregion from a three-headed segmentation model, then calibrates them with conformal prediction that (i) reweights calibration cases to match a shifted test distribution and (ii) widens each side of the interval according to whether that class tends to be over- or under-segmented. It keeps a per-class coverage guarantee and was evaluated on BraTS and a shifted CT benchmark. Asymmetric, class-specific uncertainty mirrors the asymmetric clinical costs in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study with proof and two benchmarks (University of Victoria, preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2020 (multi-class: necrotic core, oedema, enhancing tumour); synthetic multi-organ CT benchmark built under covariate shift; latent-feature calibration/test sets of 66 and 73 cases for density-ratio estimation.
papers.preprocessing: Multi-modal MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR); L2-normalised global-average-pooled TinyViT features; seed 42.
papers.modelDetails: MedSAM (TinyViT encoder) adapted with a TriadNet-style three-head decoder (lower, mean, upper volume) trained with Tversky losses (alpha/beta 0.3/0.7, 0.5/0.5, 0.7/0.3; thresholds 0.7/0.5/0.3); CA-WCP post-hoc wrapper combining latent density-ratio weighting, directional quantiles for lower/upper bounds and class-specific asymmetry factors from validation false-positive and false-negative rates.
papers.training: 200 epochs, Adam lr 3e-5 cosine decay, batch 2; logistic classifier for density ratio evaluated by 20-fold CV (ROC-AUC 0.78).
papers.evaluation: Per-class coverage of 90% volume intervals with Clopper-Pearson 95% CIs; interval width.
papers.baselines: Standard and weighted conformal prediction without class asymmetry.
papers.results: For every class on both benchmarks the 95% CI of observed coverage contained the nominal 90%, with narrower or more informative intervals than baselines.
papers.statistics: Clopper-Pearson intervals; theoretical guarantee of weighted-exchangeability coverage per class.

papers.title: Conformal Semantic Image Segmentation: Post-hoc Quantification of Predictive Uncertainty
papers.authors: Luca Mossina, Joseba Dalmau, Léo andéol
papers.aim: We propose a post-hoc, computationally lightweight method to quantify predictive uncertainty in semantic image segmentation. Our approach uses conformal prediction to generate statistically valid prediction sets that are guaranteed to include the ground-truth segmentation mask at a predefined confidence level.
papers.result: We introduce a novel visualization technique of conformalized predictions based on heatmaps, and provide metrics to assess their empirical validity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on well-known benchmark datasets and image segmentation prediction models, and conclude with practical insights.
papers.gap: Natural-image benchmarks; no medical evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors wrap any trained segmentation model with conformal risk control so that, for each pixel, a set of plausible classes is returned with a guaranteed error level, and visualise the result as heatmaps. When the required risk is too strict for the model, sets become uninformative, which is itself a warning that the model is not good enough. The idea transfers to tumour segmentation masks.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study on general segmentation benchmarks (IRT Saint Exupéry, Toulouse; CVPR workshop).
papers.datasets: Cityscapes (19 classes), ADE20K (150 classes), LoveDA (7 classes); validation data split into calibration and test, repeated shuffles.
papers.preprocessing: Pre-trained MMSegmentation models.
papers.modelDetails: Post-hoc conformal risk control for semantic segmentation producing per-pixel class sets, with binary-threshold and miscoverage losses; heatmap visualisation of conformalised predictions; PSPNet and SegFormer backbones.
papers.training: No training; pre-trained weights.
papers.evaluation: Empirical risk vs target alpha and activation ratio.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (validity check).
papers.results: Empirical risk matched targets across datasets; overly strict risk targets produced near-full sets, signalling an inadequate model.

papers.title: Anatomically-aware conformal prediction for medical image segmentation with random walks
papers.authors: Mélanie Gaillochet, Christian Desrosiers, Hervé Lombaert
papers.aim: The reliable deployment of deep learning in medical imaging requires uncertainty quantification that provides rigorous error guarantees while remaining anatomically meaningful. Conformal prediction (CP) is a powerful distribution-free framework for constructing statistically valid prediction intervals.
papers.method: However, standard applications in segmentation often ignore anatomical context, resulting in fragmented, spatially incoherent, and over-segmented prediction sets that limit clinical utility. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes Random-Walk Conformal Prediction (RW-CP), a model-agnostic framework which can be added on top of any segmentation method. RW-CP enforces spatial coherence to generate anatomically valid sets. Our method constructs a k-nearest neighbour graph from pre-trained vision foundation model features and applies a random walk to diffuse uncertainty. The random walk diffusion regularizes the non-conformity scores, making the prediction sets less sensitive to the conformal calibration parameter $λ$, ensuring more stable and continuous anatomical boundaries.
papers.result: RW-CP maintains rigorous marginal coverage while significantly improving segmentation quality. Evaluations on multi-modal public datasets show improvements of up to $35.4\%$ compared to standard CP baselines, given an allowable error rate of $α=0.1$.
papers.gap: No brain-tumour-specific or clinical evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: Standard conformal segmentation adds scattered pixels to reach coverage. RW-CP smooths the uncertainty scores over a graph built from foundation-model features before calibration, so the guaranteed set grows as an anatomically sensible region. It improves the usefulness of guaranteed segmentation uncertainty for clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study on public medical segmentation datasets (ÉTS Montréal, Polytechnique Montréal; preprint).
papers.datasets: Multi-modal public medical segmentation datasets (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Pre-trained vision foundation-model features used to build a k-nearest-neighbour graph over pixels.
papers.modelDetails: Random-Walk Conformal Prediction (RW-CP): model-agnostic conformal risk control in which non-conformity scores are diffused by a random walk on a feature graph so prediction sets are spatially coherent and anatomically plausible.
papers.training: No training of the segmenter required.
papers.evaluation: Marginal coverage/risk and segmentation quality of prediction sets; sensitivity to the calibration parameter.
papers.baselines: Standard conformal risk control for segmentation.
papers.results: Maintained marginal coverage while significantly improving the coherence and quality of prediction sets and stability with respect to the calibration parameter.

papers.title: Risk-Sensitive Conformal Prediction for Catheter Placement Detection in Chest X-rays
papers.authors: Long Hui
papers.aim: This paper presents a novel approach to catheter and line position detection in chest X-rays, combining multi-task learning with risk-sensitive conformal prediction to address critical clinical requirements. Our model simultaneously performs classification, segmentation, and landmark detection, leveraging the synergistic relationship between these tasks to improve overall performance.
papers.method: We further enhance clinical reliability through risk-sensitive conformal prediction, which provides statistically guaranteed prediction sets with higher reliability for clinically critical findings. Experimental results demonstrate excellent performance with 90.68\% overall empirical coverage and 99.29\% coverage for critical conditions, while maintaining remarkable precision in prediction sets.
papers.result: Most importantly, our risk-sensitive approach achieves zero high-risk mispredictions (cases where the system dangerously declares problematic tubes as confidently normal), making the system particularly suitable for clinical deployment. This work offers both accurate predictions and reliably quantified uncertainty -- essential features for life-critical medical applications.
papers.gap: Single-author preprint; no external validation or clinician study.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: A multi-task model locates tubes and lines on chest X-rays and classifies their position, and conformal prediction is applied with a stricter error budget for dangerous categories than for benign ones, so the system never declares a misplaced tube confidently normal. Using different guarantees for different error types is the conformal counterpart of the asymmetric clinical costs in this study's escalation rule.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on a public competition dataset (independent researcher, preprint).
papers.datasets: RANZCR CLiP: >30,000 chest X-rays with 11 categories of endotracheal tube, nasogastric tube, central venous catheter and Swan-Ganz position (normal, borderline, abnormal, incompletely imaged); pixel masks and landmark annotations for a subset.
papers.preprocessing: Multi-label targets; segmentation masks and landmarks used as auxiliary supervision.
papers.modelDetails: Multi-task network for classification, segmentation and landmark detection; risk-sensitive conformal prediction giving prediction sets with stricter guarantees for clinically critical (abnormal) findings.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Classification performance, coverage by risk class, set size, number of high-risk mispredictions (abnormal declared confidently normal).
papers.baselines: Standard conformal prediction and the multi-task model without conformal sets.
papers.results: High accuracy for critical conditions with precise prediction sets and zero high-risk mispredictions.

papers.title: Controlling False Positives in Image Segmentation via Conformal Prediction
papers.authors: Luca Mossina, Corentin Friedrich
papers.aim: Reliable semantic segmentation is essential for clinical decision making, yet deep models rarely provide explicit statistical guarantees on their errors. We introduce a simple post-hoc framework that constructs confidence masks with distribution-free, image-level control of false-positive predictions.
papers.method: Given any pretrained segmentation model, we define a nested family of shrunken masks obtained either by increasing the score threshold or by applying morphological erosion. A labeled calibration set is used to select a single shrink parameter via conformal prediction, ensuring that, for new images that are exchangeable with the calibration data, the proportion of false positives retained in the confidence mask stays below a user-specified tolerance with high probability. The method is model-agnostic, requires no retraining, and provides finite-sample guarantees regardless of the underlying predictor. Experiments on a polyp-segmentation benchmark demonstrate target-level empirical validity.
papers.result: Our framework enables practical, risk-aware segmentation in settings where over-segmentation can have clinical consequences. Code at https://github.com/deel-ai-papers/conseco.
papers.gap: Controls false positives only; 2D polyps.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: When over-segmentation is harmful, the method returns a smaller 'confidence mask' inside the predicted mask, calibrated so that, for most images, almost no false-positive pixels remain. It works with any segmentation model without retraining. For surgical planning, a guaranteed-inside region is a useful complement to a guaranteed-outside region.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study on a medical segmentation benchmark (IRT Saint Exupéry, preprint).
papers.datasets: Polyps dataset collection with pretrained PraNet; each run splits test data in half (250 calibration images); 10 seeds.
papers.preprocessing: None beyond pre-trained model outputs.
papers.modelDetails: Conformal procedure that shrinks predicted masks (higher sigmoid threshold or morphological erosion) to give confidence masks in which the proportion of accepted false-positive pixels stays below a tolerance with probability 1-alpha.
papers.training: No retraining.
papers.evaluation: Empirical validity, contraction ratio (retained area) and accepted true-positive fraction at 1-alpha = 0.90 and tolerances 0.1/0.01/0.001.
papers.baselines: Uncalibrated threshold at 0.5.
papers.results: Both conformal procedures achieved empirical validity close to the nominal 90% across tolerances, at the cost of shrinking masks.

papers.title: COMPASS: Robust Feature Conformal Prediction for Medical Segmentation Metrics
papers.authors: Matt Y. Cheung, Ashok Veeraraghavan, Guha Balakrishnan
papers.aim: In clinical applications, the utility of segmentation models is often based on the accuracy of derived downstream metrics such as organ size, rather than by the pixel-level accuracy of the segmentation masks themselves. Thus, uncertainty quantification for such metrics is crucial for decision-making.
papers.method: Conformal prediction (CP) is a popular framework to derive such principled uncertainty guarantees, but applying CP naively to the final scalar metric is inefficient because it treats the complex, non-linear segmentation-to-metric pipeline as a black box. We introduce COMPASS, a practical framework that generates efficient, metric-based CP intervals for image segmentation models by leveraging the inductive biases of their underlying deep neural networks. COMPASS performs calibration directly in the model's representation space by perturbing intermediate features along low-dimensional subspaces maximally sensitive to the target metric. We prove that COMPASS achieves valid marginal coverage under the assumption of exchangeability. Empirically, we demonstrate that COMPASS produces significantly tighter intervals than traditional CP baselines on four medical image segmentation tasks for area estimation of skin lesions and anatomical structures.
papers.result: Furthermore, we show that leveraging learned internal features to estimate importance weights allows COMPASS to also recover target coverage under covariate shifts. COMPASS paves the way for practical, metric-based uncertainty quantification for medical image segmentation.
papers.gap: No clinical decision evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of treating segmentation plus measurement as a black box, COMPASS perturbs the network's internal features in the directions that most change the measurement and calibrates those perturbations, giving tighter guaranteed intervals for quantities such as tumour volume. Feature-based weights restore coverage under shift. It is relevant for reporting guaranteed uncertainty on tumour measurements.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study (Rice University, preprint).
papers.datasets: Medical segmentation tasks where a downstream metric (e.g. organ or lesion size) matters; multiple public datasets.
papers.preprocessing: Not detailed.
papers.modelDetails: COMPASS: conformal prediction for segmentation-derived metrics performed in the network's feature space by perturbing intermediate features along low-dimensional directions most sensitive to the metric; importance weights from internal features handle covariate shift.
papers.training: Uses trained segmentation models.
papers.evaluation: Coverage and interval width for metric prediction intervals, including under covariate shift.
papers.baselines: Naive conformal prediction on the scalar metric and other CP variants.
papers.results: Valid marginal coverage with tighter intervals than black-box conformal methods; recovered target coverage under covariate shift with learned weights.

papers.title: Multi-pathology Chest X-ray Classification with Rejection Mechanisms
papers.authors: Yehudit Aperstein, Amit Tzahar, Alon Gottlib, Tal Verber, Ravit Shagan Damti, Alexander Apartsin
papers.aim: Overconfidence in deep learning models poses a significant risk in high-stakes medical imaging tasks, particularly in multi-label classification of chest X-rays, where multiple co-occurring pathologies must be detected simultaneously. This study introduces an uncertainty-aware framework for chest X-ray diagnosis based on a DenseNet-121 backbone, enhanced with two selective prediction mechanisms: entropy-based rejection and confidence interval-based rejection.
papers.method: Both methods enable the model to abstain from uncertain predictions, improving reliability by deferring ambiguous cases to clinical experts. A quantile-based calibration procedure is employed to tune rejection thresholds using either global or class-specific strategies.
papers.result: Experiments conducted on three large public datasets (PadChest, NIH ChestX-ray14, and MIMIC-CXR) demonstrate that selective rejection improves the trade-off between diagnostic accuracy and coverage, with entropy-based rejection yielding the highest average AUC across all pathologies. These results support the integration of selective prediction into AI-assisted diagnostic workflows, providing a practical step toward safer, uncertainty-aware deployment of deep learning in clinical settings.
papers.gap: No guaranteed error rate, no cost weighting, no clinician study.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The classifier abstains on a chest X-ray finding when its prediction entropy or its confidence interval indicates uncertainty, with thresholds tuned on held-out data either for all classes together or per class. Across three large public datasets, rejecting a fraction of uncertain cases raised accuracy on the rest. It is a simple multi-label selective-prediction baseline.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on public chest X-ray datasets (Afeka College, HIT Holon; preprint).
papers.datasets: 122,830 chest X-rays aggregated from PadChest, NIH ChestX-ray14 and MIMIC-CXR; four labels (cardiomegaly, effusion, oedema, consolidation); 3,869 (3.15%) multi-pathology images.
papers.preprocessing: Image-level multi-label targets; separate partition for tuning rejection thresholds.
papers.modelDetails: DenseNet-121 multi-label classifier with entropy-based rejection and confidence-interval-based rejection; quantile-based calibration of thresholds globally or per class.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy/F1 vs rejection rate (coverage) per pathology.
papers.baselines: No rejection.
papers.results: Selective rejection improved the trade-off between diagnostic accuracy and coverage on all three datasets; class-specific thresholds handled imbalance.

papers.title: Uncovering Overconfident Failures in CXR Models via Augmentation-Sensitivity Risk Scoring
papers.authors: Han-Jay Shu, Wei-Ning Chiu, Shun-Ting Chang, Meng-Ping Huang, Takeshi Tohyama, Ahram Han, Po-Chih Kuo
papers.aim: Deep learning models achieve strong performance in chest radiograph (CXR) interpretation, yet fairness and reliability concerns persist. Models often show uneven accuracy across patient subgroups, leading to hidden failures not reflected in aggregate metrics.
papers.method: Existing error detection approaches -- based on confidence calibration or out-of-distribution (OOD) detection -- struggle with subtle within-distribution errors, while image- and representation-level consistency-based methods remain underexplored in medical imaging. We propose an augmentation-sensitivity risk scoring (ASRS) framework to identify error-prone CXR cases. ASRS applies clinically plausible rotations ($\pm 15^\circ$/$\pm 30^\circ$) and measures embedding shifts with the RAD-DINO encoder.
papers.result: Sensitivity scores stratify samples into stability quartiles, where highly sensitive cases show substantially lower recall ($-0.2$ to $-0.3$) despite high AUROC and confidence. ASRS provides a label-free means for selective prediction and clinician review, improving fairness and safety in medical AI.
papers.gap: Only rotation perturbations; no deferral policy evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: ASRS measures how much a foundation encoder's representation of an X-ray changes when the image is slightly rotated; images whose representation is unstable are flagged as risky, without needing labels. On MIMIC-CXR, the most unstable quarter of cases had markedly worse recall even when models were confident, revealing failures that softmax confidence misses. Consistency under perturbation is another signal the escalation rule could use.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective method study on MIMIC-CXR (National Tsing Hua University, NTU, MIT; preprint).
papers.datasets: MIMIC-CXR-JPG frontal views with patient-level split: 30,238 train, 10,079 validation, 10,081 test patients (131,283/43,335 train/val images); tasks cardiomegaly, oedema, pleural effusion, pneumothorax.
papers.preprocessing: Rotations of +-15 and +-30 degrees applied to each image.
papers.modelDetails: Augmentation-Sensitivity Risk Scoring (ASRS): label-free score from the L2 shift of RAD-DINO embeddings under rotation; validation-derived quartiles stratify test cases into four groups; multiple classifier architectures evaluated per group.
papers.training: Classifiers trained on the training split (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: AUROC, recall, confidence and subgroup fairness by ASRS quartile.
papers.baselines: Confidence-based and OOD-based error detection.
papers.results: Highly sensitive cases had much lower recall (-0.2 to -0.3) despite high AUROC and confidence, exposing hidden overconfident failures.

papers.title: Towards Trustworthy AI for Glioma Diagnosis: A Task-Aware Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification
papers.authors: Gonzalo Esteban Mosquera Rojas, Sebastian R. van der Voort, Carolin M. Pirkl, Sandeep Kaushik, Marion Smits, Stefan Klein
papers.aim: Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is a key requirement for trustworthy AI in high-stakes medical image analysis. In this work, we evaluate UQ in a multi-task Deep Learning framework for MRI-based glioma diagnosis that performs tumor segmentation and predicts IDH mutation status, 1p/19q co-deletion status, and tumor grade.
papers.method: Monte Carlo Dropout (MCD) is used for a detailed task-aware analysis of predictive, aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainty. We assess MC sample convergence, calibration, error detection, selective prediction, associations with segmentation performance, and the effect of voxel-wise uncertainty aggregation on case-level reliability. We also compare MCD with Deep Ensembles (DE) and Monte Carlo Deep Ensembles (MCDE), examine interactions between segmentation quality and classification, and evaluate a composite trust score integrating segmentation and classification uncertainty. Across tasks, uncertainty estimates supported meaningful error detection, while calibration depended on the dropout rate, with moderate rates yielding the most reliable probabilities. Uncertainty decomposition provided task-dependent interpretability but did not consistently improve error detection over predictive uncertainty alone. DE and MCDE showed comparable operational utility, with no method consistently dominating across tasks and metrics.
papers.result: The composite trust score did not consistently outperform classification uncertainty for selective prediction. Overall, our results provide a task-aware evaluation strategy and practical guidance for the development of trustworthy AI for glioma diagnosis.
papers.gap: Single UQ family; no clinician deferral or cost analysis.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a multi-task network that segments gliomas and predicts IDH, 1p/19q and grade, the authors examined Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty task by task, separating aleatoric and epistemic parts, checking how many samples are needed, and testing whether uncertainty helps select reliable predictions. Combining tasks into one trust score did not beat simple classification uncertainty. This is the most directly relevant glioma UQ evaluation for the MRI agent.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective task-aware evaluation of uncertainty quantification (Erasmus MC, Amsterdam UMC, GE HealthCare; MELBA 2026).
papers.datasets: Pre-operative glioma MRI (T1w, T1wCE, T2w, FLAIR) from multi-centre public and institutional cohorts used for multi-task segmentation, IDH, 1p/19q and grade (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Pre-processing module (registration, skull stripping, normalisation; Appendix A.1).
papers.modelDetails: Multi-task encoder-decoder (U-Net-based) with segmentation as auxiliary task and fully connected classification heads; Monte Carlo dropout giving predictive, aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty; composite trust score combining tasks.
papers.training: Details in Appendix A.2; MC sample convergence assessed.
papers.evaluation: Uncertainty-error relationships per task, MC sample convergence, selective prediction (risk-coverage) for classification tasks.
papers.baselines: Classification uncertainty alone vs composite trust score; other UQ methods.
papers.results: Task-aware uncertainty behaved differently across tasks; the composite trust score did not consistently outperform classification uncertainty for selective prediction.

papers.title: AT-CXR: Uncertainty-Aware Agentic Triage for Chest X-rays
papers.authors: Xueyang Li, Mingze Jiang, Gelei Xu, Jun Xia, Mengzhao Jia, Danny Chen, Yiyu Shi
papers.aim: Agentic AI is advancing rapidly, yet truly autonomous medical-imaging triage, where a system decides when to stop, escalate, or defer under real constraints, remains relatively underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce AT-CXR, an uncertainty-aware agent for chest X-rays.
papers.method: The system estimates per-case confidence and distributional fit, then follows a stepwise policy to issue an automated decision or abstain with a suggested label for human intervention. We evaluate two router designs that share the same inputs and actions: a deterministic rule-based router and an LLM-decided router. Across five-fold evaluation on a balanced subset of NIH ChestX-ray14 dataset, both variants outperform strong zero-shot vision-language models and state-of-the-art supervised classifiers, achieving higher full-coverage accuracy and superior selective-prediction performance, evidenced by a lower area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) and a lower error rate at high coverage, while operating with lower latency that meets practical clinical constraints.
papers.result: The two routers provide complementary operating points, enabling deployments to prioritize maximal throughput or maximal accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/XLIAaron/uncertainty-aware-cxr-agent.
papers.gap: Fixed heuristic thresholds without risk guarantees; small balanced dataset; one finding.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: AT-CXR is an end-to-end triage agent: each new radiograph is classified, its confidence and distance from the training distribution are computed, and a router applies a stepwise policy using extra checks such as test-time augmentation stability and expert-ensemble agreement before either issuing an automatic decision or abstaining with a suggested label for a human. Deterministic and LLM-based routers were compared on the same inputs. It is a compact precursor of this study's orchestrator for a single imaging task.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with five-fold evaluation on a public subset (University of Notre Dame, preprint).
papers.datasets: Class-balanced NIH ChestX-ray14 subset of 1,000 frontal radiographs (500 pulmonary oedema positive, 500 negative), publicly available on Kaggle.
papers.preprocessing: Rib and device suppression for a lung whiteness index; reference set for Mahalanobis statistics.
papers.modelDetails: AT-CXR agent: data ingestion via folder watcher; uncertainty check (classifier confidence and Mahalanobis distribution-fit score); guardrailed stepwise routing policy over tools (test-time augmentation stability, mixture-of-experts agreement) implemented as either a deterministic rule-based router or an LLM-decided router; outputs automated decision or abstention with suggested label, plus CAMs and lung whiteness index.
papers.training: Thresholds: confidence 0.60, OOD at 95th percentile Mahalanobis, TTA posterior SD 0.05, MoE agreement threshold; supervised classifiers with 5-fold stratified CV on one A10 GPU.
papers.evaluation: Full-coverage accuracy, AURC, selective accuracy, throughput.
papers.baselines: Zero-shot VLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5, MedGemma, CheXagent, MedRAX, LLaVA-Med) and supervised classifiers (RegNetY, ResNet-50, EfficientNet-V2, RexNet).
papers.results: Both routers outperformed VLMs and supervised classifiers in full-coverage accuracy and AURC; rule-based and LLM routers gave complementary operating points (throughput vs accuracy).

papers.title: Knowing When Not to Predict: Self Supervised Learning and Abstention for Safer DR Screening
papers.authors: Muskaan Chopra, Lorenz Sparrenberg, Jan H. Terheyden, Rafet Sifa
papers.aim: Self-supervised learning (SSL) is now a standard way to pretrain medical image models, but performance is still mostly judged by downstream accuracy. For safety-critical screening tasks such as diabetic retinopathy grading, this is not enough: a model must also know when its predictions are unreliable and defer uncertain cases for clinical review.
papers.method: In this work, we examine how the length of SSL pretraining influences calibrated confidence and confidence-based abstention. We evaluate multiple SSL checkpoints under a fixed fine-tuning protocol and assess calibrated confidence, coverage, selective accuracy, and selective macro-F1. Across datasets and data regimes, SSL pretraining improves selective prediction compared to training from scratch. Unlike prior SSL studies that primarily evaluate downstream accuracy or AUROC, we analyze how SSL pretraining duration influences confidence behavior under calibrated confidence-based abstention. However, once accuracy saturates, selective performance can still change markedly across checkpoints, and longer pretraining does not consistently improve reliability.
papers.result: These results underscore the importance of abstention-aware evaluation and suggest that pretraining length should be treated as an important reliability-related design choice rather than only a computational detail. Code is available at GitHub.
papers.gap: Retinal images, not MRI; no clinician deferral study.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors pretrained fundus image encoders with self-supervised learning, saved checkpoints at different training lengths, and fine-tuned each the same way to isolate how pretraining length affects calibrated confidence and abstention in diabetic retinopathy grading. Self-supervised pretraining helped models know when not to predict, and the amount of pretraining mattered. This supports hypothesis H3, which links self-supervised pretraining to calibration.
papers.studyDesign: Controlled experimental study (University of Bonn, Fraunhofer IAIS; preprint).
papers.datasets: EyePACS (35,000 unlabelled fundus images) for SSL; APTOS-19 (3,662 images, 5 DR grades) for fine-tuning and main evaluation; Messidor (1,200) and a 7-class fundus dataset for generalisation.
papers.preprocessing: Augmentations: random crop, flip, colour jitter, Gaussian blur, light Jigsaw perturbation.
papers.modelDetails: SSL pretraining (SiCoVa non-contrastive objective and a contrastive triplet baseline) of ResNet-50 or ViT-B/16 with checkpoints at different lengths; fixed fine-tuning, calibration and confidence-based abstention.
papers.training: Fixed downstream protocol; only the SSL checkpoint varied.
papers.evaluation: Calibration, coverage, selective accuracy and selective macro-F1 at ~70% coverage.
papers.baselines: Training from scratch.
papers.results: SSL pretraining improved selective prediction over scratch training; pretraining length changed calibrated confidence and abstention quality, so it should be treated as a reliability design choice.

papers.title: OpenMIBOOD: Open Medical Imaging Benchmarks for Out-Of-Distribution Detection
papers.authors: Max Gutbrod, David Rauber, Danilo Weber Nunes, Christoph Palm
papers.aim: The growing reliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) in critical domains such as healthcare demands robust mechanisms to ensure the trustworthiness of these systems, especially when faced with unexpected or anomalous inputs. This paper introduces the Open Medical Imaging Benchmarks for Out-Of-Distribution Detection (OpenMIBOOD), a comprehensive framework for evaluating out-of-distribution (OOD) detection methods specifically in medical imaging contexts.
papers.method: OpenMIBOOD includes three benchmarks from diverse medical domains, encompassing 14 datasets divided into covariate-shifted in-distribution, near-OOD, and far-OOD categories. We evaluate 24 post-hoc methods across these benchmarks, providing a standardized reference to advance the development and fair comparison of OOD detection methods. Results reveal that findings from broad-scale OOD benchmarks in natural image domains do not translate to medical applications, underscoring the critical need for such benchmarks in the medical field.
papers.result: By mitigating the risk of exposing AI models to inputs outside their training distribution, OpenMIBOOD aims to support the advancement of reliable and trustworthy AI systems in healthcare. The repository is available at https://github.com/remic-othr/OpenMIBOOD.
papers.gap: Detection only; not linked to deferral or clinical cost.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.limitations: Specific domains; corrigendum for two methods.
papers.methodologyDetail: OpenMIBOOD provides medical imaging benchmarks in which test data are either slightly shifted, close to but outside the training classes, or very different, and evaluates 24 post-hoc out-of-distribution detectors. The finding that natural-image rankings do not transfer means the novelty check in this study's escalation rule must be validated on medical data.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation and evaluation of OOD detection in medical imaging (OTH Regensburg; CVPR 2025, with corrigendum).
papers.datasets: Three medical imaging benchmarks across domains comprising 14 datasets split into covariate-shifted in-distribution, near-OOD and far-OOD sets.
papers.preprocessing: Benchmark definitions per domain.
papers.modelDetails: Evaluation of 24 post-hoc OOD detection methods grouped as classification-based (logits/probabilities), feature-based and hybrid.
papers.training: Classifiers trained on in-distribution data.
papers.evaluation: AUROC and related metrics for near- and far-OOD detection; ranking by near-OOD AUROC.
papers.baselines: All 24 methods compared.
papers.results: Method rankings differed from natural-image benchmarks; near-OOD detection in medical images remained hard, and feature-based methods often did better than logit-based ones.

papers.title: Out-of-distribution Detection in Medical Image Analysis: A survey
papers.authors: Zesheng Hong, Yubiao Yue, Yubin Chen, Lele Cong, Huanjie Lin, Yuanmei Luo, Mini Han Wang, Weidong Wang, Jialong Xu, Xiaoqi Yang, et al.
papers.aim: Computer-aided diagnostics has benefited from the development of deep learning-based computer vision techniques in these years. Traditional supervised deep learning methods assume that the test sample is drawn from the identical distribution as the training data.
papers.method: However, it is possible to encounter out-of-distribution samples in real-world clinical scenarios, which may cause silent failure in deep learning-based medical image analysis tasks. Recently, research has explored various out-of-distribution (OOD) detection situations and techniques to enable a trustworthy medical AI system. In this survey, we systematically review the recent advances in OOD detection in medical image analysis.
