We first explore several factors that may cause a distributional shift when using a deep-learning-based model in clinic scenarios, with three different types of distributional shift well defined on top of these factors.
papers.result: Then a framework is suggested to categorize and feature existing solutions, while the previous studies are reviewed based on the methodology taxonomy. Our discussion also includes evaluation protocols and metrics, as well as the challenge and a research direction lack of exploration.
papers.gap: No quantitative comparison.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The survey defines distribution shift types in medical imaging and maps published OOD detection methods into a taxonomy for classification and segmentation, noting which require retraining. It is a reference for choosing the novelty detector in this study's escalation rule, where Mahalanobis-type feature distances and ensembles are the most widely used post-hoc options.
papers.studyDesign: Survey (HKUST Guangzhou and clinical partners, preprint).
papers.datasets: Literature on out-of-distribution detection in medical image classification and segmentation.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Taxonomy of OOD detection: post-hoc feature processing (Mahalanobis, cosine, isolation forest, Gram matrix), learning-free UQ (MSP, entropy, temperature scaling, ODIN, MC dropout, TTA, deep ensembles), learning-based deterministic UQ (evidential learning, confidence branch), OOD-aware training (outlier exposure, reject bucket, Dirichlet prior networks), and unsupervised stand-alone detectors (autoencoders, VAEs, diffusion models).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Organises existing medical OOD methods by whether they reuse, retrain or train a separate model, for classification and segmentation, and identifies open problems including evaluation standards and subtle covariate shift.

papers.title: Contrastive Deep Encoding Enables Uncertainty-aware Machine-learning-assisted Histopathology
papers.authors: Nirhoshan Sivaroopan, Chamuditha Jayanga, Chalani Ekanayake, Hasindri Watawana, Jathurshan Pradeepkumar, Mithunjha Anandakumar, Ranga Rodrigo, Chamira U. S. Edussooriya, Dushan N. Wadduwage
papers.aim: Deep neural network models can learn clinically relevant features from millions of histopathology images. However generating high-quality annotations to train such models for each hospital, each cancer type, and each diagnostic task is prohibitively laborious.
papers.method: On the other hand, terabytes of training data -- while lacking reliable annotations -- are readily available in the public domain in some cases. In this work, we explore how these large datasets can be consciously utilized to pre-train deep networks to encode informative representations. We then fine-tune our pre-trained models on a fraction of annotated training data to perform specific downstream tasks. We show that our approach can reach the state-of-the-art (SOTA) for patch-level classification with only 1-10% randomly selected annotations compared to other SOTA approaches. Moreover, we propose an uncertainty-aware loss function, to quantify the model confidence during inference. Quantified uncertainty helps experts select the best instances to label for further training. Our uncertainty-aware labeling reaches the SOTA with significantly fewer annotations compared to random labeling.
papers.result: Last, we demonstrate how our pre-trained encoders can surpass current SOTA for whole-slide image classification with weak supervision. Our work lays the foundation for data and task-agnostic pre-trained deep networks with quantified uncertainty.
papers.gap: Not brain tumours; uncertainty not calibrated against clinical decisions.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team, partly based at the University of Moratuwa, pretrained histopathology encoders with contrastive self-supervised learning on large unlabelled public data, then fine-tuned with very few labels, adding an uncertainty-aware variant that flags uncertain patches for experts. The encoder also improved slide-level classification within a multiple-instance learning pipeline. It is a Sri Lankan contribution directly relevant to label-efficient, uncertainty-aware pathology.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on public histopathology datasets (University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka, and Harvard; preprint).
papers.datasets: Patch-level datasets PCAM and NCT-CRC (fine-tuning with 1-10% of labels); Camelyon-16 whole slides for weakly supervised classification.
papers.preprocessing: Large unannotated public histopathology data used for pretraining.
papers.modelDetails: SimCLRv2 self-supervised pretraining of a ResNet (chosen over MAE and SimCLRv1), fine-tuning with few labels and distillation; uncertainty-aware variant (UA-SimCLRv2) that outputs prediction uncertainty; pretrained encoder plugged into DTFD-MIL for WSIs.
papers.training: Three-stage SimCLRv2 procedure (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Patch accuracy, F1, AUC; WSI accuracy and AUC.
papers.baselines: ImageNet-initialised encoders; MIL methods (AB-MIL, DS-MIL, CLAM, TransMIL, DTFD-MIL).
papers.results: Reached state of the art for patch classification with only 1-10% of labels; uncertainty awareness helped identify unreliable predictions; encoder improved weakly supervised WSI classification.

papers.title: Selective Conformal Risk Control
papers.authors: Yunpeng Xu, Wenge Guo, Zhi Wei
papers.aim: Reliable uncertainty quantification is essential for deploying machine learning systems in high-stakes domains. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free coverage guarantees but often produces overly large prediction sets, limiting its practical utility.
papers.method: To address this issue, we propose \textit{Selective Conformal Risk Control} (SCRC), a unified framework that integrates conformal prediction with selective classification. The framework formulates uncertainty control as a two-stage problem: the first stage selects confident samples for prediction, and the second stage applies conformal risk control on the selected subset to construct calibrated prediction sets. We develop two algorithms under this framework. The first, SCRC-T, preserves exchangeability by computing thresholds jointly over calibration and test samples, offering exact finite-sample guarantees. The second, SCRC-I, is a calibration-only variant that provides PAC-style probabilistic guarantees while being more computational efficient.
papers.result: Experiments on two public datasets show that both methods achieve the target coverage and risk levels, with nearly identical performance, while SCRC-I exhibits slightly more conservative risk control but superior computational practicality. Our results demonstrate that selective conformal risk control offers an effective and efficient path toward compact, reliable uncertainty quantification.
papers.gap: No clinical evaluation; uniform costs.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: SCRC combines abstention with conformal guarantees: the model first abstains on low-confidence inputs and then provides prediction sets with controlled risk only for the inputs it keeps, handling the fact that selection breaks the usual exchangeability assumption. This two-stage structure (decide whether to act, then guarantee what is acted on) matches the escalation rule of this study.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological and empirical study (New Jersey Institute of Technology, preprint).
papers.datasets: Two public datasets (classification tasks) used to verify coverage and risk.
papers.preprocessing: Calibration and test splits.
papers.modelDetails: Selective Conformal Risk Control: stage one selects confident samples (selective classification), stage two applies conformal risk control only to accepted samples; SCRC-T (transductive, exact finite-sample guarantee) and SCRC-I (inductive, reuses calibration thresholds, computationally cheaper).
papers.training: Uses trained classifiers.
papers.evaluation: Coverage, selective risk, prediction-set size and computation time.
papers.baselines: Standard conformal prediction/risk control without selection.
papers.results: Both variants achieved target coverage and risk with nearly identical performance; SCRC-I was computationally more efficient; prediction sets on accepted cases were more compact.

papers.title: Robust Calibration with Multi-domain Temperature Scaling
papers.authors: Yaodong Yu, Stephen Bates, Yi Ma, Michael I. Jordan
papers.aim: Uncertainty quantification is essential for the reliable deployment of machine learning models to high-stakes application domains. Uncertainty quantification is all the more challenging when training distribution and test distribution are different, even the distribution shifts are mild.
papers.method: Despite the ubiquity of distribution shifts in real-world applications, existing uncertainty quantification approaches mainly study the in-distribution setting where the train and test distributions are the same. In this paper, we develop a systematic calibration model to handle distribution shifts by leveraging data from multiple domains.
papers.result: Our proposed method -- multi-domain temperature scaling -- uses the heterogeneity in the domains to improve calibration robustness under distribution shift. Through experiments on three benchmark data sets, we find our proposed method outperforms existing methods as measured on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution test sets.
papers.gap: Not medical imaging beyond cell microscopy; needs multiple training domains.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: Standard temperature scaling uses one temperature for all data. MD-TS uses data from several domains (for example several hospitals) to learn how the right temperature depends on the input, so it calibrates better on a new, unseen domain. Tested on corrupted images, cell microscopy and federated landmark data. It is the planned calibrator for multi-site data in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological and empirical study (UC Berkeley, preprint).
papers.datasets: ImageNet-C (76 domains: 15 corruptions x 5 severities plus clean), WILDS-RxRx1 (4 validation domains as in-distribution, 14 test domains as OOD), GLDv2 federated landmarks (500 training domains; 44 evaluation domains after screening: 30 InD, 14 OOD).
papers.preprocessing: Half of in-distribution data used for calibration, half for in-distribution ECE; all OOD samples for OOD ECE.
papers.modelDetails: Multi-domain temperature scaling (MD-TS): fits per-domain temperatures and learns a regression from features to temperature, so calibration adapts to unseen domains.
papers.training: Multiple architectures (ResNet-50, EfficientNet-b1, BiT-M-R50, ViT, ResNeXt-50, DenseNet-121).
papers.evaluation: Per-domain expected calibration error on in-distribution and OOD domains.
papers.baselines: Maximum softmax probability (uncalibrated) and standard temperature scaling.
papers.results: MD-TS achieved lower ECE than standard temperature scaling on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution domains across datasets and architectures.

papers.title: Beyond Overconfidence: Foundation Models Redefine Calibration in Deep Neural Networks
papers.authors: Achim Hekler, Lukas Kuhn, Florian Buettner
papers.aim: Reliable uncertainty calibration is essential for safely deploying deep neural networks in high-stakes applications. Deep neural networks are known to exhibit systematic overconfidence, especially under distribution shifts.
papers.method: Although foundation models such as ConvNeXt, EVA and BEiT have demonstrated significant improvements in predictive performance, their calibration properties remain underexplored. This paper presents a comprehensive investigation into the calibration behavior of foundation models, revealing insights that challenge established paradigms. Our empirical analysis shows that these models tend to be underconfident in in-distribution predictions, resulting in higher calibration errors, while demonstrating improved calibration under distribution shifts. Furthermore, we demonstrate that foundation models are highly responsive to post-hoc calibration techniques in the in-distribution setting, enabling practitioners to effectively mitigate underconfidence bias.
papers.result: However, these methods become progressively less reliable under severe distribution shifts and can occasionally produce counterproductive results. Our findings highlight the complex, non-monotonic effects of architectural and training innovations on calibration, challenging established narratives of continuous improvement.
papers.gap: Classification only; no decision-level analysis.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors re-examined calibration with current pretrained architectures on both standard and biomedical datasets, including real-world distribution shifts. They found that the old rule 'networks are overconfident' no longer holds for modern models, which tend to be underconfident, and that temperature scaling fitted on clean data can make calibration worse under strong shift. Calibration must therefore be re-measured for the specific models and sites used.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic empirical study of calibration across model generations (Goethe University Frankfurt, DKFZ; preprint).
papers.datasets: ImageNet validation (90/10 test/calibration split), ImageNet-C (19 corruptions x 5 severities) and domain-specific biomedical imaging tasks with real distribution shifts.
papers.preprocessing: Standard preprocessing per dataset.
papers.modelDetails: Evaluation of inherent calibration of older CNNs and transformers versus modern pretrained hybrid models (e.g. ConvNeXt, EVA, BEiT) and of post-hoc calibration methods.
papers.training: Pretrained models fine-tuned per task.
papers.evaluation: Top-label ECE in-distribution and under synthetic and real shifts; effect of post-hoc calibration.
papers.baselines: Earlier model generations; uncalibrated outputs.
papers.results: Modern models were underconfident in-distribution (unlike the classic overconfidence) and better calibrated under shift; post-hoc calibration helped in-distribution but became less reliable and sometimes counterproductive under severe shift.

papers.title: Predictive uncertainty estimation in deep learning for lung carcinoma classification in digital pathology under real dataset shifts
papers.authors: Abdur R. Fayjie, Jutika Borah, Florencia Carbone, Jan Tack, Patrick Vandewalle
papers.aim: Deep learning has shown tremendous progress in a wide range of digital pathology and medical image classification tasks. Its integration into safe clinical decision-making support requires robust and reliable models.
papers.method: However, real-world data comes with diversities that often lie outside the intended source distribution. Moreover, when test samples are dramatically different, clinical decision-making is greatly affected. Quantifying predictive uncertainty in models is crucial for well-calibrated predictions and determining when (or not) to trust a model. Unfortunately, many works have overlooked the importance of predictive uncertainty estimation. This paper evaluates whether predictive uncertainty estimation adds robustness to deep learning-based diagnostic decision-making systems. We investigate the effect of various carcinoma distribution shift scenarios on predictive performance and calibration. We first systematically investigate three popular methods for improving predictive uncertainty: Monte Carlo dropout, deep ensemble, and few-shot learning on lung adenocarcinoma classification as a primary disease in whole slide images.
papers.result: Secondly, we compare the effectiveness of the methods in terms of performance and calibration under clinically relevant distribution shifts such as in-distribution shifts comprising primary disease sub-types and other characterization analysis data; out-of-distribution shifts comprising well-differentiated cases, different organ origin, and imaging modality shifts. While studies on uncertainty estimation exist, to our best knowledge, no rigorous large-scale benchmark compares predictive uncertainty estimation including these dataset shifts for lung carcinoma classification.
papers.gap: Lung pathology; no deferral or workload analysis.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study asks whether uncertainty estimation makes pathology classifiers safer when test data differ from training data in realistic ways: new carcinoma subtypes and new hospitals. Several uncertainty methods were compared on accuracy and calibration across these shifts. It supports testing the Pathology Agent's uncertainty on local slides that differ from public training data.
papers.studyDesign: Comparative empirical study (KU Leuven, UZ Leuven, Gauhati University; preprint).
papers.datasets: Lung carcinoma digital pathology datasets with clinically relevant shifts: in-distribution, related diseases (carcinoma subtypes), and different centres/scanners.
papers.preprocessing: Patch-based processing of whole-slide images.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of predictive uncertainty methods (e.g. MC dropout, deep ensembles, few-shot/other UQ approaches) for lung carcinoma classification.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Classification performance and calibration (ECE) under each shift scenario; uncertainty-based rejection.
papers.baselines: Deterministic baseline.
papers.results: Uncertainty estimation added robustness and better calibration, but performance and calibration degraded under strong real shifts, with differences between methods.

papers.title: Benchmarking Bayesian Deep Learning on Diabetic Retinopathy Detection Tasks
papers.authors: Neil Band, Tim G. J. Rudner, Qixuan Feng, Angelos Filos, Zachary Nado, Michael W. Dusenberry, Ghassen Jerfel, Dustin Tran, Yarin Gal
papers.aim: Bayesian deep learning seeks to equip deep neural networks with the ability to precisely quantify their predictive uncertainty, and has promised to make deep learning more reliable for safety-critical real-world applications. Yet, existing Bayesian deep learning methods fall short of this promise; new methods continue to be evaluated on unrealistic test beds that do not reflect the complexities of downstream real-world tasks that would benefit most from reliable uncertainty quantification.
papers.method: We propose the RETINA Benchmark, a set of real-world tasks that accurately reflect such complexities and are designed to assess the reliability of predictive models in safety-critical scenarios. Specifically, we curate two publicly available datasets of high-resolution human retina images exhibiting varying degrees of diabetic retinopathy, a medical condition that can lead to blindness, and use them to design a suite of automated diagnosis tasks that require reliable predictive uncertainty quantification. We use these tasks to benchmark well-established and state-of-the-art Bayesian deep learning methods on task-specific evaluation metrics.
papers.result: We provide an easy-to-use codebase for fast and easy benchmarking following reproducibility and software design principles. We provide implementations of all methods included in the benchmark as well as results computed over 100 TPU days, 20 GPU days, 400 hyperparameter configurations, and evaluation on at least 6 random seeds each.
papers.gap: Single disease; no human-in-the-loop measurement.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: RETINA turns diabetic retinopathy screening into a benchmark for uncertainty: models refer the most uncertain cases to an expert, and the accuracy on the cases they keep is measured at each referral rate, both on the training population and on a different population. Many Bayesian methods were reimplemented and compared fairly. The referral-curve evaluation is the same design as the risk-coverage analysis in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation and systematic evaluation (Oxford, Google Research; NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks).
papers.datasets: RETINA Benchmark built on EyePACS (in-domain) and APTOS 2019 (population shift, India) high-resolution retina images graded for diabetic retinopathy.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised preprocessing and splits; tasks defined for in-domain and shifted evaluation.
papers.modelDetails: Standardised implementations of Bayesian deep learning methods: MAP (deterministic), MFVI, Radial-MFVI, function-space VI, MC dropout, Rank-1 BNNs, deep ensembles and ensembles of each.
papers.training: Optimised run scripts per method (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: AUC and accuracy on retained cases as a function of referral rate (selective prediction), in-domain and under population/severity shift.
papers.baselines: Deterministic MAP model.
papers.results: Ensembles of Bayesian methods were most reliable; no method was consistently best across shifts; uncertainty-based referral improved retained-case performance in-domain but less under shift.
papers.statistics: Means with standard errors over seeds.

papers.title: A Systematic Comparison of Bayesian Deep Learning Robustness in Diabetic Retinopathy Tasks
papers.authors: Angelos Filos, Sebastian Farquhar, Aidan N. Gomez, Tim G. J. Rudner, Zachary Kenton, Lewis Smith, Milad Alizadeh, Arnoud de Kroon, Yarin Gal
papers.aim: Evaluation of Bayesian deep learning (BDL) methods is challenging. We often seek to evaluate the methods' robustness and scalability, assessing whether new tools give `better' uncertainty estimates than old ones.
papers.method: These evaluations are paramount for practitioners when choosing BDL tools on-top of which they build their applications. Current popular evaluations of BDL methods, such as the UCI experiments, are lacking: Methods that excel with these experiments often fail when used in application such as medical or automotive, suggesting a pertinent need for new benchmarks in the field. We propose a new BDL benchmark with a diverse set of tasks, inspired by a real-world medical imaging application on \emph{diabetic retinopathy diagnosis}. Visual inputs (512x512 RGB images of retinas) are considered, where model uncertainty is used for medical pre-screening---i.e. to refer patients to an expert when model diagnosis is uncertain. Methods are then ranked according to metrics derived from expert-domain to reflect real-world use of model uncertainty in automated diagnosis. We develop multiple tasks that fall under this application, including out-of-distribution detection and robustness to distribution shift. We then perform a systematic comparison of well-tuned BDL techniques on the various tasks.
papers.result: From our comparison we conclude that some current techniques which solve benchmarks such as UCI `overfit' their uncertainty to the dataset---when evaluated on our benchmark these underperform in comparison to simpler baselines. The code for the benchmark, its baselines, and a simple API for evaluating new BDL tools are made available at https://github.com/oatml/bdl-benchmarks.
papers.gap: Binary task; no cost or human performance modelling.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: An early benchmark that treated diabetic retinopathy screening as a referral task: each method's uncertainty decides which images go to an expert, and performance on the remaining images is plotted against the referral rate, with a separate Indian dataset testing shift. Ensembles of MC dropout were most useful. It established the referral-curve method used later for medical deferral.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation and comparison (University of Oxford).
papers.datasets: Kaggle Diabetic Retinopathy Detection (35,126 train, 53,576 test; 20% of train held out); binary sight-threatening DR (grades 2-4, ~19% positive); APTOS 2019 as a distribution-shift test set from India.
papers.preprocessing: Images cropped and resized to 512x512, channel-wise normalisation, affine augmentation (zoom +-10%, translation +-25 px, rotation).
papers.modelDetails: Bayesian deep learning baselines: MC dropout, mean-field VI, deep ensembles, ensemble MC dropout, deterministic; uncertainty used for pre-screening referral.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUC and accuracy as a function of the fraction of cases referred to experts (0-50%).
papers.baselines: Deterministic and random referral.
papers.results: With no referral all methods were equal; at lower referral rates ensemble MC dropout performed best; methods that excelled on UCI benchmarks did not transfer, 'overfitting' their uncertainty.

papers.title: Confidence-Uncertainty Boundary Calibration for Bayesian Deep Learning in Medical Image Analysis
papers.authors: Hua Xu, Julián D. Arias-Londoño, Juan I. Godino-Llorente
papers.aim: In critical decision support systems based on medical imaging, the reliability of AI-assisted decision-making is as relevant as predictive accuracy. Although deep learning models have demonstrated significant accuracy, they frequently suffer from miscalibration, manifested as overconfidence in erroneous predictions.
papers.method: To facilitate clinical acceptance, it is imperative that models quantify uncertainty in a manner that correlates with prediction correctness, allowing clinicians to identify unreliable outputs for further review. To address this necessity, this paper proposes a probabilistic optimization framework grounded in Bayesian deep learning. Specifically, the Confidence-Uncertainty Boundary Curve (CUBC) is first explored as an intermediate operational target. Grounded in this target, a novel Confidence-Uncertainty Boundary Loss (CUB-Loss) is proposed to regularize the alignment between prediction confidence and uncertainty estimates during training, imposing penalties on high-certainty errors and low-certainty correct predictions. Upon completion of training optimization, a Boundary Curve Calibration Error (BCCE) metric is further introduced to measure the degree of boundary alignment in the calibrated model. Building on this measurement, a Dual Temperature Scaling (DTS) strategy is devised to perform post-hoc refinement, further adjusting the posterior predictive distribution across different confidence-uncertainty regions.
papers.result: The proposed framework is validated on three distinct medical imaging tasks: automatic screening of pneumonia, diabetic retinopathy detection, and identification of skin lesions. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed approach improves uncertainty calibration across diverse modalities, maintains robust performance in data-scarce scenarios, and remains effective on severely imbalanced datasets, underscoring its potential for real clinical deployment.
papers.gap: No deferral policy or workload evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The method trains a Bayesian network so that correct predictions sit in a high-confidence, low-uncertainty region and errors fall outside it, then applies a two-temperature post-hoc correction. The goal is that uncertainty becomes a reliable flag for clinicians to review a case. Evaluated on three medical imaging tasks.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological study on three medical imaging tasks (Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, preprint).
papers.datasets: Pneumonia screening (chest X-ray), diabetic retinopathy detection and a third medical imaging identification task.
papers.preprocessing: Standard splits per dataset.
papers.modelDetails: Bayesian neural network with a Confidence-Uncertainty Boundary Calibration (CUBC) concept, a CUB-Loss training term that separates correct and incorrect predictions in confidence-uncertainty space, and a post-hoc Dual Temperature Scaling (DTS) strategy.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Calibration (ECE), correlation between uncertainty and correctness, ability to flag unreliable outputs, accuracy.
papers.baselines: Standard BNNs and post-hoc calibration methods.
papers.results: Improved alignment between uncertainty and correctness and better calibration across the three tasks.

papers.title: Comparative Benchmarking of Failure Detection Methods in Medical Image Segmentation: Unveiling the Role of Confidence Aggregation
papers.authors: Maximilian Zenk, David Zimmerer, Fabian Isensee, Jeremias Traub, Tobias Norajitra, Paul F. Jäger, Klaus Maier-Hein
papers.aim: Semantic segmentation is an essential component of medical image analysis research, with recent deep learning algorithms offering out-of-the-box applicability across diverse datasets. Despite these advancements, segmentation failures remain a significant concern for real-world clinical applications, necessitating reliable detection mechanisms.
papers.method: This paper introduces a comprehensive benchmarking framework aimed at evaluating failure detection methodologies within medical image segmentation. Through our analysis, we identify the strengths and limitations of current failure detection metrics, advocating for the risk-coverage analysis as a holistic evaluation approach. Utilizing a collective dataset comprising five public 3D medical image collections, we assess the efficacy of various failure detection strategies under realistic test-time distribution shifts.
papers.result: Our findings highlight the importance of pixel confidence aggregation and we observe superior performance of the pairwise Dice score (Roy et al., 2019) between ensemble predictions, positioning it as a simple and robust baseline for failure detection in medical image segmentation. To promote ongoing research, we make the benchmarking framework available to the community.
papers.gap: Detection only; no clinical cost or deferral to clinicians.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper defines segmentation failure detection as deciding whether to accept a segmentation for downstream use, evaluates it with risk-coverage curves using 1 - Dice as risk, and compares many ways of turning voxel uncertainties into one case-level confidence. The simplest strong method was agreement between ensemble members (pairwise Dice). This is adopted as a baseline confidence score for the MRI Agent in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study of segmentation failure detection (DKFZ Heidelberg; MELBA/preprint).
papers.datasets: Multiple public 3D medical segmentation datasets with in-distribution and shifted test sets (details in paper; includes brain and abdominal tasks).
papers.preprocessing: Ground-truth masks used only to define risk.
papers.modelDetails: Benchmarking framework: segmentation model plus confidence scoring functions (pixel confidence aggregation such as mean entropy, pairwise Dice between ensemble members, quality-regression networks, mahalanobis-type scores); failure detection by thresholding confidence.
papers.training: nnU-Net-style segmentation models; ensembles for pairwise Dice.
papers.evaluation: Risk-coverage analysis with AURC as main metric; risk = 1 - Dice (NSD in auxiliary analysis).
papers.baselines: Single-model pixel-confidence aggregates and other failure detectors.
papers.results: Confidence aggregation strongly affected performance; pairwise Dice between ensemble predictions was a simple, robust and superior baseline for failure detection.

papers.title: Better than Average: Spatially-Aware Aggregation of Segmentation Uncertainty Improves Downstream Performance
papers.authors: Vanessa Emanuela Guarino, Claudia Winklmayr, Jannik Franzen, Josef Lorenz Rumberger, Manuel Pfeuffer, Sonja Greven, Klaus Maier-Hein, Carsten T. Lüth, Christoph Karg, Dagmar Kainmueller
papers.aim: Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) is crucial for ensuring the reliability of automated image segmentations in safety-critical domains like biomedical image analysis or autonomous driving. In segmentation, UQ generates pixel-wise uncertainty scores that must be aggregated into image-level scores for downstream tasks like Out-of-Distribution (OoD) or failure detection.
papers.method: Despite routine use of aggregation strategies, their properties and impact on downstream task performance have not yet been comprehensively studied. Global Average is the default choice, yet it does not account for spatial and structural features of segmentation uncertainty. Alternatives like patch-, class- and threshold-based strategies exist, but lack systematic comparison, leading to inconsistent reporting and unclear best practices. We address this gap by (1) formally analyzing properties, limitations, and pitfalls of common strategies; (2) proposing novel strategies that incorporate spatial uncertainty structure and (3) benchmarking their performance on OoD and failure detection across ten datasets that vary in image geometry and structure.
papers.result: We find that aggregators leveraging spatial structure yield stronger performance in both downstream tasks studied. However, the performance of individual aggregators depends heavily on dataset characteristics, so we (4) propose a meta-aggregator that integrates multiple aggregators and performs robustly across datasets.
papers.gap: No link to clinical decisions or calibration.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: Segmentation uncertainty is usually summarised by averaging over all pixels. This study compares many alternative summaries, including ones that capture whether uncertainty is clustered or concentrated at edges, for detecting failures and out-of-distribution images. Spatial summaries worked better than the average. It informs how the MRI Agent should convert voxel uncertainty into one escalation score.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical study of uncertainty aggregation (MDC Berlin, DKFZ, Charité; preprint).
papers.datasets: Diverse segmentation datasets (biomedical and driving, including OoD variants) with U-Net 3D, U-Net, HoVer-NeXt, HRNet and DeepLabv3+ models.
papers.preprocessing: Uncertainty maps normalised to [0,1].
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of aggregation strategies that turn pixel uncertainty maps into a scalar: global average, patch-level maximum average, above-threshold and above-quantile averages, class-level and weighted class averages, and spatially aware structural measures (e.g. MOR, EDS).
papers.training: MC dropout main UQ method; replicated with MSP, deep ensembles and TTA.
papers.evaluation: Downstream OoD detection and failure detection performance.
papers.baselines: Global average.
papers.results: Spatially aware aggregators outperformed global averaging in both downstream tasks, but the best single aggregator depended on dataset; combining aggregators was more robust.

papers.title: Counterfactual Context Auditing for Glioma Segmentation Failure Detection Across MRI Datasets
papers.authors: Nguyen Linh Dan Le, Tran Dang Khoi, Nguyen Pham Hoang Le
papers.aim: Glioma segmentation models can lose accuracy across MRI datasets, while identifying the cases that require correction remains difficult. In this study, we introduce counterfactual context transport (CCT), which replaces a scan's feature statistics with those from training scans and measures the resulting changes in tumor masks.
papers.method: We combine this sensitivity with prediction uncertainty to rank cases for review without retraining or additional segmentation networks. Experiments on BraTS and UTSW show that context sensitivity provides evidence of segmentation failure that uncertainty in the original prediction alone does not consistently capture.
papers.result: Combining both signals gives the strongest average failure detection among the evaluated methods, including an ensemble of separately trained networks. These findings support using changes in tumor predictions under context replacement to help identify cases that require expert review.
papers.gap: Ranking only; no threshold or clinical evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: To find glioma segmentations that are likely wrong on a new dataset, the method swaps in feature statistics typical of the training data and checks whether the predicted tumour changes a lot; a large change suggests the model is relying on site-specific context. Combined with ordinary uncertainty, this ranked failures better than an ensemble on BraTS and UTSW. It offers an extra, cheap failure signal for local data.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on glioma segmentation across datasets (University of Melbourne, Vietnamese universities; preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS and UT Southwestern glioma MRI datasets (cross-dataset shift).
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Counterfactual context transport (CCT): replaces a scan's feature statistics with those of training scans and measures how much the tumour mask changes; combined with prediction uncertainty to rank cases for review without retraining or extra networks.
papers.training: Uses an existing segmentation network.
papers.evaluation: Failure detection performance (ranking of poor-Dice cases) across datasets.
papers.baselines: Prediction uncertainty alone and an ensemble of separately trained networks.
papers.results: Context sensitivity gave evidence of failure that uncertainty alone missed; combining both signals gave the strongest average failure detection, better than an ensemble.

papers.title: Automatic quality control framework for more reliable integration of machine learning-based image segmentation into medical workflows
papers.authors: Elena Williams, Sebastian Niehaus, Janis Reinelt, Alberto Merola, Paul Glad Mihai, Kersten Villringer, Konstantin Thierbach, Evelyn Medawar, Daniel Lichterfeld, Ingo Roeder, et al.
papers.aim: Machine learning algorithms underpin modern diagnostic-aiding software, which has proved valuable in clinical practice, particularly in radiology. However, inaccuracies, mainly due to the limited availability of clinical samples for training these algorithms, hamper their wider applicability, acceptance, and recognition amongst clinicians.
papers.method: We present an analysis of state-of-the-art automatic quality control (QC) approaches that can be implemented within these algorithms to estimate the certainty of their outputs. We validated the most promising approaches on a brain image segmentation task identifying white matter hyperintensities (WMH) in magnetic resonance imaging data. WMH are a correlate of small vessel disease common in mid-to-late adulthood and are particularly challenging to segment due to their varied size, and distributional patterns. Our results show that the aggregation of uncertainty and Dice prediction were most effective in failure detection for this task.
papers.result: Both methods independently improved mean Dice from 0.82 to 0.84. Our work reveals how QC methods can help to detect failed segmentation cases and therefore make automatic segmentation more reliable and suitable for clinical practice.
papers.gap: WMH, not tumours; no clinician workload measure.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built a framework that automatically checks each brain MRI segmentation before it is used, either by combining uncertainty and error estimates into a quality score or by predicting the Dice score directly, and validated it on multi-site white-matter lesion data. Removing flagged cases raised the average quality of accepted segmentations. It is a practical model for the quality check after the MRI Agent.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective framework development on public multi-site brain MRI (AICURA medical, Edinburgh, TU Dresden, Charité; preprint).
papers.datasets: 105 patients' T1 and FLAIR MRI from four public white-matter-hyperintensity / MS databases (MICCAI WMH 2017, ISBI MS 2015, MICCAI MS 2016, MS17); folds of 68 train, 16 validation, 21 test.
papers.preprocessing: Combined multi-source data to increase variation; standard preprocessing (details in paper).
papers.modelDetails: CNN segmentation with two automatic quality-control approaches: aggregation of uncertainty and error estimates into a single score, and direct prediction of Dice; cases flagged as failed are excluded or sent for review.
papers.training: Cross-validation training (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Detection of failed segmentations; mean Dice on accepted cases.
papers.baselines: No QC (all cases accepted); manual evaluation.
papers.results: Both QC methods independently improved mean Dice of accepted cases from 0.82 to 0.84 by detecting failed cases.

papers.title: Assessing Reliability and Challenges of Uncertainty Estimations for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Alain Jungo, Mauricio Reyes
papers.aim: Despite the recent improvements in overall accuracy, deep learning systems still exhibit low levels of robustness. Detecting possible failures is critical for a successful clinical integration of these systems, where each data point corresponds to an individual patient.
papers.method: Uncertainty measures are a promising direction to improve failure detection since they provide a measure of a system's confidence. Although many uncertainty estimation methods have been proposed for deep learning, little is known on their benefits and current challenges for medical image segmentation. Therefore, we report results of evaluating common voxel-wise uncertainty measures with respect to their reliability, and limitations on two medical image segmentation datasets. Results show that current uncertainty methods perform similarly and although they are well-calibrated at the dataset level, they tend to be miscalibrated at subject-level.
papers.result: Therefore, the reliability of uncertainty estimates is compromised, highlighting the importance of developing subject-wise uncertainty estimations. Additionally, among the benchmarked methods, we found auxiliary networks to be a valid alternative to common uncertainty methods since they can be applied to any previously trained segmentation model.
papers.gap: Whole-tumour only; older methods.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using the same U-Net on brain tumours and skin lesions, the study compared five common ways of estimating voxel uncertainty and checked calibration both over the whole dataset and for each patient. All methods looked well calibrated overall but not for individual patients, which is what matters clinically. This motivates subject-level calibration checks in this study.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical evaluation of voxel-wise uncertainty (University of Bern; MICCAI 2019).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018 (265 subjects: 100 train, 25 validation, 160 test; whole-tumour label) and ISIC 2017 skin lesion segmentation (2,000 train, 150 validation, 600 test).
papers.preprocessing: BraTS: per-subject z-score normalisation; ISIC: resized to 256x192 and scaled to [0,1].
papers.modelDetails: U-Net-like network (four pooling steps, dropout 0.05, batch norm) with five uncertainty measures: softmax entropy baseline, MC dropout, aleatoric uncertainty, ensembles, and auxiliary networks.
papers.training: Cross-entropy, Adam lr 1e-4, early stopping on validation Dice.
papers.evaluation: Dataset-level and subject-level calibration (ECE, uncertainty-error overlap), failure detection.
papers.baselines: Softmax entropy.
papers.results: Methods performed similarly; uncertainty was well calibrated at the dataset level but miscalibrated at the subject level, so per-patient reliability is compromised; ensembles were relatively robust.

papers.title: Information-theoretic Generalization Analysis for Expected Calibration Error
papers.authors: Futoshi Futami, Masahiro Fujisawa
papers.aim: While the expected calibration error (ECE), which employs binning, is widely adopted to evaluate the calibration performance of machine learning models, theoretical understanding of its estimation bias is limited. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive analysis of the estimation bias in the two common binning strategies, uniform mass and uniform width binning.
papers.method: Our analysis establishes upper bounds on the bias, achieving an improved convergence rate. Moreover, our bounds reveal, for the first time, the optimal number of bins to minimize the estimation bias.
papers.result: We further extend our bias analysis to generalization error analysis based on the information-theoretic approach, deriving upper bounds that enable the numerical evaluation of how small the ECE is for unknown data. Experiments using deep learning models show that our bounds are nonvacuous thanks to this information-theoretic generalization analysis approach.
papers.gap: Theoretical; no medical data.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper studies how accurate the expected calibration error itself is as a measurement, showing how binning choices bias it, how many bins to use, and how much ECE can be trusted on new data. It informs how calibration will be measured and reported in this study, especially with small local test sets.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical learning-theory study with experiments (Osaka University, RIKEN AIP; NeurIPS 2024).
papers.datasets: Deep learning benchmarks used to validate bounds.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Analysis of estimation bias of expected calibration error under uniform-mass and uniform-width binning, optimal number of bins, and information-theoretic generalisation bounds for ECE on unseen data.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Tightness of bounds; bias when reusing training data for recalibration.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Derived improved bias bounds, the optimal bin count, and non-vacuous generalisation bounds; showed extra bias when recalibrating on training data.

papers.title: Calibration tests in multi-class classification: A unifying framework
papers.authors: David Widmann, Fredrik Lindsten, Dave Zachariah
papers.venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (NeurIPS 2019)
papers.aim: In safety-critical applications a probabilistic model is usually required to be calibrated, i.e., to capture the uncertainty of its predictions accurately. In multi-class classification, calibration of the most confident predictions only is often not sufficient.
papers.method: We propose and study calibration measures for multi-class classification that generalize existing measures such as the expected calibration error, the maximum calibration error, and the maximum mean calibration error.
papers.result: We propose and evaluate empirically different consistent and unbiased estimators for a specific class of measures based on matrix-valued kernels. Importantly, these estimators can be interpreted as test statistics associated with well-defined bounds and approximations of the p-value under the null hypothesis that the model is calibrated, significantly improving the interpretability of calibration measures, which otherwise lack any meaningful unit or scale.
papers.gap: No medical application.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors give a general family of calibration measures for multi-class models and kernel-based estimators that can be used as formal statistical tests of whether a model is calibrated, instead of reporting an ECE number with no notion of significance. Simulations confirmed unbiasedness and test validity. These tests could complement ECE in this study, especially for small local test sets.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical and simulation study (Uppsala, Linköping; NeurIPS 2019).
papers.datasets: Synthetic datasets of 250 predictions over 10 classes from three generative models (one calibrated, two miscalibrated), 10^4 repetitions.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Unifying framework of multi-class calibration measures generalising ECE, MCE and MMCE; squared kernel calibration error (SKCE) with matrix-valued kernels and consistent, unbiased estimators that serve as statistical calibration tests with p-value approximations.
papers.training: Kernel bandwidth by median heuristic.
papers.evaluation: Bias and variance of estimators; type I and II error of calibration tests.
papers.baselines: Histogram-regression ECE with uniform and data-dependent binning.
papers.results: SKCE estimators were unbiased and gave valid hypothesis tests of calibration, unlike binned ECE, improving interpretability of calibration measurement.

papers.title: Towards Reliable WMH Segmentation under Domain Shift: An Application Study using Maximum Entropy Regularization to Improve Uncertainty Estimation
papers.authors: Franco Matzkin, Agostina Larrazabal, Diego H Milone, Jose Dolz, Enzo Ferrante
papers.aim: Accurate segmentation of white matter hyperintensities (WMH) is crucial for clinical decision-making, particularly in the context of multiple sclerosis. However, domain shifts, such as variations in MRI machine types or acquisition parameters, pose significant challenges to model calibration and uncertainty estimation.
papers.method: This study investigates the impact of domain shift on WMH segmentation by proposing maximum-entropy regularization techniques to enhance model calibration and uncertainty estimation, with the purpose of identifying errors post-deployment using predictive uncertainty as a proxy measure that does not require ground-truth labels.
papers.result: To do this, we conducted experiments using a U-Net architecture to evaluate these regularization schemes on two publicly available datasets, assessing performance with the Dice coefficient, expected calibration error, and entropy-based uncertainty estimates. Our results show that entropy-based uncertainty estimates can anticipate segmentation errors, and that maximum-entropy regularization further strengthens the correlation between uncertainty and segmentation performance while also improving model calibration under domain shift.
papers.gap: WMH rather than tumours; no deferral experiment.
papers.relation: Informs calibrated, uncertainty-aware escalation (O2): how confidence is calibrated and when a case should be deferred to the clinician instead of being decided automatically.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study trains white-matter-lesion segmentation networks with a penalty that discourages overconfident outputs and tests them on a second dataset from different scanners. Regularised models were better calibrated after the shift and their entropy better predicted where segmentations were wrong, without needing ground truth at deployment. It is a cheap training-time option to improve calibration before local deployment.
papers.studyDesign: Application study under domain shift (CONICET Argentina, ÉTS Montréal; preprint).
papers.datasets: WMH Segmentation Challenge and 3D-MR-MS datasets (public, different scanners and sites) for in-distribution and out-of-distribution testing.
papers.preprocessing: Standard WMH preprocessing (details in paper).
papers.modelDetails: U-Net segmentation with maximum-entropy regularisation schemes during training; voxel predictive entropy as uncertainty.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice, Hausdorff distance, expected calibration error, correlation of entropy-based uncertainty with segmentation error, in- and out-of-distribution.
papers.baselines: Standard U-Net training without regularisation.
papers.results: Entropy-based uncertainty anticipated segmentation errors in and out of distribution; maximum-entropy regularisation strengthened this correlation and improved calibration under domain shift.

heading: O3 - Data-efficient MRI and pathology models, fusion and federated learning

papers.title: nnU-Net: a self-configuring method for deep learning-based biomedical image segmentation
papers.authors: Isensee F, Jaeger PF, Kohl SAA, Petersen J, Maier-Hein KH
papers.aim: To make segmentation work out-of-the-box on any new medical dataset without manual tuning.
papers.method: Rules that set preprocessing, network (2D/3D U-Net), training and post-processing automatically from dataset properties.
papers.result: Beat most specialised methods on 23 public datasets and many challenges.
papers.tools: U-Net, PyTorch, 3D CNN
papers.gap: Needs strong GPU and no uncertainty output by default.
papers.relation: Our main baseline for tumour segmentation on Sri Lankan MRI.
papers.limitations: Heavy compute, still needs good labels. Future: lighter and label-efficient versions.
papers.methodologyDetail: nnU-Net argues that the way a U-Net is configured and trained matters more than new architecture tricks, and automates all of it. Given any new dataset, it inspects voxel spacing, image size and modality, crops to the body or brain, resamples every case to the median spacing, and normalises intensities (z-score for MRI). It then sets up three candidates - a 2D U-Net, a 3D U-Net, and a 3D cascade that first segments a down-sampled image - choosing patch size, batch size and network depth to fit GPU memory. Each is trained from scratch with Dice plus cross-entropy loss, Adam at 3e-4, heavy augmentation, and a learning-rate and stopping schedule driven by loss moving averages, in five-fold cross-validation; the best configuration or ensemble is chosen automatically. On the Medical Segmentation Decathlon, including the BraTS-based brain tumour task (cross-validation Dice about 81/62/79 for the three tumour labels with the 3D U-Net), it won the challenge and its cross-validation scores held on the test set. For our PhD nnU-Net is the baseline and starting point for the MRI tumour segmentation agent, and its recipe is the default for training on small Sri Lankan datasets.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper; automatic segmentation framework evaluated on the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (PDF read is the 2018 arXiv version; the 2021 Nature Methods version extends evaluation to 23 public datasets / 53 tasks).
papers.datasets: Medical Segmentation Decathlon phase 1: BrainTumour (BraTS multimodal MRI, 3 labels: oedema, non-enhancing, enhancing), Heart, Liver, Hippocampus, Prostate, Lung, Pancreas; held-out test sets on the challenge platform.
papers.preprocessing: Fully automatic: crop to non-zero region (reduces skull-stripped brain MRI size); resample all cases to the dataset's median voxel spacing (3rd-order spline for images, nearest neighbour for masks); intensity normalisation (z-score per case for MRI, global clipping and normalisation for CT); data augmentation on the fly (rotations, scaling, elastic deformation, gamma, mirroring).
papers.modelDetails: No new architecture: standard U-Net variants configured automatically from dataset properties - 2D U-Net, 3D U-Net, and a two-stage 3D U-Net Cascade (low-resolution then full-resolution) when the 3D patch cannot cover the image. Patch size, batch size (lower bound 2) and number of pooling layers chosen from image size and GPU memory. Final prediction may ensemble configurations chosen by cross-validation.
papers.training: Trained from scratch, five-fold cross-validation; loss = Dice + cross-entropy; Adam, initial learning rate 3e-4; epoch = 250 training batches; learning rate reduced by factor 5 if training-loss moving average does not improve by 5e-3 within 30 epochs; stop if validation-loss moving average does not improve by 5e-3 within 60 epochs.
papers.evaluation: Dice per foreground label in 5-fold cross-validation and on the held-out Decathlon test set (single submission).
papers.baselines: Comparison of its own configurations (2D, 3D, cascade) and with other Decathlon entries.
papers.results: Cross-validation Dice for BrainTumour labels 1/2/3: 2D U-Net 78.60 / 58.65 / 77.42; 3D U-Net 80.71 / 62.22 / 79.07. Heart 2D 91.36, 3D 92.45; Liver label 1 3D 94.11. Cross-validation results were recovered on the test set; only BrainTumour dropped on all labels, attributed to data/label shift typical of BraTS. nnU-Net ranked first in the Decathlon.
papers.statistics: Five-fold cross-validation means; single test submission.

papers.title: The RSNA-ASNR-MICCAI BraTS 2021 Benchmark on Brain Tumor Segmentation and Radiogenomic Classification
papers.authors: Baid U, Ghodasara S, Mohan S, Bilello M, Calabrese E, et al., Bakas S
papers.aim: To describe the BraTS 2021 dataset and tasks.
papers.method: Large multi-institution multi-parametric MRI (T1, T1Gd, T2, FLAIR) with expert labels for enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour. Also MGMT prediction task.
papers.result: Around 2,000 glioma cases, the biggest public brain tumour MRI set at that time.
papers.tools: Multi-parametric MRI, standard preprocessing (skull strip, co-registration)
papers.gap: Mostly gliomas from Western centres, pre-processed and standardised.
papers.relation: Public pre-training and benchmark set before we use local data. Also shows the gap: our data is not standardised.
papers.limitations: Population and scanner bias. Future: more tumour types and regions.
papers.methodologyDetail: BraTS 2021 assembled about 2,000 pre-operative glioma MRI scans (T1, contrast T1, T2 and FLAIR) from many institutions and scanners. Every scan goes through the same public pipeline: conversion to NIfTI (which removes patient identifiers), registration to the SRI24 brain template, resampling to 1 mm voxels and deep-learning skull stripping. Tumour sub-regions were first drawn automatically by fusing earlier winning algorithms, then corrected by trained annotators and approved by expert neuroradiologists, giving labels for enhancing tumour, necrotic core and oedema. A second task gives MGMT promoter methylation status from laboratory testing of the resected tissue. Data are split into training (with labels), validation (labels hidden) and a hidden test set; segmentation is scored with Dice and 95% Hausdorff distance on enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour. For our PhD this defines the public development dataset, the preprocessing pipeline to apply to Sri Lankan scans so models transfer, and the standard metrics for the segmentation agent.
papers.studyDesign: Challenge / benchmark description paper (RSNA-ASNR-MICCAI BraTS 2021): dataset creation, annotation protocol and evaluation framework for two tasks.
papers.datasets: About 2,000 multi-institutional glioma cases (up from 660 in earlier BraTS) with pre-operative mpMRI: native T1, post-contrast T1 (T1Gd), T2, T2-FLAIR, from different scanners and protocols. Task 1: tumour sub-region segmentation (enhancing tumour, tumour core, whole tumour). Task 2: prediction of MGMT promoter methylation status (from laboratory assessment of surgical specimens). Split into training (labels given), validation (no labels) and hidden test sets.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS pipeline (public in CaPTk and the FeTS tool): DICOM to NIfTI (removes PHI), co-registration to SRI24 anatomical template, resampling to 1 mm^3 isotropic, deep-learning skull stripping (shape-prior, sequence-agnostic). Task 1 volumes pre-segmented by STAPLE fusion of earlier top BraTS algorithms, then manually refined by annotators and approved by expert neuroradiologists.
papers.modelDetails: Not a model paper. Defines labels: GD-enhancing tumour, peritumoural oedema/invaded tissue, necrotic tumour core; evaluated regions ET, TC (ET + necrosis), WT (TC + oedema).
papers.training: Rules: participants may not use extra public/private data or pre-trained models for the ranked submission (allowed only for separate publications).
papers.evaluation: Task 1: Dice similarity coefficient and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance per region, plus sensitivity/specificity; ranking across cases. Task 2: MGMT classification evaluated on Kaggle (AUC). Platforms: Synapse (Task 1) and Kaggle (Task 2); $60,000 prizes.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (benchmark definition).
papers.results: Not applicable for model results; provides the largest public annotated glioma mpMRI dataset (~2,000 cases) and a standard pipeline and metrics.
papers.statistics: Ranking scheme with case-wise ranks across metrics (described in challenge documentation).
papers.availability: Data: https://www.synapse.org/brats (registration); preprocessing in CaPTk / FeTS tool.

papers.title: Swin UNETR: Swin Transformers for Semantic Segmentation of Brain Tumors in MRI Images
papers.authors: Hatamizadeh A, Nath V, Tang Y, Yang D, Roth HR, Xu D
papers.aim: To use a Swin transformer encoder for 3D brain tumour segmentation.
papers.method: Swin transformer encoder with shifted windows, CNN decoder, skip connections. Trained on BraTS 2021.
papers.result: Among the top methods in BraTS 2021 validation.
papers.tools: Swin Transformer, MONAI, PyTorch
papers.gap: Transformers usually need lots of data.
papers.relation: Candidate model for our MRI agent, compared with nnU-Net.
papers.limitations: Heavy model, small data risk. Future: pretraining.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors adapt the Swin Transformer to 3D brain MRI segmentation. The four MRI sequences are split into small 3D patches, and a hierarchical transformer computes self-attention inside shifted local windows at four scales; these features are passed through skip connections to a convolutional decoder that outputs enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour maps. Training uses BraTS 2021's 1,251 cases in five-fold cross-validation with 128-cube random crops, flips and intensity augmentation, soft Dice loss, learning rate 8e-4, on eight V100 GPUs in MONAI. On identical folds it slightly beat nnU-Net, SegResNet and TransBTS (average Dice 0.913 vs 0.908 for nnU-Net). For our PhD Swin UNETR is the main transformer alternative to nnU-Net for the segmentation agent, especially when combined with self-supervised pre-training (O3-P04) for small local datasets.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper evaluated by five-fold cross-validation on BraTS 2021 and on the BraTS 2021 challenge validation/test sets.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2021 training set (1,251 multi-parametric MRI cases: T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR) for five-fold cross-validation; BraTS 2021 validation and test leaderboards.
papers.preprocessing: BraTS-preprocessed volumes; intensities normalised to zero mean, unit SD over non-zero voxels; random 128x128x128 patches; random mirror flips (p = 0.5 per axis); random intensity scaling/shifting.
papers.modelDetails: Swin UNETR: 3D Swin Transformer encoder (shifted-window self-attention, hierarchical features at 4 resolutions, patch size 2, window size 7) connected by skip connections to a CNN decoder (U-Net style). Input: 4 MRI channels; output: ET, TC, WT sigmoid maps. Configurations, parameters and FLOPs in Table 1.
papers.training: PyTorch + MONAI on a DGX-1 with 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs; soft Dice loss; learning rate 0.0008 (AdamW, cosine schedule); five-fold cross-validation; ensemble of fold models for submission.
papers.evaluation: Dice per region (ET, WT, TC) and 95% Hausdorff distance; comparison with nnU-Net, SegResNet and TransBTS under the same folds.
papers.baselines: nnU-Net, SegResNet, TransBTS.
papers.results: Five-fold mean Dice (ET / WT / TC / average): Swin UNETR 0.891 / 0.933 / 0.917 / 0.913; nnU-Net 0.883 / 0.927 / 0.913 / 0.908; SegResNet 0.883 / 0.927 / 0.913 / 0.907; TransBTS 0.868 / 0.911 / 0.898 / 0.891. Swin UNETR ranked among the top teams in the BraTS 2021 validation phase.
papers.statistics: Per-fold and average Dice; no formal significance tests.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Pre-Training of Swin Transformers for 3D Medical Image Analysis
papers.authors: Tang Y, Yang D, Li W, Roth HR, Landman B, Xu D, Nath V, Hatamizadeh A
papers.aim: To pretrain 3D models on unlabelled scans so less labelled data is needed later.
papers.method: Self-supervised tasks: masked volume inpainting, rotation prediction and contrastive coding, on about 5,000 unlabelled CT scans.
papers.result: State-of-the-art results on BTCV and Medical Segmentation Decathlon after fine-tuning.
papers.tools: Swin UNETR, self-supervised learning, MONAI
papers.gap: Pretrained on CT, transfer to brain MRI not shown well.
papers.relation: Our labelled Sri Lankan data will be small. Self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled local MRI is a key option.
papers.limitations: Big compute for pretraining. Future: pretraining on MRI.
papers.methodologyDetail: Because labelled 3D medical data are scarce, the authors pre-train a 3D Swin Transformer encoder on 5,050 unlabelled CT scans using three self-supervised tasks at once: fill in randomly masked 3D regions (30% dropped), predict how a sub-volume was rotated, and pull together embeddings of two augmented views of the same sub-volume while pushing apart others. Pre-training runs 450K iterations with AdamW (lr 4e-4, warm-up cosine schedule, batch 4 per GPU on 96-cube patches). The pre-trained encoder is then joined to a convolutional decoder and fine-tuned with five-fold cross-validation on BTCV abdominal organs and on all ten Medical Segmentation Decathlon tasks, with fold ensembles for the final result. It topped both public leaderboards, and ablations show pre-training helps most with little labelled data. For our PhD this is the template for data-efficient learning: pre-train on unlabelled Sri Lankan MRI (and public scans) with these proxy tasks, then fine-tune the segmentation agent on the few labelled local cases.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper: large-scale self-supervised pre-training on unlabelled CT, fine-tuned and evaluated on public segmentation benchmarks.
papers.datasets: Pre-training: 5,050 unlabelled CT volumes from public datasets (multiple body regions). Fine-tuning: BTCV multi-organ abdominal CT (30 labelled scans, 13 organs) and Medical Segmentation Decathlon (10 tasks, CT and MRI, including brain tumour).
papers.preprocessing: Dataset-specific preprocessing in supplementary material; 96x96x96 patches for pre-training.
papers.modelDetails: Swin UNETR encoder (3D Swin Transformer, hierarchical shifted windows, 4 resolutions) pre-trained with three proxy tasks: masked volume inpainting (30% of regions dropped), 3D image rotation prediction (0/90/180/270 degrees) and 3D contrastive coding (embedding size 512). After pre-training, a CNN decoder is attached and the network fine-tuned for segmentation.
papers.training: Pre-training: AdamW, warm-up cosine scheduler 500 iterations, batch 4 per GPU, 96^3 patches, initial learning rate 4e-4, momentum 0.9, decay 1e-5, 450K iterations; PyTorch + MONAI. Fine-tuning: five-fold cross-validation, best model per fold, ensemble of folds for final predictions.
papers.evaluation: Dice and Normalised Surface Distance (NSD / surface Dice) on BTCV and MSD public leaderboards; ablations on pre-training tasks and data size.
papers.baselines: nnU-Net, UNETR, TransBTS, other leaderboard entries; Swin UNETR without pre-training.
papers.results: State-of-the-art on the BTCV leaderboard (best average Dice among submissions) and first place on the MSD public test leaderboard overall; pre-training improved performance, especially with fewer labelled training cases (exact per-task values in Tables 1-2).

papers.title: Segment Anything in Medical Images (MedSAM)
papers.authors: Ma J, He Y, Li F, Han L, You C, Wang B
papers.aim: To build one promptable segmentation model for many medical image types.
papers.method: Fine-tuned Segment Anything on over 1.5 million medical image-mask pairs across 10 modalities. User gives a bounding box.
papers.result: Better than SAM and comparable or better than specialist models on many internal and external tests.
papers.tools: SAM, ViT, box prompts
papers.gap: 2D slices, needs a box prompt, weaker on very small or unclear edges.
papers.relation: Clinician can draw a box and correct the result. Good for human-in-the-loop correction and fast labelling of local data.
papers.limitations: Not 3D native. Future: 3D and text prompts.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors build a general medical segmentation model by fine-tuning Meta's Segment Anything Model on more than 1.5 million image-mask pairs from ten modalities. Data are split by scan, video or slide to avoid leakage, images are resized to 1024x1024, and each training example is a bounding box around the target with its mask. Training uses AdamW (lr 1e-4) for 150 epochs on 20 A100 GPUs without augmentation. MedSAM is compared with the original SAM and with 20 specialist U-Net and DeepLabV3+ models on 86 internal and 60 external tasks, using Dice and surface distance. It beats SAM everywhere and matches or exceeds specialists, including on unseen modalities. For our PhD MedSAM is a candidate for the anatomical reconstruction and surgical-planning agent: a clinician or the detection agent draws a box around a tumour or structure at risk, and MedSAM produces the outline, which helps with structures not labelled in BraTS.
papers.studyDesign: Foundation model development (fine-tuning SAM on a very large medical dataset) with internal and external validation across many tasks.
papers.datasets: 1,570,263 medical image-mask pairs covering 10 modalities (CT, MRI, chest X-ray, dermoscopy, endoscopy, ultrasound, mammography, OCT, pathology, and more), over 30 cancer types and many protocols; 86 internal validation tasks and 60 external validation tasks (including brain tumour MRI).
papers.preprocessing: Random 80/10/10 split into training, tuning and validation at the 3D scan / video level (no leakage across slices or frames); whole-slide images split by slide then tiled into 1024x1024 patches; images resized to 1024x1024; bounding-box prompts derived from masks.
papers.modelDetails: MedSAM = Segment Anything Model (ViT-B image encoder, prompt encoder, mask decoder) fine-tuned for medical images with bounding-box prompts; the user (or another agent) gives a box around the target and MedSAM outputs the mask.
papers.training: AdamW, learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 0.01, global batch 160, no data augmentation, 150 epochs on 20 A100 (80 GB) GPUs; last checkpoint used. Comparison specialist models: 20 modality-specific U-Net and DeepLabV3+ models.
papers.evaluation: Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and Normalised Surface Distance (NSD) per task, median and IQR; ranking across 86 internal and 60 external tasks; qualitative examples (liver, brain, breast cancer, polyps).
papers.baselines: Original SAM; specialist U-Net and DeepLabV3+ trained per modality.
papers.results: MedSAM ranked first on most internal tasks and outperformed SAM across tasks, on par with or better than specialist models; e.g. nasopharynx cancer median DSC 87.8% (IQR 85.0-91.4%), +52.3 points over SAM, +15.5 over U-Net, +22.7 over DeepLabV3+; up to 10% better on unseen modalities (abdomen T1 in/out-phase).
papers.statistics: Median and IQR of DSC/NSD; rank frequency analysis; significance tests reported in the paper.

papers.title: Attention-based Deep Multiple Instance Learning
papers.authors: Ilse M, Tomczak JM, Welling M
papers.aim: To learn from bag-level labels only (e.g. one label per slide) and still find important instances.
papers.method: Attention pooling over instance features, trained end-to-end.
papers.result: Matched or beat other MIL methods and gives attention maps showing important patches (tested on histopathology data).
papers.tools: CNN, attention pooling
papers.gap: Assumes instances are independent.
papers.relation: Biopsy slides will have only slide-level diagnosis. This is the basic method for our pathology agent.
papers.limitations: Small datasets in paper. Future: larger WSI.
papers.methodologyDetail: In pathology a whole slide often has one label while only a few regions show the disease. The authors treat each image as a bag of patches and learn a network that embeds every patch, then combines them with a learned attention-weighted average, so patches that matter get high weights. The bag embedding goes to a classifier trained only with bag labels. They test on standard MIL benchmarks, on synthetic bags of MNIST digits, and on breast and colon histology where each image is split into small patches around nuclei. Attention pooling gave the best colon cancer results (accuracy 0.904, AUC 0.968) and its weights highlighted the epithelial patches that define the label. For our PhD attention-based MIL is the core building block for the biopsy-slide agent: it learns from slide-level diagnoses (which hospitals have) rather than pixel annotations, and its attention map shows the pathologist which regions drove the AI's decision.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with experiments on classical multiple-instance learning (MIL) benchmarks, MNIST-bags and two histopathology datasets.
papers.datasets: Classical MIL: MUSK1, MUSK2, FOX, TIGER, ELEPHANT. MNIST-bags: bags of random numbers of 28x28 MNIST digits (positive if any '9'). Histopathology: Breast Cancer (UCSB) and Colon Cancer (H&E images; 27x27 patches centred on marked nuclei; positive if epithelial cells present).
papers.preprocessing: Histology images split into 27x27 (colon) or 32x32 patches as instances; augmentation with rotations, flips and colour jitter (as described in the paper).
papers.modelDetails: Bag-level MIL with a neural network: instance embeddings from a CNN, combined by attention-based pooling z = sum_k a_k h_k, where weights a_k come from a small network (tanh, or gated tanh x sigmoid). The attention weights show which instances (patches) drive the bag label. Compared with instance-level max/mean pooling and embedding-level max/mean pooling.
papers.training: Adam optimiser; experiments repeated 5 times; settings per dataset in the appendix.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy (classical MIL); accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for histopathology (mean +/- SEM over 5 runs); attention heatmaps vs ground-truth positive patches.
papers.baselines: mi-SVM, MI-SVM, MI-Kernel, EM-DD, mi-Graph, miVLAD, miFV; instance+max/mean and embedding+max/mean pooling networks.
papers.results: Colon Cancer: Attention accuracy 0.904 +/- 0.011, AUC 0.968 +/- 0.009; Gated-Attention accuracy 0.898, AUC 0.968; best pooling baseline embedding+mean accuracy 0.860, AUC 0.940; instance+max 0.842 / 0.914. Competitive with best methods on classical MIL datasets; attention heatmaps highlighted epithelial patches.

papers.title: Data-efficient and weakly supervised computational pathology on whole-slide images (CLAM)
papers.authors: Lu MY, Williamson DFK, Chen TY, Chen RJ, Barbieri M, Mahmood F
papers.aim: To classify whole slides using only slide labels and small datasets.
papers.method: Attention MIL with clustering constraint on top of frozen pretrained features. Tested on renal cancer subtyping, lung cancer subtyping and lymph node metastasis.
papers.result: High AUC with limited labels, worked on independent test sets and even on smartphone microscopy images. Gives interpretable heatmaps.
papers.tools: ResNet-50 features, attention MIL, PyTorch, OpenSlide
papers.gap: Not tested on brain tumours. Feature extractor from ImageNet.
papers.relation: Strong baseline for our pathology agent on small Sri Lankan biopsy sets.
papers.methodologyDetail: CLAM classifies whole-slide images using only the slide's diagnosis, with no hand-drawn regions. Each slide is segmented into tissue, cut into 256-pixel patches, and every patch is turned once into a 1,024-number feature vector by an ImageNet ResNet50. An attention network then scores how important each patch is for each class and combines patches into a slide representation for the final prediction; an extra clustering loss teaches the model to separate highly attended (diagnostic) patches from weakly attended ones, which makes learning more data-efficient. Trained with 10-fold cross-validation on TCGA kidney and lung and Camelyon lymph-node slides, it reached AUCs of 0.95-0.99, kept good performance with fewer training slides, transferred from resections to biopsies, and even worked on photos taken through a microscope with a smartphone (AUC 0.87-0.92). Attention heatmaps show which areas drove the decision. For our PhD CLAM is the baseline for the biopsy-slide agent: it fits small Sri Lankan slide collections with only diagnosis labels, its heatmaps support pathologist review, and the smartphone result is relevant where slide scanners are scarce.
papers.studyDesign: Method paper with public datasets and independent test cohorts (biopsies, smartphone microscopy images).
papers.datasets: TCGA-Kidney (3-class RCC subtyping: papillary, chromophobe, clear cell); TCGA + CPTAC Lung (NSCLC: adenocarcinoma vs squamous); Camelyon16 + Camelyon17 (breast cancer lymph-node metastasis); independent in-house test cohorts including biopsy WSIs and cellphone-captured microscopy fields of view (lung and kidney CPI datasets).
papers.preprocessing: Tissue segmentation of each WSI; 256x256 patches extracted from tissue regions (20x for kidney/lung, 40x for Camelyon); each patch encoded once by an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet50 (truncated after the 3rd residual block, adaptive mean pooling) into a 1,024-dimensional feature vector.
