papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-centre study with public data (West China Hospital, Sichuan University; ethics No. 2021.1319, written consent).
papers.datasets: 472 H&E WSIs from 226 patients at West China Hospital (scanned on Hamamatsu NanoZoomer-SQ) and 1,604 WSIs from 880 TCGA patients; five subtypes (astrocytoma, anaplastic astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma, anaplastic oligodendroglioma, glioblastoma); TCGA diagnoses revised to WHO 2021.
papers.preprocessing: OpenSlide loading, DeepZoom patch tiling at 10x, Reinhard colour normalisation; damaged or blurry regions excluded; diagnoses confirmed by two senior pathologists.
papers.modelDetails: Weakly supervised ResNet-50 with an attention mechanism for slide-level classification; heatmap visualisation.
papers.training: Ten-fold cross-validation.
papers.evaluation: AUC for grade and subtype distinctions and IDH inference.
papers.baselines: Not reported.
papers.results: High AUCs for distinguishing grades of astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma; IDH status inferred in TCGA with AUC 0.9488.
papers.availability: TCGA public; hospital data on reasonable request.

papers.title: Brain Tumor/Mass Classification Framework Using Magnetic-Resonance-Imaging-Based Isolated and Developed Transfer Deep-Learning Model
papers.authors: Alanazi MF, Ali MU, Hussain SJ, Zafar A, Mohatram M, Irfan M, AlRuwaili R, Alruwaili M, Ali NH, Albarrak AM
papers.aim: With the advancement in technology, machine learning can be applied to diagnose the mass/tumor in the brain using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This work proposes a novel developed transfer deep-learning model for the early diagnosis of brain tumors into their subclasses, such as pituitary, meningioma, and glioma.
papers.method: First, various layers of isolated convolutional-neural-network (CNN) models are built from scratch to check their performances for brain MRI images. Then, the 22-layer, binary-classification (tumor or no tumor) isolated-CNN model is re-utilized to re-adjust the neurons’ weights for classifying brain MRI images into tumor subclasses using the transfer-learning concept. As a result, the developed transfer-learned model has a high accuracy of 95.75% for the MRI images of the same MRI machine. Furthermore, the developed transfer-learned model has also been tested using the brain MRI images of another machine to validate its adaptability, general capability, and reliability for real-time application in the future.
papers.result: The results showed that the proposed model has a high accuracy of 96.89% for an unseen brain MRI dataset. Thus, the proposed deep-learning framework can help doctors and radiologists diagnose brain tumors early.
papers.gap: 2D slices from web datasets; possible patient overlap; no uncertainty or external clinical test.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors trained small CNNs from scratch on public 2D brain MRI slices and then transferred the best one to other datasets for tumour detection and three-class tumour typing. Results were high on curated 2D Kaggle-type data. Such datasets are useful for quick baselines but do not reflect 3D clinical MRI, so their accuracy should not be expected locally.
papers.studyDesign: Model development on public MRI datasets (Jouf University and partners, Saudi Arabia).
papers.datasets: Dataset I: 3,000 Kaggle MRI images (tumour/no tumour); Dataset II: 2,870 Kaggle images (glioma 826, meningioma 822, no tumour 395, pituitary 827); Dataset III: 3,064 slices from 233 patients (Figshare, Chinese hospitals: glioma 1,426, meningioma 708, pituitary 930).
papers.preprocessing: Extreme-point cropping, erosion and dilation for noise removal, resizing to 227x227, scaling.
papers.modelDetails: Isolated CNNs built from scratch (19, 22, 25 layers) for 2-, 3- and 4-class tasks; best CNN reused as a transfer-learning model on another dataset.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on held-out and unseen datasets.
papers.baselines: Isolated CNNs and pretrained networks.
papers.results: Transfer-learned model reached 96.89% accuracy on an unseen brain MRI dataset.

papers.title: Deep Transfer Learning Approaches in Performance Analysis of Brain Tumor Classification Using MRI Images
papers.authors: Srinivas C, K S NP, Zakariah M, Alothaibi YA, Shaukat K, Partibane B, Awal H
papers.aim: Brain tumor classification is a very important and the most prominent step for assessing life-threatening abnormal tissues and providing an efficient treatment in patient recovery. To identify pathological conditions in the brain, there exist various medical imaging technologies.
papers.method: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is extensively used in medical imaging due to its excellent image quality and independence from ionizing radiations. The significance of deep learning, a subset of artificial intelligence in the area of medical diagnosis applications, has macadamized the path in rapid developments for brain tumor detection from MRI to higher prediction rate. For brain tumor analysis and classification, the convolution neural network (CNN) is the most extensive and widely used deep learning algorithm. In this work, we present a comparative performance analysis of transfer learning-based CNN-pretrained VGG-16, ResNet-50, and Inception-v3 models for automatic prediction of tumor cells in the brain. Pretrained models are demonstrated on the MRI brain tumor images dataset consisting of 233 images. Our paper aims to locate brain tumors with the utilization of the VGG-16 pretrained CNN model.
papers.result: The performance of our model will be evaluated on accuracy. As an outcome, we can estimate that the pretrained model VGG-16 determines highly adequate results with an increase in the accuracy rate of training and validation.
papers.gap: Very small JPEG dataset; no patient-level split, no uncertainty, no external test.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Several ImageNet-pretrained networks were fine-tuned on a very small public set of 2D brain MRI images to detect tumours, and their accuracy and errors compared. It illustrates transfer learning on scarce data but also how unstable such small-sample results are; false negatives are particularly concerning clinically.
papers.studyDesign: Model comparison on a small public dataset (India, Saudi Arabia, Australia, Ghana authors; Journal of Healthcare Engineering 2022).
papers.datasets: Kaggle brain MRI set of about 256 JPEG images labelled tumour yes/no (158 and 98 images); split into training, validation and test.
papers.preprocessing: Resizing to 256x256, intensity normalisation (z-score), cropping.
papers.modelDetails: Transfer learning with ImageNet-pretrained CNNs (VGG-16, ResNet-50, Inception-v3 and others) with frozen convolutional layers and new classification heads.
papers.training: Fine-tuning details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, confusion matrices, training/validation curves.
papers.baselines: Comparison among pretrained architectures.
papers.results: VGG-16 performed best; ResNet-50 showed unstable validation accuracy and many false negatives (11 of 31).

papers.title: Multiconvolutional Transfer Learning for 3D Brain Tumor Magnetic Resonance Images
papers.authors: Sangeetha SKB, Muthukumaran V, Deeba K, Rajadurai H, Maheshwari V, Dalu GT
papers.aim: The difficulty or cost of obtaining data or labels in applications like medical imaging has progressed less quickly. If deep learning techniques can be implemented reliably, automated workflows and more sophisticated analysis may be possible in previously unexplored areas of medical imaging.
papers.method: In addition, numerous characteristics of medical images, such as their high resolution, three-dimensional nature, and anatomical detail across multiple size scales, can increase the complexity of their analysis. This study employs multiconvolutional transfer learning (MCTL) for applying deep learning to small medical imaging datasets in an effort to address these issues. Multiconvolutional transfer learning is a model based on transfer learning that enables deep learning with small datasets. In order to learn new features on a smaller target dataset, an initial baseline is used in the transfer learning process. In this study, 3D MRI images of brain tumors are classified using a convolutional autoencoder method. In order to use unenhanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) for clinical diagnosis, expensive and invasive contrast-enhancing procedures must be performed.
papers.result: MCTL has been shown to increase accuracy by 1.5%, indicating that small targets are more easily detected with MCTL. This research can be applied to a wide range of medical imaging and diagnostic procedures, including improving the accuracy of brain tumor severity diagnosis through the use of MRI.
papers.gap: Very small cohort; low specificity; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: An autoencoder is pretrained to reconstruct 3D medical images and its features are transferred to a small tumour-classification task with 45 patients, evaluated with repeated leave-one-out cross-validation. Pretraining beat random initialisation. It is a small example of self-supervised feature learning for scarce 3D data, though specificity remained low.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on a public 3D MRI dataset (SRM, VIT and other Indian institutions; Computational Intelligence and Neuroscience 2022).
papers.datasets: REMBRANDT-derived 3D brain MRI from 45 patients (T2-weighted fat-saturated coronal images), patients aged 18-45.
papers.preprocessing: Synthetic augmentations (32 per sample, 764-image training sets).
papers.modelDetails: Multi-convolutional transfer learning (MCTL): a convolutional autoencoder learns features from different 3D medical imaging datasets, then transferred to tumour/healthy classification.
papers.training: Grid search over hyperparameters; leave-one-out cross-validation repeated 15 times.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity.
papers.baselines: SVM, KNN, naive Bayes, DNN, CNN.
papers.results: Best average validation accuracy about 94% (specificity about 73%); MCTL improved accuracy by about 1.5% over CNN baselines.

papers.title: Nationwide federated learning for histopathology: secure deployment across Germany behind firewalls
papers.authors: Babendererde N, Lemke N, Stieber J, Fuchs M, Weng Z, Eich ML, Lingscheidt T, Mairinger F, Büttner R, Tolkach Y, et al.
papers.aim: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training across institutions without sharing sensitive data, a solution for privacy-preserving AI in medical imaging. However, hospital deployment remains challenging due to strict data protection regulations, heterogeneous infrastructures, and limited network accessibility behind firewalls.
papers.method: We introduce TheODen, an open-source framework for Federated training on histopathology Whole Slide Imaging (WSI). It requires no open client-side ports, enabling training through firewalls via a secure reverse-proxy architecture. We conducted, to our knowledge, the first nationwide FL study for histopathology segmentation of colorectal cancer across three German university hospitals, using breast and colorectal cancer datasets without opening firewall ports.
papers.result: TheODen achieves robust segmentation, with global average dice scores of 0.764 on BCSS and 0.754 on SemiCOL despite data heterogeneity and network constraints. These findings underline TheODen’s potential to facilitate secure, large-scale collaborations between medical institutions and to accelerate clinical translation of AI models under real-world infrastructure constraints, providing a privacy-preserving-by-design architecture for future collaborations.
papers.gap: Segmentation of non-brain tissue; no calibration analysis after aggregation.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Three sites; public datasets partitioned to sites.
papers.methodologyDetail: TheODen was deployed on real hospital infrastructure in three German university hospitals behind their firewalls, with clients connecting outward through a secure reverse proxy so no hospital had to open network ports. Federated segmentation models for breast and colorectal pathology reached performance near central training. It addresses the practical IT barriers that federated learning will face in Sri Lankan hospitals.
papers.studyDesign: Real-world nationwide federated deployment across three German university hospitals (Cologne, Essen, Leipzig) with a new open-source framework (TU Darmstadt and partners; npj Digital Medicine 2026).
papers.datasets: BCSS: 144 TCGA breast cancer H&E WSIs (0.25 um/px, 256x256 patches; per client 34 train, 7 validation, 7 test cases); SemiCOL colorectal cancer slides from two hospitals (subset of 20 multi-site cases and more).
papers.preprocessing: Patching at 256x256; data partitioned per hospital client.
papers.modelDetails: TheODen: federated training framework requiring no open client-side ports, using a secure reverse-proxy architecture; abstract-server and control-server modes; pluggable aggregation methods, datasets and models; segmentation networks trained federatedly.
papers.training: Federated configurations and hardware per site described in methods.
papers.evaluation: Global average Dice on test sets; comparison with centralised and local training; robustness to heterogeneity and network constraints.
papers.baselines: Centralised training and single-site (local) training.
papers.results: Global average Dice 0.764 (BCSS) and 0.754 (SemiCOL) despite heterogeneity and firewall constraints, close to centralised performance.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Histopathology Image Classification: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Touhami M, Ahmad Fauzi MF, Ur Rehman Z, Mansor S
papers.aim: Background/Objective: The integration of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) has significantly enhanced medical image classification, especially in histopathology, by improving diagnostic accuracy and aiding clinical decision making. However, data privacy concerns and restrictions on sharing patient data limit the development of effective DL models.
papers.method: Federated learning (FL) offers a promising solution by enabling collaborative model training across institutions without exposing sensitive data. This systematic review aims to comprehensively evaluate the current state of FL applications in histopathological image classification by identifying prevailing methodologies, datasets, and performance metrics and highlighting existing challenges and future research directions. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, 24 studies published between 2020 and 2025 were analyzed. The literature was retrieved from ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, MDPI, Springer Nature Link, PubMed, and arXiv. Eligible studies focused on FL-based deep learning models for histopathology image classification with reported performance metrics. Studies unrelated to FL in histopathology or lacking accessible full texts were excluded. Results: The included studies utilized 10 datasets (8 public, 1 private, and 1 unspecified) and reported classification accuracies ranging from 69.37% to 99.72%. FedAvg was the most commonly used aggregation algorithm (14 studies), followed by FedProx, FedDropoutAvg, and custom approaches. Only two studies reported their FL frameworks (Flower and OpenFL). Frequently employed model architectures included VGG, ResNet, DenseNet, and EfficientNet. Performance was typically evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Federated learning demonstrates strong potential for privacy-preserving digital pathology applications. However, key challenges remain, including communication overhead, computational demands, and inconsistent reporting standards.
papers.result: Addressing these issues is essential for broader clinical adoption. Conclusions: Future work should prioritize standardized evaluation protocols, efficient aggregation methods, model personalization, robustness, and interpretability, with validation across multi-institutional clinical environments to fully realize the benefits of FL in histopathological image classification.
papers.gap: No meta-analysis; few real deployments in included studies.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The review collects federated learning studies for histopathology classification published between 2020 and 2025, tabulating datasets, methods, strengths and weaknesses. Most studies simulate federation on public data and assume similar data at each site; real multi-hospital validation is rare. It frames the gap that WP5 addresses.
papers.studyDesign: PRISMA systematic review (Multimedia University, KPJ Healthcare University, Malaysia); no registered protocol.
papers.datasets: Studies (2020-2025) applying federated learning to histopathology image classification (e.g. LC25000, TCGA CRC-DX, BreakHis, HAM10000, TCGA, MC-CRC datasets).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Systematic search, eligibility screening and data extraction of FL architectures, aggregation methods, privacy techniques and performance.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Narrative and tabular synthesis of performance, advantages and limitations.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: FL achieves performance comparable to centralised learning in many studies, but issues include IID assumptions, non-IID performance drops, communication and encryption costs, and lack of large-scale validation; recommends standardised evaluation, efficient communication and real deployments.

papers.title: Federated learning and differential privacy for medical image analysis
papers.authors: Adnan M, Kalra S, Cresswell JC, Taylor GW, Tizhoosh HR
papers.aim: The artificial intelligence revolution has been spurred forward by the availability of large-scale datasets. In contrast, the paucity of large-scale medical datasets hinders the application of machine learning in healthcare.
papers.method: The lack of publicly available multi-centric and diverse datasets mainly stems from confidentiality and privacy concerns around sharing medical data. To demonstrate a feasible path forward in medical image imaging, we conduct a case study of applying a differentially private federated learning framework for analysis of histopathology images, the largest and perhaps most complex medical images. We study the effects of IID and non-IID distributions along with the number of healthcare providers, i.e., hospitals and clinics, and the individual dataset sizes, using The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) dataset, a public repository, to simulate a distributed environment. We empirically compare the performance of private, distributed training to conventional training and demonstrate that distributed training can achieve similar performance with strong privacy guarantees.
papers.result: We also study the effect of different source domains for histopathology images by evaluating the performance using external validation. Our work indicates that differentially private federated learning is a viable and reliable framework for the collaborative development of machine learning models in medical image analysis.
papers.gap: Simulated federation; no calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: WSIs are summarised into a representative mosaic of patches, encoded with a pretrained network, and classified with attention-based multiple-instance learning. Each simulated hospital trains locally with differential privacy and the server averages models. The study varies the number of hospitals, their data size and how different their data are, and checks external validity. It supports the feasibility of private federated pathology for WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Simulation case study of differentially private federated learning on public histopathology data (University of Waterloo, Vector Institute, Layer 6; Scientific Reports 2022).
papers.datasets: TCGA whole-slide images (lung cancer subtype tasks) distributed across simulated hospitals with IID and non-IID splits and varying client numbers and dataset sizes; external validation on a different source domain.
papers.preprocessing: Mosaic patch selection per WSI: tissue thresholding, clustering of patches, random 10% per cluster; 1000x1000 patches at 20x (0.5 mpp); DenseNet features.
papers.modelDetails: Attention-based multiple-instance learning (MEM model) trained locally with DP-SGD for quantitative privacy bounds and aggregated by FedAvg.
papers.training: DP-SGD with varying privacy budgets; FedAvg rounds (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Classification accuracy/AUC vs centralised training; effect of privacy budget, number of clients, IID vs non-IID; external validation.
papers.baselines: Centralised (non-private) training.
papers.results: Differentially private federated training achieved performance close to centralised training with strong privacy guarantees; non-IID data and small sites reduced performance.

papers.title: IDH Mutation Assessment in Gliomas from Anatomical MRI Using Deep Learning: A Comparative Analysis of Centralized and Federated Learning Frameworks
papers.authors: Bas A, Ozturk-Isik E
papers.aim: Background/Objectives: Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation is a key prognostic indicator in diffuse gliomas; however, it is clinically determined from invasive tissue sampling. Non-invasive preoperative identification of IDH mutation from routine anatomical MRI could support treatment decision making.
papers.method: This study evaluated deep learning models for IDH mutation detection using routine anatomical MRI (post-contrast T1-weighted (T1c), T2-weighted, and fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI) and quantified how tumor-focused image preprocessing and different training schemes, centralized learning (CL) versus federated learning (FL) with alternative aggregation strategies, affected model performance. Methods: Anatomical MRI from 501 diffuse glioma patients in the UCSF Preoperative Diffuse Glioma MRI (UCSF-PDGM) dataset was analyzed using a deep learning classifier built on a 2D U-Net encoder, with age and sex included as covariates. Two methods of tumor-focused image preprocessing, Naïve Soft Filtering (NSF) and Gradient-Based Soft Filtering (GBSF), were compared. Centralized learning (CL) was benchmarked against federated learning (FL) using Federated Averaging (FA) and Federated Trimmed Mean (FTM) aggregation strategies. Model performance was compared in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, specificity, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC). Results: The CL model with NSF achieved the best test performance (accuracy = 0.949, F1 = 0.951, ROC-AUC = 0.971), with NSF consistently outperforming GBSF. FL’s performance decreased relative to CL’s, but the FA strategy outperformed FTM (FTM accuracy = 0.915 vs. FA accuracy = 0.949), which indicates that the FL aggregation strategy has an influence on model performance. Conclusions: Deep learning applied to routine anatomical MRI could classify IDH mutation status with high accuracy.
papers.result: Context-preserving image preprocessing with NSF substantially improved performance across training schemes. FL provides a privacy-preserving alternative to CL, but incurs a measurable performance degradation that is sensitive to the choice of aggregation strategy.
papers.gap: Simulated federation; 2D slices; no calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a public glioma dataset with expert segmentations, the authors predict IDH mutation from routine MRI slices, comparing ways of emphasising the tumour while keeping surrounding context, and compare central training with federated training across simulated sites. Keeping context helped, and federation cost some accuracy. It quantifies the federation trade-off for a brain-tumour molecular task relevant to H5.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective comparison of centralised and federated learning (Bogazici University, Istanbul; Diagnostics 2026).
papers.datasets: UCSF-PDGM: 501 pre-operative diffuse gliomas (103 IDH-mutant, 398 wild-type), 3T GE MRI (T1c IR-SPGR, 3D T2 FSE, FLAIR) with expert-corrected multi-compartment segmentations.
papers.preprocessing: Resampling to 1 mm isotropic, nonlinear co-registration with ANTs, deep-learning skull stripping; tumour ROI from combined compartments; Naive Soft Filtering (non-tumour weight 0.3) or Gradient-Based Soft Filtering; axial slices with FLAIR, T1c, T2 mapped to RGB channels.
papers.modelDetails: 2D CNN classifiers for IDH status trained centrally or with federated learning across simulated clients.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity for IDH prediction; centralised vs federated.
papers.baselines: Centralised learning; hard tumour masking.
papers.results: Context-preserving soft filtering substantially improved performance across training schemes; federated learning was a privacy-preserving alternative but with some performance cost relative to centralised training.

papers.title: Byzantine robust federated learning for heterogeneous brain MRI using multisignal gradient fingerprinting and adaptive trust aggregation
papers.authors: Karami M, Kebriaei H, Ghassemi F, Azadegan H
papers.aim: Federated learning enables collaborative training across institutions without centralizing patient data, but remains vulnerable to malicious clients and severe non-IID data heterogeneity. We propose a trust-aware federated learning framework for brain MRI that combines multi-signal gradient fingerprinting with adaptive aggregation to achieve Byzantine robustness.
papers.method: Each client update is characterized by a six-dimensional fingerprint (variational-autoencoder reconstruction error, cosine similarity to a server reference, peer similarity, gradient norm, sign consistency, and Monte Carlo Shapley contribution). A dual-attention module and a reinforcement-learning controller map these signals into trust weights and integrate with FedBN-P (Federated Batch Normalization with Proximal regularization), an optimizer co-designed for stability under heterogeneous and adversarial conditions. We evaluate on MNIST, CIFAR-10, Alzheimer’s MRI, and the OASIS brain-MRI cohort (approximately 87 test samples, used strictly as proof-of-concept) under both standard and strengthened threat models (up to 40% malicious clients). Attack-specific ablation confirms a defense-in-depth design: VAE fingerprinting is the primary noise-attack defense (3.60 pp accuracy drop upon removal), Shapley values safeguard accuracy under scaling (10.16 pp drop), and reinforcement learning improves detection consistency under dynamic attack schedules. Three-seed paired-test validation further shows detection F1 outperforms FLTrust by up to 44 pp on Non-IID Gaussian noise; a white-box adaptive attacker degrades the detector but not model accuracy, confirming the layered design. End-to-end wall-clock overhead is + 8.8% over FedAvg with identical communication volume.
papers.result: The framework achieves F1 above 0.98 for gradient-scaling attacks while preserving accuracy under magnitude-preserving attacks where explicit detection remains limited. Multi-site validation on larger federated cohorts (e.g., ADNI, UK Biobank, FeTS) is required before any clinical-deployment claim can be made.
papers.gap: Classification, not tumour segmentation; adaptive parts not fully exercised in clinical runs.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The framework protects federated training on brain MRI from malicious or corrupted hospital updates by describing each update with several signals of plausibility and contribution, learning trust weights for aggregation, and combining this with a batch-normalisation-aware optimiser suited to heterogeneous sites. It was tested on benchmark data and a clinical brain MRI cohort under strengthened attacks. Robust aggregation is a safeguard for a federation in which sites may have faulty data.
papers.studyDesign: Method development with benchmark and clinical MRI validation (Sharif University of Technology and partners; Scientific Reports 2026).
papers.datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10, an Alzheimer's MRI dataset (proof of concept) and the OASIS clinical brain-MRI cohort (clinical validation); simulated clients with IID, Dirichlet and label-skew (70%, 90%) partitions.
papers.preprocessing: Partitioned into clients; attacks injected (30-40% malicious clients: scaling, sign flip, Gaussian noise, label flip).
papers.modelDetails: Trust-aware federated learning: each client update gets a six-dimensional fingerprint (VAE reconstruction error, cosine similarity to server reference, peer similarity, gradient norm, sign consistency, Monte Carlo Shapley contribution); a dual-attention module and reinforcement-learning controller map fingerprints to trust weights within FedBN-P (FedBN with proximal regularisation).
papers.training: Multiple seeds with mean, SD and 95% CIs; 8-round clinical runs used warm-started VAE/RL modules.
papers.evaluation: Detection F1 for malicious clients, accuracy under attacks and heterogeneity, scalability.
papers.baselines: Widely used Byzantine-robust defences (e.g. Krum, trimmed mean, median, FLTrust) and FedAvg.
papers.results: Detection F1 above 0.98 for gradient-scaling attacks while preserving accuracy under magnitude-preserving attacks where explicit detection was limited; robust under non-IID splits.
papers.statistics: Means, SDs and 95% CIs; statistical comparisons with baselines.

papers.title: Federated learning for lesion segmentation in multiple sclerosis: a real-world multi-center feasibility study
papers.authors: Hindawi S, Szubstarski B, Boernert E, Tackenberg B, Wuerfel J
papers.aim: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neuroinflammatory disease driven by immune-mediated central nervous system damage, often leading to progressive disability. Accurate segmentation of MS lesions on MRI is crucial for monitoring disease and treatment efficacy; however, manual segmentation remains time-consuming and prone to variability.
papers.method: While deep learning has advanced automated segmentation, robust performance benefits from large-scale, diverse datasets, yet data pooling is restricted by privacy regulations and clinical performance remains challenged by inter-site heterogeneity. In this proof-of-concept work, we aim to apply and adopt Federated Learning (FL) in a real-world hospital setting. We assessed FL for MS lesion segmentation using the self-configuring nnU-Net model, leveraging 512 MRI cases from three sites without sharing raw patient data. The federated model achieved Dice scores ranging from 0.66 to 0.80 across held-out test sets.
papers.result: While performance varied across sites, reflecting data heterogeneity, the study demonstrates the potential of FL as a scalable and secure paradigm for advancing automated MS analysis in distributed clinical environments. This work supports adopting secure, collaborative AI in neuroimaging, offering utility for privacy-sensitive clinical research and a starting point for medical AI development, bridging the gap between model generalizability and regulatory compliance.
papers.gap: No calibration or uncertainty analysis; MS lesions rather than tumours.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Three hospitals trained one MS lesion segmentation model together using nnU-Net, an open-source imaging platform for local execution and a governance layer that kept each institution in control of what ran on its data. Fifty rounds of one local epoch each worked best, as more local training destabilised FedAvg. It is a practical template for deploying nnU-Net federatedly in hospitals.
papers.studyDesign: Real-world multi-centre feasibility study of federated learning (Roche with three hospital sites; Frontiers in Neurology 2025).
papers.datasets: 512 MRI cases from three sites for MS lesion segmentation, without sharing raw data.
papers.preprocessing: Local preprocessing and nnU-Net configuration at each site.
papers.modelDetails: Self-configuring nnU-Net trained with FedAvg in a client-server architecture built on Kaapana (open-source imaging platform) with Apheris enterprise governance for secure, governed execution.
papers.training: 50 federated rounds, one local epoch per round (more local epochs caused abrupt degradation).
papers.evaluation: Dice and lesion-level metrics per site vs local models.
papers.baselines: Locally trained models.
papers.results: Federated model achieved competitive segmentation; performance varied across sites due to heterogeneity; most loss reduction in first 10-15 rounds.

papers.title: Magnetic resonance imaging-based deep learning for predicting subtypes of glioma
papers.authors: Yang Z, Zhang P, Ding Y, Deng L, Zhang T, Liu Y
papers.aim: PurposeTo explore the value of deep learning based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in the classification of glioma subtypes.MethodsThis study retrospectively included 747 adult patients with surgically pathologically confirmed gliomas from a public database and 64 patients from our hospital. Patients were classified into IDH-wildtype (IDHwt) (490 cases), IDH-mutant/1p19q-noncodeleted (IDHmut-intact) (105 cases), and IDH-mutant/1p19q-codeleted (IDHmut-codel) (216 cases) based on their pathological findings, with the public database of patients were divided into training and validation sets, and patients from our hospital were used as an independent test set.
papers.result: The models were developed based on five categories of preoperative T1-weighted, T1-weighted gadolinium contrast-enhanced, T2-weighted and T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (T1w, T1c, T2w and FLAIR) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of four sequences and mixed imaging of the four sequences, respectively. The receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC), area under the curve (AUC) of the ROC were generated in the jupyter notebook tool using python language to evaluate the accuracy of the models in classification and comparing the predictive value of different MRI sequences.ResultsIDHwt, IDHmut-intact and IDHmut-codel were the best classified in the model containing only FLAIR sequences, with test set AUCs of 0.790, 0.737 and 0.820, respectively; and the worst classified in the model containing only T1w sequences, with test set AUCs of 0.621, 0.537 and 0.760, respectively.ConclusionWe have developed a set of models that can effectively classify glioma subtypes and that work best when only the FLAIR sequence model is included.
papers.gap: Small local test set; no uncertainty; imaging-only molecular prediction remains imperfect.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors pooled four public glioma MRI datasets for training and validation and tested on their own hospital's patients, predicting the three main WHO 2021 molecular groups from routine sequences. Using all four sequences worked best. Training on public data and testing on a local cohort mirrors the planned strategy for the MRI Agent in Sri Lanka.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-dataset study with an independent local test set (Hefei and Xuzhou hospitals, China; ethics XYFY2022-KL476-01).
papers.datasets: 811 adult gliomas: TCGA-LGG (86), TCGA-GBM (88), UCSF-PDGM (382), Erasmus Glioma Database (191) for training/validation, and 64 local patients (2019-2022) as independent test; IDH-wildtype 490, IDH-mutant 1p/19q intact 105, IDH-mutant co-deleted 216.
papers.preprocessing: Inclusion required T1w, T1c, T2w and FLAIR and clear molecular status; poor-quality scans excluded after consensus of two physicians; ROI delineation.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning models built on five input categories (each sequence and all sequences combined) for three-class WHO 2021 molecular subtype prediction.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUC, precision, recall, F1 per subtype on validation and independent test.
papers.baselines: Single-sequence models.
papers.results: The all-sequence model gave the best AUCs for the three subtypes on the independent test set (exact values in paper).
papers.statistics: Chi-square, Kruskal-Wallis with Bonferroni; ROC analysis in Python.

papers.title: Deep-learning and conventional radiomics to predict IDH genotyping status based on magnetic resonance imaging data in adult diffuse glioma
papers.authors: Zhang H, Fan X, Zhang J, Wei Z, Feng W, Hu Y, Ni J, Yao F, Zhou G, Wan C, et al.
papers.aim: ObjectivesIn adult diffuse glioma, preoperative detection of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) status helps clinicians develop surgical strategies and evaluate patient prognosis. Here, we aim to identify an optimal machine-learning model for prediction of IDH genotyping by combining deep-learning (DL) signatures and conventional radiomics (CR) features as model predictors.MethodsIn this study, a total of 486 patients with adult diffuse gliomas were retrospectively collected from our medical center (n=268) and the public database (TCGA, n=218).
papers.method: All included patients were randomly divided into the training and validation sets by using nested 10-fold cross-validation. A total of 6,736 CR features were extracted from four MRI modalities in each patient, namely T1WI, T1CE, T2WI, and FLAIR. The LASSO algorithm was performed for CR feature selection. In each MRI modality, we applied a CNN+LSTM–based neural network to extract DL features and integrate these features into a DL signature after the fully connected layer with sigmoid activation. Eight classic machine-learning models were analyzed and compared in terms of their prediction performance and stability in IDH genotyping by combining the LASSO–selected CR features and integrated DL signatures as model predictors. In the validation sets, the prediction performance was evaluated by using accuracy and the area under the curve (AUC) of the receiver operating characteristics, while the model stability was analyzed by using the relative standard deviation of the AUC (RSDAUC). Subgroup analyses of DL signatures and CR features were also individually conducted to explore their independent prediction values.ResultsLogistic regression (LR) achieved favorable prediction performance (AUC: 0.920 ± 0.043, accuracy: 0.843 ± 0.044), whereas support vector machine with the linear kernel (l-SVM) displayed low prediction performance (AUC: 0.812 ± 0.052, accuracy: 0.821 ± 0.050). With regard to stability, LR also showed high robustness against data perturbation (RSDAUC: 4.7%).
papers.result: Subgroup analyses showed that DL signatures outperformed CR features (DL, AUC: 0.915 ± 0.054, accuracy: 0.835 ± 0.061, RSDAUC: 5.9%; CR, AUC: 0.830 ± 0.066, accuracy: 0.771 ± 0.051, RSDAUC: 8.0%), while DL and DL+CR achieved similar prediction results.ConclusionIn IDH genotyping, LR is a promising machine-learning classification model. Compared with CR features, DL signatures exhibit markedly superior prediction values and discriminative capability.
papers.gap: No external test; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: From multi-vendor MRI of nearly 500 gliomas, the authors extracted both deep features and thousands of handcrafted radiomics features and built models to predict IDH mutation, evaluated by nested cross-validation. Deep features were better and combining them improved stability. It shows the heterogeneity typical of real data and a careful validation design.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective study combining public and local data (Nanjing Medical University; Frontiers in Oncology 2023).
papers.datasets: 486 adult diffuse gliomas from TCGA-GBM, TCGA-LGG and the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (2015-2020) with known IDH status and four MRI sequences from 1.5T/3T Philips, GE and Siemens scanners.
papers.preprocessing: Heterogeneous protocols; sequences of 11 consecutive slices with stride 2 (12 samples per patient per modality); 6,736 conventional radiomics features.
papers.modelDetails: Deep-learning signatures and conventional radiomics features combined as predictors in machine-learning models for IDH status.
papers.training: PyTorch, sklearn, PyCaret; SiLU activations, BCE loss, batch 32, lr 1e-6; nested 10-fold cross-validation.
papers.evaluation: AUC, accuracy and relative standard deviation of AUC across folds and subgroups.
papers.baselines: Conventional radiomics alone.
papers.results: DL signatures outperformed radiomics (AUC 0.915 +/- 0.054 vs 0.830; accuracy 0.835), and combined models were most stable.

papers.title: Clinical application of machine-based deep learning in patients with radiologically presumed adult-type diffuse glioma grades 2 or 3
papers.authors: Gómez Vecchio T, Neimantaite A, Thurin E, Furtner J, Solheim O, Pallud J, Berger M, Widhalm G, Bartek J, Häggström I, et al.
papers.aim: AbstractBackgroundRadiologically presumed diffuse lower-grade glioma (dLGG) are typically non or minimal enhancing tumors, with hyperintensity in T2w-images. The aim of this study was to test the clinical usefulness of deep learning (DL) in IDH mutation prediction in patients with radiologically presumed dLGG.MethodsThree hundred and fourteen patients were retrospectively recruited from 6 neurosurgical departments in Sweden, Norway, France, Austria, and the United States.
papers.method: Collected data included patients’ age, sex, tumor molecular characteristics (IDH, and 1p19q), and routine preoperative radiological images. A clinical model was built using multivariable logistic regression with the variables age and tumor location. DL models were built using MRI data only, and 4 DL architectures used in glioma research. In the final validation test, the clinical model and the best DL model were scored on an external validation cohort with 155 patients from the Erasmus Glioma Dataset.ResultsThe mean age in the recruited and external cohorts was 45.0 (SD 14.3) and 44.3 years (SD 14.6).
papers.result: The cohorts were rather similar, except for sex distribution (53.5% vs 64.5% males, P-value = .03) and IDH status (30.9% vs 12.9% IDH wild-type, P-value <.01). Overall, the area under the curve for the prediction of IDH mutations in the external validation cohort was 0.86, 0.82, and 0.87 for the clinical model, the DL model, and the model combining both models’ probabilities.ConclusionsIn their current state, when these complex models were applied to our clinical scenario, they did not seem to provide a net gain compared to our baseline clinical model.
papers.gap: WHO 2016 classification; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a large international cohort of presumed lower-grade gliomas, the authors compared a deep learning IDH predictor with a simple clinical model and tested both on an unseen external dataset. Deep learning did not clearly add value in this clinically realistic setting. This is an important negative result supporting cautious use of imaging-only molecular prediction and a fair comparison with simple baselines.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multicentre study with external validation (University of Gothenburg and neurosurgical departments in Sweden, Norway, France, Austria and the USA; Neuro-Oncology Advances 2024).
papers.datasets: 1,576 screened; 469 adults with WHO 2016 diffuse glioma grade 2-3 included (modelling cohort from six departments plus Erasmus Glioma Database as unseen external cohort); 75% IDH-mutant, 37% 1p/19q co-deleted.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusions for other diagnoses (570), missing molecular data (181) and missing sequences after processing (356); routine pre-operative MRI.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning model for IDH mutation from routine MRI compared with a clinical multivariable model (age, sex, imaging features) and combined models.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, clinical usefulness (e.g. high-specificity operating points) on the external cohort.
papers.baselines: Clinical model based on age and simple imaging features.
papers.results: In radiologically presumed lower-grade glioma, deep learning was not clearly superior to conventional clinical models for IDH prediction; cohorts differed in sex distribution and IDH wild-type rate (30.9% vs 12.9%).

papers.title: Federated radiomics analysis of preoperative MRI across institutions: toward integrated glioma segmentation and molecular subtyping
papers.authors: Ren R, Zhu A, Li Y, Liu H, Huang G, Gu J, Ni J, Miao Z
papers.aim: BackgroundNon-invasive and comprehensive molecular characterization of glioma is crucial for personalized treatment but remains limited by invasive biopsy procedures and stringent privacy restrictions on clinical data sharing. Federated learning (FL) provides a promising solution by enabling multi-institutional collaboration without compromising patient confidentiality.MethodsWe propose a multi-task 3D deep neural network framework based on federated learning.
papers.method: Using multi-modal MRI images, without sharing the original data, the automatic segmentation of T2w high signal region and the prediction of four molecular markers (IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion, MGMT promoter methylation, WHO grade) were completed in collaboration with multiple medical institutions. We trained the model on local patient data at independent clients and aggregated the model parameters on a central server to achieve distributed collaborative learning.
papers.result: The model was trained on five public datasets (n = 1,552) and evaluated on an external validation dataset (n = 466).ResultsThe model showed good performance in the external test set (IDH AUC = 0.88, 1p/19q AUC = 0.84, MGMT AUC = 0.85, grading AUC = 0.94), and the median Dice of the segmentation task was 0.85.ConclusionsOur federated multi-task deep learning model demonstrates the feasibility and effectiveness of predicting glioma molecular characteristics and grade from multi-parametric MRI, without compromising patient privacy. These findings suggest significant potential for clinical deployment, especially in scenarios where invasive tissue sampling is impractical or risky.
papers.gap: Simulated institutions; no calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study treats each public glioma dataset as a separate institution and trains a single federated model that both segments the tumour region and predicts several molecular markers, then tests it on an external cohort. It demonstrates federated multi-task learning for integrated glioma analysis.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective federated multi-task study with external validation (Jiangnan University and partners; Frontiers in Radiology 2025).
papers.datasets: Training on five public datasets (BraTS 2021 without overlaps, UPENN-GBM 671, TCGA-GBM, TCGA-LGG, REMBRANDT; n = 1,552) treated as separate institutions; external validation dataset of 466 patients.
papers.preprocessing: Skull stripping and co-registration as provided; no exclusion for image quality; T1w, T1c, T2w, FLAIR required.
papers.modelDetails: Federated multi-task model that segments the T2w hyperintense region and predicts four molecular markers (e.g. IDH, 1p/19q and others) from multi-modal MRI with radiomics features, without sharing raw data.
papers.training: Federated training across dataset-sites (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice for segmentation; AUC for molecular predictions on external validation.
papers.baselines: Locally trained and centralised models.
papers.results: Good segmentation and molecular-prediction performance on the external dataset of 466 patients.

papers.title: The University of Texas Southwestern Glioma Dataset - MRI, Molecular Markers and Segmentations
papers.authors: Reddy DD, Saadat N, Holcomb JM, Wagner BC, Truong NC, Bowerman J, Hatanpaa KJ, Patel TR, Pinho MC, Yu F, et al.
papers.aim: Gliomas are the most common type of primary brain tumors. Their management options and outcomes depend significantly on the underlying molecular-marker profile.
papers.method: Traditionally, molecular markers are determined through pathological testing on a tissue specimen acquired through biopsy. Several Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) based Deep Learning (DL) methods offer a promising, non-invasive approach to predict these markers. However, they often require high-quality, well-annotated datasets. To support this need, we present a well-curated brain tumor dataset developed at The University of Texas Southwestern (UTSW) Medical Center. This dataset includes multi-contrast-MRI, demographics, molecular-markers, and multi-label tumor segmentations for 625 patients treated at UTSW between 2006 and 2023. Each patient record contains four MRI contrasts: pre-contrast-T1w, post-contrast-T1w, T2w, and T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (T2w-FLAIR) images. The dataset also provides comprehensive genetic information, including IDH mutation-status, 1p19q co-deletion, MGMT promoter methylation, tumor-type, and tumor-grade.
papers.result: This dataset offers a valuable resource for exploring the relationship between MRI characteristics and tumor genetics. It also serves as a robust benchmark for developing and validating DL models for various downstream tasks.
papers.gap: Single US institution.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper releases a large single-institution glioma MRI dataset with molecular markers and segmentations, documenting acquisition, preprocessing and validation. It is a candidate external test set for the MRI Agent and for imaging-marker experiments.
papers.studyDesign: Data descriptor (UT Southwestern Medical Center; Scientific Data 2026).
papers.datasets: UTSW glioma cohort: pre-operative multi-parametric MRI with molecular markers (e.g. IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT) and tumour segmentations.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised preprocessing (registration, skull stripping) and segmentation curation described in the paper.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (dataset release with technical validation).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Technical validation of image quality and segmentations.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Provides a public benchmark linking MRI features with tumour genetics and segmentations.

papers.title: Lightweight self supervised learning framework for domain generalization in histopathology
papers.authors: Shafique A, Dy A, Qin X, Alshamlan N, Androutsos D, Done SJ, Khademi A
papers.aim: The emergence of large foundation models (FMs) in histopathology, trained on extensive image datasets using high-performance graphics processing unit (GPU) clusters, has demonstrated significant potential in advancing computational pathology. FMs have potential to overcome the domain gap between training and testing datasets, which creates more translation opportunities.
papers.method: However, the reliance on vast computational resources and large-scale data often limits accessibility and widespread adoption of FMs. To address this limitation, we present HistoLite, a lightweight self-supervised learning framework designed to enable domain-invariant representation learning in histopathology. HistoLite utilizes customizable auto-encoders within a self-supervised learning paradigm that learns generalized and transferable features in an efficient manner. We evaluated the proposed framework using breast Whole Slide Images (WSIs) and benchmarked performance with state-of-the-art FMs for domain generalization. A novel dataset was curated that is of the same tissue slides, scanned by two different scanning platforms, which allows for specific analysis of covariate shifts due to scanner bias. Aspects evaluated include the difference in embeddings across scanners using novel representation shift metrics, including a robustness index, and accuracy, which looks at performance on downstream tasks. The top performing models were UNI, Virchow2 and Prov-GigaPath, likely due to large model sizes and training datasets. In general, most FMs were found to be susceptible to scanner-bias, as shown by differences in embeddings and drop in performance on the held-out scanner.
papers.result: This has significant implications for real-world deployment of FMs in histopathology. HistoLite offered low representation shift in embeddings, the lowest performance drop on out-of-domain data with modest classification accuracy, indicating the smaller model may exhibit a tradeoff between accuracy and generalization.
papers.gap: Breast tissue; no uncertainty output.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: HistoLite trains small autoencoders with contrastive learning on public breast slides to learn features that do not change with the scanner. A carefully designed test scanned the same slides on two scanners and registered them, so the change in features and in classification could be attributed purely to scanner shift. HistoLite was more robust to that shift than much larger foundation models. A lightweight approach suits hospitals with limited GPUs.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and benchmarking against foundation models (Toronto Metropolitan University and partners; Scientific Reports 2025).
papers.datasets: Training: 2,761 public breast cancer WSIs (CAMELYON16, CAMELYON17, HEROHE, TCGA-BRCA). Evaluation: 111 FFPE breast cancer slides from OICR scanned on Aperio AT2 and Sakura VisionTek (222 WSIs), with 9,904 aligned 512x512 patches (2,959 tumour, 1,993 non-tumour per scanner) from pathologist-annotated HPFs.
papers.preprocessing: VisionTek upsampled and affinely registered to Aperio; patches extracted at identical coordinates across scanners at 0.5 mpp.
papers.modelDetails: HistoLite: lightweight dual-stream autoencoder contrastive self-supervised framework (41M parameters; encoder 7.6M per stream) learning domain-invariant features.
papers.training: Self-supervised training with augmentations (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Zero-shot representation shift across scanners; downstream tumour vs non-tumour patch classification.
papers.baselines: Histopathology foundation models (KimiaNet, PathDino, HIPT, iBOT-Path, Hibou-B, UNI, Virchow, Virchow2, Prov-GigaPath).
papers.results: HistoLite had low representation shift between scanners and the lowest performance drop under scanner shift, with far less compute than foundation models, though large FMs had higher absolute accuracy in some settings.

papers.title: Generalizable biomarker prediction from cancer pathology slides with self-supervised deep learning: A retrospective multi-centric study
papers.authors: Niehues JM, Quirke P, West NP, Grabsch HI, van Treeck M, Schirris Y, Veldhuizen GP, Hutchins GGA, Richman SD, Foersch S, et al.
papers.aim: SummaryDeep learning (DL) can predict microsatellite instability (MSI) from routine histopathology slides of colorectal cancer (CRC). However, it is unclear whether DL can also predict other biomarkers with high performance and whether DL predictions generalize to external patient populations.
papers.method: Here, we acquire CRC tissue samples from two large multi-centric studies. We systematically compare six different state-of-the-art DL architectures to predict biomarkers from pathology slides, including MSI and mutations in BRAF, KRAS, NRAS, and PIK3CA.
papers.result: Using a large external validation cohort to provide a realistic evaluation setting, we show that models using self-supervised, attention-based multiple-instance learning consistently outperform previous approaches while offering explainable visualizations of the indicative regions and morphologies. While the prediction of MSI and BRAF mutations reaches a clinical-grade performance, mutation prediction of PIK3CA, KRAS, and NRAS was clinically insufficient.
papers.gap: Colorectal, not brain; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors systematically compared six pipelines for predicting genetic biomarkers from colorectal cancer slides, training on one trial cohort and validating on a large independent cohort. Self-supervised feature extractors combined with attention-based multiple-instance learning generalised best, while some mutations were not predictable. It supports the chosen pathology pipeline (self-supervised encoder + attention MIL) for WP4.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-centric study with large external validation (Dresden, Leeds, Heidelberg and others; Cell Reports Medicine 2023).
papers.datasets: Colorectal cancer H&E slides from two large multi-centric studies (QUASAR trial for training and DACHS for external validation; thousands of patients) with MSI, BRAF, KRAS, NRAS and PIK3CA status.
papers.preprocessing: Tiling, colour normalisation; features from self-supervised encoders.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of six deep learning approaches: ImageNet-pretrained tile-level (INPT) vs self-supervised encoders (Ciga, Wang) with attention-based multiple-instance learning; multi-input models.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUROC for each biomarker, internal and external.
papers.baselines: INPT approach and other architectures.
papers.results: Self-supervised attention MIL (Wang encoder) performed best: AUROC 0.94 (MSI), 0.82 (BRAF), 0.67 (KRAS), 0.52 (NRAS), 0.57 (PIK3CA); MSI and BRAF predictable, others below clinical grade; multi-input models generalised better for BRAF.

papers.title: Self-supervised attention-based deep learning for pan-cancer mutation prediction from histopathology
papers.authors: Saldanha OL, Loeffler CML, Niehues JM, van Treeck M, Seraphin TP, Hewitt KJ, Cifci D, Veldhuizen GP, Ramesh S, Pearson AT, et al.
papers.aim: The histopathological phenotype of tumors reflects the underlying genetic makeup. Deep learning can predict genetic alterations from pathology slides, but it is unclear how well these predictions generalize to external datasets.
papers.result: We performed a systematic study on Deep-Learning-based prediction of genetic alterations from histology, using two large datasets of multiple tumor types. We show that an analysis pipeline that integrates self-supervised feature extraction and attention-based multiple instance learning achieves a robust predictability and generalizability.
papers.gap: No uncertainty; mutation prediction not diagnosis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using two large public multi-cancer collections, the authors trained mutation predictors on one and validated on the other with a standard pipeline of self-supervised tile features and attention-based multiple-instance learning, producing attention maps that show where the prediction came from. Many mutations were predictable externally. Including glioblastoma, it supports the pathology pipeline choice.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective pan-cancer study with external validation (Kather lab, Dresden/Aachen, and Chicago; npj Precision Oncology 2023).
papers.datasets: TCGA and CPTAC H&E slides with matched genetic profiling for tumour types present in both: breast (TCGA 1,066 / CPTAC 122), colorectal (534/105), glioblastoma (397/96), lung adenocarcinoma (566/110) and others; genes with >=25 mutant cases (e.g. 43 genes in endometrial, 4 in pancreatic).
papers.preprocessing: Anonymised public slides; mutation data from cBioPortal excluding variants of unknown significance; tiling.
papers.modelDetails: Open-source marugoto pipeline: self-supervised RetCCL encoder (2,048 features per tile) with attention-based MIL for patient-level mutation prediction; attention and prediction maps.
papers.training: Internal cross-validation on TCGA; external validation on CPTAC.
papers.evaluation: AUROC per gene, internal and external.
papers.baselines: Earlier single-cohort pan-cancer approaches.
papers.results: Self-supervised feature extraction plus attention MIL gave robust predictability and generalisability for many genetic alterations across tumour types, including glioblastoma.
papers.statistics: AUROC with internal and external comparison.

papers.title: Cluster-based histopathology phenotype representation learning by self-supervised multi-class-token hierarchical ViT
papers.authors: Ye J, Kalra S, Miri MS
papers.aim: Developing a clinical AI model necessitates a significant amount of highly curated and carefully annotated dataset by multiple medical experts, which results in increased development time and costs. Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a method that enables AI models to leverage unlabelled data to acquire domain-specific background knowledge that can enhance their performance on various downstream tasks.
papers.method: In this work, we introduce CypherViT, a cluster-based histo-pathology phenotype representation learning by self-supervised multi-class-token hierarchical Vision Transformer (ViT). CypherViT is a novel backbone that can be integrated into a SSL pipeline, accommodating both coarse and fine-grained feature learning for histopathological images via a hierarchical feature agglomerative attention module with multiple classification (cls) tokens in ViT. Our qualitative analysis showcases that our approach successfully learns semantically meaningful regions of interest that align with morphological phenotypes. To validate the model, we utilize the DINO self-supervised learning (SSL) framework to train CypherViT on a substantial dataset of unlabeled breast cancer histopathological images. This trained model proves to be a generalizable and robust feature extractor for colorectal cancer images.
papers.result: Notably, our model demonstrates promising performance in patch-level tissue phenotyping tasks across four public datasets. The results from our quantitative experiments highlight significant advantages over existing state-of-the-art SSL models and traditional transfer learning methods, such as those relying on ImageNet pre-training.
papers.gap: Patch-level only; no brain tissue; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: CypherViT modifies the Vision Transformer to learn both coarse and fine tissue features through several class tokens, trained without labels on breast pathology patches. On other datasets, small amounts of labelled data were enough to match fully supervised performance. It is evidence that self-supervised pathology encoders cut annotation needs.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation on public pathology datasets (Huron Digital Pathology; Scientific Reports 2024).
papers.datasets: SSL training on ~300,000 H&E breast cancer patches (NKI and Vancouver General Hospital cohorts); downstream CRC (100,000 patches, with/without Macenko normalisation), PanNuke and BreastPathQ.
papers.preprocessing: Patches cropped to 224x224 with up to 50% overlap; rotations and flips.
papers.modelDetails: CypherViT: hierarchical Vision Transformer with multiple class tokens and a hierarchical feature agglomerative attention module, trained with DINO self-supervision for cluster-based phenotype representation.
papers.training: Multi-crop augmentation; ablations of local views and stabilisation techniques.
papers.evaluation: KNN and linear-probe accuracy, regression MSE and Kendall tau on downstream tasks; semi-supervised performance with 5-10% labels.
papers.baselines: ImageNet pretraining, SimCLR, MoCo, iBOT, DINO with vanilla ViT, fully supervised.
papers.results: DINO-CypherViT gave strong patch-level phenotyping; with 5% labelled data it approached full-data performance and surpassed it at 10%.

papers.title: A clinical benchmark of public self-supervised pathology foundation models
papers.authors: Campanella G, Chen S, Singh M, Verma R, Muehlstedt S, Zeng J, Stock A, Croken M, Veremis B, Elmas A, et al.
papers.aim: The use of self-supervised learning to train pathology foundation models has increased substantially in the past few years. Notably, several models trained on large quantities of clinical data have been made publicly available in recent months.
papers.method: This will significantly enhance scientific research in computational pathology and help bridge the gap between research and clinical deployment. With the increase in availability of public foundation models of different sizes, trained using different algorithms on different datasets, it becomes important to establish a benchmark to compare the performance of such models on a variety of clinically relevant tasks spanning multiple organs and diseases. In this work, we present a collection of pathology datasets comprising clinical slides associated with clinically relevant endpoints including cancer diagnoses and a variety of biomarkers generated during standard hospital operation from three medical centers.
papers.result: We leverage these datasets to systematically assess the performance of public pathology foundation models and provide insights into best practices for training foundation models and selecting appropriate pretrained models. To enable the community to evaluate their models on our clinical datasets, we make available an automated benchmarking pipeline for external use.
papers.gap: No brain-specific tasks highlighted; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of benchmarks built from public research collections, this study uses real clinical slides to test publicly released pathology foundation models under the same downstream protocol, and examines what in their training explains performance. It provides guidance on which encoder to use as the frozen feature extractor for the Pathology Agent and shows the value of testing on local data.
papers.studyDesign: Clinical benchmark of public pathology foundation models (Mount Sinai, MSKCC and partners; Nature Communications 2025).
papers.datasets: Clinical slide datasets from routine practice across several institutions and cancer types, curated for diagnostic and biomarker tasks and released for benchmarking.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised tiling and feature extraction for each foundation model.
papers.modelDetails: Systematic evaluation of public self-supervised pathology foundation models (e.g. UNI, Virchow, Prov-GigaPath, CTransPath, Phikon and others) with a common slide-level aggregator.
papers.training: Downstream aggregator training per task with consistent protocol.
papers.evaluation: AUC across clinical tasks; analysis of pretraining data size, model size and training recipe.
papers.baselines: All foundation models compared with each other and ImageNet baselines.
papers.results: Foundation models improved over ImageNet features but no single model dominated all tasks; insights on best practices for training and selecting pretrained models; benchmark released.
papers.availability: Datasets and code released for community evaluation.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Learning for 3D Medical Image Analysis using 3D SimCLR and Monte Carlo Dropout
papers.authors: Yamen Ali, Aiham Taleb, Marina M. -C. Höhne, Christoph Lippert
papers.aim: Self-supervised learning methods can be used to learn meaningful representations from unlabeled data that can be transferred to supervised downstream tasks to reduce the need for labeled data. In this paper, we propose a 3D self-supervised method that is based on the contrastive (SimCLR) method.
papers.method: Additionally, we show that employing Bayesian neural networks (with Monte-Carlo Dropout) during the inference phase can further enhance the results on the downstream tasks.
papers.result: We showcase our models on two medical imaging segmentation tasks: i) Brain Tumor Segmentation from 3D MRI, ii) Pancreas Tumor Segmentation from 3D CT. Our experimental results demonstrate the benefits of our proposed methods in both downstream data-efficiency and performance.
papers.gap: Small workshop study; uncertainty used for accuracy, not calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors extend contrastive self-supervised learning to 3D volumes by contrasting augmented versions of the same 3D patch against other patches, then fine-tune the encoder for brain-tumour and pancreatic tumour segmentation with limited labels, and add Monte Carlo dropout at prediction time. Pretraining reduced label needs and MC dropout helped further. It directly supports H3 (self-supervised pretraining on local MRI).
papers.studyDesign: Method development and evaluation (TU Berlin, Hasso Plattner Institute; ML4H 2021).
papers.datasets: Brain tumour segmentation from 3D MRI (BraTS) and pancreas tumour segmentation from 3D CT (Medical Segmentation Decathlon); unlabelled scans for pretraining, limited labels for fine-tuning.
papers.preprocessing: Each 3D scan split into equally sized non-overlapping 3D patches; two random composite augmentations per patch (3D rotation, colour distortion, Gaussian noise/blur, Sobel filtering, identity).
papers.modelDetails: 3D SimCLR: 3D-CNN encoder with non-linear projection head trained with NT-Xent contrastive loss; encoder fine-tuned for segmentation; Monte Carlo dropout at inference.
papers.training: Pretraining then fine-tuning with varying fractions of labelled data (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice on test data with different amounts of labels; effect of MC dropout.
papers.baselines: Training from scratch; 2D SimCLR or other SSL baselines.
papers.results: 3D SimCLR pretraining improved data efficiency and segmentation Dice, and MC dropout at inference further improved results on both tasks.

papers.title: CONSULT: Contrastive Self-Supervised Learning for Few-shot Tumor Detection
papers.authors: Sin Chee Chin, Xuan Zhang, Lee Yeong Khang, Wenming Yang
papers.aim: Artificial intelligence aids in brain tumor detection via MRI scans, enhancing the accuracy and reducing the workload of medical professionals. However, in scenarios with extremely limited medical images, traditional deep learning approaches tend to fail due to the absence of anomalous images.
papers.method: Anomaly detection also suffers from ineffective feature extraction due to vague training process. Our work introduces a novel two-stage anomaly detection algorithm called CONSULT (CONtrastive Self-sUpervised Learning for few-shot Tumor detection). The first stage of CONSULT fine-tunes a pre-trained feature extractor specifically for MRI brain images, using a synthetic data generation pipeline to create tumor-like data. This process overcomes the lack of anomaly samples and enables the integration of attention mechanisms to focus on anomalous image segments. The first stage is to overcome the shortcomings of current anomaly detection in extracting features in high-variation data by incorporating Context-Aware Contrastive Learning and Self-supervised Feature Adversarial Learning. The second stage of CONSULT uses PatchCore for conventional feature extraction via the fine-tuned weights from the first stage. To summarize, we propose a self-supervised training scheme for anomaly detection, enhancing model performance and data reliability.
papers.result: Furthermore, our proposed contrastive loss, Tritanh Loss, stabilizes learning by offering a unique solution all while enhancing gradient flow. Finally, CONSULT achieves superior performance in few-shot brain tumor detection, demonstrating significant improvements over PatchCore by 9.4%, 12.9%, 10.2%, and 6.0% for 2, 4, 6, and 8 shots, respectively, while training exclusively on healthy images.
papers.gap: 2D slices; detection only; synthetic anomalies may not reflect real tumours.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: With only a handful of normal brain scans, CONSULT adapts a feature extractor to brain MRI by contrasting normal images with synthetic tumour-like defects, then detects tumours as anomalies relative to a memory of normal features. It is an approach for detecting unusual cases when labelled tumours are scarce, which can complement the out-of-distribution check in the escalation rule.
papers.studyDesign: Method development for few-shot anomaly detection (Tsinghua University, ViTrox; preprint).
papers.datasets: Public brain MRI dataset; training on 2-8 healthy images only (K2-K8 shots), all tumour images used for validation; images resized to 256x256.
papers.preprocessing: Synthetic tumour-like anomalies generated with Bezier curves; elastic distortion and translation for normal images.
papers.modelDetails: CONSULT: stage 1 fine-tunes a pretrained feature extractor with attention modules on brain MRI using contrastive learning with a new Tritanh loss on synthetic anomalies; stage 2 replaces PatchCore's feature extractor with the fine-tuned one for anomaly detection.
papers.training: Stage 1: 50 epochs, Adam lr 1e-4; stage 2: coreset ratio 10%, k=9 nearest neighbours.
papers.evaluation: Image-level AUROC for tumour detection with 2-8 shots.
papers.baselines: f-AnoGAN, GANomaly, PaDIM, EfficientAD, PatchCore.
papers.results: Outperformed state-of-the-art anomaly detectors in extreme few-shot settings, improving with more shots.

papers.title: BraTS-PEDs: Results of the Multi-Consortium International Pediatric Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge 2023
papers.authors: Anahita Fathi Kazerooni, Nastaran Khalili, Xinyang Liu, Debanjan Haldar, Zhifan Jiang, Anna Zapaishchykova, Julija Pavaine, Lubdha M. Shah, Blaise V. Jones, Nakul Sheth, et al.
papers.aim: Pediatric central nervous system tumors are the leading cause of cancer-related deaths in children. The five-year survival rate for high-grade glioma in children is less than 20%.
papers.method: The development of new treatments is dependent upon multi-institutional collaborative clinical trials requiring reproducible and accurate centralized response assessment. We present the results of the BraTS-PEDs 2023 challenge, the first Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) challenge focused on pediatric brain tumors. This challenge utilized data acquired from multiple international consortia dedicated to pediatric neuro-oncology and clinical trials. BraTS-PEDs 2023 aimed to evaluate volumetric segmentation algorithms for pediatric brain gliomas from magnetic resonance imaging using standardized quantitative performance evaluation metrics employed across the BraTS 2023 challenges. The top-performing AI approaches for pediatric tumor analysis included ensembles of nnU-Net and Swin UNETR, Auto3DSeg, or nnU-Net with a self-supervised framework.
papers.result: The BraTSPEDs 2023 challenge fostered collaboration between clinicians (neuro-oncologists, neuroradiologists) and AI/imaging scientists, promoting faster data sharing and the development of automated volumetric analysis techniques. These advancements could significantly benefit clinical trials and improve the care of children with brain tumors.
papers.gap: Segmentation only; no uncertainty ranking.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: BraTS-PEDs created the first large multi-consortium benchmark for paediatric brain-tumour segmentation, with expert labels on routine-care MRI from many institutions, and summarised the methods of competing teams. Winning approaches were ensembles of nnU-Net, Swin UNETR and related networks. It provides a public set for checking the MRI Agent on paediatric cases, which the registry will include.
