papers.studyDesign: International segmentation challenge and results paper (CBTN, DIPG/DMG Registry, CONNECT and many institutions; MELBA 2024).
papers.datasets: Multi-consortium paediatric high-grade glioma MRI (astrocytoma, DMG/DIPG) with pre- and post-contrast T1, T2 and FLAIR from treatment-naive sessions; heterogeneous protocols and scanners.
papers.preprocessing: Quality control by experienced researchers; exclusion of low-quality scans and infants under one month; standard BraTS preprocessing; expert-refined labels.
papers.modelDetails: Challenge design: participants' methods included ensembles of nnU-Net and Swin UNETR, Auto3DSeg, self-supervised nnU-Net, STU-Net, SegResNet+MedNeXt ensembles, and others.
papers.training: Per team; unlimited validation on the Synapse platform.
papers.evaluation: Lesion-wise Dice and Hausdorff distance on held-out test data; cumulative rank across subjects.
papers.baselines: Participating teams ranked against each other.
papers.results: 18 teams submitted 159 validation entries; nine completed testing; top methods were ensembles of established architectures; the challenge fostered clinician-AI collaboration and data sharing.

papers.title: Imbalance-Aware Self-Supervised Learning for 3D Radiomic Representations
papers.authors: Hongwei Li, Fei-Fei Xue, Krishna Chaitanya, Shengda Luo, Ivan Ezhov, Benedikt Wiestler, Jianguo Zhang, Bjoern Menze
papers.aim: Radiomic representations can quantify properties of regions of interest in medical image data. Classically, they account for pre-defined statistics of shape, texture, and other low-level image features.
papers.method: Alternatively, deep learning-based representations are derived from supervised learning but require expensive annotations from experts and often suffer from overfitting and data imbalance issues. In this work, we address the challenge of learning representations of 3D medical images for an effective quantification under data imbalance. We propose a \emph{self-supervised} representation learning framework to learn high-level features of 3D volumes as a complement to existing radiomics features. Specifically, we demonstrate how to learn image representations in a self-supervised fashion using a 3D Siamese network.
papers.result: More importantly, we deal with data imbalance by exploiting two unsupervised strategies: a) sample re-weighting, and b) balancing the composition of training batches. When combining our learned self-supervised feature with traditional radiomics, we show significant improvement in brain tumor classification and lung cancer staging tasks covering MRI and CT imaging modalities.
papers.gap: Single sequence; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The method learns 3D tumour representations without labels by comparing two augmented views of each scan in a memory-efficient Siamese network, and handles imbalance between classes and centres by re-weighting or rebalancing training batches based on unsupervised clusters. The representations then classify glioma grade better than handcrafted radiomics. Local registry data will also be imbalanced by site and tumour type.
papers.studyDesign: Method development (TUM, Zurich, ETH, SUSTech; MICCAI 2021 workshop/preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS (326 patients, FLAIR only, imbalanced grade labels and centres) and NSCLC-radiomics lung CT (420 patients, stage I/II/III ratio 2:1:6).
papers.preprocessing: Tumour-centred 96x96x96 bounding boxes for BraTS; 224x224x224 lung boxes resized to 112^3 for CT; intensities rescaled to [0,255].
papers.modelDetails: 3DSiam: 3D Siamese self-supervised network trained with extensive augmentation (affine, appearance, contrast, noise); RE/SE module clusters features with k-means and uses sample re-weighting or sample selection to counter data imbalance.
papers.training: Details in supplement.
papers.evaluation: Downstream classification of high vs low grade glioma and lung cancer stage using learned representations.
papers.baselines: Classical radiomics and supervised/self-supervised baselines without imbalance handling.
papers.results: Imbalance-aware self-supervised representations outperformed radiomics and other baselines on both tasks.

papers.title: Residual Vision Transformer (ResViT) Based Self-Supervised Learning Model for Brain Tumor Classification
papers.authors: Meryem Altin Karagoz, O. Ufuk Nalbantoglu, Geoffrey C. Fox
papers.aim: Deep learning has proven very promising for interpreting MRI in brain tumor diagnosis. However, deep learning models suffer from a scarcity of brain MRI datasets for effective training.
papers.method: Self-supervised learning (SSL) models provide data-efficient and remarkable solutions to limited dataset problems. Therefore, this paper introduces a generative SSL model for brain tumor classification in two stages. The first stage is designed to pre-train a Residual Vision Transformer (ResViT) model for MRI synthesis as a pretext task. The second stage includes fine-tuning a ResViT-based classifier model as a downstream task. Accordingly, we aim to leverage local features via CNN and global features via ViT, employing a hybrid CNN-transformer architecture for ResViT in pretext and downstream tasks. Moreover, synthetic MRI images are utilized to balance the training set. The proposed model performs on public BraTs 2023, Figshare, and Kaggle datasets. Furthermore, we compare the proposed model with various deep learning models, including A-UNet, ResNet-9, pix2pix, pGAN for MRI synthesis, and ConvNeXtTiny, ResNet101, DenseNet12, Residual CNN, ViT for classification. According to the results, the proposed model pretraining on the MRI dataset is superior compared to the pretraining on the ImageNet dataset.
papers.result: Overall, the proposed model attains the highest accuracy, achieving 90.56% on the BraTs dataset with T1 sequence, 98.53% on the Figshare, and 98.47% on the Kaggle brain tumor datasets. As a result, the proposed model demonstrates a robust, effective, and successful approach to handling insufficient dataset challenges in MRI analysis by incorporating SSL, fine-tuning, data augmentation, and combining CNN and ViT.
papers.gap: 2D curated datasets; no external clinical test; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: A hybrid residual-transformer network is first pretrained without labels on brain MRI and then fine-tuned to classify tumour types on several public 2D datasets, giving strong accuracy. It supports self-supervised pretraining for limited MRI data, though on curated 2D datasets.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public brain MRI datasets (preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS (T1 sequence), Figshare brain tumour dataset (3,064 slices, three tumour types) and a Kaggle brain MRI dataset.
papers.preprocessing: 2D slices with standard resizing and normalisation.
papers.modelDetails: Residual Vision Transformer (ResViT) self-supervised pretraining (e.g. masked/generative pretext) followed by fine-tuning for brain tumour classification.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Classification accuracy on each dataset.
papers.baselines: CNNs and ViTs without SSL pretraining.
papers.results: Highest accuracies among compared models: 90.56% on BraTS T1, 98.53% on Figshare, 98.47% on the Kaggle dataset.

papers.title: A self-supervised framework for learning whole slide representations
papers.authors: Xinhai Hou, Cheng Jiang, Akhil Kondepudi, Yiwei Lyu, Asadur Chowdury, Honglak Lee, Todd C. Hollon
papers.aim: Whole slide imaging is fundamental to biomedical microscopy and computational pathology. Previously, learning representations for gigapixel-sized whole slide images (WSIs) has relied on multiple instance learning with weak labels, which do not annotate the diverse morphologic features and spatial heterogeneity of WSIs.
papers.method: A high-quality self-supervised learning method for WSIs would provide transferable visual representations for downstream computational pathology tasks, without the need for dense annotations. We present Slide Pre-trained Transformers (SPT) for gigapixel-scale self-supervision of WSIs. Treating WSI patches as tokens, SPT combines data transformation strategies from language and vision modeling into a general and unified framework to generate views of WSIs for self-supervised pretraining. SPT leverages the inherent regional heterogeneity, histologic feature variability, and information redundancy within WSIs to learn high-quality whole slide representations. We benchmark SPT visual representations on five diagnostic tasks across three biomedical microscopy datasets.
papers.result: SPT significantly outperforms baselines for histopathologic diagnosis, cancer subtyping, and genetic mutation prediction. Finally, we demonstrate that SPT consistently improves whole slide representations when using off-the-shelf, in-domain, and foundational patch encoders for whole slide multiple instance learning.
papers.gap: No uncertainty or calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: SPT learns whole-slide representations without labels by treating each slide as a sequence of patch tokens and training a transformer to produce consistent representations across different transformed views of the same slide. On brain-tumour benchmarks from optical and H&E imaging and on standard TCGA tasks, it beat weakly supervised aggregators. Slide-level self-supervision is useful when diagnosis labels are few.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and benchmarking (University of Michigan; IRB HUM00083059 for SRH data).
papers.datasets: Five benchmarks: SRH CNS tumour benchmark (six CNS tumour types plus normal brain; 2,035 training and 925 evaluation WSIs, pathologist-labelled); H&E diffuse glioma molecular classification from TCGA and Digital Brain Tumour Atlas (2,309 training, 341 TCGA evaluation slides, three WHO molecular subgroups); TCGA BRCA, NSCLC and RCC.
papers.preprocessing: WSIs partitioned into non-overlapping patches; frozen pre-trained patch encoder produces tokens with coordinates.
papers.modelDetails: Slide Pre-trained Transformers (SPT): a transformer whole-slide encoder trained with self-supervision using view-generation strategies from language and vision (splitting, cropping, masking, dropping patches) on patch tokens; compatible with existing SSL objectives.
papers.training: Patch encoder frozen; large mini-batch training of slide encoder (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Slide-level classification accuracy/AUC with linear probes and fine-tuning for diagnosis, subtyping and mutation prediction.
papers.baselines: ABMIL and other MIL aggregators; slide-level SSL baselines.
papers.results: SPT significantly outperformed baselines for histopathologic diagnosis, cancer subtyping and genetic mutation prediction, including glioma molecular groups and SRH CNS tumours.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Learn Visual Concepts in Histopathology
papers.authors: Richard J. Chen, Rahul G. Krishnan
papers.aim: Tissue phenotyping is a fundamental task in learning objective characterizations of histopathologic biomarkers within the tumor-immune microenvironment in cancer pathology. However, whole-slide imaging (WSI) is a complex computer vision in which: 1) WSIs have enormous image resolutions with precludes large-scale pixel-level efforts in data curation, and 2) diversity of morphological phenotypes results in inter- and intra-observer variability in tissue labeling.
papers.method: To address these limitations, current efforts have proposed using pretrained image encoders (transfer learning from ImageNet, self-supervised pretraining) in extracting morphological features from pathology, but have not been extensively validated. In this work, we conduct a search for good representations in pathology by training a variety of self-supervised models with validation on a variety of weakly-supervised and patch-level tasks.
papers.result: Our key finding is in discovering that Vision Transformers using DINO-based knowledge distillation are able to learn data-efficient and interpretable features in histology images wherein the different attention heads learn distinct morphological phenotypes. We make evaluation code and pretrained weights publicly-available at: https://github.com/Richarizardd/Self-Supervised-ViT-Path.
papers.gap: No brain tumours; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors trained several self-supervised encoders on pathology patches and compared them with ImageNet features on slide- and patch-level tasks with varying amounts of training data. DINO-trained Vision Transformers learned meaningful tissue concepts and worked well with less data. This underlies later pathology foundation models used as frozen encoders.
papers.studyDesign: Empirical comparison of self-supervised pretraining in pathology (Harvard Medical School, University of Toronto; workshop preprint).
papers.datasets: TCGA BRCA (IDC vs ILC subtyping, 10-fold CV with 25-100% of training data) and CRC-100K patch-level tissue phenotyping with and without Macenko normalisation, plus other patch tasks.
papers.preprocessing: Macenko stain normalisation in some experiments.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of ImageNet transfer (ResNet-50), SimCLR (ResNet-50) and DINO (ViT) self-supervised encoders pretrained on histopathology; KNN on embeddings for patch tasks; weakly supervised slide classification.
papers.training: Self-supervised pretraining on TCGA patches (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: AUC for slide subtyping and patch phenotyping; attention visualisation.
papers.baselines: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50.
papers.results: ImageNet features were a strong baseline (BRCA AUC 0.884 vs SimCLR 0.879, DINO 0.886); DINO ViTs learned data-efficient, interpretable features capturing distinct tissue concepts, and were more robust without stain normalisation.

papers.title: DeepSMILE: Contrastive self-supervised pre-training benefits MSI and HRD classification directly from H&E whole-slide images in colorectal and breast cancer
papers.authors: Yoni Schirris, Efstratios Gavves, Iris Nederlof, Hugo Mark Horlings, Jonas Teuwen
papers.aim: We propose a Deep learning-based weak label learning method for analyzing whole slide images (WSIs) of Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) stained tumor tissue not requiring pixel-level or tile-level annotations using Self-supervised pre-training and heterogeneity-aware deep Multiple Instance LEarning (DeepSMILE). We apply DeepSMILE to the task of Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) and microsatellite instability (MSI) prediction.
papers.method: We utilize contrastive self-supervised learning to pre-train a feature extractor on histopathology tiles of cancer tissue. Additionally, we use variability-aware deep multiple instance learning to learn the tile feature aggregation function while modeling tumor heterogeneity. For MSI prediction in a tumor-annotated and color normalized subset of TCGA-CRC (n=360 patients), contrastive self-supervised learning improves the tile supervision baseline from 0.77 to 0.87 AUROC, on par with our proposed DeepSMILE method. On TCGA-BC (n=1041 patients) without any manual annotations, DeepSMILE improves HRD classification performance from 0.77 to 0.81 AUROC compared to tile supervision with either a self-supervised or ImageNet pre-trained feature extractor.
papers.result: Our proposed methods reach the baseline performance using only 40% of the labeled data on both datasets. These improvements suggest we can use standard self-supervised learning techniques combined with multiple instance learning in the histopathology domain to improve genomic label classification performance with fewer labeled data.
papers.gap: Colorectal and breast; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: DeepSMILE pretrains a tile encoder on cancer tissue without labels and aggregates tiles with a multiple-instance model that accounts for variation across the tumour, predicting genomic labels such as MSI and HRD from slides. With self-supervision it matched the supervised baseline using 40% of the labels. It reinforces that domain-specific self-supervised encoders reduce labelling needs.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on TCGA (Netherlands Cancer Institute, University of Amsterdam, Radboud; Medical Image Analysis 2022).
papers.datasets: TCGA-CRCk: 192,314 colour-normalised tumour tiles from 360 patients (train 260 incl. 39 MSI; test 100 incl. 26 MSI), 5-fold patient-level splits; TCGA-BC breast cancer WSIs with HRD scores (median and tertile binarisation).
papers.preprocessing: Tiles from tumour annotations; colour normalisation; HRD labels binarised at median (mHRD) or by tertiles (tHRD).
papers.modelDetails: DeepSMILE: SimCLR contrastive self-supervised pretraining of a tile feature extractor on cancer tissue, plus variability-aware deep multiple-instance learning (modelling tumour heterogeneity) for slide-level MSI and HRD prediction.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUROC for MSI and HRD with varying amounts of labelled data.
papers.baselines: ImageNet-pretrained features and standard MIL; two-stage tile-supervised methods.
papers.results: Reached baseline performance using only 40% of labelled data on both datasets and improved overall AUROC.

papers.title: Anomaly Detection-Inspired Few-Shot Medical Image Segmentation Through Self-Supervision With Supervoxels
papers.authors: Stine Hansen, Srishti Gautam, Robert Jenssen, Michael Kampffmeyer
papers.aim: Recent work has shown that label-efficient few-shot learning through self-supervision can achieve promising medical image segmentation results. However, few-shot segmentation models typically rely on prototype representations of the semantic classes, resulting in a loss of local information that can degrade performance.
papers.method: This is particularly problematic for the typically large and highly heterogeneous background class in medical image segmentation problems. Previous works have attempted to address this issue by learning additional prototypes for each class, but since the prototypes are based on a limited number of slices, we argue that this ad-hoc solution is insufficient to capture the background properties. Motivated by this, and the observation that the foreground class (e.g., one organ) is relatively homogeneous, we propose a novel anomaly detection-inspired approach to few-shot medical image segmentation in which we refrain from modeling the background explicitly. Instead, we rely solely on a single foreground prototype to compute anomaly scores for all query pixels.
papers.result: The segmentation is then performed by thresholding these anomaly scores using a learned threshold. Assisted by a novel self-supervision task that exploits the 3D structure of medical images through supervoxels, our proposed anomaly detection-inspired few-shot medical image segmentation model outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches on two representative MRI datasets for the tasks of abdominal organ segmentation and cardiac segmentation.
papers.gap: Cardiac and abdominal organs; no tumours; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of modelling both organ and background, ADNet models only the target structure from one labelled example and treats everything unlike it as anomalous, learning the threshold; training uses supervoxels as automatically generated pseudo-labels. It allows segmentation of new structures from very few annotations, relevant to delineating structures at risk for surgical planning.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public 3D segmentation datasets (UiT The Arctic University of Norway; Medical Image Analysis 2022).
papers.datasets: MS-CMRSeg bSSFP (35 cardiac MRI scans) and CHAOS abdominal MRI (20 scans) and related public sets for few-shot organ segmentation.
papers.preprocessing: Supervoxels generated offline per volume for self-supervision.
papers.modelDetails: ADNet: anomaly-detection-inspired prototypical few-shot segmentation using only a foreground prototype, anomaly scores for query features and a learned threshold; supervoxel-based self-supervision for training without labels.
papers.training: PyTorch, ResNet-101 encoder pretrained on MS-COCO with 1x1 conv to 256 channels; SGD momentum 0.9, lr 1e-3 decaying 0.98 per 1k epochs, weight decay 5e-4, 50k iterations; foreground/background weights 1.0/0.1; 1.8 h on an RTX 2080Ti.
papers.evaluation: Dice in few-shot settings.
papers.baselines: SSL-ALPNet and other prototypical few-shot methods.
papers.results: Outperformed previous few-shot segmentation methods without needing annotations for training, especially for heterogeneous backgrounds.

papers.title: Towards Foundation Models and Few-Shot Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Volumetric Organ Segmentation
papers.authors: Julio Silva-Rodríguez, Jose Dolz, Ismail Ben Ayed
papers.aim: The recent popularity of foundation models and the pre-train-and-adapt paradigm, where a large-scale model is transferred to downstream tasks, is gaining attention for volumetric medical image segmentation. However, current transfer learning strategies devoted to full fine-tuning for transfer learning may require significant resources and yield sub-optimal results when the labeled data of the target task is scarce.
papers.method: This makes its applicability in real clinical settings challenging since these institutions are usually constrained on data and computational resources to develop proprietary solutions. To address this challenge, we formalize Few-Shot Efficient Fine-Tuning (FSEFT), a novel and realistic scenario for adapting medical image segmentation foundation models. This setting considers the key role of both data- and parameter-efficiency during adaptation. Building on a foundation model pre-trained on open-access CT organ segmentation sources, we propose leveraging Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and black-box Adapters to address such challenges.
papers.result: Furthermore, novel efficient adaptation methodologies are introduced in this work, which include Spatial black-box Adapters that are more appropriate for dense prediction tasks and constrained transductive inference, leveraging task-specific prior knowledge. Our comprehensive transfer learning experiments confirm the suitability of foundation models in medical image segmentation and unveil the limitations of popular fine-tuning strategies in few-shot scenarios.
papers.gap: CT organs; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The paper defines a realistic hospital scenario in which a large pretrained segmentation model must be adapted to a new structure using only a few labelled scans and little compute, and compares lightweight adaptation methods. Small adapters beat full fine-tuning when labels are scarce. This is directly applicable to adapting brain segmentation models to local Sri Lankan scans.
papers.studyDesign: Method and benchmark development (ÉTS Montréal, CR-CHUM; preprint/Medical Image Analysis).
papers.datasets: Foundation model pretrained on 2,042 CT volumes from nine public datasets (BTCV, CHAOS, LiTS, KiTS, AbdomenCT-1K, AMOS, MSD, AbdomenCT-12organ, CT-ORG) with 29 partially labelled structures; adaptation to new tasks with K = 1, 5 or 10 labelled volumes.
papers.preprocessing: Standard CT preprocessing (details in paper).
papers.modelDetails: Few-Shot Efficient Fine-Tuning (FSEFT) scenario: supervised volumetric segmentation foundation model (CNN/ViT encoder, CNN decoder) adapted with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, BitFit, AdaptFormer) or black-box adapters (linear probing and a new Spatial Adapter).
papers.training: Few-shot adaptation with limited compute (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice on downstream organ/tumour tasks with 1-10 labelled volumes.
papers.baselines: Full fine-tuning and training from scratch.
papers.results: Parameter-efficient and spatial black-box adapters outperformed full fine-tuning in data-scarce settings at much lower compute.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Guided Mutual Consistency Learning for Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Yichi Zhang, Rushi Jiao, Qingcheng Liao, Dongyang Li, Jicong Zhang
papers.aim: Medical image segmentation is a fundamental and critical step in many clinical approaches. Semi-supervised learning has been widely applied to medical image segmentation tasks since it alleviates the heavy burden of acquiring expert-examined annotations and takes the advantage of unlabeled data which is much easier to acquire.
papers.method: Although consistency learning has been proven to be an effective approach by enforcing an invariance of predictions under different distributions, existing approaches cannot make full use of region-level shape constraint and boundary-level distance information from unlabeled data. In this paper, we propose a novel uncertainty-guided mutual consistency learning framework to effectively exploit unlabeled data by integrating intra-task consistency learning from up-to-date predictions for self-ensembling and cross-task consistency learning from task-level regularization to exploit geometric shape information.
papers.result: The framework is guided by the estimated segmentation uncertainty of models to select out relatively certain predictions for consistency learning, so as to effectively exploit more reliable information from unlabeled data. Experiments on two publicly available benchmark datasets showed that: 1) Our proposed method can achieve significant performance improvement by leveraging unlabeled data, with up to 4.13% and 9.82% in Dice coefficient compared to supervised baseline on left atrium segmentation and brain tumor segmentation, respectively. 2) Compared with other semi-supervised segmentation methods, our proposed method achieve better segmentation performance under the same backbone network and task settings on both datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness and robustness of our method and potential transferability for other medical image segmentation tasks.
papers.gap: Whole tumour from FLAIR only; uncertainty used internally, not reported for decisions.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: With only part of the scans labelled, the model learns from unlabelled scans by enforcing that its predictions are consistent over time and between two related outputs (masks and distance maps), but only where it is confident. On a glioma dataset it improved segmentation over other semi-supervised methods. It is a way to use the registry's many unlabelled scans.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public datasets (Beihang University; preprint/Medical Image Analysis).
papers.datasets: Left Atrium MRI (100 scans: 80 train with 16 labelled/64 unlabelled, 20 test) and multi-institutional pre-operative glioma MRI (335 patients; T2-FLAIR whole tumour; 250 train, 25 validation, 60 test) with labelled fractions of training data.
papers.preprocessing: Resampling to 1 mm isotropic; z-score normalisation.
papers.modelDetails: Uncertainty-guided mutual consistency: a network jointly predicts segmentation and signed distance maps; intra-task consistency with self-ensembled predictions and cross-task consistency between tasks, using only relatively certain predictions (estimated uncertainty) for consistency learning on unlabelled data.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice, Jaccard, 95HD, ASD.
papers.baselines: Supervised baseline and semi-supervised methods (mean teacher, UA-MT, SASSNet, DTC and others).
papers.results: Outperformed state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods on both datasets, including glioma whole-tumour segmentation with few labels.

papers.title: M-GenSeg: Domain Adaptation For Target Modality Tumor Segmentation With Annotation-Efficient Supervision
papers.authors: Malo Alefsen de Boisredon d'Assier, Eugene Vorontsov, Samuel Kadoury
papers.aim: Automated medical image segmentation using deep neural networks typically requires substantial supervised training. However, these models fail to generalize well across different imaging modalities.
papers.method: This shortcoming, amplified by the limited availability of expert annotated data, has been hampering the deployment of such methods at a larger scale across modalities. To address these issues, we propose M-GenSeg, a new semi-supervised generative training strategy for cross-modality tumor segmentation on unpaired bi-modal datasets. With the addition of known healthy images, an unsupervised objective encourages the model to disentangling tumors from the background, which parallels the segmentation task. Then, by teaching the model to convert images across modalities, we leverage available pixel-level annotations from the source modality to enable segmentation in the unannotated target modality. We evaluated the performance on a brain tumor segmentation dataset composed of four different contrast sequences from the public BraTS 2020 challenge data.
papers.result: We report consistent improvement in Dice scores over state-of-the-art domain-adaptive baselines on the unannotated target modality. Unlike the prior art, M-GenSeg also introduces the ability to train with a partially annotated source modality.
papers.gap: Simulated modality shift within BraTS; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: When the MRI sequence available at a new hospital differs from the one the model was trained on, M-GenSeg learns to translate between sequences and between healthy and tumour-containing images, so labels from the source sequence transfer to the target. It worked with limited source labels. This addresses sequence mismatch expected in Sri Lankan routine MRI.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on a public brain tumour dataset (Polytechnique Montréal, CR-CHUM, Paige; preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS-derived brain tumour MRI with four modalities treated as unpaired source and target domains, plus healthy images; varying fractions of pixel-level source annotations.
papers.preprocessing: Same on-the-fly augmentation as GenSeg.
papers.modelDetails: M-GenSeg: semi-supervised generative model with shared latent representations performing healthy-diseased translation (tumour disentangling and synthetic tumour generation) and cross-modality translation, so source-modality pixel labels enable segmentation in an unannotated target modality; attention gates in skip connections.
papers.training: PyTorch on one A100; batch 15, AMSGrad (beta1 0.5, beta2 0.999), lr 1e-4, 300 epochs, best validation Dice checkpoint; three seeds; loss weights given in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice on the unannotated target modality.
papers.baselines: State-of-the-art domain-adaptive segmentation methods.
papers.results: Consistent Dice improvements over domain-adaptive baselines on the target modality with limited source annotations.
papers.statistics: Mean and SD over three runs.

papers.title: Addressing data annotation scarcity in Brain Tumor Segmentation on 3D MRI scan Using a Semi-Supervised Teacher-Student Framework
papers.authors: Jiaming Liu, Cheng Ding, Daoqiang Zhang
papers.aim: Accurate brain tumor segmentation from MRI is limited by expensive annotations and data heterogeneity across scanners and sites. We propose a semi-supervised teacher-student framework that combines an uncertainty-aware pseudo-labeling teacher with a progressive, confidence-based curriculum for the student.
papers.method: The teacher produces probabilistic masks and per-pixel uncertainty; unlabeled scans are ranked by image-level confidence and introduced in stages, while a dual-loss objective trains the student to learn from high-confidence regions and unlearn low-confidence ones. Agreement-based refinement further improves pseudo-label quality. On BraTS 2021, validation DSC increased from 0.393 (10% data) to 0.872 (100%), with the largest gains in early stages, demonstrating data efficiency.
papers.result: The teacher reached a validation DSC of 0.922, and the student surpassed the teacher on tumor subregions (e.g., NCR/NET 0.797 and Edema 0.980); notably, the student recovered the Enhancing class (DSC 0.620) where the teacher failed. These results show that confidence-driven curricula and selective unlearning provide robust segmentation under limited supervision and noisy pseudo-labels.
papers.gap: Single dataset; uncertainty calibration not assessed.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: A teacher network trained on labelled scans labels unlabelled scans and estimates its uncertainty; a student then learns from the most confident pseudo-labelled scans first, adding less confident ones gradually and ignoring uncertain regions. This confidence-driven curriculum improved tumour subregion segmentation with limited annotation, a direct strategy for the registry where most scans will be unlabelled.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on BraTS 2021 (Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics; preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2021 multi-institutional multi-parametric glioma MRI (T1, T1ce, T2, FLAIR) with labelled fractions from 10% to 100%.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Semi-supervised teacher-student framework: a U-Net teacher (Dice + cross-entropy) produces probabilistic pseudo-labels and per-pixel uncertainty by stochastic inference; unlabelled scans ranked by image-level confidence and added in stages (progressive curriculum); student learns from high-confidence regions and unlearns low-confidence ones; agreement-based pseudo-label refinement.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice per subregion; confidence and error analyses.
papers.baselines: Teacher model and supervised training at each label fraction.
papers.results: Validation DSC rose from 0.393 (10% labels) to 0.872 (100%); teacher 0.922; student surpassed teacher on subregions (NCR/NET 0.797, oedema 0.980) and recovered enhancing tumour (0.620) where the teacher failed.

papers.title: Generalizable Brain Tumor Segmentation with Self-Training and Tumor-Aware Deformations
papers.authors: Henrique Zan Grande, Jeovane Honorio Alves, Rayson Laroca, Andre Gustavo Hochuli
papers.aim: This work presents an approach to the Generalizability Across Tumors (BraTS-GoAT) task of the BraTS 2026 Challenge, which focuses on robust segmentation of brain tumor sub-regions across a heterogeneous patient population. The proposed method employs the nnU-Net framework with a large residual encoder architecture, integrating a semi-supervised learning technique with pseudo-labels generated from the unlabeled training data and a tumor-aware deformable augmentation that locally deforms the lesion while preserving the surrounding anatomy.
papers.method: We evaluate the individual contributions of each component, as well as their combination, using varying proportions of the most confident pseudo-labeled cases.
papers.result: The submitted configuration for the generalization task achieves Dice and NSD scores of 0.881 and 0.473 for Whole Tumor, 0.817 and 0.490 for Tumor Core, and 0.775 and 0.533 for Enhancing Tumor on the BraTS-GoAT validation set, improving over the labeled-only baselines across all tumor regions and confirming that self-training and the proposed augmentation are complementary. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Henrique-zan/brats-goat-2026/.
papers.gap: No calibrated uncertainty output; challenge data.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint; validation on hidden challenge set.
papers.methodologyDetail: The approach trains a strong teacher, uses it to label unlabelled scans, keeps only its most confident pseudo-labels, and trains a student with a new augmentation that deforms the tumour locally without distorting the rest of the brain, aiming to generalise across tumour types. Ablations isolate each component's effect. It is a practical recipe for using unlabelled local scans with nnU-Net.
papers.studyDesign: Challenge method paper (PUCPR Brazil, University of Luxembourg; BraTS 2026 GoAT task, accepted to MICCAI 2026 BraTS cluster).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2026 Generalizability Across Tumors (GoAT) data: heterogeneous brain tumour types and populations with labelled and unlabelled training cases; hidden validation via challenge platform.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing; tumour-aware deformable augmentation locally deforms lesions while preserving surrounding anatomy.
papers.modelDetails: Self-training: teacher nnU-Net v2 3D full-resolution with large residual encoder, group normalisation, axial attention in decoder and Hausdorff loss term; pseudo-labels for unlabelled cases, top-k most confident merged with labelled data; unmodified large-residual-encoder nnU-Net student trained with tumour-aware deformation augmentation.
papers.training: All hyperparameters, code and weights publicly released.
papers.evaluation: Dice, NSD and HD95 per region on challenge validation.
papers.baselines: Student trained on labelled data only; augmentation-only and self-training-only ablations.
papers.results: Submitted configuration Dice/NSD 0.881/0.473 whole tumour and 0.817/0.490 tumour core (other regions in paper); self-training and augmentation each helped, best combined.

papers.title: Cross-Modality Brain Tumor Segmentation via Bidirectional Global-to-Local Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
papers.authors: Kelei He, Wen Ji, Tao Zhou, Zhuoyuan Li, Jing Huo, Xin Zhang, Yang Gao, Dinggang Shen, Bing Zhang, Junfeng Zhang
papers.aim: Accurate segmentation of brain tumors from multi-modal Magnetic Resonance (MR) images is essential in brain tumor diagnosis and treatment. However, due to the existence of domain shifts among different modalities, the performance of networks decreases dramatically when training on one modality and performing on another, e.g., train on T1 image while performing on T2 image, which is often required in clinical applications.
papers.method: This also prohibits a network from being trained on labeled data and then transferred to unlabeled data from a different domain. To overcome this, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) methods provide effective solutions to alleviate the domain shift between labeled source data and unlabeled target data. In this paper, we propose a novel Bidirectional Global-to-Local (BiGL) adaptation framework under a UDA scheme. Specifically, a bidirectional image synthesis and segmentation module is proposed to segment the brain tumor using the intermediate data distributions generated for the two domains, which includes an image-to-image translator and a shared-weighted segmentation network. Further, a global-to-local consistency learning module is proposed to build robust representation alignments in an integrated way.
papers.result: Extensive experiments on a multi-modal brain MR benchmark dataset demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-art unsupervised domain adaptation methods by a large margin, while a comprehensive ablation study validates the effectiveness of each key component. The implementation code of our method will be released at \url{https://github.com/KeleiHe/BiGL}.
papers.gap: Simulated modality shift; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: To segment tumours in an MRI sequence that has no labels, BiGL translates images between the labelled and unlabelled sequences in both directions and enforces consistent segmentations and features across real and synthetic images. It improved cross-sequence segmentation over other unsupervised adaptation methods, relevant when local protocols differ from training data.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on BraTS 2019 (Nanjing University and partners; preprint/IEEE journal).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2019 multi-modal glioma MRI with manual labels for three regions; modalities treated as source (e.g. T1, labelled) and target (e.g. T2, unlabelled) domains.
papers.preprocessing: Unpaired images per domain.
papers.modelDetails: Bidirectional Global-to-Local (BiGL) unsupervised domain adaptation: bidirectional image-to-image translator (pix2pix-like GAN) creates synthetic images in both directions; four weight-shared segmentation networks segment real and synthetic images; a global-to-local adaptor with feature, segmentation and attention consistency reduces domain shift.
papers.training: PyTorch on four V100 GPUs; synthesis module trained first then fixed; lr 5e-3 with polynomial decay (power 0.75), 150 epochs; discriminator lr 5e-5; consistency weights 0.001/0.1/0.1/0.1.
papers.evaluation: Dice and Hausdorff distance on target modality.
papers.baselines: State-of-the-art unsupervised domain adaptation methods.
papers.results: Outperformed several state-of-the-art UDA methods on cross-modality brain tumour segmentation.

papers.title: On the Role of MRI Sequences in Cross-Dataset Generalization for Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Henrique Zan Grande, João G. Pitol, Lucas B. Schuck, Rafael V. Serenato, Rayson Laroca, Andre Gustavo Hochuli
papers.aim: Brain tumor segmentation in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a critical task for diagnosis and treatment planning. Despite the success of deep learning architectures such as U-Net and its variants, performance degradation across datasets remains a major challenge, particularly under domain shift and limited annotated data.
papers.method: To address this issue, this study systematically evaluates how individual MRI sequences influence model robustness across two well-known datasets. A ResUNet-based framework is employed, where each modality is trained independently to isolate its effect under a controlled cross-dataset evaluation protocol with tumor size stratification, without target-domain training, or with limited domain adaptation. Results show that the T2f/FLAIR sequence achieves the best cross-dataset performance, with Dice scores exceeding 75%. It consistently outperforms other modalities across most tumor size ranges, while multi-sequence training further improves performance.
papers.result: Additionally, even limited target-domain adaptation yields rapid initial gains, reducing the need for extensive annotations and costly retraining. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/henrique-zan/brain_tumor_segmentation/.
papers.gap: Binary 2D segmentation; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study isolates how each MRI sequence affects how well a segmentation model trained on one dataset works on another, by training separate models per sequence, stratifying by tumour size, and measuring the benefit of a few labelled target cases. FLAIR transferred best and small amounts of local labels helped quickly. This guides which sequences to prioritise when local scans are incomplete and how many local labels are needed.
papers.studyDesign: Controlled cross-dataset evaluation (PUCPR, Brazil; SIBGRAPI 2026).
papers.datasets: Two well-known public brain tumour MRI datasets used as source and target for binary tumour vs non-tumour segmentation, stratified by tumour size.
papers.preprocessing: Each sequence (T1n, T1c, T2w, T2f/FLAIR) processed and trained independently; 2D slices.
papers.modelDetails: 2D ResUNet trained per sequence and with multiple sequences; fine-tuning with limited labelled target-domain data.
papers.training: Standardised pipeline (details and code public).
papers.evaluation: Dice across datasets by sequence and tumour size; performance vs amount of target-domain labels.
papers.baselines: Each sequence compared; no adaptation vs limited adaptation.
papers.results: FLAIR achieved the best cross-dataset performance (Dice >75%) across most tumour sizes; multi-sequence training improved further; even limited target-domain adaptation gave rapid gains.

papers.title: MedMAP: Promoting Incomplete Multi-modal Brain Tumor Segmentation with Alignment
papers.authors: Tianyi Liu, Zhaorui Tan, Muyin Chen, Xi Yang, Haochuan Jiang, Kaizhu Huang
papers.aim: Brain tumor segmentation is often based on multiple magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, in clinical practice, certain modalities of MRI may be missing, which presents a more difficult scenario.
papers.method: To cope with this challenge, Knowledge Distillation, Domain Adaption, and Shared Latent Space have emerged as commonly promising strategies. However, recent efforts typically overlook the modality gaps and thus fail to learn important invariant feature representations across different modalities. Such drawback consequently leads to limited performance for missing modality models. To ameliorate these problems, pre-trained models are used in natural visual segmentation tasks to minimize the gaps. However, promising pre-trained models are often unavailable in medical image segmentation tasks. Along this line, in this paper, we propose a novel paradigm that aligns latent features of involved modalities to a well-defined distribution anchor as the substitution of the pre-trained model}. As a major contribution, we prove that our novel training paradigm ensures a tight evidence lower bound, thus theoretically certifying its effectiveness.
papers.result: Extensive experiments on different backbones validate that the proposed paradigm can enable invariant feature representations and produce models with narrowed modality gaps. Models with our alignment paradigm show their superior performance on both BraTS2018 and BraTS2020 datasets.
papers.gap: Simulated missing modalities; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: MedMAP makes the features from each MRI sequence follow a common reference distribution during training, so a model can work when some sequences are missing. Added to three existing missing-modality methods, it improved Dice on BraTS, especially for mmFormer. It helps the MRI Agent handle incomplete routine protocols.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on BraTS (Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, Duke Kunshan; preprint, IEEE TMI submission).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2018 (split as in Proto-KD) and BraTS 2020 (three-fold cross-validation) with simulated missing MRI modalities.
papers.preprocessing: All modality subsets evaluated.
papers.modelDetails: MedMAP: a training paradigm that aligns latent features of each modality to a defined distribution anchor (best single modality or an adaptive mixture) in place of a pretrained model, inserted into existing missing-modality backbones (PMKL knowledge distillation, mmFormer shared latent space, ACN domain adaptation).
papers.training: Each backbone retrained with its released settings (batch sizes adjusted: mmFormer 1, PMKL 4) on one RTX 3090Ti.
papers.evaluation: Average Dice across missing-modality combinations.
papers.baselines: Same backbones without MedMAP.
papers.results: MedMAP improved all backbones, e.g. BraTS2018 mmFormer +7.67 to 78.29% and PMKL +3.68 to 69.12%; BraTS2020 mmFormer +6.76.
papers.statistics: Descriptive with proof of alignment properties.

papers.title: Rethink Domain Generalization in Heterogeneous Sequence MRI Segmentation
papers.authors: Zheyuan Zhang, Linkai Peng, Wanying Dou, Cuiling Sun, Halil Ertugrul Aktas, Andrea M. Bejar, Elif Keles, Gorkem Durak, Ulas Bagci
papers.aim: Clinical magnetic-resonance (MR) protocols generate many T1 and T2 sequences whose appearance differs more than the acquisition sites that produce them. Existing domain-generalization benchmarks focus almost on cross-center shifts and overlook this dominant source of variability.
papers.method: Pancreas segmentation remains a major challenge in abdominal imaging: the gland is small, irregularly, surrounded by organs and fat, and often suffers from low T1 contrast. State-of-the-art deep networks that already achieve >90% Dice on the liver or kidneys still miss 20-30% of the pancreas. The organ is also systematically under-represented in public cross-domain benchmarks, despite its clinical importance in early cancer detection, surgery, and diabetes research. To close this gap, we present PancreasDG, a large-scale multi-center 3D MRI pancreas segmentation dataset for investigating domain generalization in medical imaging. The dataset comprises 563 MRI scans from six institutions, spanning both venous phase and out-of-phase sequences, enabling study of both cross-center and cross-sequence variations with pixel-accurate pancreas masks created by a double-blind, two-pass protocol. Through comprehensive analysis, we reveal three insights: (i) limited sampling introduces significant variance that may be mistaken for distribution shifts, (ii) cross-center performance correlates with source domain performance for identical sequences, and (iii) cross-sequence shifts require specialized solutions. We also propose a semi-supervised approach that leverages anatomical invariances, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques with 61.63% Dice score improvements and 87.00% on two test centers for cross-sequence segmentation.
papers.result: PancreasDG sets a new benchmark for domain generalization in medical imaging. Dataset, code, and models will be available at https://pancreasdg.netlify.app.
papers.gap: Pancreas, not brain; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a new six-centre pancreas MRI dataset, the authors show that differences between MRI sequences cause larger performance drops than differences between hospitals, and that small samples can create apparent shifts. A semi-supervised pretraining approach based on anatomy that does not change with sequence greatly improved cross-sequence segmentation. The finding that sequence differences dominate is relevant to heterogeneous brain MRI protocols.
papers.studyDesign: Dataset creation and domain-generalisation benchmark with a new method (Northwestern University; preprint).
papers.datasets: PancreasDG: 563 3D MRI scans from six institutions with venous-phase and out-of-phase sequences; pixel-accurate pancreas masks from a double-blind two-pass protocol.
papers.preprocessing: Not detailed in extract.
papers.modelDetails: Analysis of cross-centre vs cross-sequence shift; semi-supervised pretraining approach exploiting anatomical invariances for cross-sequence generalisation.
papers.training: Trained only on venous-phase data for cross-sequence tests (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice on unseen centres and sequences.
papers.baselines: Domain generalisation methods, SAM-based large segmentation models, pretraining baselines.
papers.results: Cross-sequence shift posed fundamentally different challenges than cross-centre shift; limited sampling variance can be mistaken for shift; proposed method raised Dice from 43.55% to 70.39% and from 35.62% to 66.61% on two independent test centres.
papers.availability: Dataset, code and models to be released.

papers.title: Causality-inspired Single-source Domain Generalization for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Cheng Ouyang, Chen Chen, Surui Li, Zeju Li, Chen Qin, Wenjia Bai, Daniel Rueckert
papers.aim: Deep learning models usually suffer from domain shift issues, where models trained on one source domain do not generalize well to other unseen domains. In this work, we investigate the single-source domain generalization problem: training a deep network that is robust to unseen domains, under the condition that training data is only available from one source domain, which is common in medical imaging applications.
papers.method: We tackle this problem in the context of cross-domain medical image segmentation. Under this scenario, domain shifts are mainly caused by different acquisition processes. We propose a simple causality-inspired data augmentation approach to expose a segmentation model to synthesized domain-shifted training examples. Specifically, 1) to make the deep model robust to discrepancies in image intensities and textures, we employ a family of randomly-weighted shallow networks. They augment training images using diverse appearance transformations. 2) Further we show that spurious correlations among objects in an image are detrimental to domain robustness. These correlations might be taken by the network as domain-specific clues for making predictions, and they may break on unseen domains. We remove these spurious correlations via causal intervention. This is achieved by resampling the appearances of potentially correlated objects independently.
papers.result: The proposed approach is validated on three cross-domain segmentation tasks: cross-modality (CT-MRI) abdominal image segmentation, cross-sequence (bSSFP-LGE) cardiac MRI segmentation, and cross-center prostate MRI segmentation. The proposed approach yields consistent performance gains compared with competitive methods when tested on unseen domains.
papers.gap: Not tumour-specific; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: When a model can only be trained on data from one source, these augmentations expose it to many synthetic appearances generated by random shallow networks while keeping anatomy fixed, and break accidental links between background and target appearance. This made segmentation more robust to unseen scanners, sequences and modalities. It is an easy-to-add training step for the MRI Agent before local deployment.
papers.studyDesign: Method development (Imperial College London, Oxford; IEEE TMI).
papers.datasets: Three cross-domain settings: abdominal CT to T2-SPIR MRI (liver, kidneys, spleen), cardiac bSSFP to LGE MRI, and prostate MRI across six centres.
papers.preprocessing: 2D slices; standard normalisation.
papers.modelDetails: Causality-inspired single-source domain generalisation: Global Intensity Non-linear augmentation (GIN) with randomly weighted shallow networks to vary appearance while preserving shape, and Interventional Pseudo-correlation Augmentation (IPA) blending GIN-augmented images spatially to break spurious correlations between objects.
papers.training: Standard segmentation training with these augmentations added.
papers.evaluation: Dice on unseen target domains.
papers.baselines: Other single-source domain generalisation and augmentation methods.
papers.results: Consistently outperformed competing methods across cross-modality, cross-sequence and cross-centre settings.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Medical Image Classification: A Comprehensive Benchmark
papers.authors: Zhekai Zhou, Guibo Luo, Mingzhi Chen, Zhenyu Weng, Yuesheng Zhu
papers.aim: The federated learning paradigm is wellsuited for the field of medical image analysis, as it can effectively cope with machine learning on isolated multicenter data while protecting the privacy of participating parties. However, current research on optimization algorithms in federated learning often focuses on limited datasets and scenarios, primarily centered around natural images, with insufficient comparative experiments in medical contexts.
papers.method: In this work, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of several state-of-the-art federated learning algorithms in the context of medical imaging. We conduct a fair comparison of classification models trained using various federated learning algorithms across multiple medical imaging datasets. Additionally, we evaluate system performance metrics, such as communication cost and computational efficiency, while considering different federated learning architectures. Our findings show that medical imaging datasets pose substantial challenges for current federated learning optimization algorithms. No single algorithm consistently delivers optimal performance across all medical federated learning scenarios, and many optimization algorithms may underperform when applied to these datasets. Our experiments provide a benchmark and guidance for future research and application of federated learning in medical imaging contexts.
papers.result: Furthermore, we propose an efficient and robust method that combines generative techniques using denoising diffusion probabilistic models with label smoothing to augment datasets, widely enhancing the performance of federated learning on classification tasks across various medical imaging datasets. Our code will be released on GitHub, offering a reliable and comprehensive benchmark for future federated learning studies in medical imaging.
papers.gap: Classification only; no calibration.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The benchmark evaluates many federated learning algorithms under the same conditions on medical classification datasets, measuring accuracy and system costs. The main finding is that algorithm rankings vary by dataset and none wins everywhere, so plain FedAvg remains a reasonable default with targeted alternatives tested locally, as planned in WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study of federated learning algorithms on medical image classification (Peking University Shenzhen; preprint).
papers.datasets: Multiple medical imaging classification datasets (e.g. COVIDx chest X-ray, HAM10K dermoscopy, retina DR, BreakHis pathology and others) partitioned across clients with IID and non-IID settings.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised partitioning and preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Fair comparison of traditional FL optimisers (FedAvg, FedProx, FedNova, SCAFFOLD, FedDyn and others), personalised FL (FedBN, Ditto, FedKD) and one-shot FL; proposed method combining denoising diffusion generative models with label-smoothing augmentation.
papers.training: Common training configuration across algorithms.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, communication cost and computational efficiency across architectures.
papers.baselines: All listed algorithms.
papers.results: Medical datasets posed substantial challenges; no single algorithm consistently performed best; the generative augmentation method improved robustness and efficiency.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Medical Image Analysis: A Survey
papers.authors: Hao Guan, Pew-Thian Yap, Andrea Bozoki, Mingxia Liu
papers.aim: Machine learning in medical imaging often faces a fundamental dilemma, namely, the small sample size problem. Many recent studies suggest using multi-domain data pooled from different acquisition sites/centers to improve statistical power.
papers.method: However, medical images from different sites cannot be easily shared to build large datasets for model training due to privacy protection reasons. As a promising solution, federated learning, which enables collaborative training of machine learning models based on data from different sites without cross-site data sharing, has attracted considerable attention recently. In this paper, we conduct a comprehensive survey of the recent development of federated learning methods in medical image analysis. In this survey, we first introduce the background knowledge of federated learning for dealing with privacy protection and collaborative learning issues in medical imaging. We then present a comprehensive review of recent advances in federated learning methods for medical image analysis. Specifically, existing methods are categorized based on three critical aspects of a federated learning system, including client end, server end, and communication techniques. In each category, we summarize the existing federated learning methods according to specific research problems in medical image analysis and also provide insights into the motivations of different approaches. In addition, we provide a review of existing benchmark medical imaging datasets and software platforms for current federated learning research.
papers.result: We also conduct an experimental study to empirically evaluate typical federated learning methods for medical image analysis. This survey can help to better understand the current research status, challenges, and potential research opportunities in this promising research field.
papers.gap: Survey; limited calibration discussion.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: A broad survey organising federated learning research in medical imaging by where in the system each technique acts and listing applications by organ, with an empirical comparison of representative methods. It provides background and terminology for WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Survey with an experimental study (University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill; Pattern Recognition 2024).
papers.datasets: Literature on federated learning in medical image analysis 2017-2023 grouped by organ (brain, chest, lung, etc.), with tasks and datasets catalogued (e.g. BraTS, ABIDE, ADNI, RSNA, CheXpert).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Taxonomy of FL methods (client-end, server-end and communication techniques) and an empirical evaluation of typical FL methods.
papers.training: Not applicable for review; experiments use standard settings.
papers.evaluation: Empirical comparison metrics on representative tasks.
papers.baselines: Typical FL algorithms.
papers.results: Summarises progress, challenges (heterogeneity, privacy attacks, communication, evaluation) and directions; empirical results show heterogeneity strongly affects performance.

papers.title: In-depth Analysis of Privacy Threats in Federated Learning for Medical Data
papers.authors: Badhan Chandra Das, M. Hadi Amini, Yanzhao Wu
papers.aim: Federated learning is emerging as a promising machine learning technique in the medical field for analyzing medical images, as it is considered an effective method to safeguard sensitive patient data and comply with privacy regulations. However, recent studies have revealed that the default settings of federated learning may inadvertently expose private training data to privacy attacks.
papers.method: Thus, the intensity of such privacy risks and potential mitigation strategies in the medical domain remain unclear. In this paper, we make three original contributions to privacy risk analysis and mitigation in federated learning for medical data. First, we propose a holistic framework, MedPFL, for analyzing privacy risks in processing medical data in the federated learning environment and developing effective mitigation strategies for protecting privacy. Second, through our empirical analysis, we demonstrate the severe privacy risks in federated learning to process medical images, where adversaries can accurately reconstruct private medical images by performing privacy attacks. Third, we illustrate that the prevalent defense mechanism of adding random noises may not always be effective in protecting medical images against privacy attacks in federated learning, which poses unique and pressing challenges related to protecting the privacy of medical data.
papers.result: Furthermore, the paper discusses several unique research questions related to the privacy protection of medical data in the federated learning environment. We conduct extensive experiments on several benchmark medical image datasets to analyze and mitigate the privacy risks associated with federated learning for medical data.
papers.gap: Classification models; small-batch attack settings.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built a framework to attack and defend federated learning on medical images, showing that, without protection, an adversary can reconstruct brain MRI and other images from the gradients hospitals share. Common defences involve trade-offs between privacy and accuracy. This is why WP5 includes differential privacy and secure aggregation options and audit of what leaves each site.
papers.studyDesign: Framework development and empirical privacy-risk analysis (Florida International University and partners; preprint).
papers.datasets: Public medical image datasets: melanoma skin cancer images, COVID-19 X-rays and brain tumour MRI scans.
papers.preprocessing: Standard image preprocessing per dataset.
papers.modelDetails: MedPFL framework for analysing privacy risk in federated learning: gradient-inversion attacks (DLG, iDLG, GradInv, CPL) against LeNet, ResNet and U-Net, and defences (gradient perturbation, gradient compression, differential privacy, secure multi-party computation).
papers.training: FL training with shared gradients (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Attack success rate, SSIM and MSE of reconstructed images; model accuracy under defences.
papers.baselines: Undefended federated training.
papers.results: Adversaries could accurately reconstruct private medical images from shared gradients under default FL settings; prevalent defences did not always protect adequately or reduced accuracy.

papers.title: Future-Proofing Medical Imaging with Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning and Uncertainty Quantification: A Review
papers.authors: Nikolas Koutsoubis, Asim Waqas, Yasin Yilmaz, Ravi P. Ramachandran, Matthew Schabath, Ghulam Rasool
papers.aim: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has demonstrated significant potential in automating various medical imaging tasks, which could soon become routine in clinical practice for disease diagnosis, prognosis, treatment planning, and post-treatment surveillance. However, the privacy concerns surrounding patient data present a major barrier to the widespread adoption of AI in medical imaging, as large, diverse training datasets are essential for developing accurate, generalizable, and robust Artificial intelligence models.
papers.method: Federated Learning (FL) offers a solution that enables organizations to train AI models collaboratively without sharing sensitive data. federated learning exchanges model training information, such as gradients, between the participating sites. Despite its promise, federated learning is still in its developmental stages and faces several challenges. Notably, sensitive information can still be inferred from the gradients shared during model training. Quantifying AI models' uncertainty is vital due to potential data distribution shifts post-deployment, which can affect model performance. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) in FL is particularly challenging due to data heterogeneity across participating sites.
papers.result: This review provides a comprehensive examination of FL, privacy-preserving FL (PPFL), and UQ in FL. We identify key gaps in current FL methodologies and propose future research directions to enhance data privacy and trustworthiness in medical imaging applications.
papers.gap: No empirical comparison.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The review brings together federated learning, its privacy weaknesses and defences, and uncertainty quantification under federation, arguing that site heterogeneity makes uncertainty estimation in FL especially hard. It directly frames the gap this study addresses about calibration after federated aggregation.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (Moffitt Cancer Center, University of South Florida, Rowan University; preprint).
papers.datasets: Literature on federated learning, privacy-preserving FL and uncertainty quantification in FL for medical imaging.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Review of FL algorithms, privacy-preserving techniques (differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure aggregation) and UQ methods adapted to FL (ensembles, Bayesian FL, conformal prediction).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Identifies gaps: non-IID heterogeneity, gradient leakage, and the difficulty of UQ in FL because site data differ; calls for privacy-preserving FL with trustworthy uncertainty.

papers.title: Multi-Institutional Deep Learning Modeling Without Sharing Patient Data: A Feasibility Study on Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Micah J Sheller, G Anthony Reina, Brandon Edwards, Jason Martin, Spyridon Bakas
papers.aim: Deep learning models for semantic segmentation of images require large amounts of data. In the medical imaging domain, acquiring sufficient data is a significant challenge.
papers.method: Labeling medical image data requires expert knowledge. Collaboration between institutions could address this challenge, but sharing medical data to a centralized location faces various legal, privacy, technical, and data-ownership challenges, especially among international institutions. In this study, we introduce the first use of federated learning for multi-institutional collaboration, enabling deep learning modeling without sharing patient data.
papers.result: Our quantitative results demonstrate that the performance of federated semantic segmentation models (Dice=0.852) on multimodal brain scans is similar to that of models trained by sharing data (Dice=0.862). We compare federated learning with two alternative collaborative learning methods and find that they fail to match the performance of federated learning.
papers.gap: Simulated federation; no calibration.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: This was the first demonstration that brain-tumour segmentation models can be trained across institutions without moving patient data. By partitioning BraTS by source institution, the authors showed federated training reached nearly the same Dice as pooling the data, whereas sequential institution-by-institution training lost performance. It is the starting point for federated brain-tumour work.
papers.studyDesign: Simulated federated learning feasibility study on BraTS (Intel and University of Pennsylvania; MICCAI BrainLes 2018).
papers.datasets: BraTS multimodal brain tumour MRI partitioned by original institution into simulated federations of 4 to 32 institutions.
papers.preprocessing: Standard BraTS preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: U-Net segmentation trained with federated learning (weighted averaging of institutional updates by data fraction), compared with cyclic institutional incremental learning (CIIL), institutional incremental learning (IIL) and centralised data sharing.
papers.training: Adam lr 0.0005, loss = negative log Dice with Laplace smoothing 1; epochs per round studied.
papers.evaluation: Whole-tumour Dice on validation; percentage of data-sharing performance.
papers.baselines: Centralised data sharing, CIIL, IIL.
papers.results: Federated Dice 0.852, close to data-sharing performance and to expert inter-rater agreement (0.85 +/- 0.08), and better than incremental approaches as institutions increased.

papers.title: FedFMS: Exploring Federated Foundation Models for Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Yuxi Liu, Guibo Luo, Yuesheng Zhu
papers.aim: Medical image segmentation is crucial for clinical diagnosis. The Segmentation Anything Model (SAM) serves as a powerful foundation model for visual segmentation and can be adapted for medical image segmentation.
papers.method: However, medical imaging data typically contain privacy-sensitive information, making it challenging to train foundation models with centralized storage and sharing. To date, there are few foundation models tailored for medical image deployment within the federated learning framework, and the segmentation performance, as well as the efficiency of communication and training, remain unexplored. In response to these issues, we developed Federated Foundation models for Medical image Segmentation (FedFMS), which includes the Federated SAM (FedSAM) and a communication and training-efficient Federated SAM with Medical SAM Adapter (FedMSA). Comprehensive experiments on diverse datasets are conducted to investigate the performance disparities between centralized training and federated learning across various configurations of FedFMS. The experiments revealed that FedFMS could achieve performance comparable to models trained via centralized training methods while maintaining privacy.
papers.result: Furthermore, FedMSA demonstrated the potential to enhance communication and training efficiency. Our model implementation codes are available at https://github.com/LIU-YUXI/FedFMS.
papers.gap: No brain-tumour focus; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study asks whether a large segmentation foundation model can be trained federatedly and shows that full federated SAM matches centralised training, while training only small adapters cuts communication substantially. Adapter-based federation suits hospitals with slow connections.
papers.studyDesign: Exploratory study of federated foundation models for segmentation (Peking University Shenzhen; preprint).
papers.datasets: Diverse public medical segmentation datasets partitioned across clients (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Standard preprocessing for SAM inputs.
papers.modelDetails: FedFMS: Federated SAM (FedSAM, full model with ViT-B/16 or ViT-L/16 encoder and lightweight decoder) and FedMSA (Medical SAM Adapter, training only adapters and decoder for communication and compute efficiency), with multi-class segmentation head.
papers.training: Federated rounds with FedAvg (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice vs centralised training; communication and training cost; effect of pretraining.
papers.baselines: Centralised SAM training.
papers.results: Federated foundation models performed comparably to centralised training; FedMSA reduced communication and training cost while keeping performance; pretraining enriched prior knowledge.

papers.title: Cross-Domain Federated Learning in Medical Imaging
papers.authors: Vishwa S Parekh, Shuhao Lai, Vladimir Braverman, Jeff Leal, Steven Rowe, Jay J Pillai, Michael A Jacobs
papers.aim: Federated learning is increasingly being explored in the field of medical imaging to train deep learning models on large scale datasets distributed across different data centers while preserving privacy by avoiding the need to transfer sensitive patient information. In this manuscript, we explore federated learning in a multi-domain, multi-task setting wherein different participating nodes may contain datasets sourced from different domains and are trained to solve different tasks.
papers.method: We evaluated cross-domain federated learning for the tasks of object detection and segmentation across two different experimental settings: multi-modal and multi-organ.
papers.result: The result from our experiments on cross-domain federated learning framework were very encouraging with an overlap similarity of 0.79 for organ localization and 0.65 for lesion segmentation. Our results demonstrate the potential of federated learning in developing multi-domain, multi-task deep learning models without sharing data from different domains.
papers.gap: Small cohorts; no calibration.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study tests whether federated learning still helps when participating sites hold different imaging modalities or tasks, by training one U-Net with CT at one node and PET at another for kidney localisation, plus other multi-task settings. Cross-domain federation gave reasonable results. It is relevant because Sri Lankan hospitals may hold different sequences or data types.
