papers.studyDesign: Exploratory multi-domain, multi-task federated learning study (Johns Hopkins University; MIDL 2022 submission, IRB-approved retrospective clinical data).
papers.datasets: Experiment 1: 50 patients with whole-body 18F-DCFPyL PET/CT (35 train, 15 test) for kidney localisation, CT at one node and PET at another; further experiments with multi-task settings (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Split of modalities across nodes.
papers.modelDetails: U-Net (five encoder, one bridge, five decoder blocks; batch norm, ReLU) trained with FedAvg across nodes holding different modalities and tasks; one local epoch per communication round.
papers.training: Batch size 4, sigmoid output, binary cross-entropy, Adam.
papers.evaluation: Overlap similarity (Dice) for organ localisation and segmentation.
papers.baselines: Locally trained models.
papers.results: Encouraging cross-domain results, e.g. overlap similarity of 0.79 for organ localisation across PET and CT nodes.

papers.title: FedSODA: Federated Cross-assessment and Dynamic Aggregation for Histopathology Segmentation
papers.authors: Yuan Zhang, Yaolei Qi, Xiaoming Qi, Lotfi Senhadji, Yongyue Wei, Feng Chen, Guanyu Yang
papers.aim: Federated learning (FL) for histopathology image segmentation involving multiple medical sites plays a crucial role in advancing the field of accurate disease diagnosis and treatment. However, it is still a task of great challenges due to the sample imbalance across clients and large data heterogeneity from disparate organs, variable segmentation tasks, and diverse distribution.
papers.method: Thus, we propose a novel FL approach for histopathology nuclei and tissue segmentation, FedSODA, via synthetic-driven cross-assessment operation (SO) and dynamic stratified-layer aggregation (DA). Our SO constructs a cross-assessment strategy to connect clients and mitigate the representation bias under sample imbalance. Our DA utilizes layer-wise interaction and dynamic aggregation to diminish heterogeneity and enhance generalization.
papers.result: The effectiveness of our FedSODA has been evaluated on the most extensive histopathology image segmentation dataset from 7 independent datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/yuanzhang7/FedSODA.
papers.gap: Non-brain tissue; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: FedSODA tackles very different pathology datasets acting as sites by evaluating each client's contribution with synthetic data and by aggregating different network layers differently, plus a loss that stops large structures dominating small cells. It improved federated segmentation across seven datasets. Layer-wise aggregation is one option for heterogeneous sites in WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public histopathology segmentation datasets (Southeast University and partners; preprint).
papers.datasets: Seven datasets as clients: CoNSeP, CPM-17, CRAG, CryoNuSeg, GlaS, Kumar and others (nuclei and tissue segmentation across organs).
papers.preprocessing: Standard patching per dataset.
papers.modelDetails: FedSODA: synthetic-driven cross-assessment operation (Gaussian synthetic information with a memory bank uploaded to the server to evaluate clients) with a segmentation consistency loss, and dynamic stratified-layer aggregation that adaptively combines shallow and deep layers.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Dice/AJI-type segmentation metrics across clients.
papers.baselines: FedAvg, FedProx and other FL methods.
papers.results: Outperformed FL baselines on the largest multi-site histopathology segmentation benchmark assembled from seven datasets.

papers.title: FedDropoutAvg: Generalizable federated learning for histopathology image classification
papers.authors: Gozde N. Gunesli, Mohsin Bilal, Shan E Ahmed Raza, Nasir M. Rajpoot
papers.aim: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative learning of a deep learning model without sharing the data of participating sites. FL in medical image analysis tasks is relatively new and open for enhancements.
papers.method: In this study, we propose FedDropoutAvg, a new federated learning approach for training a generalizable model. The proposed method takes advantage of randomness, both in client selection and also in federated averaging process. We compare FedDropoutAvg to several algorithms in an FL scenario for real-world multi-site histopathology image classification task. We show that with FedDropoutAvg, the final model can achieve performance better than other FL approaches and closer to a classical deep learning model that requires all data to be shared for centralized training. We test the trained models on a large dataset consisting of 1.2 million image tiles from 21 different centers. To evaluate the generalization ability of the proposed approach, we use held-out test sets from centers whose data was used in the FL and for unseen data from other independent centers whose data was not used in the federated training.
papers.result: We show that the proposed approach is more generalizable than other state-of-the-art federated training approaches. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first study to use a randomized client and local model parameter selection procedure in a federated setting for a medical image analysis task.
papers.gap: No calibration or uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using real centre boundaries in TCGA as federation sites, the authors add randomness to which sites contribute each round and which parameters are averaged, which acts as regularisation. Tested on held-out data from training centres and on completely unseen centres, it generalised better than FedAvg and FedProx. It is a simple aggregation option for small, heterogeneous federations.
papers.studyDesign: Method development and multi-site evaluation on real centre partitions (University of Warwick; preprint).
papers.datasets: TCGA CRC-DX: 599 diagnostic WSIs from 591 colorectal cancer patients from 36 centres; centres with <5 patients excluded; ~1.2 million tiles from 21 centres used for testing, including independent centres not in training; tumour tiles selected by a ResNet18 tumour classifier (99% accuracy).
papers.preprocessing: Otsu tissue thresholding; 512x512 tiles at 20x; tumour vs non-tumour filtering.
papers.modelDetails: FedDropoutAvg: federated training with randomness in client selection and random dropout of parameters during federated averaging to improve generalisation; classifier for slide-derived tile labels (e.g. MSI-type task).
papers.training: 3-fold experiments (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Mean F1 and AUROC on held-out test sets of training centres and on independent centres.
papers.baselines: Centralised model, FedAvg, FedProx.
papers.results: FedDropoutAvg outperformed other FL approaches and came closer to centralised training, especially on independent unseen centres.
papers.statistics: Mean and SD across folds and centres.

papers.title: Benchmarking Differentially Private Residual Networks for Medical Imagery
papers.authors: Sahib Singh, Harshvardhan Sikka, Sasikanth Kotti, Andrew Trask
papers.aim: In this paper we measure the effectiveness of $ε$-Differential Privacy (DP) when applied to medical imaging. We compare two robust differential privacy mechanisms: Local-DP and DP-SGD and benchmark their performance when analyzing medical imagery records.
papers.result: We compare two robust differential privacy mechanisms: Local-DP and DP-SGD and benchmark their performance when analyzing medical imagery records. We analyze the trade-off between the model's accuracy and the level of privacy it guarantees, and also take a closer look to evaluate how useful these theoretical privacy guarantees actually prove to be in the real world medical setting.
papers.gap: Simple 2D tasks; no federated or calibration analysis.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors trained medical image classifiers with two forms of differential privacy across a range of privacy budgets and measured the cost to accuracy, discussing what the guarantees mean in practice. It provides reference points for choosing a privacy budget in WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study of differential privacy for medical imaging (OpenMined, Harvard, Oxford and others; preprint).
papers.datasets: Chest X-ray pneumonia dataset (~5,800 images) and APTOS 2019 diabetic retinopathy dataset (~3,600 training fundus images, grades 0-4).
papers.preprocessing: Standard image preprocessing.
papers.modelDetails: Residual networks trained with Local Differential Privacy and with DP-SGD at varying epsilon values.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy versus privacy budget epsilon; practical usefulness of guarantees.
papers.baselines: Non-private training.
papers.results: Showed the accuracy-privacy trade-off: stronger privacy (smaller epsilon) reduced accuracy, with DP-SGD and Local-DP behaving differently.

papers.title: Privacy-Preserving in Medical Image Analysis: A Review of Methods and Applications
papers.authors: Yanming Zhu, Xuefei Yin, Alan Wee-Chung Liew, Hui Tian
papers.aim: With the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence and deep learning, medical image analysis has become a critical tool in modern healthcare, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. However, AI-based methods also raise serious privacy concerns, as medical images often contain highly sensitive patient information.
papers.method: This review offers a comprehensive overview of privacy-preserving techniques in medical image analysis, including encryption, differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, federated learning, and generative adversarial networks. We explore the application of these techniques across various medical image analysis tasks, such as diagnosis, pathology, and telemedicine. Notably, we organizes the review based on specific challenges and their corresponding solutions in different medical image analysis applications, so that technical applications are directly aligned with practical issues, addressing gaps in the current research landscape.
papers.result: Additionally, we discuss emerging trends, such as zero-knowledge proofs and secure multi-party computation, offering insights for future research. This review serves as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners and can help advance privacy-preserving in medical image analysis.
papers.gap: No empirical comparison.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The review organises privacy-preserving techniques in medical imaging according to the practical problems they solve rather than by technology, and discusses newer cryptographic approaches. It is background for designing the registry's de-identification and federated privacy protections.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (Griffith University, Australia; preprint).
papers.datasets: Literature on privacy-preserving medical image analysis across diagnosis, pathology and telemedicine.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Review organised by privacy challenge: encryption, differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, federated learning, image obfuscation/deformation, and emerging methods such as zero-knowledge proofs and secure multi-party computation.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Maps techniques to concrete privacy problems and highlights trade-offs and emerging directions.

papers.title: Vision Through the Veil: Differential Privacy in Federated Learning for Medical Image Classification
papers.authors: Kishore Babu Nampalle, Pradeep Singh, Uppala Vivek Narayan, Balasubramanian Raman
papers.aim: The proliferation of deep learning applications in healthcare calls for data aggregation across various institutions, a practice often associated with significant privacy concerns. This concern intensifies in medical image analysis, where privacy-preserving mechanisms are paramount due to the data being sensitive in nature.
papers.method: Federated learning, which enables cooperative model training without direct data exchange, presents a promising solution. Nevertheless, the inherent vulnerabilities of federated learning necessitate further privacy safeguards. This study addresses this need by integrating differential privacy, a leading privacy-preserving technique, into a federated learning framework for medical image classification. We introduce a novel differentially private federated learning model and meticulously examine its impacts on privacy preservation and model performance.
papers.result: Our research confirms the existence of a trade-off between model accuracy and privacy settings. However, we demonstrate that strategic calibration of the privacy budget in differential privacy can uphold robust image classification performance while providing substantial privacy protection.
papers.gap: Classification on dermatoscopy; no calibration of predictions.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Each simulated hospital adds calibrated noise to its model update before sending it, with the amount of noise adapted over training rounds, so that privacy is formally protected. Accuracy fell less than with naive noise. It gives a concrete differentially private federated design for WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Method development (IIT Roorkee; preprint).
papers.datasets: HAM10000 dermatoscopic images (10,015: 8,902 benign, 1,113 malignant) and other medical image classification data distributed across simulated clients.
papers.preprocessing: Standard preprocessing and partitioning.
papers.modelDetails: Differentially private federated learning: Laplace noise added to each client's model update with a noise calibration mechanism and adaptive privacy budget allocation across rounds; formal privacy-utility analysis.
papers.training: Details in Algorithm 1.
papers.evaluation: Classification accuracy across privacy budgets.
papers.baselines: Non-private federated learning.
papers.results: Confirmed an accuracy-privacy trade-off, but strategic noise calibration and budget allocation preserved accuracy while giving meaningful privacy.

papers.title: Multiple Instance Learning for Digital Pathology: A Review on the State-of-the-Art, Limitations & Future Potential
papers.authors: Michael Gadermayr, Maximilian Tschuchnig
papers.aim: Digital whole slides images contain an enormous amount of information providing a strong motivation for the development of automated image analysis tools. Particularly deep neural networks show high potential with respect to various tasks in the field of digital pathology.
papers.method: However, a limitation is given by the fact that typical deep learning algorithms require (manual) annotations in addition to the large amounts of image data, to enable effective training. Multiple instance learning exhibits a powerful tool for learning deep neural networks in a scenario without fully annotated data. These methods are particularly effective in this domain, due to the fact that labels for a complete whole slide image are often captured routinely, whereas labels for patches, regions or pixels are not. This potential already resulted in a considerable number of publications, with the majority published in the last three years.
papers.result: Besides the availability of data and a high motivation from the medical perspective, the availability of powerful graphics processing units exhibits an accelerator in this field. In this paper, we provide an overview of widely and effectively used concepts of used deep multiple instance learning approaches, recent advances and also critically discuss remaining challenges and future potential.
papers.gap: No quantitative comparison.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The review explains how multiple instance learning lets models learn from slide-level labels, surveys the main families of MIL methods and discusses open problems. It provides the conceptual basis for the slide-level Pathology Agent.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (Salzburg University of Applied Sciences; Computerized Medical Imaging and Graphics).
papers.datasets: Literature on deep multiple instance learning in digital pathology.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Overview of MIL concepts (instance vs embedding level, pooling operators, attention-based MIL, transformer MIL, graph MIL, multi-scale, self-supervised features) and their use for WSI classification and segmentation.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: MIL is effective because slide labels are routinely available while patch labels are not; remaining challenges include interpretability, data efficiency, multi-scale context, label noise and validation.

papers.title: CAMIL: Context-Aware Multiple Instance Learning for Cancer Detection and Subtyping in Whole Slide Images
papers.authors: Olga Fourkioti, Matt De Vries, Chen Jin, Daniel C. Alexander, Chris Bakal
papers.venue: The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations, ICLR 2024
papers.aim: The visual examination of tissue biopsy sections is fundamental for cancer diagnosis, with pathologists analyzing sections at multiple magnifications to discern tumor cells and their subtypes. However, existing attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) models used for analyzing Whole Slide Images (WSIs) in cancer diagnostics often overlook the contextual information of tumor and neighboring tiles, leading to misclassifications.
papers.method: To address this, we propose the Context-Aware Multiple Instance Learning (CAMIL) architecture. CAMIL incorporates neighbor-constrained attention to consider dependencies among tiles within a WSI and integrates contextual constraints as prior knowledge into the MIL model.
papers.result: We evaluated CAMIL on subtyping non-small cell lung cancer (TCGA-NSCLC) and detecting lymph node (CAMELYON16 and CAMELYON17) metastasis, achieving test AUCs of 97.5\%, 95.9\%, and 88.1\%, respectively, outperforming other state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, CAMIL enhances model interpretability by identifying regions of high diagnostic value.
papers.gap: No brain tumours; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: CAMIL mimics how pathologists look at a region and its surroundings: each tile's importance is adjusted according to its neighbours, so isolated high-attention tiles likely to be noise are down-weighted. It improved slide classification and tumour localisation over standard attention MIL. Context-aware attention may help with heterogeneous gliomas.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public WSI benchmarks (Institute of Cancer Research and UCL; ICLR 2024).
papers.datasets: TCGA-NSCLC (subtyping), CAMELYON16 and CAMELYON17 (lymph-node metastasis detection).
papers.preprocessing: Automatic tissue segmentation and tiling into 256x256 tiles.
papers.modelDetails: CAMIL: tile feature extraction followed by a Nystromformer-based global transformer and neighbour-constrained attention that recalibrates each tile's attention by its neighbourhood, then attention pooling for slide classification.
papers.training: Details in appendix.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy and AUC; localisation of tumour regions.
papers.baselines: CLAM-SB, CLAM-MB, TransMIL, DTFD-MIL, GTP, DSMIL.
papers.results: Outperformed baselines on subtyping and metastasis detection (reported AUCs above 0.95 on the benchmarks) and improved localisation by using tile context.

papers.title: Federated Learning for Computational Pathology on Gigapixel Whole Slide Images
papers.authors: Ming Y. Lu, Dehan Kong, Jana Lipkova, Richard J. Chen, Rajendra Singh, Drew F. K. Williamson, Tiffany Y. Chen, Faisal Mahmood
papers.aim: Deep Learning-based computational pathology algorithms have demonstrated profound ability to excel in a wide array of tasks that range from characterization of well known morphological phenotypes to predicting non-human-identifiable features from histology such as molecular alterations. However, the development of robust, adaptable, and accurate deep learning-based models often rely on the collection and time-costly curation large high-quality annotated training data that should ideally come from diverse sources and patient populations to cater for the heterogeneity that exists in such datasets.
papers.method: Multi-centric and collaborative integration of medical data across multiple institutions can naturally help overcome this challenge and boost the model performance but is limited by privacy concerns amongst other difficulties that may arise in the complex data sharing process as models scale towards using hundreds of thousands of gigapixel whole slide images. In this paper, we introduce privacy-preserving federated learning for gigapixel whole slide images in computational pathology using weakly-supervised attention multiple instance learning and differential privacy. We evaluated our approach on two different diagnostic problems using thousands of histology whole slide images with only slide-level labels.
papers.result: Additionally, we present a weakly-supervised learning framework for survival prediction and patient stratification from whole slide images and demonstrate its effectiveness in a federated setting. Our results show that using federated learning, we can effectively develop accurate weakly supervised deep learning models from distributed data silos without direct data sharing and its associated complexities, while also preserving differential privacy using randomized noise generation.
papers.gap: No calibration; non-brain cancers.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: This early study combined attention-based multiple instance learning on gigapixel slides with federated learning and differential privacy, showing that institutions can jointly train slide-level diagnostic and survival models from slide labels only without sharing slides. It is the template for federated pathology in WP5.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on multi-institutional WSIs (Brigham and Women's / Harvard, Northwell; Medical Image Analysis).
papers.datasets: Thousands of H&E WSIs with slide-level labels for two diagnostic problems (e.g. breast and renal cell carcinoma subtyping) and survival prediction, partitioned across institutions as federated clients.
papers.preprocessing: Tissue segmentation and patching; frozen feature extraction.
papers.modelDetails: Weakly supervised attention-based multiple instance learning (CLAM-style) trained with federated averaging across institutions, with differential privacy via randomised noise added to model updates; weakly supervised survival prediction framework.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Classification AUC and accuracy; C-index for survival; comparison with centralised and single-institution training.
papers.baselines: Centralised training and individual-site models.
papers.results: Federated models reached accuracy close to centralised training and better than single-site models while preserving differential privacy; survival stratification effective in federated setting.

papers.title: Glioma Classification Using Multimodal Radiology and Histology Data
papers.authors: Azam Hamidinekoo, Tomasz Pieciak, Maryam Afzali, Otar Akanyeti, Yinyin Yuan
papers.aim: Gliomas are brain tumours with a high mortality rate. There are various grades and sub-types of this tumour, and the treatment procedure varies accordingly.
papers.method: Clinicians and oncologists diagnose and categorise these tumours based on visual inspection of radiology and histology data. However, this process can be time-consuming and subjective. The computer-assisted methods can help clinicians to make better and faster decisions. In this paper, we propose a pipeline for automatic classification of gliomas into three sub-types: oligodendroglioma, astrocytoma, and glioblastoma, using both radiology and histopathology images. The proposed approach implements distinct classification models for radiographic and histologic modalities and combines them through an ensemble method. The classification algorithm initially carries out tile-level (for histology) and slice-level (for radiology) classification via a deep learning method, then tile/slice-level latent features are combined for a whole-slide and whole-volume sub-type prediction. The classification algorithm was evaluated using the data set provided in the CPM-RadPath 2020 challenge.
papers.result: The proposed pipeline achieved the F1-Score of 0.886, Cohen's Kappa score of 0.811 and Balance accuracy of 0.860. The ability of the proposed model for end-to-end learning of diverse features enables it to give a comparable prediction of glioma tumour sub-types.
papers.gap: Assumes both modalities present; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The pipeline trains one network on MRI and another on pathology slides for the same patients and combines their predictions to classify glioma subtype. The fused model reached high agreement with the reference labels in the challenge. It is an early demonstration of the radiology-pathology fusion planned in WP4.
papers.studyDesign: Method development in the CPM-RadPath challenge (Institute of Cancer Research and partners; preprint).
papers.datasets: CPM-RadPath 2020: paired multi-institutional mp-MRI (T1w, T2w, Gd-T1w, FLAIR; co-registered, 1 mm, skull-stripped) and one H&E WSI per patient; labels A (IDH-mutant astrocytoma), O (oligodendroglioma) and G (glioblastoma/IDH-wildtype); 221 training (133 G, 54 O, 34 A), 35 validation, 73 test.
papers.preprocessing: Challenge preprocessing for MRI; WSI patching at varying magnifications.
papers.modelDetails: Separate DenseNet-based classifiers for radiology and histology, combined in an ensemble/fusion pipeline for three-class glioma classification.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: F1, Cohen's kappa, balanced accuracy.
papers.baselines: Single-modality models.
papers.results: F1 0.886, kappa 0.811, balanced accuracy 0.860 on validation.

papers.title: Glioma subtype classification from histopathological images using in-domain and out-of-domain transfer learning: An experimental study
papers.authors: Vladimir Despotovic, Sang-Yoon Kim, Ann-Christin Hau, Aliaksandra Kakoichankava, Gilbert Georg Klamminger, Felix Bruno Kleine Borgmann, Katrin B. M. Frauenknecht, Michel Mittelbronn, Petr V. Nazarov
papers.aim: We provide in this paper a comprehensive comparison of various transfer learning strategies and deep learning architectures for computer-aided classification of adult-type diffuse gliomas. We evaluate the generalizability of out-of-domain ImageNet representations for a target domain of histopathological images, and study the impact of in-domain adaptation using self-supervised and multi-task learning approaches for pretraining the models using the medium-to-large scale datasets of histopathological images.
papers.method: A semi-supervised learning approach is furthermore proposed, where the fine-tuned models are utilized to predict the labels of unannotated regions of the whole slide images (WSI).
papers.result: The models are subsequently retrained using the ground-truth labels and weak labels determined in the previous step, providing superior performance in comparison to standard in-domain transfer learning with balanced accuracy of 96.91% and F1-score 97.07%, and minimizing the pathologist's efforts for annotation. Finally, we provide a visualization tool working at WSI level which generates heatmaps that highlight tumor areas; thus, providing insights to pathologists concerning the most informative parts of the WSI.
papers.gap: Very small cohort; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: With a small national glioma cohort annotated by a neuropathologist under WHO 2021, the authors compared ImageNet and histopathology-pretrained networks and then used the trained models to label unannotated regions and retrain, gaining performance. A small-country cohort with expert annotation is comparable to the situation in Sri Lanka.
papers.studyDesign: Experimental comparison study with an in-house cohort (Luxembourg Institute of Health, National Center of Pathology Luxembourg, Frankfurt; ethics CNER REC-LRNO-20110708).
papers.datasets: 75 H&E WSIs from 28 adult-type diffuse glioma cases (2017-2021) scanned on Philips IntelliSite at 0.25 um/px; WHO CNS5 classes: IDH-mutant 1p/19q co-deleted oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-wildtype glioblastoma, plus normal brain; region annotations by a neuropathologist.
papers.preprocessing: FFPE processing; pseudonymised region-annotated images; patch extraction from annotated regions.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of transfer-learning strategies (out-of-domain ImageNet vs in-domain histopathology pretraining) and architectures for patch-level glioma subtype classification; semi-supervised step in which fine-tuned models label unannotated regions and models are retrained on ground-truth plus weak labels.
papers.training: Details in paper.
papers.evaluation: Patch and slide-level accuracy, balanced accuracy, F1.
papers.baselines: Different architectures and pretraining sources.
papers.results: In-domain pretraining and the semi-supervised weak-label retraining improved performance over standard transfer learning.

papers.title: Multi-Beholder: Biomarker Prediction for Low-Grade Glioma with Multiple Instance Learning and One-Class Classification
papers.authors: Zijie Fang, Yihan Liu, Yifeng Wang, Xiangyang Zhang, Yang Chen, Changjing Cai, Yiyang Lin, Ying Han, Zhi Wang, Shan Zeng, et al.
papers.aim: Biomarker detection is an indispensable part of the diagnosis and treatment of low-grade glioma (LGG). However, current LGG biomarker detection methods rely on expensive and complex molecular genetic testing, for which professionals are required to analyze the results, and intra-rater variability is often reported.
papers.method: To overcome these challenges, we propose an interpretable deep learning pipeline, named Multi-Biomarker Histomorphology Discoverer (Multi-Beholder), to predict the status of five biomarkers in LGG using only hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole slide images. Specifically, Multi-Beholder incorporates one-class classification into the multiple instance learning framework to achieve accurate instance-level pseudo-labeling, thereby complementing slide-level labels and improving prediction performance. Multi-Beholder demonstrates high performance on two LGG cohorts with diverse races and scanning protocols, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve up to 0.973 on the internal-validated TCGA-LGG dataset and 0.820 on the external-validated Xiangya cohort. Moreover, the interpretability of Multi-Beholder allows for discovering quantitative and qualitative correlations between biomarker status and histomorphology characteristics.
papers.result: Our pipeline not only provides a novel approach for biomarker prediction, enhancing the applicability of molecular treatments for LGG patients but also facilitates the discovery of new mechanisms in molecular functionality and LGG progression. Code can be accessed at https://github.com/Vison307/Multi-Beholder.
papers.gap: No calibration or deferral when marker prediction is uncertain.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Multi-Beholder predicts several molecular markers of low-grade glioma directly from routine slides. It adds one-class classification to multiple instance learning so that confident patches get pseudo-labels, improving learning from slide-level labels, and adapts predictions at test time. It is relevant to estimating markers when molecular tests are unavailable, though such estimates must stay advisory.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on two LGG cohorts (Central South University and partners; preprint).
papers.datasets: Two low-grade glioma cohorts with diverse races and scanners, H&E WSIs and five biomarkers (e.g. 1p/19q N = 831 with 39% positive; ATRX N = 828 with 34% positive; IDH, TERT, others).
papers.preprocessing: WSIs cut into non-overlapping patches.
papers.modelDetails: Multi-Beholder: attention-based MIL with one-class classification (OCSVM) to pseudo-label confident instances in negative and positive bags, instance feature refinement, and test-time adaptation (T3A) of the final prediction.
papers.training: Hyperparameters (number of confident instances, noisy-instance ratio, OCSVM nu) listed in paper.
papers.evaluation: AUC, accuracy, F1 with 95% CIs per biomarker.
papers.baselines: ABMIL, CLAM-SB and other MIL methods.
papers.results: Outperformed MIL baselines across biomarkers (e.g. ABMIL 1p/19q AUC 0.830 vs higher for Multi-Beholder) and gave interpretable histomorphology.

papers.title: Benchmarking Pathology Foundation Models: Adaptation Strategies and Scenarios
papers.authors: Jeaung Lee, Jeewoo Lim, Keunho Byeon, Jin Tae Kwak
papers.aim: In computational pathology, several foundation models have recently emerged and demonstrated enhanced learning capability for analyzing pathology images. However, adapting these models to various downstream tasks remains challenging, particularly when faced with datasets from different sources and acquisition conditions, as well as limited data availability.
papers.method: In this study, we benchmark four pathology-specific foundation models across 14 datasets and two scenarios-consistency assessment and flexibility assessment-addressing diverse adaptation scenarios and downstream tasks. In the consistency assessment scenario, involving five fine-tuning methods, we found that the parameter-efficient fine-tuning approach was both efficient and effective for adapting pathology-specific foundation models to diverse datasets within the same downstream task. In the flexibility assessment scenario under data-limited environments, utilizing five few-shot learning methods, we observed that the foundation models benefited more from the few-shot learning methods that involve modification during the testing phase only.
papers.result: These findings provide insights that could guide the deployment of pathology-specific foundation models in real clinical settings, potentially improving the accuracy and reliability of pathology image analysis. The code for this study is available at: https://github.com/QuIIL/BenchmarkingPathologyFoundationModels.
papers.gap: No brain tissue; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors tested how best to adapt pathology foundation models to new datasets from different hospitals and scanners, and how they behave when only a few labelled examples exist. Lightweight adaptation worked best in most cases. This informs how the Pathology Agent's encoder will be adapted to local slides.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark study of pathology foundation models (Korea University; preprint).
papers.datasets: 14 public pathology datasets across breast (PCam, BACH, BRACS), colorectal (Kather19, Kather16, CRC-TP, KBSMC Colon I/II, DigestPath, Chaoyang), prostate (PANDA, AGGC22, UBC), gastric (KBSMC Gastric) and lung/colorectal (LC25000), with different scanners, magnifications and pixel sizes.
papers.preprocessing: Native patch sizes and resolutions per dataset.
papers.modelDetails: Four pathology-specific foundation models evaluated in two scenarios: consistency assessment with five fine-tuning methods (including parameter-efficient fine-tuning) and flexibility assessment with five few-shot learning methods.
papers.training: Standardised fine-tuning and few-shot protocols.
papers.evaluation: Classification accuracy/F1 across datasets and scenarios.
papers.baselines: Full fine-tuning, linear probing and other adaptation methods.
papers.results: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning was efficient and effective across datasets; in data-limited settings, foundation models benefited most from few-shot methods that modify only test-time behaviour.

papers.title: Domain-Specific Foundation Model Improves AI-Based Analysis of Neuropathology
papers.authors: Ruchika Verma, Shrishtee Kandoi, Robina Afzal, Shengjia Chen, Jannes Jegminat, Michael W. Karlovich, Melissa Umphlett, Timothy E. Richardson, Kevin Clare, Quazi Hossain, et al.
papers.aim: Foundation models have transformed computational pathology by providing generalizable representations from large-scale histology datasets. However, existing models are predominantly trained on surgical pathology data, which is enriched for non-nervous tissue and overrepresents neoplastic, inflammatory, metabolic, and other non-neurological diseases.
papers.method: Neuropathology represents a markedly different domain of histopathology, characterized by unique cell types (neurons, glia, etc.), distinct cytoarchitecture, and disease-specific pathological features including neurofibrillary tangles, amyloid plaques, Lewy bodies, and pattern-specific neurodegeneration. This domain mismatch may limit the ability of general-purpose foundation models to capture the morphological patterns critical for interpreting neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and cerebellar ataxias. To address this gap, we developed NeuroFM, a foundation model trained specifically on whole-slide images of brain tissue spanning diverse neurodegenerative pathologies. NeuroFM demonstrates superior performance compared to general-purpose models across multiple neuropathology-specific downstream tasks, including mixed dementia disease classification, hippocampal region segmentation, and neurodegenerative ataxia identification encompassing cerebellar essential tremor and spinocerebellar ataxia subtypes.
papers.result: This work establishes that domain-specialized foundation models trained on brain tissue can better capture neuropathology-specific features than models trained on general surgical pathology datasets. By tailoring foundation models to the unique morphological landscape of neurodegenerative diseases, NeuroFM enables more accurate and reliable AI-based analysis for brain disease diagnosis and research, setting a precedent for domain-specific model development in specialized areas of digital pathology.
papers.gap: Mostly neurodegenerative tasks; tumour tasks less emphasised; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.limitations: Preprint; model availability may be restricted.
papers.methodologyDetail: NeuroFM is pretrained on hundreds of thousands of slides, enriched with brain tissue from neurodegenerative and neuro-oncological sources, and benchmarked against general pathology foundation models. Brain-specific pretraining helped. It is a candidate encoder for brain-tumour slides in the Pathology Agent, alongside general models.
papers.studyDesign: Foundation model development and benchmarking (Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and collaborators; preprint).
papers.datasets: Pretraining corpus of 585,657 H&E and Luxol fast blue-H&E WSIs; neuropathology data 23,144 slides (~800 million tiles) from Mount Sinai autopsy, diagnostic and brain bank services, PSP/CBD, Boston University CTE and Columbia Essential Tremor collections, plus 200 million tiles from general pathology.
papers.preprocessing: Standardised to 20x (0.5 um/px).
papers.modelDetails: NeuroFM: domain-specific self-supervised foundation model for neuropathology, compared with general pathology foundation models on neuropathology tasks.
papers.training: Monte Carlo cross-validation with 20 random 80/20 splits, two runs each; majority-class subsampling for slide classification.
papers.evaluation: Slide- and tile-level classification and regression metrics on neuropathology benchmarks.
papers.baselines: General-purpose pathology foundation models (e.g. UNI, Virchow, Prov-GigaPath).
papers.results: The neuropathology-specific model captured brain-tissue features better and outperformed general models on neuropathology tasks.

papers.title: RandStainNA: Learning Stain-Agnostic Features from Histology Slides by Bridging Stain Augmentation and Normalization
papers.authors: Yiqing Shen, Yulin Luo, Dinggang Shen, Jing Ke
papers.aim: Stain variations often decrease the generalization ability of deep learning based approaches in digital histopathology analysis. Two separate proposals, namely stain normalization (SN) and stain augmentation (SA), have been spotlighted to reduce the generalization error, where the former alleviates the stain shift across different medical centers using template image and the latter enriches the accessible stain styles by the simulation of more stain variations.
papers.method: However, their applications are bounded by the selection of template images and the construction of unrealistic styles. To address the problems, we unify SN and SA with a novel RandStainNA scheme, which constrains variable stain styles in a practicable range to train a stain agnostic deep learning model. The RandStainNA is applicable to stain normalization in a collection of color spaces i.e. HED, HSV, LAB. Additionally, we propose a random color space selection scheme to gain extra performance improvement. We evaluate our method by two diagnostic tasks i.e. tissue subtype classification and nuclei segmentation, with various network backbones.
papers.result: The performance superiority over both SA and SN yields that the proposed RandStainNA can consistently improve the generalization ability, that our models can cope with more incoming clinical datasets with unpredicted stain styles. The codes is available at https://github.com/yiqings/RandStainNA.
papers.gap: Colorectal tissue; no uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of normalising all slides to one template or randomly distorting colours, RandStainNA samples realistic stain styles from the distribution seen in training data and applies them as augmentation. Models trained this way generalised better to slides from other centres. It is a simple preprocessing option for local slides stained differently from public data.
papers.studyDesign: Method development (Shanghai Jiao Tong University, ShanghaiTech; MICCAI 2022).
papers.datasets: NCT-CRC-HE-100K-NONORM (100,000 patches, 80/20 train/validation, background class removed) and CRC-VAL-HE-7K (7,180 patches) for external testing of 8-class classification; MoNuSeg for nuclei segmentation.
papers.preprocessing: Images converted to LAB colour space; stain style characterised by mean and SD of each channel.
papers.modelDetails: RandStainNA: random stain normalisation and augmentation that samples a virtual template from estimated stain-style distributions, bridging normalisation and augmentation; tested on ResNet-18/50, MobileNetV3, EfficientNet-B0, ViT-Tiny and Swin-Tiny.
papers.training: Standard training per backbone (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Top-1 accuracy (classification); Dice and IoU (segmentation) on external data.
papers.baselines: Stain normalisation alone and stain augmentation alone.
papers.results: Consistently improved generalisation over both normalisation and augmentation across architectures.

papers.title: Do Histopathological Foundation Models Eliminate Batch Effects? A Comparative Study
papers.authors: Jonah Kömen, Hannah Marienwald, Jonas Dippel, Julius Hense
papers.aim: Deep learning has led to remarkable advancements in computational histopathology, e.g., in diagnostics, biomarker prediction, and outcome prognosis. Yet, the lack of annotated data and the impact of batch effects, e.g., systematic technical data differences across hospitals, hamper model robustness and generalization.
papers.method: Recent histopathological foundation models -- pretrained on millions to billions of images -- have been reported to improve generalization performances on various downstream tasks. However, it has not been systematically assessed whether they fully eliminate batch effects. In this study, we empirically show that the feature embeddings of the foundation models still contain distinct hospital signatures that can lead to biased predictions and misclassifications.
papers.result: We further find that the signatures are not removed by stain normalization methods, dominate distances in feature space, and are evident across various principal components. Our work provides a novel perspective on the evaluation of medical foundation models, paving the way for more robust pretraining strategies and downstream predictors.
papers.gap: No mitigation method proposed.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study checks whether pathology foundation models remove differences between hospitals and finds they do not: the site a slide came from can be predicted from its features, and site differences dominate. This means local validation and site-aware calibration remain necessary even with foundation encoders.
papers.studyDesign: Comparative empirical study (TU Berlin, BIFOLD, Aignostics; preprint).
papers.datasets: TCGA-LUSC-5: up to 50 patients from each of five tissue source sites; CAMELYON16: 400 sentinel lymph node slides from two Dutch hospitals with tumour annotations.
papers.preprocessing: 256x256 patches at 20x, Otsu background removal, minimum patch SD of 8; patches labelled by site and tumour status.
papers.modelDetails: Analysis of embeddings from several histopathological foundation models for site-specific signatures (batch effects): site prediction from features, feature-space distances, principal components, and effect of stain normalisation.
papers.training: Linear and other probes on frozen features.
papers.evaluation: Site-prediction accuracy, contribution of site vs biology to feature distances, downstream bias.
papers.baselines: ImageNet features.
papers.results: Foundation model embeddings still contained strong hospital signatures that could bias predictions; these signatures were not removed by stain normalisation and dominated feature distances.

papers.title: PRISM: Privacy-preserving Inter-Site MRI Harmonization via Disentangled Representation Learning
papers.authors: Sarang Galada, Tanurima Halder, Kunal Deo, Ram P Krish, Kshitij Jadhav
papers.aim: Multi-site MRI studies often suffer from site-specific variations arising from differences in methodology, hardware, and acquisition protocols, thereby compromising accuracy and reliability in clinical AI/ML tasks. We present PRISM (Privacy-preserving Inter-Site MRI Harmonization), a novel Deep Learning framework for harmonizing structural brain MRI across multiple sites while preserving data privacy.
papers.method: PRISM employs a dual-branch autoencoder with contrastive learning and variational inference to disentangle anatomical features from style and site-specific variations, enabling unpaired image translation without traveling subjects or multiple MRI modalities. Our modular design allows harmonization to any target site and seamless integration of new sites without the need for retraining or fine-tuning. Using multi-site structural MRI data, we demonstrate PRISM's effectiveness in downstream tasks such as brain tissue segmentation and validate its harmonization performance through multiple experiments.
papers.result: Our framework addresses key challenges in medical AI/ML, including data privacy, distribution shifts, model generalizability and interpretability. Code is available at https://github.com/saranggalada/PRISM
papers.gap: 2D single slices; healthy brains, not tumours.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: PRISM lets hospitals make their MRI look like a chosen reference site without sharing images: each site learns to separate anatomy from scanner style, and the reference site shares only the parts of its model that encode style. It is a possible preprocessing step to reduce scanner differences across Sri Lankan sites before federated training.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on public multi-site brain MRI (IIT Bombay, Sai University; preprint).
papers.datasets: T2-weighted brain MRI from IXI (Guys 319, HH 185 slices) and ADNI (77 slices); middle axial slice per subject; 90/10 train-test split.
papers.preprocessing: FSL BET brain extraction; padding, centre-cropping, normalisation, background removal, resizing to 256x256; gamma augmentations (0.5, 1.5); brain masks.
papers.modelDetails: PRISM: dual-branch autoencoder with contrastive learning and variational inference disentangling anatomy (sensitive) from style/site (non-sensitive); each site trains locally; the target site shares only its style encoder and decoder so other sites harmonise to it without sharing images.
papers.training: Local training per site (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Harmonisation quality and downstream brain tissue segmentation consistency across sites.
papers.baselines: Other harmonisation methods requiring traveling subjects or paired data.
papers.results: Effective privacy-preserving harmonisation enabling consistent downstream segmentation; new sites can be added without retraining.

papers.title: Few-Shot Generation of Brain Tumors for Secure and Fair Data Sharing
papers.authors: Yongyi Shi, Ge Wang
papers.aim: Leveraging multi-center data for medical analytics presents challenges due to privacy concerns and data heterogeneity. While distributed approaches such as federated learning has gained traction, they remain vulnerable to privacy breaches, particularly in sensitive domains like medical imaging.
papers.method: Generative models, such as diffusion models, enhance privacy by synthesizing realistic data. However, they are prone to memorization, especially when trained on small datasets. This study proposes a decentralized few-shot generative model (DFGM) to synthesize brain tumor images while fully preserving privacy. DFGM harmonizes private tumor data with publicly shareable healthy images from multiple medical centers, constructing a new dataset by blending tumor foregrounds with healthy backgrounds.
papers.result: This approach ensures stringent privacy protection and enables controllable, high-quality synthesis by preserving both the healthy backgrounds and tumor foregrounds. We assess DFGM's effectiveness in brain tumor segmentation using a UNet, achieving Dice score improvements of 3.9% for data augmentation and 4.6% for fairness on a separate dataset.
papers.gap: 2D; synthetic realism and residual privacy risk need clinical checking.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Instead of sharing real tumour scans, each centre blends its tumours into healthy brains taken from public data using a diffusion model, producing synthetic images that can be shared. Training segmentation networks with this shared synthetic data improved performance at each centre. It is an alternative or complement to federated learning when sites cannot participate in live training.
papers.studyDesign: Method development on BraTS 2020 (Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute; preprint).
papers.datasets: BraTS 2020 GBM: 309 scans from CBICA (103 train, 26 test) and TCIA (134 train, 33 test); public healthy brain images from multiple centres; 2D tumour slices every five slices; whole tumour in T2.
papers.preprocessing: Patient-level split by centre; 2D slice extraction.
papers.modelDetails: Decentralised few-shot generative model (DFGM): a diffusion model harmonises private tumour foregrounds with publicly shareable healthy backgrounds from other centres to create synthetic tumour images for sharing, reducing memorisation risk.
papers.training: Few-shot diffusion training (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: UNet segmentation Dice when training with shared synthetic data; fairness across centres; few-shot rare-disease scenario.
papers.baselines: Training on local data only; federated learning; standard generative models.
papers.results: Synthetic shared data improved segmentation Dice across centres and supported fairness while protecting privacy.

papers.title: Deep learning can differentiate IDH-mutant from IDH-wild type GBM
papers.authors: Luca Pasquini, Antonio Napolitano, Emanuela Tagliente, Francesco Dellepiane, Martina Lucignani, Antonello Vidiri, Giulio Ranazzi, Antonella Stoppacciaro, Giulia Moltoni, Matteo Nicolai, et al.
papers.aim: Background: Distinction of IDH mutant and wildtype GBMs is challenging on MRI, since conventional imaging shows considerable overlap. While few studies employed deep-learning in a mixed low/high grade glioma population, a GBM-specific model is still lacking in the literature.
papers.method: Our objective was to develop a deep-learning model for IDH prediction in GBM by using Convoluted Neural Networks (CNN) on multiparametric MRI. Methods: We included 100 adult patients with pathologically proven GBM and IDH testing. MRI data included: morphologic sequences, rCBV and ADC maps. Tumor area was obtained by a bounding box function on the axial slice with widest tumor extension on T2 images and was projected on every sequence. Data was split into training and test (80:20) sets. A 4 block 2D - CNN architecture was implemented for IDH prediction on every MRI sequence. IDH mutation probability was calculated with softmax activation function from the last dense layer. Highest performance was calculated accounting for model accuracy and categorical cross-entropy loss (CCEL) in the test cohort. Results: Our model achieved the following performance: T1 (accuracy 77%, CCEL 1.4), T2 (accuracy 67%, CCEL 2.41), FLAIR (accuracy 77%, CCEL 1.98), MPRAGE (accuracy 66%, CCEL 2.55), rCBV (accuracy 83%, CCEL 0.64). ADC achieved lower performance. Conclusion: We built a GBM-tailored deep-learning model for IDH mutation prediction, achieving accuracy of 83% with rCBV maps.
papers.result: High predictivity of perfusion images may reflect the known correlation between IDH, hypoxia inducible factor (HIF) and neoangiogenesis. This model may set a path for non-invasive evaluation of IDH mutation in GBM.
papers.gap: Very few positives; no external validation; WHO 2016 GBM definition (IDH-mutant GBM no longer exists under WHO 2021).
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a single-centre GBM cohort, the authors trained separate networks on each structural, diffusion and perfusion sequence to predict IDH status and found perfusion images most informative. The small number of IDH-mutant cases limits conclusions. It indicates that advanced sequences, if available locally, may add molecular information.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective observational single-centre study (Sant'Andrea Hospital, Sapienza University, Rome; IRB 19 SA_2020).
papers.datasets: 156 adults with pathology-proven GBM (2005-2019); 100 with IDH testing: 83 IDH-wildtype, 17 IDH-mutant; preoperative T1, T2, FLAIR, MPRAGE, rCBV perfusion and ADC diffusion images.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusion for motion artefacts; IDH by IHC (R132H) with sequencing of negatives.
papers.modelDetails: CNN classifiers trained per MRI sequence for IDH mutation prediction.
papers.training: Five random train/test splits averaged.
papers.evaluation: AUC per sequence.
papers.baselines: Comparison across sequences.
papers.results: Mean AUCs: T1 0.71, T2 0.63, FLAIR 0.74, MPRAGE 0.62, rCBV 0.86, ADC 0.45; perfusion was most predictive, possibly reflecting IDH-related angiogenesis.

papers.title: FoundBioNet: A Foundation-Based Model for IDH Genotyping of Glioma from Multi-Parametric MRI
papers.authors: Somayeh Farahani, Marjaneh Hejazi, Antonio Di Ieva, Sidong Liu
papers.aim: Accurate, noninvasive detection of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation is essential for effective glioma management. Traditional methods rely on invasive tissue sampling, which may fail to capture a tumor's spatial heterogeneity.
papers.method: While deep learning models have shown promise in molecular profiling, their performance is often limited by scarce annotated data. In contrast, foundation deep learning models offer a more generalizable approach for glioma imaging biomarkers. We propose a Foundation-based Biomarker Network (FoundBioNet) that utilizes a SWIN-UNETR-based architecture to noninvasively predict IDH mutation status from multi-parametric MRI. Two key modules are incorporated: Tumor-Aware Feature Encoding (TAFE) for extracting multi-scale, tumor-focused features, and Cross-Modality Differential (CMD) for highlighting subtle T2-FLAIR mismatch signals associated with IDH mutation. The model was trained and validated on a diverse, multi-center cohort of 1705 glioma patients from six public datasets. Our model achieved AUCs of 90.58%, 88.08%, 65.41%, and 80.31% on independent test sets from EGD, TCGA, Ivy GAP, RHUH, and UPenn, consistently outperforming baseline approaches (p <= 0.05). Ablation studies confirmed that both the TAFE and CMD modules are essential for improving predictive accuracy.
papers.result: By integrating large-scale pretraining and task-specific fine-tuning, FoundBioNet enables generalizable glioma characterization. This approach enhances diagnostic accuracy and interpretability, with the potential to enable more personalized patient care.
papers.gap: No calibration or deferral; public Western cohorts.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The model builds on a large pretrained 3D transformer encoder and fine-tunes it to predict IDH mutation from routine MRI, trained on some public cohorts and tested on entirely separate ones. Large-scale pretraining improved generalisation. Still, MRI-based IDH prediction is advisory and must defer to tissue testing in the framework.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-cohort study (Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Macquarie University; preprint).
papers.datasets: 2,428 glioma patients from six public datasets (TCGA 213, UCSF-PDGM 489, EGD 415, Ivy GAP 34, UPenn 514, RHUH 40); after exclusions (missing scans 228, incomplete pathology 204, preprocessing failure 81) 1,705 patients: 354 IDH-mutant, 1,351 IDH-wildtype.
papers.preprocessing: I3CR-WANO pipeline for registration and skull stripping where needed; no exclusion by acquisition parameters or quality.
papers.modelDetails: FoundBioNet: Swin-UNETR-based foundation model pretrained at scale and fine-tuned for IDH genotyping from T1, T1C, T2 and FLAIR, with tumour-aware feature modules.
papers.training: Two scenarios: train on TCGA+UCSF-PDGM and test on others; train on EGD+UCSF-PDGM and test on TCGA (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity on internal and independent external cohorts.
papers.baselines: Conventional CNN and radiomics models.
papers.results: Generalisable IDH prediction across multiple external cohorts, outperforming baselines.

papers.title: Towards a Multimodal MRI-Based Foundation Model for Multi-Level Feature Exploration in Segmentation, Molecular Subtyping, and Grading of Glioma
papers.authors: Somayeh Farahani, Marjaneh Hejazi, Antonio Di Ieva, Emad Fatemizadeh, Sidong Liu
papers.aim: Accurate, noninvasive glioma characterization is crucial for effective clinical management. Traditional methods, dependent on invasive tissue sampling, often fail to capture the spatial heterogeneity of the tumor.
papers.method: While deep learning has improved segmentation and molecular profiling, few approaches simultaneously integrate tumor morphology and molecular features. Foundation deep learning models, which learn robust, task-agnostic representations from large-scale datasets, hold great promise but remain underutilized in glioma imaging biomarkers. We propose the Multi-Task SWIN-UNETR (MTS-UNET) model, a novel foundation-based framework built on the BrainSegFounder model, pretrained on large-scale neuroimaging data. MTS-UNET simultaneously performs glioma segmentation, histological grading, and molecular subtyping (IDH mutation and 1p/19q co-deletion). It incorporates two key modules: Tumor-Aware Feature Encoding (TAFE) for multi-scale, tumor-focused feature extraction and Cross-Modality Differential (CMD) for highlighting subtle T2-FLAIR mismatch signals associated with IDH mutation. The model was trained and validated on a diverse, multi-center cohort of 2,249 glioma patients from seven public datasets. MTS-UNET achieved a mean Dice score of 84% for segmentation, along with AUCs of 90.58% for IDH mutation, 69.22% for 1p/19q co-deletion prediction, and 87.54% for grading, significantly outperforming baseline models (p<=0.05). Ablation studies validated the essential contributions of the TAFE and CMD modules and demonstrated the robustness of the framework.
papers.result: The foundation-based MTS-UNET model effectively integrates tumor segmentation with multi-level classification, exhibiting strong generalizability across diverse MRI datasets. This framework shows significant potential for advancing noninvasive, personalized glioma management by improving predictive accuracy and interpretability.
papers.gap: No uncertainty or deferral; public Western data.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: MTS-UNET uses one foundation-based network to segment gliomas and predict three molecular and grading targets together, trained and externally tested on several public cohorts. Multi-task learning lets segmentation information support classification. It is a design option for the MRI Agent if multiple outputs are produced from one model.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-cohort study (Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Macquarie University, Sharif University; preprint).
papers.datasets: 2,587 glioma patients from seven public datasets (TCGA, Ivy GAP, RHUH-GBM, UPenn-GBM, UCSF-PDGM, EGD, LGG-1p19q); 2,249 included across tasks; task-specific training/internal validation and external validation cohorts (e.g. IDH: train TCGA+UCSF-PDGM, external RHUH, UPenn, Ivy GAP, EGD).
papers.preprocessing: Standard preprocessing; inclusion based on available sequences per task (all four for IDH; T1C and T2 for 1p/19q and grade).
papers.modelDetails: MTS-UNET: foundation-based multi-task Swin-UNETR model that jointly performs glioma segmentation, IDH mutation prediction, 1p/19q co-deletion detection and histological grading.
papers.training: Large-scale pretraining with task-specific fine-tuning (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice for segmentation; AUC, accuracy for classification tasks on internal and external sets.
papers.baselines: Single-task models and conventional baselines.
papers.results: Integrated segmentation with multi-level classification and showed strong generalisability across external cohorts.

papers.title: Semi-supervised Contrastive Learning for Label-efficient Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Xinrong Hu, Dewen Zeng, Xiaowei Xu, Yiyu Shi
papers.aim: The success of deep learning methods in medical image segmentation tasks heavily depends on a large amount of labeled data to supervise the training. On the other hand, the annotation of biomedical images requires domain knowledge and can be laborious.
papers.method: Recently, contrastive learning has demonstrated great potential in learning latent representation of images even without any label. Existing works have explored its application to biomedical image segmentation where only a small portion of data is labeled, through a pre-training phase based on self-supervised contrastive learning without using any labels followed by a supervised fine-tuning phase on the labeled portion of data only. In this paper, we establish that by including the limited label in formation in the pre-training phase, it is possible to boost the performance of contrastive learning. We propose a supervised local contrastive loss that leverages limited pixel-wise annotation to force pixels with the same label to gather around in the embedding space. Such loss needs pixel-wise computation which can be expensive for large images, and we further propose two strategies, downsampling and block division, to address the issue.
papers.result: We evaluate our methods on two public biomedical image datasets of different modalities. With different amounts of labeled data, our methods consistently outperform the state-of-the-art contrast-based methods and other semi-supervised learning techniques.
papers.gap: Not tumour-specific; 2D.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The method improves contrastive pretraining for segmentation by also using the few pixel labels available: pixels with the same label are pulled together in feature space. Pretraining in two steps (unlabelled then labelled) improved segmentation with little data. It is another label-efficient option for WP2.
papers.studyDesign: Method development (University of Notre Dame, Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital; MICCAI 2021).
papers.datasets: Hippocampus MRI (Medical Segmentation Decathlon) and MMWHS cardiac CT/MRI with varying percentages of labelled training data.
papers.preprocessing: 2D slices with random augmentations for contrastive pairs.
papers.modelDetails: Two-step pretraining: self-supervised global contrastive learning on unlabelled data (encoder), then supervised local contrastive loss using limited pixel labels (encoder and decoder; stride or block sampling), followed by segmentation fine-tuning.
papers.training: Adam; lr 1e-4 contrastive (70 epochs), 1e-5 segmentation (120 epochs); GTX 1080 and Tesla P100 GPUs.
papers.evaluation: Dice with different labelled fractions.
papers.baselines: Random initialisation, global contrastive (SimCLR), global+local self-supervised, Mixup, TCSM.
papers.results: Global+local supervised contrastive variants outperformed other semi-supervised and self-supervised methods across label fractions.

papers.title: CoRe-BT: A Multimodal Radiology-Pathology-Text Benchmark for Robust Brain Tumor Typing
papers.authors: Juampablo E. Heras Rivera, Daniel K. Low, Xavier Xiong, Jacob J. Ruzevick, Daniel D. Child, Wen-wai Yim, Mehmet Kurt, Asma Ben Abacha
papers.aim: Accurate brain tumor typing requires integrating heterogeneous clinical evidence, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), histopathology, and pathology reports, which are often incomplete at the time of diagnosis. We introduce CoRe-BT, a cross-modal radiology-pathology-text benchmark for brain tumor typing, designed to study robust multimodal learning under missing modality conditions.
papers.method: The dataset comprises 310 patients with multi-sequence brain MRI (T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR), including 95 cases with paired H&E-stained whole-slide pathology images and pathology reports. All cases are annotated with tumor type and grade, and MRI volumes include expert-annotated tumor masks, enabling both region-aware modeling and auxiliary learning tasks. Tumors are categorized into six clinically relevant classes capturing the heterogeneity of common and rare glioma subtypes. We evaluate tumor typing under variable modality availability by comparing MRI-only models with multimodal approaches that incorporate pathology information when present.
papers.result: Baseline experiments demonstrate the feasibility of multimodal fusion and highlight complementary modality contributions across clinically relevant typing tasks. CoRe-BT provides a grounded testbed for advancing multimodal glioma typing and representation learning in realistic scenarios with incomplete clinical data.
papers.gap: Small paired subset; no calibration.
papers.relation: Informs data-efficient modelling (O3): learning reliable MRI / histopathology models from small datasets, including self-supervised, transfer, domain-adaptation and privacy-preserving federated learning.
papers.methodologyDetail: CoRe-BT provides brain-tumour cases with MRI, and for some cases pathology slides and reports, so methods can be tested when some modalities are missing, as in real practice. The baseline fuses embeddings from large MRI and pathology foundation models. It is a public test bed for the Diagnosis and Staging Agent's fusion under incompleteness.
papers.studyDesign: Benchmark creation with baseline experiments (University of Washington, Microsoft Health AI; preprint).
papers.datasets: 310 patients with multi-sequence brain MRI (T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR), of whom 95 have paired H&E WSIs and pathology reports; annotated with tumour type and grade and tumour masks; six clinically relevant glioma classes.
papers.preprocessing: MRI volumes embedded per sequence; WSIs tiled into 256x256 tiles.
papers.modelDetails: CoRe-BT-Fusion: NeuroVFM (volumetric neuroimaging foundation model trained on 5.24 million MRI/CT volumes) for subject-level MRI embeddings and Prov-GigaPath (1.3 billion tiles from 171,189 WSIs) for slide embeddings, fused for supervised tumour typing under variable modality availability.
papers.training: Supervised fusion head trained on embeddings (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Classification metrics for tumour typing with MRI only vs multimodal.
papers.baselines: MRI-only models.
papers.results: Multimodal fusion was feasible and modalities contributed complementary information across typing tasks.

heading: O4 - Clinical evaluation: performance, escalation appropriateness, workload, usability, trust and safety

papers.title: Reporting guideline for the early-stage clinical evaluation of decision support systems driven by artificial intelligence: DECIDE-AI
papers.authors: Vasey B, Nagendran M, Campbell B, Clifton DA, Collins GS, et al., McCulloch P
papers.aim: To give a reporting guideline for the first live clinical studies of AI decision support.
papers.method: International Delphi consensus with experts and stakeholders.
papers.result: Checklist of 17 AI-specific items and 10 generic items, covering human factors, safety, and user interaction.
papers.tools: Reporting guideline
papers.gap: Guideline only, it does not say which metrics to use for deferral.
papers.relation: Our O4 study is exactly this early stage. We should design and report it using DECIDE-AI.
papers.limitations: Needs adoption by journals. Future: updates as field changes.
papers.methodologyDetail: DECIDE-AI is a reporting checklist for the early, small-scale clinical evaluation of AI decision support - the stage after lab validation and before large trials, which is exactly the stage of our O4 study. It was built with a two-round modified Delphi survey of 123 and 138 experts from 20 stakeholder groups (clinicians, engineers, regulators, patients, journal editors and others), a consensus meeting of 16 people and a qualitative check by 16 more. It asks studies to report, for example, who the users were and how they were trained, the exact AI version, how inputs were obtained and handled when missing, how outputs were shown, human factors such as usability and trust, errors and safety events, and how often users agreed with or overrode the AI. For our PhD this is the main reporting standard for the clinician evaluation in O4.
papers.studyDesign: Consensus-based reporting guideline development (modified Delphi, consensus meeting, qualitative evaluation).
papers.datasets: Expert panel from 20 pre-defined stakeholder categories: 123 experts in Delphi round 1, 138 in round 2, 16 at the virtual consensus meeting and 16 in the qualitative evaluation.
papers.preprocessing: Initial candidate item list from literature review and steering group; items added after round 1 feedback.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (guideline). Output: DECIDE-AI checklist of 17 AI-specific items (28 subitems) and 10 generic items, each with an Explanation & Elaboration paragraph.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Delphi agreement thresholds on importance of each item; consensus meeting voting; qualitative evaluation of clarity and usability.
papers.baselines: Existing guidelines (TRIPOD, STARD, CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, IDEAL) - DECIDE-AI covers the early clinical stage between them.
papers.results: Final guideline with 17 AI-specific reporting items (28 subitems) and 10 generic items covering intended use, users and their training, AI system version and inputs/outputs, human factors (usability, learning curve, user trust), safety and errors, and human-AI agreement.
papers.availability: Checklist and E&E published open access (Nature Medicine 2022; BMJ).

papers.title: Reporting guidelines for clinical trial reports for interventions involving artificial intelligence: the CONSORT-AI extension
papers.authors: Liu X, Cruz Rivera S, Moher D, Calvert MJ, Denniston AK; SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI Working Group
papers.aim: To extend CONSORT for randomised trials that test AI interventions.
papers.method: Delphi process and consensus meeting.
papers.result: 14 new items, for example describing the AI version, input data, how humans interact with the output, and error analysis.
papers.tools: Reporting guideline
papers.gap: For RCTs, which come after early-stage studies.
papers.relation: Our study is not an RCT, but these items help us describe AI version, input and human interaction. Useful for future trial.
papers.limitations: Not for early studies. Future: updates.
papers.methodologyDetail: CONSORT-AI extends the standard checklist for reporting randomized trials so that trials testing AI tools describe the AI clearly. Candidate items were rated by 103 international experts over two Delphi rounds, agreed at a two-day meeting of 31 experts and piloted with 34 users, producing 14 new items. Trials must state which AI version was used, how input data were collected and what happened with poor-quality or missing inputs, how clinicians interacted with the AI and what skills they needed, how its output fed into decisions, and how errors were analysed. For our PhD it defines what a later randomized evaluation of the system must report, and several items (input quality handling, human-AI interaction, error analysis) should already be built into our O4 study design.
papers.studyDesign: Consensus-based extension of the CONSORT 2010 reporting guideline for randomized trials of AI interventions.
papers.datasets: 29 candidate items assessed by 103 international stakeholders in a two-stage Delphi survey; 31 stakeholders at a two-day consensus meeting; checklist pilot with 34 participants. Ethics approval University of Birmingham (ERN_19-1100).
papers.preprocessing: Literature review and steering group consultation to generate candidate items (developed together with SPIRIT-AI).
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (guideline). Output: 14 new AI-specific items (extensions and elaborations) added to CONSORT 2010.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Delphi rating and consensus meeting agreement on each item; pilot testing.
papers.baselines: CONSORT 2010 core items.
papers.results: 14 new items, including: state the AI intervention and its intended use; inclusion criteria at participant and input-data level; how the AI was integrated in the trial setting; AI version; how input data were acquired and handled when poor or missing; human-AI interaction and user skills; output of the AI and how it was used in decisions; analysis of performance errors; and access to the AI code.
papers.availability: Published open access in Nature Medicine, BMJ and Lancet Digital Health (2020).

papers.title: TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods
papers.authors: Collins GS, Moons KGM, Dhiman P, Riley RD, Beam AL, et al., Logullo P
papers.aim: To update TRIPOD for prediction models built with machine learning.
papers.method: Delphi survey and consensus meeting.
