papers.methodologyDetail: Many papers claim AI can strengthen health care in poorer countries, but how often has it actually been tested there? This review searched five databases and grey literature from 2009 to 2021 and found only 10 studies that evaluated AI in real use in low- and middle-income countries - decision support in rural Chinese clinics, radiotherapy planning in South Africa, TB screening in Peru, COVID-19 triage and chatbots. Half did not even say what algorithm or data were used. Common problems were unreliable performance, disrupted workflows, hard-to-use interfaces, poor fit with local practice, lack of local data, low trust and no proof of cost-effectiveness. For our PhD it underlines the novelty and need for a real-world, context-adapted evaluation of AI for brain tumour care in Sri Lanka, with attention to these barriers in O4.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic scoping review.
papers.datasets: Records 2009-2021 from 5 databases plus grey literature; 10 included studies from LMICs (e.g., China rural CDSS, South Africa radiotherapy planning for 14 cervical cancer patients, Peru TB CAD in primary care, COVID-19 CT triage).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (applications included deep learning computer vision CAD, CDSS, NLP chatbots).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Narrative synthesis of effectiveness, implementation challenges and barriers.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: 10 studies; 5 reported algorithms/datasets; themes: reliability issues, mixed workflow effects, poor usability, contextual mismatch, data scarcity, trust and cost barriers.

papers.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Assessment of Diabetic Retinopathy on Referral Service Uptake in a Low-Resource Setting: The RAIDERS Randomized Trial
papers.authors: Mathenge W, Whitestone N, Nkurikiye J, et al.
papers.aim: To test whether immediate AI-supported diabetic retinopathy screening feedback increases referral uptake in a low-resource African setting.
papers.method: RAIDERS: investigator-masked, parallel-group RCT at 4 Rwandan facilities (March-July 2021); patients with AI-detected referable DR randomised 1:1 to immediate AI feedback versus referral advice after human grading 3-5 days later; outcome = attending referral within 30 days.
papers.result: Of 823 eligible patients, 275 (33.4%) had referable DR and were randomised (136 intervention, 139 control); referral adherence 51.5% vs 39.6% (p=0.048), a 30.1% relative increase; intervention OR 1.74 (1.05-2.88), with older age, male sex and rural residence also associated with uptake.
papers.tools: Orbis Cybersight AI for retinal image grading, logistic regression.
papers.gap: AI accuracy not separately validated in this population; 60% urban participants; short follow-up.
papers.relation: A randomised clinical evaluation of AI with referral to clinicians in a low-resource setting, a close analogue to O4's escalation-based design.
papers.limitations: Single country; outcome is attendance, not visual outcomes.
papers.methodologyDetail: In Rwanda, patients with diabetes had eye photos graded by an AI system. Those the AI flagged as needing specialist referral were randomly split: half were told immediately at the visit, half were told only after a human grader reviewed the images 3-5 days later (usual practice). Among 275 randomised patients, 51.5% of those told immediately attended the referral within 30 days versus 39.6% of the others, a 30% relative increase. For our PhD this is a rare randomised trial of AI in a low-resource health system that measures a real care outcome, and it shows that faster AI-supported decisions can improve referral completion - an outcome type O4 could measure for brain tumour referral pathways in Sri Lanka.
papers.studyDesign: Investigator-masked parallel-group randomized controlled trial.
papers.datasets: 823 adults (>=18 years) with diabetes screened at 4 clinics in Rwanda; 275 with referable DR randomised (mean age 50.7 years; 58.2% women); outcome data for 100%.
papers.preprocessing: Retinal fundus imaging at clinic; AI grading of referable DR.
papers.modelDetails: Cybersight AI (Orbis International) deep learning DR grading system.
papers.training: Not applicable (deployed commercial/non-profit AI).
papers.evaluation: Proportion presenting for referral within 30 days; multivariable predictors of adherence.
papers.baselines: Usual care: referral advice after human grading 3-5 days later.
papers.statistics: Chi-square and multivariable logistic regression with 95% CI.

papers.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence-Based Autosegmentation of Organs at Risk in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
papers.authors: Kibudde S, Kavuma A, Hao Y, et al.
papers.aim: To assess the time savings and contour quality of AI auto-segmentation of organs at risk for radiotherapy in two low- and middle-income countries.
papers.method: 10 randomly selected patients (5 head and neck, 5 prostate) had planning CT contoured by an FDA-approved AI tool (CARINA-AI) and manually by radiation oncologists at Uganda Cancer Institute and National Cancer Center of Mongolia; compared with reference contours from a US academic centre using Dice, Hausdorff distance and mean surface distance, plus timing.
papers.result: AI took about 2 minutes per patient vs 57-84 minutes manually (about 10 minutes total human time including review); AI pelvic contours agreed better with the reference than LMIC manual contours (mean DSC 0.834 vs 0.807 and 0.844 vs 0.801); head and neck AI better for most OARs (0.823 vs 0.821; 0.792 vs 0.748); bladder best (DSC 0.971), penile bulb worst (0.536).
papers.tools: CARINA-AI auto-contouring (cloud), Eclipse treatment planning system, Dice/HD/MSD analysis.
papers.gap: Only 10 patients; small structures still poor; requires internet/cloud access.
papers.relation: Evaluates AI segmentation for treatment planning in low- and middle-income clinics, including clinician time and acceptability, which mirrors O4's planning proof of concept.
papers.limitations: Tiny sample; one AI vendor; reference from one US oncologist.
papers.methodologyDetail: Radiotherapy planning needs experts to outline the tumour and nearby healthy organs on CT, which takes time that low-resource centres often lack. In Uganda and Mongolia, the authors took CT scans of 10 patients (5 head and neck, 5 prostate) and compared outlines drawn by an FDA-approved AI tool with those of local radiation oncologists, using a US expert's outlines as reference. The AI needed about 2 minutes per patient against roughly one to one and a half hours manually, and its outlines agreed with the reference as well as or better than local manual ones for most organs, though tiny structures remained hard for everyone. For our PhD it shows that AI segmentation with clinician review can save large amounts of specialist time in LMIC centres, supporting the planning agent's design and O4's time-saving outcomes.
papers.studyDesign: Cross-sectional comparative evaluation in two LMIC radiotherapy centres.
papers.datasets: 10 planning CT scans (5 head and neck, 5 prostate cancer); LMIC1 Uganda Cancer Institute, LMIC2 National Cancer Center of Mongolia; reference contours from Washington University in St. Louis.
papers.preprocessing: Upload of anonymised planning CT to cloud AI; AI contours reviewed and approved by radiation oncologists, then imported into Eclipse.
papers.modelDetails: Generic FDA-cleared deep learning auto-segmentation models (CARINA-AI) for head and neck and pelvic OARs.
papers.training: Not applicable (vendor model).
papers.evaluation: Dice similarity coefficient, Hausdorff distance, mean surface distance against reference; contouring time.
papers.baselines: Manual contours by experienced LMIC radiation oncologists.
papers.results: Time 2 min AI vs 57-84 min manual; pelvic DSC AI 0.834/0.844 vs manual 0.807/0.801; HN DSC AI 0.823/0.792 vs manual 0.821/0.748; small OARs (penile bulb, seminal vesicles, some HN structures) poorly matched by both.
papers.statistics: Mean DSC, HD, MSD per structure.

papers.title: Attitudes of the Surgical Team Toward Artificial Intelligence in Neurosurgery: International 2-Stage Cross-Sectional Survey
papers.authors: Layard Horsfall H, Palmisciano P, Khan DZ, et al.
papers.aim: To evaluate the attitudes of neurosurgeons and the wider surgical team toward AI in neurosurgery.
papers.method: Two-stage cross-sectional survey: stage 1 open-question qualitative survey (33 respondents) with thematic analysis; stage 2 quantitative 5-point Likert survey distributed via social media (100 respondents) covering surgeons, anaesthetists, nurses and operating room practitioners.
papers.result: Six themes: imaging interpretation and preoperative diagnosis, team coordination, operative planning, real-time hazard alerts, autonomous surgery, postoperative follow-up. Agreement: imaging interpretation 62%, operative planning 82%, team coordination 70%, real-time hazard alerts 85%, autonomous surgery 66%, postoperative management 49%.
papers.tools: Online qualitative and Likert surveys, thematic analysis.
papers.gap: Convenience sample via social media; mainly high-income respondents; attitudes not behaviour.
papers.relation: Reports neurosurgical teams' trust in and acceptance of AI, background for O4's clinician trust and usability assessment in surgical planning.
papers.limitations: Self-selection bias; small sample; no response rate.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors first asked 33 members of neurosurgical teams open questions about AI, found six themes - from reading scans and planning operations to warning of hazards during surgery, autonomous surgery and follow-up - and then turned these into a Likert questionnaire answered by 100 surgeons, anaesthetists, nurses and theatre staff. Most agreed with AI for real-time hazard alerts (85%), operative planning (82%), team coordination (70%), autonomous surgery (66%) and imaging interpretation (62%), but fewer for postoperative care (49%). For our PhD it shows that surgical teams are open to AI for diagnosis and planning, and its themes can guide the attitude survey of Sri Lankan neurosurgical teams in O4.
papers.studyDesign: International two-stage cross-sectional survey (qualitative then quantitative).
papers.datasets: Stage 1: 33 respondents; Stage 2: 100 respondents (neurosurgeons, anaesthetists, nurses, operating room practitioners).
papers.preprocessing: Thematic analysis of stage 1 responses to build stage 2 items.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Percentage agreement and comfort with AI applications on 5-point Likert scales.
papers.baselines: Prior patient and relative attitude survey by the same group.
papers.results: Agreement 49-85% across applications; highest for real-time hazard alerts (85%) and operative planning (82%); lowest for postoperative management (49%).

papers.title: Neuro-oncology access in Sub-Saharan Africa: A literature review of challenges and opportunities
papers.authors: Yevudza WE, Buckman V, Darko K, et al.
papers.aim: To identify barriers and opportunities for access to neuro-oncology care in Sub-Saharan Africa.
papers.method: PRISMA-guided literature review of PubMed and Google Scholar (1 Jan 2003 - 20 Jun 2023), excluding systematic reviews and meta-analyses, with independent screening and structured data extraction by all authors.
papers.result: Barriers: constrained resources (scanners, neurosurgeons, pathology, radiotherapy), insufficient training, cultural beliefs, low awareness, delayed diagnosis and treatment, and poor incidence data; opportunities: research, advocacy, training and mentorship programmes, and international collaboration.
papers.tools: PRISMA framework, structured extraction tables.
papers.gap: Heterogeneous, mostly small single-centre studies; lack of registry data.
papers.relation: Describes the workforce and infrastructure limits of brain-tumour care in low-resource settings, which justify and constrain O4's workload and deployment evaluation.
papers.limitations: Narrative synthesis; publication bias towards larger centres.
papers.methodologyDetail: This review searched 20 years of literature on brain tumour care in Sub-Saharan Africa. It found that patients are diagnosed and treated late because of too few scanners, neurosurgeons, neuropathologists and radiotherapy units, gaps in training, cultural beliefs and low awareness, and that the true number of brain tumours is unknown because registries are missing. It also highlights opportunities: research, advocacy, training and mentoring programmes, and international partnerships. For our PhD it describes constraints very similar to Sri Lanka's and supports the argument that an AI system which works with limited data and defers uncertain cases to scarce specialists can improve access to neuro-oncology care.
papers.studyDesign: Literature review (PRISMA-guided, narrative synthesis).
papers.datasets: Studies 2003-2023 on neuro-oncology capacity and challenges in Sub-Saharan Africa from PubMed and Google Scholar (e.g., Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya studies on low-field MRI accuracy, pituitary tumours, paediatric tumours, smear vs frozen section).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Narrative synthesis of challenges and opportunities.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Key barriers: resources, workforce and training deficits, cultural factors, low awareness, diagnostic delay, missing epidemiological data; opportunities in research, advocacy, training, mentorship and collaboration.

papers.title: Common pitfalls and recommendations for using machine learning to detect and prognosticate for COVID-19 using chest radiographs and CT scans
papers.authors: Michael Roberts, Derek Driggs, Matthew Thorpe et al.
papers.aim: To systematically review machine learning models for COVID-19 diagnosis or prognosis from chest X-ray and CT and assess whether any are fit for clinical use.
papers.method: Systematic review of bioRxiv, medRxiv, arXiv, EMBASE and MEDLINE (2020); quality screening with CLAIM, RQS and PROBAST-type checks; analysis of methodological pitfalls; recommendations.
papers.result: 2,212 studies found, 2,150 after de-duplication, 415 relevant, 320 full-text screened, 62 included after quality review (37 deep learning). None of the models was judged of potential clinical use, mainly because of biased or duplicated datasets ('Frankenstein' data), poor validation, lack of external testing and incomplete reporting.
papers.tools: CLAIM checklist, Radiomics Quality Score, PROBAST risk of bias.
papers.gap: Specific to COVID-19 imaging, but pitfalls generalise.
papers.relation: Checklist of mistakes O3 and O4 must avoid: patient-level splits, no overlapping public datasets, external validation, clear reporting and bias assessment.
papers.limitations: Covers the first pandemic year; fast-moving literature.
papers.methodologyDetail: During the first pandemic year thousands of AI papers claimed to detect COVID-19 from chest X-rays or CT. This review screened 2,212 papers, quality-checked 320 in full and examined 62 in detail with standard reporting and bias tools. None of the models was considered ready for clinical use: many mixed public datasets that overlapped or came from different populations (for example children's X-rays used as normal controls), did not test on external data, or reported too little to judge. The authors give concrete recommendations for data, training, evaluation and reporting. For our PhD it is a list of pitfalls to avoid in building and evaluating the brain tumour agents: patient-level splits, careful dataset provenance, external validation and full reporting.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review.
papers.datasets: 2,212 records from 5 databases (1 Jan - 3 Oct 2020); 62 studies included.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (reviewed deep learning and traditional ML / radiomics models).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Quality and risk-of-bias assessment; identification of pitfalls in data, development and evaluation.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: 0 of 62 models clinically usable; recurring issues: small or duplicated public datasets, children's images as controls, no external validation, unclear reporting.

papers.title: The STARD-AI reporting guideline for diagnostic accuracy studies using artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Viknesh Sounderajah, Ahmad Guni, Xiaoxuan Liu et al.
papers.aim: To develop a reporting guideline for diagnostic accuracy studies that evaluate AI (STARD-AI).
papers.method: Literature review (55 candidate items), international scoping survey, patient and public involvement, two-round modified Delphi (209 then 143 participants; more than 240 stakeholders overall) and consensus meeting; finalised by the Steering Committee.
papers.result: 40-item checklist: STARD 2015 items plus 18 new or modified items (4 modified, 14 new) covering dataset eligibility at dataset and participant level, data source and collection, annotation, capture devices and software versions, acquisition and preprocessing, data partitioning, test-set characteristics and representativeness, algorithmic bias and fairness, commercial interests, and availability of data and code.
papers.tools: Delphi consensus; checklist and abstract checklist.
papers.gap: Reporting standard only; does not judge study quality.
papers.relation: Reporting standard for the diagnostic-accuracy parts of O3/O4 (MRI and pathology agents), alongside TRIPOD+AI and DECIDE-AI.
papers.methodologyDetail: STARD-AI updates the standard checklist for reporting how accurate a diagnostic test is, so that it fits AI tools. The team reviewed the literature, surveyed experts, involved patients and the public, and ran two Delphi rounds with over 240 international stakeholders before a consensus meeting. The final checklist has 40 items, 18 of them new or changed for AI: how datasets were chosen and labelled, which devices and software versions captured the data, how data were preprocessed and split into training, validation and test sets, how representative the test set is, bias and fairness checks, conflicts of interest, and whether code and data are shared. For our PhD it is the reporting checklist for the accuracy evaluation of the MRI and pathology agents.
papers.studyDesign: Reporting guideline development (modified Delphi consensus).
papers.datasets: Delphi round 1: 209 participants (45 items); round 2: 143 participants (26 items); over 240 international stakeholders overall.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable. Output: STARD-AI checklist (40 items) and abstracts checklist.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Delphi agreement thresholds and consensus meeting.
papers.baselines: STARD 2015.
papers.results: 40 essential items; 14 new and 4 modified AI-specific items.

papers.title: When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Thomas W. Malone, Michelle Anna Vaccaro, Andres Campero et al.
papers.aim: To find out when combinations of humans and AI perform better than humans or AI alone.
papers.method: Preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies (ACM DL, Web of Science, AIS eLibrary; 1 Jan 2020 - 30 Jun 2023) that measured humans alone, AI alone and human-AI combinations; random-effects models with moderators (task type, relative performance, explanation, confidence display, etc.).
papers.result: 106 studies with 370 effect sizes. On average, human-AI combinations performed worse than the best of humans or AI alone (Hedges' g = -0.23, 95% CI -0.39 to -0.07), but better than humans alone. Losses occurred in decision-making tasks and gains in content-creation tasks; when humans were better than the AI, combinations gained, but when the AI was better than humans, combinations lost. Explanations and confidence displays did not significantly change synergy.
papers.tools: Three-level random-effects meta-analysis, meta-regression.
papers.gap: Most studies used lay participants and short tasks; few clinical deployments.
papers.relation: Key design evidence for O2/O4: in medical decisions, simply showing AI advice often fails; our approach routes cases so the AI decides when it is clearly better and the clinician when they are, which is what produces gains.
papers.methodologyDetail: This preregistered meta-analysis pooled 106 experiments (370 results) from 2020-2023 where people worked alone, the AI worked alone, and people worked with the AI. On average the team did worse than whichever of the two was best alone (Hedges' g -0.23), although it usually beat the person alone. Teams lost ground in decision tasks such as classification and gained in creative tasks; and when the AI was better than people, adding people made results worse, while when people were better, AI help improved them. Showing explanations or confidence did not reliably fix this. For our PhD it is strong support for selective autonomy - deciding case by case who should decide - rather than always showing AI advice to clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.datasets: 106 experimental studies, 370 effect sizes (2020-2023).
papers.preprocessing: Extraction of performance for human, AI and human-AI conditions; computation of Hedges' g for synergy versus best single agent and versus humans.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Pooled Hedges' g; moderator analyses.
papers.baselines: Best of human alone or AI alone.
papers.results: g = -0.23 vs best single agent; positive vs humans alone; decision tasks negative, creation tasks positive; human-superior settings positive, AI-superior settings negative.
papers.statistics: Random-effects meta-analysis with 95% CI; heterogeneity statistics.

papers.title: Diagnostic accuracy of deep learning in medical imaging: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.authors: Ravi Aggarwal, Viknesh Sounderajah, Guy Martin et al.
papers.aim: To estimate the diagnostic accuracy of deep learning for identifying pathology in medical imaging and to appraise study methods and reporting.
papers.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Medline and EMBASE to January 2020) of peer-reviewed studies reporting DL diagnostic accuracy; two investigators extracted data; QUADAS-2 risk of bias; bivariate diagnostic meta-analysis and DerSimonian-Laird random effects.
papers.result: 11,921 records identified, 503 studies included; 273-279 meta-analysed (82 ophthalmology, 82 breast, 115 respiratory) and 224 in other specialties reviewed qualitatively (including 78 in neurology/neurosurgery). DL showed high diagnostic accuracy in these specialties but with extensive heterogeneity, high risk of bias, few external validations and inconsistent terminology and reporting.
papers.tools: QUADAS-2, bivariate random-effects meta-analysis.
papers.gap: Few prospective or externally validated studies; segmentation excluded.
papers.relation: Benchmark context and warning for O4: high reported accuracy often comes from biased designs, so our evaluation needs external, prospective-style testing and AI-specific reporting (STARD-AI).
papers.limitations: Search ends January 2020; heterogeneity limits pooled estimates.
papers.methodologyDetail: This large meta-analysis pooled studies up to early 2020 that tested deep learning for spotting disease on medical images. From almost 12,000 records, 503 studies qualified; those in eye, breast and lung imaging were pooled statistically, and the rest - including 78 in neurology and neurosurgery - were reviewed. Accuracy looked high, but results varied widely and most studies had a high risk of bias, used internal test sets only and reported methods inconsistently. For our PhD it shows that impressive accuracy figures are not enough: the brain tumour agents must be validated on external, realistic data and reported with AI-specific guidelines.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.datasets: 11,921 records (Medline, EMBASE); 503 included studies; meta-analysis in ophthalmology (82), breast (82) and respiratory (115).
papers.preprocessing: Extraction of 2x2 data and AUC, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV by study.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable (reviewed CNN-based diagnostic models).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Pooled AUC, sensitivity and specificity by specialty and modality; risk of bias.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: High pooled accuracy across the three specialties with large heterogeneity; widespread methodological and reporting weaknesses.

papers.title: Towards Human-Centered Explainable AI: A Survey of User Studies for Model Explanations
papers.authors: Yao Rong, Tobias Leemann, Thai-trang Nguyen et al.
papers.venue: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
papers.aim: To review how user studies evaluate explainable AI and give guidelines for human-centred XAI evaluation.
papers.method: Systematic literature review of 97 core papers (past five years) with human-based XAI evaluations, categorised by measured outcome - trust, understanding, usability, and human-AI collaboration performance - and by study design choices.
papers.result: User evaluations of XAI are still sparse and rarely use insights from cognitive or social science; applications cluster in domains such as recommender systems; the authors propose practical guidelines for study design, measures and reporting and list open problems.
papers.tools: Systematic review and taxonomy.
papers.gap: Few studies in high-stakes medical settings with expert users.
papers.relation: Guides O4's measurement of explanation effects (trust, understanding, usability, team performance) with validated instruments rather than ad-hoc questions.
papers.limitations: Limited to explanation user studies; heterogeneous measures.
papers.methodologyDetail: Many AI systems add explanations, but are they tested with real users? This survey examined 97 studies that evaluated explanations with people and sorted them by what they measured - trust, understanding, usability and how well the person-AI team performed - and how the studies were designed. User studies were still rare, often lacked grounding in psychology, and were concentrated in domains like recommender systems. The authors give practical guidance on choosing tasks, participants, measures and controls. For our PhD it helps design the explanation part of O4 so trust, understanding, usability and joint accuracy are measured properly with clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic literature review.
papers.datasets: 97 core papers with human-subject XAI evaluations.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Not applicable.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Categorisation of evaluation measures and study designs.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Taxonomy of user-study measures; design guidelines; open challenges.

papers.title: Reader bias in breast cancer screening related to cancer prevalence and artificial intelligence decision support-a reader study
papers.authors: Al-Bazzaz H, Janicijevic M, Strand F
papers.aim: ObjectivesThe aim of our study was to examine how breast radiologists would be affected by high cancer prevalence and the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for decision support.Materials and methodThis reader study was based on selection of screening mammograms, including the original radiologist assessment, acquired in 2010 to 2013 at the Karolinska University Hospital, with a ratio of 1:1 cancer versus healthy based on a 2-year follow-up. A commercial AI system generated an exam-level positive or negative read, and image markers.
papers.method: Double-reading and consensus discussions were first performed without AI and later with AI, with a 6-week wash-out period in between. The chi-squared test was used to test for differences in contingency tables.ResultsMammograms of 758 women were included, half with cancer and half healthy. 52% were 40–55 years; 48% were 56–75 years. In the original non-enriched screening setting, the sensitivity was 61% (232/379) at specificity 98% (323/379). In the reader study, the sensitivity without and with AI was 81% (307/379) and 75% (284/379) respectively (p < 0.001). The specificity without and with AI was 67% (255/379) and 86% (326/379) respectively (p < 0.001). The tendency to change assessment from positive to negative based on erroneous AI information differed between readers and was affected by type and number of image signs of malignancy.ConclusionBreast radiologists reading a list with high cancer prevalence performed at considerably higher sensitivity and lower specificity than the original screen-readers. Adding AI information, calibrated to a screening setting, decreased sensitivity and increased specificity.Clinical relevance statementRadiologist screening mammography assessments will be biased towards higher sensitivity and lower specificity by high-risk triaging and nudged towards the sensitivity and specificity setting of AI reads.
papers.result: After AI implementation in clinical practice, there is reason to carefully follow screening metrics to ensure the impact is desired.Key Points • Breast radiologists’ sensitivity and specificity will be affected by changes brought by artificial intelligence. • Reading in a high cancer prevalence setting markedly increased sensitivity and decreased specificity. • Reviewing the binary reads by AI, negative or positive, biased screening radiologists towards the sensitivity and specificity of the AI system. Graphical abstract
papers.gap: Breast screening; AI without confidence-based deferral.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Enriched set not representative of screening.
papers.methodologyDetail: Radiologists re-read an enriched set of screening mammograms with and without AI, with a washout between sessions, and their decisions were compared with the original screening reads. Both the unusually high cancer prevalence and the AI support shifted their operating points. Prevalence and AI effects must be considered when designing the reader study in WP7 with an enriched case set.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective reader study (Karolinska Institutet; European Radiology 2024; ethics approved, consent waived).
papers.datasets: CSAW-CC cancer-enriched case-control set: most recent screening mammogram before diagnosis for 379 women with breast cancer and 379 healthy women (2010-2013, Karolinska), reference standard from pathology-verified registry within 2 years.
papers.preprocessing: Four standard views on Hologic FFDM.
papers.modelDetails: Radiologists performed double reading and consensus discussion first without AI and then with an AI decision-support system, with a 6-week washout, in a high-prevalence (50%) setting; compared with original screening reads.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Sensitivity, specificity and recall rates by reading condition.
papers.baselines: Original screening reads; reading without AI.
papers.results: High cancer prevalence and AI support both changed radiologists' sensitivity and specificity, showing reader bias; screening metrics should be monitored after AI implementation.

papers.title: Evaluation of the impact of artificial intelligence-assisted image interpretation on the diagnostic performance of clinicians in identifying pneumothoraces on plain chest X-ray: a multi-case multi-reader study
papers.authors: Novak A, Ather S, Gill A, Aylward P, Maskell G, Cowell GW, Espinosa Morgado AT, Duggan T, Keevill M, Gamble O, et al.
papers.aim: AbstractBackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI)-assisted image interpretation is a fast-developing area of clinical innovation. Most research to date has focused on the performance of AI-assisted algorithms in comparison with that of radiologists rather than evaluating the algorithms’ impact on the clinicians who often undertake initial image interpretation in routine clinical practice.
papers.method: This study assessed the impact of AI-assisted image interpretation on the diagnostic performance of frontline acute care clinicians for the detection of pneumothoraces (PTX).MethodsA multicentre blinded multi-case multi-reader study was conducted between October 2021 and January 2022. The online study recruited 18 clinician readers from six different clinical specialties, with differing levels of seniority, across four English hospitals. The study included 395 plain CXR images, 189 positive for PTX and 206 negative. The reference standard was the consensus opinion of two thoracic radiologists with a third acting as arbitrator. General Electric Healthcare Critical Care Suite (GEHC CCS) PTX algorithm was applied to the final dataset. Readers individually interpreted the dataset without AI assistance, recording the presence or absence of a PTX and a confidence rating. Following a ‘washout’ period, this process was repeated including the AI output.ResultsAnalysis of the performance of the algorithm for detecting or ruling out a PTX revealed an overall AUROC of 0.939. Overall reader sensitivity increased by 11.4% (95% CI 4.8, 18.0, p=0.002) from 66.8% (95% CI 57.3, 76.2) unaided to 78.1% aided (95% CI 72.2, 84.0, p=0.002), specificity 93.9% (95% CI 90.9, 97.0) without AI to 95.8% (95% CI 93.7, 97.9, p=0.247). The junior reader subgroup showed the largest improvement at 21.7% (95% CI 10.9, 32.6), increasing from 56.0% (95% CI 37.7, 74.3) to 77.7% (95% CI 65.8, 89.7, p<0.01).ConclusionThe study indicates that AI-assisted image interpretation significantly enhances the diagnostic accuracy of clinicians in detecting PTX, particularly benefiting less experienced practitioners.
papers.result: While overall interpretation time remained unchanged, the use of AI improved diagnostic confidence and sensitivity, especially among junior clinicians. These findings underscore the potential of AI to support less skilled clinicians in acute care settings.
papers.gap: Detection task only; AI confidence not calibrated or used for deferral.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Eighteen frontline clinicians from six specialties read 400 chest X-rays first without and then with an AI tool that shows a heatmap and confidence score for pneumothorax, after brief training; correct answers required clicking the right region. AI help raised sensitivity and confidence, particularly for junior staff. Its two-phase multi-reader design with seniority strata is a template for WP7.
papers.studyDesign: Multicentre multi-case multi-reader study (Oxford University Hospitals and Thames Valley sites, Oct 2021-Jan 2022); reported to STARD.
papers.datasets: 400 de-identified adult chest X-rays from Oxford (200 pneumothorax-positive across subtypes, 200 negative) curated via the NCIMI databank; 18 readers from six specialties at three seniority levels across four hospitals.
papers.preprocessing: Ground truth contoured by expert radiologists; clinical indication shown to readers.
papers.modelDetails: FDA-cleared GE Critical Care Suite pneumothorax algorithm giving a heatmap and confidence score with a variable threshold; two reader phases (unaided then aided) on the RAIQC platform after training with five test cases.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial algorithm).
papers.evaluation: Sensitivity, specificity, accuracy (correct localisation required), confidence on a 4-point Likert scale, interpretation time; subgroup by seniority and specialty.
papers.baselines: Unaided reading.
papers.results: AI improved diagnostic confidence and sensitivity, especially for junior clinicians, without changing overall interpretation time.
papers.statistics: Paired comparisons and mixed-effects analyses (details in paper).

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted breast ultrasound: modest AUROC improvement and shorter interpretation time without significant change in diagnostic accuracy
papers.authors: Kwon H, Kim SM, Oh SH, Jang M, Kim MG, Bae HM, Choi SI, Cho SM, Kim Y, Jung G, et al.
papers.aim: ObjectivesTo evaluate whether Vis-BUS, a commercial artificial intelligence (AI) breast ultrasound detection and analysis software, improves diagnostic discrimination and interpretation efficiency in breast ultrasound examinations.Materials and methodsThis retrospective multi-reader study included 258 breast ultrasound examinations (129 malignant and 129 benign lesions). Six radiologists independently interpreted all cases without AI and, after a two-week washout, with AI assistance.
papers.method: Diagnostic performance metrics, including the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under the precision–recall curve (AUPRC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, were compared using multi-reader analysis. Median interpretation time per case was recorded and compared using paired statistical tests.ResultsVis-BUS assistance modestly increased the pooled AUROC (0.921 vs. 0.953, p = 0.002) and reduced median reading time (6.0 vs. 3.0 s, p < 0.001), whereas AUPRC, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity did not differ significantly (all p > 0.06). Accuracy (79.1% vs. 83.9%, p = 0.061), sensitivity (94.2% vs. 96.3%, p = 0.243), and specificity (64.0% vs. 71.6%, p = 0.069) showed no significant differences. Median interpretation time decreased from 6.0 to 3.0 s (p < 0.001). Subgroup analyses demonstrated significant AUROC improvements for dense breasts and tumors ≤ 2 cm (p < 0.001 for both).ConclusionVis-BUS AI assistance was associated with improved diagnostic discrimination and shorter interpretation time.
papers.result: However, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity did not differ significantly. These findings suggest potential efficiency benefits, while the clinical impact remains to be confirmed in prospective multi-center studies.
papers.gap: No confidence-based deferral; balanced enriched set.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Readers interpreted a balanced set of breast ultrasound lesions with and without a commercial AI tool. AI slightly improved discrimination and reduced reading time but did not significantly change accuracy. It shows that efficiency gains can occur without accuracy gains, so WP7 should measure both.
papers.studyDesign: Single-centre retrospective multi-reader multi-case study (Seoul National University Bundang Hospital; IRB E-2310-858-301, consent waived).
papers.datasets: 258 diagnostic breast ultrasound examinations (2015-2020): 129 malignant (112 invasive, 17 DCIS, pathology-proven) and 129 benign (55 biopsy-proven, 74 stable >=12 months); index lesion per case.
papers.preprocessing: De-identified images from PACS.
papers.modelDetails: Commercial AI software (Vis-BUS) for breast lesion detection and analysis used by readers with and without assistance.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: AUROC, AUPRC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and interpretation time.
papers.baselines: Unaided reading.
papers.results: Modest AUROC improvement and shorter interpretation time with AI; accuracy, sensitivity and specificity did not change significantly.

papers.title: Improving traumatic fracture detection on radiographs with artificial intelligence support: a multi-reader study
papers.authors: Bachmann R, Gunes G, Hangaard S, Nexmann A, Lisouski P, Boesen M, Lundemann M, Baginski SG
papers.aim: AbstractObjectivesThe aim of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic performance of nonspecialist readers with and without the use of an artificial intelligence (AI) support tool to detect traumatic fractures on radiographs of the appendicular skeleton.MethodsThe design was a retrospective, fully crossed multi-reader, multi-case study on a balanced dataset of patients (≥2 years of age) with an AI tool as a diagnostic intervention. Fifteen readers assessed 340 radiographic exams, with and without the AI tool in 2 different sessions and the time spent was automatically recorded.
papers.method: Reference standard was established by 3 consultant radiologists. Sensitivity, specificity, and false positives per patient were calculated.ResultsPatient-wise sensitivity increased from 72% to 80% (P < .05) and patient-wise specificity increased from 81% to 85% (P < .05) in exams aided by the AI tool compared to the unaided exams. The increase in sensitivity resulted in a relative reduction of missed fractures of 29%. The average rate of false positives per patient decreased from 0.16 to 0.14, corresponding to a relative reduction of 21%. There was no significant difference in average reading time spent per exam.
papers.result: The largest gain in fracture detection performance, with AI support, across all readers, was on nonobvious fractures with a significant increase in sensitivity of 11 percentage points (pp) (60%-71%).ConclusionsThe diagnostic performance for detection of traumatic fractures on radiographs of the appendicular skeleton improved among nonspecialist readers tested AI fracture detection support tool showed an overall reader improvement in sensitivity and specificity when supported by an AI tool. Improvement was seen in both sensitivity and specificity without negatively affecting the interpretation time.Advances in knowledgeThe division and analysis of obvious and nonobvious fractures are novel in AI reader comparison studies like this.
papers.gap: Vendor-led; no deferral or uncertainty display.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Non-specialist readers interpreted a balanced, stratified set of trauma radiographs with and without an AI fracture-detection aid in a fully crossed design, against a three-radiologist reference standard. AI helped most on subtle fractures. The stratified case selection and sample-size justification are good models for designing the WP7 case set.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective fully crossed multi-reader multi-case study (Radiobotics, Copenhagen University Hospitals, Virtual Radiologic; IRB WCG 20240639); reported to STARD 2015.
papers.datasets: 340 trauma radiographs from a US teleradiology provider, stratified random sample from >4,800 exams not used in AI development: adults 40 per region (shoulder/clavicle, arm/elbow, hand/wrist, knee/leg, foot/ankle, hip/pelvis), children 20 per region; ~50% with fracture per stratum; exclusions for implants and casts.
papers.preprocessing: Reference standard by three consultant radiologists.
papers.modelDetails: Commercial fracture-detection AI support tool used by non-specialist readers with and without assistance.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Sensitivity, specificity, false positives per patient; subgroup for non-obvious fractures.
papers.baselines: Unaided reading.
papers.results: AI improved fracture detection, with the largest gain in sensitivity for non-obvious fractures across all readers.

papers.title: Impact of a Decision-Support Interface on Mental Workload and Stress in Prehospital Stroke Triage: A Randomized Crossover Trial
papers.authors: Lu YC, Tang SC, Tsai LK, Jeng JS, Lee YC, Hsieh MJ
papers.venue: The western journal of emergency medicine
papers.aim: IntroductionPrehospital triage challenges often lead to suboptimal choices and delayed treatment for stroke patients. The objective of the study was to evaluate whether a decision-support interface to assist in stroke triage to an appropriate hospital could reduce emergency medical technicians’ (EMT) mental workload.MethodsThis randomized crossover study was conducted between February and March 2025.
papers.method: Each participant completed two 12-minute simulated trials in randomized order: current dispatch orders without decision support and a decision-support interface. We assessed mental workload—the mental effort required to make hospital transport decisions under time pressure during prehospital stroke triage—using heart rate variability (HRV) metrics and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Task Load Index (NASA-TLX). System usability was assessed using the System Usability Scale. The primary outcome was the root mean square of successive differences for each participant after completing the two trials. The secondary outcomes included the differences of NASA-TLX, System Usability Scale, and other heart rate variability parameters, including mean R-R interval (meanRR), mean heart rate, percentage of successive R-R intervals that differ by more than 50 milliseconds, low-frequency power (LF), high-frequency (HF) power, and the LF/HF ratio. Subgroup analyses examined differences by sex, education, age, and years of service.ResultsA total of 35 emergency medical technician (EMT)-intermediate participants (mean age, 27.5 [5.3] years) completed the study. For the primary outcome, the root mean square of successive differences increased significantly (28.1 [13.0] vs 32.4 [13.6] milliseconds; mean difference, 4.3 milliseconds [95% CI, 1.57–6.99]; P < .01), indicating reduced mental workload when the participants used the decision-support interface. For the secondary outcomes, mean heart rate (77.5 [8.6] vs 73.8 [10.6], P < .01) decreased, mean R (784.2 [89.5] vs 808.9 [87.3], P < .01) increased, and HF power (370.1 [291.7] versus 482.6 [433.9], P = .02) increased, suggesting reduced mental workload when the participants used the decision-support interface.
papers.result: The mental demand scores in NASA-TLX decreased from 62.5 (14.6) to 35.5 (17.0). Emergency medical technicians with 1.0–1.5 years of service reported higher System Usability Scale scores than those with 1.5–3.0 years (84.4 versus 71.3, P = .02), and 82.9% of participants rated the system as acceptable (System Usability Scale score ≥ 70).ConclusionThis study demonstrated that integrating a web-based decision-support interface effectively reduces mental workload and psychological stress among EMTs in stroke triage.
papers.gap: Simulation; not AI with uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Paramedics completed time-limited simulated stroke triage tasks with and without a decision-support interface, in random order, while workload was measured by questionnaire and physiology. Mental demand nearly halved with support. It shows NASA-TLX and crossover design as practical tools for measuring workload effects in WP7.
papers.studyDesign: Randomised crossover simulation trial (National Tsing Hua University, National Taiwan University Hospital); reported to CONSORT.
papers.datasets: Emergency medical technicians completing two 12-minute simulated trials of eight stroke scenarios each (varying location, onset time and G-FAST score).
papers.preprocessing: Latin square randomisation of trial order.
papers.modelDetails: Decision-support interface for prehospital stroke transport destination vs current dispatch orders without decision support.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: NASA-TLX subjective workload, physiological stress indicators, decision outcomes and user experience.
papers.baselines: Current dispatch orders.
papers.results: NASA-TLX mental demand fell from 62.5 (SD 14.6) to 35.5 (SD 17.0) with the interface; effects varied with years of service.

papers.title: User experience study to evaluate a clinical decision support system prototype supporting continuous kidney replacement therapy in a simulated ICU environment
papers.authors: Kunz LM, Metzger M, Schaefer C, Pohlmeier R, Petrovic Vorkapic J, Nosch M
papers.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
papers.aim: BackgroundThe increasing amount of data routinely collected on ICUs poses a challenge for clinicians which is aggravated with data-heavy therapies like Continuous Kidney Replacement Therapy (CKRT). We developed the CKRT Supporting Software Prototype (CKRT-SSP), a clinical decision support system for use before, during and after CKRT.
papers.method: The aim of this user experience (UX) study was to prospectively evaluate CKRT–SSP in terms of usability, user experience, and workload in a simulated ICU setting.MethodsWe simulated CKRT treatments in a fully equipped single patient room in the ICU and evaluated CKRT-SSP using validated questionnaires: System Usability Scale (SUS) and User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ). Furthermore, a modified NASA-TLX (task load index) compared the workload before and after using CKRT-SSP. Twelve clinicians and nurses participated in this study.ResultsThe SUS reached a median value of 87.5 for CKRT-SSP, reflecting excellent usability. In the UEQ, CKRT-SSP scored clearly positive in the attractiveness dimension and the three task-related dimensions of clarity, efficiency, and dependability (95% CI fully > 0.8). For the two non-task-related dimensions, stimulation and novelty, there was a positive trend (mean > 0.8, lower limit of 95% CI < 0.8).
papers.result: The modified NASA-TLX suggests a trend to less total workload with CKRT-SSP which mainly is attributable to less physical demand and less effort.ConclusionCKRT-SSP is a promising tool for improving the workload in ICUs and the specific application of CKRT. We obtained valuable insights for further user-centric development.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12911-025-03165-7.
papers.gap: Very small sample; industry-led; not AI with uncertainty.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Clinicians used a decision-support prototype in realistic simulated ICU scenarios and then rated usability with SUS, user experience with UEQ, and workload with NASA-TLX, against current practice. The combination of standard questionnaires in a pre-deployment simulation is a template for the usability part of WP7.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective non-clinical user experience study in a simulated ICU setting (Fresenius Medical Care with Marienhospital Bottrop, Germany).
papers.datasets: 8 healthcare professionals evaluating a CKRT clinical decision support prototype in simulated scenarios.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: CKRT-SSP: stand-alone web-based decision support integrating CKRT device, blood gas analyser and PDMS data for prescription support, remote monitoring and quality metrics, developed by human-centred design.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: System Usability Scale, User Experience Questionnaire (attractiveness, clarity, efficiency, dependability, stimulation, novelty), modified NASA-TLX; hypotheses H1-H3 on effectiveness, UX and workload.
papers.baselines: Current CKRT prescription and monitoring without the software.
papers.results: Mean SUS 87.5 (SD 8.39, 'excellent'); positive UEQ scores for attractiveness and task-related dimensions; trend to lower total workload mainly from less physical demand and effort.

papers.title: Exploring the feasibility of an artificial intelligence based clinical decision support system for cutaneous melanoma detection in primary care - a mixed method study
papers.authors: Helenason J, Ekström C, Falk M, Papachristou P
papers.venue: Scandinavian journal of primary health care
papers.aim: AbstractObjective: Skin examination to detect cutaneous melanomas is commonly performed in primary care. In recent years, clinical decision support systems (CDSS) based on artificial intelligence (AI) have been introduced within several diagnostic fields.Setting: This study employs a variety of qualitative and quantitative methodologies to investigate the feasibility of an AI-based CDSS to detect cutaneous melanoma in primary care.Subjects and Design: Fifteen primary care physicians (PCPs) underwent near-live simulations using the CDSS on a simulated patient, and subsequent individual semi-structured interviews were explored with a hybrid thematic analysis approach.
papers.method: Additionally, twenty-five PCPs performed a reader study (diagnostic assessment on the basis of image interpretation) of 18 dermoscopic images, both with and without help from AI, investigating the value of adding AI support to a PCPs decision. Perceived instrument usability was rated on the System Usability Scale (SUS).Results: From the interviews, the importance of trust in the CDSS emerged as a central concern. Scientific evidence supporting sufficient diagnostic accuracy of the CDSS was expressed as an important factor that could increase trust.
papers.result: Access to AI decision support when evaluating dermoscopic images proved valuable as it formally increased the physician’s diagnostic accuracy. A mean SUS score of 84.8, corresponding to ‘good’ usability, was measured.Conclusion: AI-based CDSS might play an important future role in cutaneous melanoma diagnostics, provided sufficient evidence of diagnostic accuracy and usability supporting its trustworthiness among the users.
papers.gap: Binary output without calibrated confidence; small samples.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The study combined realistic simulated consultations, think-aloud and interviews with a small reader study to judge whether an AI melanoma aid would work in primary care. Trust, usability and clinical context emerged as key themes, and accuracy improved with AI. Combining qualitative and reader-study methods mirrors the explanatory mixed-methods design of WP7.
papers.studyDesign: Exploratory mixed-methods feasibility study in Swedish primary care (AI Medical Technology, Linköping University, Karolinska Institutet), March-May 2021.
papers.datasets: 15 primary care physicians in near-live simulations with think-aloud and semi-structured interviews at five centres; 25 PCPs in a reader study of 18 dermoscopic images.
papers.preprocessing: Simulated patient consultations video-recorded.
papers.modelDetails: Dermalyser CDSS prototype: CNN trained on 6,714 ISIC 2020 dermoscopic images giving a binary statement ('Melanoma cannot be excluded' / 'No signs of melanoma'); synthetic test sensitivity 90%, specificity 65%.
papers.training: Not applicable for study.
papers.evaluation: Hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis (COREQ); reader diagnostic accuracy with and without AI.
papers.baselines: Reading without AI support.
papers.results: Three themes (trust, usability and user experience, clinical context) with ten subthemes from 75 codes; AI access increased PCPs' diagnostic accuracy in the reader study.

papers.title: User-centred design of a clinical decision support system for palliative care: Insights from healthcare professionals
papers.authors: Blanes-Selva V, Asensio-Cuesta S, Doñate-Martínez A, Pereira Mesquita F, García-Gómez JM
papers.aim: Objective:Although clinical decision support systems (CDSS) have many benefits for clinical practice, they also have several barriers to their acceptance by professionals. Our objective in this study was to design and validate The Aleph palliative care (PC) CDSS through a user-centred method, considering the predictions of the artificial intelligence (AI) core, usability and user experience (UX).Methods:We performed two rounds of individual evaluation sessions with potential users.
papers.method: Each session included a model evaluation, a task test and a usability and UX assessment.Results:The machine learning (ML) predictive models outperformed the participants in the three predictive tasks. System Usability Scale (SUS) reported 62.7 ± 14.1 and 65 ± 26.2 on a 100-point rating scale for both rounds, respectively, while User Experience Questionnaire – Short Version (UEQ-S) scores were 1.42 and 1.5 on the −3 to 3 scale.Conclusions:The think-aloud method and including the UX dimension helped us to identify most of the workflow implementation issues.
papers.result: The system has good UX hedonic qualities; participants were interested in the tool and responded positively to it. Performance regarding usability was modest but acceptable.
papers.gap: Small, heterogeneous sample; usability only moderate; no clinical outcome evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Potential users ran through cases on the CDSS in two iterative rounds, first predicting outcomes themselves to compare with the ML models, then completing tasks while thinking aloud, and finally rating usability and user experience. Findings from round 1 were used to improve the interface before round 2. This iterative user-centred loop with explanation plots informs the clinician-facing escalation interface of the PhD.
papers.studyDesign: User-centred design and validation study of The Aleph palliative care CDSS (Universitat Politècnica de València, InAdvance project), two rounds of individual evaluation sessions.
papers.datasets: Round 1: 15 healthcare professionals; round 2: 6 (21 in total: 15 physicians, 6 nurses) from Italy, Brazil, Spain, Greece, Scotland and Portugal, recruited by snowball sampling.
papers.preprocessing: Test cases built from patient data (Barthel and Charlson indexes, laboratory results, diagnoses).
papers.modelDetails: Open-access web CDSS with ML models predicting 1-year mortality, frailty and related palliative-care needs, with SHAP explanation plots for each prediction.
papers.training: Models trained previously; not retrained in this study.
papers.evaluation: Each session: model evaluation (clinicians predicted the same tasks as the ML), task test with think-aloud, System Usability Scale and UEQ-Short.
papers.baselines: Clinician predictions versus ML predictions.
papers.results: ML outperformed participants in all three predictive tasks; SUS 62.7 ± 14.1 (round 1) and 65 ± 26.2 (round 2); UEQ-S 1.42 and 1.5 on the -3 to 3 scale; good hedonic qualities, usability below ideal.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-assisted Endoscopy and Examiner Confidence: A Study on Human-Artificial Intelligence Interaction in Barrett's Esophagus (With Video)
papers.authors: Roser D, Meinikheim M, Muzalyova A, Mendel R, Palm C, Probst A, Nagl S, Scheppach MW, Römmele C, Schnoy E, et al.
papers.aim: ABSTRACTObjectiveDespite high stand‐alone performance, studies demonstrate that artificial intelligence (AI)‐supported endoscopic diagnostics often fall short in clinical applications due to human‐AI interaction factors. This video‐based trial on Barrett's esophagus aimed to investigate how examiner behavior, their levels of confidence, and system usability influence the diagnostic outcomes of AI‐assisted endoscopy.MethodsThe present analysis employed data from a multicenter randomized controlled tandem video trial involving 22 endoscopists with varying degrees of expertise.
papers.method: Participants were tasked with evaluating a set of 96 endoscopic videos of Barrett's esophagus in two distinct rounds, with and without AI assistance. Diagnostic confidence levels were recorded, and decision changes were categorized according to the AI prediction. Additional surveys assessed user experience and system usability ratings.ResultsAI assistance significantly increased examiner confidence levels (p < 0.001) and accuracy. Withdrawing AI assistance decreased confidence (p < 0.001), but not accuracy. Experts consistently reported higher confidence than non‐experts (p < 0.001), regardless of performance. Despite improved confidence, correct AI guidance was disregarded in 16% of all cases, and 9% of initially correct diagnoses were changed to incorrect ones. Overreliance on AI, algorithm aversion, and uncertainty in AI predictions were identified as key factors influencing outcomes. The System Usability Scale questionnaire scores indicated good to excellent usability, with non‐experts scoring 73.5 and experts 85.6.ConclusionsOur findings highlight the pivotal function of examiner behavior in AI‐assisted endoscopy.
papers.result: To fully realize the benefits of AI, implementing explainable AI, improving user interfaces, and providing targeted training are essential. Addressing these factors could enhance diagnostic accuracy and confidence in clinical practice.
papers.gap: Confidence only, not the reasons for reliance; no uncertainty display tested.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Video-based, not live procedures; few experts.
papers.methodologyDetail: Endoscopists read the same set of Barrett's videos with and without an AI aid in randomised order and rated their confidence after each case. The analysis compared confidence when the AI was right versus wrong, separately for experts and non-experts. This shows how AI advice can sway confidence and over-reliance, a key safety concern that the PhD's calibrated escalation and reader study (WP7) must measure.
papers.studyDesign: Secondary analysis of a multicentre randomised controlled tandem video trial (University Hospital Augsburg, Germany) on human-AI interaction in Barrett's oesophagus.
papers.datasets: 22 endoscopists from 12 centres in four countries (4 experts, 18 non-experts); 96 endoscopic videos of non-dysplastic BE and Barrett's neoplasia, block-randomised into two blocks of 48.
papers.preprocessing: Videos split into blocks with a custom R script; arms A and B with crossover order (without AI then with AI, and vice versa).
papers.modelDetails: Verit-AI computer-aided detection system for Barrett's neoplasia; examiner confidence recorded on a 0-9 scale after every assessment.
papers.training: Not applicable (pre-trained system).
papers.evaluation: Confidence levels with and without AI, by expertise and by whether the AI prediction was correct or incorrect.
papers.baselines: Assessment without AI assistance.
papers.results: AI support changed examiner confidence; non-experts relied on the AI more and were influenced by incorrect predictions, so stand-alone AI performance did not fully translate to human-AI performance; authors call for explainable AI, better interfaces and targeted training.
papers.statistics: Mixed-effects / comparative statistical tests of confidence by group and AI correctness.

papers.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: Automation Bias, Deskilling, and Cognitive Implications - A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Al-Anezi FM
papers.aim: BackgroundGenerative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming eHealthcare, promising substantial gains in diagnostic accuracy, workflow efficiency, and decision support, yet raising concerns about automation bias and clinician deskilling that may erode core diagnostic expertise and professional judgment over time.Aim and ObjectivesThis systematic review investigates the dual impact of GenAI in eHealthcare, focusing on how it enhances clinical efficiency and decision support while potentially diminishing clinicians’ diagnostic expertise and professional judgment.MethodsA systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. A total of 11,269 records were identified, and 29 studies met inclusion criteria following PRISMA 2020 guidelines.
papers.method: Studies were synthesized using a narrative approach due to heterogeneity in design, clinical domains, and AI system maturity.ResultsAcross the included studies, recurrent themes included automation bias (reported in 10 studies), concerns regarding clinician deskilling (9 studies), and impacts on diagnostic reasoning (9 studies). Evidence was predominantly observational, experimental simulation-based, or conceptual in nature. Findings reveal that GenAI significantly improves diagnostic accuracy, workflow efficiency, and decision quality across radiology, telehealth, and education domains. However, overreliance introduces risks of automation bias, cognitive deskilling, and loss of interpretive autonomy.
papers.result: The review identifies key mitigation strategies, including human-in-the-loop frameworks, explainable AI (XAI), ethical governance, and continuous clinician reskilling. Theoretically, the results redefine the clinician–AI relationship as a dynamic cognitive partnership, while practically they emphasize responsible integration through education and regulation.ConclusionSustainable adoption of GenAI demands balanced implementation—leveraging its analytical capabilities without compromising human judgment, clinical reasoning, or professional accountability.
papers.gap: Little empirical longitudinal evidence on deskilling; no quantitative pooling.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single author; heterogeneous studies; narrative synthesis.
papers.methodologyDetail: The author searched six databases for ten years of studies on generative AI in healthcare, screened over eleven thousand records to 29 studies, and synthesised them narratively because designs and domains varied too much for meta-analysis. The review weighs efficiency gains against automation bias and deskilling and lists mitigations. It supports the PhD's argument that human-in-the-loop escalation must actively protect clinician judgement.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020 and Tranfield et al. principles (Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University, Saudi Arabia).
papers.datasets: 11,269 records from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore and Google Scholar (January 2015 to June 2025); 29 studies (2022-2025) included.
papers.preprocessing: Boolean search strings combining GenAI/LLM terms (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Med-PaLM, BioGPT) with healthcare and decision-support terms; screening against inclusion criteria; data extraction.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis of empirical, review and conceptual studies on generative AI benefits versus automation bias and deskilling.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Thematic synthesis of efficiency gains, diagnostic support, automation bias, deskilling and cognitive effects; quality appraisal of included studies.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: GenAI improves efficiency and decision support but brings automation bias and risk of eroding diagnostic expertise; mitigation includes human-in-the-loop frameworks, explainable AI, ethical governance and continuous training.

papers.title: Automation bias in AI-assisted detection of cerebral aneurysms on time-of-flight MR angiography
papers.authors: Kim SH, Schramm S, Riedel EO, Schmitzer L, Rosenkranz E, Kertels O, Bodden J, Paprottka K, Sepp D, Renz M, et al.
papers.aim: PurposeTo determine how automation bias (inclination of humans to overly trust-automated decision-making systems) can affect radiologists when interpreting AI-detected cerebral aneurysm findings in time-of-flight magnetic resonance angiography (TOF-MRA) studies.Material and MethodsNine radiologists with varying levels of experience evaluated twenty TOF-MRA examinations for the presence of cerebral aneurysms. Every case was evaluated with and without assistance by the AI software © mdbrain, with a washout period of at least four weeks in-between.
papers.method: Half of the cases included at least one false-positive AI finding. Aneurysm ratings, follow-up recommendations, and reading times were assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.ResultsFalse-positive AI results led to significantly higher suspicion of aneurysm findings (p = 0.01). Inexperienced readers further recommended significantly more intense follow-up examinations when presented with false-positive AI findings (p = 0.005).
papers.result: Reading times were significantly shorter with AI assistance in inexperienced (164.1 vs 228.2 s; p < 0.001), moderately experienced (126.2 vs 156.5 s; p < 0.009), and very experienced (117.9 vs 153.5 s; p < 0.001) readers alike.ConclusionOur results demonstrate the susceptibility of radiology readers to automation bias in detecting cerebral aneurysms in TOF-MRA studies when encountering false-positive AI findings. While AI systems for cerebral aneurysm detection can provide benefits, challenges in human–AI interaction need to be mitigated to ensure safe and effective adoption.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s11547-025-01964-6.
papers.gap: No uncertainty or explanation display tested as mitigation.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Small enriched dataset; single centre; artificial prevalence.
papers.methodologyDetail: Nine radiologists read twenty aneurysm MRA scans twice, once with AI marks and once without, separated by a washout period; half of the cases contained a deliberately included false-positive AI finding. Comparing ratings, follow-up decisions and reading times showed that wrong AI marks pulled readers, especially less experienced ones, towards over-calling. This design is a direct model for testing automation bias in the PhD's neuro-oncology reader study.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective reader study with crossover design (Technical University of Munich, Germany); IRB approved, consent waived.
papers.datasets: 20 3D TOF-MRA studies (06/2021-12/2023) from an outpatient practice using mdbrain v4 routinely: 10 cases with at least one false-positive AI finding, 10 with true-positive findings only; 12 aneurysms; 9 radiologists of varying experience; 360 readings.
papers.preprocessing: Cases found by RIS full-text search and verified by a board-certified interventional neuroradiologist; anterior circulation only; 3T and 1.5T Siemens/Philips scanners; washout of at least four weeks between sessions.
papers.modelDetails: Commercial CAD AI (mdbrain, Mediaire) providing aneurysm segmentations on TOF-MRA.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial model).
papers.evaluation: Likert aneurysm ratings, follow-up recommendations and reading times with versus without AI; power analysis for sample size.
papers.baselines: Reading without AI assistance.
papers.results: False-positive AI findings significantly raised suspicion ratings (p = 0.01); inexperienced readers rating such cases unremarkable fell from 63.3% to 23.3%; reading times shorter with AI (inexperienced 164.1 vs 228.2 s, p < 0.001).
papers.statistics: Statistical comparisons (p-values) across experience groups; power analysis.

papers.title: Clinical validation of AI-assisted contouring in prostate radiation therapy treatment planning: Highlighting automation bias and the need for standardized quality assurance
papers.authors: Arjmandi N, Sebzari AR, Molaei F, Rezaei S, Rezaie-Yazdi M, Rezaie-Yazdi M
papers.venue: Journal of applied clinical medical physics
papers.aim: AbstractPurposeThis study evaluated the impact of a commercial AI‐assisted contouring tool on intra‐ and inter‐observer variability in prostate radiation therapy and assessed the dosimetric consequences of geometric contour differences.MethodsTwo experienced radiation oncologists independently delineated clinical target volume (CTV) and organs at risk (OARs) for prostate cancer patients. Manual contours (Cman) and AI‐generated contours (CAI) were compared with adjusted AI contours (CAI,adj).
papers.method: A consensus reference (Cref) served as the benchmark. To evaluate clinical impact, treatment plans were recalculated and replanned on each contour set under identical beam geometries to assess dose–volume histogram (DVH) parameters.ResultsAI‐assisted contouring significantly improved both intra‐ and inter‐observer agreement. Inter‐observer analysis revealed that the Dice similarity coefficient (DSCs) for CTV increased from 0.78 (± 0.11) for Cman to 0.89 (± 0.09) for CAI, adj. Similarly, intra‐observer analysis revealed that both oncologists showed significantly higher DSCs for CAI, adj compared to Cman. A thorough geometric comparison to the Cref revealed that while adjustments to CAI improved accuracy, they generally did not surpass Cman for CTV and rectum. Dosimetric analyses demonstrated that, under fixed plan geometry, both Cman and CAI,adj contours yielded lower planning target volume (PTV) D95% values compared with Cref, whereas after replanning, all plans met institutional criteria with no clinically significant differences among contour sets.ConclusionAI‐assisted contouring in prostate radiotherapy reduced intra‐ and inter‐observer variability and improved contouring consistency. However, CAI, adj did not consistently surpass Cman, especially for the CTV and rectum, where automation bias or selective clinical acceptance may have influenced edits. Fixed‐plan recalculations revealed dose differences from minor geometric deviations.
papers.result: These findings underscore the importance of structured quality assurance (QA) and human oversight to mitigate automation bias while leveraging AI's efficiency. The single‐institution design with two oncologists and one AI software limits generalizability, underscoring the need for multi‐observer validation.
papers.gap: Few observers and patients; no uncertainty maps to guide editing.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Single centre; retrospective; one commercial tool.
papers.methodologyDetail: Two experienced oncologists contoured the same prostate CT scans manually and later with AI-proposed contours they could edit; all contours were compared with a consensus reference and the treatment plans were recalculated on each set. AI support reduced variability but clinicians tended to keep AI contours with few changes, showing automation bias. The paper argues for structured quality assurance and human oversight, which supports the PhD's review-and-escalate design for surgical planning.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective clinical validation study in radiation oncology (Iran Mehr Hospital, Birjand University of Medical Sciences, Iran), two phases separated by 2 months.
papers.datasets: Non-contrast planning CT scans of 17 randomly selected patients with localised early-stage prostate cancer (GE LightSpeed 16, 120 kVp, 512×512, 0.82-0.97 mm in-plane, 3-5 mm slices); two radiation oncologists with over 10 years' experience.
papers.preprocessing: Patients without prostatectomy, rectal spacer or femoral implants; each oncologist contoured each case twice at least 2 weeks apart; consensus reference contour (Cref) as benchmark.
papers.modelDetails: Three workflows: manual contouring (Cman), unedited commercial AI contours, and AI contours adjusted by oncologists (CAI,adj) for CTV, rectum, bladder and femoral heads in a 3D PCRT TPS.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial tool).
papers.evaluation: Dice similarity coefficient and HD95 for intra- and inter-observer variability; dosimetric impact by recalculating and replanning on each contour set.
papers.baselines: Manual contouring from scratch.
papers.results: AI-adjusted contours improved agreement: CTV DSC 0.86 to 0.90 (p = 0.044) and HD95 6.3 to 2.6 mm for oncologist 1; 0.83 to 0.92 (p < 0.001) for oncologist 2; evidence of automation bias when clinicians accepted AI contours with minimal edits.
papers.statistics: Paired statistical tests (p-values) on geometric and dosimetric metrics.

papers.title: Explainability in context: calibrating appropriate trust and reliance in artificial intelligence
papers.authors: Davis SE, Salwei ME
papers.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
papers.aim: AbstractBackground and SignificancePredictive artificial intelligence (AI) promises to transform care delivery, enhance patient safety, and improve health outcomes. Realizing these benefits will require careful design, implementation, and monitoring strategies to avoid unintended consequences, including automation bias (i.e., erroneously favoring recommendations from automated systems).
papers.method: Automation bias is particularly concerning due to the variability of AI performance across time and populations, leading to predictions that may be variably incorrect, uncertain, or unfair.ApproachWe advocate for an expanded view of explainable AI that uses contextual information to help end users calibrate appropriate levels of trust and reliance.
papers.result: We propose multiple levels of contextualization—model, setting, subpopulation, and patient—that together provide insight for clinicians to evaluate the reliability of individual predictions. This includes information about historical and in-the-moment AI performance, algorithmic fairness, and prediction uncertainty.ConclusionWe outline an approach to integrate context-based explanations into decision support workflows to aid clinician interpretation without adding cognitive burden.
papers.gap: Framework not yet empirically evaluated.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors argue that explaining why a model made a prediction is not enough; clinicians also need to know how reliable the model is in their setting, for the patient's subgroup, and for this particular case, including uncertainty. They propose layered contextual information built into decision support workflows. This directly supports the PhD's design of showing calibrated uncertainty and site-level performance at the point of escalation.
papers.studyDesign: Perspective / conceptual paper (Vanderbilt University Medical Center, USA) in JAMIA.
papers.datasets: Not applicable (conceptual framework drawing on literature).
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Context-based explainable AI framework with four levels of contextualisation (model, setting, subpopulation and patient), including historical and in-the-moment performance, algorithmic fairness and prediction uncertainty.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable; illustrative workflow integration proposed.
papers.baselines: Conventional feature-attribution XAI.
