papers.aim: AbstractBackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) assistance has been considered as a promising way to improve colonoscopic polyp detection, but there are limited prospective studies on real‐time use of AI systems.MethodsWe conducted a prospective, multicenter, randomized controlled trial of patients undergoing colonoscopy at six centers. Eligible patients were randomly assigned to conventional colonoscopy (control group) or AI‐assisted colonoscopy (AI group).
papers.method: AI assistance was our newly developed AI system for real‐time colonoscopic polyp detection. Primary outcome is polyp detection rate (PDR). Secondary outcomes include polyps per positive patient (PPP), polyps per colonoscopy (PPC), and non‐first polyps per colonoscopy (PPC‐Plus).ResultsA total of 2352 patients were included in the final analysis. Compared with the control, AI group did not show significant increment in PDR (38.8% vs. 36.2%, p = 0.183), but its PPC‐Plus was significantly higher (0.5 vs. 0.4, p < 0.05). In addition, AI group detected more diminutive polyps (76.0% vs. 68.8%, p < 0.01) and flat polyps (5.9% vs. 3.3%, p < 0.05).
papers.result: The effects varied somewhat between centers. In further logistic regression analysis, AI assistance independently contributed to the increment of PDR, and the impact was more pronounced for male endoscopists, shorter insertion time but longer withdrawal time, and elderly patients with larger waist circumference.ConclusionThe intervention of AI plays a limited role in overall polyp detection, but increases detection of easily missed polyps; ChiCTR.org.cn number, ChiCTR1800015607.
papers.gap: No adenoma or cancer outcomes; centre variability unexplained.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Patients at six hospitals were randomly allocated to colonoscopy with or without a real-time AI polyp detector, and detection rates were compared. AI did not significantly raise the overall polyp detection rate but helped find small, flat and additional polyps, with benefit varying by centre and operator. This shows that AI value depends on the setting and user, which the PhD's multi-site evaluation must account for.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective multicentre randomised controlled trial at six centres in Zhejiang, China (ChiCTR1800015607).
papers.datasets: 2,352 patients undergoing colonoscopy included in final analysis.
papers.preprocessing: Eligible patients randomly assigned to conventional colonoscopy or AI-assisted colonoscopy.
papers.modelDetails: Newly developed real-time deep learning system for colonoscopic polyp detection overlaid on the endoscopy video.
papers.training: Developed previously by the team (details referenced).
papers.evaluation: Primary: polyp detection rate (PDR); secondary: polyps per positive patient, polyps per colonoscopy, non-first polyps per colonoscopy (PPC-Plus); subgroup by centre, endoscopist and patient factors.
papers.baselines: Conventional colonoscopy.
papers.results: PDR not significantly higher with AI (38.8% vs 36.2%, p = 0.183); PPC-Plus higher (0.5 vs 0.4, p < 0.05); more diminutive (76.0% vs 68.8%) and flat polyps (5.9% vs 3.3%) detected; effects varied between centres; in regression AI independently increased PDR, especially for certain endoscopist and patient subgroups.

papers.title: A responsible AI framework for infection surveillance in low-resource settings: ethics, opportunities and threats for LMICs (EOT-LMICs)
papers.authors: Alzyood M
papers.aim: AbstractThe integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into infection surveillance represents a significant shift in public health; however, most AI frameworks and implementation guidance neglect the distinct constraints of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This commentary presents the ethics, opportunities, and threats for LMICs (EOT-LMICs) framework, developed through synthesis of the literature on AI adoption, digital health implementation and infection surveillance in resource-limited settings.
papers.result: The framework provides an integrated analytical structure: ethical foundations (equity, data governance, contextual validity) establish preconditions for adoption, opportunities (workforce augmentation, standardised surveillance, outbreak detection) define potential benefits warranting investment and threats (misclassification, infrastructure fragility, model drift, regulatory gaps) identify risks requiring mitigation before and during implementation. Aligned with the 4Ps model (precision, partnership, practice, people), this framework offers policymakers and infection prevention practitioners a pathway for context-appropriate AI implementation that prioritises local needs and human-centred care.
papers.gap: Framework not empirically tested.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The author combined literature on AI, digital health and infection surveillance in low-resource settings into a framework that first checks ethical preconditions, then weighs opportunities against threats such as model drift and fragile infrastructure. Although focused on infection surveillance, the framework applies to deploying the PhD's system in Sri Lanka, an LMIC, and supports its attention to data governance, local validation and drift monitoring.
papers.studyDesign: Short communication / conceptual framework (Oxford Brookes University, UK) in International Health.
papers.datasets: Not applicable; synthesis of literature on AI adoption, digital health implementation and infection surveillance in resource-limited settings.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: EOT-LMICs framework: ethical foundations (equity, data governance, contextual validity) as preconditions; opportunities (workforce augmentation, standardised surveillance, outbreak detection); threats (misclassification, infrastructure fragility, model drift, regulatory gaps); aligned with the 4Ps model (precision, partnership, practice, people).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Not applicable.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Provides policymakers and practitioners with a structured pathway for context-appropriate, human-centred AI implementation in LMICs.

papers.title: Effectiveness of AI-Based Tools in Detecting Diabetic Retinopathy in Low- and Middle-Income Countries: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic Performance and Implementation Feasibility
papers.authors: Onyeze N, Sartawi S, Nayyer Z
papers.aim: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide, with a disproportionate impact in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a potential means to address workforce and infrastructure gaps that limit access to DR screening in these settings, but evidence on its performance and feasibility remains scattered.
papers.method: A systematic review of studies published between January 2015 and June 2025 was conducted using six databases. Eligible studies evaluated AI, machine learning, or deep learning applied to retinal imaging for DR detection and reported quantitative diagnostic or implementation outcomes, while studies limited to high-income countries or non-original research were excluded. Only a small number of eligible studies were identified. Across these, AI-based tools generally showed high diagnostic accuracy and were feasible to implement in resource-limited environments.
papers.result: Early evidence suggested potential benefits, such as reduced screening costs, decreased clinician workload, and improved patient follow-up, though reporting on infrastructure needs, regulatory considerations, and long-term sustainability was limited. Overall, AI-based tools show promise for scaling DR screening in LMICs, with encouraging indications of good accuracy and operational efficiency, but further large-scale and implementation-focused research is required to guide their integration into health systems.
papers.gap: Only six studies; few RCTs or cost analyses.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched six databases for studies of AI diabetic retinopathy screening carried out in low- and middle-income countries and found six with usable accuracy or implementation data. They summarised both how accurate the tools were and how well they worked in practice, including a randomised trial showing better referral uptake. This LMIC evidence supports the PhD's argument that AI can help fill specialist gaps in Sri Lanka if implementation is planned carefully.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review of diagnostic performance and implementation feasibility (Ninewells Hospital, Dundee, UK), PRISMA; studies January 2015 to June 2025 from six databases.
papers.datasets: 109 records, 86 screened, 58 full texts, 6 studies included from LMICs (World Bank FY25 classification), e.g. Thailand (nine primary care sites), Rwanda RCT (n = 275), Brazil portable-camera pilot (n = 1,046), India.
papers.preprocessing: Inclusion: AI/ML/DL on retinal images for DR detection in LMICs with quantitative accuracy or implementation outcomes; English peer-reviewed or high-quality preprints.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis of diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, AUC) and implementation outcomes (referral uptake, cost, workload, feasibility) of AI DR screening tools.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Tabulated accuracy and implementation outcomes; quality appraisal.
papers.baselines: Human graders / retina specialists.
papers.results: High accuracy (e.g. Thai DL system for vision-threatening DR: accuracy 94.7%, sensitivity 91.4%, specificity 95.4%); immediate AI feedback raised referral uptake in Rwanda (51.5% vs 39.6%, p = 0.048); handheld embedded AI feasible in rural Brazil; early evidence of lower costs and workload, but infrastructure and integration challenges.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted chest X-ray for tuberculosis case finding in low- and middle-income countries: implementation experiences and impact
papers.authors: Vijayan S, Nair AM, Dominic N, Chiramal JA, Pawar S, Goswami L
papers.aim: AbstractMedical imaging is fundamental to healthcare systems, aiding in the detection of internal abnormalities related to medical conditions beyond their physical symptoms. In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), limited access to advanced imaging and scarcity of radiologists for image interpretation are evident.
papers.method: Upgrading available resources with artificial intelligence can expand the diagnostic capacity of LMICs to manage the growing prevalence and incidence of infectious diseases such as tuberculosis (TB). Chest X-rays can act as an effective triage tool for TB screening, and multiple models have been reported to improve the number of cases detected in high-burden settings. The case-finding strategies reported in literature have also demonstrated improved diagnostic accuracy and turnaround time post adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) for chest X-ray interpretation. AI assistance can help in identifying radiological involvement of TB, irrespective of their clinical symptoms.
papers.result: Furthermore, cost-effective, integrated workflows can also efficiently support LMICs by facilitating parallel diagnosis and appropriate linkage to care for multiple chest disorders through a unified pathway, thereby broadening the capabilities of chest X-ray based TB screening. By optimizing and strengthening LMIC health systems with AI, further scale-up and implementation can foster a supportive ecosystem for early disease diagnosis and decentralized care delivery.
papers.gap: No systematic method; vendor perspective.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Authors from an AI company summarised how AI reading of chest X-rays has been used to find tuberculosis cases in low- and middle-income countries, describing deployment models and their reported effects on case detection and speed. It shows that AI can extend scarce radiology capacity in LMICs, relevant to Sri Lanka's limited neuroradiology workforce, though the industry authorship is a potential conflict of interest.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review of implementation experiences (Qure.ai Technologies, India and USA) in BJR|Open.
papers.datasets: Published studies and programme reports on AI-assisted chest X-ray for TB case finding in LMICs.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis of AI CXR deployment models (triage before molecular testing, active case finding, mobile vans, integrated multi-disease pathways).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative summary of reported case-detection, accuracy, turnaround time and cost outcomes.
papers.baselines: Human radiologist reading or symptom screening.
papers.results: AI CXR improved case detection, diagnostic accuracy and turnaround time in high-burden settings, identified subclinical TB, and enabled integrated workflows for multiple chest diseases and decentralised care.

papers.title: Effectiveness of Human-Artificial Intelligence Collaboration in Cephalometric Landmark Detection
papers.authors: Le VNT, Kang J, Oh IS, Kim JG, Yang YM, Lee DW
papers.aim: Detection of cephalometric landmarks has contributed to the analysis of malocclusion during orthodontic diagnosis. Many recent studies involving deep learning have focused on head-to-head comparisons of accuracy in landmark identification between artificial intelligence (AI) and humans.
papers.method: However, a human–AI collaboration for the identification of cephalometric landmarks has not been evaluated. We selected 1193 cephalograms and used them to train the deep anatomical context feature learning (DACFL) model. The number of target landmarks was 41. To evaluate the effect of human–AI collaboration on landmark detection, 10 images were extracted randomly from 100 test images. The experiment included 20 dental students as beginners in landmark localization. The outcomes were determined by measuring the mean radial error (MRE), successful detection rate (SDR), and successful classification rate (SCR). On the dataset, the DACFL model exhibited an average MRE of 1.87 ± 2.04 mm and an average SDR of 73.17% within a 2 mm threshold. Compared with the beginner group, beginner–AI collaboration improved the SDR by 5.33% within a 2 mm threshold and also improved the SCR by 8.38%.
papers.result: Thus, the beginner–AI collaboration was effective in the detection of cephalometric landmarks. Further studies should be performed to demonstrate the benefits of an orthodontist–AI collaboration.
papers.gap: Only beginners tested; no uncertainty on landmarks.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team trained a deep learning model on over a thousand children's cephalograms to locate 41 landmarks, then had less experienced clinicians mark the same landmarks on test images alone and again with the AI suggestions, comparing errors at several distance thresholds. Collaboration made beginners more accurate. It is evidence that human-AI teamwork helps less experienced users most, relevant to supporting junior clinicians in the PhD's setting.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and human-AI collaboration study (Jeonbuk National University, South Korea); IRB approved (CUH2019-05-057).
papers.datasets: 1,293 lateral cephalograms of children and adolescents aged 6-18 years (2008-2018) from the hospital PACS; 1,193 for training and 100 for testing; 41 landmarks.
papers.preprocessing: De-identified JPG images (550×550 to 4066×4345 pixels); random training/test split; expert landmark annotation.
papers.modelDetails: DACFL deep learning model for cephalometric landmark detection; beginner clinicians detected landmarks alone and with AI-suggested positions (beginner-AI collaboration).
papers.training: Details in paper (CNN trained on 1,193 images).
papers.evaluation: Mean radial error (MRE) and successful detection rate (SDR) within 2, 2.5, 3 and 4 mm thresholds per landmark, for AI alone, beginners alone and beginner-AI collaboration.
papers.baselines: Beginners alone; AI alone.
papers.results: AI MRE 1.87 ± 2.04 mm (sella lowest at 0.76 mm, glabella highest at 5.18 mm); beginner-AI collaboration improved SDR over beginners alone for many landmarks.
papers.statistics: t-tests comparing SDR between beginner-only and beginner-AI groups (SPSS, PRISM), p < 0.05.

papers.title: A scoping review of human-AI collaboration patterns and task divisions in healthcare applications
papers.authors: You Y, Li X
papers.aim: With the widespread use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare, how human physicians work with AI, a new colleague, has become an issue of increasing concern. This review systematically explores the collaboration between humans and AI in the medical field, focusing on the prevalent human-AI collaboration patterns, the task division mechanisms, and the evaluation metrics.
papers.method: Following the PRISMA guidelines for scoping reviews, we screened the relevant literature and finally included 85 journal papers. Our analysis reveals that human-AI collaboration patterns in healthcare tend to be associated with the inherent risk and automation level of medical tasks, and the collaboration process demonstrates a clear division of labor between human physicians and AI.
papers.result: Furthermore, the evaluation of the human-AI collaboration effect is shifting from single technical metrics (e.g., diagnostic accuracy) to multidimensional aspects incorporating clinical efficiency and user experience. Overall, this review presents collaboration patterns in various medical tasks and serves as a theoretical basis for optimizing the clinical workflows for human-AI collaboration.
papers.gap: Few studies on dynamic or uncertainty-based task allocation.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors screened the literature for studies comparing humans working with AI against either alone, included 85, and classified how the AI was inserted into the workflow (before the human's decision, after it, or as a filter) and how tasks were divided. Higher-risk tasks kept more human control. This taxonomy helps the PhD position its confidence-based escalation as a risk-aware division of labour and supports multidimensional evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR (npj Digital Medicine).
papers.datasets: 85 journal papers (2016-July 2025) comparing human-AI collaboration with AI-only or human-only benchmarks in healthcare.
papers.preprocessing: Screening with explicit inclusion criteria (human-AI collaboration, healthcare application, benchmark comparison, English); VOSviewer keyword co-occurrence analysis of titles and abstracts.
papers.modelDetails: Classification of collaboration patterns (e.g. AI-prior aid, AI-late aid / second opinion, AI triage and filtering, task division), task allocation mechanisms and evaluation metrics.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Descriptive mapping of patterns versus task risk and automation level; evaluation metrics used.
papers.baselines: AI-only and human-only benchmarks in included studies.
papers.results: Collaboration patterns relate to task risk and automation level, with clear division of labour; evaluation is shifting from single accuracy metrics to multidimensional outcomes including efficiency and user experience.

papers.title: A Dataset for Understanding Radiologist-Artificial Intelligence Collaboration
papers.authors: Moehring A, Kutwal M, Huang R, Banerjee O, Jacobi A, Eber C, Mendoza D, Chung M, Dayan E, Gupta Y, et al.
papers.aim: This dataset, Collab-CXR, provides a unique resource to study human-AI collaboration in chest X-ray interpretation. We present experimentally generated data from 227 professional radiologists who assessed 324 historical cases under varying information conditions: with and without AI assistance, and with and without clinical history.
papers.method: Using a custom-designed interface, we collected probabilistic assessments for 104 thoracic pathologies using a comprehensive hierarchical reporting structure. This dataset is the largest known comparison of human-AI collaborative performance to either AI or humans alone in radiology, offering assessments across an extensive range of pathologies with rich metadata on radiologist characteristics and decision-making processes. Multiple experimental designs enable both within-subject and between-subject analyses.
papers.result: Researchers can leverage this dataset to investigate how radiologists incorporate AI assistance, factors influencing collaborative effectiveness, and impacts on diagnostic accuracy, speed, and confidence across different cases and pathologies. By enabling rigorous study of human-AI integration in clinical workflows, this dataset can inform AI tool development, implementation strategies, and ultimately improve patient care through optimized collaboration in medical imaging.
papers.gap: Remote experimental setting; single modality.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Historical cases; incentive variation across designs.
papers.methodologyDetail: Hundreds of radiologists read historical chest X-rays through an online interface while the researchers randomly varied whether they saw AI predictions and clinical history, collecting probability judgements for over a hundred findings. The resulting dataset lets others study when and how humans benefit from AI advice. Its randomised information-condition design is a useful template for the PhD's reader study comparing reads with and without calibrated AI and escalation cues.
papers.studyDesign: Experimental data descriptor (MIT, Harvard, Stanford and partners) in Scientific Data; MIT COUHES exempt protocol E-2953.
papers.datasets: Collab-CXR: 227 professional radiologists (mean 22 years' experience; 17% US-based; recruited including via a Vietnamese healthcare system) assessing subsets of 324 historical chest X-ray cases.
papers.preprocessing: Remote custom interface mimicking clinical reading with training, consent and practice cases; randomised information conditions; monetary accuracy incentives for a random subset in designs 1 and 3.
papers.modelDetails: Three experimental designs varying AI assistance (CheXpert-type AI probabilities) and clinical history availability; probabilistic assessments for 104 thoracic pathologies in a hierarchical reporting structure.
papers.training: Not applicable (existing AI model).
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy, speed and confidence under each condition; within- and between-subject comparisons enabled.
papers.baselines: Radiologists alone; AI alone.
papers.results: Largest known dataset comparing human-AI collaboration with AI or humans alone in radiology, with rich metadata on radiologist characteristics and decisions, released for research on how radiologists incorporate AI.

papers.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Healthcare: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Strong J, Rogers H, Sun E, Todsen AL, Ede J, Lumley C, Yeung N, Higham H, Noble JA
papers.aim: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in clinical pathways, making effective human-AI collaboration (HAIC) a practical and policy priority in healthcare. We conducted a scoping review of empirical studies of HAIC in healthcare published from January 2015 to October 2025, using Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting.
papers.method: Of 17,463 records identified, 140 studies were included. Evidence was concentrated in diagnostic interpretation, with fewer studies in screening and triage, therapeutic decision-making, and administrative workflows. Effectiveness was defined inconsistently across task contexts and was usually assessed using short-term task-level metrics rather than patient or system outcomes. Most studies, particularly in diagnostic interpretation, reported benefits for human-AI teams. These depended on task fit, workflow integration, training, and appropriately calibrated trust.
papers.result: Ethical and governance issues, including accountability and patient safety, were often discussed but rarely evaluated empirically. These findings provide a foundation for more task-specific, longitudinal, and governance-aware evaluation of HAIC in healthcare.
papers.gap: Few studies with patient outcomes or empirical governance evaluation.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a registered protocol, the team screened over seventeen thousand records and charted 140 empirical studies of clinicians working with AI. They found that benefits are common but depend on fit with the task and workflow, training and calibrated trust, and that effects on patients and accountability are seldom measured. This directly supports the PhD's plan to evaluate workflow, trust calibration and accountability alongside accuracy.
papers.studyDesign: Scoping review using Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR (University of Oxford), protocol registered on OSF.
papers.datasets: MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane and Google Scholar, January 2015 to October 2025: 17,463 records, 269 full texts, 140 empirical studies included.
papers.preprocessing: Predefined eligibility; dual screening; data charting; five registered research questions consolidated into three (effectiveness in task context, determinants of collaboration, ethics and governance).
papers.modelDetails: Charting and thematic synthesis of human-AI collaboration studies by task context (diagnostic interpretation, screening and triage, therapeutic decisions, administration).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: How effectiveness was defined and measured; success factors; ethics and governance evaluation.
papers.baselines: Human-only and AI-only comparators in included studies.
papers.results: Evidence concentrated on diagnostic interpretation; effectiveness usually measured with short-term task metrics rather than patient or system outcomes; most studies reported team benefits that depended on task fit, workflow integration, training and calibrated trust; ethics and accountability discussed but rarely evaluated empirically.

papers.title: A quantitative study of pathologists' perceptions towards artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic system
papers.authors: Ye Z, Lu Q, Wang J, Jiang Y, Xue P
papers.aim: The successful implementation of artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostic system (AIADS) in pathology relies not only on the maturity of AI technology but also on pathologists’ cognition and acceptance of AI. However, research on pathologists’ perceptions towards AIADS is limited.
papers.method: This study aims to explore pathologists’ knowledge, attitudes, and practice toward AIADS and identify key factors influencing their willingness to use it, providing insights for the effective integration of AI technology in pathology. An online, nationwide, cross-sectional survey is to investigate pathologists’ knowledge, attitudes and behavioral intention/practice regarding AIADS with a 5-point Likert scale. Descriptive analysis is used to present the results, while logistic regression examines factors influencing AIADS adoption. The mediating effect of attitude in the association between knowledge and behavioral intention is also explored. A total of 224 pathologists were surveyed, with 85 (37.9%) having used AIADS and 139 (62.1%) not using it. The mean scores for knowledge, attitude, and behavioral intention were 3.42 ± 0.97, 3.48 ± 0.44, and 3.47 ± 0.44, respectively. Pathologists who had used AIADS scored higher in knowledge, attitude, and behavioral intention, with clearer attitudes toward AIADS. Over 80% of pathologists supported the use of AIADS in clinical diagnostics, citing improved diagnostic speed and reduced workload as key reasons. The main concerns about AIADS were its diagnostic accuracy. Logistic regression analysis indicated that a greater likelihood of willingness to use AIADS was associated with not having used it before (OR=2.462, 95%CI 1.087-5.573), as well as with higher knowledge scores (OR=1.140, 95%CI 1.076-1.208) and more positive attitude scores (OR=1.119, 95%CI 1.053-1.189). Mediation analysis indicated an indirect path from knowledge to behavioral intention through attitude among individuals who have used AIADS, with the mediation effect accounting for 59.4%.
papers.result: In conclusion, most pathologists support the use of AIADS in clinical practice, but improvements in diagnostic performance are necessary. Enhancing pathologists’ knowledge, attitudes, and user experience is crucial for the broader adoption of AIADS.
papers.gap: Intentions rather than observed use; cervical-cytology network focus.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Pathologists across China completed a piloted online questionnaire about what they know about AI diagnostic aids, how they feel about them and whether they intend to use them, and regression identified the factors linked to willingness. Most were supportive but wanted more accurate systems. This informs how the PhD should engage Sri Lankan pathologists for the pathology arm and its trust measures.
papers.studyDesign: Online nationwide cross-sectional KAP survey of pathologists in China (Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College), August 2024; IRB approved, written consent.
papers.datasets: 235 questionnaires, 224 valid (95.3%) from pathologists at over 120 hospitals in 27 provinces; 73.2% female; mean age 40.3; 37.9% had used an AI-assisted diagnostic system (AIADS).
papers.preprocessing: Recruitment through a national multicentre cervical cancer cohort network plus snowball sampling; questionnaire piloted (n = 30) and expert-reviewed; one response per IP; mandatory fields; quality-control question.
papers.modelDetails: Questionnaire on knowledge, attitudes and behavioural intention/practice toward AIADS, with demographic and influencing-factor sections.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Scale scores for knowledge, attitudes and intention; factors associated with willingness to use AIADS.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Most pathologists supported clinical use of AIADS but wanted better diagnostic performance; knowledge, prior use and perceived usefulness were associated with willingness to use; training and trust-building recommended.
papers.statistics: t-tests/ANOVA, chi-square tests, logistic regression of behavioural intention (SPSS 29.0, α = 0.05).

papers.title: Impact of a deep learning assistant on the histopathologic classification of liver cancer
papers.authors: Kiani A, Uyumazturk B, Rajpurkar P, Wang A, Gao R, Jones E, Yu Y, Langlotz CP, Ball RL, Montine TJ, et al.
papers.aim: Artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms continue to rival human performance on a variety of clinical tasks, while their actual impact on human diagnosticians, when incorporated into clinical workflows, remains relatively unexplored. In this study, we developed a deep learning-based assistant to help pathologists differentiate between two subtypes of primary liver cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma, on hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images (WSI), and evaluated its effect on the diagnostic performance of 11 pathologists with varying levels of expertise.
papers.method: Our model achieved accuracies of 0.885 on a validation set of 26 WSI, and 0.842 on an independent test set of 80 WSI. Although use of the assistant did not change the mean accuracy of the 11 pathologists (p = 0.184, OR = 1.281), it significantly improved the accuracy (p = 0.045, OR = 1.499) of a subset of nine pathologists who fell within well-defined experience levels (GI subspecialists, non-GI subspecialists, and trainees). In the assisted state, model accuracy significantly impacted the diagnostic decisions of all 11 pathologists.
papers.result: As expected, when the model’s prediction was correct, assistance significantly improved accuracy (p = 0.000, OR = 4.289), whereas when the model’s prediction was incorrect, assistance significantly decreased accuracy (p = 0.000, OR = 0.253), with both effects holding across all pathologist experience levels and case difficulty levels. Our results highlight the challenges of translating AI models into the clinical setting, and emphasize the importance of taking into account potential unintended negative consequences of model assistance when designing and testing medical AI-assistance tools.
papers.gap: No uncertainty display to warn of likely-wrong predictions.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Binary task; small number of pathologists.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team trained a deep learning classifier on TCGA liver cancer slides and put it into a web tool, then had eleven pathologists classify eighty slides with and without the tool in randomised order separated by a washout. Overall accuracy did not change, because correct AI advice helped and wrong advice harmed. This is a key motivation for the PhD's escalation design: uncertain predictions should be flagged rather than shown as confident advice.
papers.studyDesign: Diagnostic assistant development and randomised crossover reader study (Stanford University, USA).
papers.datasets: Training from 70 TCGA H&E WSI (35 HCC from LIHC, 35 cholangiocarcinoma from CHOL): 25,000 patches of 512×512 px (128×128 µm); validation 26 WSI; independent Stanford test set of 80 WSI; 11 pathologists of varying expertise.
papers.preprocessing: Tumour regions patched; random split at slide level (20,000 training patches from 20 WSI, 2,400 tuning from 24 WSI, 2,600 validation from 26 WSI) with 50:50 class balance.
papers.modelDetails: CNN patch classifier in a web-based assistant showing predicted probabilities and class activation maps for HCC versus cholangiocarcinoma.
papers.training: Patch-level training with tuning set for model selection (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Model accuracy on validation and test sets; pathologist accuracy with and without assistance in randomised order (assisted first or unassisted first) with a 2-week washout; effect stratified by correctness of model prediction.
papers.baselines: Unassisted pathologists.
papers.results: Model accuracy 0.885 (validation) and 0.842 (test); assistance did not change mean pathologist accuracy (p = 0.184, OR 1.281) but significantly improved accuracy when the model was correct (OR 4.289) and significantly reduced it when the model was wrong.
papers.statistics: Mixed-effects logistic regression with odds ratios.
papers.availability: Code and model details in paper/supplement.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted cancer diagnosis improves the efficiency of pathologists in prostatic biopsies
papers.authors: Eloy C, Marques A, Pinto J, Pinheiro J, Campelos S, Curado M, Vale J, Polónia A
papers.venue: Virchows Archiv : an international journal of pathology
papers.aim: Paige Prostate is a clinical-grade artificial intelligence tool designed to assist the pathologist in detecting, grading, and quantifying prostate cancer. In this work, a cohort of 105 prostate core needle biopsies (CNBs) was evaluated through digital pathology.
papers.method: Then, we compared the diagnostic performance of four pathologists diagnosing prostatic CNB unaided and, in a second phase, assisted by Paige Prostate. In phase 1, pathologists had a diagnostic accuracy for prostate cancer of 95.00%, maintaining their performance in phase 2 (93.81%), with an intraobserver concordance rate between phases of 98.81%. In phase 2, pathologists reported atypical small acinar proliferation (ASAP) less often (about 30% less). Additionally, they requested significantly fewer immunohistochemistry (IHC) studies (about 20% less) and second opinions (about 40% less). The median time required for reading and reporting each slide was about 20% lower in phase 2, in both negative and cancer cases. Lastly, the average total agreement with the software performance was observed in about 70% of the cases, being significantly higher in negative cases (about 90%) than in cancer cases (about 30%).
papers.result: Most of the diagnostic discordances occurred in distinguishing negative cases with ASAP from small foci of well-differentiated (less than 1.5 mm) acinar adenocarcinoma. In conclusion, the synergic usage of Paige Prostate contributes to a significant decrease in IHC studies, second opinion requests, and time for reporting while maintaining highly accurate diagnostic standards.Supplementary informationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00428-023-03518-5.
papers.gap: Small reader and case numbers; single centre.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Four pathologists diagnosed the same prostate biopsies first without and later with an AI tool, and their accuracy, agreement and use of extra tests were compared. Accuracy stayed similar but pathologists needed fewer immunostains and second opinions, saving time and cost. This shows that efficiency and resource use, not only accuracy, are important outcomes for the PhD's pathology evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Two-phase retrospective reader study (IPATIMUP and University of Porto, Portugal).
papers.datasets: 105 prostate core needle biopsy slides from 41 men (median age 69): 66 benign, 39 acinar adenocarcinoma (GrG1-5); 4 pathologists.
papers.preprocessing: Digitised whole-slide images; ground truth established by reference diagnosis; phase 1 unaided, phase 2 assisted after interval.
papers.modelDetails: Paige Prostate clinical-grade AI tool for detecting, grading and quantifying prostate cancer on WSI.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial tool).
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy, intra- and interobserver concordance, ASAP reporting rate, number of IHC requests and second opinions, reading time.
papers.baselines: Unaided pathologists (phase 1).
papers.results: Accuracy 95.00% unaided and 93.81% assisted, intraobserver concordance 98.81%; with AI, ASAP reported about 30% less, IHC requests about 20% fewer and fewer second opinions; discordances mainly between ASAP and small well-differentiated cancer foci.
papers.statistics: Chi-square and McNemar tests; Kruskal-Wallis; simple and quadratic weighted kappa with Landis-Koch interpretation (SPSS 27).

papers.title: Artificial intelligence assistance significantly improves Gleason grading of prostate biopsies by pathologists
papers.authors: Bulten W, Balkenhol M, Belinga JA, Brilhante A, Çakır A, Egevad L, Eklund M, Farré X, Geronatsiou K, Molinié V, et al.
papers.venue: Modern pathology : an official journal of the United States and Canadian Academy of Pathology, Inc
papers.aim: The Gleason score is the most important prognostic marker for prostate cancer patients, but it suffers from significant observer variability. Artificial intelligence (AI) systems based on deep learning can achieve pathologist-level performance at Gleason grading.
papers.method: However, the performance of such systems can degrade in the presence of artifacts, foreign tissue, or other anomalies. Pathologists integrating their expertise with feedback from an AI system could result in a synergy that outperforms both the individual pathologist and the system. Despite the hype around AI assistance, existing literature on this topic within the pathology domain is limited. We investigated the value of AI assistance for grading prostate biopsies. A panel of 14 observers graded 160 biopsies with and without AI assistance. Using AI, the agreement of the panel with an expert reference standard increased significantly (quadratically weighted Cohen’s kappa, 0.799 vs. 0.872; p = 0.019). On an external validation set of 87 cases, the panel showed a significant increase in agreement with a panel of international experts in prostate pathology (quadratically weighted Cohen’s kappa, 0.733 vs. 0.786; p = 0.003).
papers.result: In both experiments, on a group-level, AI-assisted pathologists outperformed the unassisted pathologists and the standalone AI system. Our results show the potential of AI systems for Gleason grading, but more importantly, show the benefits of pathologist-AI synergy.
papers.gap: No uncertainty-based routing; retrospective reads only.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: A panel of pathologists graded a set of prostate biopsies without help and later with an AI showing predicted Gleason patterns, and both reads were scored against an expert consensus. With AI support, the human-AI team graded better than either pathologists alone or the AI alone, and variation fell. This is strong evidence for the PhD's premise that human-AI teams with clear AI output can beat either alone, especially in difficult grading tasks.
papers.studyDesign: International observer study with crossover reads (Radboud University Medical Center, Netherlands, with ISUP expert panel); ethics waiver IRB 2016-2275.
papers.datasets: System trained on 5,759 H&E biopsies from 1,243 patients (Radboud 2012-2017, scanned at 20×, 0.24 µm/pixel); 550 independent test biopsies; observer panel of 14 pathologists from 16 invited (board-certified and residents), multiple countries.
papers.preprocessing: Consensus reference standard from three uropathology experts with majority-vote rules; anonymised slides; reads with and without AI separated by washout.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning Gleason grading system showing grade-group prediction and overlaid Gleason pattern maps as assistance.
papers.training: Previously developed system (semi-automatic labelling and CNN segmentation, details in earlier study).
papers.evaluation: Quadratic weighted Cohen's kappa against reference (median kappa at group level); sensitivity/specificity for cancer detection; comparison with stand-alone AI.
papers.baselines: Unassisted pathologists; stand-alone AI.
papers.results: AI-assisted pathologists outperformed both unassisted pathologists and the stand-alone AI at group level; kappa improved significantly with assistance, with the largest gains for less experienced pathologists.
papers.statistics: Shapiro-Wilk test; Wilcoxon signed-rank test on paired kappa differences.
papers.availability: Test data available via grand-challenge (details in paper).

papers.title: How can artificial intelligence models assist PD-L1 expression scoring in breast cancer: results of multi-institutional ring studies
papers.authors: Wang X, Wang L, Bu H, Zhang N, Yue M, Jia Z, Cai L, He J, Wang Y, Xu X, et al.
papers.aim: Programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) expression is a key biomarker to screen patients for PD-1/PD-L1-targeted immunotherapy. However, a subjective assessment guide on PD-L1 expression of tumor-infiltrating immune cells (IC) scoring is currently adopted in clinical practice with low concordance.
papers.method: Therefore, a repeatable and quantifiable PD-L1 IC scoring method of breast cancer is desirable. In this study, we propose a deep learning-based artificial intelligence-assisted (AI-assisted) model for PD-L1 IC scoring. Three rounds of ring studies (RSs) involving 31 pathologists from 10 hospitals were carried out, using the current guideline in the first two rounds (RS1, RS2) and our AI scoring model in the last round (RS3). A total of 109 PD-L1 (Ventana SP142) immunohistochemistry (IHC) stained images were assessed and the role of the AI-assisted model was evaluated. With the assistance of AI, the scoring concordance across pathologists was boosted to excellent in RS3 (0.950, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.936–0.962) from moderate in RS1 (0.674, 95% CI: 0.614–0.735) and RS2 (0.736, 95% CI: 0.683–0.789). The 2- and 4-category scoring accuracy were improved by 4.2% (0.959, 95% CI: 0.953–0.964) and 13% (0.815, 95% CI: 0.803–0.827) (p < 0.001). The AI results were generally accepted by pathologists with 61% “fully accepted” and 91% “almost accepted”.
papers.result: The proposed AI-assisted method can help pathologists at all levels to improve the PD-L1 assay (SP-142) IC assessment in breast cancer in terms of both accuracy and concordance. The AI tool provides a scheme to standardize the PD-L1 IC scoring in clinical practice.
papers.gap: Single antibody clone and single source of slides.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Image patches rather than whole slides.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team built a deep learning model that quantifies PD-L1-positive immune cells in breast cancer images, then ran three rounds in which 31 pathologists from 10 hospitals scored the same 109 images, the last round with AI help. Agreement and accuracy rose with assistance at every experience level. The multi-institutional ring-study design is a useful template for the PhD's multi-site reader evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Model development and three-round multi-institutional ring study (Fourth Hospital of Hebei Medical University with Tencent AI Lab and other hospitals, China).
papers.datasets: 100 invasive breast cancer resection blocks (January-June 2019) stained with PD-L1 SP142; 4,246 patches cut from tumour regions, 2,395 after exclusions; 109 test images; 31 pathologists from 10 hospitals.
papers.preprocessing: 4 µm sections, Ventana BenchMark staining, scanned at ×40 (Unic); tumour, necrosis, in situ and normal areas annotated per Roche SP142 guide; non-overlapping 3290×3290 patches resized to 2160×2160 (~×20).
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning AI-assisted PD-L1 immune-cell (IC) scoring model segmenting tumour area and PD-L1-positive immune cells to compute IC percentage and categories.
papers.training: Supervised training on annotated patches (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Model 2- and 4-category accuracy, AUC and weighted F1; pathologist concordance (ICC, kappa), accuracy against gold standard and acceptance of AI results across ring studies RS1-RS2 (guideline) and RS3 (AI-assisted).
papers.baselines: Guideline-based visual scoring in RS1 and RS2.
papers.results: Model 2-category accuracy 0.963 (105/109), AUC 0.888, weighted F1 0.962; AI assistance raised inter-pathologist concordance and accuracy for pathologists at all experience levels.
papers.statistics: Intraclass correlation coefficients, kappa and accuracy comparisons across rounds.

papers.title: Assessing the influence of two deep-learning assistance modes on pathologists in cancer identification
papers.authors: Chuang WY, Yu WH, Liu YJ, Huang CC, Lee KF, Hwang CC, Chang LC, Ueng SH, Yeh CJ, Chuang HC, et al.
papers.aim: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) has achieved good performance in image recognition, including identifying cancer cells in pathology images. However, the best mode of AI assistance in diagnostic pathology remains to be explored.MethodsWe compared the influence of two deep-learning assistance modes on pathologists in cancer identification.
papers.method: Ten board-certified pathologists classified 60 cases of nasopharyngeal biopsy as carcinoma or benign with or without AI assistance, which was either a heatmap of cancer probability accompanying a whole-slide image (AI-heatmap mode) or ten high-power field images with the highest cancer probability (AI-HPF mode).ResultsBoth assisting modes significantly accelerated the diagnostic process, lowered the subjective difficulty, and maintained high accuracy compared to the unassisted mode. Notably, the acceleration of diagnosis was more significant in AI-HPF mode than in AI-heatmap mode (time reduction: 35.1% vs. 28.1%; P = 0.040), especially for benign cases (time reduction: 49.4% vs. 32.9%; P = 0.0000072). For benign cases, an increased area proportion of false-positive AI prediction slowed down the diagnostic process in AI-heatmap mode (P = 0.00000084) but not in AI-HPF mode (P = 0.62).ConclusionsWe show for the first time that an AI-HPF assistance mode was superior to the commonly used AI-heatmap mode in accelerating cancer identification by pathologists.
papers.result: In our scenario, the AI-HPF mode maintained high diagnostic accuracy and was robust to the influence of false-positive AI prediction. The potential risk caused by AI assistance is also discussed.
papers.gap: Binary task; no calibrated uncertainty display tested.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Small case set; one centre group.
papers.methodologyDetail: Ten pathologists classified nasopharyngeal biopsies with no AI, with a full-slide AI heatmap, or with AI-selected high-power fields, and their speed, accuracy and perceived difficulty were modelled with mixed-effects statistics. Showing selected fields kept accuracy high and limited the pull of false-positive predictions. This shows that how AI output is presented changes automation bias, which matters for the PhD's escalation interface design.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-reader study comparing two AI assistance modes (Chang Gung Memorial Hospital and aetherAI, Taiwan); IRB 202000956B0.
papers.datasets: 70 nasopharyngeal biopsies (35 carcinoma, 35 benign) from three hospital branches, one H&E slide each, scanned at 40× (NanoZoomer S360); 60 cases used in the experiment; 10 board-certified pathologists.
papers.preprocessing: Diagnoses confirmed by two senior pathologists excluded from reading; three review modes prepared for each case.
papers.modelDetails: ResNeXt-based nasopharyngeal carcinoma detector (trained on 726 independent cases, patch AUC 0.99) presented either as a whole-slide cancer probability heatmap (AI-heatmap) or as AI-selected high-power fields (AI-HPF).
papers.training: Pre-trained model from earlier study.
papers.evaluation: Review time, diagnostic accuracy and subjective difficulty in unassisted, AI-heatmap and AI-HPF modes; influence of false-positive AI predictions.
papers.baselines: Unassisted review.
papers.results: AI-HPF mode kept high diagnostic accuracy and was robust to false-positive AI predictions, while assistance modes affected review time and perceived difficulty differently.
papers.statistics: Generalised linear mixed-effect models with readers and cases as random effects; ANOVA model comparison; TukeyHSD or simple main effects.

papers.title: Computer-assisted mitotic count using a deep learning-based algorithm improves interobserver reproducibility and accuracy
papers.authors: Bertram CA, Aubreville M, Donovan TA, Bartel A, Wilm F, Marzahl C, Assenmacher CA, Becker K, Bennett M, Corner S, et al.
papers.aim: The mitotic count (MC) is an important histological parameter for prognostication of malignant neoplasms. However, it has inter- and intraobserver discrepancies due to difficulties in selecting the region of interest (MC-ROI) and in identifying or classifying mitotic figures (MFs).
papers.method: Recent progress in the field of artificial intelligence has allowed the development of high-performance algorithms that may improve standardization of the MC. As algorithmic predictions are not flawless, computer-assisted review by pathologists may ensure reliability. In the present study, we compared partial (MC-ROI preselection) and full (additional visualization of MF candidates and display of algorithmic confidence values) computer-assisted MC analysis to the routine (unaided) MC analysis by 23 pathologists for whole-slide images of 50 canine cutaneous mast cell tumors (ccMCTs). Algorithmic predictions aimed to assist pathologists in detecting mitotic hotspot locations, reducing omission of MFs, and improving classification against imposters. The interobserver consistency for the MC significantly increased with computer assistance (interobserver correlation coefficient, ICC = 0.92) compared to the unaided approach (ICC = 0.70). Classification into prognostic stratifications had a higher accuracy with computer assistance. The algorithmically preselected hotspot MC-ROIs had a consistently higher MCs than the manually selected MC-ROIs.
papers.result: Compared to a ground truth (developed with immunohistochemistry for phosphohistone H3), pathologist performance in detecting individual MF was augmented when using computer assistance (F1-score of 0.68 increased to 0.79) with a reduction in false negatives by 38%. The results of this study demonstrate that computer assistance may lead to more reproducible and accurate MCs in ccMCTs.
papers.gap: Sequential non-randomised order; veterinary tumour type.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Pathologists counted mitoses on the same tumour slides three times: alone, with an AI-chosen hotspot, and with the hotspot plus AI-marked candidate mitoses and their confidence scores, compared with an immunostain-based ground truth. Agreement and accuracy rose with more assistance. Showing confidence values alongside detections is directly relevant to the PhD's plan to present calibrated confidence to clinicians.
papers.studyDesign: Multi-centre, three-stage reader study with increasing computer assistance (University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna, FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg and international partners).
papers.datasets: WSIs of 50 canine cutaneous mast cell tumours; 23 of 26 pathologists from 11 laboratories completed (96% board-certified diplomates).
papers.preprocessing: Ground truth by destaining H&E sections, re-staining with phosphohistone H3 IHC and registering both images at cellular level; at least 3 days between stages.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning mitotic-figure detector over the whole slide; stage 1 no assistance, stage 2 algorithm-selected mitotic hotspot ROI, stage 3 ROI plus overlay of detected mitotic figures and lookalikes with algorithmic confidence values.
papers.training: Algorithm trained previously on annotated canine tumour datasets.
papers.evaluation: Mitotic count reproducibility (ICC) between pathologists; accuracy of mitotic figure detection (sensitivity, precision, F1) and MC against pHH3-assisted ground truth.
papers.baselines: Unassisted pathologists (stage 1).
papers.results: Computer assistance improved interobserver reproducibility of the mitotic count and accuracy of mitotic figure detection versus unassisted counting; full assistance with confidence overlays gave the largest improvement.
papers.statistics: Intraclass correlation and accuracy comparisons across stages.
papers.availability: Datasets and algorithm referenced from earlier open datasets.

papers.title: Assessing the impact of deep-learning assistance on the histopathological diagnosis of serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC) in fallopian tubes
papers.authors: Bogaerts JM, Steenbeek MP, Bokhorst JM, van Bommel MH, Abete L, Addante F, Brinkhuis M, Chrzan A, Cordier F, Devouassoux-Shisheboran M, et al.
papers.venue: The journal of pathology. Clinical research
papers.aim: AbstractIn recent years, it has become clear that artificial intelligence (AI) models can achieve high accuracy in specific pathology‐related tasks. An example is our deep‐learning model, designed to automatically detect serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), the precursor lesion to high‐grade serous ovarian carcinoma, found in the fallopian tube.
papers.method: However, the standalone performance of a model is insufficient to determine its value in the diagnostic setting. To evaluate the impact of the use of this model on pathologists' performance, we set up a fully crossed multireader, multicase study, in which 26 participants, from 11 countries, reviewed 100 digitalized H&E‐stained slides of fallopian tubes (30 cases/70 controls) with and without AI assistance, with a washout period between the sessions. We evaluated the effect of the deep‐learning model on accuracy, slide review time and (subjectively perceived) diagnostic certainty, using mixed‐models analysis. With AI assistance, we found a significant increase in accuracy (p < 0.01) whereby the average sensitivity increased from 82% to 93%. Further, there was a significant 44 s (32%) reduction in slide review time (p < 0.01). The level of certainty that the participants felt versus their own assessment also significantly increased, by 0.24 on a 10‐point scale (p < 0.01).
papers.result: In conclusion, we found that, in a diverse group of pathologists and pathology residents, AI support resulted in a significant improvement in the accuracy of STIC diagnosis and was coupled with a substantial reduction in slide review time. This model has the potential to provide meaningful support to pathologists in the diagnosis of STIC, ultimately streamlining and optimizing the overall diagnostic process.
papers.gap: Enriched case mix; no uncertainty communication.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: A diverse international group of pathologists and residents diagnosed fallopian tube slides for early serous carcinoma with and without an AI model that highlights suspicious areas, against an expert-panel reference standard. AI support improved accuracy and saved time. It shows the value of measuring both accuracy and efficiency in a held-out, multi-source case set, as planned for the PhD reader study.
papers.studyDesign: International multi-reader crossover study (Radboud University Medical Center, Netherlands, with AI-STIC Study Group); ethics 2019-5879 and partner approvals.
papers.datasets: 100 fallopian tube slides (21 STIC, 9 STIL, 70 controls) from Radboudumc, PALGA, Johns Hopkins, CWZ and Rijnstate, held out from model training; diverse group of pathologists and residents.
papers.preprocessing: Reference standard from an international panel of 15 gynaecological pathologists; one slide per specimen; reads with and without AI separated by washout.
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning STIC detection model producing heatmaps/region highlights of suspicious epithelium.
papers.training: Model developed in earlier study.
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, inter-observer agreement and reading time with versus without AI support.
papers.baselines: Unassisted reading.
papers.results: AI support significantly improved diagnostic accuracy and reduced reading time for STIC across pathologists and residents.
papers.statistics: Mixed-effects or paired statistical comparisons; kappa agreement.

papers.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Patient Safety Outcomes: Systematic Literature Review
papers.authors: Choudhury A, Asan O
papers.aim: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) provides opportunities to identify the health risks of patients and thus influence patient safety outcomes.ObjectiveThe purpose of this systematic literature review was to identify and analyze quantitative studies utilizing or integrating AI to address and report clinical-level patient safety outcomes.MethodsWe restricted our search to the PubMed, PubMed Central, and Web of Science databases to retrieve research articles published in English between January 2009 and August 2019. We focused on quantitative studies that reported positive, negative, or intermediate changes in patient safety outcomes using AI apps, specifically those based on machine-learning algorithms and natural language processing.
papers.method: Quantitative studies reporting only AI performance but not its influence on patient safety outcomes were excluded from further review.ResultsWe identified 53 eligible studies, which were summarized concerning their patient safety subcategories, the most frequently used AI, and reported performance metrics. Recognized safety subcategories were clinical alarms (n=9; mainly based on decision tree models), clinical reports (n=21; based on support vector machine models), and drug safety (n=23; mainly based on decision tree models).
papers.result: Analysis of these 53 studies also identified two essential findings: (1) the lack of a standardized benchmark and (2) heterogeneity in AI reporting.ConclusionsThis systematic review indicates that AI-enabled decision support systems, when implemented correctly, can aid in enhancing patient safety by improving error detection, patient stratification, and drug management. Future work is still needed for robust validation of these systems in prospective and real-world clinical environments to understand how well AI can predict safety outcomes in health care settings.
papers.gap: Lack of standardised safety benchmarks and reporting.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched three databases for ten years of studies that measured how AI actually changed patient safety outcomes, not just model accuracy, and analysed 53 such studies. They found promising effects but no common benchmark and inconsistent reporting. This supports the PhD's emphasis on measuring safety outcomes such as missed escalations and on transparent, standard reporting.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic literature review following PRISMA, protocol registered on OSF 15 September 2019 (Stevens Institute of Technology, USA).
papers.datasets: PubMed, PubMed Central and Web of Science, English, January 2009 to August 2019; 53 quantitative studies included.
papers.preprocessing: Librarian-assisted MeSH-based Boolean search; studies reporting only AI performance without patient safety outcomes excluded.
papers.modelDetails: Synthesis of quantitative studies using ML or NLP applications that reported positive, negative or intermediate changes in clinical-level patient safety outcomes (e.g. adverse drug events, falls, pressure ulcers, sepsis, clinical deterioration).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Categorisation by safety outcome, AI type and data source; assessment of reporting standards.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: AI applications showed potential to improve safety outcomes, but there was no standardised benchmark and AI reporting was heterogeneous, limiting comparison and evidence of real clinical impact.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence related safety issues associated with FDA medical device reports
papers.authors: Handley JL, Krevat SA, Fong A, Ratwani RM
papers.aim: The Biden 2023 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Executive Order calls for the creation of a patient safety program. Patient safety reports are a natural starting point for identifying issues.
papers.method: We examined the feasibility of this approach by analyzing reports associated with AI/Machine Learning (ML)-enabled medical devices.
papers.result: Of the 429 reports reviewed, 108 (25.2%) were potentially AI/ML related, with 148 (34.5%) containing insufficient information to determine an AI/ML contribution. A more comprehensive approach is needed.
papers.gap: Report data too sparse for causal attribution.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Reliance on voluntary and mandatory reports; name-matching may miss events.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team matched the FDA's list of AI-enabled devices to the national device adverse-event database and read each report to judge whether AI could have contributed. A quarter could have, but a third did not contain enough detail to tell. This shows the need for better AI incident logging, supporting the PhD's audit trail and post-deployment monitoring design.
papers.studyDesign: Brief communication: retrospective analysis of FDA MAUDE adverse event reports (MedStar Health National Center for Human Factors in Healthcare, USA).
papers.datasets: 429 MAUDE reports matched to FDA-listed AI/ML-enabled medical devices up to 18 October 2023.
papers.preprocessing: Device brand, generic and manufacturer names matched to MAUDE via the openFDA Elasticsearch API (exact or partial match); reports reviewed manually.
papers.modelDetails: Human-factors content review classifying each report as potentially AI/ML-related, not related, or insufficient information.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Proportion of reports with possible AI/ML contribution to safety events.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: 108 of 429 reports (25.2%) were potentially AI/ML related and 148 (34.5%) lacked enough information to judge an AI/ML contribution; current reporting is insufficient for AI safety surveillance.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare: transforming patient safety with intelligent systems-A systematic review
papers.authors: De Micco F, Di Palma G, Ferorelli D, De Benedictis A, Tomassini L, Tambone V, Cingolani M, Scendoni R
papers.aim: IntroductionAdverse events in hospitals significantly compromise patient safety and trust in healthcare systems, with medical errors being a leading cause of death globally. Despite efforts to reduce these errors, reporting remains low, and effective system changes are rare.
papers.method: This systematic review explores the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical risk management.MethodsThe systematic review was conducted using the PRISMA Statement 2020 guidelines to ensure a comprehensive and transparent approach. We utilized the online tool Rayyan for efficient screening and selection of relevant studies from three different online bibliographic.ResultsAI systems, including machine learning and natural language processing, show promise in detecting adverse events, predicting medication errors, assessing fall risks, and preventing pressure injuries. Studies reveal that AI can improve incident reporting accuracy, identify high-risk incidents, and automate classification processes.
papers.result: However, challenges such as socio-technical issues, implementation barriers, and the need for standardization persist.DiscussionThe review highlights the effectiveness of AI in various applications but underscores the necessity for further research to ensure safe and consistent integration into clinical practices. Future directions involve refining AI tools through continuous feedback and addressing regulatory standards to enhance patient safety and care quality.
papers.gap: Few implementation studies; heterogeneous outcomes.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched three databases for studies in which AI was actually tested to prevent adverse events, screened them with set criteria, and grouped the evidence by the kind of harm addressed. AI looks promising for risk prediction and prevention, but implementation and standardisation remain problems. It frames the PhD's escalation system as a clinical risk-management tool whose safety benefit must be demonstrated.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review following PRISMA-DTA guidance (Università Campus Bio-Medico di Roma and University of Macerata, Italy).
papers.datasets: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science searched February 2024: 662 records, 489 after de-duplication, 68 initially included and further screened (16 excluded at full review).
papers.preprocessing: Search string combining risk management/clinical governance, patient safety/quality and AI/ML/DL terms; Rayyan for screening; five inclusion criteria (AI system, healthcare, clinical risk management, active experimentation results, prevention of adverse events).
papers.modelDetails: Synthesis of AI applications in clinical risk management grouped by adverse event type (e.g. medication errors, falls, infections, diagnostic errors, surgical complications).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative and descriptive synthesis of reported effectiveness in preventing adverse events.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: AI shows potential to predict and prevent adverse events and support risk management, but socio-technical issues, implementation barriers and lack of standardisation persist.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Patient Safety and Surgical Education in Neurosurgery
papers.authors: Sugiyama T, Sugimori H, Tang M, Fujimura M
papers.aim: Neurosurgery has evolved alongside technological innovations; however, these advances have also introduced greater complexity into clinical practice. Neurosurgery remains a demanding and high-risk field that requires a broad range of skills.
papers.method: Artificial intelligence (AI) has immense potential in neurosurgery given its ability to rapidly analyze large volumes of clinical data generated in modern clinical environments. An expanding body of literature has demonstrated that AI enhances various aspects of neurosurgery, including diagnostics, prognostication, decision-making, data management, education, and clinical studies. AI applications are expected to reduce medical errors and costs, broaden healthcare accessibility, and ultimately boost patient safety and surgical education.
papers.result: Nevertheless, AI application in neurosurgery remains practically limited because of several challenges, such as the diversity and volume of clinical training data collection, concerns regarding data quality, algorithmic bias, transparency (explainability and interpretability), ethical issues, and regulatory implications. To comprehensively discuss the potential benefits, future directions, and limitations of AI in neurosurgery, this review examined recent studies on AI technology and its applications in this field, focusing on intraoperative decision support and surgical education.
papers.gap: No systematic method; few prospective validations.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors review how AI, especially computer vision on surgical video, can improve neurosurgical safety and training, for example by assessing microsurgical skill and analysing operations. They note that preventable technical errors are common in neurosurgery and that data and transparency problems limit adoption. It supports the patient-safety motivation and surgical-planning use case of the PhD.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (Hokkaido University, Japan) in JMA Journal.
papers.datasets: Recent studies on AI in neurosurgery related to patient safety and surgical education.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis of ML, deep learning and computer vision applications: diagnosis and outcome prediction, intra-operative video analysis, instrument tracking, microsurgical skill assessment and surgical education.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: AI can reduce errors and costs, broaden access and improve safety and training in neurosurgery, where about 25% of adverse events are attributed to preventable technical errors; practical use remains limited by data volume and diversity, quality, algorithmic bias, explainability, ethics and regulation.

papers.title: Evaluation of a Deep Learning and XAI based Facial Phenotyping Tool for Genetic Syndromes: A Clinical User Study
papers.authors: Sümer Ö, Huber T, Duong D, Ledgister Hanchard SE, Conati C, André E, Solomon BD, Waikel RL
papers.venue: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
papers.aim: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly employed in clinical genetics to assist in diagnosing genetic conditions by assessing photographs of patients. For medical uses of AI, explainable AI (XAI) methods offer a promising approach by providing interpretable outputs, such as saliency maps and region relevance visualizations.
papers.method: XAI has been discussed as important for regulatory purposes and to enable clinicians to better understand how AI tools work in practice. However, the real-world effects of XAI on clinician performance, confidence, and trust remain underexplored. This study involved a web-based user experiment with 31 medical geneticists to assess the impact of AI-only diagnostic assistance compared to XAI-supported diagnostics. Participants were randomly assigned to either group and completed diagnostic tasks with 18 facial images of individuals with known genetic syndromes and unaffected individuals, before and after experiencing the AI outputs. The results show that both AI-only and XAI approaches improved diagnostic accuracy and clinician confidence. The effects varied according to the accuracy of AI predictions and the clarity of syndromic features (sample difficulty). While AI support was viewed positively, users approached XAI with skepticism. Interestingly, we found a positive correlation between diagnostic improvement and XAI intervention.
papers.result: Although XAI support did not significantly enhance overall performance relative to AI alone, it prompted users to critically evaluate images with false predictions and influenced their confidence levels. These findings highlight the complexities of trust, perceived usefulness, and interpretability in AI-assisted diagnostics, with important implications for developing and implementing clinical decision-support tools in facial phenotyping for rare genetic diseases.
papers.gap: Small sample; no calibrated uncertainty shown.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Preprint; public images may differ from clinical photos.
papers.methodologyDetail: Medical geneticists diagnosed syndromes from face photos, then revised their answers after seeing either AI probabilities alone or probabilities with saliency-based explanations. Explanations did not raise overall accuracy but made users more critical when the AI was wrong. This supports the PhD's view that explanations help users question AI but need to be paired with calibrated confidence to improve accuracy.
papers.studyDesign: Clinical user study with randomised AI-only versus XAI groups (University of Augsburg, TH Ingolstadt, NHGRI/NIH, UBC); medRxiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Publicly available facial images of individuals with 22q11.2 deletion, Angelman, Kabuki, Noonan and Williams syndromes plus unaffected controls; medical geneticists as participants.
papers.preprocessing: Image selection from prior work; participants first diagnosed unaided, then saw AI output (pre/post design).
papers.modelDetails: ResNet-50 CNN classifying face images into five syndromes or unaffected, with probabilities; XAI group additionally saw DeepLIFT saliency maps and region relevance scores.
papers.training: CNN trained as in earlier work (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Prediction improvement after AI or XAI support, stratified by whether the AI was correct; user perceptions.
papers.baselines: AI-only output (probabilities without explanation); unaided performance.
papers.results: Mean improvement 0.031 ± 0.129 for XAI vs 0.056 ± 0.11 for AI-only (not significantly different); when AI was correct AI-only improved more (0.190 vs 0.146); XAI prompted users to critically evaluate images when the AI was wrong.
papers.statistics: Group comparisons of prediction improvement with significance testing.

papers.title: Reducing the workload of medical diagnosis through artificial intelligence: A narrative review
papers.authors: Jeong J, Kim S, Pan L, Hwang D, Kim D, Choi J, Kwon Y, Yi P, Jeong J, Yoo SJ
papers.aim: Artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized medical diagnostics by enhancing efficiency, improving accuracy, and reducing variability. By alleviating the workload of medical staff, AI addresses challenges such as increasing diagnostic demands, workforce shortages, and reliance on subjective interpretation.
papers.method: This review examines the role of AI in reducing diagnostic workload and enhancing efficiency across medical fields from January 2019 to February 2024, identifying limitations and areas for improvement. A comprehensive PubMed search using the keywords “artificial intelligence” or “AI,” “efficiency” or “workload,” and “patient” or “clinical” identified 2587 articles, of which 51 were reviewed. These studies analyzed the impact of AI on radiology, pathology, and other specialties, focusing on efficiency, accuracy, and workload reduction. The final 51 articles were categorized into 4 groups based on diagnostic efficiency, where category A included studies with supporting material provided, category B consisted of those with reduced data volume, category C focused on independent AI diagnosis, and category D included studies that reported data reduction without changes in diagnostic time. In radiology and pathology, which require skilled techniques and large-scale data processing, AI improved accuracy and reduced diagnostic time by approximately 90% or more. Radiology, in particular, showed a high proportion of category C studies, as digitized data and standardized protocols facilitated independent AI diagnoses. AI has significant potential to optimize workload management, improve diagnostic efficiency, and enhance accuracy.
