papers.result: However, challenges remain in standardizing applications and addressing ethical concerns. Integrating AI into healthcare workforce planning is essential for fostering collaboration between technology and clinicians, ultimately improving patient care.
papers.gap: Mostly retrospective, heterogeneous efficiency measures.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched PubMed for five years of studies measuring how AI changes diagnostic time or workload and sorted 51 studies into four types according to how AI saves effort. Most reported large time savings, especially when AI pre-screens or highlights findings. This evidence supports the PhD's workload hypothesis and the use of time and workload measures in its evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review with structured PubMed search (Korean authors) in Medicine.
papers.datasets: PubMed search January 2019 to February 2024 with terms for AI, efficiency/workload and patient/clinical: 2,587 articles, 51 reviewed.
papers.preprocessing: Screening for studies quantifying diagnostic efficiency changes.
papers.modelDetails: Classification of studies into four categories (A-D) by efficiency mechanism: supporting material for clinicians' decisions, AI triage or pre-screening, AI replacing a reading step, and reduction of data volume/workload.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Reported percentage reductions in diagnosis time or workload, by specialty (radiology, pathology, gastroenterology, haematology, others).
papers.baselines: Conventional unaided workflows in included studies.
papers.results: AI reduced diagnosis time substantially across specialties (e.g. 22-99% reductions in radiology; 39.6% workload reduction in DBT screening), though standardisation of applications and ethical concerns remain challenges.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence as triage in breast screening: simulated impact on workload and detection
papers.authors: Riccardi MT, Nurchis MC, Savoia C, Gigli S, Marotta D, Di Lullo F, Damiani G, Pettinicchio V
papers.venue: The European Journal of Public Health
papers.aim: AbstractBackgroundArtificial intelligence(AI) is increasingly proposed as a triage tool in mammography screening to reduce double reading workload. However, its impact on cancer detection and screening performance remains uncertain.
papers.method: Within a project funded by the Italian Ministry of Health on the evaluation of AI in mammography screening, this study evaluated, through simulation, the impact of AI-based triage in a population-based screening programme.MethodsA retrospective simulation was conducted on the 2025 cohort of the largest Italian Local Health Unit. AI scores (Lunit INSIGHT) were analysed using a predefined threshold(2.9).Exams below threshold were considered for single reading. Outcomes included workload reduction and potential missed cancers compared with standard double reading.ResultsAmong 38,075 mammograms, 4,542(11.9%) had AI scores below threshold. Among those,96% were also negative at double reading, while 201 women were referred to second-level assessment, resulting in 18 cancers. Cancers not identified by AI were predominantly associated with microcalcifications(61%), followed by distortions(22%),opacities(9%) and asymmetries(8%). In the simulated scenario, 4,542 exams would have undergone single reading. Of the 201 recalls,46 cases(concordant positive or symptomatic) would certainly have been recalled, identifying 17 cancers and 2 lesions of uncertain malignant potential. The outcome of discordant cases cannot be predicted; therefore, up to one additional cancer could potentially be missed. Workload reduction was estimated at approximately 5% of annual reading volume.ConclusionsAI-based triage may reduce workload and support sustainability of screening programmes.
papers.result: However, current performance shows limitations in detecting cancers presenting as microcalcifications, with possible implications for diagnostic sensitivity. These findings highlight the need for cautious implementation and careful integration with radiologist interpretation and quality assurance processes.Key messages• AI triage can reduce screening workload but introduces uncertainty in cancer detection.• Careful AI evaluation is needed to ensure safe and sustainable integration in breast screening workflow.
papers.gap: Simulation only; threshold not optimised.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a year of real screening data, the authors simulated sending mammograms with low AI scores to a single reader instead of two and counted the reading saved and the cancers that might be missed. Workload fell only modestly and some cancers with microcalcifications scored low. This shows that a triage threshold must be set with care and checked for systematic blind spots, which is central to the PhD's escalation threshold design.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective simulation study (conference abstract) in a population-based screening programme (Local Health Unit Roma 2 and Università Cattolica, Italy), funded by the Italian Ministry of Health.
papers.datasets: 38,075 screening mammograms from the 2025 cohort of the largest Italian Local Health Unit.
papers.preprocessing: AI scores compared with a predefined threshold (2.9); exams below threshold assigned to simulated single reading.
papers.modelDetails: Lunit INSIGHT MMG AI score used as triage: below-threshold exams single-read, others double-read.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial AI).
papers.evaluation: Workload reduction and potentially missed cancers versus standard double reading; characteristics of AI-missed cancers.
papers.baselines: Standard double reading.
papers.results: 4,542 exams (11.9%) below threshold; 96% of these were negative at double reading, 201 recalled with 18 cancers; up to one extra cancer could be missed; workload reduction about 5% of annual reading volume; AI-missed cancers mainly microcalcifications (61%), distortions (22%).

papers.title: Can we reduce the workload of mammographic screening by automatic identification of normal exams with artificial intelligence? A feasibility study
papers.authors: Rodriguez-Ruiz A, Lång K, Gubern-Merida A, Teuwen J, Broeders M, Gennaro G, Clauser P, Helbich TH, Chevalier M, Mertelmeier T, et al.
papers.aim: PurposeTo study the feasibility of automatically identifying normal digital mammography (DM) exams with artificial intelligence (AI) to reduce the breast cancer screening reading workload.Methods and materialsA total of 2652 DM exams (653 cancer) and interpretations by 101 radiologists were gathered from nine previously performed multi-reader multi-case receiver operating characteristic (MRMC ROC) studies. An AI system was used to obtain a score between 1 and 10 for each exam, representing the likelihood of cancer present.
papers.method: Using all AI scores between 1 and 9 as possible thresholds, the exams were divided into groups of low- and high likelihood of cancer present. It was assumed that, under the pre-selection scenario, only the high-likelihood group would be read by radiologists, while all low-likelihood exams would be reported as normal. The area under the reader-averaged ROC curve (AUC) was calculated for the original evaluations and for the pre-selection scenarios and compared using a non-inferiority hypothesis.ResultsSetting the low/high-likelihood threshold at an AI score of 5 (high likelihood > 5) results in a trade-off of approximately halving (− 47%) the workload to be read by radiologists while excluding 7% of true-positive exams.
papers.result: Using an AI score of 2 as threshold yields a workload reduction of 17% while only excluding 1% of true-positive exams. Pre-selection did not change the average AUC of radiologists (inferior 95% CI > − 0.05) for any threshold except at the extreme AI score of 9.ConclusionIt is possible to automatically pre-select exams using AI to significantly reduce the breast cancer screening reading workload.Key Points • There is potential to use artificial intelligence to automatically reduce the breast cancer screening reading workload by excluding exams with a low likelihood of cancer. • The exclusion of exams with the lowest likelihood of cancer in screening might not change radiologists’ breast cancer detection performance. • When excluding exams with the lowest likelihood of cancer, the decrease in true-positive recalls would be balanced by a simultaneous reduction in false-positive recalls.
papers.gap: Enriched data; not prospective screening.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using exams and radiologist reads from nine earlier reader studies, the team scored each mammogram with an AI and tested every possible cut-off for removing low-risk exams from human reading. A low cut-off cut workload by about a sixth while losing very few cancers. This threshold-sweep method is a direct template for choosing the PhD's escalation threshold by trading workload against missed cases.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multicentre feasibility study (Radboud University Medical Center and international partners) in European Radiology.
papers.datasets: 2,652 digital mammography exams (653 cancers, 768 benign, 1,233 normal) from nine previous MRMC ROC studies, with 28,296 interpretations by 101 radiologists (USA and Europe); four vendors, seven countries.
papers.preprocessing: Ground truth from histopathology and/or at least one year follow-up; enriched datasets; anonymised data with ethics waivers.
papers.modelDetails: Transpara 1.4.0 deep learning CNN AI system assigning a 1-10 cancer-likelihood score; thresholds 1-9 tested to exclude low-score exams from radiologist reading.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial AI).
papers.evaluation: Workload reduction and proportion of excluded true-positive exams at each threshold; effect of pre-selection on radiologists' simulated performance (AUC).
papers.baselines: All exams read by radiologists.
papers.results: 72.5% of cancers scored 10 and 95.1% scored 5-10; threshold of 2 gave 17% workload reduction excluding only 1% of true-positive exams; pre-selection did not change radiologists' performance; higher thresholds traded more workload savings for more missed cancers.

papers.title: Diagnostic capabilities of artificial intelligence as an additional reader in a breast cancer screening program
papers.authors: Seker ME, Koyluoglu YO, Ozaydin AN, Gurdal SO, Ozcinar B, Cabioglu N, Ozmen V, Aribal E
papers.aim: ObjectivesWe aimed to evaluate the early-detection capabilities of AI in a screening program over its duration, with a specific focus on the detection of interval cancers, the early detection of cancers with the assistance of AI from prior visits, and its impact on workload for various reading scenarios.Materials and methodsThe study included 22,621 mammograms of 8825 women within a 10-year biennial two-reader screening program. The statistical analysis focused on 5136 mammograms from 4282 women due to data retrieval issues, among whom 105 were diagnosed with breast cancer.
papers.method: The AI software assigned scores from 1 to 100. Histopathology results determined the ground truth, and Youden’s index was used to establish a threshold. Tumor characteristics were analyzed with ANOVA and chi-squared test, and different workflow scenarios were evaluated using bootstrapping.ResultsThe AI software achieved an AUC of 89.6% (86.1–93.2%, 95% CI). The optimal threshold was 30.44, yielding 72.38% sensitivity and 92.86% specificity. Initially, AI identified 57 screening-detected cancers (83.82%), 15 interval cancers (51.72%), and 4 missed cancers (50%). AI as a second reader could have led to earlier diagnosis in 24 patients (average 29.92 ± 19.67 months earlier). No significant differences were found in cancer-characteristics groups.
papers.result: A hybrid triage workflow scenario showed a potential 69.5% reduction in workload and a 30.5% increase in accuracy.ConclusionThis AI system exhibits high sensitivity and specificity in screening mammograms, effectively identifying interval and missed cancers and identifying 23% of cancers earlier in prior mammograms. Adopting AI as a triage mechanism has the potential to reduce workload by nearly 70%.Clinical relevance statementThe study proposes a more efficient method for screening programs, both in terms of workload and accuracy.Key Points • Incorporating AI as a triage tool in screening workflow improves sensitivity (72.38%) and specificity (92.86%), enhancing detection rates for interval and missed cancers. • AI-assisted triaging is effective in differentiating low and high-risk cases, reduces radiologist workload, and potentially enables broader screening coverage. • AI has the potential to facilitate early diagnosis compared to human reading.
papers.gap: Retrospective simulation; single institution.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Small cancer numbers; Youden threshold not clinically tuned.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team scored screening mammograms and the earlier mammograms of women later diagnosed with cancer using an AI system, chose a threshold from the ROC curve, and simulated a workflow in which AI triages exams. AI could have flagged some cancers a round earlier and greatly reduced reading workload in the hybrid scenario. This supports using a data-driven threshold for routing cases between AI and humans, as in the PhD's escalation design.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective observational single-institution study of AI as an additional reader in a population screening programme (Acibadem and partner universities, Istanbul, Turkey).
papers.datasets: Screening mammograms from a Turkish breast screening programme: 4,893 negative exams and exams of 105 cancer patients, plus 138 prior mammograms of these patients.
papers.preprocessing: Ground truth from histopathology; analysis of current and prior screening rounds; subgroup factors (density, tumour size, mass/calcification type, stage, molecular subtype).
papers.modelDetails: Commercial AI software assigning risk scores 1-100; Youden-index threshold for cancer identification; simulated hybrid triage workflow.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial AI).
papers.evaluation: ROC AUC, sensitivity, specificity at threshold, detection of cancers on prior (earlier) mammograms, workload and accuracy in hybrid triage scenario.
papers.baselines: Radiologist screening reads.
papers.results: AUC 89.6% (95% CI 86.1-93.2); threshold score 30.44 gave sensitivity 72.38% and specificity 92.86%; AI flagged 35 prior mammograms of 24 cancer patients (earlier detection); hybrid triage scenario showed potential 69.5% workload reduction and 30.5% accuracy increase.
papers.statistics: ROC analysis, Youden's index, Kolmogorov-Smirnov normality tests and group comparisons in R 4.1.0.

papers.title: Current practical experience with artificial intelligence in clinical radiology: a survey of the European Society of Radiology
papers.authors: European Society of Radiology (ESR)
papers.aim: A survey among the members of European Society of Radiology (ESR) was conducted regarding the current practical clinical experience of radiologists with Artificial Intelligence (AI)-powered tools. 690 radiologists completed the survey. Among these were 276 radiologists from 229 institutions in 32 countries who had practical clinical experience with an AI-based algorithm and formed the basis of this study.
papers.method: The respondents with clinical AI experience included 143 radiologists (52%) from academic institutions, 102 radiologists (37%) from regional hospitals, and 31 radiologists (11%) from private practice. The use case scenarios of the AI algorithm were mainly related to diagnostic interpretation, image post-processing, and prioritisation of workflow. Technical difficulties with integration of AI-based tools into the workflow were experienced by only 49 respondents (17.8%). Of 185 radiologists who used AI-based algorithms for diagnostic purposes, 140 (75.7%) considered the results of the algorithms generally reliable. The use of a diagnostic algorithm was mentioned in the report by 64 respondents (34.6%) and disclosed to patients by 32 (17.3%). Only 42 (22.7%) experienced a significant reduction of their workload, whereas 129 (69.8%) found that there was no such effect. Of 111 respondents who used AI-based algorithms for clinical workflow prioritisation, 26 (23.4%) considered algorithms to be very helpful for reducing the workload of the medical staff whereas the others found them only moderately helpful (62.2%) or not helpful at all (14.4%).
papers.result: Only 92 (13.3%) of the total 690 respondents indicated that they had intentions to acquire AI tools. In summary, although the assistance of AI algorithms was found to be reliable for different use case scenarios, the majority of radiologists experienced no reduction of practical clinical workload.
papers.gap: Low response rate; self-reported experience.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: European radiologists were asked about their real clinical experience with certified AI tools, including how well they integrate, how reliable they seem and whether they save time. Most users found results reliable, but workload savings were rare and few planned to buy AI. This tempers expectations and shows the PhD should measure real workload effects rather than assume them.
papers.studyDesign: Online survey of European Society of Radiology members by the ESR eHealth and Informatics Subcommittee.
papers.datasets: 690 radiologist respondents from 44 countries (response rate 2.5%); 276 with practical clinical AI experience from 229 institutions in 32 countries (52% academic, 37% regional hospitals, 11% private practice).
papers.preprocessing: Brief questionnaire stating answers should reflect clinical routine, not research use.
papers.modelDetails: Questions on certified AI algorithms used, integration difficulties, use cases (diagnostic interpretation, post-processing, prioritisation), confidence in performance, quality control, communication to patients and reports, and workload effect.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Descriptive frequencies of responses.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Main uses were diagnostic interpretation, post-processing and prioritisation; integration problems reported by 17.8%; 75.7% of diagnostic users found results generally reliable; few reported workload reduction; only 13.3% of all respondents intended to acquire AI tools.

papers.title: Constrained-Spherical Deconvolution Tractography in the Evaluation of the Corticospinal Tract in Glioma Surgery
papers.authors: Sheng Z, Yu J, Chen Z, Sun Y, Bu X, Wang M, Sarica C, Hernesniemi J, Nelson BJ, Zemmar A, et al.
papers.aim: Introduction: Tractography has demonstrated utility for surgical resection in the setting of primary brain tumors involving eloquent white matter (WM) pathways.Methods: Twelve patients with glioma in or near eloquent motor areas were analyzed. The motor status was recorded before and after surgery.
papers.method: Two different tractography approaches were used to generate the motor corticospinal tract (CST): Constrained spherical deconvolution probabilistic tractography (CSD-Prob) and single tensor deterministic tractography (Tens-DET). To define the degree of disruption of the CST after surgical resection of the tumor, we calculated the percentage of the CST affected by surgical resection, which was then correlated with the postoperative motor status. Moreover, the fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), axial diffusivity (AD), and radial diffusivity (RD) of the CST generated by the CSD-Prob and the Tens-DET was measured and compared between the ipsilesional and contralesional side.Results: The CST was identified in all patients and its trajectory was displaced by the tumor. Only the CSD-Prob approach showed the CST with the characteristic fan-like projections from the precentral gyrus to the brainstem. Disruption of the CST was identified in 6/6 with postoperative motor deficit by CSD-Prob approach and in 5/6 in the Tens-DET. The degree of disruption was significantly associated with the motor deficit with the CSD-Prob approach (rho = −0.88, p = 0.021). However, with the Tens-DET approach the CST disruption did not show significant association with the motor function (rho = −0.27, p = 0.6).
papers.result: There was a significant decrease in FA (p = 0.006) and a significant increase in MD (p = 0.0004) and RD (p = 0.005) on the ipsilesional CST compared with the contralesional CST only with the CSD-Prob approach.Conclusion: CSD-Prob accurately represented the known anatomy of the CST and provided a meaningful estimate of microstructural changes of the CST affected by the tumor and its macrostructural damage after surgery. Newer surgical planning stations should include advanced models and algorithms of tractography in order to obtain more meaningful reconstructions of the WM pathways during glioma surgery.
papers.gap: Very small sample; no validation with stimulation mapping.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Retrospective; selection excluded brain shift cases.
papers.methodologyDetail: In twelve glioma patients, the team reconstructed the motor pathway with an advanced probabilistic method and a standard tensor method, compared how each showed the tract around the tumour, and related tract injury after surgery to motor outcome. The advanced method gave a more complete tract, which matters for planning safe resections. This supports using advanced tractography inputs in the PhD's surgical-planning demonstrator.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective methodological imaging study (Henan Provincial People's Hospital, China, with Toronto and ETH Zurich partners); ethics approved, consent obtained.
papers.datasets: 12 of 53 glioma patients operated January 2017 to January 2019 (4 WHO grade II, 8 GBM; mean age 50) with tumours in or near motor areas and mild or no motor deficit; 3T Siemens MRI pre- and postoperatively (within 2 days).
papers.preprocessing: Exclusion of significant brain shift or oedema; co-registration of pre- and postoperative T1-gadolinium and diffusion images; extent of resection (GTR > 90%) and permanent motor deficit (MRC scale at ~2 months) recorded.
papers.modelDetails: Two tractography approaches for the corticospinal tract: constrained spherical deconvolution probabilistic (CSD-Prob) versus tensor-based deterministic (Tens-DET); diffusion metrics (FA, MD, RD) along ipsilesional and contralesional CST.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: CST reconstruction pattern and displacement; overlap of resection cavity with CST; diffusion metric differences; relation to postoperative motor outcome.
papers.baselines: Tensor-based deterministic tractography.
papers.results: CST identified in all patients by both methods; CSD-Prob showed the anatomically expected fan-shaped tract while Tens-DET showed a narrow straight path missing lateral fibres; ipsilesional CST had lower FA (p = 0.006) and higher MD (p = 0.0004) and RD (p = 0.005); cavity-CST overlap related to permanent deficits.

papers.title: Tractography for Subcortical Resection of Gliomas Is Highly Accurate for Motor and Language Function: ioMRI-Based Elastic Fusion Disproves the Severity of Brain Shift
papers.authors: Ille S, Schwendner M, Zhang W, Schroeder A, Meyer B, Krieg SM
papers.aim: Simple SummaryTractography enables the visualization of eloquent white matter pathways. Inaccuracies due to brain shift might occur intraoperatively.
papers.method: The aim of this study was to evaluate the impact of intraoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based elastic fusion on preoperative tractography for subcortical resection of gliomas. We confirmed the high accuracy of tractography during the whole course of surgery.AbstractWhen using preoperative tractography intraoperatively, inaccuracies due to brain shift might occur. Intraoperative tractography is rarely performed. Elastic fusion (EF) is a tool developed to compensate for brain shift, gravity, and tissue resection based on intraoperative images. Our hypothesis was that preoperative tractography is accurate and adjustments of tractography by intraoperative magnetic resonance imaging (ioMRI)-based EF (IBEF) compensate for brain shift. Between February 2018 and June 2019, 78 patients underwent eloquent (46 motor, 32 language) glioma resection in our department using intraoperative MRI. Mean distances between the resection cavity and tractography were analyzed and correlated with clinical outcomes. The mean ± standard deviation (range) distance after the application of IBEF was 5.0 ± 2.9 mm (0–10 mm) in patients without surgery-related motor deficits compared with 1.1 ± 1.6 mm (0–5 mm) in patients who showed new permanent surgery-related motor deficits postoperatively (p < 0.001). For language, the distance was 0.7 ± 1.2 mm (0–2 mm) in patients with new permanent deficits compared with 3.1 ± 4.5 mm (0–14 mm) in patients without new permanent surgery-related language deficits (p = 0.541).
papers.result: Preoperative tractography corrected by IBEF for subcortical resection of gliomas is highly accurate. However, at least for such subcortical anatomy, the severity of brain shift was considerably overestimated in the past.
papers.gap: Single centre; specialised nTMS and ioMRI equipment not widely available.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: For glioma patients near motor or language pathways, the team mapped function with magnetic stimulation, built tractography from it, and after resection measured how close the cavity came to the tracts, both before and after correcting for brain shift with intraoperative MRI, relating this to new deficits. Corrected tractography predicted function well. This informs the PhD's surgical-planning proof of concept and the need to account for brain shift.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective cohort study (Technical University of Munich, Germany); ethics 336/17 and 192/18, written consent.
papers.datasets: 78 cases of eloquent gliomas with preoperative nTMS-based fibre tracking and intraoperative MRI: 46 motor tracking, 32 left-hemispheric language tracking (12 awake surgeries).
papers.preprocessing: nTMS used to seed function-based DTI fibre tracking; resection with neuronavigation and continuous MEP monitoring; ioMRI after resection; ioMRI-based elastic fusion (IBEF) to correct preoperative tracts for brain shift.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of distances between resection cavity and preoperative tractography with and without IBEF correction, correlated with new motor and language deficits.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Distance from cavity to tracts; postoperative functional status at different time points; accuracy of tractography for predicting deficits.
papers.baselines: Uncorrected preoperative tractography.
papers.results: Preoperative tractography corrected by IBEF was highly accurate for subcortical resections; brain shift had less effect on tract accuracy than often assumed for such resections.
papers.statistics: Statistical correlation of distance with functional outcome.

papers.title: The Relevant Role of Navigated Tractography in Speech Eloquent Area Glioma Surgery: Single Center Experience
papers.authors: Salvati LF, De Marco R, Palmieri G, Minardi M, Massara A, Pesaresi A, Cagetti B, Melcarne A, Garbossa D
papers.aim: Background: Gliomas are among the most challenging pathologies for neurosurgeons due to their infiltrative and recurrent nature in functionally relevant regions. Current knowledge confirms that gross total resection highly influence survival in patient with glioma.
papers.method: However, surgery performed in eloquent brain area, could seriously compromise the quality of life in patient with reduced life expectancy even more if it concerns the language function. Methods: 18 right-handed patients with perisylvian gliomas on the left hemisphere were prospectively analyzed over a period of 12 months. Standardized preoperative Diffusion-Tensor-Imaging based tractography of the five main language Tracts (Arcuate Fasciculus, Frontal Aslant Tract, Inferior Fronto-Occipital Fasciculus, Inferior Longitudinal Fasciculus, Uncinate Fasciculus) was navigated during the surgical procedure. Using a validated method, correlations were made between the pre-operative fascicles and their possible infiltration and surgical damage. The language status was assessed using the Aachen Aphasia Test. Results: In all nine patients who developed a permanent disorder there was pre-operative involvement of at least one fascicle and resection of at least one of these.
papers.result: In this way, areas of high risk of permanent language damage have emerged as a result of surgical injury: the temporoparietal junction, the middle portion of the FAT and the temporal stem. Conclusions: Navigated tractography has proven to be a user-friendly tool that can assess perioperative risk, guide surgical resection, and help the neurosurgeon to find that balance between tumor resection and function preservation.
papers.gap: Small uncontrolled series.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Eighteen patients with gliomas near language areas had language pathways mapped with tractography and loaded into the navigation system, and their language was tested before surgery, a week after and at three months. The series describes resection extent, outcomes and anatomical zones where damage tends to be permanent. It supports the surgical-planning use case of the PhD, where AI would add to such tractography-based planning.
papers.studyDesign: Prospective observational single-centre study (Department of Neurosurgery, Turin, Italy) over about one year to August 2020; written consent.
papers.datasets: 18 adults (11 women, 7 men; median age 52) with left gliomas near presumed language areas: 13 high-grade, 5 low-grade; 6 awake surgeries.
papers.preprocessing: 3T Philips Ingenia MRI (T1, T2, 3D FLAIR, subtraction); manual tumour segmentation and volumes in Brainlab iPlan; extent of resection from subtraction or FLAIR; language assessed with Italian Aachen Aphasia Test before, within 7 days and at 3 months (4-level aphasia score).
papers.modelDetails: Navigated DTI tractography of language tracts (arcuate, SLF, IFOF, uncinate, etc.) integrated into neuronavigation for resection planning.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Extent of resection (gross total, subtotal, partial), postoperative and 3-month aphasia scores, relation of tumour location and tract involvement to language outcome.
papers.baselines: Not applicable (no control group).
papers.results: Gross total resection in 9 patients, subtotal in 6, partial in 3; areas at high risk of permanent language damage identified (e.g. temporoparietal junction and related regions); navigated tractography supported maximal safe resection.

papers.title: Significance of navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation and tractography to preserve motor function in patients undergoing surgery for motor eloquent gliomas
papers.authors: Eibl T, Schrey M, Liebert A, Ritter L, Lange R, Steiner HH, Schebesch KM
papers.aim: Resection of gliomas in or close to motor areas is at high risk for morbidity and development of surgery-related deficits. Navigated transcranial magnetic stimulation (nTMS) including nTMS-based tractography is suitable for presurgical planning and risk assessment.
papers.method: The aim of this study was to investigate the association of postoperative motor status and the spatial relation to motor eloquent brain tissue in order to increase the understanding of postoperative motor deficits.Patient data, nTMS examinations and imaging studies were retrospectively reviewed, corticospinal tracts (CST) were reconstructed with two different approaches of nTMS-based seeding. Postoperative imaging and nTMS-augmented preoperative imaging were merged to identify the relation between motor positive cortical and subcortical areas and the resection cavity.38 tumor surgeries were performed in 36 glioma patients (28.9% female) aged 55.1 ± 13.8 years. Mean distance between the CST and the lesion was 6.9 ± 5.1 mm at 75% of the patient-individual fractional anisotropy threshold and median tumor volume reduction was 97.7 ± 11.6%. The positive predictive value for permanent deficits after resection of nTMS positive areas was 66.7% and the corresponding negative predictive value was 90.6%.
papers.result: Distances between the resection cavity and the CST were higher in patients with postoperative stable motor function. Extent of resection and distance between resection cavity and CST correlated well.The present study strongly supports preoperative nTMS as an important surgical tool for preserving motor function in glioma patients at risk.
papers.gap: Retrospective; no intraoperative stimulation in all cases.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors reviewed glioma patients whose motor areas and pathways were mapped before surgery with magnetic stimulation and tractography, then measured how close the resection came to the motor tract on postoperative MRI and related this to motor outcome. Keeping a larger distance was linked to preserved function. Such distance-based risk measures are candidate inputs and evaluation endpoints for the PhD's surgical-planning demonstrator.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective cohort study (Paracelsus Medical University Nuremberg, Germany), April 2016 to June 2021; IRB-2020-022 and IRB-2022-012, consent waived.
papers.datasets: Adults with WHO grade 2-4 motor-eloquent gliomas with preoperative nTMS motor mapping and DTI, and pre- and postoperative MRI.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusions: lesion-to-tract distance > 20 mm, postoperative subcortical ischaemia, in-hospital death; 5-ALA fluorescence-guided microsurgery with nTMS data in neuronavigation.
papers.modelDetails: nTMS motor mapping and nTMS-based tractography of the corticospinal tract; measurement of cavity-to-tract distance (CTD) and lesion-to-tract distance on MRI.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Association of postoperative motor status with CTD, extent of resection and nTMS-derived risk factors; positive and negative predictive values.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Distances between resection cavity and CST were larger in patients with stable postoperative motor function; extent of resection and distance-related nTMS measures were associated with motor outcomes.
papers.statistics: Fisher exact and Fisher-Freeman-Halton tests with Cramer's V; Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests; PPV/NPV (SPSS 27).

papers.title: Preoperative tractography algorithm for safe resection of tumors located in the descending motor pathways zone
papers.authors: Ordonez-Rubiano EG, Johnson JM, Abdalá-Vargas N, Zorro OF, Marin-Munoz JH, Álvarez-Tobián R, Forlizzi V, Rangel CC, Luzzi S, Campero A, et al.
papers.aim: Background: Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) tractography facilitates maximal safe resection and optimizes planning to avoid injury during subcortical dissection along descending motor pathways (DMPs). We provide an affordable, safe, and timely algorithm for preoperative DTI motor reconstruction for gliomas adjacent to DMPs.Methods: Preoperative DTI reconstructions were extracted from a prospectively acquired registry of glioma resections adjacent to DMPs.
papers.method: The surgeries were performed over a 7-year period. Demographic, clinical, and radiographic data were extracted from patients’ electronic medical records.Results: Nineteen patients (12 male) underwent preoperative tractography between January 1, 2013, and May 31, 2020. The average age was 44.5 years (range, 19–81 years). A complete radiological resection was achieved in nine patients, a subtotal resection in five, a partial resection in three, and a biopsy in two. Histopathological diagnoses included 10 patients with high-grade glioma and nine with low-grade glioma. A total of 16 perirolandic locations (10 frontal and six frontoparietal) were recorded, as well as two in the insula and one in the basal ganglia. In 9 patients (47.3%), the lesion was in the dominant hemisphere.
papers.result: The median preoperative and postoperative Karnofsky Performance Scores were 78 and 80, respectively. Motor function was unchanged or improved over time in 15 cases (78.9%).Conclusion: This protocol of DTI reconstruction for glioma removal near the DMP shows good results in low-term neurological functional outcomes.
papers.gap: Small uncontrolled series; no intraoperative mapping comparison.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors reviewed glioma patients whose motor pathways were traced before surgery and classified each tract as reduced, displaced, infiltrated or disrupted, using this to plan the resection. Most patients kept or improved motor function. The structured classification of tract involvement is the type of planning information an AI surgical-planning tool in the PhD could support or automate.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective review of a prospectively acquired database at two academic institutions (Hospital de San José, Bogotá, Colombia, with MD Anderson and international co-authors), January 2013 to May 2020; ethics approved.
papers.datasets: 25 glioma patients with DTI fibre tracking and neuronavigation; 19 resections with preoperative tracking of descending motor pathways (12 male; age 19-81, mean 44.5; 10 HGG, 9 LGG).
papers.preprocessing: Tumour location confirmed by neuroradiologist and neurosurgeon; fibre tracking by a dedicated neuroradiologist; extent of resection from ABC/2 volumes (GTR 100%, STR ≥ 90%, partial < 90%).
papers.modelDetails: Preoperative tractography algorithm classifying the relation of descending motor pathways to tumour as volume reduction, displacement (preserved FA), infiltration (reduced FA) or disruption, to guide surgical approach.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Karnofsky Performance Score and motor function before and after surgery; extent of resection.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Descending motor pathways identified bilaterally in all patients; median KPS 78 preoperatively and 80 postoperatively; motor function unchanged or improved in most patients.

papers.title: Emerging paradigms in connectome-guided neurosurgery for central nervous system tumors: a narrative review of structural and functional connectomics
papers.authors: Patel T, Yousuf Ibrahim H, Abbas M, Amir Ali M, Sohrab S, Nawaz K, Zehra SF, Patel BD, Anand N
papers.aim: Connectomics is a comprehensive mapping of structural and functional brain networks. It has introduced a paradigm shift in neurosurgery by redefining brain tumors as network disorders rather than isolated lesions.
papers.method: Unlike traditional surgeries, connectome-guided neurosurgery conceptualizes brain tumors as network disorders and aims to preserve brain function in resection. The objective was to study the role of connectome-guided neurosurgery in the management of Central Nervous System tumors and the use of structural and functional connectomics in tumor resection while preserving neurological function. Articles have been identified by searches of PubMed, Scopus and Google scholar from January 2000 to May 2025, using a combination of search terms like “connectomes,” “neurosurgery,” “central nervous system tumors,” “brain mapping,” “glioma surgery,” “tractography,” “neuroimaging,” “functional MRI,” “brain tumors,” “functional connectomics,” “structural connectomics,” “connectome-guided neurosurgery,” and “artificial intelligence” and addition of relevant references of articles. Included studies addressed both conventional and novel treatments for CNS tumors, including gliomas. Structural (DTI/tractography) and functional (fMRI, MEG, EEG) connectomes support preoperative planning, intraoperative guidance, and postoperative outcomes in CNS tumors. However, to reduce tumor size, a multiphase strategy is proposed by medical professionals, which includes rehabilitation, possible second surgery, and chemotherapy. Limitations of this study include tractography errors, fMRI neurovascular coupling, high costs, limited availability, and barriers to neurosurgeon training.
papers.result: Connectome-guided neurosurgery provides a paradigm shift from lesion-centric to network centric neurosurgery of CNS tumors. Although challenges remain, the use of connectomics with AI, intraoperative, and supramaximal resection strategies provides safe resection, reduces morbidity, and improves quality of life.
papers.gap: Narrative; limited clinical outcome evidence.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched three databases and summarised how mapping brain networks, both structural wiring and functional activity, is changing brain tumour surgery from removing a lesion to protecting networks, and how AI may help. They also list technical limitations. This review frames future extensions of the PhD's surgical-planning component and shows where uncertainty in tractography must be communicated.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review with structured search and dual screening (authors from USA, Pakistan and India) in Annals of Medicine & Surgery.
papers.datasets: PubMed, Scopus and Google Scholar, January 2000 to May 2025, using connectome, neurosurgery, CNS tumour, brain mapping, tractography, fMRI and AI terms.
papers.preprocessing: Two independent reviewers with third-reviewer arbitration; English peer-reviewed studies, trials, meta-analyses and reviews included; abstracts, editorials and animal studies excluded.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative synthesis of structural (DTI/tractography) and functional (fMRI, MEG, EEG) connectomics for preoperative planning, intraoperative guidance, connectome-based predictive modelling and AI integration.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Connectome-guided neurosurgery shifts from lesion-centric to network-centric surgery, supporting function preservation; limitations include tractography errors, fMRI neurovascular uncoupling, cost and lack of standardisation.

papers.title: Tracking the Corticospinal Tract in Patients With High-Grade Glioma: Clinical Evaluation of Multi-Level Fiber Tracking and Comparison to Conventional Deterministic Approaches
papers.authors: Zhylka A, Sollmann N, Kofler F, Radwan A, De Luca A, Gempt J, Wiestler B, Menze B, Krieg SM, Zimmer C, et al.
papers.aim: While the diagnosis of high-grade glioma (HGG) is still associated with a considerably poor prognosis, neurosurgical tumor resection provides an opportunity for prolonged survival and improved quality of life for affected patients. However, successful tumor resection is dependent on a proper surgical planning to avoid surgery-induced functional deficits whilst achieving a maximum extent of resection (EOR).
papers.method: With diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) providing insight into individual white matter neuroanatomy, the challenge remains to disentangle that information as correctly and as completely as possible. In particular, due to the lack of sensitivity and accuracy, the clinical value of widely used diffusion tensor imaging (DTI)-based tractography is increasingly questioned. We evaluated whether the recently developed multi-level fiber tracking (MLFT) technique can improve tractography of the corticospinal tract (CST) in patients with motor-eloquent HGGs. Forty patients with therapy-naïve HGGs (mean age: 62.6 ± 13.4 years, 57.5% males) and preoperative diffusion MRI [repetition time (TR)/echo time (TE): 5000/78 ms, voxel size: 2x2x2 mm3, one volume at b=0 s/mm2, 32 volumes at b=1000 s/mm2] underwent reconstruction of the CST of the tumor-affected and unaffected hemispheres using MLFT in addition to deterministic DTI-based and deterministic constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD)-based fiber tractography. The brain stem was used as a seeding region, with a motor cortex mask serving as a target region for MLFT and a region of interest (ROI) for the other two algorithms. Application of the MLFT method substantially improved bundle reconstruction, leading to CST bundles with higher radial extent compared to the two other algorithms (delineation of CST fanning with a wider range; median radial extent for tumor-affected vs. unaffected hemisphere – DTI: 19.46° vs. 18.99°, p=0.8931; CSD: 30.54° vs. 27.63°, p=0.0546; MLFT: 81.17° vs. 74.59°, p=0.0134).
papers.result: In addition, reconstructions by MLFT and CSD-based tractography nearly completely included respective bundles derived from DTI-based tractography, which was however favorable for MLFT compared to CSD-based tractography (median coverage of the DTI-based CST for affected vs. unaffected hemispheres – CSD: 68.16% vs. 77.59%, p=0.0075; MLFT: 93.09% vs. 95.49%; p=0.0046). Thus, a more complete picture of the CST in patients with motor-eloquent HGGs might be achieved based on routinely acquired diffusion MRI data using MLFT.
papers.gap: No intraoperative stimulation ground truth.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: In forty high-grade glioma patients, the motor tract was reconstructed with a standard tensor method and two advanced methods, and the results were compared visually and by overlap. The advanced methods captured more of the tract, including parts close to the tumour that the standard method missed. This highlights method-dependent uncertainty in tract maps that the PhD's surgical-planning tool should communicate to surgeons.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective clinical evaluation study (Eindhoven University of Technology, Technical University of Munich, KU Leuven, UMC Utrecht); IRB approved, consent waived.
papers.datasets: 40 adults with high-grade glioma in suspected motor-eloquent locations (mean age 62.6; 17 female) with preoperative 3T MRI including diffusion imaging, identified from PACS February 2019 to February 2020.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusion of implant or motion artefacts and prior brain surgery; diffusion preprocessing and registration to anatomical scans.
papers.modelDetails: Three corticospinal tract reconstruction methods: DTI-based deterministic tractography, constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD)-based tractography, and multi-level fibre tracking (MLFT) designed to disentangle crossing and tumour-affected fibres.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative assessment of CST anatomy and tumour contact; quantitative overlap and volume comparison between methods; plausibility of reconstructions.
papers.baselines: Conventional DTI-based deterministic tractography.
papers.results: All methods traced the CST through internal capsule and cerebral crus; MLFT and CSD reconstructed more complete, fan-shaped tracts and almost fully included DTI-derived bundles, while DTI often missed lateral projections; tumour contact detected more often with advanced methods.
papers.statistics: Statistical comparison of overlap and volumes between methods.

papers.title: Standardized evaluation of the extent of resection in glioblastoma with automated early post-operative segmentation
papers.authors: Luque L, Skogen K, MacIntosh BJ, Emblem KE, Larsson C, Bouget D, Helland RH, Reinertsen I, Solheim O, Schellhorn T, et al.
papers.aim: Standard treatment of patients with glioblastoma includes surgical resection of the tumor. The extent of resection (EOR) achieved during surgery significantly impacts prognosis and is used to stratify patients in clinical trials.
papers.method: In this study, we developed a U-Net-based deep-learning model to segment contrast-enhancing tumor on post-operative MRI exams taken within 72 h of resection surgery and used these segmentations to classify the EOR as either maximal or submaximal. The model was trained on 122 multiparametric MRI scans from our institution and achieved a mean Dice score of 0.52 ± 0.03 on an external dataset (n = 248), a performance ­on par with the interrater agreement between expert annotators as reported in literature. We obtained an EOR classification precision/recall of 0.72/0.78 on the internal test dataset (n = 462) and 0.90/0.87 on the external dataset. Furthermore, Kaplan-Meier curves were used to compare the overall survival between patients with maximal and submaximal resection in the internal test dataset, as determined by either clinicians or the model. There was no significant difference between the survival predictions using the model's and clinical EOR classification.
papers.result: We find that the proposed segmentation model is capable of reliably classifying the EOR of glioblastoma tumors on early post-operative MRI scans. Moreover, we show that stratification of patients based on the model's predictions offers at least the same prognostic value as when done by clinicians.
papers.gap: Enhancing tumour only; early postoperative blood products remain challenging.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team trained a U-Net to outline remaining enhancing tumour on MRI scans taken within three days of glioblastoma surgery and tested whether it could judge if resection was complete, on internal and external hospital data. Its judgements matched experts reliably. Automated postoperative assessment like this could provide objective outcome measures for the PhD's surgical-planning evaluation.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective development and external validation study (Oslo University Hospital and St. Olavs/SINTEF Trondheim, Norway).
papers.datasets: Internal cohort of 616 glioblastoma patients operated 2003-2020 with early postoperative MRI (within 72 h: T1w, T1wc, T2w, FLAIR); labelled train/validation subset of 122 exams (87 with 3D sequences, 2016-2020); external dataset of 248 patients from another national institution.
papers.preprocessing: Expert manual segmentation of residual contrast-enhancing tumour; co-registration of sequences; scans differ by manufacturer, field strength and 2D/3D acquisition.
papers.modelDetails: U-Net-based deep learning model segmenting residual contrast-enhancing tumour on early postoperative MRI to classify extent of resection (gross total vs residual).
papers.training: Cross-validation on labelled internal subset (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Segmentation Dice and volume agreement; EOR classification accuracy, sensitivity and specificity versus expert ratings on internal and external data.
papers.baselines: Expert radiologist assessment.
papers.results: Model reliably classified EOR of glioblastoma on early postoperative MRI in both internal and external datasets, comparable to expert raters, supporting standardised EOR evaluation.
papers.availability: Model shared via Raidionics-related tools (details in paper).

papers.title: The effect of editing clinical contours on deep-learning segmentation accuracy of the gross tumor volume in glioblastoma
papers.authors: Hochreuter KM, Ren J, Nijkamp J, Korreman SS, Lukacova S, Kallehauge JF, Trip AK
papers.venue: Physics and imaging in radiation oncology
papers.aim: Background and purposeDeep-learning (DL) models for segmentation of the gross tumor volume (GTV) in radiotherapy are generally based on clinical delineations which suffer from inter-observer variability. The aim of this study was to compare performance of a DL-model based on clinical glioblastoma GTVs to a model based on a single-observer edited version of the same GTVs.Materials and methodsThe dataset included imaging data (Computed Tomography (CT), T1, contrast-T1 (T1C), and fluid-attenuated-inversion-recovery (FLAIR)) of 259 glioblastoma patients treated with post-operative radiotherapy between 2012 and 2019 at a single institute.
papers.method: The clinical GTVs were edited using all imaging data. The dataset was split into 207 cases for training/validation and 52 for testing.GTV segmentation models (nnUNet) were trained on clinical and edited GTVs separately and compared using Surface Dice with 1 mm tolerance (sDSC1mm). We also evaluated model performance with respect to extent of resection (EOR), and different imaging combinations (T1C/T1/FLAIR/CT, T1C/FLAIR/CT, T1C/FLAIR, T1C/CT, T1C/T1, T1C). A Wilcoxon test was used for significance testing.ResultsThe median (range) sDSC1mm of the clinical-GTV-model and edited-GTV-model both evaluated with the edited contours, was 0.76 (0.43–0.94) vs. 0.92 (0.60–0.98) respectively (p < 0.001). sDSC1mm was not significantly different between patients with a biopsy, partial, and complete resection. T1C as single input performed as good as use of imaging combinations.ConclusionsHigh segmentation accuracy was obtained by the DL-models.
papers.result: Editing of the clinical GTVs significantly increased DL performance with a relevant effect size. DL performance was robust for EOR and highly accurate using only T1C.
papers.gap: Single editor; single centre.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Edited labels may encode one observer's bias.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team trained two tumour-contouring models for glioblastoma radiotherapy, one on the original clinical outlines drawn by several oncologists and one on outlines carefully corrected by a single expert, then compared them on matched test sets. Cleaner, consistent labels gave significantly better models. This underlines the PhD's plan for careful clinician annotation protocols when building the Sri Lankan dataset.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective single-centre deep learning study (Danish Centre for Particle Therapy, Aarhus University Hospital, Denmark); approved by the Danish Patient Safety Authority and Danish Neuro-Oncology Registry.
papers.datasets: 406 eligible glioblastoma patients treated with postoperative radiotherapy 2012-2019 identified through DNOR; 292 with complete planning MRI and CT; 259 used (207 training/validation, 52 test).
papers.preprocessing: T1, T1C and FLAIR rigidly registered to planning CT (mutual information, skull ROI); clinical GTVs delineated by at least five oncologists were edited by a single observer using all imaging (tightening, excluding subdural haematoma, including enhancement and cavity).
papers.modelDetails: Deep learning segmentation models trained on clinical GTVs versus single-observer edited GTVs, using T1C/T1/FLAIR/CT inputs; robustness by extent of resection (complete, partial, biopsy).
papers.training: Details in paper (nnU-Net-type training on 207 cases).
papers.evaluation: Surface DSC at 1 mm tolerance, DSC, mean surface distance and HD95; head-to-head comparison of models on clinical and edited test sets; subgroup analysis by EOR.
papers.baselines: Model trained on unedited clinical GTVs.
papers.results: Editing changed GTV volumes slightly (median 0.85 cc; 65% decreased) but significantly improved DL performance with a relevant effect size; performance robust across extent of resection.
papers.statistics: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests in R, significance level 0.01.

papers.title: DeepEOR: automated perioperative volumetric assessment of variable grade gliomas using deep learning
papers.authors: Zanier O, Da Mutten R, Vieli M, Regli L, Serra C, Staartjes VE
papers.aim: PurposeVolumetric assessments, such as extent of resection (EOR) or residual tumor volume, are essential criterions in glioma resection surgery. Our goal is to develop and validate segmentation machine learning models for pre- and postoperative magnetic resonance imaging scans, allowing us to assess the percentagewise tumor reduction after intracranial surgery for gliomas.MethodsFor the development of the preoperative segmentation model (U-Net), MRI scans of 1053 patients from the Multimodal Brain Tumor Segmentation Challenge (BraTS) 2021 as well as from patients who underwent surgery at the University Hospital in Zurich were used.
papers.method: Subsequently, the model was evaluated on a holdout set containing 285 images from the same sources. The postoperative model was developed using 72 scans and validated on 45 scans obtained from the BraTS 2015 and Zurich dataset. Performance is evaluated using Dice Similarity score, Jaccard coefficient and Hausdorff 95%.ResultsWe were able to achieve an overall mean Dice Similarity Score of 0.59 and 0.29 on the pre- and postoperative holdout sets, respectively.
papers.result: Our algorithm managed to determine correct EOR in 44.1%.ConclusionAlthough our models are not suitable for clinical use at this point, the possible applications are vast, going from automated lesion detection to disease progression evaluation. Precise determination of EOR is a challenging task, but we managed to show that deep learning can provide fast and objective estimates.
papers.gap: Small postoperative training set; student labels.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors trained U-Net ensembles on public BraTS and local Zurich scans to outline glioma components before and after surgery and calculate how much tumour was removed. Preoperative segmentation was good, but postoperative segmentation was hard and resection category was correct in fewer than half of cases. This shows that postoperative assessment is a difficult, uncertain task where the PhD's escalation to human review is essential.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective model development and validation study (University Hospital Zurich, Switzerland); Cantonal Ethics Committee Zürich BASEC 2021-01147.
papers.datasets: Preoperative: 1,053 MRI scans from BraTS 2021 training set and Zurich (87 pre-op), holdout 285; postoperative: 72 training and 45 validation scans from BraTS 2015 and Zurich (92 post-op); LGG and HGG.
papers.preprocessing: Zurich images hand-labelled by medical students after expert teaching; segmentation of enhancing tumour (ET), non-enhancing tumour (NET) and whole tumour (WT).
papers.modelDetails: DeepEOR: ensembles of U-Nets for pre- and postoperative segmentation to compute extent of resection and residual tumour volume automatically.
papers.training: Ensemble U-Net training (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Dice and volumetric agreement for ET, NET, WT; accuracy of EOR category against ground truth.
papers.baselines: Manual segmentation.
papers.results: Preoperative segmentation performed well, but postoperative segmentation was weaker and the algorithm determined correct EOR in only 44.1% of cases; not yet suitable for clinical use.

papers.title: Augmented and virtual reality usage in awake craniotomy: a systematic review
papers.authors: Mofatteh M, Mashayekhi MS, Arfaie S, Chen Y, Mirza AB, Fares J, Bandyopadhyay S, Henich E, Liao X, Bernstein M
papers.aim: Augmented and virtual reality (AR, VR) are becoming promising tools in neurosurgery. AR and VR can reduce challenges associated with conventional approaches via the simulation and mimicry of specific environments of choice for surgeons.
papers.method: Awake craniotomy (AC) enables the resection of lesions from eloquent brain areas while monitoring higher cortical and subcortical functions. Evidence suggests that both surgeons and patients benefit from the various applications of AR and VR in AC. This paper investigates the application of AR and VR in AC and assesses its prospective utility in neurosurgery. A systematic review of the literature was performed using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. Our search results yielded 220 articles. A total of six articles consisting of 118 patients have been included in this review. VR was used in four papers, and the other two used AR. Tumour was the most common pathology in 108 patients, followed by vascular lesions in eight patients. VR was used for intraoperative mapping of language, vision, and social cognition, while AR was incorporated in preoperative training of white matter dissection and intraoperative visualisation and navigation. Overall, patients and surgeons were satisfied with the applications of AR and VR in their cases.
papers.result: AR and VR can be safely incorporated during AC to supplement, augment, or even replace conventional approaches in neurosurgery. Future investigations are required to assess the feasibility of AR and VR in various phases of AC.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s10143-022-01929-7.
papers.gap: Very small evidence base; no comparative outcomes.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.limitations: Only six studies from two countries.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors searched three databases for original studies using augmented or virtual reality during awake brain surgery and found six small studies. They describe the devices used and the functions tested, concluding that these tools are safe and can extend intraoperative mapping. It is background for how planning outputs from the PhD's system might eventually be displayed to surgeons.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic review following PRISMA (international authors; senior author University of Toronto).
papers.datasets: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science from inception to 20 May 2022; 6 studies included (4 France, 2 Germany) with 118 patients in total (cohorts 3 to 55; ages 14-81).
papers.preprocessing: Boolean search combining AR/VR/mixed reality terms with awake craniotomy terms; title/abstract and full-text screening; reference-list checking by three authors; English original human studies only.
papers.modelDetails: Data extraction on AR/VR type, hardware and software (e.g. Oculus DK1/DK2, Samsung Gear VR), user (patient or staff), timing (pre-, intra-, postoperative) and mapped function (visual field, optic radiation, language, social cognition).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Narrative synthesis of feasibility, safety and outcomes.
papers.baselines: Conventional awake mapping tasks.
papers.results: AR and VR can be safely incorporated during awake craniotomy to supplement, augment or replace conventional testing, e.g. VR for visual field and social cognition mapping and AR for navigation; evidence is limited to small studies.

papers.title: Augmented reality for intracranial meningioma resection: a mini-review
papers.authors: Gómez Amarillo DF, Ordóñez-Rubiano EG, Ramírez-Sanabria AD, Figueredo LF, Vargas-Osorio MP, Ramon JF, Mejia JA, Hakim F
papers.aim: Augmented reality (AR) integrates computer-generated content and real-world scenarios. Artificial intelligence's continuous development has allowed AR to be integrated into medicine.
papers.method: Neurosurgery has progressively introduced image-guided technologies. Integration of AR into the operating room has permitted a new perception of neurosurgical diseases, not only for neurosurgical planning, patient positioning, and incision design but also for intraoperative maneuvering and identification of critical neurovascular structures and tumor boundaries. Implementing AR, virtual reality, and mixed reality has introduced neurosurgeons into a new era of artificial interfaces. Meningiomas are the most frequent primary benign tumors commonly related to paramount neurovascular structures and bone landmarks.
papers.result: Integration of preoperative 3D reconstructions used for surgical planning into AR can now be inserted into the microsurgical field, injecting information into head-up displays and microscopes with integrated head-up displays, aiming to guide neurosurgeons intraoperatively to prevent potential injuries. This manuscript aims to provide a mini-review of the usage of AR for intracranial meningioma resection.
papers.gap: No systematic method or outcome comparisons.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors review how augmented reality overlays 3D models built from preoperative imaging onto the surgeon's view during meningioma surgery, describing the workflow and its benefits and limits. It shows a route for presenting planning outputs, such as AI segmentations from the PhD's system, directly in the operative field, while noting accuracy problems such as brain shift.
papers.studyDesign: Mini-review (Fundación Santa Fe de Bogotá and partners, Colombia) in Frontiers in Neurology.
papers.datasets: Published literature on augmented reality in intracranial meningioma surgery.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative review of AR workflows: preoperative 3D reconstruction of tumour, vessels and venous sinuses, registration to the patient, and overlay into the operating microscope or head-mounted display for planning and intraoperative guidance.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative.
papers.baselines: Conventional neuronavigation.
papers.results: Integrating preoperative 3D reconstructions into the microsurgical field with AR improves spatial understanding of anatomy for meningioma resection; limitations include registration error, brain shift and cost.

papers.title: Cerebral Anatomy Detection and Surgical Planning in Patients with Anterior Skull Base Meningiomas Using a Virtual Reality Technique
papers.authors: Zawy Alsofy S, Nakamura M, Suleiman A, Sakellaropoulou I, Welzel Saravia H, Shalamberidze D, Salma A, Stroop R
papers.aim: Anterior skull base meningiomas represent a wide cohort of tumors with different locations, extensions, configurations, and anatomical relationships. Diagnosis of these tumors and review of their therapies are inseparably connected with cranial imaging.
papers.method: We analyzed the influence of three-dimensional-virtual reality (3D-VR) reconstructions versus conventional computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images (two-dimensional (2D) and screen 3D) on the identification of anatomical structures and on the surgical planning in patients with anterior skull base meningiomas. Medical files were retrospectively analyzed regarding patient- and disease-related data. Preoperative 2D-CT and 2D-MRI scans were retrospectively reconstructed to 3D-VR images and visualized via VR software to detect the characteristics of tumors. A questionnaire of experienced neurosurgeons evaluated the influence of the VR visualization technique on identification of tumor morphology and relevant anatomy and on surgical strategy. Thirty patients were included and 600 answer sheets were evaluated.
papers.result: The 3D-VR modality significantly influenced the detection of tumor-related anatomical structures (p = 0.002), recommended head positioning (p = 0.005), and surgical approach (p = 0.03). Therefore, the reconstruction of conventional preoperative 2D scans into 3D images and the spatial and anatomical presentation in VR models enabled greater understanding of anatomy and pathology, and thus influenced operation planning and strategy.
papers.gap: Decisions not linked to patient outcomes.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Experienced neurosurgeons planned meningioma operations first from standard scans and, four weeks later, from 3D virtual reality reconstructions of the same patients presented in a different order. VR changed which structures they identified and how they would position the patient and approach the tumour. The within-rater design with washout is a model for testing whether the PhD's planning outputs change surgical decisions.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective within-surgeon comparison study (Witten/Herdecke University and partners, Germany); ethics Ref-Nr. 201/2018.
papers.datasets: Adults with anterior skull base meningiomas operated 2016-2019 with thin-slice CT/CTA and MRI/MRA; experienced board-certified neurosurgeons (not the operating surgeons) as raters.
papers.preprocessing: Exclusions for multimorbidity, other pathologies, prior craniotomy, recurrent or multiple meningiomas; clinical data withheld from raters; 3D-VR reconstructions built from CT/MRI.
papers.modelDetails: Raters reviewed conventional 2D and screen-3D CT/MRI, then four weeks later reconstructed 3D virtual reality (3D-VR) images of the same patients in a different order, completing the same questionnaire on anatomical structures, head positioning and surgical approach.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Detection of tumour-related anatomical structures; recommended positioning and approach; comparison between modalities.
papers.baselines: Conventional 2D and screen-3D imaging.
papers.results: 3D-VR significantly influenced detection of tumour-related anatomical structures (p = 0.002) and recommended head positioning and surgical approach.
papers.statistics: Paired statistical tests comparing questionnaire responses across modalities.

papers.title: Intraoperative Imaging and Optical Visualization Techniques for Brain Tumor Resection: A Narrative Review
papers.authors: Bin-Alamer O, Abou-Al-Shaar H, Gersey ZC, Huq S, Kallos JA, McCarthy DJ, Head JR, Andrews E, Zhang X, Hadjipanayis CG
papers.aim: Simple SummaryBrain tumors are difficult to treat, and surgeons need the best tools to safely remove them. This review looks at the various technologies that help surgeons see tumors more clearly during surgery.
papers.method: These technologies range from special microscopes and exoscopes to advanced imaging like handheld molecular diagnostic tools. While these tools have made surgery safer and more effective, they are not without challenges, such as complex usage and interpretation. Our aim is to present an overview of these technologies, discuss their pros and cons, and look at the future, where artificial intelligence and virtual reality could make these surgeries even more precise. This research could guide future innovations that improve patient outcomes.AbstractAdvancements in intraoperative visualization and imaging techniques are increasingly central to the success and safety of brain tumor surgery, leading to transformative improvements in patient outcomes. This comprehensive review intricately describes the evolution of conventional and emerging technologies for intraoperative imaging, encompassing the surgical microscope, exoscope, Raman spectroscopy, confocal microscopy, fluorescence-guided surgery, intraoperative ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, and computed tomography. We detail how each of these imaging modalities contributes uniquely to the precision, safety, and efficacy of neurosurgical procedures. Despite their substantial benefits, these technologies share common challenges, including difficulties in image interpretation and steep learning curves.
papers.result: Looking forward, innovations in this field are poised to incorporate artificial intelligence, integrated multimodal imaging approaches, and augmented and virtual reality technologies. This rapidly evolving landscape represents fertile ground for future research and technological development, aiming to further elevate surgical precision, safety, and, most critically, patient outcomes in the management of brain tumors.
papers.gap: No systematic evidence grading.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors describe the main tools that help surgeons see brain tumours during surgery, from microscopes and fluorescence to intraoperative MRI and molecular imaging, with their pros and cons. They expect AI to help interpret these data. This gives the PhD context on intraoperative information that a future version of the planning assistant could use.
papers.studyDesign: Narrative review (University of Pittsburgh Medical Center Center for Image-Guided Neurosurgery, USA) in Cancers.
papers.datasets: Literature on intraoperative imaging and optical visualisation for brain tumour resection.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Narrative review of operating microscope, exoscope, Raman spectroscopy, confocal microscopy, fluorescence-guided surgery (5-ALA, fluorescein, ICG), intraoperative ultrasound, MRI and CT.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative comparison of benefits, limitations and evidence.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Each modality improves precision and safety of resection but faces challenges in usage, interpretation and learning curve; future directions include AI, integrated multimodal imaging and VR.

papers.title: Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice Among Chinese Physicians: Nationwide Cross-Sectional Survey Using Extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology and Explainable Machine Learning
papers.authors: Shi X, Tian Z, Guo Q, Qiao B, Wang X
papers.aim: AbstractBackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming clinical practice, yet empirical evidence on Chinese physicians’ acceptance of AI medical tools remains scarce at the national level.ObjectiveThis study aimed to evaluate the current acceptance of AI medical tools among Chinese physicians, identify key determinants, and elucidate underlying mechanisms using an extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and explainable machine learning.MethodsA nationwide cross-sectional survey was conducted from January to April 2024, recruiting 4024 in-service physicians across 29 provincial-level administrative units in China via stratified random sampling. The questionnaire incorporated 5 UTAUT constructs—performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions (FC), and a newly introduced “positive impact” dimension.
papers.method: Psychometric properties were validated through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Structural equation modeling assessed direct and moderated effects, with hospital level, professional title, AI familiarity, and future optimism as moderators. Six classification models were compared for predictive performance; balanced random forest was selected, and model interpretability was evaluated using Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP).ResultsOverall acceptance exceeded 90% across subgroups. Structural equation modeling showed that performance expectancy, social influence, FC, and positive impact significantly and positively predicted physicians’ behavioral intention to use AI medical tools. Six negative moderation effects were identified.
papers.result: The random forest achieved 85.6% accuracy and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.836; SHAP analysis identified organizational support (FC_HospPromoteAI) as the feature with the highest mean absolute SHAP value, though all effect sizes were modest.ConclusionsChinese physicians exhibit high acceptance of AI medical tools, mainly driven by organizational support and perceived clinical benefits. The combined use of extended UTAUT and explainable AI provides actionable insights for targeted AI implementation strategies in health care.
papers.gap: Intentions, not actual use; senior-heavy sample.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Over four thousand Chinese physicians completed a validated questionnaire based on a technology-acceptance model, and the team analysed it both with structural equation modelling and with an explainable machine learning model to see which factors best predict acceptance of AI. Organisational support and expected performance mattered most. The combination of SEM with SHAP is a useful approach for the PhD's acceptance analysis.
papers.studyDesign: Nationwide cross-sectional survey of physicians in mainland China (Shuguang Hospital Shanghai, KINGYEE and Zhejiang University), January-April, distributed via Medlive.
papers.datasets: 4,024 in-service physicians from 29 provinces (77.4% tertiary hospitals; 72.9% senior titles).
papers.preprocessing: Stratified random sampling by province and hospital tier; questionnaire adapted from UTAUT with an added perceived-impact (PI) construct; exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis for psychometric validation.
papers.modelDetails: Extended UTAUT model (performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, perceived impact) tested with structural equation modelling; random forest classifier with SHAP explanations to identify key predictors of acceptance.
papers.training: Random forest trained on survey features (scikit-learn).
papers.evaluation: SEM path coefficients and mediation; random forest accuracy and AUC; SHAP feature importance.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Random forest accuracy 85.6% and AUC 0.836; SHAP identified organisational and expectancy factors (e.g. facilitating conditions, performance expectancy) as key drivers of acceptance; SEM confirmed direct and mediated effects.
