papers.statistics: Paired t-tests; Welch t-tests and Welch ANOVA with Holm adjustment; linear models with HC3 robust standard errors.

papers.title: Dermatologist-like explainable AI enhances trust and confidence in diagnosing melanoma
papers.authors: Tirtha Chanda, Katja Hauser, Sarah Hobelsberger, Tabea-Clara Bucher, Carina Nogueira Garcia, Christoph Wies, Harald Kittler, Philipp Tschandl, Cristian Navarrete-Dechent, Sebastian Podlipnik, et al.
papers.aim: Although artificial intelligence (AI) systems have been shown to improve the accuracy of initial melanoma diagnosis, the lack of transparency in how these systems identify melanoma poses severe obstacles to user acceptance. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods can help to increase transparency, but most XAI methods are unable to produce precisely located domain-specific explanations, making the explanations difficult to interpret.
papers.method: Moreover, the impact of XAI methods on dermatologists has not yet been evaluated. Extending on two existing classifiers, we developed an XAI system that produces text and region based explanations that are easily interpretable by dermatologists alongside its differential diagnoses of melanomas and nevi. To evaluate this system, we conducted a three-part reader study to assess its impact on clinicians' diagnostic accuracy, confidence, and trust in the XAI-support. We showed that our XAI's explanations were highly aligned with clinicians' explanations and that both the clinicians' trust in the support system and their confidence in their diagnoses were significantly increased when using our XAI compared to using a conventional AI system.
papers.result: The clinicians' diagnostic accuracy was numerically, albeit not significantly, increased. This work demonstrates that clinicians are willing to adopt such an XAI system, motivating their future use in the clinic.
papers.gap: Accuracy improvement not significant; trust may be miscalibrated.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team built a melanoma classifier that explains its decision using the same features dermatologists use, checked it was as accurate as a standard model, and then ran a reader study comparing plain AI with the explainable version. Explanations increased clinicians' trust and confidence, though accuracy gains were not significant. This highlights that explanations can raise trust without proven accuracy gains, a risk for over-reliance that the PhD's calibration aims to manage.
papers.studyDesign: Two-phase reader study with preregistered hypotheses (OSF g3keh) and STARD reporting (DKFZ Heidelberg and international dermatology centres); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Dermoscopic images of melanomas and nevi (biopsy-verified public datasets) for training/testing; international dermatologists in the reader study.
papers.preprocessing: Explanatory ontology of melanoma and nevus features built from pattern analysis literature, pilot feedback and board-certified panel approval; ground-truth feature annotations by dermatologists.
papers.modelDetails: Dermatologist-like XAI extending two classifiers to predict diagnosis and corresponding ontology features with localisation; phase 1 AI-only support, phase 2 XAI support.
papers.training: Details in supplementary information.
papers.evaluation: Balanced accuracy of XAI vs baseline classifier; Grad-CAM attention inside vs outside lesion; clinicians' diagnostic accuracy, confidence and trust with AI vs XAI.
papers.baselines: State-of-the-art non-explainable classifier; AI support without explanation.
papers.results: XAI balanced accuracy 81% (95% CI 75.6-86.3) vs 80% for baseline; XAI attended significantly more to lesion areas; XAI increased clinicians' trust and confidence, with a numerical but non-significant increase in diagnostic accuracy.

papers.title: Engaging with AI: How Interface Design Shapes Human-AI Collaboration in High-Stakes Decision-Making
papers.authors: Zichen Chen, Yunhao Luo, Misha Sra
papers.aim: As reliance on AI systems for decision-making grows, it becomes critical to ensure that human users can appropriately balance trust in AI suggestions with their own judgment, especially in high-stakes domains like healthcare. However, human + AI teams have been shown to perform worse than AI alone, with evidence indicating automation bias as the reason for poorer performance, particularly because humans tend to follow AI's recommendations even when they are incorrect.
papers.method: In many existing human + AI systems, decision-making support is typically provided in the form of text explanations (XAI) to help users understand the AI's reasoning. Since human decision-making often relies on System 1 thinking, users may ignore or insufficiently engage with the explanations, leading to poor decision-making. Previous research suggests that there is a need for new approaches that encourage users to engage with the explanations and one proposed method is the use of cognitive forcing functions (CFFs). In this work, we examine how various decision-support mechanisms impact user engagement, trust, and human-AI collaborative task performance in a diabetes management decision-making scenario. In a controlled experiment with 108 participants, we evaluated the effects of six decision-support mechanisms split into two categories of explanations (text, visual) and four CFFs. Our findings reveal that mechanisms like AI confidence levels, text explanations, and performance visualizations enhanced human-AI collaborative task performance, and improved trust when AI reasoning clues were provided.
papers.result: Mechanisms like human feedback and AI-driven questions encouraged deeper reflection but often reduced task performance by increasing cognitive effort, which in turn affected trust. Simple mechanisms like visual explanations had little effect on trust, highlighting the importance of striking a balance in CFF and XAI design.
papers.gap: Lay users and non-clinical task.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Participants made meal decisions first alone, then with AI suggestions, and then with one of six types of support such as explanations, confidence levels or prompting questions, in random assignment. People followed wrong AI advice often, and heavier interventions made them think more but sometimes perform worse. For the PhD, showing calibrated confidence with a light explanation may be the best balance for the escalation interface.
papers.studyDesign: Online randomised between-subjects experiment with three within-subject phases (University of California, Santa Barbara); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 108 Prolific participants (18 per condition, power analysis for r = 0.60, 80% power) performing diabetes meal-planning decisions.
papers.preprocessing: Phase 1 decision without AI; phase 2 with AI suggestion but no explanation; phase 3 with condition-specific decision-support mechanism.
papers.modelDetails: Six decision-support mechanisms: textual explanation, visual explanation (segmentation/labelling), AI and estimated user confidence levels, human feedback on confidence, AI-driven questions, and performance visualisation of past AI and user correctness.
papers.training: Not applicable (generative AI in simulated interface).
papers.evaluation: Decision accuracy, agreement with correct and incorrect AI suggestions (over-reliance), trust and cognitive load across phases and conditions; hypotheses H1-H3 on over-reliance, critical engagement and explanation information load.
papers.baselines: No AI and AI-without-explanation phases.
papers.results: Users over-relied on AI suggestions even when incorrect; mechanisms such as human feedback and AI-driven questions encouraged reflection but often reduced performance by increasing cognitive load; balanced explanation load and confidence displays best supported trust calibration.

papers.title: From Trust to Appropriate Reliance: Measurement Constructs in Human-AI Decision-Making
papers.authors: Muhammad Raees, Konstantinos Papangelis
papers.aim: While human-AI decision-making research has primarily used trust measurements to assess the practical usage of AI systems by their end-users, recent empirical evidence suggests that trust measurements do not inform users' appropriate reliance on AI systems. While examining the human-AI decision-making literature, in this work, we review empirical studies that assess people's appropriate reliance on AI advice, differentiating measurements and constructs of appropriate reliance from trust and mere reliance.
papers.method: Our analysis of literature shows that constructs for human-AI appropriate reliance are still fragmented in research. We present three views on appropriate reliance, namely Traditional, Appropriateness, and Dominance, as discussed in research. Using these views, we evaluate objective metrics reported in studies and argue for their consensus to facilitate the comparison across empirical research.
papers.result: We also discuss how studies employ objective metrics and examine their validity in application contexts. Our work contributes to the critical body of research on exploring objective metrics for assessing humans' appropriate reliance on AI advice.
papers.gap: Few studies with domain experts such as clinicians.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors reviewed studies that measured whether people relied on AI advice appropriately, accepting it when right and rejecting it when wrong, and separated these measures from trust. They group definitions into three views and argue for common objective metrics. This guides the PhD to measure appropriate reliance on escalation advice with objective switch-based metrics, not only trust questionnaires.
papers.studyDesign: Systematic literature review following PRISMA (Rochester Institute of Technology, USA); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 729 search results from Scopus (mid-2025) and ACM Digital Library (December 2025), 2018 onwards; 22 empirical studies of appropriate reliance included.
papers.preprocessing: Keyword development by skimming; inclusion funnel: peer-reviewed full papers, human-subject human-AI decision-making studies measuring appropriate reliance.
papers.modelDetails: Analysis of constructs and objective metrics of appropriate reliance, organised into three views: Traditional, Appropriateness and Dominance; examination of experimental designs and validity of metrics.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Comparison of metrics (e.g. relative AI reliance, relative self-reliance, switching rates, over/under-reliance) and study designs.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Trust measures do not capture appropriate reliance; reliance constructs are fragmented; most studies (20 of 22) used lay users or crowd workers; authors argue for consensus metrics to compare studies.

papers.title: Adjust for Trust: Mitigating Trust-Induced Inappropriate Reliance on AI Assistance
papers.authors: Tejas Srinivasan, Jesse Thomason
papers.aim: Trust biases how users rely on AI recommendations in AI-assisted decision-making tasks, with low and high levels of trust resulting in increased under- and over-reliance, respectively. We propose that AI assistants should adapt their behavior through trust-adaptive interventions to mitigate such inappropriate reliance.
papers.method: For instance, when user trust is low, providing an explanation can elicit more careful consideration of the assistant's advice by the user. In two decision-making scenarios -- laypeople answering science questions and doctors making medical diagnoses -- we find that providing supporting and counter-explanations during moments of low and high trust, respectively, yields up to 38% reduction in inappropriate reliance and 20% improvement in decision accuracy.
papers.result: We are similarly able to reduce over-reliance by adaptively inserting forced pauses to promote deliberation. Our results highlight how AI adaptation to user trust facilitates appropriate reliance, presenting exciting avenues for improving human-AI collaboration.
papers.gap: Trust self-report needed; simulated assistant.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: People, including doctors making diagnoses, received AI advice while repeatedly reporting their trust, and the AI adapted its behaviour: giving supporting reasons when trust was low and counter-arguments or pauses when trust was high. Adapting to trust reduced both over- and under-reliance and improved accuracy. The PhD's escalation interface could similarly adapt prompts to user state to protect against automation bias.
papers.studyDesign: Controlled user experiments in two decision-making settings (University of Southern California); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Laypeople answering science questions (ARC) and medical doctors making diagnoses with AI assistance (participant numbers in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Users report trust level repeatedly during tasks; initial independent answer, then AI advice, then final decision.
papers.modelDetails: Trust-adaptive interventions: supporting explanations when user trust is low, counter-explanations when trust is high, and adaptively inserted forced pauses to promote deliberation; compared with no intervention and persistent interventions.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Switch rate, over-reliance, under-reliance, total inappropriate reliance and final decision accuracy; correlation of trust with reliance.
papers.baselines: No intervention; persistent (non-adaptive) explanations.
papers.results: Trust strongly correlated with switch rate (0.796-0.949) and over-reliance (0.500-0.780); trust-adaptive explanations reduced inappropriate reliance by up to 38% and improved accuracy by up to 20%; counter-explanations at high trust reduced over-reliance 10-23%; adaptive forced pauses also reduced over-reliance; adaptive was better than persistent.

papers.title: Proxy Tasks and Subjective Measures Can Be Misleading in Evaluating Explainable AI Systems
papers.authors: Zana Buçinca, Phoebe Lin, Krzysztof Z. Gajos, Elena L. Glassman
papers.aim: Explainable artificially intelligent (XAI) systems form part of sociotechnical systems, e.g., human+AI teams tasked with making decisions. Yet, current XAI systems are rarely evaluated by measuring the performance of human+AI teams on actual decision-making tasks.
papers.method: We conducted two online experiments and one in-person think-aloud study to evaluate two currently common techniques for evaluating XAI systems: (1) using proxy, artificial tasks such as how well humans predict the AI's decision from the given explanations, and (2) using subjective measures of trust and preference as predictors of actual performance. The results of our experiments demonstrate that evaluations with proxy tasks did not predict the results of the evaluations with the actual decision-making tasks.
papers.result: Further, the subjective measures on evaluations with actual decision-making tasks did not predict the objective performance on those same tasks. Our results suggest that by employing misleading evaluation methods, our field may be inadvertently slowing its progress toward developing human+AI teams that can reliably perform better than humans or AIs alone.
papers.gap: Non-clinical task; simulated AI.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The researchers tested whether common shortcuts for evaluating explanations, namely asking people to guess what the AI will do, or asking how much they trust or like it, predict how well human-AI teams actually decide. They do not. The PhD must therefore evaluate escalation and explanations on real diagnostic decisions with objective accuracy and reliance measures, not only questionnaires.
papers.studyDesign: Two online experiments and one in-person think-aloud study (Harvard University); arXiv preprint (IUI 2020).
papers.datasets: Online participants (e.g. 183+ in proxy-task experiment) and think-aloud participants judging food-plate images for fat content.
papers.preprocessing: 24 food images with ground-truth fat percentage; simulated AI with controlled accuracy.
papers.modelDetails: Comparison of two XAI evaluation practices: proxy tasks (predicting what the AI will decide from explanations) versus actual decision-making tasks; inductive (example-based) versus deductive (rule/feature-based) explanations; subjective trust and preference measures.
papers.training: Not applicable (simulated AI).
papers.evaluation: Accuracy on proxy and actual tasks, self-reported trust and preference, and their correlation with objective performance.
papers.baselines: Different explanation designs and no-explanation conditions.
papers.results: Proxy-task results did not predict performance on actual decision tasks, and subjective trust and preference did not predict objective human-AI performance (e.g. trust higher for inductive explanations, M = 3.55 vs 3.40, p = 0.02, without matching performance gains).

papers.title: Knowing About Knowing: An Illusion of Human Competence Can Hinder Appropriate Reliance on AI Systems
papers.authors: Gaole He, Lucie Kuiper, Ujwal Gadiraju
papers.aim: The dazzling promises of AI systems to augment humans in various tasks hinge on whether humans can appropriately rely on them. Recent research has shown that appropriate reliance is the key to achieving complementary team performance in AI-assisted decision making.
papers.method: This paper addresses an under-explored problem of whether the Dunning-Kruger Effect (DKE) among people can hinder their appropriate reliance on AI systems. DKE is a metacognitive bias due to which less-competent individuals overestimate their own skill and performance. Through an empirical study (N = 249), we explored the impact of DKE on human reliance on an AI system, and whether such effects can be mitigated using a tutorial intervention that reveals the fallibility of AI advice, and exploiting logic units-based explanations to improve user understanding of AI advice. We found that participants who overestimate their performance tend to exhibit under-reliance on AI systems, which hinders optimal team performance. Logic units-based explanations did not help users in either improving the calibration of their competence or facilitating appropriate reliance. While the tutorial intervention was highly effective in helping users calibrate their self-assessment and facilitating appropriate reliance among participants with overestimated self-assessment, we found that it can potentially hurt the appropriate reliance of participants with underestimated self-assessment. Our work has broad implications on the design of methods to tackle user cognitive biases while facilitating appropriate reliance on AI systems.
papers.result: Our findings advance the current understanding of the role of self-assessment in shaping trust and reliance in human-AI decision making. This lays out promising future directions for relevant HCI research in this community.
papers.gap: Non-clinical task; lay users.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Crowd participants solved reasoning problems with AI advice in a factorial design varying whether they first saw a tutorial showing the AI can be wrong and whether advice came with explanations, while their self-assessed skill was measured. People who overrated themselves ignored good AI advice. For the PhD, user self-confidence should be considered alongside AI confidence when deciding how escalation advice is presented.
papers.studyDesign: Online 2×2 factorial experiment (Delft University of Technology, Netherlands); CHI 2023; arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 314 Prolific participants recruited, 249 analysed after attention checks (power analysis via G*Power required 244; Bonferroni α = 0.0125); 16 logical reasoning trial cases.
papers.preprocessing: Two-stage decisions (initial, then after AI advice); £2.5 payment with £0.1 bonus per correct decision; English-proficient adults with ≥ 90% approval.
papers.modelDetails: Factors: tutorial revealing AI fallibility (with performance feedback and contrastive explanations) and logic-unit-based XAI explanations; self-assessment measured to identify Dunning-Kruger overestimation.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Reliance patterns (positive/negative AI reliance and self-reliance), relative AI reliance (RAIR), relative self-reliance (RSR), accuracy and trust, by self-assessment calibration.
papers.baselines: No tutorial, no XAI condition.
papers.results: Participants who overestimated their own performance showed under-reliance on AI; the tutorial helped recalibrate self-assessment and improved appropriate reliance for some, while logic-unit explanations had limited effect.
papers.statistics: ANOVA/ANCOVA and non-parametric tests with Bonferroni correction.

papers.title: Towards Effective Human-AI Decision-Making: The Role of Human Learning in Appropriate Reliance on AI Advice
papers.authors: Max Schemmer, Andrea Bartos, Philipp Spitzer, Patrick Hemmer, Niklas Kühl, Jonas Liebschner, Gerhard Satzger
papers.aim: The true potential of human-AI collaboration lies in exploiting the complementary capabilities of humans and AI to achieve a joint performance superior to that of the individual AI or human, i.e., to achieve complementary team performance (CTP). To realize this complementarity potential, humans need to exercise discretion in following AI 's advice, i.e., appropriately relying on the AI's advice.
papers.method: While previous work has focused on building a mental model of the AI to assess AI recommendations, recent research has shown that the mental model alone cannot explain appropriate reliance. We hypothesize that, in addition to the mental model, human learning is a key mediator of appropriate reliance and, thus, CTP.
papers.result: In this study, we demonstrate the relationship between learning and appropriate reliance in an experiment with 100 participants. This work provides fundamental concepts for analyzing reliance and derives implications for the effective design of human-AI decision-making.
papers.gap: Non-medical lay task.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Participants identified bird species with an AI advisor, some receiving example-based explanations, and the authors tested whether learning the task explains when people rely appropriately on AI. Learning improved appropriate reliance, and examples helped people learn. This suggests that showing similar reference cases could help Sri Lankan clinicians calibrate reliance on the PhD's system over time.
papers.studyDesign: Online behavioural experiment testing a research model (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and University of Bayreuth, Germany); ICIS 2023.
papers.datasets: 100 participants classifying bird images from four similar black-coloured classes of Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (11,788 images, 200 classes).
papers.preprocessing: Two-stage decision procedure (initial decision, then AI advice); explanation and learning conditions.
papers.modelDetails: Hypothesised model: example-based explanations increase human learning, which in turn increases appropriate reliance measured as relative self-reliance (RSR) and relative AI reliance (RAIR), alongside mental model effects.
papers.training: Image classifier used as AI advisor (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: RSR, RAIR, human learning (performance improvement) and complementary team performance; path analysis of hypotheses H1-H3.
papers.baselines: Condition without example-based explanations.
papers.results: Human learning was positively related to appropriate reliance, and example-based explanations supported learning, helping move towards complementary team performance.

papers.title: Designing for Appropriate Reliance: The Roles of AI Uncertainty Presentation, Initial User Decision, and User Demographics in AI-Assisted Decision-Making
papers.authors: Shiye Cao, Anqi Liu, Chien-Ming Huang
papers.aim: Appropriate reliance is critical to achieving synergistic human-AI collaboration. For instance, when users over-rely on AI assistance, their human-AI team performance is bounded by the model's capability.
papers.method: This work studies how the presentation of model uncertainty may steer users' decision-making toward fostering appropriate reliance. Our results demonstrate that showing the calibrated model uncertainty alone is inadequate. Rather, calibrating model uncertainty and presenting it in a frequency format allow users to adjust their reliance accordingly and help reduce the effect of confirmation bias on their decisions. Furthermore, the critical nature of our skin cancer screening task skews participants' judgment, causing their reliance to vary depending on their initial decision.
papers.result: Additionally, step-wise multiple regression analyses revealed how user demographics such as age and familiarity with probability and statistics influence human-AI collaborative decision-making. We discuss the potential for model uncertainty presentation, initial user decision, and user demographics to be incorporated in designing personalized AI aids for appropriate reliance.
papers.gap: Lay participants; small sample.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Participants judged skin lesions, then saw AI advice with no uncertainty, with calibrated uncertainty, or with calibrated uncertainty phrased as frequencies, and could change their answer. Only the frequency format helped people adjust their reliance appropriately, and their own first answer and background shaped behaviour. This is directly relevant to how the PhD should present calibrated confidence at escalation, for example as frequencies.
papers.studyDesign: Online between-subjects user study with exploratory regression analyses (Johns Hopkins University, USA); IRB approved; arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 50 non-medical participants (27 female; mean age 26.2) from the local community; 15 ISIC 2018 dermoscopic cases (3 melanoma, 12 nevi; 25% prevalence).
papers.preprocessing: Initial decision, then AI advice with uncertainty, then final decision; $8 compensation.
papers.modelDetails: Presentation of AI uncertainty as between-subjects factor: no uncertainty, calibrated uncertainty, and calibrated uncertainty in a frequency format (e.g. 'X out of 10 similar cases').
papers.training: Not applicable (simulated calibrated AI).
papers.evaluation: Switching (reliance) behaviour, appropriate reliance, team accuracy; step-wise multiple regression on demographics (age, familiarity with probability and statistics) and initial decision.
papers.baselines: AI advice without uncertainty.
papers.results: Showing calibrated uncertainty alone was inadequate; calibrated uncertainty in a frequency format helped users adjust reliance and reduced confirmation bias; reliance depended on initial decision (users erred on the side of caution in cancer screening); age and statistical familiarity influenced reliance.
papers.statistics: Between-group tests and step-wise multiple regression.

papers.title: In Search of Verifiability: Explanations Rarely Enable Complementary Performance in AI-Advised Decision Making
papers.authors: Raymond Fok, Daniel S. Weld
papers.aim: The current literature on AI-advised decision making -- involving explainable AI systems advising human decision makers -- presents a series of inconclusive and confounding results. To synthesize these findings, we propose a simple theory that elucidates the frequent failure of AI explanations to engender appropriate reliance and complementary decision making performance.
papers.method: We argue explanations are only useful to the extent that they allow a human decision maker to verify the correctness of an AI's prediction, in contrast to other desiderata, e.g., interpretability or spelling out the AI's reasoning process. Prior studies find in many decision making contexts AI explanations do not facilitate such verification.
papers.result: Moreover, most tasks fundamentally do not allow easy verification, regardless of explanation method, limiting the potential benefit of any type of explanation. We also compare the objective of complementary performance with that of appropriate reliance, decomposing the latter into the notions of outcome-graded and strategy-graded reliance.
papers.gap: No new experiment.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors argue that AI explanations help decisions only when they allow the human to check whether the AI is right, and show that most studied tasks do not allow this, explaining the mixed results in the literature. They distinguish judging reliance by outcomes versus by sensible strategy. This supports the PhD's choice to prioritise calibrated confidence and evidence that clinicians can verify, such as highlighted image regions, over generic explanations.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical perspective and literature synthesis (University of Washington and Allen Institute for AI); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Prior empirical studies of AI-advised decision making with explanations.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Proposed theory that explanations help only when they let the decision maker verify the correctness of the AI prediction; decomposition of appropriate reliance into outcome-graded and strategy-graded reliance; comparison of complementary performance and appropriate reliance objectives.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Conceptual analysis of task verifiability across published studies.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Explanations rarely enable complementary performance because most tasks do not permit easy verification; explanations can increase over-reliance; displaying AI confidence often performs as well; verifiability should guide explanation design.

papers.title: Majority Voting of Doctors Improves Appropriateness of AI Reliance in Pathology
papers.authors: Hongyan Gu, Chunxu Yang, Shino Magaki, Neda Zarrin-Khameh, Nelli S. Lakis, Inma Cobos, Negar Khanlou, Xinhai R. Zhang, Jasmeet Assi, Joshua T. Byers, et al.
papers.aim: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) making advancements in medical decision-making, there is a growing need to ensure doctors develop appropriate reliance on AI to avoid adverse outcomes. However, existing methods in enabling appropriate AI reliance might encounter challenges while being applied in the medical domain.
papers.method: With this regard, this work employs and provides the validation of an alternative approach -- majority voting -- to facilitate appropriate reliance on AI in medical decision-making. This is achieved by a multi-institutional user study involving 32 medical professionals with various backgrounds, focusing on the pathology task of visually detecting a pattern, mitoses, in tumor images. Here, the majority voting process was conducted by synthesizing decisions under AI assistance from a group of pathology doctors (pathologists). Two metrics were used to evaluate the appropriateness of AI reliance: Relative AI Reliance (RAIR) and Relative Self-Reliance (RSR). Results showed that even with groups of three pathologists, majority-voted decisions significantly increased both RAIR and RSR -- by approximately 9% and 31%, respectively -- compared to decisions made by one pathologist collaborating with AI.
papers.result: This increased appropriateness resulted in better precision and recall in the detection of mitoses. While our study is centered on pathology, we believe these insights can be extended to general high-stakes decision-making processes involving similar visual tasks.
papers.gap: Image tiles rather than whole slides; group reading costly.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Pathologists from many centres detected mitoses in images first without and then with AI, and the authors combined several doctors' AI-assisted answers by majority vote. Grouping reduced individuals' inappropriate reliance and improved detection quality. For the PhD, escalation to more than one clinician for uncertain cases could similarly improve decision quality.
papers.studyDesign: Multi-institutional two-stage online user study (UCLA and 10 US medical centres); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 32 pathology professionals (12 specialist pathologists, 6 general pathologists, 10 residents, 4 trained medical students) examining 48 images for mitoses; 29 AI users analysed (25 for reliance analysis).
papers.preprocessing: Unmoderated online sessions with tutorial; stage 2 images randomly flipped and rotated to reduce learning effects; users chose AI sensitivity settings.
papers.modelDetails: AI mitosis detection with XAI support; majority voting across groups of pathologists' AI-assisted decisions as an approach to improve appropriateness of AI reliance.
papers.training: Pre-trained mitosis detector.
papers.evaluation: Two quantifiable metrics of appropriateness of AI reliance; precision and recall of mitosis detection for individuals versus majority-voted groups; AI/XAI utilisation.
papers.baselines: Individual AI-assisted pathologists; unassisted stage 1.
papers.results: AI activation rate 99.21% and active time 71.39%; majority voting of grouped doctors improved appropriateness of AI reliance, which increased precision and recall of mitosis detection.
papers.statistics: Descriptive statistics with 95% CIs and group comparisons.

papers.title: A Decision Theoretic Framework for Measuring AI Reliance
papers.authors: Ziyang Guo, Yifan Wu, Jason Hartline, Jessica Hullman
papers.aim: Humans frequently make decisions with the aid of artificially intelligent (AI) systems. A common pattern is for the AI to recommend an action to the human who retains control over the final decision.
papers.method: Researchers have identified ensuring that a human has appropriate reliance on an AI as a critical component of achieving complementary performance. We argue that the current definition of appropriate reliance used in such research lacks formal statistical grounding and can lead to contradictions. We propose a formal definition of reliance, based on statistical decision theory, which separates the concepts of reliance as the probability the decision-maker follows the AI's recommendation from challenges a human may face in differentiating the signals and forming accurate beliefs about the situation. Our definition gives rise to a framework that can be used to guide the design and interpretation of studies on human-AI complementarity and reliance.
papers.result: Using recent AI-advised decision making studies from literature, we demonstrate how our framework can be used to separate the loss due to mis-reliance from the loss due to not accurately differentiating the signals. We evaluate these losses by comparing to a baseline and a benchmark for complementary performance defined by the expected payoff achieved by a rational decision-maker facing the same decision task as the behavioral decision-makers.
papers.gap: Theory; requires known signal distributions.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors define reliance formally using decision theory and show how to split a human-AI team's shortfall into the part caused by following the AI at the wrong times and the part caused by not being able to tell cases apart. Applied to published studies, this clarifies how much better teams could do. The PhD can use this framework to analyse escalation-study results more rigorously.
papers.studyDesign: Theoretical framework paper with re-analysis of published studies (Northwestern University, USA); ACM FAccT 2024.
papers.datasets: Data from recent AI-advised decision-making studies in the literature.
papers.preprocessing: Not applicable.
papers.modelDetails: Formal definition of reliance from statistical decision theory as the probability that the decision maker follows the AI recommendation, separated from the human's ability to distinguish signals and form accurate beliefs; rational decision-maker baseline and benchmark for complementary performance.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Decomposition of performance loss into loss from mis-reliance and loss from failing to differentiate signals, relative to rational baseline and benchmark payoffs.
papers.baselines: Rational decision-maker baseline and benchmark.
papers.results: Current definitions of appropriate reliance lack statistical grounding and can be contradictory; the framework separates mis-reliance losses from discrimination losses and clarifies what improvement is achievable in each study.

papers.title: Accuracy-Time Tradeoffs in AI-Assisted Decision Making under Time Pressure
papers.authors: Siddharth Swaroop, Zana Buçinca, Krzysztof Z. Gajos, Finale Doshi-Velez
papers.aim: In settings where users both need high accuracy and are time-pressured, such as doctors working in emergency rooms, we want to provide AI assistance that both increases decision accuracy and reduces decision-making time. Current literature focusses on how users interact with AI assistance when there is no time pressure, finding that different AI assistances have different benefits: some can reduce time taken while increasing overreliance on AI, while others do the opposite.
papers.method: The precise benefit can depend on both the user and task. In time-pressured scenarios, adapting when we show AI assistance is especially important: relying on the AI assistance can save time, and can therefore be beneficial when the AI is likely to be right. We would ideally adapt what AI assistance we show depending on various properties (of the task and of the user) in order to best trade off accuracy and time. We introduce a study where users have to answer a series of logic puzzles. We find that time pressure affects how users use different AI assistances, making some assistances more beneficial than others when compared to no-time-pressure settings. We also find that a user's overreliance rate is a key predictor of their behaviour: overreliers and not-overreliers use different AI assistance types differently.
papers.result: We find marginal correlations between a user's overreliance rate (which is related to the user's trust in AI recommendations) and their personality traits (Big Five Personality traits). Overall, our work suggests that AI assistances have different accuracy-time tradeoffs when people are under time pressure compared to no time pressure, and we explore how we might adapt AI assistances in this setting.
papers.gap: Lay task; not clinical time pressure.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Participants solved puzzles with AI advice shown before or after their own answer, with and without time pressure. Under pressure, seeing the AI first saved time but increased blind following of wrong advice, and individuals differed in their tendency to over-rely. Busy Sri Lankan clinics face time pressure, so the PhD should consider when to show AI advice and reserve 'AI-first' display for high-confidence cases.
papers.studyDesign: Online randomised user experiment (Harvard University); IUI 2024; arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Crowd participants solving a series of logic puzzles with AI assistance under no time pressure and time pressure (about 138-139 per analysis).
papers.preprocessing: Between-subjects AI assistance conditions with within-subject time-pressure manipulation; Big Five personality questionnaire.
papers.modelDetails: Three AI assistance types: AI-before (recommendation shown first), AI-after (shown after initial answer), and mixed; analysis of overreliers versus non-overreliers to inform adaptive assistance.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy, response time and overreliance by condition and time pressure; correlation of overreliance with personality traits.
papers.baselines: No time pressure; between assistance types.
papers.results: Without time pressure, conditions had similar accuracy, time and overreliance; under time pressure, AI-before was faster but had higher overreliance (p = 0.04), and mixed had lower accuracy; overreliance rate predicted how users used assistance; marginal correlations with personality traits.
papers.statistics: ANOVA (e.g. F(2,135) = 5.09, p = 0.0073 for time) with post hoc tests.

papers.title: NASA-TLX Web App: An Online Tool to Analyse Subjective Workload
papers.authors: Vinoth Pandian Sermuga Pandian, Sarah Suleri
papers.aim: NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) is a widely used assessment technique to compute subjective workload experienced during a task. It evaluates workload using six dimensions: mental demand, physical demand, temporal demand, frustration, effort, and performance.
papers.method: This paper presents a web app to assist experimenters in using NASA-TLX to commute subjective workload. The web app enables the experimenter to conduct various experiments simultaneously and offers the participants a concise interface to provide their subjective evaluation. It performs the calculations at the backend and provides the computed results comprehensively.
papers.result: The web app provides a dashboard for the experimenter to visualize and export the summary of results. Qualitative feedback from 12 experimenters indicated that the NASA-TLX web app is relevant, helpful, and easy to use.
papers.gap: No validation beyond user feedback.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built a free web tool for running the NASA Task Load Index workload questionnaire, which handles ratings, pairwise weighting, calculation and export, and asked twelve researchers for feedback. It is a practical tool the PhD can use to measure clinician workload with and without the escalation system in WP7.
papers.studyDesign: Software tool paper with qualitative user feedback (Fraunhofer FIT, Germany); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 12 experimenters providing feedback on the tool.
papers.preprocessing: Review of nine existing NASA-TLX tools; six free tools compared.
papers.modelDetails: NASA-TLX web app: participants rate six dimensions (mental, physical and temporal demand, performance, effort, frustration) on 0-100 and complete pairwise weighting; backend computes weighted workload; dashboard to manage multiple experiments and export results.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative feedback on relevance, helpfulness and ease of use.
papers.baselines: Existing NASA-TLX apps and websites.
papers.results: Experimenters found the web app relevant, helpful and easy to use; it supports multiple simultaneous experiments and data export.

papers.title: iSurgARy: A mobile augmented reality solution for ventriculostomy in resource-limited settings
papers.authors: Zahra Asadi, Joshua Pardillo Castillo, Mehrdad Asadi, David S. Sinclair, Marta Kersten-Oertel
papers.aim: Global disparities in neurosurgical care necessitate innovations addressing affordability and accuracy, particularly for critical procedures like ventriculostomy. This intervention, vital for managing life-threatening intracranial pressure increases, is associated with catheter misplacement rates exceeding 30% when using a freehand technique.
papers.method: Such misplacements hold severe consequences including haemorrhage, infection, prolonged hospital stays, and even morbidity and mortality. To address this issue, we present a novel, stand-alone mobile-based augmented reality system (iSurgARy) aimed at significantly improving ventriculostomy accuracy, particularly in resource-limited settings such as those in low- and middle-income countries. iSurgARy uses landmark based registration by taking advantage of Light Detection and Ranging (LiDaR) to allow for accurate surgical guidance. To evaluate iSurgARy, we conducted a two-phase user study.
papers.result: Initially, we assessed usability and learnability with novice participants using the System Usability Scale (SUS), incorporating their feedback to refine the application. In the second phase, we engaged human-computer interaction (HCI) and clinical domain experts to evaluate our application, measuring Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), System Usability Scale (SUS) and NASA Task Load Index (TLX) metrics to assess accuracy usability, and cognitive workload, respectively
papers.gap: Phantom testing only; no clinical trial.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team built a smartphone augmented reality app that uses the phone's depth sensor to register a patient's preoperative scan and guide drain insertion into the brain ventricles, then tested it with novices and experts for accuracy, usability and workload. It offers affordable guidance where expensive navigation systems are unavailable, which is directly relevant to neurosurgical planning tools for Sri Lanka.
papers.studyDesign: System development with two-phase user study (Concordia University and Montreal Neurological Institute, McGill, Canada); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Phase 1: novice participants; phase 2: HCI and clinical domain experts performing simulated ventriculostomy guidance (phantom).
papers.preprocessing: Preoperative CT-based landmarks; feedback from phase 1 used to refine the app.
papers.modelDetails: iSurgARy: stand-alone mobile augmented reality app using LiDAR-based landmark registration to overlay ventricle targets and trajectory for external ventricular drain placement, designed for resource-limited settings.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Root mean square error of registration/placement accuracy, System Usability Scale, NASA-TLX cognitive workload.
papers.baselines: Freehand landmark-based technique (misplacement > 30% in literature); costly image-guided navigation (USD 650,000-900,000).
papers.results: The app achieved accurate guidance with good usability and acceptable workload in expert evaluation, showing promise as a low-cost alternative to navigation systems in LMICs.

papers.title: Automation Bias in AI-Assisted Medical Decision-Making under Time Pressure in Computational Pathology
papers.authors: Emely Rosbach, Jonathan Ganz, Jonas Ammeling, Andreas Riener, Marc Aubreville
papers.aim: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based clinical decision support systems (CDSS) promise to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency in computational pathology. However, human-AI collaboration might introduce automation bias, where users uncritically follow automated cues.
papers.method: This bias may worsen when time pressure strains practitioners' cognitive resources. We quantified automation bias by measuring the adoption of negative system consultations and examined the role of time pressure in a web-based experiment, where trained pathology experts (n=28) estimated tumor cell percentages. Our results indicate that while AI integration led to a statistically significant increase in overall performance, it also resulted in a 7% automation bias rate, where initially correct evaluations were overturned by erroneous AI advice.
papers.result: Conversely, time pressure did not exacerbate automation bias occurrence, but appeared to increase its severity, evidenced by heightened reliance on the system's negative consultations and subsequent performance decline. These findings highlight potential risks of AI use in healthcare.
papers.gap: Simulated AI; single task.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Pathology experts estimated tumour cell percentages on tissue images with and without AI suggestions, some of them wrong, and with or without a time limit. AI helped overall, but in 7% of cases correct answers were changed to wrong ones, and time pressure made such errors larger. This quantifies automation bias in pathology and supports the PhD's plan to flag low-confidence AI outputs rather than present them as advice.
papers.studyDesign: Web-based experiment with expert users (Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt and Flensburg University of Applied Sciences, Germany); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 28 trained pathology experts (pathologists, residents and non-physician pathology staff) estimating tumour cell percentage on 23 H&E tissue patches.
papers.preprocessing: Recruitment from professional network; conditions with and without AI advice and with and without time pressure.
papers.modelDetails: Simulated AI CDSS giving tumour cell percentage estimates, including deliberately erroneous (negative) consultations to quantify automation bias.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Overall estimation performance; automation bias rate (initially correct estimates overturned by wrong AI advice); severity of reliance under time pressure.
papers.baselines: Estimation without AI; no time pressure.
papers.results: AI integration significantly improved overall performance but produced a 7% automation bias rate; time pressure did not increase automation bias frequency but increased its severity through heavier reliance on wrong advice.

papers.title: On the Influence of Explainable AI on Automation Bias
papers.authors: Max Schemmer, Niklas Kühl, Carina Benz, Gerhard Satzger
papers.aim: Artificial intelligence (AI) is gaining momentum, and its importance for the future of work in many areas, such as medicine and banking, is continuously rising. However, insights on the effective collaboration of humans and AI are still rare.
papers.method: Typically, AI supports humans in decision-making by addressing human limitations. However, it may also evoke human bias, especially in the form of automation bias as an over-reliance on AI advice. We aim to shed light on the potential to influence automation bias by explainable AI (XAI). In this pre-test, we derive a research model and describe our study design.
papers.result: Subsequentially, we conduct an online experiment with regard to hotel review classifications and discuss first results. We expect our research to contribute to the design and development of safe hybrid intelligence systems.
papers.gap: Preliminary results only; non-medical task.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Participants judged whether hotel reviews were fake, with AI advice either alone or accompanied by highlighted explanatory words, to see whether explanations reduce blind following of wrong advice. This early study frames the question of whether explanations reduce automation bias, which the PhD addresses using calibrated confidence and escalation instead.
papers.studyDesign: Research-in-progress online between-subjects experiment (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Germany); ECIS 2022.
papers.datasets: Deceptive hotel review classification task using Ott et al. dataset (400 deceptive, 400 genuine reviews); online participants (pre-test sample).
papers.preprocessing: Clear ground truth from dataset; two experimental conditions.
papers.modelDetails: Support vector machine classifier (86% accuracy) giving recommendations alone or with LIME feature-importance explanations shown as highlighted words with direction and three effect-size levels; research model linking XAI to automation bias.
papers.training: SVM trained on review dataset.
papers.evaluation: Automation bias (following incorrect AI advice), accuracy, and related constructs between conditions.
papers.baselines: AI recommendation without explanation.
papers.results: Pre-test results suggest explanations may influence automation bias, with first results discussed; full study planned to inform design of safe hybrid intelligence systems.

papers.title: Stuck on Suggestions: Automation Bias, the Anchoring Effect, and the Factors That Shape Them in Computational Pathology
papers.authors: Emely Rosbach, Jonas Ammeling, Jonathan Ganz, Christof Albert Bertram, Thomas Conrad, Andreas Riener, Marc Aubreville
papers.aim: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven decision support systems can improve diagnostic accuracy and efficiency in computational pathology. However, collaboration between human experts and AI may introduce cognitive biases such as automation and anchoring bias, where users adopt system predictions blindly or are disproportionately influenced by AI advice, even when inaccurate.
papers.method: These effects may be amplified under time pressure, common in routine pathology, or shaped by individual user characteristics. We conducted an online experiment in which pathology experts (n = 28) estimated tumor cell percentages: once independently and once with AI support. A subset of estimations in each condition was performed under time strain. Overall, AI assistance improved diagnostic performance but introduced a 7% automation bias rate, defined as accepted negative consultations where previously correct independent judgments were overturned by incorrect AI advice. While time pressure did not increase the frequency of automation bias, it appeared to intensify its severity, reflected in stronger performance declines associated with increased AI reliance under cognitive load. A linear mixed-effects model (LMM) simulating weighted averaging showed a statistically significant positive coefficient for AI advice, indicating moderate anchoring on system output. This effect increased under time pressure, suggesting anchoring bias becomes more pronounced when cognitive resources are limited.
papers.result: A second LMM assessing automation reliance, a proxy for automation and anchoring bias, showed that professional experience and self-efficacy were associated with lower dependence on AI, whereas higher confidence during AI-assisted decisions was tied to increased AI reliance. These findings highlight the dual nature of AI integration in clinical workflows: improving performance while introducing risks of bias-driven diagnostic errors.
papers.gap: Simulated AI; single estimation task.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Extending their earlier study, the authors had pathology experts estimate tumour cell percentages with and without AI suggestions and time limits, and used mixed-effects models to see who is most pulled towards AI values. Both automation bias and anchoring occurred, influenced by experience and self-belief. This shows the PhD that user characteristics should be recorded and analysed in its reader study.
papers.studyDesign: Web-based 2×2 within-subjects experiment (TH Ingolstadt, Vetmeduni Vienna, FU Berlin, Flensburg UAS); Machine Learning for Biomedical Imaging; arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 28 trained pathology experts estimating tumour cell percentage (0-100%) on H&E tissue patches.
papers.preprocessing: Factors: inclusion of AI suggestions and time pressure; measures of professional experience, self-efficacy and decision confidence.
papers.modelDetails: Simulated AI decision support providing TCP estimates including inaccurate suggestions; quantification of automation bias (adopting wrong AI advice) and anchoring effect (estimates pulled towards AI value).
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Accuracy of estimates, automation bias and anchoring magnitude; automation reliance modelled with linear mixed-effects models including experience, self-efficacy and confidence.
papers.baselines: Estimation without AI and without time pressure.
papers.results: AI improved overall accuracy but induced automation and anchoring bias; time pressure increased severity of reliance; LMMs showed professional experience and self-efficacy were associated with automation reliance.

papers.title: A Research Framework for Virtual Reality Neurosurgery Based on Open-Source Tools
papers.authors: Lukas D. J. Fiederer, Hisham Alwanni, Martin Völker, Oliver Schnell, Jürgen Beck, Tonio Ball
papers.aim: Fully immersive virtual reality (VR) has the potential to improve neurosurgical planning. For example, it may offer 3D visualizations of relevant anatomical structures with complex shapes, such as blood vessels and tumors.
papers.method: However, there is a lack of research tools specifically tailored for this area. We present a research framework for VR neurosurgery based on open-source tools and preliminary evaluation results. We showcase the potential of such a framework using clinical data of two patients and research data of one subject.
papers.result: As a first step toward practical evaluations, two certified senior neurosurgeons positively assessed the usefulness of the VR visualizations using head-mounted displays. The methods and findings described in our study thus provide a foundation for research and development aiming at versatile and user-friendly VR tools for improving neurosurgical planning and training.
papers.gap: Pilot with three subjects; manual pipeline steps.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team assembled open-source tools into a pipeline that segments patients' scans into 3D models of vessels, tumours and skull that surgeons can explore in virtual reality, and two senior neurosurgeons judged it useful. It is an example of how AI segmentations from the PhD's MRI models could feed an immersive planning view.
papers.studyDesign: Technical framework paper with pilot evaluation (Translational Neurotechnology Lab and Department of Neurosurgery, University of Freiburg, Germany); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Routine pre-surgical MRI and CT of 2 patients and MRI of 1 healthy subject.
papers.preprocessing: DICOM to NIfTI conversion; co-registration and reslicing to T1 MRA or TOF MRA with FSL FLIRT; skull and implant segmentation from CT by semi-automatic multi-stage region growing; skull-masked vessel segmentation from CTA/MRA; patient-specific pipeline adaptation.
papers.modelDetails: Open-source research framework for fully immersive VR neurosurgical planning, building detailed 3D models of brain, vessels, tumours and implants for interaction in VR; planned replacement with a deep learning segmentation pipeline.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Qualitative assessment of VR visualisation usefulness by two certified senior neurosurgeons.
papers.baselines: Conventional 2D imaging review.
papers.results: Senior neurosurgeons positively assessed the usefulness of VR visualisations for understanding complex anatomy and planning.

papers.title: Web-based Augmented Reality with Auto-Scaling and Real-Time Head Tracking towards Markerless Neurointerventional Preoperative Planning and Training of Head-mounted Robotic Needle Insertion
papers.authors: Hon Lung Ho, Yupeng Wang, An Wang, Long Bai, Hongliang Ren
papers.aim: Neurosurgery requires exceptional precision and comprehensive preoperative planning to ensure optimal patient outcomes. Despite technological advancements, there remains a need for intuitive, accessible tools to enhance surgical preparation and medical education in this field.
papers.method: Traditional methods often lack the immersive experience necessary for surgeons to visualize complex procedures and critical neurovascular structures, while existing advanced solutions may be cost-prohibitive or require specialized hardware. This research presents a novel markerless web-based augmented reality (AR) application designed to address these challenges in neurointerventional preoperative planning and education. Utilizing MediaPipe for precise facial localization and segmentation, and React Three Fiber for immersive 3D visualization, the application offers an intuitive platform for complex preoperative procedures. A virtual 2-RPS parallel positioner or Skull-Bot model is projected onto the user's face in real-time, simulating surgical tool control with high precision. Key features include the ability to import and auto-scale head anatomy to the user's dimensions and real-time auto-tracking of head movements once aligned. The web-based nature enables simultaneous access by multiple users, facilitating collaboration during surgeries and allowing medical students to observe live procedures. A pilot study involving three participants evaluated the application's auto-scaling and auto-tracking capabilities through various head rotation exercises.
papers.result: This research contributes to the field by offering a cost-effective, accessible, and collaborative tool for improving neurosurgical planning and education, potentially leading to better surgical outcomes and more comprehensive training for medical professionals. The source code of our application is publicly available at https://github.com/Hillllllllton/skullbot_web_ar.
papers.gap: No clinical validation; accuracy not tested on patients.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The authors built a browser-based augmented reality app that tracks a person's face through a normal webcam and overlays a head model and a robotic needle-guide so that procedures can be planned or practised without special equipment. Low-cost tools like this are relevant to delivering the PhD's planning outputs in resource-limited Sri Lankan hospitals.
papers.studyDesign: System development paper (The Chinese University of Hong Kong); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Webcam video of users' faces; 3D head and neurovascular models for planning (details in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Real-time facial landmark detection and segmentation with MediaPipe; auto-scaling of models to face boundary.
papers.modelDetails: Markerless web-based AR application using Three.js and React Three Fiber, projecting a virtual 2-RPS parallel positioner ('Skull-Bot') and head models onto the user's face with real-time head tracking for neurointerventional planning and training of robotic needle insertion.
papers.training: Not applicable (pre-trained MediaPipe models).
papers.evaluation: Tracking and alignment accuracy, responsiveness and qualitative assessment of usability for planning and education.
papers.baselines: Marker-based or specialised-hardware AR systems.
papers.results: The app provided accurate real-time markerless tracking and auto-scaling in a standard browser, offering a cost-effective, accessible and collaborative tool for neurosurgical planning and education.

papers.title: Assessment of user-interaction strategies for neurosurgical data navigation and annotation in virtual reality
papers.authors: Owen Hellum, Marta Kersten-Oertel, Yiming Xiao
papers.aim: While virtual-reality (VR) has shown great promise in radiological tasks, effective user-interaction strategies that can improve efficiency and ergonomics are still under-explored and systematic evaluations of VR interaction techniques in the context of complex anatomical models are rare. Therefore, our study aims to identify the most effective interaction techniques for two common neurosurgical planning tasks in VR (point annotation and note-taking) from the state-of-the-arts, and propose a novel technique for efficient sub-volume selection necessary in neuroanatomical navigation.
papers.method: We assessed seven user-interaction methods with multiple input modalities (gaze, head motion, controller, and voice) for point placement and note-taking in the context of annotating brain aneurysms for cerebrovascular surgery. Furthermore, we proposed and evaluated a novel technique, called magnified selection diorama (Maserama) for easy navigation and selection of complex 3D anatomies in VR. Both quantitative and semi-quantitative (i.e., NASA Task Load Index) metrics were employed through user studies to reveal the performance of each interaction scheme in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and usability. Our evaluations demonstrated that controller-based interaction is preferred over eye-tracking-based methods for point placement while voice recording and virtual keyboard typing are better than freehand writing for note-taking. Furthermore, our new Maserama sub-volume selection technique was proven to be highly efficient and easy-to-use.
papers.result: Our study is the first to provide a systematic assessment of existing and new VR interaction schemes for neurosurgical data navigation and annotation. It offers valuable insights and tools to guide the design of future VR systems for radiological and surgical applications.
papers.gap: Synthetic tasks; few clinicians.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Participants marked brain aneurysms and took notes in virtual reality using seven different interaction methods, and a new magnified selection technique was tested, with accuracy, time and workload measured. Controllers and voice worked best. These findings guide interface choices if the PhD's surgical-planning outputs are reviewed in 3D or VR.
papers.studyDesign: Controlled user study of VR interaction techniques (Concordia University and PERFORM Centre, Montreal, Canada); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Participants performing aneurysm annotation tasks on cerebrovascular 3D models in VR (sample size in paper).
papers.preprocessing: Artificial aneurysm targets with known surfaces for accuracy measurement.
papers.modelDetails: Seven interaction methods using gaze, head motion, controller and voice for point placement and note-taking; novel magnified selection diorama (Maserama) for sub-volume selection in neuroanatomical navigation.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Point placement accuracy (Euclidean distance to aneurysm surface), task time, NASA-TLX workload and usability ratings.
papers.baselines: Existing state-of-the-art VR interaction techniques.
papers.results: Controller-based interaction outperformed eye-tracking for point placement (controller methods achieved 0 mm mean error); voice recording and virtual keyboard beat freehand writing for notes; Maserama was highly efficient and easy to use.
papers.statistics: Statistical comparisons of accuracy, time and NASA-TLX across techniques.

papers.title: Dense Error Map Estimation for MRI-Ultrasound Registration in Brain Tumor Surgery Using Swin UNETR
papers.authors: Soorena Salari, Amirhossein Rasoulian, Hassan Rivaz, Yiming Xiao
papers.aim: Early surgical treatment of brain tumors is crucial in reducing patient mortality rates. However, brain tissue deformation (called brain shift) occurs during the surgery, rendering pre-operative images invalid.
papers.method: As a cost-effective and portable tool, intra-operative ultrasound (iUS) can track brain shift, and accurate MRI-iUS registration techniques can update pre-surgical plans and facilitate the interpretation of iUS. This can boost surgical safety and outcomes by maximizing tumor removal while avoiding eloquent regions. However, manual assessment of MRI-iUS registration results in real-time is difficult and prone to errors due to the 3D nature of the data.
papers.result: Automatic algorithms that can quantify the quality of inter-modal medical image registration outcomes can be highly beneficial. Therefore, we propose a novel deep-learning (DL) based framework with the Swin UNETR to automatically assess 3D-patch-wise dense error maps for MRI-iUS registration in iUS-guided brain tumor resection and show its performance with real clinical data for the first time.
papers.gap: Simulated misalignments; small dataset.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: During brain tumour surgery the brain shifts, so preoperative MRI must be re-aligned to intraoperative ultrasound, and surgeons need to know how good the alignment is. The authors trained a transformer-based network to predict, voxel by voxel, how large the alignment error is. Estimating local error like this is a form of spatial uncertainty that the PhD's planning tool could show surgeons.
papers.studyDesign: Deep learning methods study for registration quality assessment (Concordia University, Canada); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: RESECT dataset: preoperative MRI and intraoperative ultrasound from 23 low-grade glioma resections; 22 cases with T2-FLAIR and pre-resection iUS used.
papers.preprocessing: Silver ground truth by landmark-based 3D B-spline nonlinear registration; T2-FLAIR cropped to iUS field of view; resampling to 0.5 mm isotropic; simulated random misalignments with B-spline transforms for training and testing.
papers.modelDetails: Swin UNETR network estimating dense voxel-wise registration error maps for MRI-iUS registration, patch-wise 3D processing.
papers.training: Trained on augmented misaligned pairs (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Error between predicted and true registration error maps; patch-wise regression accuracy; comparison with baselines.
papers.baselines: Alternative CNN-based error estimation approaches.
papers.results: The model estimated dense registration error maps accurately, enabling automatic real-time quality assessment of MRI-iUS alignment for brain shift correction.

papers.title: Development of Advanced FEM Simulation Technology for Pre-Operative Surgical Planning
papers.authors: Zhanyue Zhao, Yiwei Jiang, Charles Bales, Yang Wang, Gregory Fischer
papers.aim: Intracorporeal needle-based therapeutic ultrasound (NBTU) offers a minimally invasive approach for the thermal ablation of malignant brain tumors, including both primary and metastatic cancers. NBTU utilizes a high-frequency alternating electric field to excite a piezoelectric transducer, generating acoustic waves that cause localized heating and tumor cell ablation, and it provides a more precise ablation by delivering lower acoustic power doses directly to targeted tumors while sparing surrounding healthy tissue.
papers.method: Building on our previous work, this study introduces a database for optimizing pre-operative surgical planning by simulating ablation effects in varied tissue environments and develops an extended simulation model incorporating various tumor types and sizes to evaluate thermal damage under trans-tissue conditions. A comprehensive database is created from these simulations, detailing critical parameters such as CEM43 isodose maps, temperature changes, thermal dose areas, and maximum ablation distances for four directional probes. This database serves as a valuable resource for future studies, aiding in complex trajectory planning and parameter optimization for NBTU procedures. Moreover, a novel probe selection method is proposed to enhance pre-surgical planning, providing a strategic approach to selecting probes that maximize therapeutic efficiency and minimize ablation time.
papers.result: By avoiding unnecessary thermal propagation and optimizing probe angles, this method has the potential to improve patient outcomes and streamline surgical procedures. Overall, the findings of this study contribute significantly to the field of NBTU, offering a robust framework for enhancing treatment precision and efficacy in clinical settings.
papers.gap: Simulation only; no patient validation.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: The team simulated how a needle-based ultrasound probe heats and destroys brain tumour tissue in many tissue and tumour scenarios, building a database of expected ablation zones and proposing a rule for choosing the best probe direction. This is an example of physics-based surgical planning support that could complement the PhD's imaging-based planning component.
papers.studyDesign: Computational simulation study (Worcester Polytechnic Institute, USA; NIH/NCI funded); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Finite element simulations across varied tissue environments, tumour types and sizes for needle-based therapeutic ultrasound (NBTU) brain tumour ablation.
papers.preprocessing: Model set-up building on prior acoustic-thermal models validated with MR thermometry in gel phantoms.
papers.modelDetails: Extended finite element model coupling acoustic pressure fields from piezoelectric transducers with bioheat transfer to compute CEM43 thermal dose isodose maps, temperature changes, thermal dose areas and maximum ablation distances for four directional probes; novel probe selection method.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Simulated ablation extent, thermal dose distributions and ablation time per probe and tissue condition.
papers.baselines: Previous single-condition simulation models.
papers.results: A comprehensive simulation database was created and a probe selection method proposed that maximises therapeutic efficiency, minimises ablation time and avoids unnecessary thermal spread.

papers.title: Clinician-AI Collaboration in Endovascular Neurointerventions: In-Vitro User Study of Copilot Assistance Modes for Robotic Navigation Across the Autonomy Spectrum
papers.authors: Nikola Fischer, Harry Robertshaw, S. M. Hadi Sadati, Xingyu Chen, Weiyuan Deng, Benjamin Jackson, Michael Adofo Kwakye, Sara Sciacca, Naga Kandasamy, Parthiban Balasundaram, et al.
papers.aim: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is an effective treatment for acute ischemic stroke, yet access remains limited by the availability of neurointerventional expertise. Telerobotic and AI-assisted systems may help address this challenge, but it remains unclear how clinicians interact with different levels of autonomy and how autonomous navigation systems perform in realistic environments.
papers.method: This work introduces Copilot Assistance Modes (CAMs), a framework for clinician-AI collaboration in robotic endovascular navigation spanning the autonomy spectrum from manual operation to full autonomy. In the first in-vitro user study comparing clinician-AI collaboration strategies, 11 experts and two students evaluated six navigation modes in a patient-specific vascular phantom. Objective performance metrics were combined with subjective assessments, including workload and usability. Autonomous performance was additionally evaluated both in silico and in vitro to investigate sim-to-real transfer. Hands-on manual navigation achieved the strongest overall performance (100% success). While fully autonomous navigation achieved 81% success in simulation, performance dropped to 23% in vitro. In contrast, several clinician-AI shared-autonomy modes achieved success rates of 92-97%, approximately four times higher than full autonomy and comparable to direct robotic control (95%), demonstrating mitigation of sim-to-real domain shift through clinician-AI collaboration.
papers.result: Among the evaluated AI-driven approaches, user-directed task delegation and rotational shared control demonstrated the most favorable balance between performance and clinician acceptance. These findings suggest that effective clinician-AI collaboration and allocation of control authority may currently be more important for reliable robotic neurointerventional navigation than increasing autonomy alone.
papers.gap: Phantom only; small sample.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Experts and students steered a robotic catheter through a realistic vessel model using six modes ranging from fully manual to fully autonomous AI. Full autonomy often failed, while modes where the clinician delegated specific steps or shared control did best. This supports the PhD's position that shared, human-directed autonomy is safer than full automation in neuro-interventions.
papers.studyDesign: In-vitro user study comparing clinician-AI collaboration modes in robotic endovascular navigation (King's College London and King's College Hospital, UK); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 11 expert neurointerventionalists and 2 students navigating a patient-specific vascular phantom from aortic arch to right internal and external carotid arteries.
papers.preprocessing: Phantom set-up with robotic manipulator and user control interface; repeated runs per mode.
papers.modelDetails: Copilot Assistance Modes (CAMs) spanning the autonomy spectrum: manual, AI translation, rotational shared control, user-directed task delegation, and full autonomy, driven by an AI navigation agent.
papers.training: AI agent trained previously (reinforcement learning, details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Success rate, navigation time, safety measures (e.g. forces, path), workload and user preference.
papers.baselines: Manual robotic navigation.
papers.results: Full autonomy had the lowest success rate (23%) and AI translation 38%; user-directed task delegation and rotational shared control gave the best balance of performance, safety and user experience.
