papers.title: Selective Prediction Reduces the Negative Effects of Automation Bias Overall but Increases False Negatives
papers.authors: Sarah Jabbour, David Fouhey, Nikola Banovic, Stephanie D. Shepard, Ella Kazerooni, Michael W. Sjoding, Jenna Wiens
papers.aim: AI has the potential to augment human decision making. However, even high-performing models can produce inaccurate predictions when deployed.
papers.method: These inaccuracies, combined with automation bias, where humans overrely on AI predictions, can result in worse decisions. Selective prediction, in which potentially unreliable model predictions are hidden from users, has been proposed as a solution. This approach assumes that when AI abstains and informs the user so, humans make decisions as they would without AI involvement. To test this assumption, we study the effects of selective prediction on human decisions in a clinical context. We conducted a user study of 259 clinicians tasked with diagnosing and treating hospitalized patients. We compared their baseline performance without any AI involvement to their AI-assisted accuracy with and without selective prediction. Our findings indicate that selective prediction mitigates the negative effects of inaccurate AI in terms of decision accuracy. Compared to no AI assistance, clinician accuracy declined when shown inaccurate AI predictions (66% [95% CI: 56%-75%] vs. 56% [95% CI: 46%-66%]), but recovered under selective prediction (64% [95% CI: 54%-73%]).
papers.result: However, while selective prediction nearly maintains overall accuracy, our results suggest that it alters patterns of mistakes: when informed the AI abstains, clinicians underdiagnose (18% increase in missed diagnoses) and undertreat (35% increase in missed treatments) compared to no AI input at all. Our findings underscore the importance of empirically validating assumptions about how humans engage with AI within human-AI systems.
papers.gap: Vignette setting; one clinical domain.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Clinicians treated realistic respiratory failure cases alone, with full AI advice, or with AI that hid its likely-wrong predictions and said it was deferring. Hiding bad predictions reduced harm overall, but when told the AI deferred, clinicians missed more treatments. This is crucial for the PhD: escalation messages must be designed so deferral does not cause under-treatment, and false negatives must be monitored.
papers.studyDesign: Pre-registered vignette-based randomised study with clinicians (University of Michigan and NYU, USA); IRB exempt; arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 259 clinicians treating 45 vignette cases of patients hospitalised with acute respiratory failure (pneumonia, heart failure, COPD) from a large academic medical centre; ground truth from multi-physician chart review.
papers.preprocessing: Cases include presentation, history, medications, examination, laboratory results and chest X-ray, slightly modified for privacy.
papers.modelDetails: Three conditions: Clinician Alone, Clinician + AI (all AI likelihood scores shown), and Clinician + Selective Prediction (potentially harmful predictions withheld, with message 'The model defers to you').
papers.training: Not applicable (AI outputs constructed for the study).
papers.evaluation: Primary: diagnostic accuracy mapped to treatment decisions (antibiotics, IV diuretics, steroids); error types (false positives and false negatives).
papers.baselines: Clinician Alone; Clinician + AI.
papers.results: Selective prediction partly mitigated the harm of inaccurate AI and nearly maintained overall accuracy, but changed error patterns: when the AI abstained, clinicians made more false-negative decisions (under-treatment) than without AI.
papers.statistics: Pre-registered comparisons of accuracy and error types between arms.

papers.title: Evaluating Explainable AI on a Multi-Modal Medical Imaging Task: Can Existing Algorithms Fulfill Clinical Requirements?
papers.authors: Weina Jin, Xiaoxiao Li, Ghassan Hamarneh
papers.aim: Being able to explain the prediction to clinical end-users is a necessity to leverage the power of artificial intelligence (AI) models for clinical decision support. For medical images, a feature attribution map, or heatmap, is the most common form of explanation that highlights important features for AI models' prediction.
papers.method: However, it is unknown how well heatmaps perform on explaining decisions on multi-modal medical images, where each image modality or channel visualizes distinct clinical information of the same underlying biomedical phenomenon. Understanding such modality-dependent features is essential for clinical users' interpretation of AI decisions. To tackle this clinically important but technically ignored problem, we propose the modality-specific feature importance (MSFI) metric. It encodes clinical image and explanation interpretation patterns of modality prioritization and modality-specific feature localization. We conduct a clinical requirement-grounded, systematic evaluation using computational methods and a clinician user study.
papers.result: Results show that the examined 16 heatmap algorithms failed to fulfill clinical requirements to correctly indicate AI model decision process or decision quality. The evaluation and MSFI metric can guide the design and selection of XAI algorithms to meet clinical requirements on multi-modal explanation.
papers.gap: No new explanation method proposed beyond requirements.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a brain tumour MRI model, the authors tested sixteen popular heatmap explanation methods against clinical expectations of which MRI sequence shows which feature, and asked clinicians to judge them. None met clinical requirements. This directly warns the PhD against relying on standard heatmaps for its multi-sequence MRI models and supports using calibrated confidence instead.
papers.studyDesign: Clinical-requirement-grounded evaluation of XAI algorithms with computational metrics and a clinician user study (Simon Fraser University and UBC, Canada); AAAI 2022 workshop; arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: Multi-modal brain MRI (e.g. BraTS glioma, T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR) with a model trained for tumour grading; clinicians in a user study.
papers.preprocessing: Modality-specific ground-truth feature maps derived from clinical knowledge of which modalities show which tumour features.
papers.modelDetails: Evaluation of 16 post-hoc heatmap (feature attribution) algorithms for modality-specific feature importance and localisation in multi-modal images.
papers.training: CNN classifier trained on multi-modal MRI (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Modality importance correctness, modality-specific feature localisation, and clinician assessment of whether heatmaps reveal decision process and quality.
papers.baselines: Comparison among 16 heatmap methods.
papers.results: All 16 heatmap algorithms failed to meet clinical requirements for correctly indicating the AI decision process or decision quality on multi-modal images.
papers.statistics: Quantitative localisation metrics and user-study statistics.

papers.title: One Map Does Not Fit All: Evaluating Saliency Map Explanation on Multi-Modal Medical Images
papers.authors: Weina Jin, Xiaoxiao Li, Ghassan Hamarneh
papers.aim: Being able to explain the prediction to clinical end-users is a necessity to leverage the power of AI models for clinical decision support. For medical images, saliency maps are the most common form of explanation.
papers.method: The maps highlight important features for AI model's prediction. Although many saliency map methods have been proposed, it is unknown how well they perform on explaining decisions on multi-modal medical images, where each modality/channel carries distinct clinical meanings of the same underlying biomedical phenomenon. Understanding such modality-dependent features is essential for clinical users' interpretation of AI decisions. To tackle this clinically important but technically ignored problem, we propose the MSFI (Modality-Specific Feature Importance) metric to examine whether saliency maps can highlight modality-specific important features. MSFI encodes the clinical requirements on modality prioritization and modality-specific feature localization.
papers.result: Our evaluations on 16 commonly used saliency map methods, including a clinician user study, show that although most saliency map methods captured modality importance information in general, most of them failed to highlight modality-specific important features consistently and precisely. The evaluation results guide the choices of saliency map methods and provide insights to propose new ones targeting clinical applications.
papers.gap: Classification only; no segmentation explanations.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Using a brain tumour grading model on BraTS MRI, the authors created two metrics that check whether saliency maps highlight the right MRI sequence and the right tumour features within it, and tested sixteen methods plus clinician opinions. Maps usually identified important sequences but not the specific features clinicians expect. This directly informs how the PhD should evaluate any explanation shown alongside its MRI models.
papers.studyDesign: Methodological evaluation study with clinician user study (Simon Fraser University and UBC, Canada); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: BraTS 2020 multi-modal brain MRI (T1, T1c, T2, FLAIR; 76 LGG and 293 HGG) with tumour segmentation masks; synthetic dataset for sanity checks.
papers.preprocessing: Pre-registered, pre-processed BraTS volumes (4×240×240×155); five-fold cross-validation.
papers.modelDetails: VGG-like 3D CNN for LGG vs HGG grading; evaluation of 16 post-hoc saliency methods (activation-, gradient- and perturbation-based) using two proposed metrics: Modality Importance (MI, Shapley-value ground truth, Kendall's tau-b) and Modality-Specific Feature Importance (MSFI, encoding clinical modality prioritisation and feature localisation).
papers.training: Five-fold cross-validated training of the 3D CNN.
papers.evaluation: MI correlation, MSFI scores and clinician ratings of saliency maps.
papers.baselines: Comparison among saliency methods.
papers.results: Most saliency methods captured modality importance in general, but most failed to consistently and precisely highlight modality-specific important features aligned with clinical knowledge.

papers.title: Clinicians' Voice: Fundamental Considerations for XAI in Healthcare
papers.authors: T. E. Röber, R. Goedhart, S. İ. Birbil
papers.aim: Explainable AI (XAI) holds the promise of advancing the implementation and adoption of AI-based tools in practice, especially in high-stakes environments like healthcare. However, most of the current research lacks input from end users, and therefore their practical value is limited.
papers.method: To address this, we conducted semi-structured interviews with clinicians to discuss their thoughts, hopes, and concerns. Clinicians from our sample generally think positively about developing AI-based tools for clinical practice, but they have concerns about how these will fit into their workflow and how it will impact clinician-patient relations.
papers.result: We further identify training of clinicians on AI as a crucial factor for the success of AI in healthcare and highlight aspects clinicians are looking for in (X)AI-based tools. In contrast to other studies, we take on a holistic and exploratory perspective to identify general requirements for (X)AI products for healthcare before moving on to testing specific tools.
papers.gap: Small, single-country sample.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Eleven Dutch clinicians from several specialties were interviewed openly about what they want from AI and explanations before any specific tool was tested. They welcomed AI but worried about workflow and patient relationships and stressed the need for training. These general requirements complement the PhD's planned clinician interviews in Sri Lanka.
papers.studyDesign: Qualitative semi-structured interview study (Amsterdam Business School, University of Amsterdam, Netherlands); ethics approved, written consent.
papers.datasets: 11 clinicians trained and working in the Netherlands (6 women, 5 men; 2-30 years' experience) from general practice, oncology, paediatric oncology, radiology, health psychology, obstetrics and gynaecology, and surgery.
papers.preprocessing: Recruitment by networking and word of mouth; 30-minute mostly online interviews; interview materials in appendix.
papers.modelDetails: Exploratory interviews on clinicians' thoughts, hopes and concerns about AI and XAI, analysed thematically.
papers.training: Not applicable.
papers.evaluation: Thematic analysis of interview transcripts.
papers.baselines: Not applicable.
papers.results: Clinicians were generally positive about AI tools but concerned about workflow fit and effects on clinician-patient relationships; training of clinicians on AI was seen as crucial; requirements for (X)AI tools were identified.

papers.title: Explainable AI for Clinical Outcome Prediction: A Survey of Clinician Perceptions and Preferences
papers.authors: Jun Hou, Lucy Lu Wang
papers.aim: Explainable AI (XAI) techniques are necessary to help clinicians make sense of AI predictions and integrate predictions into their decision-making workflow. In this work, we conduct a survey study to understand clinician preference among different XAI techniques when they are used to interpret model predictions over text-based EHR data.
papers.method: We implement four XAI techniques (LIME, Attention-based span highlights, exemplar patient retrieval, and free-text rationales generated by LLMs) on an outcome prediction model that uses ICU admission notes to predict a patient's likelihood of experiencing in-hospital mortality.
papers.result: Using these XAI implementations, we design and conduct a survey study of 32 practicing clinicians, collecting their feedback and preferences on the four techniques. We synthesize our findings into a set of recommendations describing when each of the XAI techniques may be more appropriate, their potential limitations, as well as recommendations for improvement.
papers.gap: Text-only task; mostly nurses.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Clinicians were shown four different ways of explaining an AI mortality prediction from ICU notes and asked which helped and why. Preferences varied, with natural-language rationales and similar-patient examples often favoured. This informs the PhD's choice of explanation formats, such as showing similar prior cases alongside calibrated confidence.
papers.studyDesign: Survey study of clinician perceptions of XAI techniques (Virginia Tech and University of Washington, USA); AMIA 2025 Informatics Summit; arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 32 practising clinicians (mostly registered nurses; 78.1% female; most with > 5 years' experience) evaluating explanations for ICU admission notes.
papers.preprocessing: Outcome prediction model trained on ICU admission notes to predict in-hospital mortality; explanation examples generated for survey cases.
papers.modelDetails: Four XAI techniques: LIME, attention-based span highlights, exemplar patient retrieval, and free-text rationales generated by LLMs.
papers.training: Text classification model for mortality prediction (details in paper).
papers.evaluation: Likert ratings and open-ended feedback on usefulness, clarity and trust per technique; thematic analysis.
papers.baselines: Comparison among the four XAI methods.
papers.results: Clinicians had differing preferences, with LLM free-text rationales and exemplar patients valued for context, and highlights for quick scanning; each method had limitations; recommendations given for when each is appropriate and how to improve them.

papers.title: Enhancing Early Lung Cancer Detection on Chest Radiographs with AI-assistance: A Multi-Reader Study
papers.authors: Gaetan Dissez, Nicole Tay, Tom Dyer, Matthew Tam, Richard Dittrich, David Doyne, James Hoare, Jackson J. Pat, Stephanie Patterson, Amanda Stockham, et al.
papers.aim: Objectives: The present study evaluated the impact of a commercially available explainable AI algorithm in augmenting the ability of clinicians to identify lung cancer on chest X-rays (CXR). Design: This retrospective study evaluated the performance of 11 clinicians for detecting lung cancer from chest radiographs, with and without assistance from a commercially available AI algorithm (red dot, Behold.ai) that predicts suspected lung cancer from CXRs.
papers.method: Clinician performance was evaluated against clinically confirmed diagnoses. Setting: The study analysed anonymised patient data from an NHS hospital; the dataset consisted of 400 chest radiographs from adult patients (18 years and above) who had a CXR performed in 2020, with corresponding clinical text reports. Participants: A panel of readers consisting of 11 clinicians (consultant radiologists, radiologist trainees and reporting radiographers) participated in this study. Main outcome measures: Overall accuracy, sensitivity, specificity and precision for detecting lung cancer on CXRs by clinicians, with and without AI input. Agreement rates between clinicians and performance standard deviation were also evaluated, with and without AI input.
papers.result: Results: The use of the AI algorithm by clinicians led to an improved overall performance for lung tumour detection, achieving an overall increase of 17.4% of lung cancers being identified on CXRs which would have otherwise been missed, an overall increase in detection of smaller tumours, a 24% and 13% increased detection of stage 1 and stage 2 lung cancers respectively, and standardisation of clinician performance. Conclusions: This study showed great promise in the clinical utility of AI algorithms in improving early lung cancer diagnosis and promoting health equity through overall improvement in reader performances, without impacting downstream imaging resources.
papers.gap: Enriched dataset; vendor-led.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Eleven clinicians read 400 chest X-rays for possible lung cancer with and without an AI that marks suspicious areas, and their results were checked against confirmed diagnoses. AI support increased detection, particularly for less experienced readers. This is another example of a multi-reader design with clinical-outcome ground truth that the PhD can follow.
papers.studyDesign: Retrospective multi-reader multi-case study (Behold.ai with NHS hospitals, UK); local radiology board approval, Caldicott guardian endorsement; arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 400 adult chest radiographs from an NHS hospital in 2020: 200 randomly sampled from 650 suspicious CXRs requiring follow-up CT, and 200 without urgent findings; 11 clinicians of varying experience.
papers.preprocessing: Python text search of reports for terms (CT, alert, mass, nodule, hilar enlargement, urgent) and manual filtering; ground truth from clinical outcomes and expert labelling; reads with and without AI.
papers.modelDetails: Commercial explainable AI algorithm (red dot) detecting suspected lung cancer on CXR with localisation.
papers.training: Not applicable (commercial algorithm).
papers.evaluation: AI accuracy, sensitivity and specificity versus ground truth; clinician sensitivity, specificity and agreement for lung tumour detection with and without AI against clinical outcomes.
papers.baselines: Unassisted clinicians.
papers.results: AI assistance improved clinicians' overall lung tumour detection performance, with gains in sensitivity especially for less experienced readers, and improved agreement.
papers.statistics: Accuracy metrics with confidence intervals; agreement statistics.

papers.title: 2-Factor Retrieval for Improved Human-AI Decision Making in Radiology
papers.authors: Jim Solomon, Laleh Jalilian, Alexander Vilesov, Meryl Mathew, Tristan Grogan, Arash Bedayat, Achuta Kadambi
papers.aim: Human-machine teaming in medical AI requires us to understand to what degree a trained clinician should weigh AI predictions. While previous work has shown the potential of AI assistance at improving clinical predictions, existing clinical decision support systems either provide no explainability of their predictions or use techniques like saliency and Shapley values, which do not allow for physician-based verification.
papers.method: To address this gap, this study compares previously used explainable AI techniques with a newly proposed technique termed '2-factor retrieval (2FR)', which is a combination of interface design and search retrieval that returns similarly labeled data without processing this data. This results in a 2-factor security blanket where: (a) correct images need to be retrieved by the AI; and (b) humans should associate the retrieved images with the current pathology under test.
papers.result: We find that when tested on chest X-ray diagnoses, 2FR leads to increases in clinician accuracy, with particular improvements when clinicians are radiologists and have low confidence in their decision. Our results highlight the importance of understanding how different modes of human-AI decision making may impact clinician accuracy in clinical decision support systems.
papers.gap: Online setting; public dataset labels.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Physicians diagnosed chest X-rays with AI help presented either as a saliency map or as a set of retrieved confirmed examples of the predicted diagnosis that they could compare against. The example-based retrieval improved accuracy, especially for radiologists unsure of their answer. This verifiable, example-based approach could complement calibrated confidence in the PhD's escalation interface.
papers.studyDesign: Online randomised experiment with physicians (UCLA, USA); IRB exempt, informed consent; arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 69 physicians: radiologists (task experts) and internal medicine, anaesthesiology, surgery and emergency physicians (non-task experts) in the USA/Canada; 24 images from the NIH Chest X-ray dataset with 12 diagnostic questions.
papers.preprocessing: Public web interface; demographic survey; 10-15 minute session with raffle compensation.
papers.modelDetails: 2-factor retrieval (2FR): interface plus search retrieval that shows physician-confirmed images with the same AI-predicted label as canonical examples, so humans can verify the AI by comparison; compared with saliency maps and no-explanation AI.
papers.training: Not applicable (retrieval over labelled images).
papers.evaluation: Diagnostic accuracy and confidence by explanation mode, expertise and AI correctness.
papers.baselines: AI prediction alone; saliency map explanations.
papers.results: 2FR increased clinician accuracy, with particular improvements for radiologists and when clinicians had low confidence, compared with saliency maps.

papers.title: Explainability and AI Confidence in Clinical Decision Support Systems: Effects on Trust, Diagnostic Performance, and Cognitive Load in Breast Cancer Care
papers.authors: Olya Rezaeian, Alparslan Emrah Bayrak, Onur Asan
papers.aim: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has demonstrated potential in healthcare, particularly in enhancing diagnostic accuracy and decision-making through Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSSs). However, the successful implementation of these systems relies on user trust and reliance, which can be influenced by explainable AI.
papers.method: This study explores the impact of varying explainability levels on clinicians trust, cognitive load, and diagnostic performance in breast cancer detection. Utilizing an interrupted time series design, we conducted a web-based experiment involving 28 healthcare professionals. The results revealed that high confidence scores substantially increased trust but also led to overreliance, reducing diagnostic accuracy. In contrast, low confidence scores decreased trust and agreement while increasing diagnosis duration, reflecting more cautious behavior. Some explainability features influenced cognitive load by increasing stress levels. Additionally, demographic factors such as age, gender, and professional role shaped participants' perceptions and interactions with the system.
papers.result: This study provides valuable insights into how explainability impact clinicians' behavior and decision-making. The findings highlight the importance of designing AI-driven CDSSs that balance transparency, usability, and cognitive demands to foster trust and improve integration into clinical workflows.
papers.gap: Small sample; configured rather than real AI confidence.
papers.relation: Informs the human-in-the-loop clinical evaluation (O4): reader-study design, usability, workload, trust and safety outcomes, and AI-assisted neurosurgical planning.
papers.methodologyDetail: Breast imaging clinicians used AI decision support in a series of phases varying how much explanation and what confidence level the AI showed, while trust, accuracy, time and mental workload were measured. High stated confidence made people over-trust the AI, while low confidence made them slower and more careful. This shows the PhD that the confidence shown must be well calibrated, because it strongly steers clinician behaviour.
papers.studyDesign: Web-based experiment with interrupted time-series design across explainability conditions (Stevens Institute of Technology and Lehigh University, USA); arXiv preprint.
papers.datasets: 28 US healthcare professionals in breast cancer care (≈ 60% radiologists, 18% oncologists; mean age 42.6) recruited January-August 2024, compensated $80; multiple breast imaging diagnostic cases.
papers.preprocessing: Pre-experiment demographic survey; workload and stress surveys after each CDSS variant.
papers.modelDetails: AI breast cancer CDSS variants with different explainability levels and AI confidence scores (high vs low), including explanation features.
papers.training: Not applicable (configured AI outputs).
papers.evaluation: Trust, agreement with AI, diagnostic accuracy, diagnosis duration, and cognitive load (NASA-TLX-type mental demand and stress).
papers.baselines: CDSS without explanation.
papers.results: High confidence scores substantially increased trust but led to over-reliance and lower accuracy; low confidence scores decreased trust and agreement and increased diagnosis time (more cautious behaviour); some explainability features helped while others increased load.
